Egypt's Sisi pledges to leave office when term ends in 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:34:55 UTC
20:34:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt's Sisi pledges to leave office when term ends in 2030
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that he would not seek to remain in office when his current term expires in 2030, describing the matter as "completely settled".
Sisi, 71, a former army general who became president in 2014, made the remarks at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital, one of his flagship megaprojects.
Speaking to graduates and state officials in the sprawling new city east of Cairo, Sisi said the Egyptian constitution "would not be touched".
"The period leading up to 2030 will be the end of my term as president of the state, if I am still alive. This is completely settled, and there will be no discussion about it," he said.
The Egyptian constitution, approved in 2014 following the 2013 military ouster of late president Mohamed Morsi, originally limited presidents to two four-year terms.
Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four to six years and included transitional provisions that allowed Sisi to run for an additional term.
Under those amendments, Sisi was re-elected in 2023 for a six-year term that expires in 2030.
Critics and opposition figures have speculated about further constitutional changes that could allow him to remain in office beyond 2030.
Before running for president, Sisi denied having political ambitions, but he resigned as defence minister in 2014 and entered the race he went on to win.
On Saturday, he said the run-up to 2030 would groom a new generation of leaders, with the Military Academy training hundreds of prospective officials, ministers and presidential candidates in statecraft and leadership.
During his 12 years in power, Sisi has overseen an ambitious state-led development programme centred on megaprojects which critics say have relied heavily on borrowing and contributed to Egypt's mounting debt burden and economic pressures.
Sisi's presidency has also faced sustained criticism from international human rights organisations over restrictions on political opposition, civil society and freedom of expression, allegations the government rejects, saying its policies are necessary to preserve stability and security.

Russia wants blackout in Ukraine as winter comes — Zelenskyy

Ukraine: Zelenskyy urges allies to pressure Russia as energy sites hit
October 17, 2026
Russia is stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in a bid to cut electricity and heating in the country as winter approaches, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.
His remarks come as Moscow intensifies its attacks on civilian targets in the capital, Kyiv, and elsewhere, with key observers saying its objective is to render the country virtually unlivable.
What did Zelenskyy say?
In a post on social media platform X, Zelenskyy said Russia had just carried out one of its biggest attacks on Ukraine's energy sector since it began its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.
"More than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine," he wrote.
"Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved," he added.
Zelenskyy said that Russia was planning to leave Ukrainian citizens in the cold this winter.
"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine — right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating," he wrote, calling on allies to put pressure on Moscow to stop this happening.
He said Russia had "expanded its campaign against the energy system" and was trying "to stretch Ukraine's reserves and repair capacity as thinly as possible." 
Russia claims multiple infrastructure attacks
The Russian Defense Ministry, for its part, said on Saturday that its forces had attacked several infrastructure targets in Ukraine overnight.
Among those named was an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr.
However, it also said Ukraine's largest steelworks, in the city of Kryvyi Rih, had been hit, saying the facility supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.
It said another steel plant in Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front line, had also been struck.
Ukrainian authorities have also said that one person — an ambulance driver — was killed and 19 others injured, including a child, in a Russian airstrike on Kherson in southern Ukraine.
Russian state news agency TASS has also reported the death of one woman as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region that also injured a man.
Trump's sanctions waiver a boost for Putin: Zelenskyy
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy also reacted to US President Donald Trump's decision to waive a package of new sanctions on Moscow, saying the move would only encourage Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
"A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelenskyy said.
On Friday, Trump signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect.
The waiver has been hailed by a Russian presidential envoy as a "historic moment."
"The Trump administration's suspension of the [Lindsey] Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said on social media.
Dmitriev said the act, named for the late US senator who sponsored the bill, "would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets."
Trump's move came as he increasingly criticizes Zelenskyy, fueling speculation that the US leader is siding with Moscow in the conflict.

Police, protesters clash ahead of mass demonstrations in France
Unknown

A protester lights smoke flares next to a fire during a demonstration to protest against the "high cost of living", Place de la Victoire in Bordeaux, southwestern France, on October 17, 2026. | Christophe Aarchambault/ AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — Clashes broke out early on Saturday between protesters and police, ahead of nationwide protests in France that are expected to gather several hundred thousand people throughout the country.
Media reported incidents in the nation’s largest cities including Lyon, Marseille and Paris. Clashes have been taking place across the capital, including on Place de la République, a few hours before authorized demonstrations were scheduled to start from Paris’s central square.
A police station was vandalized in Marseille, more than 100 people had already been arrested in the French capital already at midday and the headquarters of right-wing TV channel CNews was targeted, authorities said.
Advertisement
Students, farmers and members of the Yellow Jacket movement, among others, are slated to take to the streets on Saturday in a “convergence of struggles” to protest raising living costs, sluggish wages and deep disagreements with the government.
The government expects “a fairly large turnout,” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Friday.
Saturday’s demonstrations originated in the student protests that began last month with school blockades and calls for better studying conditions, more teachers and more funding. The movement has since spread nationwide — and become a political issue as the campaign for next year’s presidential election heats up.
The government has struggled to deal with the crisis — which Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu described as “urban violence” — and is hoping the student movement will now fade because of a two-week school holiday that started Friday evening.
The government has also defended the law enforcement response to the student protests despite numerous allegations of police brutality, including incidents that left one teenager with a severed hand and another blind in one eye. Nuñez said the use of “stun grenades” was authorized on Saturday, after a temporary ban on their use against students.
While far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon is backing protesters, far-right leader Jordan Bardella pledged support for the police.

The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:33:20 UTC
20:33:20 KST

“I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare.
It was Labour conference, with everyone from ministers to activists jubilant at Andy Burnham’s takeover and a bounce in the polls after the change of leader.
But a number of senior Labour figures were privately starting to name the power of AI as the thing worrying them most, alongside the immediate pressures on the cost of living and fragile economy.
One cabinet minister – with a brief unrelated to technology – told the Guardian that dangerous, out-of-control AI was the issue keeping them up at night, fretting about the threat to humanity. It was “not killer robots” causing the worry, they explained, but the idea of a huge amount of concentrated, super-intelligent power potentially ending up in the hands of bad actors.
Another expressed concern that the government was “falling behind the public” in terms of dealing with worries about AI safety – and that it needed to catch up fast.
In his conference speech, Ed Miliband was the most strident about the “daunting” dangers of AI, making the case that politicians could not and would not allow the profits of tech companies “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”.
And it has not taken long for these alarm bells to ring even louder, with the last seven days looking like the week Westminster fully woke up to the warnings.
A flurry of activity started on Monday with Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, stating it was “likely, if not inevitable” that rogue agents would hack the British state, and saying the UK was looking to strengthen its forthcoming cybersecurity legislation.
It was the main topic of discussion at cabinet on Tuesday, and that was followed by the MI5 chief Ken McCallum warning AI was “supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders”. He said the biggest threat was extremist groups using the technology to unleash bioweapons – toxins used to cause death and disease.
Liam Byrne, the chair of the business, innovation, science and trade committee, said the change of government from Keir Starmer to Burnham was partly behind the increased focus on protecting the UK from AI threats but more still had to be done. “The reality is that the Starmer administration was much too close to the big tech companies,” Byrne said. “And Burnham is not, frankly, so there has been a change of posture. Those things, plus the security services issuing their warning, that is what has changed the weather on this.”
One senior Labour government figure agreed that Burnham’s government was taking AI safety warnings more seriously. “I do feel there has been a shift. Under the last lot, too many of them had drunk the tech-bro Kool-Aid,” he said.
Byrne’s committee held an evidence session this week with civil service leaders in charge of AI security and executives from the key companies – Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind and Meta – with a split between them about whether government testing of new models should be mandatory.
He said his committee was “lighting up” the issue, particularly in terms of working with the US to regulate and monitor new models. It had been reported that Donald Trump’s administration had asked AI companies not to share their latest models with the UK’s cutting-edge AI Security Institute for testing, though Narayan confirmed this week that they had managed to retain cooperation.
But Byrne said the government now needed to seize the moment and take the lead on new regulation, particularly if Trump’s Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections to the Democrats.
“I think the government is still caught in a dilemma between how to keep model access, given a capricious US president, and the safeguards that the industry itself now says are essential. It’s make-your-mind-up time, I would say,” Byrne said.
“The companies want to cooperate … It’s not in their commercial interest to issue models which are lethal. Now they too have got to navigate the White House. So I just think this is a moment when the government has actually got to do what is right for the country because Congress is about to change the dynamics on this in the US.”
The UK’s upcoming G20 presidency will be the key moment to push for international action to rein in AI. Geoffrey Irving, the former chief scientist at AISI who spoke at this week’s parliamentary hearing, believes Whitehall concerns are justified. OpenAI and Anthropic’s technology has already shown its hacking capabilities but their models are released with safety guardrails in place that at least mitigate against the threat of malicious behaviour.
However, so-called open source AI models are freely available and can be adapted. Typically, they caught up with the paid-for models such as OpenAI’s within less than a year, said Irving, although they could cause disruption already.
“It’s very likely that open source models are already powerful enough to do serious damage,” Irving told the Guardian, adding that he expected open source technology to reach the capabilities of OpenAI and Anthropic products “soon”. Safety guardrails “either don’t exist or can be trivially removed” from open source models, he added.
The business committee heard this week that AI-enabled bioweapons could become the next serious threat to manifest itself, in the wake of cybersecurity, as models become more powerful and therefore capable of designing novel bio-harms – although experts suggest there is a gap between designing dangerous pathogens and weaponising them.
Concerns over cybersecurity and bioweapons can escalate rapidly to fears about AI wiping out humanity in a variety of scenarios – a concern that is widespread within the AI community, and is shared by Irving.
However, some experts argue that the government should focus on immediate risks from AI. Prof Elena Simperl, a co-director of the Institute for Artificial Intelligence at King’s College London, said the existential risk argument had “no evidence” and was a “theory” rather than a credible threat.
“There are bigger, more immediate risks that AI technology is posing now and are actually evidenced, like hacking and signs that AI can be as addictive as social media,” Simperl said.
In the absence of international AI regulation, there are some in Whitehall worried about whether the UK is doing enough preparation to defend against AI warfare and attacks.
Defence sources said there was concern about the cancellation last year of the AI programme at the government’s Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl), based at Porton Down, with worries that this was shortsighted given the need for cutting-edge research on advancing the nation’s capabilities and defending against its risks.
This was countered by an MoD spokesperson who said AI was “transforming defence from industry to the battlefield and will play a decisive role in how we fight and defend” and that it must be “integrated across all workstreams, rather than a standalone programme”. They pointed to a £400m investment in AI-focused capabilities over the next four years to “prepare the UK for the future of warfare”.
Others in Whitehall have the opposite concern: that worries about safety could become too dominant – and end up holding back the government’s adoption of tools that could be transformative for productivity and solving longstanding problems in public services, from medical care to reducing waiting lists.
The former cabinet secretary Gus O’Donnell told the Guardian that ministers needed to be as aware of “the risk of being left behind” when it came to AI as being aware of the need for guardrails.
Launching a Global Government Forum report on AI with the tech firm Cognizant, O’Donnell told the Guardian: “There is a big need to get it better and to really push on. I’m really optimistic, but the challenge for us, obviously, is managing the risks along the way, making sure that we don’t make mistakes, which reduce people’s trust, which means that that sets us back.”

Demand-side strategies could halve battery emissions by 2050: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:31:27 CST
20:31:27 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Demand-side strategies, including reducing battery sizes, extending battery lifetimes and promoting shared mobility, could cut global lithium-ion battery supply-chain emissions by around half by 2050, an Australian-led study finds.
The study found that demand for lithium-ion batteries used in electric vehicles and battery energy storage systems could increase twentyfold by 2050, driving a tenfold rise in related supply-chain greenhouse gas emissions, according to a statement released Saturday by Australia's University of Melbourne.
The study was one of the first detailed global assessments to examine both supply-side and demand-side factors, researchers said, adding that supply-side strategies reduce emissions from battery production through cleaner electricity, greener factories, switching battery chemistries and recycling.
While cleaner production remains essential, the findings suggest that reducing battery demand could offer a substantial additional opportunity to curb emissions, said University of Melbourne Associate Professor Li Wen, lead contact of the study published in One Earth.
Researchers from Australia, China and Britain estimated that without additional measures, the global battery supply chain could generate 19 billion to 23 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions through 2050.
Combining ambitious supply- and demand-side strategies could reduce the total to 9 billion to 12 billion tonnes, with demand-side measures accounting for 6 billion to 7 billion tonnes of the reduction, Li said.
The study assessed battery material and component production, manufacturing and end-of-life treatment from 2024 to 2050, with the researchers saying battery decarbonization policies should move beyond regulating production emissions to consider how much battery capacity is needed to provide transport and energy storage services. ■

ISLAMABAD, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Pakistan's information technology (IT) and tech exports rose 18 percent year on year to 435 million U.S. dollars in September 2026, marking the second-highest monthly figure on record, an official said Friday.
In a post on social media platform X, Adviser to the Finance Minister Khurram Schehzad said the September figure was 2 million dollars below the record high of 437 million dollars set in December 2025. Exports also increased 10 percent from August.
IT exports during the first quarter of fiscal year (FY) 2026-27, covering July to September, reached 1.25 billion dollars, up about 18 percent from the same period last year, Schehzad said.
Separately, the country's IT-related freelance earnings reached a record 197 million dollars in September, up 49 percent year on year and 11 percent month on month, according to figures shared by Schehzad.
Freelance earnings totalled around 550 million dollars in the first quarter of FY 2026-27, up 46 percent from the same period a year earlier. For the full fiscal year 2025-26, they reached 1.76 billion dollars.
Schehzad attributed the growth to targeted incentives introduced in the FY 2026-27 budget for exporters, particularly those in the IT sector, and the expansion of the country's digital economy.
The measures are supporting exports, generating foreign exchange without adding to debt, creating high-value jobs and strengthening Pakistan's integration with global markets, he added. ■

YEREVAN, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Four years after the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, its first global progress report has found uneven progress toward the 2030 targets, with the biggest gaps in efforts to address the drivers of biodiversity loss.
The State of Biodiversity Action report, released by the United Nations on Thursday, will inform the first global review of collective progress under the framework at the upcoming 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP17) to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) in the Armenian capital.
With the conference opening on Oct. 19, the challenge is to turn the review's findings into concrete action.
UNEVEN PROGRESS
Countries have taken action across all 23 targets of the framework for 2030, but none presents an entirely positive picture, according to the report. Unless collective implementation accelerates, the 2030 targets and mission will not be achieved.
The report identifies two gaps: national targets do not fully reflect the scope and ambition of global commitments, and implementation falls short even of those less ambitious targets.
Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the CBD, said in August that fewer than half of the national targets assessed by parties and aligned with the framework were on track. The largest gaps concerned resource mobilization, harmful subsidy reform, business impacts and the transition to sustainable consumption.
Schomaker has noted promising conservation efforts, alongside slow progress on resource mobilization, harmful subsidy reform and inclusive governance.
The framework calls for reducing incentives harmful to biodiversity, including subsidies, by at least 500 billion U.S. dollars annually by 2030.
Yet an analysis by the Britain-based website Carbon Brief found that only about 5 percent of countries had set quantitative targets for subsidy reductions. Some countries reported that reform faced obstacles from vested interests and political resistance.
ECONOMIC OBSTACLES
A recent report by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) points to tightening public finances and immediate pressures over food and energy security as reasons why some countries have shown insufficient political will for biodiversity protection.
The problem becomes more acute when reforms affect powerful interest groups or impose immediate costs on certain sectors, while conservation benefits are shared across society and take longer to emerge.
International financing presents another challenge. Under the framework, international biodiversity finance from developed countries and other contributors to developing countries was to reach at least 20 billion dollars annually by 2025, increasing to at least 30 billion dollars by 2030.
However, the State of Biodiversity Action report shows that reported international public finance totaled only 17.7 billion dollars between 2020 and 2023, averaging about 4.4 billion dollars a year.
An assessment by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services warns that delaying action could double the costs and increase the risk of irreversible losses, including species extinctions. Current economic models are also exacerbating biodiversity loss, climate change, water scarcity, food insecurity and health risks, with unaccounted-for costs estimated at 10 trillion to 25 trillion dollars annually.
Within and between countries, the central tension is who should bear the immediate costs of protecting nature and when. The longer action is delayed, the greater the overall costs.
TURNING REVIEW INTO ACTION
The key test for COP17 is whether the review can provide clear guidance for further action, according to the Institute for Sustainable Development and International Relations, a French think tank.
Under the convention's procedures, the global review materials will be submitted to COP17, where parties will examine implementation gaps and consider follow-up action.
Observers say three questions will be central to the conference.
First, what signals will its decisions send? Harmful subsidy reform and the integration of biodiversity into economic decision-making are among the areas lagging most. A general call to accelerate action would carry different weight from specific measures addressing these obstacles.
Second, how will funding be secured and managed? Financing is a major weakness identified by the review and an important measure by which developing countries will judge the conference's outcome. The WWF has called on COP17 to deliver results rather than further promises, including a credible path toward mobilizing at least 30 billion dollars annually in international biodiversity finance by 2030.
Third, how will supporting measures be implemented? At the Kunming Dialogue on the framework's implementation in September, participants broadly agreed that finance, capacity-building and technology were equally important. They also noted that support remained insufficient, while reliance on short-term funding hampered long-term planning and implementation.
Despite the gaps exposed by the report, Schomaker has stressed that the 2030 targets remain achievable, provided major changes are made.
COP17 will need to address who bears the costs of protecting nature and how to overcome resistance to reforms that bring short-term difficulties but long-term benefits. Its decisions will help determine whether the framework remains a set of commitments on paper or is translated into national budgets, subsidies and investment. ■

Interview: IMO chief urges ships to avoid Strait of Hormuz amid escalating attacks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:30:44 CST
20:30:44 KST

LONDON, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez has urged ships to avoid transiting the Strait of Hormuz and trading in the region as attacks on commercial vessels continue to escalate.
He warned that safe shipping operations cannot resume until the underlying causes of the conflict are addressed.
In an interview with Xinhua at the IMO headquarters in London on Friday, Dominguez said the organization's advice remained unchanged: ships should avoid transiting the Strait of Hormuz and trading in the region.
"The situation continues to escalate," he said.
He further said more than 110 vessels have been hit since the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran began in late February, while at least 24 seafarers have been confirmed dead.
Attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz have intensified recently, with the security situation continuing to deteriorate, data published on the IMO website showed.
A total of 12 attacks on vessels were reported in the strait and nearby waters between Oct. 5 and 11, the highest weekly figure since the conflict began. On Oct. 11 alone, six vessels came under attack.
Dominguez cited two recent incidents to illustrate the increasingly serious consequences of the attacks.
"Just in the last couple of days, we have two vessels that were hit, one a total loss, the other one still trying to reach a berth where it could be assisted," he said.
Dominguez expressed concern that too many shipowners and operators continued to take risks despite the dangers.
He warned that prolonged disruption to shipping could have wider consequences beyond the maritime sector.
"It may have an even bigger impact when it comes to the global economy and supplies of energy sources as well as food security," he said.
The IMO chief said the organization was continuing to support around 6,000 seafarers who had remained trapped in the region since the beginning of the conflict.
However, Dominguez stressed that protecting seafarers must remain a priority, even if avoiding high-risk waters leads to higher costs.
"Costs will increase globally; it's a reality, but we cannot put the lives of innocent seafarers at risk anymore," he said.
Asked whether the IMO had been in contact with the parties involved in the conflict, Dominguez said the organization was maintaining communications with all its member states, particularly those directly involved, as well as countries beyond the region and other United Nations agencies.
He acknowledged mediation efforts by several countries but said they had yet to produce the decisions needed to allow shipping operations to return to normal.
"The root causes are not being addressed," Dominguez said. "So from our side, we can only work on the operational aspects of shipping, but it's been very clear that until the parties in the conflict sit down and find a solution to why this crisis started, we will not be able to resume operations safely around the region."
On the protection of seafarers, Dominguez said the IMO was reviewing existing rules and guidance on risk assessments before vessels enter conflict zones or high-risk areas.
The organization was also engaging with shipowners, operators and seafarers' representatives to explore ways to help seafarers obtain necessary supplies and uphold their rights under the Maritime Labour Convention.
These include the right to refuse to transit dangerous areas without retaliation and the right to receive repatriation support.
He said the IMO was also examining how existing regulations could be better enforced, including the detention of non-compliant vessels until they demonstrate compliance with international requirements.
Dominguez noted that geopolitical conflicts were affecting shipping across several regions, including the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
Until these areas become more peaceful and shipping is no longer used as leverage in conflicts, vessels should avoid operating in such high-risk waters, he said. ■

The Best LED Grow Lights for Houseplants This Winter (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Summer is officially over, along with its allotment of free sunlight. You might be sad about this, but your indoor plants might be even sadder. A good LED grow light can replicate sunlight with full-spectrum light and day/night cycles, keeping plants lush and thriving even in a dark, windowless corner or basement.
I have no fewer than 40 houseplants in my home at any given time, as well as a fair number of grow lights, and what I've found to be important for a general consumer (i.e., someone not doing that kind of indoor grow) isn't necessarily certain colored light wavelengths but whether a grow light is easy to live with in your house.
Many grow lights are more or less going to serve the same purpose, so what you really need to know is this: Is the light so bright that it's disruptive? Does it require complicated installation? Is it easy for kids or pets to knock over? The grow lights recommended below are ones that WIRED staffers have lived with for months, if not years, and have found them both effective and easy to integrate into our lives.
Also be sure to check out our guides to the Best Indoor Gardening Systems, Best Gifts for Plant Lovers, and Best Kitchen Composters.
Featured Lights
What Is PPFD?
Photosynthetic photon flux Ddensity, or PPFD, expressed in micromoles per square meter per second (μmol/m²/s), is a measurement of how much light reaches your plant that's usable for photosynthesis. In general, the higher the plant's energy needs, such as producing a flower or a fruit, the higher the PPFD number you want. Though different lights have different height requirements given the plants they're made for, for standardization purposes, I measured the PPFD of each grow light at 18 inches with the Photone app and a light diffuser. Keep in mind these measurements are general and approximate.
How I Test Grow Lights
Some of these grow lights I bought myself, with my own money, before I even began working at WIRED. Others were owned by staffers and recommended to me. I also have press samples from other guides I worked on, which I liked so much I ended up keeping around.
For the traditional grow lights, I tested them at home under normal-life conditions. I put them where they'd fit, tested their timers, and noted whether or not they were dimmable. I also measured each light's PPFD (see above) and noted whether certain lights could be daisy-chained for more extensive coverage.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Grow Light for Small Plants and Seedlings
There are a lot of options out there for starting seeds and helping houseplants along in the winter, and many of them are bulky, fussy, or require elaborate hanging setups. This simple, 15-inch-long light from Vego sticks to its 3M adhesive mount with a magnet, so it's easy to take on and off and use with existing racks or, as I do, under a kitchen cabinet. Up to four Vego lights can be daisy-chained together, and the five preprogrammed modes (Seeds, Leafy, Fruits, Herbs, Microgreens) have varying intensities and automatic built-in off periods to simulate nighttime. I have not found this light especially disruptive, especially since it's easy to turn on and off with the button on the back.
WIRED commerce SEO director Stewart Savin used these lights to start her garden earlier this year and had 138 successful germinations across 144 seedling cells. ("The vast majority of those plants went on to have long lives in my garden after I hardened them off," she says.) Note that because this light can only go beneath a rack, shelf, or cabinet, it’s not inherently adjustable, and therefore is best for small plants (like seedlings) that aren’t going to grow especially tall.
Most Versatile Grow Light
This do-anything light, with a broad 2 x 3-foot head, can hang from the ceiling or swivel on its included stand where you need it. (Up to 20 of these lights can be daisy-chained.) Note that while the stand is useful, the 1-inch-diameter pole and offset base aren't the sturdiest, and it's easy to knock over, so I'd recommend hanging it if you have pets and small kids. I learned this the hard way while trying to revive a corn plant in a dark corner at the top of my stairs.
While this light is quite bright and potentially disruptive, it's easily dimmable via the remote, which hangs on a cord. At first I thought this was weird, but I found it extremely useful when the light was behind plants or in another hard-to-reach spot.
Also worth noting: While the stand height is supposed to be adjustable up to 72 inches, mine only goes up to about 64 inches, so it may not be the best option for extremely tall plants.
Best Grow Light for Serious Indoor Growers
Vivosun is a long-respected brand among indoor growers, and its LumaLight panels are sturdy and all business. In fact, you'll be hard-pressed to find a higher-quality grow light for the price. This is not necessarily a light for casual houseplant parents—the 100-watt, 12 x 12-inch model weighs 4.4 pounds and needs to be attached to the ceiling or inside one of Vivosun's grow tents using the included adjustable ropes and carabiners.
If you're growing fruiting or flowering plants, though, this is the grow light you want—none of the other lights I tested even came close to its level of brightness. That said, you probably won't want it in a main living area, though it is dimmable via a dial on top. The LumaLight is IP65-rated for water resistance, and up to seven units can be daisy-chained if you need.
Best Budget Grow Light
Former WIRED commerce director Martin Cizmar loved and recommended this grow light for his houseplants, which features three bendable heads on a clip you can attach to a table or shelf. It has a timer for three, nine, or twelve hours, plus a 10-foot cord if you need to place it away from an outlet. It also has warm and cool lighting options in addition to full spectrum, if you want to use it for ambiance (despite it looking, in my opinion, sort of like a creepy Freddy Krueger glove), plus 10 dimming modes. Right now, the base price on Amazon is for a two-pack.
Alternatives to Traditional Grow Lights
If you don’t have the space or desire for a classic grow light, I’ve used all three options below for at least a year, and all resulted in happy plants.
Other Grow Lights Tested
Sansi Pot Clip-On Plant Lights for $30: These Sansi grow lights came in handy when I was living in a dark basement with minimal light for plants and hardly any space to store them. They clip directly onto the pot, so you don't need a dedicated stand or extra space, and they run on a three-, six-, or twelve-hour timer. The long cord (just over 6 feet) also helps in awkward or tight spaces. These lights helped my Monstera stay alive over winter with almost no natural light. Just be aware that the clips work best on thin pots, though you can also stick them on a chopstick or stake if needed, thanks to the adjustable gooseneck, depending on how tall your plant is. —Louryn Strampe

U.S. Army’s Arctic division gets its own supply brigade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:27:41 UTC
20:27:41 KST

- The U.S. Army activated the 11th Airborne Division Sustainment Brigade (Arctic) at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Alaska, on Oct. 16, 2026.
- The brigade includes a reactivated intelligence and electronic warfare battalion, a renamed sustainment support battalion and a new troops battalion.
The U.S. Army has activated a new sustainment brigade for the 11th Airborne Division in Alaska, giving the Arctic-focused division its own formation to keep troops supplied and supported in some of the harshest conditions the U.S. military operates in.
The 11th Airborne Division Sustainment Brigade (Arctic) uncased its colors on Oct. 16, 2026, at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson near Anchorage, the division said. The ceremony also stood up the brigade’s subordinate battalions and companies: the 106th Intelligence and Electronic Warfare Battalion was reactivated, the 17th Combat Sustainment Support Battalion was renamed the 17th Division Sustainment Support Battalion, and a new 11th Airborne Division Sustainment Troops Battalion was activated.
“Today’s uncasing ceremony represents much more than the unfurling of our unit colors,” said Col. George Plys, the brigade’s commander. “It symbolizes the beginning of a new chapter, the commitment to a mission, and the readiness of our Soldiers to answer the call wherever and whenever our nation needs them.”
A division sustainment brigade handles the logistics that keep combat units moving, including fuel, ammunition, food, maintenance and transportation. In Alaska, where winter temperatures can fall far below freezing and distances between bases are vast, that support is central to whether troops can operate for long periods at all.
The U.S. Army reactivated the 11th Airborne Division in 2022, replacing the U.S. Army Alaska headquarters, and the division describes itself as both the youngest division in the active force and the fastest growing among comparable units. Until now, its main combat power has rested on two infantry brigade combat teams, one based at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson and one at Fort Wainwright near Fairbanks.
“Our ability to endure and sustain ourselves in the crucible of large-scale combat operations is impossible without the formations you see in front of you today,” said Maj. Gen. John Cogbill, the division’s commanding general.
The activation follows the U.S. Army’s release of new foundational doctrine, titled “How the Army Fights,” which names endurance as one of four linked operational elements alongside convergence, strike and close battle.
Plys said the brigade’s two main battalions do different but connected jobs, with the 17th sustaining the force and the 106th giving commanders intelligence and electronic warfare capabilities to understand the battlefield.
“While these two battalions have distinct missions, both are essential to our Army’s ability to fight and win,” said Plys. “One sustains the force; the other provides the intelligence and electronic warfare capabilities that help commanders understand the battlefield and make informed decisions.”

Moscow blasts UN for ignoring torture of Russian POWs
The UN should resist pressure from Kiev’s Western backers and finally address the issue of widespread abuse of captured Russian servicemen in Ukrainian secret prisons, Russian Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik has said.
During a conversation with the chairman of the UN Committee Against Torture Claude Heller on Thursday, Miroshnik said that Moscow is aware of a whole network of such detention facilities, operating in Ukraine’s Kharkov, Dnepropetrovsk, and Sumy Regions as well as in the country’s capital, Kiev.
The Russian servicemen are “going through hell” in so-called “transit prisons,” which are set up at deployment points of Ukrainian military units and nationalist battalions, he said.
“The thugs, who hide their faces behind masks... and address each other only by their call signs, subject the captured Russian troops to inhuman abuse. Waterboarding, electrocuting, baiting with dogs and amputations performed without anesthesia are just a few examples of the techniques systematically employed by the Ukrainian tormentors,” the envoy, who is charged with documenting Kiev’s war crimes, stressed.
According to Miroshnik, captured troops are usually sent to those facilities in the early stages of their imprisonment, where they are held in cages, pits, and stone dungeons.
The Kiev government does not allow ombudsmen and human rights activists into those “torture chambers,” but the Russian authorities have gathered hundreds of accounts of survivors detailing what has been happening there, he said.
“This information had been passed on to the UN Secretariat on more than one occasion,” but no action followed, Miroshnik added.
By ignoring the existence of the secret prisons and systematic torture of Russian troops, the global body “encourages the spread of such criminal practices and disregard for the relevant UN Convention,” he added.
“Many experts are aware of this disgraceful phenomenon, yet there is a lack of political will to overcome the pressure from the foreign accomplices to the conflict, who shield the Kiev regime from accountability and prevent a thorough investigation of its conduct,” the envoy said.
While turning a blind eye to the torture of Russian troops, the UN published several reports accusing Russia of mistreating Ukrainian prisoners, based on accounts by POWs returned by Moscow to Kiev. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has labeled those accusations of abuse “disinformation.”
Last month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that the UN Secretariat was unable to properly perform its duties as most key positions are occupied by representatives of NATO countries.
The current team, led by [UN General-Secretary] Antonio Guterres, who is a Portuguese national, “promotes biased approaches and double standards, effectively serving the interests of a group of Western nations,” Lavrov insisted during a press conference on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

Demonstrations began in mid-September at schools and have expanded, tapping into wider grievances.
Paris, France – Saturday is a day of many unknowns. That was how the French newspaper Le Monde described it as France braced for possible nationwide demonstrations bringing together high school students, trade unions and “yellow vest” activists.
The protests began in mid-September at a high school in the Paris suburb of Creteil, where students took to the streets over dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and what they see as a deeply unequal education system.
Since then, the mobilisation has spread to thousands of “lycees”, or upper secondary schools, across the country. It is now beginning to reflect broader anxieties in a country grappling with a combination of fiscal pressures, economic stagnation and mounting social discontent.
Teachers, trade unions and university students have joined the movement.
On Saturday, some “yellow vest” activists – remnants of the participants in the grassroots cost-of-living protests that shook President Emmanuel Macron’s first term in 2018 – have also called on supporters to join the students.
“High school students are fighting for their future. Workers are fighting to earn a living from their labour. Retirees are fighting to preserve their dignity. Our paths may differ, but our concerns can converge,” Jerome Rodrigues, a prominent “yellow vest” activist, said in a video message released last week that called on people to join Saturday’s demonstrations.
Now France is waiting to see whether those calls will translate into a large, coordinated mobilisation.
Warlike injuries
Authorities have described the unrest as among the most violent in decades, saying more than 900 police have been injured since the start of the protests. But critics argued that although some demonstrators have engaged in violence, they represent a minority and the actions of a few risk overshadowing the grievances of the wider movement.
The government has also faced criticism over its response to the protests, including the detention of thousands of minors and the use of force against young demonstrators.
More than 6,700 children had been taken into police custody since mid-September, according to reports published this week.
Human rights lawyers said several teenage students have suffered warlike injuries.
Two cases have drawn particular attention: A 15-year-old lost his hand in the explosion of a stun grenade outside a school in the northern city of Lens, and a 16-year-old in western Tours lost his sight due to an injury caused by a rubber bullet.
There are fears of further clashes on Saturday.
“This is a moment of fatigue in the country,” Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu said on Thursday. “We are in an atmosphere of perma-crisis: wars, inflation and issues surrounding purchasing power.”
The government has accused the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of inflaming the protests. The party has rejected the accusation.
While France suspended the use of stun grenades for the student demonstrations, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday that he authorised police to use them in the event of what he called “urban violence”.
Nunez also said he is expecting a “fairly significant” turnout on Saturday.
Hundreds of protest sites
Calls on social media for members of past protest movements to join the current one have been made for weeks. The website 17octobregiletjaune.net, which tracks “yellow vest” actions, listed more than 1,750 planned protest locations across the country.
The government has tried to quell student anger by scrapping plans to increase some higher education registration fees and promising to deploy 3,000 substitute teachers to high schools. This week, it set up a national online survey for pupils to hear their concerns.
But Mathieu Roger-Lacan, a French literature teacher in a disadvantaged area and author of A Language of One’s Own, a book about the growing language gap, argued that these measures fail to address the deeper problem: an education system that struggles to provide equal opportunities.
“If you have a pool that is leaking, the answer should not be to put more water into it but to work on its structure – and that costs money too,” he said.
For Roger-Lacan, the problem is not simply how much France spends on education but how it distributes those resources.
A government report published this week said that 32 percent of the French education ministry’s budget for next year will go towards funding the pensions of retired civil servants.
Students are not only complaining about deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms but also expressing a deeper anxiety about their future.
For many, a diploma no longer feels like a guarantee of stable employment or social mobility. That concern is compounded by questions about the quality of education itself amid evidence of persistent weaknesses in French students’ academic performance.
In September, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said that French 15-year-olds’ results in mathematics and reading had fallen to among their lowest levels on record.
“There is a gap between the diploma we give at the end of school, which is given to a huge part of the population, and the reality around us, which is that many of these young students have great difficulties even in writing French,” Roger-Lacan said.
Competing demands
The protests come at a very difficult time for the government, which is caught between demands for better-funded public services and the need to rein in France’s debt.
The government recorded a deficit of 152.5 billion euros ($171.3bn) last year, equivalent to 5.1 percent of France’s gross domestic product (GDP). By contrast, the European Union average is 3.1 percent.
Meanwhile, public debt ballooned to 115.6 percent of GDP, the third highest in the EU after Greece and Italy.
Lecornu’s proposed 2027 budget seeks to reduce the deficit through spending restraint and tax measures, including a freeze on public sector pay and limits on pension increases.
Whether the government can make those savings without deepening public anger is another question.
The debate touches a nerve in France, where the welfare state and access to public services remain central political issues.
Macron’s decision to raise the retirement age from 62 to 64 triggered months of mass demonstrations in 2023, exposing deep opposition to reforms that many saw as unfairly burdening workers.
Now as the government prepares its next budget, it faces the challenge of persuading the public that spending cuts and other savings are necessary without further eroding confidence in public institutions.
The political stakes are high. The budget bill will be debated in a deeply divided parliament as parties position themselves before the 2027 presidential election, which will mark the end of Macron’s presidency.

====================================================================================================

Beyond oil: The Gulf crisis is becoming a food security crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:18:06 UTC
20:18:06 KST

Ask most people what the Gulf crisis will cost the world and they will say oil. Fair enough. Prices are the part we can watch every morning. But the bill that worries me more will arrive later and quietly: a farmer who buys less fertilizer than he needs, a thinner harvest, a family that can no longer afford a decent meal.
Two things are happening at once. The Gulf states import most of what they eat, so every delayed ship is a problem for their own tables. And the same region sells the raw materials that farmers elsewhere rely on to grow food. Block the sea lanes and you hurt the people eating in the Gulf and the people growing crops thousands of kilometres away.
On 14th October, UN Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva, who leads the UN task force on fertilizer shipments, warned that failure to reach an agreement could bring a food-security crisis to parts of Asia and Africa. His mechanism, he said, could start working within seven to ten days of a deal between Washington and Tehran. The scale of what he asked for is striking. Five vessels a day would be enough to keep fertilizer flowing to the countries most in need. Five ships, in a conflict that has put whole fleets at risk.
Why does this matter so much? Because of what the Gulf supplies. The FAO Director-General has said the region provides roughly 30–35 per cent of the world’s urea, about half of its sulphur exports and 20–30 per cent of its ammonia. FAO’s estimates, as reported by Fertilizer Daily, put the fertilizer trade delayed each month at between 1.5 and three million tonnes. Those are not cargoes sitting in a warehouse waiting for better days. They are next season’s wheat, rice and maize.
Farming does not negotiate. Fertilizer that arrives after the right weeks have passed cannot undo the damage, and no ceasefire can bring back a missed window.
Moreira da Silva made the same point in May, saying the planting season cannot wait. He also said that even if the strait reopened immediately, getting back to normal would take three to four months.
That gap between cause and effect is what makes this crisis easy to miss. Input prices jump at once. Smaller harvests show up in the statistics many months later, by which time the chance to prevent them is gone. Governments watching only the daily oil price are watching the wrong clock. They need to read this crisis against the planting and fertilizer calendar.
READ: Gulf countries seek alternative export routes amid Hormuz crisis
Freight adds another layer. Reuters reported on October 13 that oil shipping costs had hit new highs, with Hormuz risks among the causes. A few days earlier, the cost of hiring a supertanker to carry US oil to Asia had passed $77 million, over 700 per cent above its 2025 average. Dearer fuel raises the price of running a tractor, trucking inputs to a village and delivering food to a market. A country that buys little from the Gulf can still pay more for dinner.
The Gulf itself is hardly safe. Reuters has described the region as 80–90 per cent dependent on imported food, and Chatham House’s Neil Quilliam told the agency that over 70 per cent of GCC food comes in through Hormuz. He added that stockpiles and wider supplier networks could carry the region for only a few months. Money helps. It buys cargo and pays for air freight. It does not make a ship move through a closed passage.
There is a lesson here that goes beyond the Gulf. Buying from ten countries is not the same as having ten routes. If every shipment must pass through one strait, one port or one distribution hub, the diversity exists on paper only. Reserves give a government time, but only if they can be replaced and moved quickly.
Real food security means following a sack of grain from the foreign supplier to the local shop: the ship, the port, the warehouse, customs, the truck. If any one link fails, the rest count for little.
Nor will the pain be shared fairly. A large agribusiness can draw on stocks, credit and other suppliers. A small farmer facing a higher price simply buys less, or plants less. A well-off household grumbles about the grocery bill; a poor one skips meals. Hunger can grow even when shelves are full, because people can no longer afford what is on them.
Pakistan should not assume it is either safe or doomed. It should find out. How much fertilizer do we produce, how much do we import, what is in stock, when is the next delivery due, and can a farmer in a given district actually afford it? Pakistan should not assume it is either safe or doomed. It should find out. How much fertilizer do we produce, how much do we import, what is in stock, when is the next delivery due, and can a farmer in a given district actually afford it? National totals can hide a great deal. A tonne in a warehouse in Karachi does nothing for a grower who needs it in the right district, at a price he can pay, in the right week of the crop cycle. Preparedness is measured at the farm gate, and the numbers should be published so that farmers, provinces and traders can plan. National totals can hide a great deal. A tonne in a warehouse in Karachi does nothing for a grower who needs it in the right district, at a price he can pay, in the right week of the crop cycle. Preparedness is measured at the farm gate, and the numbers should be published so that farmers, provinces and traders can plan.
The good news is that a diplomatic answer already exists. The UN task force has designed a mechanism built on registering vessels, keeping them out of each other’s way, monitoring, verifying and reporting, modelled on earlier UN-backed arrangements for grain. It covers fertilizer and related inputs only, and it is meant to be temporary. It does not claim to settle freedom of navigation. UN officials say it was developed in consultation with the parties and has drawn strong support from member states, especially the poorer countries that depend on fertilizer imports. The idea is to build a little trust while the larger talks go on.
Governments that care about food prices should say so loudly and put weight behind it. But a protected lane on paper is not a protected lane at sea. Crews, shipowners, insurers and port operators will use it only if they believe it is safe. The test is simple: how much fertilizer arrives, how predictable the sailing times are, and whether farmers get what they need before the window shuts.
READ: Iran’s navy reports oil tanker fire in Gulf of Oman
Looking further ahead, the crisis makes a strong case for routes that do not depend on one strait. Oman’s ports at Sohar, Duqm and Salalah sit outside Hormuz and connect to global shipping, so they are a natural place to start. But a port on the right side of the map is only the first step. Food landed there still has to travel on, by road or by sea, and that takes trucks, border clearances, cold storage and money. Moreira da Silva has also pointed to attacks in the Red Sea and on Black Sea cargo vessels as adding to the pressure on global food supplies. Escaping one chokepoint only to meet delay or cost at the next is not much of an escape.
One idea that deserves serious study is a corridor linking Central Asian producers through Afghanistan and Pakistan to Arabian Sea ports, and from there to Oman and the Gulf.
I would treat it as a long-term business proposition, tested against real demand, freight rates and reliability, and not as an answer to this season’s emergency. It would need far more than a road. Traders would want open borders they can count on, transit rules that are actually enforced, fast customs, warehouses and, for fresh produce, a cold chain that never breaks. The hardest question is political. Would Pakistan and Afghanistan keep transit open through a bad patch in their relations? A corridor that closes whenever tempers rise just swaps one risk for another. Shared profit may encourage both sides to keep it running, but encouragement is not a guarantee.
If Pakistan wants a role, reliability will earn it. Food traders care about clearance times, honest charges and cargo that arrives intact far more than they care about grand announcements. Gulf partners might back it through purchase commitments, logistics deals or investment in storage and distribution that makes commercial sense, with clear responsibilities and protection against disruption.
None of this replaces the urgent job of getting this season’s shipments through. Importing countries should say openly what stocks they hold and what is due to arrive, compare it with what their crops need, and buy together where that helps. Help should go first to the farmers whose harvests are most at risk, along with sensible advice on how to use less fertilizer well. Poor households need protection too. FAO has urged governments to keep trade open, be transparent about markets and target social support. Each government panicking alone only makes prices swing more.
A global food crisis is a risk, not a certainty. How bad it gets will depend on how long the disruption lasts, what other supplies appear, the weather, the size of stocks and the decisions governments make. Corridors will not rescue anyone this season, and nobody should pretend otherwise.
So the work divides into three. Diplomats must get the cargo moving. Governments at home must look after their farmers and their poorest families. And over the longer run, investors and planners must build supply lines that can lose one route and yet survive.
In the end, the people who will judge this crisis have no say in how it is fought. For them, security at sea means fertilizer in the shop, a harvest in the field and bread they can afford. Oil prices show one cost of this war within hours. A failed harvest shows another within months. The world should count both.

€32.54 million to be invested in green innovation in Latvian companies with support from Norway grants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:17:55 UTC
20:17:55 KST

A total of €32.54 million has been allocated to support green and digital innovation in Latvia, develop new products and technologies, strengthen business competitiveness, and remediate a contaminated site in the Liepāja Special Economic Zone. The funding is provided under the Norway Grants programme “Green Business and Innovation”, following an agreement signed by the Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Latvia and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Norway. The programme will be administered by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), which plans to launch three calls for project proposals in 2027, offering grants ranging from €50,000 to €3 million.
The programme aims to support Latvian companies in transitioning towards more environmentally friendly and resource-efficient business operations while promoting innovation and bringing new products to market. Funding will be available both for the development of new solutions and prototypes and for scaling up green technologies already introduced to the market.
“More efficient use of energy, raw materials and other resources helps companies reduce costs and strengthen their competitiveness. At the same time, independently developed products, technologies and services can become valuable export offerings. Latvian companies and research organisations have the expertise needed to develop such solutions. The programme will enable investment in prototype development and testing, preparation of green innovations for market entry, and wider deployment of existing solutions. Cooperation with Norwegian partners will help combine the expertise of both countries, facilitate technology transfer and jointly develop solutions for international markets,” emphasises Ieva Jāgere, Director of the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA).
Three Funding Calls Planned for 2027
The programme envisages three calls for project proposals in 2027, providing support at different stages of innovation development:
- First quarter of 2027 — Scaling up green innovations already on the market. Grants ranging from €500,000 to €3 million will support the wider deployment of innovative green products and technologies that have already been developed and introduced to the market, including resource efficiency and renewable energy solutions. A total of €9.37 million has been allocated to this call.
- Second quarter of 2027 — Development and commercialisation of green innovations. Grants ranging from €100,000 to €499,999 will support the development and market introduction of new environmentally friendly products and technologies, with particular emphasis on the circular economy, efficient resource use, wastewater treatment and pollution reduction. A total of €12.53 million has been allocated to this call.
- Fourth quarter of 2027 — Prototype development for women entrepreneurs and startups. Grants ranging from €50,000 to €99,999 will support the development of prototypes for new products, services, processes and technologies. A total of €2 million has been allocated to this call, with funding distributed approximately equally between women entrepreneurs and startups.
Support will be available to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises registered in Latvia, as well as large companies in which public sector ownership does not exceed 25%. At least €17.87 million of the programme’s funding is expected to be allocated to small and medium-sized enterprises.
Eligible activities will include green and digital innovations, environmentally friendly products and manufacturing processes, circular economy solutions, renewable energy technologies — including biofuels and hydrogen solutions — as well as wastewater treatment and pollution reduction.
The exact launch dates, application procedures and funding conditions for each call will be published on the LIAA website.
€5.88 Million for Environmental Remediation in Liepāja
In addition to business support measures, the programme includes a project to remediate a contaminated site in the Liepāja Special Economic Zone, with the aim of returning the land to productive economic use and creating conditions for further business development.
The project will be implemented by the Liepāja Special Economic Zone Authority, with a maximum allocation of €5.88 million.
To promote knowledge and technology transfer, establish new partnerships and encourage joint innovation development, the programme also includes €190,000 in funding for bilateral cooperation activities. Project applications involving Norwegian partners will receive priority during the selection process.
Norway Grants to Provide €27.69 Million
The programme’s total budget amounts to €32.54 million, of which €27.69 million will be provided through Norway Grants and €4.85 million through co-financing from the Latvian state budget.
The programme will be managed by LIAA in cooperation with Innovation Norway, the programme partner representing the donor country.

Congress gave Trump 30 days to hit Russia’s oil buyers with 100% tariffs. He waives them two days before deadline, citing US interests. Moscow calls it historic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:15:35 UTC
20:15:35 KST

US President Donald Trump has suspended the tariffs and sanctions on the biggest buyers of Russian oil set by the Lindsey Graham Act, the law he signed himself in September. He says the move serves US national interests, according to an executive order published on the White House site.
The act required the president, within 30 days, to impose 100% tariffs on all goods from the five biggest buyers of Russian oil, to sanction a range of Russian entities and to put 500% tariffs on all Russian energy imports to the US. The deadline for those measures fell on 18 October.
Trump has used the president’s power under Section 115 of the Graham Act, which allows him to waive sanctions, restrictions, and duties by certifying to Congress in writing that doing so serves US national interests and submitting a report explaining why. The act does not, however, allow him to cancel sanctions that have already been announced.
Moscow calls it historic, Kyiv calls it a gift to Putin
The two capitals read the same order in opposite ways. Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy for Russian leader Vladimir Putin, called it “an important and truly historic moment” on X, claiming the sanctions had mainly harmed the US economy and world markets.
“Economic cooperation between Russia and the US serves the interests of both nations, contributes to global economic stability and lays the foundation for building trust and achieving lasting peace,” Dmitriev writes.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy answered from under fire. Russia struck Ukraine’s energy system on 17 October, and at that very moment Washington chose “to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to impose real, effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” he says.
A law its own backers say is being gutted
The waiver lands amid a bipartisan revolt in Congress. Seven Republican and Democratic senators had already warned on 11 October that Trump’s move to allow Russian diesel imports had broken the law Congress passed after the full-scale invasion, urging the administration to reverse it so US money would not help finance Russia’s war.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy argued the law can still work if Washington lets it.
“This law could, and still can, help a great deal. But the law has actually to work, and every vote for it matters,” he said, warning that the step only pushes Moscow to strike harder.
The world must not give up ground and must try to end the war, Zelenskyy added.
“To end it, and not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely,” he stressed, thanking everyone who “is truly fighting for peace and helping Ukraine," he stated.
The word from the Ukrainian opposition
The Ukrainian opposition also commented on Trump’s decision. Iryna Herashchenko, co-chair of the European Solidarity parliamentary faction, said that “the most cynical and stupid decisions are usually made by rulers on Saturday night,” when public attention is scattered, and people are preparing for the weekend.
“Rehabilitating Putin harms not only Ukraine but also the US itself, strengthens the axis of authoritarian regimes, and undermines international security,” she claimed.

Plants move to get away from their decaying brethren
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:11:26 UTC
20:11:26 KST

Plants seem stationary: they don’t skip, fly or walk around. But that doesn’t mean they don’t move. The organisms bend their roots and shoots in response to stimuli such as water, light, salt and gravity. These responsive movements, called tropisms, are crucial for plants’ survival.
Now researchers have discovered a new way plants move, which they call “saprotropism”: the bending of roots to avoid dead or rotting plant tissue. The results were published in Science.
The discovery began with a failed experiment and an unexpected observation. Yuzhou Zhang, a biologist at Northwest A&F University in China, was studying how plants move in response to gravity in a laboratory in Austria when one of his agar plates became contaminated with airborne microbes. Just before he threw it away, he noticed something striking: almost every single one of the plants’ roots in the plate was bent away from the spoilage. The consistency “immediately made me wonder whether this was more than a random response,” Zhang says.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
His team decided to investigate further. The researchers grew the common research plant Arabidopsis thaliana in containers, some of which were dotted with patches of rotting apple. The plants that encountered “decay zones” bent their roots to avoid the bad apple, whereas the ones in containers lacking decay grew straight through. Repeating the experiment with other plants, including tomatoes and wheat, yielded similar results—but an encounter with putrefying animal tissues had no effect. Zhang and his colleagues theorize that this reaction might help plants avoid pathogens, similar to the way unpleasant smells help animals steer clear of rotten food.
Saprotropism seems to operate differently than most other plant tropisms. “It does not follow the classical mechanism,” Zhang says. For example, gravitropism, or movement in response to gravity, and phototropism—in response to light—occur when plants redistribute the hormone auxin in their stems or roots, causing them to change their growth direction.
In contrast, saprotropism relies on a hormone called abscisic acid (ABA). When the plant roots encounter an area acidified by decaying plant matter—a chemical gradient distinct from that of animal matter—ABA builds up on the side facing the rot, encouraging growth in the other direction.
The work’s scope is impressive, says Chris Wolverton, a plant biologist at Ohio Wesleyan University, who was not involved in the study. He adds, however, that “there’s still a lot of open space in the signaling mechanism for more detail to get fleshed out.” At what point, for instance, does decaying plant tissue break down enough to become nutritious compost?
Zhang’s team hopes to fill those gaps in future studies. Ultimately the research could help illuminate how plants sense and interact with the world around them.

Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:10:22 UTC
20:10:22 KST

Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas?
Analysts say Russia will benefit most from US sanctions waiver.
United States President Donald Trump has signed an executive order waiving newly-passed Russia sanctions, claiming the move is in the US’s “national interest”.
Earlier this month, Trump also announced a deal to bring stocks of Russian diesel into global markets, in a bid to drive down energy prices that have spiked during the US-Israel war on Iran. The US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027.
Trump’s embrace of Russian energy has angered Ukraine, European partners and many US officials, who say the move rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war against its neighbour.
Ukraine’s President Volodmyr Zelenskyy slammed Trump’s diesel deal as “a gift” to Russia’s President Vladimir Putin that will help fund his war effort.
While European countries have also criticised Trump’s embrace of Russian energy, the US president has accused them of “hypocrisy”, as figures show that European Union countries continue to import Russian gas.
Here’s what we know:
Which sanctions has Trump waived?
In his executive order on Friday, Trump called off numerous planned Russia-related sanctions days before they were due to take effect, including duties on Russian goods and penalties for buying the country’s oil and gas.
The now-blocked measures were part of legislation passed in Congress with bipartisan support last month, named after the late US Senator Lindsay Graham, an outspoken critic of Russia.
They would have included up to 100 percent tariffs on all goods brought into the US from the five top importers of Russian crude oil or gas, including China and India. They could also have imposed equal penalties on countries deemed to have knowingly bought oil or gas from Russia 30 days after the law’s implementation, or to be among the top five countries helping Moscow circumvent sanctions on sales of its oil.
The waiver will hold until the Trump administration believes “further action is appropriate”, according to the executive order.
US Congressman Don Beyer, a Democrat from Virginia, said the sanctions waiver amounts to a “surrender to Putin” that “betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent”.
Who will benefit from this?
Vasily Astrov, an economist at the Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Russian government will likely be the greatest beneficiary because the easing of sanctions means Russian oil will not have to be further discounted.
He estimated that about 60 cents of every extra dollar in the price of a barrel of Russian oil would “end up in state coffers”.
Russian official Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy for Putin, hailed the US decision to waive the sanctions as “an important and truly historic moment”.
Other beneficiaries include major importers of Russian oil and gas, such as China and India, who are now less exposed to the risk of secondary US penalties.
While Trump hopes the measures will also help bring down oil prices for US consumers before November mid-term elections, experts say that is less certain.
Addressing the US’s recent diesel deal with Russia, EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis said it is unlikely to have a significant impact on global prices.
According to Trump, that deal would bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel into US and global markets “immediately”, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November, and 1 million tonnes afterwards.
“If we look at the volumes, they are not of any macroeconomic significance, and frankly, there are strong doubts whether Russia is even able to supply those volumes, and according also to US quality standards, those are big question marks,” Dombrovskis told the AFP news agency.
Which countries still buy oil from Russia?
China and India are the largest buyers of Russian crude oil, purchasing 6 billion euros ($6.74bn) and 3.6 billion euros ($4.04bn) worth respectively in September, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a nonprofit think tank.
Hungary and Slovakia, the landlocked EU members that have exemptions to the bloc’s ban on Russian crude, also remain big customers, buying a combined 290 million euros ($326m) worth of the commodity in September, said CREA. Turkiye imported 172 million euros ($193m) worth of Russian crude oil the same month, the think tank added.
Since the end of 2022, the largest importers of Russian oil products, which include diesel, have been Turkiye, China, Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Singapore.
Saudi Arabia imported the most Russian oil products in September at 534 million euros ($600m), followed by Turkiye with 321 million euros ($361m), China with 304 million euros ($342m) and India with 161 million euros ($181m).
Is Europe buying increasing amounts of gas from Russia?
“The European Council regrets the United States’ decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel,” European leaders said in a joint statement adopted following a two-day European Council meeting in Brussels this week.
But despite its own near-blanket ban on Russian oil, the EU has continued to import large quantities of Russian gas, though it plans to phase out those imports next year.
Urgewald, a Germany-based group that researches coal companies, reported this week that more than 12 million tonnes of Russian Arctic LNG was transported into EU ports from January to September this year, a 9.5 percent jump from the same period last year.
In September, EU countries imported 817 million euros ($918m) of pipeline gas, and 615 million euros ($691m) of liquefied natural gas (LNG), according to CREA.
EU members France and the Netherlands were the largest LNG importers, bringing in 446 million euros ($501m) and 116 million euros ($130m) respectively, according to the think tank. France’s LNG imports represented a 103 percent increase from the previous month, it added.
France’s President Emmanuel Macron has been among the most outspoken about Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, saying on Friday that it “sends a negative message” and would have no impact on global prices.
Hungary imported the most Russian pipeline gas of any EU member by far during the month, with 414 million euros ($465m) worth. Slovakia and Bulgaria brought in 161 million euros ($181m) and 132 million euros ($148m), respectively, according to CREA data.
