Syria’s Kurdish autonomy is fading as Arab unrest challenges Damascus’s control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:10:04 UTC
20:10:04 KST

Sunni Arab Syrians held large-scale demonstrations after Friday prayers in the northern Syrian city of Hasakah. The demonstrators, many of whom were members of Arab tribes, came from neighborhoods surrounding Hasakah, with some arriving from the adjoining Deir al-Zur province in Syria’s southeast.
Protesters assembled outside the Abu Bakr al-Siddiq Mosque in Ghweiran, where the protests began last week. After Friday prayers, they marched to the city’s main square, Liberation Square, carrying the flag of the new Syrian regime. The demonstrators were accompanied by members of the government’s internal security forces.
Regional outlets have given the unrest in Hasakah over the last week only minor attention, and almost none in the international media. The tensions in the city are noteworthy, however, because they attest to the ongoing instability bubbling beneath the surface in Syria, even as the new regime seeks to present an image of firm and exclusive authority.
Hasakah was the main city of the Kurdish-led Autonomous Administration of Northeast Syria, prior to the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), which partnered with the US-led coalition in the fight against Islamic State in the 2014-19 period, were the armed element of that administration.
However, after a swift military push by the Damascus government across the Euphrates in January, the SDF and the administration quickly agreed to dissolve. An agreement concluded on January 29 formally terminated the autonomous administration, and the SDF was formally dissolved on August 26.
But while the Kurdish-led authority was dissolved on paper, many of its institutions continued to function in reality. The SDF’s leaders deliberately sought to avoid confronting the new authorities. They understood that without external backing or protection, following the US abandonment of the Kurds and withdrawal, such a path would surely lead to bloodshed and their own forceful suppression.
Instead, they have sought to preserve as much autonomy as possible while remaining in formal cooperation with the central authorities. At the same time, semi-independent Kurdish political formations linked to the circles of the SDF remain.
This approach derives from a basic mistrust between the Kurdish structures and the new authorities, combined with the Kurds’ desire to make the best of the new situation and avoid the government-facilitated sectarian slaughters that have taken place in the Druze south and the Alawi western coastal area since the fall of the Assad regime.
The Syrian Kurds note the apparent reluctance of the Damascus authorities to punish those elements among its supporters who have engaged in violence against minorities. Only a tiny number of people have been tried, and only one or two convicted for involvement in the sectarian massacres in Sweida and Latakia.
Arab population appears determined to force the dissolution of Kurdish autonomous structures
THE LATEST incidents appear to derive from a determination by elements among the Arab population of Hasakah to force the pace of the dissolution of the Kurdish-led autonomous structures, and to demand the imposition by the central authorities in Damascus of speedy, full, and immediate control.
A source in the Kurdish authority in Hasakah told The Jerusalem Post: “The situation began approximately a week ago, when a coordinated campaign emerged on social media involving fake accounts and certain Syrians residing in Europe, particularly Germany.
“These accounts called upon Arab residents of the Ghweiran neighborhood in Hasakah to organize demonstrations and raise the Syrian national flag in the city center, under the pretext of ‘restoring state authority’ throughout Syrian territory.
“The Kurdish governor of Hasakah and the local authorities had already decided to raise the Syrian flag themselves during an official ceremony. But the social media campaign continued, calling on people from outside Hasakah city and the governorate to participate.
“It is particularly significant that the local Arab tribal leaders did not participate in these demonstrations. Instead, the gatherings consisted largely of groups of young agitators, including individuals reportedly associated with the former Islamic State and elements of the former Ba’athist establishment.
“During the demonstrations, participants raised portraits of Saddam Hussein, chanted inflammatory and explicitly sectarian slogans, including ‘Syria without minorities,’ and attacked Kurdish national symbols, flags, and banners. These actions appeared deliberately calculated to provoke a Kurdish reaction and potentially trigger wider ethnic confrontation.”
The source in Hasakah added: “These developments raise serious questions about the intentions of certain elements within Damascus. There are strong grounds to suspect that factions opposed to the integration process are actively seeking to undermine its implementation.
“These factions are believed to maintain close ties with Turkey, which may itself be encouraging such destabilizing activities, given Ankara’s apparent dissatisfaction with certain aspects of the integration agreement and its outcomes.”
'There is no deterrence or law to stop the tension in Hasakah by the government'
THE ROLE OF the Damascus authorities in the latest events remains open to question. A civilian source in Hasakah told the Post: “There is no deterrence or law to stop the tension in Hasakah by the government. Kurds and Arabs started to become afraid of moving inside the city. The risk of kidnapping has started to rise.”
The source from the Hasakah authority suspects that a broader political agenda may lie behind the latest events, namely “to exploit divisions between Arab and Kurdish communities, particularly through the mobilization of sections of the Arab tribal population, to create conditions conducive to sectarian or ethnic confrontation.
“Should such tensions escalate into widespread violence, the Kurdish authorities could find themselves under considerable pressure to request intervention by the central government to restore order.
“Damascus could then use such a request, or the wider deterioration of security, as justification for deploying additional government forces and progressively assuming direct security and administrative control over Hasakah.
“This would bear certain similarities to the approach initially envisaged toward Sweida and its Druze population, whereby internal instability could provide a political and security justification for expanding central government authority.”
A report on the Enab Baladi website, meanwhile, which is sympathetic to the Damascus authorities, blamed the Kurdish “Revolutionary Youth” for the tensions. This term is used to denote a Kurdish youth organization linked to the political organizations behind the Syrian Democratic Forces.
According to individuals quoted in the article, at Enab Baladi, the Revolutionary Youth established checkpoints in areas of the city, and “stopped passersby, searched their phones, and treated them in a humiliating manner.”
According to Abdulrahman al-Hassan, an Arab resident of Ghweiran, “The city was experiencing severe tensions because of the Revolutionary Youth’s conduct.” Al-Hassan said that in his assessment, “residents were not seeing sufficient intervention by government security forces to stop these practices or establish control throughout the city.”
In the period ahead, the stage appears to be set for further steps by the authorities in Damascus to terminate the remnants of Kurdish autonomy east of the Euphrates, and to extend the authority of the new Islamist regime to this area in its entirety.
Recent experience in southwest Syria indicates that such efforts have been conducted via a combination of local unrest, and then the entry of a combination of government-aligned “irregular” forces and official security forces into the area in question. The coming period will indicate whether such an effort is now beginning in northeast Syria.

Voices from the Arab press: Yemen’s fight to retake Sana'a mirrors Syria’s liberation of Damascus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:09:54 UTC
20:09:54 KST

Retaking Sanaa: Like Liberating Damascus
Asharq al-Awsat, London, October 10
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The current war in Yemen could bring about historic change, just as happened in Syria with the overthrow of another Iranian-backed regime.
Yemen’s internationally recognized government now controls more than two-thirds of the country and is fighting to reclaim the remainder. But that final third will be no walk in the park, given the terrain and military challenges involved. It may not be decided quickly, despite the gains achieved in the north and southwest.
This is a war against Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and Lebanon’s Hezbollah, whose operatives serve within the Houthi leadership and ranks.
This war differs in several important respects from the previous Yemen war, which began in 2015.
For years, the Houthi militia has operated under the supervision of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. Its fighters are not the barefoot cave dwellers some portray them as. They have trained in Lebanon and Iraq and spent years preparing for this confrontation, making it another regional war with Tehran.
Reliable reports indicate that Abdul Reza Shahlai, a commander in Iran’s Quds Force, directed the Houthis’ latest offensive on the Tihama plain.
Several new factors distinguish today’s war from yesterday’s.
The international community, once divided, is now almost united against the Houthis and increasingly convinced that this is a just war on behalf of the Yemeni people. The conflict has also become a matter of regional security and international trade. There is now a desire to end Houthi control, as part of a broader effort to reduce Iranian influence in the region, an effort that reached a milestone with the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime nearly two years ago.
During the previous war, Britain and the US sought to prevent an advance toward Hodeidah and Sanaa, believing that a political settlement through the Stockholm negotiations would achieve the desired outcome.
After nearly a decade of Houthi rule, however, it has become clear that the movement differs little from terrorist organizations such as ISIS and Hezbollah. It is another branch of the Iranian regime’s network, notwithstanding certain differences.
The Houthis have become an even greater international threat this year, as the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has grown in strategic importance.
With the Strait of Hormuz nearly closed because of the war with Iran, the Red Sea has become an alternative outlet for energy exports.
In coordination with Tehran, the Houthis announced their intention to close the strait. Consistent with Iran’s attacks on oil shipments, they declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia and began targeting its tankers. It was for this purpose that they seized Perim island and the Mocha area last month, both of which have recently been liberated.
Previously, the international community showed little interest in correcting Yemen’s disastrous situation. That changed when the crisis ceased to concern only Yemenis and their neighbors and became a threat to international shipping. The European Union, Britain and the American administration quickly condemned the Houthis and offered logistical support for operations against them.
If the current war achieves its objectives, it will end Houthi domination of the Yemeni people and bring relief to millions. Some 22 million Yemenis living under Houthi control could be rescued from the brink of famine and epidemics. According to World Health Organization figures, cholera cases have tripled in just three weeks. Millions of children could return to school after years without education.
The extremist religious movement has also transformed Yemen into a transit route for people fleeing wars and famine in East Africa, a corridor for drug smugglers and a haven for al-Qaeda and ISIS, both of which operate there and maintain dealings with the Houthis. The movement also has an arms-smuggling relationship with the Somalia-based terrorist organization al-Shabaab.
Twelve years have passed since the Houthis forcibly seized Sanaa. Like Lebanon’s Hezbollah, they imposed their rule through coercion, adopted a similar name – Ansar Allah – and displayed portraits of their leaders.
This war is different from previous wars and skirmishes. For the first time, Yemen’s legitimate government is fighting as a unified force, bringing together diverse Yemeni factions under one banner. Earlier confrontations were largely fought by the Arab coalition alongside government forces with limited domestic reach.
The coming weeks and months could prove decisive. The chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council has clearly identified the objective: the liberation of Sanaa.
If Yemenis succeed in defeating Iran’s proxy, it will constitute a major regional victory, much like the achievement of Ahmed al-Sharaa’s forces when they advanced from Idlib province and liberated the Syrian capital from Assad’s regime. – Abdulrahman Al-Rashed
Iraq’s Kurds: Little Choice But To Work With Baghdad
An-Nahar, Lebanon, October 9
As Iraq celebrates the withdrawal of coalition forces from its territory, Iraqi Kurds are hardly in a celebratory mood. A Kurdish researcher at the London Dialogue research center believes the withdrawal calls for a funeral rather than a celebration.
“It is not good, but it is an Iraqi decision,” said Sirwan Barzani, a Kurdish military commander turned businessman. “They asked them to come to their country, and now they are telling them they are no longer needed.”
Barzani warned of renewed activity by ISIS terrorists. His forces and those of the Iraqi government have observed four or five Islamist cells operating near Makhmour in Nineveh province after months of inactivity. This is an alarming development.
“We know what happened in 2014. There will certainly be terrorist cell activity now, and we can already see it.”
Iraqi and Kurdish forces are nevertheless better trained and organized than they were in 2014, when ISIS captured a third of Iraq and extensive areas of Syria. The organization was eventually driven out of Iraq in 2017 and Syria in 2019 through counteroffensives by local forces supported by the international coalition.
In 2024, Iraqi and Iranian officials agreed that coalition forces would withdraw from Iraq by September 30, 2026.
Today, however, the greatest threat to Iraqi Kurds is not ISIS but continuing Iranian drone attacks, occurring amid the confrontation between Washington and Tehran and the possibility that Iraqi Kurds could help their Iranian counterparts conduct operations against the Islamic Republic.
On the very day coalition forces withdrew, an Iranian drone struck a civilian camp housing Iranian Kurds near Iraqi Kurdistan.
Since February 28, when the US and Israel launched their attack on Iran, the Kurdish Region of Iraq has faced approximately 1,000 drone and missile attacks from Iran and Iraqi armed groups loyal to it. These attacks have killed around 32 people, including 19 members of Iranian Kurdish parties.
In March, rumors circulated that Iranian Kurdish forces would launch a ground invasion of Iran with American and Israeli backing, but no such operation materialized.
On September 27, the Kurdistan Regional Government’s media office confirmed that Iranian Kurdish groups were aware of the 2023 security agreement between Erbil, Baghdad, and Tehran, intended to prevent armed Iranian Kurdish organizations from attacking neighboring countries.
Meanwhile, Iraq had set September 20 as the deadline for disarming Iraqi militias in response to American pressure, only to postpone it until June 30, 2027.
“The foremost internal Iraqi threat comes from pro-Iranian militias, which have attacked Iraqi Kurdistan and neighboring countries more than 100 times this year,” said retired US Army Col. Myles Caggins, a former coalition spokesman.
Baghdad faces a substantial challenge in confronting these illegal militias, which continue launching drones without serious consequences.
Barzani therefore believes the Kurds must be provided with air defenses. After all, this is Iraqi airspace. Even if Iraq itself lacks adequate defenses, it will remain vulnerable to these threats, and the hope is that any new air-defense systems supplied to Baghdad will also be extended to Kurdistan.
Joey Hood, a former senior State Department official for Near Eastern affairs who also served in Iraq, considers it unlikely that Iranian attacks across the Middle East, including Iraqi Kurdistan, will cease.
Iran has targeted not only American troops but also American interests, using that justification to strike a power station in Kurdistan and a water-analysis facility in Kuwait.
The federal government in Baghdad and the regional government in Erbil must work together, with partners such as the US, to acquire and deploy air-defense systems capable of countering these attacks.
Even before the American-Iranian war, Iran and its affiliated groups targeted positions belonging to Iranian opposition forces, Kurdish oil and gas facilities, and Kurdish businessmen.
On January 16, 2024, for example, Kurdish billionaire Peshraw Dizayee and his 11-year-old daughter were killed in a ballistic missile strike that Iran justified by claiming it had targeted an Israeli espionage headquarters.
On September 30, US Central Command chief Brad Cooper stated that Iraqi security forces, including the Kurdish Peshmerga, now possess the capabilities, leadership, and operational independence needed to confront threats to their territory. Yet another CENTCOM officer expressed concern that Baghdad would show little interest in protecting Kurdish areas, particularly amid fears of incursions across their boundaries.
The Kurds must therefore increasingly rely on themselves and on their relationship with Baghdad, according to a coalition official who previously advised the Peshmerga.
Unfortunately, the coalition is now leaving. Its continued presence would have been valuable both for confronting ISIS and for maintaining military assistance. Only time will tell whether these concerns prove justified.
At a farewell ceremony for American troops, Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani acknowledged one reality the Kurds cannot avoid: their growing dependence on Baghdad. This means entering a formative stage in which Iraq itself must assume an active and meaningful national role. – Sarkis Naoum
Resuming the Iran War: Congress vs Pentagon
Al-Ittihad, UAE, October 10
Developments within the Pentagon and Congress, alongside competing centers of influence in the American decision-making establishment, particularly the administration itself, reveal a growing dispute over how the war with Iran should be managed, how much should be spent on it, the mechanisms of oversight, and the limits of authority in conducting military operations.
Differences over the war have spread from Democratic leaders to figures within the Republican Party, many of them supporters of President Donald Trump. The debate also involves military and political leaders and reaches as far as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth himself.
At the heart of these disagreements are the war’s cost and the prospect of continued operations. Expenditure had already reached $43 billion by September, including additional costs and nearly $28b. for replenishing ammunition and other requested allocations.
This has prompted lawmakers from both parties to demand comprehensive accounting of operational costs, damage sustained by American bases, and the expense of repairing aircraft, ships, and other equipment.
The Congressional Budget Office has also presented estimates of the war’s costs and its impact on military stockpiles, further complicating the administration’s request for at least $67b. in additional funding. This comes alongside a proposed defense budget that could reach $1 trillion in 2027, with the possibility of still greater spending should full-scale war resume.
The central disagreement is that the Pentagon seeks additional resources, while Congress wants to define the objectives for which money may be allocated and restrict its use. Lawmakers from both parties may not fully appreciate the breadth of the military requirements involved.
The War Powers Resolution of 1973 will undoubtedly remain a source of contention if war with Iran resumes, particularly over whether Congress must approve a declaration of war or provide explicit authorization for military action.
There is also concern about the effects of renewed military operations on the armed forces themselves, the performance of the defense secretary and senior commanders, and the broader turmoil within the military establishment. Recent dismissals and resignations, together with delays in military appointments, point to the possibility of further confusion and even disorder within one of America’s most strategically important institutions.
Members of Congress are therefore pressing for serious consultations and a firm approach rather than direct confrontation, especially as the US faces challenges extending well beyond the Middle East. These include the Indo-Pacific, the growing demands posed by China and Russia, and security concerns closer to Europe.
Washington must consider its readiness to confront multiple contingencies, including the possibility of simultaneous military engagements in different regions.
Congress is consequently moving to rebuild a framework of understanding with the administration without waiting for the midterm elections. Several military priorities cannot be postponed, including investment in strategic programs such as missile defense, interception systems, early warning capabilities, and space technology.
Congress is also expected to examine the scale of American military deployments worldwide.
Virtually every major military issue may now be reopened as Congress moves urgently to reaffirm its political role in national decision-making, while the Pentagon continues operating with Trump’s direct support.
The consequences will be felt in both funding for military operations and the authority to wage war. Proposed increases in the 2027 defense budget, particularly for research, development, and procurement, underscore the scale of the decisions awaiting lawmakers.
The disputes between Congress, the Pentagon, the administration, and influential military institutions are unlikely to disappear. All sides may also be waiting for the midterm elections before reassessing their policies. Each has its own priorities, and reconciling them will require greater agreement, candor, and transparency, as American military involvement in the Middle East continues and the possibility of renewed war with Iran remains.
For now, the major policies under consideration will remain politically contested. – Tarek Fahmy
Hosni Mubarak, Military Commander
Al-Masry Al-Youm, Egypt, October 8
The anniversary of Egypt’s great October victory has arrived, and we have heard much said about it, yet almost nothing about Hosni Mubarak. I mean Mubarak the commander of the Egyptian Air Force during the October War, not Mubarak the politician, whose legacy remains controversial and always will.
It is the military commander who concerns me here, for one simple reason: we should imagine what might have happened had the airstrike he led at the opening moment of the crossing of the Suez Canal failed. Any ground forces fighting on the battlefield remain exposed to the enemy unless they have air cover protecting their positions.
The initial airstrike under Mubarak’s command provided that protection. Without it, our forces would have found it extremely difficult to cross the Suez Canal itself, let alone penetrate the earthen defenses of the Bar Lev Line. This was Mubarak’s contribution, alongside the airmen under his command, and it deserves to be remembered.
One of the principal reasons for the crushing defeat of June 5, 1967, was that the enemy struck our aircraft while they were still on the ground. Once our air force had been neutralized, the enemy knew our ground forces were completely exposed. What followed were horrors almost beyond belief, as anyone reading the political memoirs of those dark days can attest.
The heroic Anwar Sadat absorbed that lesson, as did the Egyptian Air Force. When our army went into battle and secured victory on October 6, 1973, every soldier knew that Egyptian aircraft were protecting him from above. Our ground forces advanced and kept advancing because Mubarak and his pilots provided a protective aerial umbrella.
Nor was that his only achievement. The Battle of Mansoura was also fought under his command, and anyone familiar with its details knows that it stands almost without parallel in the history of aerial warfare. Military academies continue devoting extensive attention to it when teaching the landmark battles of military history.
Israel launched 120 aircraft to destroy air bases in the Nile Delta, only to find our air force waiting for them. An extraordinary aerial battle followed, lasting a full 53 minutes. By its conclusion on October 14, 1973, the Israeli aircraft had been divided into two groups: those destroyed and those forced to flee. Mubarak led that effort.
The Koran teaches: “Do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just.” In other words, disliking someone must not keep us from giving them the credit they deserve. Another verse instructs us: “Do not deprive people of what is rightfully theirs.”
We have deprived Mubarak the military commander – not Mubarak the politician, I repeat – of the recognition he deserves in many respects.
– Soliman Gouda ■

How public opinion on transgender bathroom access shifted between 2016 and 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:59 UTC
20:00:59 KST

Public opinion in the United States has grown more conservative regarding restroom access for transgender individuals over the past several years, a shift the researchers link to changing beliefs about safety and discrimination. When people hold conflicting views about the rights and risks involved in this debate, they are now much more likely to side with restrictive policies than they were in the past. These shifts are detailed in a new study published in Politics, Groups, and Identities.
Over the last decade, lawmakers across multiple states have proposed and passed legislation regulating which public restrooms transgender people can use. These bills typically require individuals to use facilities that match the sex listed on their original birth certificates rather than their current gender identities.
Public restrooms have historically served as a political battleground regarding gender, space, and safety. As the study notes, the modern sex-segregated restroom emerged during the Industrial Revolution as women entered the paid workforce. At the time, separate facilities were framed as necessary safe spaces for women. Similar arguments about restroom safety appeared during the mid-twentieth century to police the behavior of gay men, and again in the 1970s by opponents of the Equal Rights Amendment.
Today, political rhetoric surrounding transgender bathroom policies tends to rely on three main arguments. Proponents of bathroom restrictions often argue that allowing transgender women into women’s restrooms poses a security risk to women and children. Opponents counter this by framing bathroom restrictions as a form of discrimination against transgender people. They also argue that forcing transgender individuals into facilities that do not match their outward appearance places those individuals at physical risk.
Patrick R. Miller, a political scientist at Kent State University, led a team of researchers to investigate how these three political arguments influence public opinion. The researchers wanted to understand which of these beliefs resonate most with the public. They also wanted to see how Americans formulate their policy preferences when they happen to agree with arguments from both sides of the political aisle.
The research team utilized data from two nationally representative online surveys. The first survey polled 1,291 adults in 2016, a year when national media coverage of bathroom legislation peaked. The second survey polled 1,618 adults in 2022, a period when media attention on this specific issue had cooled but conservative political focus on transgender policies remained high.
In both surveys, participants read three statements reflecting the main political arguments about bathroom access. They rated their level of agreement on a seven-point scale. The statements asked whether unrestricted restroom access poses a security risk to women and children, whether restroom restrictions discriminate against transgender individuals, and whether such restrictions endanger the safety of transgender people.
Participants also indicated their ultimate policy preferences. They were asked whether they agreed or disagreed with the statement that transgender people should only be allowed to use public restrooms consistent with the sex listed on their official state identification cards.
To ensure their findings isolated the impact of specific arguments, the researchers applied a robust statistical model to the survey responses. They accounted for a wide range of demographic and psychological variables known to influence political opinions. These included age, sex, income, religious attendance, and political partisanship.
The team also measured underlying psychological traits, such as moral traditionalism, egalitarianism, and a person’s baseline sensitivity to disgust. By accounting for these broad traits, the researchers could better isolate how the three specific bathroom-related arguments independently swayed policy preferences.
The researchers found that overall support for restrictive bathroom policies grew between the two survey periods. In 2016, about 54 percent of respondents supported laws restricting restroom access based on state identification. By 2022, support for these restrictions had risen to roughly 62 percent.
When examining the underlying beliefs, the researchers noticed shifting patterns. The belief that transgender restroom access poses a security risk to women and children grew stronger in the population by 2022. At the same time, the belief that bathroom restrictions discriminate against transgender individuals also grew slightly, while concerns about the physical safety of transgender people remained relatively stable.
Because people do not always hold perfectly aligned political views, the research team looked closely at respondents who agreed with conflicting statements. A substantial portion of participants believed both that open restroom policies pose a security risk to women and that restrictive policies discriminate against transgender people. The way these conflicted individuals resolved their internal tension changed dramatically over the six-year gap.
In 2016, conflicted respondents were highly likely to resolve their ambivalence in favor of transgender rights. A person who held both beliefs had about a 62 percent chance of opposing restrictive bathroom policies. They appeared to discount their own security concerns and elevate their concerns about discrimination when deciding on a final policy stance.
By 2022, this pattern flipped entirely. Conflicted respondents became much more likely to support restrictive bathroom laws. A person holding those same competing beliefs in 2022 had only about a 29 percent chance of opposing bathroom restrictions. They began weighing the perceived security risks much more heavily than their concerns about discrimination.
The researchers also observed changes in how education influenced attitudes among political liberals. In 2016, highly educated liberals held the most consistently pro-transgender beliefs about the bathroom issue, standing apart from less educated liberals. By 2022, this educational divide vanished, as highly educated liberals shifted toward a more neutral stance that matched the rest of their ideological cohort.
The study relies on observational survey data, which means it cannot establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship between political messaging and changing public opinion. The surveys capture snapshots in time, and the researchers note that self-reported attitudes do not entirely capture how these policies operate in reality.
Future research could rely on experimental designs to test how specific messages or news frames actively alter a person’s viewpoint. Researchers might also investigate why the argument regarding the security of women and children remains so persuasive to the public, as previous studies have not found empirical evidence of an actual security threat linked to inclusive bathroom policies.
The study, “Policing gender in the bathroom: attitudes toward the transgender bathroom issue,” was authored by Patrick R. Miller, Andrew R. Flores, Donald P. Haider-Markel, Daniel C. Lewis, and Jami K. Taylor.

Plaque telling story of African-Caribbean prisoners in Britain stolen within days

20:00:58 KST

The theft of a plaque in Hampshire that told the little-known story of African-Caribbean prisoners in 18th-century Britain reflects the enduring racism that has fuelled centuries of atrocities against Black and Indigenous Caribbean people, their descendants say.
Drummer Ronald Raymond McDonald was part of a delegation that travelled from Belize and elsewhere to Portchester Castle last week to honour their ancestors: 2,500 men, women and children transported to Britain as prisoners of war in 1796.
McDonald, whose Garifuna ancestors from St Vincent and the Grenadines were among the prisoners, said he was heartbroken to learn that the plaque had been stolen and a nearby bench vandalised with hateful graffiti.
“Why would somebody do something like that when people are simply honouring their ancestors … It’s very sad,” he said.
The plaque, installed at the castle, commemorated the more than 2,000 prisoners held there, marking an extraordinary chapter of Black British history: one of the largest known arrivals of African-Caribbean people in Britain before the Windrush era.
The unveiling was part of a ceremony organised by the St Vincent and the Grenadines 2nd Generation (SV2G), in partnership with the University of Warwick and English Heritage, and was attended by Caribbean communities, diplomats, researchers and heritage organisations.
But days later, English Heritage staff discovered the plaque was missing. They said a padlock to one of the castle gates had been removed and the incident had been reported to police.
Garifuna advocate Princess Eulogia said the theft reflected “a spirit of racism that haunts generation after generation and hides in plain sight”. It was time, she said, to recognise that “we are all connected” and to end the hate.
Queen Mother Chief Freda Paulino-Sideroff, who is Garifuna and had travelled to the UK for the ceremony, was returning home to the US when she learned of the theft.
“Hate will never define who we are as a people. We are resilient survivors of our ancestors who have endured,” she said. In the 1700s, her Garifuna ancestors were expelled from St Vincent by British forces and left to perish on the barren island of Baliceaux as Britain sought to crush decades of resistance to colonisation.
Emilio ‘Sásamu’ Thomas, a Garifuna cultural ambassador who also travelled from Belize for the ceremony, echoed Paulino-Sideroff’s defiance, saying Garifuna people would not allow themselves to be victimised. His message to the perpetrators, he said, was: “Whatever pain that they are experiencing, we’re here to help them to relieve that pain.”
The missing plaque was meant to honour the prisoners, whose story, researchers say, had been largely lost to history. They came from a coalition that included formerly enslaved Africans, Caribbean-born people, Indigenous people and French soldiers who fought against British control of St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines and Grenada. Their defeat and removal helped strengthen British rule in the region.
It was unveiled on 9 October, exactly 230 years after one of the ships carrying the prisoners was wrecked at Rapparee Cove in Devon, with many of those on board losing their lives.
Iona Keen of English Heritage called the removal an act of vandalism, while University of Warwick professor Katherine Astbury said the plaque was intended to provide a visible memorial of the prisoners, and a reminder of “an important, forgotten part of Caribbean history”.
The incident comes during Black History Month and amid renewed debate over slavery reparations. Campaigner and author Sir Patrick Vernon said vandalism of memorials representing Black British history had occurred repeatedly over decades, citing damage to other memorials.
He described the theft as symbolic of an “ongoing battle and the legacy of enslavement”.
Jacqueline Roberts, SV2G chief executive, said the theft could not erase history, and stressed the importance of continuing research to uncover more hidden stories. “Our history is intertwined with British history,” she said. “It’s important to understand that part of our journey, because it is part of the complexity of our identity, and affects our sense of belonging.”
Anthony Severin, St Lucia’s high commissioner and chair of the Caribbean community diplomatic caucus in the UK, described the theft as a “desecration of the memory and spirit of our commemorated ancestors”. He pledged that the plaque “whether returned or replaced, will remain affixed to the walls of Portchester Castle”.

US corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:31 UTC
20:00:31 KST

US corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth.
Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influence the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in more than 350 meetings, the advocacy group found.
US company representatives and industry groups deny there was a concerted campaign to derail the deforestation rules, saying their meetings with EU officials raised legitimate concerns around implementation.
The EUDR prohibits imports of commodities such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood from deforested land. When the ban was put forward in 2003, the then European environment commissioner, Virginijus Sinkevičius, described it as “the most ambitious legislative attempt to tackle these issues worldwide ever” and some US lawmakers said it should be a model for similar rules in the United States.
In the years since, its official implementation has been delayed twice and the original goal to rigorously trace the origin of commodities has been revised so much that some of its initial supporters claimed the policy has been in effect “dismantled”. The law will come into effect in December.
Lobbyists from many countries, including Brazil and several EU nations, are known to have contributed to this dilution. Mighty Earth has provided the most detailed analysis yet of the role of organisations from the United States.
It found 24 major US companies, trade associations and industry organizations discussed the EUDR in at least 173 meetings with members of the European parliament and 178 meetings with senior European Commission officials between July 2024 and July 2026.
The US organisations with the highest number of meetings with the European Commission were the National Alliance of Forest Owners, Advanced Woody Biomass Alliance, the US Soybean Export Council, Bunge, the American Chamber of Commerce to the European Union and Cargill.
Cargill had two meetings, Bunge one meeting and Mondlēz eight meetings.
Mighty Earth said lobbying was also conducted through the US Congress, the US Department of Agriculture, the Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House.
Two weeks after a July 2025 meeting at a Scottish golf course between Trump and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, the two sides released a joint statement that promised the US special treatment with regard to the EUDR.
The commission stated the US “poses negligible risk to global deforestation” (even though many of its biggest financial and trading companies have been repeatedly implicated in destruction of the Amazon and similar biomes). The statement also talked about the EU working “to address the concerns of US producers and exporters regarding EUDR, with a view to avoiding undue impact on US-EU trade”.
Mighty Earth said its investigation highlighted the need for the EU to adopt greater transparency about lobbying activities and to give more access to civil society to ensure balance.
“Our analysis found a relentless and aggressive campaign by major US businesses, trade bodies and government officials, going all the way to President Trump, who offered to personally intervene, to further pressure EU policymakers,” Isabel Fernandez, senior adviser for Mighty Earth, said. “Some of the companies lobbying the EU, include the most egregious who are still linked to the illegal clearing of forests for commodities, such as soy that make their way into European markets.”
Earlier this year a delegation of Trump administration officials went to EU capitals arguing the law would put the US off exporting to the European market because it would raise costs for US producers. In an opinion piece published in Agence France, Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, said the law was: “… sold as a bold strike against global forest loss. In reality it will impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit when enforced against countries that pose no deforestation risk.”
US corporate organisations said their engagement was designed to better understand and enhance the EUDR.
The American Chamber of Commerce to the EU said it had raised concerns about EUDR implementation challenges, such as IT system shortcomings and a lack of clarity around the obligations of companies. But a spokesperson said its role had been constructive: “AmCham EU has consistently supported the EUDR’s objective of tackling global deforestation and promoting sustainable supply chains ... We have asked to allow sufficient time for companies and authorities to prepare and ensure the regulation can be effectively enforced without undermining its environmental objectives.”
The US Soybean Export Council said it was focused on ways to support industry compliance with the EU’s rules. “USSEC does not seek delay or exemption; rather we favour a transition period as the Regulation comes into force. This would allow companies, control authorities, the European Commission, and the entire value chain to gain experience and learnings on how compliance works in practice, allowing for greater understanding and adaptations to implementation if needed moving forwards,” a spokesperson said.
The agribusiness company Bunge said it was committed to deforestation-free supply chains and was investing in monitoring and traceability that had, it said, achieved 100% traceability to farm for both direct and indirect soy sourcing in priority areas of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. A spokesperson said: “Bunge supports the objectives of the European Union Deforestation Regulation while observing our own non-deforestation commitment and strengthening responsible sourcing. We are also in contact with relevant EU bodies and national competent authorities via sector organizations and directly to request clarification on certain specific complex scenarios regarding the practical implementation requirements of the EUDR.”
Cargill and Mondelēz did not send an on-the-record response to the Guardian’s request for a comment.

====================================================================================================

Fake Linda and me: the Agatha Christie-worthy mystery of the fraudster who stole my byline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:30 UTC
20:00:30 KST

It started with an entirely ordinary interaction on LinkedIn. Someone had tagged me in a post, saying how much they’d enjoyed contributing to a New York Post article I’d written about “chronoworking”. As the author of a book about circadian rhythms, it was exactly the sort of subject I might write about. Except I’d never heard of this person, let alone interviewed them.
I clicked on the link and my stomach dropped. There, above an article about people who organise their working lives around their biological clocks, was my name: Linda Geddes.
It was the latest in a string of increasingly bizarre events that had begun three weeks earlier, when a friend who works as an editor at the scientific journal Nature texted to ask whether I’d been pitching stories to one of her colleagues. I hadn’t.
It turned out that someone had been approaching Nature editors using my name and an email address that wasn’t mine, referencing articles I’d previously written to make their pitches more convincing. Worse, the journal had recently encountered another impersonator posing as Caroline Williams, a former colleague of mine. That person had convinced an editor at Science to commission and publish an article under Caroline’s name, receiving about $1,000 for it.
Further digging revealed that Fake Linda had also pitched a story to Science, unsuccessfully. Then, last week, an editor at Nature Medicine contacted me to ask whether I’d been pitching to them and Nature Health as well.
I donned my sleuthing cap and discovered a potential link between Fake Linda and Fake Caroline. Entering my impersonator’s email address into Outlook.com’s account recovery system revealed a partially obscured Gmail recovery address. An editor at Science had independently discovered the same address pattern associated with Fake Caroline’s email.
As someone whose livelihood depends on the reputation I’ve spent decades building, I find this deeply unsettling. Someone is potentially making money by passing themselves off as me, while putting my professional credibility at risk. Apart from one interview conducted by email, the quotes in the New York Post article were lifted from previously published features, without attribution. Many of Fake Linda’s pitches also bear the hallmarks of AI-assisted writing. Even unsuccessful pitches could damage relationships with editors.
The New York Post has since removed the article, conducted an internal review and referred the matter to the appropriate authorities, a spokesperson said.
What I find particularly baffling is the motive. Freelance science journalism is hardly a lucrative profession, and is quite niche. My best guess is that a struggling freelancer is impersonating more established peers to boost their earnings, perhaps using AI to make the process more efficient. But how would they receive payment without revealing their identity?
Other possibilities have crossed my mind. Could it be a PR professional trying to secure coverage for a client, or someone testing how easily publishers can be fooled? Perhaps it is someone with a personal grudge. But as Caroline put it: “Why us? We’re nice!”
Dr Simon Miller, the director of policy, strategy and communications at the UK fraud prevention service Cifas, is equally bemused. “Ordinarily, if you’re seeking to defraud, you’re seeking to do it at scale, in a relatively light-touch way, using mechanised, industrialised processes,” he said. “This is tantalisingly unusual. It’s almost the stuff of Agatha Christie, but with 21st-century technology.”
Journalists are far from the only people finding their names attached to work they didn’t produce. In April, Prof Eric Topol, of the Scripps Institute in California, discovered his name on a scientific paper he knew nothing about. Four of his five supposed co-authors were similarly unaware of the paper, while the fifth could not be identified. Within hours of Topol flagging the incident on X, the journal’s website had disappeared.
Topol, who is a bestselling author, said he has discovered at least 12 books on Amazon with his name on that he didn’t write, including several cookbooks. “I don’t even know how to cook,” he said. Particularly upsetting was when a patient told him he’d read his supposed memoir. “They said: ‘I was reading it, and a lot of those things don’t seem to be accurate.’ That’s how I found out about it.”
Leslie McIntosh, a vice-president of research integrity and security at Digital Science, said someone might add a respected name to a scientific paper without permission to make the work appear more credible. Fraudsters also sometimes added respected researchers as editors to make bogus journals appear legitimate and attract publication fees. Even more nightmarish would be someone deliberately publishing misleading information under someone else’s name to damage their reputation. “If their name ended up on a retracted paper, they would then have to explain that retraction,” she said.
Employers are encountering yet another form of impersonation. Jamie Collier, a researcher at Google Threat Intelligence, said criminals had used stolen personal information to secure remote jobs under other people’s names, sometimes without the victim’s knowledge.
Generative AI is making such deception easier, “mainly by stripping away the usual tell-tale red flags that hiring managers relied on to spot fraud,” Collier said. Large language models can generate convincing CVs, tailored cover letters and fabricated evidence of professional experience.
“Real-time video filters and voice-cloning tools are the next step. While live deepfakes are still relatively nascent … threat actors are already testing them to bypass quick video screenings and mask regional accents,” Collier said.
The Society of Authors and the Writers’ Guild of Great Britain have warned of increasingly sophisticated scams involving people impersonating literary agents and publishers, in an attempt to get writers to part with money or sign away their rights.
The Society of Authors’ chief executive, Anna Ganley, said she personally received between five and 10 scam emails a day, supposedly from book festivals, literary agents, publishers and others. Some writers had lost thousands of pounds after responding to genuine-sounding offers. “It’s incredibly difficult for writers, because you are often looking for opportunities to market your books,” she said.
Unlike those scams, Fake Linda’s activities seem like a lot of work for relatively small financial gain. But the latest technology could make such impersonations easier. Miller said: “AI is allowing criminals to create sophisticated impersonations at unprecedented speed and scale.”
Or multiple impersonations. I’ve since identified a third science journalist, Sara Novak, with a potential link to Fake Linda and Fake Caroline. Fake Sara apparently pitched a story to Chemical and Engineering News in August, which was declined. When Real Sara shared her impersonator’s email address with me, I discovered it links to the same masked recovery address.
The consequences extend beyond those being impersonated. “The risk for journals and publishers is huge,” said Dr Ben Johnson, the chief editor at Nature Health, who turned down a pitch by Fake Linda. “People trust the Nature brand as a source of evidence-based quality information. If an AI-generated story from a fake journalist is submitted then I will likely spend hours editing it from AI slop into Nature prose, including all the fake quotes from people never interviewed.”
All of this raises uncomfortable questions about how you can be sure you know who you’re dealing with when communicating online. When I emailed the New York Post about my impersonator, it agreed to help rectify the situation, then asked: “I see that you’re emailing me from a Guardian email address. Is there any other info you can provide to verify who you are?”
After discovering that Science had inadvertently published a news story by Fake Caroline, its managing news editor, John Travis, said his team had started running all pitches and drafts through AI detectors, “though they are not perfect”. “We also require Zoom calls for any new writers,” he said.
The experience has also put editors at Nature on higher alert. “Sadly, for early career freelancers, this makes me less likely to commission news stories from journalists that I haven’t worked with before,” Johnson said. “I will also have to try to find the time to have a call with new freelancers before they write, to check they are who they say they are.”
Even video calls are no guarantee of identity. Google Threat Intelligence recently documented North Korea-linked hackers using real-time deepfakes to lure executives into Zoom calls with trusted peers. “They faked video and audio glitches to get the target to download a ‘troubleshooting tool’ that wiped out their credentials and wallets,” Collier said.
Miller advises independently checking unexpected approaches through an established email address or telephone number. McIntosh advocates several layers of verification, like the multiple identity checks at airports. “You have to have multiple ways to ensure and triangulate that you’re speaking to the person you think you’re speaking to,” she said.
For people whose identities have been hijacked, Miller advises warning professional networks and monitoring for further impersonation attempts.
There may also be legal remedies. Rupert Earle, senior counsel at the London law firm Bates Wells, said that under UK law, impersonating someone to secure paid work could constitute fraud. Victims could also have civil claims for “passing off” – misleading people into believing that work or services come from an established person or business – or false attribution, if work they didn’t create was published under their name.
However, identifying the perpetrator and taking legal action can be difficult, particularly when the publications are overseas and the impersonator’s location is unknown. Despite uncovering several clues linking Fake Linda and Fake Caroline, we still don’t know who is behind the accounts.
But the hunt for Fake Linda continues. I’ll be reporting the incident to the UK’s Report Fraud service. I’ve also sent a cease-and-desist email to my impersonator, demanding they stop.
For such a prolific writer, they’ve gone surprisingly quiet.

‘We are in hiding’: Briton with severe health issues fears deportation from Sweden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:30 UTC
20:00:30 KST

A seriously ill British man living in Sweden has been forced into hiding amid fears he will be deported as a result of what he says is a government Brexit residency error.
Mark Smith, 60, who has had hearts attacks, strokes, severe headaches and chronically high blood pressure that has been difficult to treat, was told on the phone he should leave Sweden by 17 October as he was an “alien” without permission to stay.
Terrified of deportation, he and his wife have moved out of their home in Falkenberg, in south-west Sweden, to a caravan park. “We are in hiding, we daren’t go back to our apartment. We are scared to go out as we don’t know if the police will come and take us,” Smith said.
A court ruled on 12 October that a decision on deportation would not be suspended but gave him until 20 October to “submit his application for a retrial” in relation to “the grounds for the decision on indefinite deportation”.
Smith has been in Sweden since 2017 and says he was told by authorities he did not need to do anything to stay after Brexit in 2020. He worked, had private health insurance, supported his wife and registered on the population register administered by the national tax authority, as required under Swedish rules.
He was unaware, however, that Sweden was among 13 of the 27 EU member states that required Britons living in the country before Brexit to make a formal application to remain. Other countries, such as Spain, did not opt for that system and just required Britons to declare they were a resident.
Smith said: “I asked the tax authorities three times on different occasions if I had to do anything because of Brexit and they said no, telling me I had to wait for five years to apply for permanent residency.
“Because it was the tax authority, a government body, I took it for granted that what they told me was correct,” he added.
David Milstead, a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights activist working through the Brits in Sweden group, said Smith’s case was typical of many Britons living in Sweden.
Milstead said: “Mark’s experience is far from unusual. I have encountered many British citizens who actively sought information from the Swedish authorities about their residence rights after Brexit, only to receive vague, unhelpful answers, sometimes being told that they needed to do nothing.”
They include the 78-year-old widow Joyce Thomas, whose husband also inquired about Brexit residency and was told by the tax authorities there was nothing to do, and who is now fighting a removal order.
Smith had a minor heart attack on Wednesday night but wanted his situation publicised because he said the British government needed to know what was happening to expats in Sweden, “not just to me but others”.
His wife, Petra, said his health conditions had left him so vulnerable she was not sure “if he will last until Christmas”.
She said: “He has been told he can’t drive, he can’t fly – what do they expect him to do? Get up and walk to England? Come on, Sweden, we need to step back from all of this and be better.”
After 12 years together, she said deportation would be devastating for her and her 15-year-old son who has special needs, who Smith co-parents. “It is wrong what they are doing, I feel ashamed to be Swedish. What they are doing is racist to British people,” Petra said.
Milstead said Smith’s case was “depressingly familiar” and should warrant the urgent attention of the European Commission, which has previously said Sweden was not breaking any laws.
“A gentleman with Mark’s serious health conditions should not be having to fight deportation. It is difficult to understand how the European Commission has concluded that Sweden’s treatment of late applications under the [Brexit] withdrawal agreement does not warrant a challenge,” he said.
“Sweden stands out so starkly from other EU countries, and there are serious questions that remain unanswered, particularly about proportionality and the treatment of vulnerable people. These are precisely the kinds of cases where the protections of the withdrawal agreement ought to matter most.”
The Scandinavian country has found itself under mounting pressure over its approach to the withdrawal agreements having deported 458 Britons, including one man who had been in the country since he was 10 years old, and a 65-year-old man married to a Swede with no family or property in the UK.
Sweden has also issued removal orders to a man with dementia who is in 24-hour care and who has been in the country for 25 years.
Under the legally binding treaty, it was agreed governments would communicate the Brexit residency rules, consider late applications on reasonable grounds, and exercise “proportionate” decisions including in the case of vulnerable people.
Smith’s troubles began in 2021 when he started to get ill and applied for sickness benefit. He was told by officials that he should have applied for post-Brexit residency. The couple immediately did so; they recall making the application at the end of 2021, in time for Sweden’s 31 December 2021 deadline.
They waited more than two years to hear back and when they did it was a rejection on the grounds that they were not married and therefore did not have a family connection to merit his residency in Sweden.
They were married in 2023 and had been living together since 2017.
It is not clear if Smith applied for the specific Brexit residency or through the usual immigration route, an important difference and one that may not have been made clear to British protected by the withdrawal agreement. Family connections are not a criteria under free movement rights, which apply to any individual regardless of marital status, so campaigners believe they have a strong case.
Smith said: “We were so much in love, we lived together, we did everything together, even now we hold hands walking down the streets. We wanted to get married, we wanted to do it the right way. I wanted to ask Petra’s father for permission and have him give her away, but two weeks after he gave me permission to marry his daughter, he passed.
“So we were looking into marriage but things just kept happening. But we don’t understand why this matters.”
They also said they had not been given the full court paperwork from the first case appealing against the migration agency’s decision, so they appealed to a higher courtwithout the full arguments against them.
After speaking to a judge this week, Petra has had assurances that all the paperwork will be sent to them by post, but they feel angry that they were not apprised of the information that the migration agency was arguing before the courts.
Sweden’s migration agency has said there is no evidence Sweden has taken an extreme approach to the withdrawal agreement.
The UK Foreign Office has raised concerns about Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement with the European Commission on numerous occasions, but has been told Sweden is not breaching the agreement.
A spokesperson said: “We are in touch with Mr Smith and are providing consular support. We know this is a distressing and challenging time for those concerned and we are urgently raising the situation with both the Swedish authorities and the European Commission.”
The Foreign Office welcomed a statement by Sweden’s former migration minister Johan Forssell in August that Sweden would examine “additional measures” that would address the issue of Brexit deportation, and a similar declaration by Magdalena Andersson, who is on track to form the new government.

‘Drones all night. By morning, you smell the smoke’: life in the last hotel on Ukraine’s frontline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:30 UTC
20:00:30 KST

There is one important rule in the Richelievsky, Kherson’s last functioning hotel: close the curtains before dusk. Less than a kilometre away lies the Dnipro, the river that has formed the frontline since Ukrainian forces liberated Kherson in November 2022; Moscow’s troops are on the opposite bank.
In a city where Russian drone operators hunt civilians in what is now widely known as the “human safari”, even a sliver of light escaping through a window may be enough to reveal someone’s location after dark.
In the lobby, Yevhen Emtsov, the hotel’s manager, sits at a small round table almost buried beneath papers. Outside, explosions punctuate the evening, joined at intervals by the mechanical hum of drones patrolling the streets in the red zone. Inside, residents pass through, pausing with questions and requests at the table that now serves as Emtsov’s office.
In more peaceful times, the Richelievsky accommodated tourists and business travellers attending conferences. The three-star hotel belonged to a different Kherson, one in which the river drew visitors rather than marking a frontline.
But in March 2022, as Russian forces closed in, Emtsov began taking in people fleeing heavily shelled communities along the Dnipro without waiting for the hotel owners’ approval. By the time the city came under occupation, the building had already begun its transformation from a commercial hotel into a refuge.
In the months that followed the invasion, between 200 and 300 people were staying, far beyond its intended maximum capacity of 120. Russian patrols would enter the building, questioning residents and recording their fingerprints. “Imagine you are sitting at home, strangers come in and begin doing whatever they want,” Emtsov says.
Today, the hotel is home to 41 displaced people, with rooms and three meals a day provided free of charge. “People come to us,” Emtsov says. “You can sleep here today, and tomorrow we will see. Nobody sleeps on the street. Nobody.”
It is close to midnight when the power cuts out, leaving the hotel and the city in complete darkness. “Drones and artillery can be heard throughout the night,” Emtsov says. “By morning, you will be able to smell the smoke.”
Hours later, kept awake by the noise of bombing outside, I make my way towards the top of the building, where the seventh floor lies deserted.
From up here, Kherson is almost entirely dark, its streets and buildings barely distinguishable in the blackout. Brief flashes flare among the stars, while explosions and the buzz of drones carry through the night.
When daylight returns, the building shows no sign of stirring. At this hour, the Richelievsky feels like a ghost hotel, mirroring the emptied neighbourhoods of Kherson’s red zone.
The first people to emerge are in the hotel kitchen: Natalia Yastreb and Iryna Rybalchenko reheat fishcakes and stew from the previous evening. Residents drift wearily into the adjoining dining room with their plates, exchanging few words as detonations continue outside.
While some residents have already left for work, Nina and Viktor Tsokurenko begin the day in room 43 with exercises and tea. Since suffering a stroke, Viktor has struggled to speak. “There was a powerful explosion at one o’clock,” Nina says. “After that, I did not sleep again until morning.” Still, she offers coffee and honey; before the war, the couple kept bees.
One floor below, four cats pad around room 37. Tatyana Nesterchuk, one of the hotel’s longest-standing residents, has returned from a shift at a laundry in Kherson’s Dniprovskyi district. The minibus journey to work takes her through some of the city’s most dangerous streets, with an emergency bag always at her side.
“It is like a one-way road,” she says. “You do not know whether you will return. Before setting out, it is as though I am leaving a will behind.”
When warnings of incoming guided aerial bombs reach the hotel, she heads to the shelter with family photographs and other keepsakes packed into her suitcase, which weighs about 10kg. “It is heavy,” she says. “My son tells me to take half of it out. I tell him, ‘I can’t.’”
Nesterchuk has been told that her house has since burned down. Even the fences are gone. “But the land, at least, will remain, I suppose.” She remembers drinking coffee on a small terrace before leaving for work or taking a hoe into the garden to tend fruit and vegetables.
“I always loved the mornings at home,” she says. “The birds were singing. It was quiet and peaceful. There was no buzzing, no humming.”
Another air raid siren cuts across the city. In room 54, Alisia Logvinenko, 11, the only child among the hotel’s residents, answers my knock. She speaks in a breathless rush that makes her difficult to follow. Her mother, Iryna, stands behind her.
The 50-year-old tries to put the war into words a child can understand. “Someone wants to take away our home.”
“To conquer a country,” Alisia adds. “Did I say that correctly?”
“Yes, you did,” her mother says.
When Iryna mentions the few friends they still have in Kherson, Alisia cuts in. “Not mine, hers.”
Most of the children she knew before the war have left Kherson. “I don’t really miss them,” she says, opening her YouTube channel and turning the screen towards me. What makes her happy now, she says, is “lots of likes on my videos”.
Before the invasion, Iryna had planned to take Alisia camping in Ukraine’s nature reserves. The landscape her daughter has learned to navigate instead is governed by a different set of rules.
“Look at the sky. Listen and try to go where there are more trees and walls,” Iryna says. The hotel may offer a measure of shelter, but she has no illusions about its limits. “There is no feeling of safety anywhere.”
Downstairs, Svitlana Salii, Emtsov’s right hand, is behind the reception desk when her phone rings. As she listens, her expression tightens. A Russian FPV drone has struck the van carrying the hotel’s manager and several helpers on their way back from collecting groceries.
Outside, the mechanical hum rises and fades, and I find Emtsov and the others about 15 minutes away, gathered around the white Mercedes. “What can I tell you?” he says. “We heard the buzzing, saw the drone ahead and got out in time to take cover before it crashed into the vehicle.”
The attack is another reminder of what it costs to keep the place running. “As a hotel, we will not be able to operate. But as a hub, we will continue for as long as we have enough strength.”
As conditions in Kherson continue to deteriorate, Emtsov is trying to find a way out of the city for Iryna and Alisia; charities are seeking a place for them in Odesa. For now, mother and daughter remain in room 54, behind curtains drawn before dusk.

‘I spent five years with criminals’: dissident Cuban artist embraces new life in US after prison release
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:30 UTC
20:00:30 KST

When Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara was pushed into the back of a police car on 11 July 2021, during the biggest protests Cuba had seen in nearly three decades, he expected to be in custody for “one, maybe two days”. Instead five years would pass before he was free, and only then after he’d agreed to exile.
“I remember that Sunday,” he says as he opens a beer in El Espacio 23, an art gallery in the Allapattah neighbourhood of Miami. “I was at my girlfriend’s. Friends started writing to tell me there were demonstrations in the streets. It felt like the day we all longed for had arrived – the end of the dictatorship – and I went out into the street.”
He walked for an hour to Old Havana, but was suddenly picked up by Cuba’s revolutionary police. First he was taken to a former seminary in Havana’s suburbs, the much-feared state security interrogation centre of Villa Marista; then, after two days, to Cuba’s maximum security prison, in Guanajay.
There he became the best known of the more than 1,000 political prisoners believed to be incarcerated in Cuba.
He also became the most corrosive to the reputation of Cuba’s government. In contrast to José Daniel Ferrer, the 56-year-old hard-fighting and political former prisoner who was released in October 2025, Otero Alcántara is an artist: unruly certainly, but young, mischievous, mixed race, self-taught and from a poor background.
For many Cubans on the island, the treatment he received encapsulated a sense that the state had come down too hard on young people following 11 July. There’s no doubt that in the run-up to the protests, Otero Alcántara had been troublesome to Cuba’s embattled government. In 2018 he had co-founded the San Isidro collective in a poor part of Old Havana, protesting against a new law, decree 349, that required all artistic endeavours to be pre-approved by the state.
His performance pieces were pointed. He mocked a new $500-a-night hotel that none of his neighbours could afford by asking what had happened to the statue of Julio Antonio Mella, student leader and Marxist, which had previously stood outside. Or he hung out under a balcony in a hard hat after one collapsed, killing three young girls.
These pieces cut through. He believes the authorities would have tolerated such work if he’d agreed to show it in galleries. “I refused, because no one who mattered to me would see it,” he says. “Instead, I tried to speak directly to people on the street, and that wasn’t acceptable.”
The San Isidro collective was cut off by police and surveilled, its occupants harassed. Otero Alcántara says those within drew confidence from each other as the pressure, and the public interest, increased.
“There were so many points of view in San Isidro,” he says now. “There was a babalao [a high priest of Santeria, Cuba’s syncretic religion], a Muslim, a gay person – all the layers that make up a society. San Isidro united them, and from there it generated a ripple effect.”
The reality of prison, he says, was horrific. “The first month I spent with people taken on 11 July. But then they were released, and I spent five years with criminals, often murderers – people who aren’t normal, people who are sadistic, people who are cruel, people who kill women, kill children.
“You come to terms with the fact that you’re in an extremely violent place, and begin to understand the different ways. That normalisation is where confinement is the worst. I think it’s one of the worst experiences a human being can have.”
Told he would never be free to walk the streets of Cuba, he accepted exile in the US, and arrived in Miami on 18 July in good physical shape, having disappeared for the week after his prison term ended. It turned out he had been taken to a beachside state security safe house, where he was allowed to see family and drink Chinese whiskey with his guards.
Once in the US, he appeared in Washington to receive the 2026 Democracy Award from the National Endowment for Democracy, an institution that’s a bugaboo for supporters of the Cuban government. More bizarrely, former president George W Bush, who has also taken up art, painted his portrait for a forthcoming book about political prisoners and dissidents.
His exit from Cuba did not play well with sections of the exile community in Miami, some of whom accused him of having sold out. “Who drinks beer and toasts with their captors right before being exiled? This looks like a staged performance by G2 (Cuban state intelligence),” said Alexander Otaola, a popular Cuban American commentator.
“There was a lot of pre-judgment,” says Michael Bustamante, chair of Cuban and Cuban American studies at the University of Miami.
Otero Alcántara only added to the fire during a round of interviews with exile media. During one, with the 87-year-old former political prisoner Ángel de Fana, he said that, no longer living in Cuba, he would miss the “taste of a woman on the island” (“la sabrosura”).
The remark caused laughter among some in Havana, but less so in Miami. “His form of speaking is very off the cuff,” says Bustamante. “It’s very Cuban-everyman, and relatable, but for guardians of certain traditions it’s seen as a departure. And it’s hard not to see a subtext about race.”
Otero Alcántara blames the criticism on the prevalence of social media, something that has exploded in the five years he was in prison. “There’s this phenomenon where a lot of influencers are actually making a living off likes, and views, so they get caught up in an algorithm that keeps the conversation going, without even assuming any civic responsibility toward Cuba.”
He does, however, agree he received better treatment than some others, that the authorities were in some ways frightened of him. “There were moments when, especially when state security wanted to get me out, they eased up a bit, because I went on more than six hunger strikes in prison, and they knew they could cause me to have a mental breakdown, so they started to give in.”
“I could come here and say, ‘Oh, in prison they beat me senseless, they broke my head,’ but that wouldn’t be honest,” he adds. “I can’t give a speech for the cameras just to keep influencers happy.”
On the floor of EL Espacio 23 is a pile of paintings he made in jail, which he was allowed to bring with him (another black mark in some eyes). A triptych shows the bars of the jail with various things in front: a tree or a cross. “It’s about what you think about in jail,” he says.
The gallery, which belongs to the Cuban American billionaire and Democrat Jorge M Pérez, is something of a sanctuary: it offers month-long residencies to young artists from around the world so he is among friends.
Meanwhile, back in Cuba, the authorities have a new problem on their hands. Anna Sofía Benítez, 21, better known as Anna Bensi, was sentenced last week along with her mother to two years of “restriction of liberty”, which means having to report regularly to police and inform them of any travel plans.
An enthusiastic Christian, Benítez had been using social media to rail against the Cuban government and the collapsing conditions in Cuba. She was charged with “acts against personal and family privacy” after filming a police officer serving her a summons, and this subsequent sentence means she could be jailed for any further infraction. The sentence has been heavily criticised by religious leaders, and on Wednesday Mike Hammer, the US chargé d’affaires in Havana, visited the family, further stirring up the situation.
Young Cubans are watching her closely, as they still are Otero Alcántara. He said he wants to move to New York, where he can slot into an artistic crowd outside the Miami exile bubble – perhaps a smart move given the issues facing young Cubans in Florida, many of whom are now actively hiding from ICE.
In the US today it’s hard to see how he won’t get himself into further trouble. He says he would have been a Cuban revolutionary if he’d been born 50 years earlier. “But I’m almost certain I would have gone to prison when the revolution triumphed. Like many who realised the revolution had become a dictatorship, I would have rebelled against it.”
Given Cuba’s turbulent history, has there been any period where he wouldn’t have ended up in prison? “In the future,” he says.
