‘Is this too little, too late?’: Cornell students on school’s response to gang-rape allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:30 UTC
20:00:30 KST

In the wake of a lawsuit over an alleged gang-rape that took place at Cornell University in 2024, the school announced this week that it would be suspending parties and social gatherings at fraternity houses for the remainder of the academic year.
Last month, a former student, referred to in court documents by the pseudonym “Jane Doe”, filed a civil lawsuit against multiple parties, including the university, accusing seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity of sexually assaulting her at a party at their fraternity house on campus in October 2024. All of the men named in the lawsuit have denied wrongdoing, and none have been criminally charged.
In a letter to the Cornell community, the school’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, said that the ban on frat parties will be “provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue”.
The Guardian spoke with several undergraduate students at Cornell about the university’s decision, as well as their handling of the alleged assault and its aftermath. The measure, which Kotlikoff referred to as an effort to “strengthen campus safety”, was announced on 13 October in a letter to the Cornell community. While some students welcome the ban on frat parties, others argue that the move is an attempt by the administration to avoid a perception of culpability in the case.
When asked for comment, Cornell referred the Guardian to Kotlikoff’s letter to the community from 13 October, in which he said: “I have spent the past weeks listening to students, faculty, staff, parents, alumni, and trustees, who have shared their feelings of deep connection and sympathy with Jane Doe, anger and frustration that this could happen at Cornell, and outrage at the broader prevalence of sexual violence against women in our society. These conversations, and campus protests, have underscored my deep conviction that we must do better: that the time for meaningful and lasting change at Cornell, and at campuses across the country, is now.”
A sophomore at Cornell’s school of industrial and labor relations, who asked to remain anonymous, supports the school’s latest decision. She acknowledged that Greek life “wasn’t something that really added to my experience at Cornell” and that the ban was “so necessary in light of Jane Doe’s experience”.
The student added that while she is not in Greek life herself, many of her friends are. “I think it’s been upsetting for people that are super involved in Greek life,” she said, noting that some members of Greek life feel that they’re being penalized for the actions of others. They “think that [the ban is] somewhat unnecessary because this happened two years ago, and it’s a completely different group of people”.
“I have many friends that have opposing viewpoints,” she said.
Some students argued that the opposition is the point, and believe that the administration’s decision was intended to further a divide between the student body.
“The fact that [the administration] thinks a one-year moratorium will solve this is, I wouldn’t say it’s misguided. I would say it is purposefully manipulative to the student body,” said Jack Huber, a sophomore at the school of industrial and labor relations and member of Students for a Democratic Cornell (SDC), an independent, student-run organization that advocates for free speech on campus. “I believe it’s a very intentional choice, because what it’s done is create a sentiment that many students are angry, and are blaming protesters for their inability to party.
“Cornell is not ready to commit itself to institutional change, and is using this moratorium to essentially scapegoat fraternities when this is a campus-wide issue,” he added. Huber added that issues of sexual assault will remain until the school has implemented an independent judicial system, which was previously in effect from 1969 to 2020.
Huber said that school’s current judiciary process operates as “a tool to be used to sweep incidences of sexual violence under the rug because they harm Cornell’s reputation, and persecute protesters because they harm the board of trustees’ investments”.
“That’s the system that allowed essays to get written by two of the [Cornell 7]” he said.
SDC is demanding that the administration rewrite a portion of its student code of conduct to require independent hearings and minimum sanctions for sexual assault.
Darius Pierce, a sophomore at Cornell’s college of architecture, art and planning, remembered hearing about the incident, which had resulted in Chi Phi being disbarred and removed from campus during his first few weeks of college in 2025.
“I was walking past the Chi Phi house, heading back to campus, and a person in my group pointed out [the house] and I asked why I’ve never heard of them, and they explained that there was an issue with ketamine and assault at that house, and that was it,” he said.
“No one ever expanded upon that. I hadn’t heard anything about it until the story broke with the Cornell Sun.”
Like Huber, Pierce believes that the administration’s decision to ban frat parties is an attempt to “cover up for their own faults and own mistakes”.
“They’re trying to make it seem like they’re actually responding to [the alleged assault] and taking action instead of addressing the real issue,” he said.
Following the alleged assault, Cornell issued a statement in November 2024 informing the community that there would be an internal investigation while the Cornell University Police Department continued their criminal investigation. Per Jane Doe’s lawsuit, Cornell University Police did not end up pursuing criminal charges. The investigation was reopened in September 2026 in response to public outrage. None of the defendants in the civil lawsuit have been charged and all have denied wrongdoing.
Pierce, who rushed a fraternity but decided not to join one, also spoke of the endemic culture of drinking and substance use he has witnessed within Greek life at Cornell. He recalled an experience at a fraternity party where “this group of girls kept screaming that it was their first time doing coke at that frat party, and that these frat guys were just handing out lines of coke like candy”.
“If you go to a frat, you plan on drinking,” Pierce said. “But it seems like for women specifically who go to these frats, they’re kind of pressured to do more.”
The Guardian previously reported on how Jane Doe’s lawsuit has reignited debates over Greek life and the relationship between fraternity parties, drinking culture and sexual assault. A 2019 survey from the Association of American Universities revealed that a quarter of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual conduct, with fraternities being the setting where it was most likely to occur.
At Cornell, 35% of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact since arriving at school, according to a 2025 survey conducted by the university.
Saya Taylor, a sophomore who is also a member of SDC, believes that the frat ban is a “Band-Aid” solution to a much deeper problem. “They’re trying to give the appearance that they are changing when they are not,” she said. “Cornell University does not want this to [have] a lasting impact.”
In addition to the fraternity ban, Kotlikoff also announced that the university would be adding a case manager to Cornell’s office of civil rights to help those who report sexual misconduct at the school navigate the processes. He also pledged that Cornell would work with the New York state police and allow their trauma-informed criminal investigators, who are independent of Cornell, to investigate allegations.
The sophomore believes that this week’s announcement is a step in the right direction. “For the vast majority, people like me, we want justice and we want the administration to change the structural way that they address sexual assault,” she said.
But others need more convincing.
“Is this too little, too late? The answer there is a resounding yes,” said Huber. “Jane Doe never got the justice she deserved in the moment.”

How the quirky puffin became a symbol of the climate crisis – and hope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:29 UTC
20:00:29 KST

For centuries human beings have exploited puffins, harvesting them by the thousand on their breeding grounds for their food and feathers. Over time, though, this relationship has changed, so that today we have come to love them, celebrating their quirky character and comical appearance and giving them a central place in our affections – a journey described by the environmental historian Dr Rob Lambert as the shift “from use to delight”.
How ironic, then, that just as we have come to truly appreciate them, our own existence now threatens theirs. The climate crisis threatens almost all the world’s roughly 11,000 species of birds, but its consequences have particularly dire significance for seabirds, whose life cycle is so intimately connected to the timing and abundance of their food supplies.
Warming oceans result in fish such as sand eels shifting their range into cooler waters, and thus either declining or disappearing from the seas around seabird breeding colonies. If puffins need to travel further to their feeding areas, or take longer to find and catch food once they get there, then their chicks have a lower chance of fledging.
Even if they do, they are less likely to survive the following winter. Our changing climate has already led to an increase in the frequency and severity of extreme weather events such as autumn and winter storms, which leads to a higher mortality of birds outside the breeding season.
It is often forgotten that the climate crisis is not the only negative factor affecting these birds’ lives. As we have seen, increased marine pollution, especially from oil and plastic, along with less severe yet still serious issues such as disturbance and predation, are already reducing the puffin’s breeding success at many once-thriving colonies.
The dire prediction that nine out of 10 puffins could disappear before the middle of this century is hopefully pessimistic, yet we do know that serious declines are already occurring.
In early 2026, BBC News reported that following that winter’s severe storms hundreds of dead and dying puffins, guillemots and razorbills had been washed up on beaches in Cornwall, Scotland and north-east England. Conservation organisations have also reported more than 20,000 stranded birds, mostly puffins, along the Atlantic coasts of France, Spain and Portugal.
Samuel Wrobel, the RSPB’s senior marine officer, noted that this was the worst wreck for over a decade, since the catastrophic events of winter 2013-14, and warned that “after the impact of avian flu this is the last thing our seabirds need”. Moreover, as most birds are likely to have died at sea, so will never be found, the true death toll is likely to be much higher.
Peter Harrison has spent his life watching, painting and studying seabirds, and has a special affection for the puffin. I asked him what he thought about the species’ future, and he began by confirming the many threats the birds face, including a reduction in their prey due to the climate crisis, threats to nest sites and the resulting lower breeding success.
Rather to my surprise, however, Harrison feels some optimism for the puffin’s future, pointing to that famous legal victory that stopped industrial sand eel fishing in the waters around England and Scotland. He is also enthusiastic about the use of technology to track the movements and survival of all seabirds, including the puffin, since this began in the 1980s.
“Prior to that time, there was a huge void in our knowledge of what puffins and other seabirds did in their non-breeding period,” he says. “They simply went to sea, only to reappear again in their breeding areas the following season. Rapid technological advances over the last four decades have greatly increased our understanding of their movements, revealing details of seabird distribution and behaviour at sea, including important foraging areas.”
And as he points out, this knowledge does not just benefit the puffin. “Auks – including puffins – fulfil a role as important canaries in the cage, indicators of global health and sustainability. If auks are doing well, the oceans will be doing well,” Harrison says.
The one thing we have on our side, Harrison believes, is that, unlike landbirds which often only live for a few years, even small seabirds can live for several decades. As he notes, although they might have gone through bad times, seabirds have in the past shown that they can make a rapid comeback, especially if we are able to rid their breeding islands of invasive predators.
Scientists have a crucial role to play, too. In 2004 BirdLife International developed the BirdLife Seabird Tracking Database (STDB) to collate tracking data using a range of different, and rapidly improving, technologies that can track the presence and movements of seabirds when they are away from their breeding colonies, as they are for most of their lives.
The records enabled them to identify six previously unrecognised oceanic routes used by the birds on their journeys: the Atlantic Ocean, North Indian Ocean, East Ocean, West Pacific Ocean, Pacific Ocean, and the Southern Ocean Flyways. The data obtained is also used for seabird research and conservation by BirdLife scientists and their collaborators throughout the world.
As Dr Stephen Kress, the scientist who has devoted his life to successfully bringing back puffins to the US, points out: “Seabirds were once abundant along the coastlines of North America and throughout the world, but the declines we’re seeing in their populations are directly related to things humans are doing – they would be fine if we weren’t tampering with their world and messing things up.
“And so I feel that we have an ethical responsibility as stewards of the Earth to do something where we can. That’s why we’ve developed these restoration techniques. If we hadn’t done that, we wouldn’t be documenting puffin recovery, we’d be documenting extinction.”
Yet perhaps we can maintain at least a small fragment of hope for the future not just of the puffin, but of all the world’s seabirds. They may be outside our day-to-day experience for much of our – and their – lives, yet the huge affection for the puffin, held by millions of people around the world, must surely count for something.
- This is an edited extract from The Puffin by Stephen Moss published by Vintage at £14.99. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Key player in false Talarico rumor has history of online posts invoking Nazi Germany

An influencer who played a key role in hoax claims that James Talarico was in a mental health facility has a long history of social media posts that favorably invoke Nazi Germany, express antisemitism and anti-Black racism, criticize miscegenation and call for “remigration” of refugees.
On X, the Lake Oswego, Oregon, resident Ryan Amacher, known online as Rhein Amacher, has described Muslims as “sub-human”, claimed that Black Africans are “monkeys” with low IQ, characterized immigrants as “vermin” and expressed support for the far right, including Germany’s AfD and the UK’s Tommy Robinson.
His attempt to damage Talarico’s campaign with false claims about a supposed inpatient admission to an Ohio facility fell apart quickly on Sunday night, but not before his claims were boosted by a staffer on the campaign of Talarico’s Republican rival, Ken Paxton. Since working for the Trump campaign in 2024, he has remained in the milieu of Republican politics and rightwing influencers.
Neither Amacher nor the Paxton campaign responded to requests for comment.
Last week, Amacher phoned the Lindner Center of Hope, a psychiatric hospital in Mason, Ohio, three times, trying to confirm a false rumor that Talarico had been admitted there. The rumor apparently began with a 9 October post by an anonymous X account, TickleTexts, which claimed Talarico had been “hospitalized at Lindner Center for HOPE”, and was picked up by the Republican fundraiser Caroline Wren, who falsely tied it to a private flight between Ohio and Austin. Before calling, Amacher had posted as fact that Talarico “was hospitalized at the @LindnerCtrHope” and tagged the hospital asking it to confirm.
In the full recording of the second call, he gives his name as “Tim”, says he wants to send a care package to his cousin, and offers a four-digit patient code. “I simply made one up (2244) in an attempt to bypass the facility’s security restrictions to discuss the patient,” he later wrote on X. For most of the six-minute call the employee tells him she has no record of Talarico. In its final seconds she says a man that looks like Talarico “was just discharged this evening”.
An excerpt of the recording was incorporated into a 47-second clip that Nick Sortor posted on Sunday afternoon under the headline “Ohio mental hospital CONFIRMS James Talarico was discharged from the facility earlier this week”. Amacher posted his own version minutes later, and Elon Musk replied with a characteristic “!!”. Amacher had first offered the recording to Blaze Media and the Daily Mail, which reportedly declined to run it, and said in an X Space that evening that influencers are “not held to the same journalistic standards”. By Tuesday he had reportedly pulled out of an interview with the writer and podcaster Jesse Singal, saying his attorney had given him a “stand down order”.
The purported legal advice coincides with coverage of the fiasco, which has included speculation that Amacher’s attempt to access private health information may land him in legal trouble.
Previous coverage, however, has not probed Amacher’s long history of extremist commentary.
‘Modern Freikorps volunteers are needed’
Amacher often invokes Nazi Germany, and the paramilitary movement that preceded it, with apparent admiration.
“In 1919, Germany’s defeated soldiers came home only to be stabbed in the back by socialists and communists who wanted to burn the nation down and install a Soviet-style dictatorship,” he wrote on 29 July, over an AI-generated image of German soldiers beneath Soviet flags beside uniformed men under crescent moons at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate. In a follow-up post he wrote: “Modern Freikorps volunteers are needed to step up to purge the German nation of the filth destroying it from within.” An AI-generated image accompanying it showed a masked soldier wearing “Freikorps” and “Deutsches Reich” patches, with the black, white and red flag of imperial Germany flying over the Reichstag.
The Freikorps were paramilitary units of demobilized soldiers that crushed leftwing uprisings in Germany after the first world war. In January 1919, Freikorps troops murdered the communist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht. In June, Amacher told critics to “read up on the German Freikorps after 1919–and what became of Luxemburg and Liebknecht”.
“History has a way of repeating itself when revolutionary movements collide with a nation pushed to the brink,” he added. The Freikorps are widely seen as an ideological ancestor of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi party, though he later turned against them.
In July, replying to a post that said “we fought the wrong enemy in WW2, just like General Patton said before the jews assassinated him in 1945”, Amacher wrote: “We should have immediately re-armed the German Wehrmacht and auxiliary troops and joined forces to defeat Soviet communism, once and for all!”
Patton died in December 1945 after a car crash in occupied Germany; conspiratorial claims that he was assassinated have long been debunked.
When fellow influencer Cam Higby complained in February that saying Nick Shirley was not a Nazi had led others to call him one, Amacher replied that “a colleague’s great-grandfather served as a paramilitary adjunct in Germany’s ‘other’ military force (not the Wehrmacht)”. He went on: “By your logic, does that make him a Nazi? Asking for a friend…” and attaching an “OK” emoji.
He has captioned a photo of a figure skater with her right arm raised “Heil yes!” and offered to recruit a man “straight into my elite Panzer division”. Panzer divisions were armored tank units in Nazi Germany’s army. In July 2025 he joked that his ancestors “fled to Argentina as well, but way back in 1945, departing from the Deutsches Reich”.
He has also called for the return of the late Spanish dictator Francisco Franco, writing: “Bring back Francisco Franco!” in July under a post claiming that “African military-aged males by the THOUSANDS” were entering the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. And he has praised Germany’s AfD, which the country’s domestic intelligence agency labeled a “confirmed rightwing extremist” force last year. “The @AfD is the ONLY party left that will actually SAVE Germany from destruction,” he wrote in April. “We will restore traditional German societal norms, identity, and culture.”
‘He looks like a Jew’
In January, replying to a post attacking the San Francisco Democrat Scott Wiener, Amacher wrote: “He looks like a Jew–I’m guessing he is a Jew!,” and included a nose emoji.
In May 2025, after another user wrote of a man that “He’s also jewish, no surprise there”, Amacher replied: “A ginger Jew? Worst of both worlds…” Under a December post blaming Somali Muslims in Minnesota for “the largest theft of tax payer dollars in American History”, he wrote: “Both peoples are despicable, but the Somalis are ahead of the Jews by far!”
He has told a pro-Israel account that it was “a hollowed-out puppet dancing on Zionist strings” whose loyalty was “to a parasitic regime halfway across the world”, and written that “Zionist infiltrators have sunk their claws deep into U.S. policy”.
Another recurring subject is George Soros, the Jewish financier who is a frequent target of antisemitic conspiracy theories. Amacher has called him “a spawn of the Devil himself”, and in February 2025 wrote that Soros “allegedly turned in his own people during WWII just to save his own skin”, a claim factcheckers have repeatedly debunked.
‘Monkeys typically have an estimated IQ below 70’
In June, TickleTexts, the anonymous account that started the Talarico rumor, baselessly claimed, “as a born South African”, that “some villages believe r*ping a 6 month old baby girl will cure their AIDS”. Amacher replied: “Monkeys typically have an estimated IQ below 70.”
Replying in January to a post about a Somali asylum seeker who, it claimed, had raped a 10-year-old girl in Denmark, he wrote: “Seriously, f*ck international obligations! These people are sub-human animals meant for zoos for viewing purposes only!” In February, he wrote that a dog said to have led police in Louisville, Kentucky, to a missing three-year-old had “demonstrated an intelligence far superior to that of any illegal Somali invader!”
In June, he credited Nick Shirley, whose videos about Somali-run daycare centers in Minnesota set off a national panic, with exposing a “mastermind” who, Amacher wrote, had “funded the savage, low-IQ black Tusken Raiders fleecing Minnesota taxpayers”. In January, under a post about Trump’s claim that fraud in Minnesota could reach $80bn, he proposed “one-way, remigration flights back to Somalia as starters!”
‘Future super predators in the making’
In June 2025, after another user told the Hodgetwins, a pair of Black conservative YouTubers, that they were “NO longer welcome”, Amacher wrote: “I’m waiting for their response of, ‘hey sorry, blame it on my negro brain!’”
On 7 October he replied to a comment about “the white girl in the front” of an image: “Getting strong mudshark vibes with that one.” “Mudshark” is a racist slur for a white woman who partners with Black men.
Last November, under a post about “a mob of black ‘kids’” accused of attacking a pregnant woman in Chicago, he wrote: “F*cking savages and future super predators in the making!” In May, replying to a post about a weekend of shootings in Chicago, he wrote: “You can’t override biology or selectively breed out the ‘predator’ gene in certain populations.”
In June, under a post claiming that “the biggest scandal in American history” was “convincing millions of people that Michelle Obama is beautiful”, Amacher wrote: “Hey now–‘BIG Mike’ ain’t playing around! No monkey business here…” The reference to “Big Mike” probably comes from a baseless conspiracy theory that Michelle Obama is a man.
That month, Karmelo Anthony was convicted of murder in Texas for the 2025 stabbing of a fellow student, 17-year-old Austin Metcalf. Replying to a video of a crowd of Anthony’s supporters, most of them Black, outside the trial, Amacher wrote: “I hope none of these animals breed.”
‘Remigration is the ONLY answer’
Since November 2025, Amacher has used the word “remigration” in more than 30 posts. The term, promoted by Europe’s far right, describes the mass deportation of migrants; plans discussed at a meeting in Potsdam attended by AfD members included people with German citizenship. Last month Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, accused the AfD of pursuing an “ethnic cleansing” policy.
“The word for 2026 is remigration!” Amacher posted in January. Asked by another user in November 2025 what should happen to Muslims in America, he replied: “Remigration to native homelands for those with insufficient loyalties.” In April he shared an AfD video with the comment: “Remigration is the ONLY answer–great video by the @AfD!”
In June, under a post complaining about the Muslim call to prayer in Dearborn, Michigan, he wrote: “These sub-humans must be forcibly extracted from America and shipped off in crates back to the Middle East.”
He has also cheered Jake Lang, a pardoned January 6 rioter who has led anti-Muslim protests. Replying last November to a post about clashes between Muslim residents and Christian protesters in Dearborn, where rightwing influencers have staged anti-Islam rallies, Amacher wrote: “Jake is the general leading our generation’s Crusade to save our nation’s cultural identity and heritage. Brave, fearsome, and ready to drive out the foreign invaders!” When Lang led a protest in Plano, Texas, in December “against the Islamic takeover of America”, Amacher tagged him in a post calling him “the leader for the next Crusades!” On 21 December he wrote that he had texted Lang to confirm he was “not Jewish”. Earlier this month, he posted: “We need another Crusades–except on our own home turf!”
Two national guard members were shot in Washington DC last November, and an Afghan man, Rahmanullah Lakanwal, was arrested as the suspect. That evening Amacher wrote that the attacker “should be publicly executed in Lafayette Square using bacon grease, with the entire nation watching”. He added: “This will send a clear message to third world invaders that we will not tolerate their presence!”
Other posts urge that migrants be shot, or rounded up by ordinary citizens. Under a June 2025 post by the British far-right activist Tommy Robinson about a defaced statue of Joan of Arc in Paris, he wrote: “These invaders don’t deserve deportation–better yet, shoot them and save the cost!” This June he wrote that “those uncivilized savages can leave Britain on their own–or be removed at gunpoint by a mob of furious native Britons”.
Replying in April to Nick Sortor’s post that “hard choices are going to have to be made soon”, he wrote that if the federal government would not deport “these third-world invaders, then we, the American people, will have no choice but to hunt them down ourselves, round them up like the illegal trash they are, and throw their asses back across the border where they belong!”
“Bounty hunters get paid to track down bail jumpers and hand them over,” he wrote in July. “We should be able to do the exact same thing with illegal immigrants–hunt them down, turn them in to @ICEgov, and get rewarded.”
Public records show Amacher has used two first names. Oregon business filings list Ryan David Amacher, at a house in Lake Oswego, as the registered agent of Amacher & Company LLC, formed in 2012. In 2018, a letter from “Ryan Amacher” calling for the repeal of US immigration law drew a rebuttal in the Lake Oswego Review. By 2024 he was signing himself Rhein: federal campaign finance records list “Rhein Amacher”, at the same address, as the company’s president, and his columns in the Review now carry that name. Last year a Portland police dispatcher logged a call from “RYAN AMACHER” at the city’s ICE facility, while officers ran a records check on “Rhein David” Amacher. The Daily Mail has reported that his “real name is Ryan”.
Until now, Amacher has been a lower-tier player in a rightwing influencer economy whose currency includes live streams of contentious events, tendentious coverage of perceived political foes, and disinformation campaigns.
Even now, his social media following is relatively modest. His biggest platform is X, where his follower count (about 35,000) is dwarfed by those of similar rightwing creators such as Nick Shirley (1.8m), Nick Sortor (1.6m) and Katie Daviscourt (512,000).
His first brushes with broader notoriety came during anti-ICE protests in his native Portland, Oregon, last year, when his antagonism toward protesters extended to the self-confessed theft of leaf blowers and other items from an abandoned protest camp.

Family Matters: The Secret History Behind Why Vincent van Gogh Cut Off His Ear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

After riding a series of escalators to the fifth floor of New York’s Museum of Modern Art, I stepped into a gallery where, on display, were a dozen paintings and lithographs by late-nineteenth and early twentieth-century artists, including Pablo Picasso, Paul Cézanne, and Georges Seurat.
But most visitors were gathered around one explosively colorful painting in swirling shades of light and dark blue, bottle green, and pale gold.
Instantly recognizable.
One of the most famous paintings in the world.
The Starry Night by Vincent van Gogh.
These were the early days of my research about a little-known woman who is key to shedding light on three inevitable questions when it comes to Vincent van Gogh. Why did he cut off his ear? Why did he commit suicide? And how, after dying in obscurity, did he eventually become regarded as one of the world’s greatest artists?
Gauging Van Gogh
Watching and talking to people as they engaged with this particular masterpiece seemed an apropos way to gauge the interest of Van Gogh lovers.
I, for one, could remember, as a child, first seeing The Starry Night reprinted in one of my parents’ art history books. It was my modern art “aha” moment. No one was standing over my shoulder telling me to pay it special attention, but I was mesmerized. The painting became imprinted on my young imagination, and I never forgot it.
As I observed the gallery, I quickly learned my reaction is hardly unique.
A man from Southern California named Paul Duelo was laughing. “I know this painting, and I don’t know anything about art,” he said with a chuckle, nodding at the crowd standing around The Starry Night. “Look at everyone!”
A woman from Seattle stood gazing quietly with her arms folded. Sheri Larison first saw a picture of The Starry Night more than 30 years ago in her high school art class. A reproduction of the iconic painting hung in her office. This was her very first time seeing the original.
“It’s overwhelming,” Larison whispered, with tears in her eyes. “It evokes something. It’s magical.”
She was interested in the painting’s origin story. “His mental health was declining,” she said, and that was true, although perhaps also misleading.
Van Gogh painted The Starry Night in June of 1889 during a year he spent in a mental asylum in the south of France.
It does not represent an actual place but a compilation of elements—a village, starry sky, moon, dark hills, and a cypress tree—all things that Vincent had seen at one time and brought together in this composition. The sight of stars, he said, always made him dream.
Hanging just to the left of The Starry Night was a Paul Gauguin’s painting, The Moon and the Earth. The juxtaposition provoked a curious thought. Gauguin and Van Gogh lived and worked together in Vincent’s yellow house in Arles in the south of France for several weeks. What would the hot-tempered, competitive Gauguin have thought seeing so many people gathered around Vincent’s painting at this moment while his was comparatively ignored? And what would Vincent have made of all the attention given to The Starry Night?
It is generally believed that it was an argument with Gauguin, who was threatening to quit Arles (in effect abandoning Van Gogh), which spun the mentally unstable Vincent into such a state of despair and frustration that he mutilated himself by slicing off his left ear.
The fine art of family matters
But, as I was learning, family matters also very likely played a part in the most notorious instance of self-harm in art history.
It’s a tragic story of dependence and the limits of love. And it’s where Jo van Gogh-Bonger comes in. Biographical details about her—revealed in her diaries and letters—have only recently been made public by the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam. They paint a picture of a determined woman to whom the world of art owes a tremendous debt.
Jo was married to Vincent’s younger brother, Theo, who was an art dealer in Paris and Vincent’s only source of income. Theo supported Vincent with a monthly allowance, and in exchange Vincent gave Theo his paintings to try to market and sell. The financial arrangement, as it would in most families, put an emotional strain on both brothers. Theo was not rich, and Vincent constantly complained about being broke, with not even enough money for food, and often practically begged his brother for more money.
Over the course of 10 years, Vincent created more than 800 paintings and 700 drawings, desperately hoping for financial independence and commercial success. But in Vincent’s lifetime, Theo is known to have sold just one painting: Red Vineyard at Arles.
In July of 1890, believing himself a failure as an artist and a man, Vincent shot himself in the chest. He was only 37.
Six months after Vincent’s suicide, Theo died from the ravages of syphilis, leaving Jo a young widow with a baby to support, not much money, and an unusual inheritance—Vincent’s paintings—more than 400 in total.
They filled the walls of their Paris apartment, were stored in closets, under beds, and at a nearby art supply store. The Potato Eaters, Irises, Sunflowers, self-portraits, and The Starry Night. Celebrated as masterpieces today, at the time they were regarded as the unpolished works of a depressed, crazy man and commercially worthless. Jo thought differently. She had no formal art training, but she loved his work and her instincts told her that Vincent was (as Theo had come to believe) a genius.
Jo also inherited hundreds of letters that Vincent wrote and received, most exchanged with Theo. Jo read and re-read those letters, initially to feel closer to Theo, but she was also captivated by Vincent’s compassion and intelligence. She decided the world should read them too. It was part of her plan: to organize exhibitions, lobby critics, and publicize the letters, which showed how vulnerable and anguished Vincent was, yes, but also how deliberate he was in his craft and how close Vincent and Theo were to each other. Eventually, in 1914, Jo succeeded in publishing Vincent’s letters in an ambitious three-volume book, which today is considered one of the most revealing and important works of art history.
An infamous ear
As much as she would play a vital role in propelling him to fame, Jo was also someone who unwittingly played a part in Vincent’s self-destructive descent, something she at times admitted feeling guilt about after his death. Jo understood Vincent was lonely and that he became more isolated after she married his brother.
That infamous act of self-mutilation, when Vincent cut off his ear, happened the very day Vincent likely received the surprising news that Theo and Jo were engaged, triggering what some Van Gogh experts, including Martin Bailey, suspect were unquenchable fears that Theo might eventually abandon him.
And Vincent shot himself just days after a stressful visit with Jo and Theo in Paris. Theo was thinking about quitting his job to start his own business, which meant, for a time, no income. The couple (who by now had a baby son they named after Vincent) hoped to rent a better apartment on a lower floor. But budgets were tight, arguments ensued, and Vincent eventually rushed out of the apartment, unable to shake the thought that he was a burden that Theo would or could no longer bear.
Jo didn’t seek to put herself at the center of this story, but she is there, nonetheless. A surprisingly relatable woman (at times insecure, at times doggedly persistent), she courageously stood up to the male-dominated art world as a champion for Vincent and spent 30 years of her life promoting his work and life story in Holland, Germany, France, England, and even, for a time, in America.
Interestingly, of all the paintings Jo inherited, no one—not Jo or Theo or Vincent—considered The Starry Night one of Vincent’s best. Vincent didn’t even sign it. Research recently published by the Van Gogh Museum points out that Vincent signed only about 16% of his paintings, hypothesizing he did so usually when he was completely satisfied or wanted to make them a gift to friends or family. In the brothers’ correspondence, The Starry Night was referred to rather than named. Theo called it simply “the village in the moonlight,” critically writing to Vincent that “I feel that the search for style takes away the real sentiment of things.”
Vincent conceded the painting lacked character and considered it a mistake that “…once again I’m allowing myself to do stars too big…new setback, and I’ve had enough of that.”
Jo also didn’t seem to consider The Starry Night as especially important. She sold it early on but reacquired it briefly in time for a major exhibition she organized in Amsterdam in 1905. It was painting number 199, called De Sterren (The Stars), and it changed hands two more times before MoMA acquired it in 1941. By then, it had been rechristened The Starry Night. The name stuck.
There is a world of personal stories behind the paintings of Vincent van Gogh, and they reaffirm an old adage: we can’t separate the art from the artist. I believe Jo would agree.
Paul Duelo, the man from California I met while admiring MoMA’s The Starry Night, lit up when I told him about Jo van Gogh-Bonger.
He had never heard of her before.
But he wanted to know more.

Slovak PM says Slovakia and Hungary will not fund EU aid for Ukraine in 2027

Source: European Pravda, citing Denník N

Ukraine’s grain trap: where to put the 2026 harvest and what prolonged export restrictions could lead to
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:59:00 EEST
19:59:00 KST

Ukraine’s grain trap: where to put the 2026 harvest and what prolonged export restrictions could lead to
Kyiv • UNN
Russian attacks and logistics problems have reduced grain exports from Ukraine. Surpluses could lower farmers’ incomes and the 2027 harvest.
Ukraine is harvesting a decent grain crop, but selling it is becoming increasingly difficult due to Russian strikes on ports, railways, and other logistics routes. There is currently a high probability that the grain may remain in storage instead of generating funds for farmers for the next sowing campaign.
The farms most at risk are those without their own storage facilities and forced to sell their produce to intermediaries at reduced prices. What could be the scale of grain accumulation, and what consequences could this have for the 2027 harvest? The CEO of the Ukrainian Agrarian Confederation (UAC), Pavlo Koval, explained to UNN.
The 2026 grain harvest — how much Ukraine has already collected and what volumes need to be exported
As of October 13, Ukrainian farmers had harvested 37.14 million tonnes of grain and leguminous crops, covering 65.2% of the planned area. According to Pavlo Koval's estimate, by October 15, up to 38 million tonnes had been collected from the fields. Separately, according to the Ministry of Agrarian Policy, about 13.9 million tonnes of oilseed crops had been harvested, including sunflower, rapeseed, and soybeans. It should be noted here that the previous state forecast projected a grain harvest of approximately 60.4 million tonnes.
Pavlo Koval explains that the discrepancy arose because of corn: its gross harvest may reach 30–31 million tonnes, but by mid-October only about 3.5 million tonnes had been harvested. Therefore, the final figures summarizing this year's grain harvest will emerge once farmers harvest this crop. And this is precisely where major problems begin.
"Due to the rain and high grain moisture, part of the harvest may remain in the fields until winter. Drying requires additional funds, which not every farm can afford," the expert warned.
Speaking about the wheat harvest, the UAC CEO estimated it at 26.2 million tonnes, of which approximately 12 million tonnes are planned for export. (For corn, the benchmark is 22 million tonnes of exports out of an expected production volume of 30 million tonnes.) However, these volumes represent export potential, because it is not enough to sell grain abroad — it must also be physically delivered to the buyer.
Maritime exports under threat — how much Ukrainian grain could remain in the country due to supply restrictions
According to the State Customs Service, as of October 16, since the beginning of the 2026/27 marketing year, Ukraine had exported 5.929 million tonnes of grain and leguminous crops. This is 24.9% less than during the corresponding period of the previous season.
Koval calculates that current shipments amount to approximately half of the required pace, given the size of the harvest. According to him, additional wheat stocks of 5–6 million tonnes could accumulate by the end of the season. If significant logistics restrictions persist during the period of mass corn deliveries, the risk of grain accumulation will increase sharply.
"The Danube route is of particular concern. In 2022, it made it possible to transport up to 2.5 million tonnes of cargo per month and partially offset restrictions on the operation of major seaports. Now it is being affected by strikes on terminals, infrastructure problems, and shipping disruptions. In the area of the Sulina Canal alone (the middle of the three major straits of the Danube Delta and the main navigable channel at the mouth of the Danube in Romania — ed.), about 150 grain vessels have accumulated," the expert said.
Rail crossings with the EU and road routes also cannot fully replace maritime transport: their capacity is limited, and transportation is more expensive. As a result, even when buyers are available, farmers cannot always ship their produce on time.
This season, Ukraine reduced wheat exports but increased corn exports12.08.26, 17:03 • 17890 views
Will Ukraine have sufficient storage capacity for the harvest, and what will happen to the surplus?
As of the end of 2025, Ukraine’s total grain storage capacity was estimated at 52.67 million tonnes of simultaneous storage. However, it is important to understand that some storage facilities are already occupied, some are located far from producers, and grain transportation and elevator services cost money. Therefore, under the most difficult scenario, according to a source speaking to UNN, if the current pace of exports and corn accumulation is maintained, carryover stocks could reach 30–35 million tonnes. As a result, the grain may have to wait for sale, while keeping it throughout this period will require the farmer to have storage space and financing.
"Having grain in the storage facility does not yet guarantee money in the account," Pavlo Koval emphasized.
According to him, small and medium-sized farms often have only three options:
-  pay for storage at an elevator;  
-  sell directly from the field at an unfavorable price;  
-  leave the produce in their own unsuitable facilities. 
Each of them entails its own costs and risks.
Additionally, excess supply within the country will put pressure on purchase prices. Even if grain becomes more expensive on the global market, Ukrainian producers will not necessarily benefit, as higher logistics costs and transportation risks may absorb the difference.
Export restrictions and farmers’ losses — how the grain crisis will affect sown areas and grain production in 2027
Ukrainian farmers have already felt the consequences of the current difficulties during the autumn sowing campaign. In an exclusive comment to UNN , Pavlo Koval said that by mid-October, approximately 3.5 million hectares of winter wheat had been sown. If the area reaches 4 million hectares by the end of the campaign, he will consider that an acceptable result. The situation is worse with winter barley: according to the expert’s estimate, about 280,000 hectares have been sown, compared with approximately 500,000 hectares planned.
"Amid difficulties selling grain, producers may cut spending on fertilizers, crop protection products and technological operations, which will affect next year’s yields. Some farms will also revise their crop structure in favor of crops that have higher margins and require less logistics capacity," the UAC director general forecast.
Among such options, he named rapeseed and sunflower. However, according to him, changing the "cropping map" will not solve the problem of the destruction of export routes.
The situation is quite difficult. I do not want to say that it is catastrophic, but it is quite challenging
He emphasized that the most vulnerable remain small producers without their own transport or financial reserves. For them, a delay in selling grain may result in lower profits and the risk of being unable to finance the next sowing campaign. Therefore, if export restrictions continue, the Ukrainian economy could suffer a double blow: lower foreign-currency revenues now and weaker grain-production potential in 2027.
How Russian attacks threaten Ukraine’s exports and whether alternative routes exist
Russian attacks on Black Sea ports threaten to cause grain accumulation and losses for farmers. Whether there is an alternative to maritime exports and what will happen if restrictions persist was explained in an exclusive comment to UNN by TEUS logistics company owner and director Dmytro Kazanin.
According to the expert’s estimate, Ukraine needs to export about 5 million tonnes of grain per month to avoid accumulating excess stocks.
"When it is necessary to ship about five million tonnes per month, we are shipping approximately two and a half million," Kazanin said.
Instead, he estimates current shipment volumes at only 2.5 million tonnes: the shortfall amounts to nearly half of the requirement.
Overall statistics also point to a slowdown in exports. According to the State Customs Service, as of October 16, since the beginning of the 2026/27 marketing year, Ukraine had exported 5.929 million tonnes of grain and pulses, 24.9% less than during the corresponding period of the previous season. The reason is that, due to higher transportation costs, farmers are forced to choose between selling at a loss and storing their crops.
Alternative export routes—can railways, road transport, and Danube ports replace the Black Sea ports?
At present, grain exports through the western borders, by rail, by truck, and via the Danube remain possible. But there is an important caveat: according to Kazanin's assessment, the combined capacity of these routes is insufficient to compensate for what Ukraine is losing because of the downtime at the Black Sea ports, which are constantly being attacked by the Russian armed forces.
"This cannot be compensated for. Our ports are designed (specifically—the editor) for this kind of work. All the border crossings and the Danube ports together cannot compensate for it," the logistics expert explained.
On the railway route that can be used to export grain, congestion is emerging, according to Kazanin. At crossings with EU countries, there are not enough European railcars to transfer grain from Ukrainian rolling stock. In addition, specific transshipment rules in the EU further complicate movement.
There are also problems with transporting agricultural cargo along the Danube.
"Danube shipping is being constrained by low water levels. Look, a barge with a capacity of 2,000 tonnes can load only about 1,000 tonnes in shallow sections in order to travel along the route to the Romanian port of Constanța. The movement of vessels from the Upper Danube to the Lower Danube is also limited," Dmytro Kazanin explained.
He clarified that some routes are nevertheless operating and cited his own company's experience as an example. Kazanin noted that in September, TEUS sent 72 containers of wheat to Indonesia via Gdańsk. At the same time, he immediately emphasized that this would not replace bulk shipments and would not significantly affect the global logistics problems that domestic farmers have faced this year.
More expensive logistics and loss of competitiveness—how Russian attacks are affecting the cost of Ukrainian grain exports
According to Kazanin's assessment, logistics costs have increased three- to fourfold recently. Since Ukrainian producers do not determine global grain prices, the additional costs of delivering it effectively reduce the amount that the farmer ultimately receives for their work.
Our farmer is losing income. Today, they have to sell grain at a loss because logistics costs have increased three- to fourfold
As an example, he cited a grain production cost of $150–160 per tonne, while sales revenue for a farm may amount to $120–125. If the situation does not change going forward, Dmytro Kazanin assumes that grain exports may become even more unprofitable. Moreover, Ukraine will feel the consequences of this as early as the next sowing season.
Due to a lack of funds, farmers are cutting back on fertilizer purchases. This could reduce yields in 2027, as well as export revenues and budget income. And because of unprofitable prices, some of the corn may remain in the fields over the winter altogether
The threat of grain accumulation—is it relevant for Ukraine, and why?
In response to questions from UNN journalists, Dmytro Kazanin explained that if the gap between the harvested crop and its exports—2.5 million tonnes per month—persists, it will mathematically amount to about 5 million tonnes after two months and 7.5 million tonnes after three. At the same time, the expert cautioned against equating delayed exports with the physical loss of grain. He emphasized that, for now, the issue is primarily the inability to deliver the necessary volumes to buyers on time.
"This is not about loss, but about the possibility of exporting it (the grain — Ed.). At present, there is no possibility of exporting the amount that is needed," he emphasized.
According to Kazanin, problems with exporting the harvest arise for Ukrainian farmers simultaneously in all directions: there is a shortage of railcars and railway capacity, transshipment at the border slows things down, while the Danube is constrained by shallow waters. Therefore, no single alternative route will save exports.
The available corridors need to be used simultaneously, along with the stable operation of Black Sea ports. Because prolonged restrictions could also affect next year's harvest
As a reminder
Russia is increasingly targeting Ukrainian grain export corridors in the Black Sea, increasing security risks for the entire region. Romania and Bulgaria are already asking NATO to strengthen protection against drones from the Russian Armed Forces.

Pro-Palestinian politician threatens Berlin left's election victory over Israel stance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:56:15 UTC
19:56:15 KST

Until a month ago, no one outside Germany's internal left-wing politics had heard of  Vanessa Emde. This week, she became a central figure in German and Berlin politics, with her positions threatening to deny her party, Die Linke (The Left), which won the Berlin elections in late September, the opportunity to form a government. Moreover, the controversy Emde sparked this week threatens to tear Die Linke apart from within, triggering a genuine struggle over the party's fundamental identity. At the heart of the dispute, unsurprisingly, is its attitude toward Israel.
After Die Linke won more than a quarter of the vote in Berlin, it was clear that forming a coalition under its leadership would require negotiations with the Greens and Social Democrats (SPD), its two natural partners in establishing a left-wing government.
However, before agreeing even to enter talks with Die Linke, the leaders of both parties demanded clarification and unequivocal commitments on two main issues: that the party distance itself from any ties to criminal clans in Berlin and, above all, that it commit to combating antisemitism, protecting Jewish lives, acknowledging the October 7 massacre, opposing Hamas and unequivocally recognizing Israel's right to exist.
Die Linke found itself in a trap. Signing such agreements would run counter to a central principle held by its voters, particularly younger voters and immigrant communities. But refusing the conditions would reinforce the public perception that it was an antisemitic party. Without the Greens and SPD, it had no chance of forming a coalition. Die Linke's representatives in Berlin signed the memorandum of understanding on the issue, and the parties agreed to begin talks.
But the agreement began to unravel almost immediately afterward, when Die Linke decided to admit Vanessa Emde to its parliamentary group. Although she had been directly elected in the Neukölln district with nearly 50% of the vote, the SPD and Greens had demanded that she not be admitted to the group. For them, she was a red line.
Emde, a queer feminist activist, rode a wave of political success largely on the strength of her explicitly anti-Israel platform. She belongs to a group called Palestine Solidarity Working Group (AG Palästina-Solidarität), whose members have previously claimed that "the Palestinian struggle will end when Tel Aviv is in Palestinian hands." On election night, she proudly posed for a photograph with Ibrahim Ibrahim, a prominent supporter of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) in Germany who is active in the United Palestinian National Committee, which also includes Hamas supporters.
She is best remembered for a statement she made in May, when she said she "does not believe in the right of states to exist, only in the right of human beings to exist." Although the statement did not refer directly to Israel, its context was clear. She supports a one-state solution and explained her friendly photograph with Ibrahim by saying she rejects the authority of Germany's domestic intelligence agency to determine who may establish political ties in the country.
Within Die Linke, the Berlin branch is considered the most radical, particularly regarding policy toward Israel. Within the Berlin branch, Neukölln, a district with a large Muslim immigrant population, is regarded as the most radical of all. Die Linke cannot afford to lose its support, either electorally or because of the work local activists do to bring voters to the polls.
Now, the local branch and its voters have demanded that the party not give in. Calls have grown louder to preserve the party's policies and the positions that brought it electoral victory at all costs, particularly on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, even if that means remaining in opposition.
The grassroots pressure worked. On Thursday, Emde posted a three-minute video on her Instagram account in which she repudiated her signature on the memorandum of understanding with the other two parties and reaffirmed all her previous statements, including her rejection of the right of states to exist.
"The fact that I, as an individual, am being used as a bargaining chip in the talks is, to put it mildly, a democratic scandal that must be investigated," she wrote in the accompanying post.
According to Emde, "The starting point for this madness: A few months ago, I published a video in which I paraphrased a self-evident principle of international law: 'States do not have a right to exist — people have a right to exist.'
"I also said: 'The demand for a democratic one-state solution with equal rights for all people, regardless of their ethnic origin or religion, is a legitimate political demand and must not be criminalized.'"
The SPD and Greens announced the cancellation of coalition talks, saying they suspected Die Linke was conducting two parallel sets of negotiations and signing separate memorandums of understanding: one in coalition negotiations with them and the other in internal party negotiations, with each agreement undermining the other.
Die Linke's leaders have now announced that the parliamentary group distances itself from Emde's remarks and disavows her political positions. Discussions about her future in the group are scheduled to begin Tuesday, with Emde in attendance.
The Palestinian issue and the war in Gaza have dominated Berlin's streets for the three years since October 7 and were an important factor in the city's election campaign. Now, they threaten both the stability of a potential local coalition and the unity of the radical left-wing party, confronting it with a fateful question: Does Die Linke have an identity without its distinctly anti-Israel stance?
It remains to be seen whether the party's argument that its position constitutes criticism of Israeli policy rather than antisemitism will be accepted, and whether it can preserve its unity and its chances of governing without abandoning that position.

Gilad Schalit’s release, 15 years later: Why Israel must remember joy of his homecoming - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:51:26 UTC
19:51:26 KST

Last Sunday, October 11, an important anniversary passed almost unnoticed.
On June 25, 2006, a 19-year-old Israeli soldier was abducted during a Hamas attack near the Gaza border. For the next five years, his name became part of the daily consciousness of Jews worldwide.
We saw his photograph everywhere. We watched the demonstrations. We followed every rumor of negotiations, every hopeful report and every subsequent disappointment.
We prayed for him in our synagogues, attended rallies, and signed petitions. His name became familiar to people who had never met him and probably never would.
I was living in Britain at the time, and I remember vividly how deeply his captivity affected Jewish communities far beyond Israel’s borders.
Gilad Schalit was not simply another soldier. He was somebody’s son, somebody’s brother, a young man who should have been enjoying the ordinary experiences of early adulthood.
Instead, he was being held in isolation, deprived of his freedom, and separated from everyone he loved.
For five long years, we prayed and hoped he would somehow return.
And then, suddenly, the extraordinary news came.
There was an agreement. He was coming home.
On October 11, 2011, 15 years ago, Israel announced that an agreement had finally been reached to secure Gilad’s release after more than five years of hell on earth. One week later, on October 18, he came home.
It was a moment of almost indescribable national joy. And perhaps, amid everything that has happened since, we should pause to remember it.
Of course, the Schalit prisoner exchange has been analyzed, criticized, and debated endlessly.
Much has been written about the price Israel paid, the prisoners who were released, the precedent it established, and the possible consequences for the horrific events of October 7, 2023. These are serious questions, and history has made some of them even more painful.
I do not dismiss the argument. But that is not what I want to write about today.
I want to remember something simpler, something profoundly human. I want to remember how it felt when we heard that Gilad was coming home.
I remember the overwhelming relief, happiness, excitement, and, above all, gratitude. After years in which hope had repeatedly been raised and dashed, something truly wonderful was happening.
For a brief moment, it seemed that an entire nation could share in one family’s happiness. The joy was almost overwhelming; we wanted to laugh out loud and greet perfect strangers with a grin and a hug.
When Gilad finally appeared on our television screens on October 18, thin, pale, and visibly affected by his ordeal, the emotion was extraordinary.
Here was the young man whose photograph we had studied for years. Here he was, alive. Here he was, back on Israeli soil.
And then came the images of him reunited with his family.
How could anyone watch without being moved?
We had never met him, yet somehow we felt we knew him. His parents’ relief became our relief. Their happiness became our happiness. The prayers of five years seemed to find their answer in that single embrace.
Of course, even then there were families for whom the release of convicted terrorists brought renewed anguish rather than celebration. Their pain was real and deserves recognition.
Remembering the joy of Gilad’s return does not require us to dismiss their suffering or ignore the difficult decisions involved, far from it.
But surely we can acknowledge that, whatever our views about the agreement, the return of a young man from captivity was itself something worth celebrating. And there are two people whose extraordinary contribution should never be forgotten.
A place for gratitude
Noam and Aviva Schalit, Gilad’s parents, refused to allow their son to disappear from public consciousness.
For five years, they campaigned tirelessly. They attended meetings, confronted politicians, spoke to journalists, and kept their son’s photograph before the eyes of the nation.
Noam, in particular, became the public face of a family’s determination never to give up. He was not a professional campaigner or a politician. He was a father who wanted his son back.
What could be more human about that simple truth?
In 2022, Noam died after a battle with cancer. He was only 68. But he lived to see his son return, embrace him again, and, in 2021, accompany him to his wedding.
What a blessing that was. What a reward for years of anguish and perseverance.
And what of Gilad himself?
Thankfully, after the extraordinary public attention surrounding his captivity and release, he has largely chosen, and achieved, a quieter life.
He married Nitzan Shabbat and has worked as a sports journalist, pursuing an interest that existed long before his abduction.
In many ways, that is perhaps the most heartening part of his story.
We sometimes imagine that the happy ending to a dramatic story must itself be dramatic. But perhaps the greatest victory for someone who has endured years of captivity is the ability to live an ordinary life.
To go to work. To enjoy sport. To spend time with family and friends. To marry, laugh, make plans, and wake up each morning without fear of what the day might bring.
Most of us take these things for granted. For somebody who has had them forcibly taken away, they must assume an entirely different significance.
We cannot know everything that Gilad has experienced since his release, nor should we presume to understand the lasting effects of his captivity. He deserves his privacy and the freedom to build his life away from the public gaze.
But it brings great joy to know that the young man whose face once appeared on countless posters has been able to move forward with his life.
The events of October 7 brought the terrible reality of hostage-taking back into our lives on a scale that none of us could have imagined.
Once again, we became familiar with photographs, names, families, and campaigns. Once again, prayers for the return of captives became part of our daily existence.
And once again, we were reminded how precious a single human life can be.
We live in an age of relentless argument. Every event is immediately subjected to political analysis. Every decision is judged, often with considerable bitterness, and every moment of happiness seems destined to be overshadowed by the next crisis.
There is a place for criticism, accountability, and historical reflection. But there must also be a place for gratitude.
Not every memory needs to become an argument. Not every anniversary needs to reopen a political battle.
Sometimes we should allow ourselves simply to remember that something good happened.
Fifteen years ago, after 1,941 days in captivity, a young Israeli soldier returned to his family. A mother embraced her son. A father saw the culmination of five years of tireless effort. And millions of people, in Israel and across the Jewish world, shared a moment of extraordinary happiness.
Whatever happened afterward should not erase that moment.
As we approach the anniversary of Gilad’s homecoming on Sunday, let us remember the tears of joy, the relief, and the gratitude.
Let us remember Noam and Aviva and the extraordinary love that sustained their campaign.
And let us wish Gilad many more years of peace, happiness, and the ordinary pleasures of a life lived in freedom.
The world has enough darkness. Sometimes we need to remind ourselves that there is light, too.
And do you know what? Fifteen years later, it is still worth stopping to say thank you.
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman

The rise in nationalist violence, just one week into the olive harvest season, has prompted plans for a security assessment in the coming days.
Security officials concerned continued violence could further inflame tensions across West Bank
With another month of the olive harvest remaining, security officials worry continued violence could further inflame tensions across the West Bank.
"The IDF is deployed in locations where the olive harvest has been coordinated in order to prevent friction," the security official said. "At the same time, there has been an increase in warnings of terrorist attacks. Dozens of warnings come in every week."
"Just this week, a cell of four terrorists who were planning to carry out an attack was arrested in the Jenin area," he added. "On the other hand, those same forces also need to protect the olive harvest."
The official also criticized rabbis who encourage the violence surrounding the olive harvest, arguing that their support contributes to the continued attacks.
"This should not happen. There are various reasons for nationalist crime, but it is also because they receive backing," the official said.

Automatic extensions of deferments from mobilization have begun in Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Automatic extensions of deferments for 22 categories of citizens will continue until October 30. The result will appear in Reserve+ after the registers are checked.
Automatic extensions of mobilization deferments have begun in Ukraine. This may affect more than 90% of current deferments. The Ministry of Defense of Ukraine reported this on October 17, UNN reports.
Details
"Automatic extensions of mobilization deferments have begun. More than 90% of current deferments may be extended automatically—without repeat applications or visits to government institutions. The grounds for extending deferments are being verified according to uniform rules based on data from state registers. After that, users will be able to see in Reserve+ whether the deferment has been extended and for what period," the ministry said in a post.
According to the available information, automatic extensions will continue until October 30. Deferments will be updated gradually, so notifications will not arrive for everyone at the same time.Automatic extension is available for 22 categories of citizens. For this, the grounds for the deferment must remain valid and be confirmed by data from state registers.
How can you find out the result?
"You will receive a notification in Reserve+ in any case—both if the deferment is extended automatically and if it is not. If you have not received a notification yet, wait for the verification result. After the extension is successfully completed, update your electronic military registration document and check the new validity period," the post says.
The ministry also said that the absence of an automatic extension of a deferment does not necessarily mean that a person has lost the right to a deferment.
"This does not necessarily mean that the right to a deferment has been lost. The reason may be missing or outdated data in state registers. Check the data and update it if necessary. After that, you can submit a new request through Reserve+ if your category is available for online processing, or visit a CNAP with the relevant documents. The current deferment remains valid until its expiration date," the post says.
Reminder
The Office of the Military Ombudsman prepared legislative proposals that provide for stricter requirements for obtaining a mobilization deferment for parents of children with disabilities, husbands and wives, and other relatives of people with disabilities.

Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:46:41 BST
19:46:41 KST

Rare pink diamond goes on display in France 100 years after amateur heist
- Published
A rare pink diamond is going on display in France for the first time since it was stolen almost 100 years ago to the day - the last time it was shown to the public.
The nine-carat, pear-shaped gemstone known as the "Grand Condé" was pilfered in an overnight raid on the Château de Chantilly in October 1926 and concealed in a hollowed-out apple.
The diamond - one of few royal jewels to survive the French Revolution - was recovered a few weeks later when a hungry maid at the hotel in which the thieves were staying took a bite of the apple.
It will once again be on display in the Condé Museum at the Château de Chantilly until 3 January.
The museum's director Mathieu Deldicque said that while the apple story may sounds far-fetched, it was widely covered by newspapers at the time.
Deldicque has faced questions about whether the exhibition may be tempting fate, especially given the string of heists on European cultural institutions in the past 12 months, including the daring daylight robbery of jewellery from the Louvre museum in Paris.
While he declined to reveal to CNN how much the diamond was insured for, he noted that extensive academic study into the properties of the diamond had taken place to make it uniquely identifiable.
The results of this analysis, as well as previously unseen archive material about the gem's history and theft, form part of the exhibition, according to the museum.
Naturally occurring pink diamonds are exceptionally rare and often sell for tens of millions of dollars. The highest price ever fetched for one at auction was $71.2m (£53.6m) in 2017, according to Sotheby's.
The exact origins of the Grand Condé remain a mystery.
It was first mentioned in 1740 in an inventory of Louis Henri de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, drawn up following his death, the Château de Chantilly said.
It then became part of the collection of Queen Marie-Amélie of Bourbon-Sicily, the wife of French King Louis Philippe I, and then her son, Prince Henri of Orléans, the Duke of Aumale.
He bequeathed it to the Institut de France, which now owns the Château de Chantilly, 50km (31 miles) north of Paris, along with thousands of artworks and manuscripts which became the Musée Condé collection.

Yerevan Declaration urges faster action to halt biodiversity loss
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:42:39 CST
19:42:39 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- The Yerevan Declaration was adopted at a biodiversity leaders' summit in the Armenian capital on Friday, calling for stronger international cooperation and accelerated efforts to halt and reverse biodiversity loss.
Held ahead of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), the summit brought together heads of state and government, alongside representatives of international organizations, local communities and other stakeholders.
Armenian Environment Minister and COP17 President-designate Hambardzum Matevosyan presented the declaration, entitled "Taking Action for Nature," as the summit's outcome document.
The declaration reaffirmed commitments to the Convention on Biological Diversity and to the effective implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, with its mission of halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030 and its vision of living in harmony with nature by 2050.
While welcoming growing global mobilization for biodiversity, it said the first global report on the framework's implementation showed that collective efforts and progress remained insufficient and that accelerated implementation was urgently needed.
In the declaration, leaders committed to strengthening national implementation through whole-of-government and whole-of-society approaches, in accordance with national circumstances, priorities and capabilities. They also committed to integrating biodiversity considerations into public policies and economic sectors and strengthening the conservation, restoration, management and sustainable use of terrestrial, freshwater, coastal and marine ecosystems.
The declaration also set out commitments to strengthen monitoring, planning, reporting and review, improve biodiversity data and knowledge systems, and promote science-based decision-making and the responsible use of innovative technology.
On financing, it stressed the need to mobilize increased public and private funding for biodiversity from all sources, ensuring that funding is adequate, predictable, timely and accessible. It also emphasized capacity-building, scientific and technical cooperation, access to and transfer of technology, and innovation, alongside stronger international partnerships to support implementation in developing countries, particularly the least developed and small-island developing ones.
It looked ahead to the first global review of collective progress in implementing the framework as an important milestone for strengthening transparency, accountability and collective learning, addressing implementation gaps, promoting effective solutions and accelerating action.
The declaration also called for an effective, results-oriented outcome in Yerevan, with a clear pathway toward accelerated implementation of the framework and achievement of its targets. ■

A major wave of Ukrainian strike drones targeted the Moscow region and multiple regions early Saturday morning, Oct. 17, forcing civil aviation authorities to shut down airspace across the Russian capital and divert international flights to alternative hubs.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin reported that Russian air defense units intercepted 75 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) heading toward the metropolitan capital. Sobyanin stated that municipal emergency services and defense specialists deployed to the sites of falling debris, without specifying the intended targets of the drone strikes.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The aerial incursions prompted Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsiya, to enact emergency ground stops and flight restrictions across Moscow’s primary airport cluster shortly before midnight.
Among the disrupted commercial flights was a Pegasus Airlines flight transiting from Antalya, Turkey, to Moscow. Passengers reported departing Turkey at 7:35 p.m., only to be informed prior to descent that the airspace above Moscow had been sealed.
The airliner diverted to Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg, landing at approximately 1:00 a.m. local time, where passengers were instructed to remain on board until Moscow airspace reopened.
Similar flight restrictions and ground delays were instituted across regional air hubs in western Russia as air raid warnings sounded.
Ministry claims 610 drones intercepted across 15 regions
According to an operational bulletin issued by the Russian Ministry of Defense, Russian air defenses intercepted and destroyed 610 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones across the country between Friday evening and Saturday morning.

The ministry claimed the overnight wave engaged targets across a broad geographical footprint spanning 15 administrative regions alongside occupied territories.
Regions targeted included the Moscow region, Leningrad, Novgorod, Tver, Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Oryol, Kaluga, Voronezh, Rostov, Smolensk, and Tula regions, as well as the Krasnodar region, the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug in western Siberia, and occupied Crimea.
Compounding disruptions to Russian civil aviation
The Saturday morning aviation shutdown marks the third time in ten days that drone alerts paralyzed Moscow’s airspace.
Overnight into Friday, Oct. 16, Moscow’s four primary airports – Vnukovo, Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky – suspended all inbound and outbound flights, forcing more than 20 commercial airliners to divert to alternate airports and causing over 200 flight cancellations before restrictions were lifted around 5:45 a.m. local time.
That disruption followed an earlier overnight shutdown on Oct. 13–14, during which more than 500 flights were delayed or canceled across the capital’s hubs.
Civil aviation data released by Rosaviatsiya head Dmitry Yadrov indicates that recurring airspace closures and drone threats have contracted commercial passenger traffic, with Russian carriers transporting 39.5 million passengers between May and August – a 7 percent decline compared to 42.6 million passengers carried during the corresponding period in 2025.
Ukrainian officials have stated that interdiction operations do not target civilian aircraft, but aim to constrain military transport and highlight the risks of utilizing Russian sovereign airspace during wartime.
In September, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned international air carriers and insurers of escalating hazards across Russian skies, stating that active airfields and logistics nodes supporting Moscow’s war effort remain valid operational targets.
