Poland moves to allow more municipalities to charge tourist fee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:37:35 UTC
19:37:35 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Many more municipalities in Poland will be allowed to charge a daily fee for tourists and other overnight visitors after a change to the law dropping environmental requirements for levying such charges.
Kraków, which received 8.7 million overnight tourists last year, had in particular been pushing for the change. However, Poland as a whole has seen a recent boom in visitor numbers, recording the EU’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights in tourist accommodation last year.
#Krakow #opłataturystyczna #ustawa 🚨🔥Z OSTATNIEJ CHWILI! 🔥🚨
📢 Prezydent RP podpisał nowelizację przepisów dotyczących podatków i opłat lokalnych, PIT oraz PCC.
🏨 Najważniejsze zmiany dla branży turystycznej dotyczą opłaty miejscowej i uzdrowiskowej.
🗓️ Od 2027 r. za jej… pic.twitter.com/9ATvENvNol
— Kraków (@krakow_pl) October 15, 2026
Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts.
Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue.
Now, under new legislation proposed by the government earlier this year and signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki this week, the requirement for beneficial climatic features has been scrapped, meaning many more places will be able to charge the visitor’s fee.
From 1 January, municipalities with scenic qualities will be able to charge visitors up to 5 zloty (€1.14) for each night they stay in hotels, guesthouses and short-term rental accommodation for up to one month, a rise on the current maximum of 3.46 zloty.
Additionally, whereas previously only people visiting for the purposes of tourism had to pay, the fee now applies to all visits, including for work or health purposes, reports broadcaster TVN. People with significant disabilities, children with certified disabilities and their carers will be exempt from the fee.
In another change, fees will be collected directly by accommodation providers, who will be required to maintain detailed records, reports the Infor news service. Passing fees on in a timely manner will entitle providers to receive at least 10% of the money they collect.
Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026
In 2024, Kraków appealed to the government to be allowed to charge tourists a fee, noting that “overtourism leads to tensions and social discontent”, as the “local community suffers” and “residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”.
With its UNESCO-listed Old Town, Wawel royal castle, and former Jewish district of Kazimierz, Kraków is regularly named as one of Europe’s best tourist destinations. Last year, a record 16.25 million people visited the city, of whom 8.7 million stayed overnight.
While that is a boon to the local economy, it also often causes tensions with residents, who complain about noise and disruption. In 2024, the city created the new position of “night mayor”, whose role is to reconcile the needs of tourists, businesses and residents.
Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb.
Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026
Following this week’s change to the law, Kraków city hall confirmed that it would now again be able to collect a visitor’s fee “if the statutory conditions are satisfied and the municipal council adopts an appropriate resolution”.
The city’s recently elected new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, who will be sworn in next week, said before Sunday’s election that he was in favour of a tourist tax of at least 20 zloty per night, four times the new maximum.
“In western European cities there are rates of that size and higher,” Gibała said, quoted by financial news service Money.pl. “Maintaining the city in the face of the influx of tourists is costly. In Kraków, private business owners profit from tourism, whilst the city and its residents foot the bill.”
Poland as a whole has also experienced a boom in tourism. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%).

Protest calling for Kyiv Mayor Klitschko's resignation under way outside Kyiv City State Administration

A protest calling for the resignation of Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko is under way outside Kyiv City State Administration building in the centre of the capital.
According to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, several hundred participants had gathered outside the administration building at 36 Khreshchatyk Street as of 12:20. The rally began with speeches by activists and organisers.
The protesters are holding cardboard signs reading "Klitschko, resign," "Glass bus stops won't protect us from missiles and drones," "It's Time," "Mayor or Looter," "Kyiv Isn't Ready Even for Autumn," "Klitschko, It's Time for You to Go," "Who to Call When the Mayor Steals Money," "Schrödinger's Mayor – Klitschko exists separately from his powers," "Russia strikes, and you just add to it," and others.
The protesters are also chanting "Resign!"
Passing cars occasionally honk in support of the protesters.
At the same time, a small number of participants supporting the current mayor and opposing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are also present outside Kyiv City State Administration building. They are holding signs reading "Klitschko – Our Mayor" and "Hands Off Klitschko." Police asked them to move away from the main protest, but they refused.
Seven police minibuses and five patrol cars are parked near Kyiv City State Administration building. More than three dozen officers from the National Police, Patrol Police and Dialogue Police are present at the rally site, while others remain in patrol vehicles.
In addition, representatives of the OZON civil society organisation and the Red Cross Society are monitoring the protest.
"Klitschko has had the authority and resources for all 12 years. He must bear political responsibility and step down from office," a statement issued by the rally organisers the previous day said.
In particular, the statement points to what the protesters describe as systemic, long-standing problems in city governance, including the city's lack of preparedness for the challenges of war, such as insufficient mobile and stationary shelters, a lack of alternative water, heating and sewage systems, and failures to address the consequences of destruction and assist those affected. It also cites allegations of corruption involving the mayor's team, favouring developers' interests, the lack of decisions to protect valuable historic buildings, deterioration of the public transport system, disregard for petitions and public opinion among city residents, and other problems.
The organisers said populist strategies were being developed without any intention of implementing them, decisions were being postponed for years and responsibility was constantly being shifted. They said the division of powers between the city authorities and district administrations could not serve as an excuse for the lack of results.
According to the protest organisers, the mayor could resign voluntarily, lose office as a result of a court ruling or an election, transfer his powers to a military administration, or leave office as a result of voluntary mobilisation.
The organisers' demands were signed, among others, by the All-Ukrainian Association Automaidan, the Green Teremky Initiative, the Legal Platform Kyiv Ecological and Cultural Center NGO, the March for Kyiv Association, the Passengers of Kyiv NGO, the Right to the City NGO, the Repair Together NGO, the Seven-Tiered Mountain Youth Center, the Kyiv Heritage NGO and the Spalah! NGO.
Ahead of the event, the UDAR Vitali Klitschko faction in Kyiv City Council, citing the security situation, called on Kyiv residents to refrain from mass gatherings on Saturday, October 17.
The faction said those calling on people to gather for protests should consider who would bear responsibility if a Russian attack occurred during the gathering and people were harmed. It said destabilising the situation in the capital, which Russia was attacking and seeking to deprive of electricity, heat and water, would only benefit the enemy. It added that responsibility, unity and joint efforts were needed to ensure Kyiv's resilience.
In response, the rally organisers published instructions on what participants should do in the event of an air raid alert.
The organisers said people with access to a map showing enemy aerial targets would be present at the rally and would be able to provide additional warnings about potential threats to the city centre. In the event of a threat, the rally would be suspended and participants would be asked to take shelter. They identified the TSUM shopping centre car park, Khreshchatyk and Teatralna metro stations, as well as nearby underground passages if there was little time, as the nearest shelters.
As previously reported, Vitali Klitschko, who was serving as Kyiv mayor at the time, won the first round of the October 2020 local election with 50.9% of the vote. Klitschko was first elected mayor of the capital in a special election in May 2014.
Under the Law of Ukraine On Local Self-Government, a mayor's powers may be terminated early in the event of a personal resignation; loss of Ukrainian citizenship; a conviction becoming final; a final court ruling holding the mayor liable for a corruption-related offence or declaring assets to be of unjustified origin; recall through a popular initiative; a court ruling declaring the mayor legally incapacitated, missing or presumed dead; or the mayor's death.
The mayor's powers may also be terminated early if the mayor violates the Constitution or laws of Ukraine or the rights and freedoms of citizens, or fails to exercise the powers granted to the office, based on a local referendum or a decision by the relevant council adopted by secret ballot with at least two-thirds of council members voting in favour. Early termination is also possible in cases provided for by the laws of Ukraine On Military-Civilian Administrations and On the Legal Regime of Martial Law.

Iran women’s wheelchair basketball suffer loss against Thailand
TEHRAN - Iran’s women’s wheelchair basketball team suffered a 64–33 defeat to Thailand in their second Group Stage match at the fifth edition of the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games on Saturday.
Despite showing improved performance in the second quarter, Iran were unable to overcome Thailand, who maintained control throughout the contest to secure a convincing victory.
Thailand made a strong start, taking the opening quarter 16–6. Iran responded with a more competitive display in the second quarter but still fell 16–13, leaving Thailand with a 32–19 lead at half-time.
The third quarter saw the two sides compete more evenly in the opening stages, but Thailand gradually pulled away, winning the period 15–7 to extend their advantage.
Thailand then closed out the game strongly, taking the final quarter 17–7 to seal a 64–33 victory.
The result marked Iran’s second consecutive defeat in the group stage. The Iranian side had opened their campaign with a 65–20 loss to hosts Japan in their first match.
Iran will look to bounce back when they face Cambodia on Monday in their next group-stage fixture, aiming to deliver a stronger performance and secure a better result.

The G7 countries plan to allocate €260 million for the restoration of the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant’s New Safe Confinement

Gallery: Central Estonia's upgraded Mäo junction reopens to traffic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:35:00 UTC
19:35:00 KST

Gallery: Central Estonia's upgraded Mäo junction reopens to traffic
Mäo's upgraded highway junction has reopened with five bus stops, two roundabouts and a 30-space parking lot, improving long-distance bus connections in Central Estonia.
A Lux Express bus made the symbolic first stop at Mäo on Friday, marking the completion of construction and the launch of bus service at the junction.
"By Monday morning, ten Lux Express routes en route to Tallinn and another ten en route to Tartu will be stopping here," said Urmas Kupp, executive director of the Järva County Public Transport Center (JÜTK).
Other bus operators are also interested and could begin stopping there as early as November 2.
One key amenity, however, is still missing. Despite assurances at the opening that the upgraded junction is safer and ready to accommodate long-distance buses, passengers have no proper public bathroom at Mäo, with only a temporary portable toilet installed next to one of the bus shelters.
The Transport Administration says building a passenger terminal is not its responsibility.
"Our job is to maintain and develop national roads," said Transport Administration director general Priit Sauk, adding that it's up to public transport centers and local governments to build stops and passenger terminals.
JÜTK plans to sell an unused terminal and use the proceeds to build a new one at Mäo, which would also solve the bathroom problem. Infrastructure Minister Kuldar Leis (Reform) said the project should be a joint effort with the state.
"I think the most logical approach for projects like this is for the state and local governments to work together," Leis said.
Next stretch of Tallinn–Tartu Highway roadwork begins
Friday also marked the start of reconstruction on an eight-kilometer stretch of Tallinn–Tartu Highway between Käsukonna and Imavere. The work, expected to take about two years, includes a multilevel interchange at Imavere that will connect traffic from Viljandi to the highway.
Sauk said another 15 to 16 kilometers between Mäo and Käsukonna also need rebuilding.
"It's included in our road maintenance plan and long-term plans," he noted. "If the next funding period allows, we'd like to get started on it within the next couple of years."

Germany news: Merz faces conservative youth wing in Bonn

- The increasingly unpopular leader's approval ratings have been in free fall of late

- In the northern state of Schleswig-Holstein, police expect 3,000 participants to show up for an Alternative for Germany (AfD) youth rally and a pro-democracy counter-rally
Here is a roundup of the main news from and about Germany on Saturday, October 17:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Merz pushes reform agenda
Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Saturday acknowledged that his administration's reform plans "shake up the country, shake up our party," but insisted that they are the only choice for the CDU going forward.
Speaking of his plan for a fundamental overhaul of Germany's retirement, nursing care and health insurance systems, Merz said: "If we can't show that we've gotten our economy growing sustainably again before the next parliamentary election, that we've sustainably reformed and future-proofed our welfare system by the next parliamentary election, we won't stand a chance in the next parliamentary election."
Merz insisted that his Cabinet should sign off on the reforms by the end of the year.
Among these is a controversial reform that would raise Germany's retirement age.
Social Democrat (SPD) coalition partners in the federal government are against the move, as are three CDU state premiers in eastern Germany.
Merz addresses party youth at annual convention
Chancellor Friedrich Merz was in Bonn Saturday to address an annual national meeting of his Christian Democratic and Christian Social Unions' (CDU/CSU) youth wing, the Young Union (Junge Union/JU).
Things were testy the last time Merz addressed the 90,000-member group — when they fought over pension policy— and he will now face them with dwindling approval numbers and growing dissatisfaction over the way he has led Germany and his party.
Merz will greet a youth wing that is self-confident as he himself reels from disastrous election results in recent state and municipal elections.
On Friday, the JU overwhelmingly re-elected Johannes Winkel as their chairman, with the CDU federal parliamentarian taking 94.3% of the vote.
"Our generation still has big plans," said Winkel as he spoke to JU attendees, "and we will be the ones who successfully continue to write the history of the CDU and CSU as a people's party."
On Friday, North Rhine-Westphalia State Premier Hendrik Wüst, a rising star within the party, addressed attendees. On Sunday, Bavarian State Premier Markus Söder will take the stage. Both represent potential replacements for Merz.
Despite the number of prominent party leaders addressing the JU amid talk of Merz's possible political demise, Johannes Winkel vowed: "We're not some applause meter. This isn't a casting show for the chancellorship."
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Morgen from the DW news team in gray and blustery Bonn, where, just across the street, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is addressing the Junge Union (JU) youth wing of his CDU and its Bavarian sister party CSU at an annual national conference.
Last time Merz spoke to the group, things got confrontational over pension policy. The chancellor will have a number of thorny issues to navigate this time around, not least whether the party thinks it can survive under his leadership.
As Germany struggles with budget cuts, the country's development minister asked for a debt spending exemption to cover shortfalls in critical funding assistance for Ukraine. Reem Alabali Radovan warned that Ukraine is suffering more death and destruction than ever but "as budget cuts for development assistance continue, we simply will not be able to maintain our support."
In the northern state of Schleswig-Holstein, "Generation Deutschland," the youth wing of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), is holding a rally under the motto: "Secure the Future — Safeguard Identity." A "Rally for Democracy" counterdemonstration will also take place. Police say they expect roughly 3,000 participants in all.

Israeli firm exploited online ads to spy on Al Jazeera and Palestinian sites, researchers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:33:10 UTC
19:33:10 KST

Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, two research groups said on Thursday.
Its services gave Israel's Candiru – a spyware company blacklisted by the U.S. government – as well as other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, Russia's Yandex and others, according to separate reports from Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.
The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.
Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group.
In a statement, Al Jazeera said it "condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff" and that it was taking steps to protect its employees and its systems. "Those responsible must be held accountable," it said.
"The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Christl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike."
Discover-Tech's online ads – often for ordinary products such as phones or earbuds – reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.
Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.
Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume.
Malicious ads shown in hundreds of sensitive networks
Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements – called cookie matching – allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements.
"Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said.
Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.
Reuters' attempts to reach Candiru's owners were similarly unsuccessful. The U.S. Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for allegedly supplying spyware that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm's ads.
"You go to almost any site in Palestine – any site – you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he said.
Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia, Sandisk, Broadcom and Micron, as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.
In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech's users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.
Measures against Discover-Tech
Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.
Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies."
IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.
Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform "following recent activity," Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.
Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that U.S. forces deployed to war zones had been targeted using location data harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since disabled ad tracking on some devices.

Source: Andrii Kovaliov, spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Quote: "Due to the lack of significant battlefield successes, the Russian military leadership continues to create an illusion of major victories for its own political leadership and domestic audience. The latest example is a briefing by Valery Gerasimov, Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, based on blatant lies, manipulation and exaggeration.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has evidence that refutes the Russian command's false claims about the situation along the contact line."
Details: Kovaliov recalled that in his briefing, Gerasimov claimed that since 1 September, Russian forces had captured more than 1,800 square kilometres of Ukrainian territory and 92 settlements.
The spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this was untrue. "In fact, thanks to active operations by Ukraine's Defence Forces, more territory has been liberated since the beginning of autumn than the enemy has managed to capture," he said.
Kovaliov also stressed that Gerasimov's claims about the capture of Dobropillia were equally false, adding that the city remains under Ukrainian control.
"This is not the first time the Russian leadership has presented wishful thinking as reality. On 1 September, Putin claimed that Sviatohirsk had been captured when, in fact, it was and remains under the control of Ukraine's defence forces," he recalled.
In addition, the General Staff described claims that Russian forces had captured Kostiantynivka and Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka and reached the outskirts of Kramatorsk as false.
"As of the morning of 17 October, Ukraine's defence forces still have positions in Kostiantynivka, where fighting is ongoing. Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka has also not been captured by the enemy, and claims that Russian forces have reached Kramatorsk do not reflect the actual situation on the battlefield," Kovaliov said.
The spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said claims that Russian forces were advancing in the outskirts of Sloviansk and controlled more than 50% of Mykolaivka were also untrue.
"In fact, a small enemy group infiltrated the southern outskirts of Mykolaivka. Ukraine's defence forces are conducting strike-and-search operations to eliminate it," he clarified.
Kovaliov also commented on Gerasimov's claims about fighting for Orikhiv and the capture of Novopavlivka and Novoandriivka.
"In fact, as of 17 October, all three settlements remain under the control of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," he said.
According to the spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the claim that Russian forces had advanced to within 5 kilometres of the southern outskirts of Zaporizhzhia is also false. The contact line has remained 22 kilometres from the regional capital for a considerable time.
"Another fabrication is the claim that Velykomykhailivka in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast has been captured. Russian forces have repeatedly claimed to have captured this settlement, attempting to present wishful thinking as reality. As of 17 October, Velykomykhailivka remains under Ukrainian control, and the contact line is 8 kilometres east of the settlement," Kovaliov said.

Stadler Rail builds world’s first narrow-gauge hydrogen train
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:30:47 UTC
19:30:47 KST

Stadler Rail builds world’s first narrow-gauge hydrogen train
Stadler Rail has achieved a world's first: a narrow-gauge hydrogen-powered train. The train is intended for use in Sardinia and is currently being tested on a dedicated test track built in Switzerland.
Regional transport in southern Italy is partly characterised by lines with a track gauge of 950 millimetres, the company notes in a press release. Trains designed for this particular track gauge operate, for example, in Puglia, Sicily, the Naples area and Sardinia.
To test the rolling stock intended for these networks, Stadler Rail built a dedicated test track in the spring, running between Hemishofen and Ramsen stations in the canton of Schaffhausen. Almost 4 kilometres long, it features a third rail within the existing standard-gauge track.
It was on this very standard-gauge line that the FLIRT H2 hydrogen-powered train, built for California, underwent its tests: the idea to extend the line stems precisely from the success of this project. The systems of the rolling stock built for the Sardinian Regional Transport Company (ARST) will now be tested.
+ Swiss firm Stadler Rail will supply eight locomotives to Italy
“The imminent delivery of the new hydrogen-powered trains represents a decisive step for ARST,” says Carlo Poledrini, the railway company’s director-general, as quoted in the press release. “The trains arriving in Sardinia will have already completed a major phase of testing, enabling us to swiftly begin final trials on our network. This will allow us to make concrete progress towards zero-emission transport and greater energy self-sufficiency. This is a significant operational milestone that confirms our excellent collaboration with Stadler Rail,” concludes the manager.
Over the next three years, the new Schaffhausen track will play a key role in the commissioning of the hydrogen-powered fleet that Stadler Rail is building for the Italian regions of Sardinia, Calabria and Sicily. To date, tests are scheduled for a total of 21 vehicles.
Since the start of January, Stadler Rail’s share price has risen by 44%, and over the past twelve months the increase has been 57%.
Stadler Rail traces its origins back to the engineering firm founded by Ernst Stadler in Zurich in 1942. The company is now based in Bussnang in canton Thurgau and manufactures a wide range of rolling stock, from high-speed trains to regional trains, as well as trams and metro vehicles, which also operate on railway lines in Switzerland and Ticino. It employs 18,000 people, 6,000 of whom are based in Switzerland. In 2025, it achieved a turnover of CHF3.7 billion ($4.48 billion).

HTC Made Smart Glasses That Are Way More Private
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

You can’t really talk about smart glasses without bringing up Meta. HTC, the company behind 2010-era virtual reality headsets and a failed smartphone business, seems quite eager to tackle that comparison directly.
In September, HTC started selling its $499 Vive Eagle smart glasses in the US. The Eagles have lots of the same features as other glasses on the market—cameras for capturing photos and video, speakers in the frames for music playback and calls, an embedded AI agent you can ask questions of and even get recipes from by taking pictures of stuff in your fridge.
But HTC also wants to steer clear of the ongoing debate about privacy in camera-equipped smart glasses. Meta has been dogged by controversy for its smart glasses, with people worried about the company’s interest in enabling face-recognition features, and calling the people who wear them creepy. HTC is aware of that discourse and thinks it is completely possible to make smart glasses that aren’t a privacy nightmare.
“It's not just about protecting the consumer, but it's also about protecting people around the consumer,” Dan McDowell, HTC Vive’s head of enterprise sales, tells WIRED. “People can usher in, I think, what are really tremendous experiences with a new layer of confidence and protection.”
I’ve been wandering around with the glasses for a couple of weeks, and so far they meet my expectations for what smart glasses have become. They protect my eyes from the sun. They snap good photos and videos. You can record and transcribe voice notes. The music playback has decent sound quality. (I’ll always prefer a solid pair of headphones if I’m actually trying to listen to music, but the speakers work just fine.) They come in two styles—one with square Wayfarer-esque lenses and the other more rounded.
The Vive Eagle glasses can get 4.5 hours of battery life on continuous music playback. They can last 36 hours on standby. HTC also sells a companion clip-on battery pack called Power Boost that costs $49. It clips right onto the frame and is noticeable but not as obnoxious as you might think.
Don’t forget the AI assistant, Vive AI, which can utilize OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini. It doesn’t require a login, so users are “de-identified” in a way that keeps the services from retaining personal information. (That also means, by default, you won’t be able to enjoy many of the personalization features these chatbots offer by gleaning information from your emails and messages.) The glasses come with Vive’s AI Plus, free for the first two years. After that, users must pay a monthly $2.50 subscription fee.
Right by the cameras is a bright indicator light. If you cover the light, it won’t record. If someone around you says stop recording, that will stop the recording. Video footage you capture is encrypted and stored on the glasses—it’s not automatically sent to the phone or cloud. If you want to import photos or videos, you have to do it manually in the app.
Meta has faced scrutiny over the indicator light before, as some users have blocked the LED with stickers or broken into the hardware to turn it off. Meta has responded with software updates that disable the camera if someone tampers with the indicator light, along with other privacy-focused measures.
I ask McDowell how HTC, and really any smart glasses maker, can get past the “trust me, bro”–style privacy promises companies tend to make.
“We're not a social media company,” McDowell says. “There's no benefit to me to have any of your info. We don't train our AI model or any third-party AI models with any of the information that is used on the glasses.”
The real problem may be that with cameras on the frames, smart glasses are hard to distinguish between brands. The Vive Eagles look a lot like Meta glasses, and people worried about those privacy issues may not know that the Eagles are different and not tied to Mark Zuckerberg’s company. I’ve had friends see me wearing them and ask if they’re smart glasses. Yeah, I replied, but not the ones they’re thinking of. That didn’t seem to dispel any of their suspicions.
The hope, at least how HTC frames it, is that more players with better privacy practices will help shift cultural disdain for smart glasses. A bunch of other companies are going cameraless, like Even Realities, Viture, and Halliday. Others are building theirs with privacy shields or focusing on virtual displays instead of capturing the world around you. That said, no one has captured the market quite like Meta.
“We'd like to make sure that our technology adapts to society's expectations, not the other way around,” McDowell says. “I hope that everybody that's making products like these takes steps in the right direction.”

Don’t Let a Crypto Inheritance Get Stuck on the Blockchain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

If someone you know has cryptocurrency that you might inherit, let me just say ahoy matey! I hope your pirate spirit is alive and your treasure-hunting skills sharp, because that's what it might take to get those assets. And if you're the one holding crypto, know that if you do nothing, it's very possible those funds will die with you.
In the US, cryptocurrency is considered a digital asset rather than money in terms of probate and estate law. With money and physical assets, you can sign a beneficiary form and create an estate plan or write a last will and testament naming who should get what when you die. With digital assets, however, the law says we should not assume that a deceased person wanted their private materials—everything from emails to photos—given to another person unless they explicitly said so. This puts cryptocurrency, as a digital asset, in an awkward position.
The options for arranging a transfer of cryptocurrency upon one's death or incapacitation breaks down by one big division: whether the crypto is held by a custodian or in a noncustodial crypto wallet.
Two Types of Wallets
A custodian or custodial wallet means a third party, such as a bank or a cryptocurrency marketplace, holds and manages the assets for you. Typically, transferring assets after death is much easier with a custodian, especially if it's a bank.
Noncustodial wallets eliminate the middleman and let a person hold their assets directly. For crypto enthusiasts whose interest in digital currency is driven by a distaste for the traditional banking system, then using a noncustodial wallet is kind of the whole point.
Noncustodial wallets can be software or hardware-based. It can even be a piece of paper with the instructions and passwords for accessing the cryptocurrency on it. (I use "password" here and throughout to refer to any string of letters, numbers, and characters needed to gain access to someone’s cryptocurrency.) Whatever kind of noncustodial wallet you choose, passing on your assets will require a DIY solution.
Pros and Cons of a Custodial Wallet
When you use a third-party custodian to hold your cryptocurrency, you can choose one that has a beneficiary process in place.
Charles Schwab and Chase are just two examples of large, well-known financial institutions that offer crypto services and have experience transferring assets after death. Schwab, for example, houses its cryptocurrency services within brokerage accounts. Signing a beneficiary form for a brokerage account applies to the crypto account as well. One and done.
Another benefit of using a bank is that at least three entities know you have an account: the bank, the government, and the credit reporting bureaus. Avenues exist for finding the banked money of deceased people. With a noncustodial wallet, this is not at all the case.
Similarly, if you get locked out of your online bank account, you can go to a bank branch with ID (I've had to do it) and get back in. More important to your heirs, it doesn't matter if you were locked out of the online portal when you died—that has no bearing on the account or a beneficiary's ability to receive the funds. This is not the case with noncustodial wallets.
Note that cryptocurrency accounts, even when held through a bank, are not FDIC-insured.
Other custodians include crypto marketplaces, such as Coinbase, and peer-to-peer payment services, like PayPal. Neither Coinbase nor PayPal have beneficiary forms as of this writing, though they do have a clear process for proving a person is entitled to a decedent's account. In both cases, you must have legal documents saying you are the executor of the estate (for PayPal) or are entitled to inherit the account (Coinbase), as well as a death certificate and other documentation. So the process is clunky and takes some advance planning, but it's still straightforward.
How many disadvantages there are to using a custodian depends on your outlook. As mentioned, crypto enthusiasts who eschew traditional banking may not see any value in using a custodian. Banks require ID, so you cannot hold the crypto anonymously. Banks and many other custodians report your transactions to the federal government, holding you accountable to an honest tax filing. Custodial wallets also cost money. They typically charge transaction fees, usually a small percentage of each trade.
Pros and Cons of a Noncustodial Wallet
The primary benefit of a noncustodial wallet is that everything is in your control. You hold the assets directly. You're responsible for knowing and keeping safe the information you need to access your assets. You also have to come up with a plan for informing your beneficiaries that a crypto account exists and making sure they can access it.
The first and biggest problem is that if you get locked out while you're alive, it's game over. "If you lose your cryptographic key, there's no company that you can appeal to," says Benjamin Orzeske, chief counsel for Uniform Law Commission and a staff attorney for the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, the law that guides how digital inheritance is handled in most states.
In the case of a hardware key, a corrupted device or one lost to fire or theft may also cut off a person and their heirs from their crypto, permanently and irreversibly.
The other major hurdle is that your fiduciary needs to know the crypto exists. No government or credit reporting bureau has a record of you holding the account. The only people who know are the ones you tell.
Now let's get procedural. Because of how the blockchain works, you must figure out a secure way to give your heirs instructions for obtaining the assets. Your system has to be safe. It doesn't come with any backups or failsafes unless you create them. And whether you can test your system to make sure it works before you die will require a huge amount of trust.
Ideas from Reddit users for how to build a system for passing on cryptocurrency include email dead-man switches, printed instructions given to a trusted person, and splitting instructions across two people who will need to come together to obtain access. All these solutions could work but have obvious flaws: the failure of an email system, a trusted person dying alongside you, someone forgetting you gave them instructions, and so forth.
The best option may be to put the bulk of the instructions into your estate plan, including your named fiduciary, but crucially omitting any passwords. As Catherine Hodder, a senior attorney editor at FindLaw, explained to me, “The will is a public document,” and you should never put any usernames or passwords in your will.
An excellent place to put your password is inside a safe-deposit box at a bank. The existence of the deposit box should also be listed in your will. Some crypto owners have suggested stamping the password into a metal plate, which I suppose is a fine idea if you don't trust ink and paper to last longer than you.
One potential flaw is still that you can't do a dry run to make sure your system works unless you trust your fiduciary completely. Something as simple as needing your fingerprint to unlock a device could spell the end of your plan.
An objection that some staunchly anti-capitalistic investors may have is that by including your cryptocurrency in your estate plan, you've returned it to the realm of traditional law and governance.
Then again, you'll be dead.

After years in power, Egypt's el-Sisi vows to step down in 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:27:52 UTC
19:27:52 KST

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi announced Saturday that he intends to leave office in 2030, in accordance with Egypt's amended constitution, ruling out the possibility of further constitutional changes. He said his departure was "settled and not open for discussion."
Amendments to Egypt's constitution were approved in 2019, allowing el-Sisi to remain president until 2030. At the time, critics argued that the changes marked another step toward consolidating authoritarian rule in Egypt, potentially creating a regime even more repressive than that of President Hosni Mubarak, who was ousted in a popular uprising in 2011. Mubarak's overthrow, after 29 years in power, had raised hopes of establishing a genuine democracy.
In recent days, el-Sisi has also addressed the question of when he will leave office in several other speeches. Speaking Saturday at a ceremony at Egypt's military academy, he added: "My duty is to protect the country and hand over its flag while it is still flying high. We are committed to preparing people capable of assuming the responsibility of leading the country. We will not allow people who are incapable of taking on that responsibility to lead."
He also expressed unequivocal support for the Gulf states and Saudi Arabia, which is currently facing attacks by the Houthis in Yemen.
"We stand firmly with our brothers in the Gulf and fully support the defense of their territories. We will take any measure Saudi Arabia requests to protect its security and sovereignty," he said.
El-Sisi came to power more than a decade ago after ousting Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohamed Morsi in a military coup in 2013. Morsi had been elected president following the revolution that toppled Mubarak.
Since the military takeover, el-Sisi has ruled Egypt virtually unchecked. During his decade in power, he has overseen a sweeping crackdown on liberals, left-wing activists and Islamists alike, with human rights organizations alleging that tens of thousands of people have been imprisoned. El-Sisi and his supporters maintain that the arrests were necessary to stabilize Egypt and curb radical Islamism.
After winning the 2014 presidential election with 97% of the vote and securing a similar result in 2018, el-Sisi won 89% of the vote in 2023, in yet another election whose outcome was widely seen as a foregone conclusion.

The number of war casualties is at a record high, rising by 85% in September - UN
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:27:46 EEST

The number of war casualties is at a record high, rising by 85% in September - UN
Kyiv • UNN
In September, 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 were injured in Russian attacks. The number of casualties was 85% higher than in September 2025.
The number of civilian casualties of the war in Ukraine remains at a record-high level amid intensified attacks on energy infrastructure as winter approaches. In September, at least 328 civilians were killed and another 2,105 were injured in Russian attacks in Ukraine. The total number of those killed and injured exceeded the September 2025 figures by 85%. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported this in a new report, UNN reports.
Details
"The intensification of attacks by the Russian Federation across Ukraine in September continued the trend of 2026, when the number of civilian casualties significantly exceeded the figures confirmed in previous years, with devastating consequences for the civilian population," the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported as it published its monthly update on harm caused to civilians in Ukraine.
"Repeated attacks on energy infrastructure threaten to further intensify this suffering," the statement said.
In September, at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 were injured, bringing the total number of those killed and injured to 85 percent higher than in September 2025 (249 killed and 1,068 injured)
The UN mission confirmed that civilians were killed or injured in September in 22 regions of Ukraine and in Kyiv. The highest number of casualties was recorded in the capital, Kherson, Kharkiv, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia.
"In Kyiv alone, civilian casualties were recorded on 22 of the 30 days—more frequently than in any previous month since the beginning of the full-scale invasion," the report said.
According to available information, the number of casualties also remained high in October. In particular, on the night of October 6–7, Russian forces attacked several regions with cruise missiles and drones. At that time, 22 civilians were killed and another 45 were injured in Pryluky, Chernihiv region. In addition, the mission documented other attacks with large numbers of civilian casualties, including in Kramatorsk on October 8, Zaporizhzhia on October 10 and Lutsk on October 14.
"The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest for civilians in recent years. In just a few days, attacks by the Russian armed forces caused mass-casualty incidents in Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kramatorsk and Kyiv," said Danielle Bell, the head of the mission.
"The confirmed figures for September include 18 civilians killed and 44 injured in territory of Ukraine occupied by the Russian Federation," the press release said.
As noted, the actual number is likely significantly higher, since the lack of access and independent sources of information makes it difficult to verify many incidents.
"The high number of civilian casualties in September and October occurred against the backdrop of the Russian armed forces' resumption of systematic attacks on energy infrastructure across Ukraine," the report said.

Writing on X on October 17, he said that the worst-hit areas included Lutsk, Rivne, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsya, Shepetivka, Slavuta, and Netishyn, and that "energy facilities in the Kharkiv, Kyiv, Dnipro, and other regions were also hit."

"Between 7 p.m. yesterday and 7 a.m. today alone, more than 320 jet-powered and gasoline-powered 'shaheds,' along with loitering munitions, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles, were used against our energy sector, our cities, and our communities."
Russia launched four Kalibr cruise missiles and 332 attack drones, including 31 jet-powered drones, as well as Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles and Kh-22/32 cruise missiles, according to Ukraine's air force.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 293 aerial targets, including all four Kalibr missiles and 289 drones, the air force said. Impacts were recorded at 22 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at three others.
In the southern city of Kherson, a Russian air strike on the Korabelniy district killed a 64-year-old emergency medical services driver, regional military administration head Yaroslav Shanko said.
In Slovyansk, in the eastern Donetsk region, Russian forces struck a residential neighborhood with FAB-250 aerial bombs in the early hours of the morning, hitting two apartment buildings, according to local authorities.

Eight apartment buildings were damaged, two of them partially destroyed. A total of 16 people were wounded in Slovyansk over the past 24 hours, including a 17-year-old girl. Vehicles and municipal equipment were also damaged.
The strikes also placed further strain on Ukraine's electricity system. National grid operator Ukrenergo announced emergency power cuts in several regions, saying previously published outage schedules would not apply in areas affected by the measures.
Energy workers were working to restore supplies, and authorities urged consumers who still had electricity to use it sparingly.
In Vinnytsya, the regional capital in central Ukraine, Russian attacks left the city without electricity, Mayor Serhiy Morhunov said. Officials were assessing the extent of the damage, while critical infrastructure switched to backup power.
The latest barrage came as US President Donald Trump announced that he had waived nearly all substantive sanctions, tariffs, and restrictions included in a bipartisan law aimed at pressuring Russia to end its war against Ukraine, prompting sharp criticism from Ukraine advocates and lawmakers from both parties who say the move undermines efforts to force Moscow to negotiate.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's General Staff said on October 17 that Ukrainian forces remained in control of the eastern town of Dobropillia, rejecting a claim by Russian President Vladimir Putin a day earlier that Russian forces had captured the town.
Kyiv also disputed Moscow's claim that Russian forces had seized more than 1,800 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory and 92 settlements since September 1, Reuters reported.

“We came here for a reason, and we achieved it. Look at this chair statement, it clearly says that all members agreed to the statement, so that’s what matters,” the chair of the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC) told Reuters.
Al-Jadaan told a news conference that the global economy was demonstrating “remarkable resilience” in the face of profound ongoing challenges, including wars, threats to energy and food security, high public debt levels, and risks linked to the rapid development of artificial intelligence, while warning finance officials against letting down their guard.
“The message from the IMFC members is clear: there is no room for complacency,” Al-Jadaan said in the final news conference of a week of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that brought more than 18,000 people to Bangkok.
“Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security,” the chair's statement said.
Fiscal authorities should work to rebuild buffers while protecting vulnerable populations and growth-enhancing investments, Al-Jadaan told reporters, underscoring the need for continued central bank independence and policies that supported private sector-led growth and investment.
“International cooperation remains critical to addressing excessive global imbalances and trade tensions,” he said.

Many lower-income countries that were not part of the AI value chain feared they were falling behind, she said.
“These meetings also have shown that in a world of repetitive shocks and geopolitical fragmentation, still there is desire for multilateral dialogue and cooperation,” she said. “It is there.”

Ukraine Launches Pilot Project Using Drones to Transport Medical Supplies Donor Organs
The Ukrainian government has approved an experimental project using unmanned aerial vehicles for medical logistics, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced on October 16.
The Heart Institute of the Ministry of Health of Ukraine will serve as the first testing site, equipped with 3 specialized drones with a flight range of up to 700 km that can land directly on hospital grounds.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Digital Transformation are implementing the experimental project.
Serhii Koretskyi explained that Ukraine plans to use the trial to build its own Unmanned Traffic Management system for civilian drones and establish safety regulations for civil UAV operations.
Flight operations will follow a clear approval process with military authorities. The drones will carry a special status and identification in the air. Procedures for air raid alerts are also established, including the ability to land at backup locations.
"In conditions of war and a difficult road situation, transporting medical cargo by car can take up life-saving time. This especially applies to transplantation, where delivery speed is critical. Drones will be able to deliver medicines, medical devices, blood samples for testing, and donor organs between hospitals faster, particularly from remote areas," the Prime Minister wrote.
Due to conditions under Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and challenging road conditions, ground transport can delay urgent medical deliveries.
Unmanned flights will accelerate the movement of donor organs, blood samples, and essential medical supplies between medical facilities.
Meanwhile, Ukraine began front-line testing of StarGate, its first aerial drone designed to evacuate wounded soldiers from high-risk zones, as reported by Associated Press.
Developed over the past year by the Ukrainian defense technology company SkyFall at the request of a military commander, the unmanned aircraft was built to reach casualties in hazardous areas extending 10 to 15 kilometers into the battlefield.
The drone possessed a payload capacity of up to 150 kilograms, enabling it to transport a fully equipped soldier on medical stretchers at speeds ranging from 65 to 105 kilometers per hour.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Saturday that he would leave office when his current term ends in 2030, ruling out any further constitutional amendments to extend his rule as he also pledged to defend Saudi Arabia’s security and sovereignty if requested.
“The year 2030 will mark the end of my presidential term. This matter is completely settled,” Sisi said during a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital, according to state-run Al-Ahram newspaper.
“I said that the Egyptian constitution would not be touched,” he added. “This is an entirely settled matter and will not be discussed.”
The 71-year-old president, a former army general who has led Egypt since 2014, is serving a six-year term after winning re-election in December 2023. Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four years to six and allowed Sisi to seek an additional term, enabling him to remain in office until 2030.
The amendments reshaped Egypt’s presidential limits and drew criticism from opponents who warned they would consolidate power in the hands of the president.
Sisi came to power in 2013 after the military ousted Mohamed Morsi, Egypt’s first democratically elected president, following mass protests against his rule. Sisi subsequently won the presidency in 2014 and has maintained a tight grip on the country’s political system.
His latest remarks appeared aimed at ending speculation about whether he might seek another constitutional change to remain in power beyond his current mandate.
Sisi also spoke about the role of the military and the need to prepare a new generation of leaders, linking the armed forces to the protection of Egypt’s constitutional order and state institutions.
He said the constitution defines the military’s responsibility to safeguard democracy, the constitutional framework and the fundamental pillars of the state.
“I will not leave the Egyptian state until it is brimming with its own people capable of shouldering responsibility,” Sisi said, referring to efforts to prepare younger generations to take on leadership roles through the Egyptian Military Academy.
The comments did not provide further details about how the transition to new leadership would be managed or what role Sisi might play after leaving office.
Sisi also declared that Egypt was prepared to take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect the kingdom’s security and sovereignty, underscoring Cairo’s stated commitment to the defense of its Gulf partners.
“We will take any measure to protect Saudi Arabia,” he said, adding that he would call on parliament to convene an emergency session to authorize such action if Riyadh requested it.
“We stand firmly to protect and defend the territories of our brothers in the Gulf,” he added.
Sisi did not specify what measures Egypt might take or identify a particular threat that would prompt such a response.

Solar power booms in Philippines as war on Iran spikes energy costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:12:01 UTC
19:12:01 KST

Solar power booms in Philippines as war on Iran spikes energy costs
With Southeast Asia’s largest electricity bills rising even higher, Filipinos invest in rooftop panels.
Manila, Philippines – Keith Cantera and his family have been thinking about having their own solar power grid at home for years. But spending up to $5,000 for solar panels was nothing to scoff at, so they put the idea on the back burner.
It all changed this year when the United States-Israel war on Iran rattled global energy markets and sent electricity prices soaring. From paying a monthly bill of about $150 before the war began in late February, Cantera said his family went to forking out as much as $220.
Eight months later, they are having solar panels installed on their rooftop.
“The cost is about the same as paying our electric bills for three or four years based on the current rate,” Cantera said. “But in the fifth year, we’ll have recovered our investment, and electricity will essentially be free.”
Cantera is one of a growing number of Filipino homeowners turning to solar power in a country that had Southeast Asia’s highest electricity costs even before the war. They were comparable only to Singapore, where the average income is more than 10 times higher.
A report by the energy think tank Ember estimated that rooftop panels had nearly doubled in the Philippines since early 2025.
And in the first months of the war from March to May, the rush for solar power led to $407m in panel imports, according to government trade data from China, where most panels are manufactured. The Philippines became the biggest single overseas market for that period. Only the Netherlands bought more, but it redistributes them to the rest of Europe.
Lexus Grepo, CEO of the solar power supplier Solarmaxx, can attest to the boom.
“There is a 30-day wait because solar panel shipments can’t keep up,” Grepo said. “In March, we had 40 projects, which was almost triple our monthly clientele. Since then, we have been setting up 25 to 30 systems a month.”
Grepo does not expect demand to slow down even if tensions in the Middle East ease and shipping routes for energy supplies reopen.
“I think people now realise that the world is an unpredictable place, so they have to be ready for any eventuality. Filipinos now see that they don’t necessarily have to be at the mercy of the global energy market.”
The Philippines, one of the few countries in the region where electricity is not subsidised, relies on imported coal and gas for more than 70 percent of its power mix. The value of its currency, the peso, which has slid to a record low of more than 63 to the US dollar, is making these imports even costlier.
In late March, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr declared a national energy emergency in response to the war and what he described as the “imminent danger” posed to the national energy supply. Still, electricity rates have continued to increase.
The shift to solar is also partly driven by anger at electric companies that have come under scrutiny for charging customers for so-called system losses, which include illegal connections.
Cantera said learning about having to pay for someone else’s electricity consumption was the last straw.
“Who would agree to paying for something that you did not use? It’s not like the money we spend for electricity just fell from heaven,” he added.
But while the soaring demand is real, the upfront cost of a solar power system is still too high for most Filipinos. The government in March launched a new initiative offering loans for residential rooftop installations, but these are available only to public sector workers.
What officials hope can bring power rates down for the majority of people are the dozens of renewable energy projects in the pipeline, including a 3,500-hectare (8,650-acre) solar farm north of the capital, Manila, that is projected to be the largest in the world. When fully operational, the project is expected to generate 850 megawatts of electricity for 2.4 million households.
But some consumers said such projects could take years to complete, leaving them with ballooning electricity bills unless they take action themselves.
“It’s just so unpredictable nowadays. You have the impending El Nino weather pattern. There’s still war, the continuing fuel price hikes and so much more,” Cantera said. “So why not utilise a natural resource?”

One emergency medical worker was killed and 33 other civilians were injured – including a one-month-old infant and an 11-year-old child – after Russian forces carried out consecutive guided aerial bomb (KAB) strikes on the Korabelnyi district of Kherson on Saturday morning, Oct. 17.
Head of the Kherson City Military Administration Yaroslav Shanko reported that Russian tactical aviation launched eight guided aerial bombs against residential buildings and civilian social infrastructure during two consecutive strike waves conducted within an hour.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A secondary strike was launched as emergency medical personnel arrived at the scene of the initial impacts to administer first aid, killing an emergency ambulance driver and injuring a female medical worker.
“The occupiers carried out two airstrikes within an hour, dropping eight KABs on residential buildings and social infrastructure facilities,” Shanko stated.
“The repeat strike was delivered after the arrival of medics. An ambulance driver was killed, and another female medic was injured.”
Emergency rescue operations and rubble clearance
According to the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS), the aerial bombardment damaged 10 multi-story residential buildings across the district, igniting localized fires and trapping residents beneath collapsed structural elements.
SES rescue crews, municipal utility workers, and emergency responders deployed immediately to secure damaged perimeters, extinguish fires, and conduct search-and-rescue operations. Rescuers extracted seven injured residents from beneath the rubble of damaged residential high-rises.
Russia Hits 15 Energy Sites in Massive Strike, Zelensky Says
Medical personnel treated 22 injured individuals at the scene and in regional clinical facilities, confirming that the wounded included a one-month-old infant and an 11-year-old child.
Engineering brigades and civil defense units initiated structural assessments across the 10 damaged high-rises to stabilize damaged facades and clear shattered glass and masonry from surrounding municipal thoroughfares.
Subsequently, the Kherson Regional State Administration reported that the number of casualties had risen to 27. Three more women, aged 64, 55, and 54, sought medical attention.
They suffered concussions, blast injuries, and closed head injuries. Two of the victims are currently in the hospital.
Later, Yaroslav Shanko stated that the number of casualties had risen to 33.
Wave of weekend bombardments
The morning bombardment of Kherson followed a series of coordinated Russian strikes directed against civilians and municipal infrastructure across several Ukrainian regions early Saturday morning.
In the eastern city of Sloviansk in the Donetsk region, Russian aircraft dropped FAB-250 aerial bombs on an urban residential neighborhood at approximately 3:40 a.m. local time, killing one civilian, injuring 10 others, and damaging eight high-rises, two of which sustained partial structural collapses.
Concurrently in the Vinnytsia region, Russian forces launched one of their largest aerial assaults on the region since the full-scale invasion, injuring six people and damaging critical municipal infrastructure.
Ukrainian air defenses downed 24 strike drones over the region, but impacts forced utility dispatchers to transfer municipal water and life-support facilities onto backup emergency generators.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force Command, the nationwide overnight barrage involved ballistic missiles – including Iskander-M and KN-23 systems – alongside Kh-22 and Kh-32 cruise missiles, four sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles, and 332 unmanned aerial vehicles.
Ukrainian air defense forces, combat aviation, electronic warfare teams, and mobile interceptor groups downed or suppressed 293 aerial targets by 8:00 a.m. on Saturday.
The overnight operations also produced civilian casualties in Kharkiv, where missile strikes on the Nemyshlianskyi district wounded 15 people, including three children, and in Zaporizhzhia, where early morning missile arrivals injured two civilians and set parked vehicles ablaze.

Ukraine Hits Russian Rail Bridge, Ammunition Warehouses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:11:00 UTC
19:11:00 KST

Ukrainian Defense Forces have struck a strategic railway bridge inside Russia’s Bryansk region, alongside multiple military logistics depots and a drone command post across occupied Donetsk region.
According to an official dispatch released by the General Staff, precision strikes were conducted throughout Friday, Oct. 16, and overnight into Saturday morning, targeting logistical nodes that sustain Russian military formations.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Inside Russia, Ukrainian fire engaged a railway bridge spanning the Unecha River near the settlement of Sloboda-Seletska in the Bryansk region.
Ukrainian defense planners noted that severing or degrading the crossing is engineered to disrupt Russian military rail transport, specifically interdicting shipments of ammunition, petroleum products, and heavy combat vehicles toward frontline formations.
“Damage was recorded to a railway bridge across the Unecha River in the area of Sloboda-Seletska, Bryansk region of the Russian Federation,” the General Staff announced.
“This will complicate rail logistics for Russian forces, in particular the supply of ammunition, fuel, and military equipment.”
Depots and drone control posts hit in occupied Donetsk region
Simultaneously, Ukrainian precision units targeted rear logistics hubs and unmanned aviation command installations across Russian-occupied sectors of the Donetsk region.
Military authorities confirmed direct impacts on Russian material and technical supply warehouses in the areas of Novoandriivka, Mykilske, and the port city of Mariupol.
Zelensky: ‘Putin’s Real Enemy Is the Rules-Based Order’ – Key Takeaways From Brussels
The destruction of concentrated storage depots restricts frontline Russian tactical groups from rapidly replenishing ammunition, vehicular parts, and fuel reserves along contested southern and eastern sectors.
In the vicinity of Malynivka in the Donetsk region, Ukrainian fire struck an active Russian unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) command and control post, suppressing enemy drone reconnaissance and strike coordination.
The General Staff emphasized that systematic interdiction of transport arteries, supply bases, and drone command centers forms part of a sustained campaign to degrade the combat potential and logistical stamina of Russian forces.
Asymmetric interdiction of supply corridors
The strikes across the Bryansk and Donetsk regions follow an expanding Ukrainian operational effort to dismantle critical transport bridges and chokepoints linking Russian staging bases with occupied Ukrainian territory.
In late September, Ukrainian strikes damaged the Chonhar road bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russian-held sectors of the Kherson region. Independent open-source satellite intelligence published by Dnipro OSINT showed that consecutive precision strikes blasted large craters into the roadway before causing a full bridge span to collapse by Sept. 30.
The collapse of the Chonhar span severely constrained Russian vehicular transport between the Crimean peninsula and occupied southern Ukraine, forcing Russian military logistics units onto longer, more vulnerable detours along the Sea of Azov coastal corridor.

Trump faults aides as Republican midterm prospects dim
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:10:38 UTC
19:10:38 KST

Trump faults aides as Republican midterm prospects dim
- Trump is blaming aides for weak Republican midterm results, including campaign spending, redistricting, and candidate choices, while Democrats may win the House and the Senate is still close.
- Tension is rising between James Blair and Susie Wiles, with Trump criticising Blair’s outside work and some officials questioning Wiles’ oversight, creating a “circular firing squad”.
- The stakes are high: losing the House could block Trump’s agenda and give Democrats subpoena power, while Republicans fear redistricting in Texas may backfire and hurt incumbents.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump is blaming senior aides and political operatives for a faltering midterm strategy, questioning campaign spending, faulting redistricting and second-guessing candidate choices as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress, said three people familiar with internal discussions.
Trump is not on the Nov 3 ballot but repeatedly tells supporters to pretend that he is, hoping to mobilise voters who might otherwise skip the election.
He has embarked on a frenetic campaign schedule while largely avoiding acknowledging his own role in shaping the strategy and how his unpopularity is weighing on Republican candidates in competitive races.
Much of the friction has centred on James Blair, the long-time aide who runs Trump’s super PAC MAGA, and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who until now had largely escaped criticism.
Trump has faulted Blair’s handling of campaign funds, while some White House officials and allies have questioned Wiles’ oversight of the political operation.
As Trump questions why campaign spending has failed to improve Republican polling numbers, his advisers are also blaming one another.
Wiles has pointed to Blair, while Blair has faulted the White House legislative affairs team, one of the people said.
“What’s really happening is a circular firing squad,” the person said.
Opinion polls suggest Democrats will win the House of Representatives, while the Senate remains too close to call.
Losing the House would hamper Trump’s legislative agenda in the final two years of his term and give Democrats subpoena power to investigate his administration.
Trump defended Wiles on Oct 16, calling her “smart” and “tough” and saying she would remain in her job.
“Susie is here, and she’s going to be here for a long time,” he said.
White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected the sources’ characterisation, saying they were “armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation”.
Wiles did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump has long distanced himself from political setbacks
Trump has long sought to distance himself from political setbacks.
He refused to accept his defeat in the 2020 election and said ahead of the 2022 midterm results that he deserved “all the credit” if Republicans won but “should not be blamed at all” if they lost.
More recently, he has reminded audiences that the president's party typically struggles in midterm elections.
But Trump helped devise and drive some of the strategies he is now questioning, including the redistricting effort and candidate choices shaped by his personal loyalties or grievances.
His approval rating is at the lowest point of his presidency, weighed down by voter concern over high prices and dissatisfaction with the Iran war.
Trump’s frustrations with his political team spilt into public view after Blair and Chris LaCivita, who co-managed Trump’s 2024 campaign, travelled in early October to Republika Srpska, a self-governing region of Bosnia.
The New York Times reported the men received substantial payments to advise the regional government ahead of local elections.
Trump distanced himself from both men, describing them as “outside consultants” in an Oct 7 Truth Social post and warning that if he found a conflict of interest, he would “terminate them, immediately”.
Senior White House officials questioned why Blair was taking on lucrative work overseas when he was supposed to be overseeing the final stretch of the Republican campaign, three people said.
One person said Wiles approved the trip without informing Trump, raising questions about how closely she was overseeing his political advisers.
For Trump, the larger concern is that Blair’s outside work has distracted him from his political responsibilities, two people said.
In a statement, Blair said: “All of this mudslinging is ridiculous, and counterproductive. President Trump and me are focused on helping Republicans win in November. Every other Republican should be doing the same.”
In a separate statement, LaCivita said: “President Trump and his team are and always have been focused on the midterms.
“That’s demonstrated through the money, message and motivation that the president is bringing on the road and all year.
“Sniping from unnamed cowards who’ve never been in a fight is not worth responding to.”
US$200 million and redistricting
With Trump asking why Republican polling in pivotal races has not improved despite MAGA’s campaign spending, which public records put at US$200 million (S$256.4 million) so far, it remains unclear whether he will approve more spending before the election, one of the sources said.
Trump also has pressed political aides and advisers in the past week to explain why the redistricting effort he personally pushed has failed to deliver more clear-cut Republican gains, two sources said.
Texas is a particular concern. Republicans redrew the state’s congressional map to gain seats, but the strategy relies in part on Hispanic voters turning out as they did for the 2024 election.
Opinion polls suggest that support may be difficult to replicate amid concerns about the cost of living and Trump’s handling of the economy.
Some Republicans fear the new boundaries could backfire, leaving incumbents more vulnerable instead of giving the party an advantage.
“The redistricting diced up the Trump voters too much,” one of the sources said.
Trump had said Blair was expected to return to the White House after the midterms, describing his departure as a “short leave of absence”. But two sources said his return was now unlikely.
“He’s not coming back. That is not happening,” one of them said.
It was less clear how things would play out for Wiles, who played a central role in Trump’s 2024 victory and has been credited by Trump allies and aides with bringing greater discipline to his White House in his second term.
Trump “may be annoyed at certain things but she has effectively kept that machine going”, a fourth source close to the White House said. REUTERS
