18:31:47 KST

IMF urges support for poorer nations facing high inflation, war spillovers
Low-income countries spend up to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, IMF chief says.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has a responsibility to help poorer nations struggling with rising debt, high inflation and price shocks caused by war spillovers, the head of the global lender says.
Speaking as the IMF’s annual meetings in Bangkok wrapped up on Saturday, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said discussions with global policymakers showed both “optimism and worry”.
“Optimism from the resilience of the global economy, the promise of AI, the dynamism of Asia,” Georgieva told reporters. “But AI is also recognised to be a source of worry and so are inflation, high levels of debt, wars, climate risks.”
Georgieva said vulnerable nations are missing out on the AI investment boom that is driving growth in richer countries while at the same time dealing with higher borrowing costs.
Higher global interest rates mean low-income countries now spend 8 to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, up from previous years, she said.
“I can tell you that people everywhere, but especially in poorer countries, don’t like inflation. Inflation is like a tax on the poor,” Georgieva said.
The warnings came as low-income, oil-importing countries take the strongest hit from rising global energy costs. Prices have soared since February when the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran, leading to retaliatory strikes in the Middle East and disrupted oil and gas flows.
“Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security,” said a statement issued by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, the chairman of the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC).
The IMFC is the main steering committee for the 191-member crisis lender.
Debt relief and regional support
Georgieva said her organisation has a responsibility to help countries restructure debt if needed to assist with domestic resource mobilisation, bring in international finance and create conditions for private investment.
Such countries need to set spending targets that prioritise growth and protect the most vulnerable people, she said, adding that the IMF has a “relentless pursuit of more resources for low-income countries”.
“When we do our best, it translates into better lives for people,” she said.
Georgieva also said the IMF plans to back Iraq “very firmly” with a requested loan programme while talks with Lebanese authorities are making progress.
“We will get to Iraq both money and policy support,” she said. “In the case of Lebanon, we are in very intense discussions with Lebanese authorities. We have made significant progress towards the programme. We have still a bit more work to do together, and I’m confident we will be successful.”

Estonia, Latvia at odds over cross-border wind farm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:29:00 UTC
18:29:00 KST

Estonia, Latvia at odds over cross-border wind farm
A hybrid wind farm under construction in northern Latvia is stirring tensions across the border, where nearby Estonian villages are facing the greater impact.
Utilitas Wind is building Lode Hybrid Park just across the border in Latvia, with 18 wind turbines and battery storage, and company executives say the site was chosen largely for its connection to the third electricity interconnection between Estonia and Latvia.
The Lode project is the first wind farm to be built directly on the border.
Earthworks are underway near Arakste, where the first foundations have been poured and equipment ordered. The park is expected to start generating electricity in about a year, with full completion planned for the first half of 2028.
The €200 million project also includes battery storage, and Utilitas hopes to build four additional turbines on the Estonian side as well.
"We have 18 wind turbines, along with battery storage capable of delivering 60 megawatts (MW) of power for four hours," said Utilitas Group CEO Priit Koit.
He said the entire complex is connected to the third Estonian-Latvian power link, "so electricity can flow in either direction depending on where demand is higher."
100 trucks a day
Latvia's Ministry of Climate and Energy says the project will bring local economic benefits.
"Up to €300,000 a year will go to the municipality and local residents," said ministry parliamentary secretary Einars Cilinskis, emphasizing that people will see economic benefits and regional development spurred by the wind farm.
But construction has also brought disruption to nearby Estonian villages. For the next six months, around 100 big trucks a day are expected to pass through the usually quiet village of Penuja, hauling sand and gravel from Estonia.
New speed limit signs have been installed and truck drivers are being careful, but a road originally intended to support tourism in the area is now carrying mainly construction traffic.
"We have a very good working relationship with the developer," said Penuja resident Reet Paju. "Some residents do object, of course, but since we had no say in the decision to build the wind farm, we have to accept it."
Mulgi Municipality tried to challenge the project in a Latvian court but lost, as Estonian local governments have no legal standing to appeal decisions made by Latvian ones.
'Too many wind farms'
Local leaders, however, say the concern extends beyond Lode, with several other wind farm projects planned in the wider area.
"This isn't just about the Lode wind farm, but wind farms more broadly," said Mulgi Municipal Mayor Imre Jagomäe.
He pointed to eight potential turbine sites in his municipality, two projects in neighboring Saarde Municipality and a planned development on the Latvian side in Ipiķi.
"Clearly, that's just too many wind farms for this area," he stressed.
With the municipality's support, the nonprofit Looduse ja Inimeste Eest is conducting environmental studies in the area.
"Underway and also partially completed are environmental studies of birdlife, bats and ecological coherence," said board member Urmas Maranik.
Lode Hybrid Park is expected to produce enough electricity to meet the annual needs of 110,000 households.

Ukraine downed four thousand seven hundred air targets
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:28:26 BST
18:28:26 KST

Ukrainian air defences destroyed more than 4,700 drones and missiles during September while repelling large-scale Russian attacks, and neutralised more than 48,000 tactical uncrewed aerial vehicles over the same month, according to the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.
The figures, attributed to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, break down into a pattern dominated overwhelmingly by one-way attack drones. Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 types accounted for 2,722 of the interceptions and the jet-powered Shahed-238 for a further 1,935, with 1,009 reconnaissance drones and 719 Lancet loitering munitions also brought down.
Missile interceptions made up a far smaller share of the total, with Ukrainian defences stopping 24 Kh-101 cruise missiles, 12 Kalibr cruise missiles, eight Iskander-M and KN-23 ballistic missiles, six Iskander-K cruise missiles, six Kh-59 and Kh-69 guided air-launched missiles, and eight Zircon anti-ship missiles. Another 86 S8000 Banderol missiles were destroyed.
The ministry said the targets were destroyed “through the efforts of aviation, surface-to-air missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defence Forces of Ukraine.”
On where the difficulty now lies, the department said: “Ballistic missiles remain a challenge for Ukraine’s air defense. At the same time, the enemy is increasingly using jet-powered drones that fly at speeds of around 400 km/h, reducing the time available to detect and intercept them.”
It added: “In addition, the enemy sends small groups of several jet-powered drones to different regions. To counter such targets, Ukraine uses aviation, among other means, and is developing innovative interception capabilities.”
Jet-powered Shaheds were shot down at nearly thirteen times the rate of every Russian missile type combined, which is a measure of how far the campaign has shifted away from missiles. A propeller-driven Shahed cruises at around 180 kilometres an hour and can be engaged by a gun truck, a helicopter or a cheap interceptor drone. At 400 kilometres an hour the engagement window halves, mobile fire groups lose much of their usefulness, and the problem starts to look more like intercepting a cruise missile than swatting a lawnmower.
Sending them in small packets to widely separated regions compounds the problem, because a defence designed around massed raids on a few cities has to be spread thinly to cover dispersed single-target attacks, and the aircraft Ukraine is using to run down the fast drones are the same F-16s and Mirages it needs for other tasks.
Evgeniy Khmara, the Ukrainian Defence Minister, raised munitions supply for the F-16 force in a recent conversation with German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, saying deliveries help ensure their effectiveness in shooting down Russian drones. The two also discussed protection of critical infrastructure and the need for more air defence assets including interceptors for the IRIS-T system.
Britain’s contribution to this problem has been concentrated on the cheap end, which is where the arithmetic works. The Lightweight Multirole Missile, built by Thales at Belfast and known in Royal Navy service as Martlet, has been supplied in quantity for counter-drone use, and the company confirmed this week that it has quadrupled production capacity at the site. Gravehawk, the British and Danish funded system that puts Soviet air-to-air missiles into a shipping container with a British sensor fit, was developed specifically to give Ukraine more launchers without waiting for Western interceptor stocks.

“We Will Strike Strategic Bridges”: Russia Threatens to Split Kyiv in Two
Russian military forces intend to split Kyiv in two by carrying out strikes on strategic bridges across Ukraine, according to statements by Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov.
The announcement came as Moscow initiated massive strikes against the country's energy infrastructure, while official Kremlin statements explicitly ruled out discussing border safety zones in future negotiations, according to 24tv.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
During a military briefing at an auxiliary command post, Vladimir Putin met with defense officials to outline current priorities during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Officials addressed several operational metrics and military objectives. Kremlin representatives stated that around 10% of the Donetsk region and roughly 16.5% of the Zaporizhzhia region remain under Ukrainian control.

Kremlin statements highlighted that the capture of the Donetsk region remains a primary task, while claiming the Luhansk region is under total Russian control. Russian officials reported that steel production in Ukraine has stopped and operations across key Black Sea ports have ceased.
Addressing air defense and overall strategy, Vladimir Putin stated that “Russia needs to increase the effectiveness of air defense” and directed that “launching massive and group strikes against Ukrainian facilities must be continued.” Meanwhile, Valery Gerasimov announced: “We will strike strategic bridges in Ukraine.”
On October 14, 2026, Russia launched a massive overnight attack against Ukrainian infrastructure, firing 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones at Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv. Ukrainian air defenses neutralized 115 UAVs and four ballistic missiles, but the strikes damaged 26 power grid facilities and four oil and gas sites, leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity.
Monitoring channels reported that a record barrage of roughly 25 Zircon hypersonic missiles targeted the capital and surrounding areas. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the assault as a deliberate strike on energy infrastructure previously covered by a ceasefire, calling the scale of the operation an open display of disrespect toward the United States.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

The IRGC navy accused the tanker of having turned off its positioning and radar systems in an effort to evade detection.
A super tanker has caught fire after striking a sea mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Saturday.
In a statement shared via Iranian state media, the IRGC's navy said a tanker carrying more than two million barrels of oil struck a mine whilst "attempting to pass through an unauthorised route" in the Strait, causing a "massive explosion" and a "fierce fire." It is unclear exactly where the incident took place.
Iran's Fars news agency posted a video appearing to show the vessel ablaze.
The IRGC navy accused the tanker of having turned off its positioning and radar systems in an effort to evade detection.
"The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the consequence of defying Iranian regulations in the Strait of Hormuz is burning in the fire of trust in the terrorist US army," the IRGC navy added in its statement.
The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial gas and oil transit chokepoint that has been at the heart of tensions between Washington and Tehran since the Iran war broke out in late February.
Iran effectively cut off the passage, which usually carries around 25% of the world’s seaborne oil trade, following US and Israeli strikes on the country, prompting the US to impose a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The US military has repeatedly pushed back on claims that the IRGC has control of the Strait, saying commercial vessels have continued to transit the region "despite unwarranted IRGC aggression."
Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of US Central Command (CENTCOM), said in an update on Friday that US forces were working with regional allies and partners in the shipping industry to help protect vessels navigating the Strait.
"Let me be clear, the Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran," he said. "It remains open for business."

Polish military to practise deploying forces in Ukraine in event of ceasefire with Russia – media
According to The Times, 1,500 European troops will practise deploying forces to Ukraine in Poland in November in preparation for a possible ceasefire with Russia.
Source: European Pravda, citing The Times
Details: The exercises are said to be the first of their kind. They will focus on preparing for the post-war situation, in which the presence of European troops on Ukrainian territory would serve as a deterrent.
Soldiers from several countries, including France and Germany, will practise troop movements and logistical support as part of a multinational peacekeeping operation.
The publication learned that at least 1,500 British, French and German troops, along with the Polish Armed Forces, will take part in the exercises.
A source in the UK Ministry of Defence said that troops would rehearse a scenario in which "multinational forces are together in a particular area", but declined to provide further details.
A senior Polish official said the exercises would underscore the unity of Europe's major military powers in the face of the Russian threat and the need to continue supporting Ukraine.
UK Defence Secretary John Healey said in Washington that next month, "thousands of troops will take part in major exercises in Poland to ensure we are ready to support the military training and post-war reconstruction that Ukraine will need".
He made the remarks following his first in-person meeting with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon.
Background:
- The exercises were agreed upon at a summit in Paris in July and announced by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
- The Coalition of the Willing, led by France and the UK, is working on a plan to deploy a mission to Ukraine to guarantee a future ceasefire.

The Ministry of Defence is working towards starting the British Army Training Unit Suffield commitment in April 2027, and funding is still being allocated through the department’s planning cycle, according to an answer given in Parliament.

The British Army Training Unit Suffield has been the Army’s armoured manoeuvre training base since 1972, occupying part of a Canadian Forces training area in southern Alberta that runs to around 2,700 square kilometres.
The space allows a battlegroup to manoeuvre and fire live at distances that cannot be reproduced on Salisbury Plain or at Otterburn, and tank and infantry fighting vehicle crews have traditionally completed their collective training there before being declared ready.

Iran-backed Houthis strike Yemen’s Aden: What that means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:16:48 UTC
18:16:48 KST

Houthis strike Yemen’s Aden: What that means
Armed group has hit the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the city’s airport as war spreads across the region.
The Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have fired missiles at the presidential palace in the southern Yemeni city of Aden, killing five people and wounding 16, on Thursday.
On Friday, two missiles landed on the grounds of Aden International Airport as a passenger plane prepared to take off for Cairo.
After the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014, the internationally recognised government of Yemen decamped to Aden with the backing of a Saudi-led coalition of Arab countries.
The latest attacks come as Yemen’s war, largely frozen under a 2022 truce, has reignited and become another front in the wider regional conflict involving Iran.
So what has happened in Aden, and why does it matter?
Here’s what you need to know:
What happened at Maashiq Palace?
The Houthis hit the Al-Maashiq Presidential Palace with five missiles, according to Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani.
Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said the dead and wounded included guards and civilian employees.
The government said Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and other officials were safe, but two of his bodyguards had been killed.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had struck what he called the “Saudi military operations headquarters” in Aden.
What happened at the airport?
On Friday, two missiles landed on the airport’s grounds, according to the Aden Security Department, which blamed the Houthis. It said it was the second attack on the facility in less than a week.
Yemenia Flight 612 to Cairo was preparing for takeoff. Al-Eryani said the missiles landed about 500 metres (1,600ft) from the aircraft. No casualties were reported.
Al-Eryani called the strike “a direct threat to the lives of passengers and aviation crews”.
The Houthi-run Saba agency claimed the group was targeting a military headquarters and weapons depots inside Badr Camp, a military site next to the airport.
Why are attacks on Aden significant?
Aden is the interim capital of Yemen.
The government moved there after the Houthis took control of the capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government.
The al-Maashiq Palace is the internationally recognised government’s headquarters and its seat of power.
The Houthis currently control much of the country’s north and west. Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi coalition supporting the government had largely ended following a 2022 ceasefire.
But in September, the Houthis launched a lightning offensive along the Red Sea coast, seizing territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Nearly two weeks ago, government forces launched a counteroffensive dubbed “Operation Dawn of Yemen” with Saudi air support, but have so far failed to reverse those gains.
Saree said the Houthi attacks on Aden were part of the group’s declared policy of targeting “Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located”.
The city has been hit before.
In December 2020, an attack on Aden airport as a new cabinet arrived from Saudi Arabia killed at least 22 people.
A second attack hit the palace where ministers had been taken to safety. The coalition blamed the Houthis, who denied responsibility.
What reaction has there been?
On Thursday, Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, blamed Iran for having “encouraged” the escalation.
He said the Iran-backed Houthis had rejected an offer to meet for talks in Oman when the latest round of hostilities began.
Tehran denied the claim on Friday. “The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.
Baghaei said Iran “has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities”, offering again to mediate.
Canada’s embassy in Saudi Arabia condemned the palace attack and called for “an immediate de-escalation of hostilities”.
“We stand in solidarity with the internationally recognised Government of Yemen and the Yemeni people,” the Canadian embassy in Saudi Arabia said in a post on X.
On Thursday, the United Nations Security Council condemned escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including those affecting civil aviation and energy infrastructure.
The governing council of the UN’s International Civil Aviation Organization also condemned recent attacks on civilian airports and aircraft in Saudi Arabia.
On October 9, Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, told the UNSC the country had slid back into “full-scale war”.
What is happening in the wider conflict?
Fighting resumed in July, ending a 2022 truce.
Last month, the Houthis took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most important waterways. Since the Strait of Hormuz was closed by Iran in March amid US strikes, Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on sending oil exports to the Red Sea via its East-West pipeline instead. The Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ships there earlier in the year.
On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, president of the Presidential Leadership Council, announced Operation Dawn of Yemen to retake Houthi-held territory, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition said 100 fighter jets took part, its first acknowledgement since 2022 that it had resumed air attacks on the Houthis.
The Houthis, in turn, have repeatedly fired missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure.
On Friday, the coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile headed for Yanbu, a Red Sea oil hub which Saudi Arabia has been using to export crude.
On the ground, fighting has intensified in Taiz governorate, where the Houthis have been holding the city of Taiz under siege, and which borders the Red Sea. State-run Saba media outlet, citing the Taiz Axis military command, reported that 168 Houthi fighters had been killed and 210 wounded there.
In Houthi-held areas, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what it called “Saudi aggression” since September 3.
Early on Saturday, Houthi-affiliated media reported attacks east of Saada, with the coalition saying it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers there.

Former Haitian President Joseph Michel Martelly registered online Friday as a presidential candidate for the upcoming election, bringing the total number of registered contenders to 16, The Haitian Times reported.
Martelly registered under Debloke, a political coalition that includes former members of the Haitian Tet Kale Party (PHTK), which he once led. His registration remains preliminary pending document submission and approval by Haiti’s Provisional Electoral Council (CEP).
The move follows an Oct. 6 amendment to the electoral decree that removed a requirement for candidates to submit a certificate from the Bank of the Republic of Haiti. The change eased a hurdle for individuals affected by sanctions, although US sanctions remain a potential barrier for designated candidates.
Sanctions, backlash and election delays
Martelly is not on the UN sanctions list, but UN experts have accused him of helping finance armed groups and benefiting from illicit activities. He has denied the allegations. Canada sanctioned him in November 2022, the US in August 2024, and the EU in December 2025 over allegations including gang financing and drug trafficking.
Martelly returned to Haiti on July 15 after spending years abroad. His potential political comeback has drawn criticism from Haitians at home and overseas, with concerns about his record and the strength of the opposition.
“As I always say, the most important thing was not to let him register, but everyone stayed silent,” Ronmdy Francois, a young auto mechanic, told The Haitian Times.
“However, from what I’m hearing, if it’s true that he has registered, then he is already president because I don’t see which candidate could stop him.”
No major political leaders had publicly supported or condemned his candidacy as of publication, according to The Haitian Times.
The election process faces persistent insecurity fueled by gang violence and technical challenges. The campaign, initially scheduled to begin on Thursday, has been postponed, while candidate registration has been extended through Oct. 31. The CEP has pledged to issue a revised electoral calendar.
As of Friday, the CEP had recorded 16 presidential candidates, 302 Senate candidates, and 1,050 candidates for the Chamber of Deputies. Registration and document submissions began Aug. 20.

A Chinese court on Friday sentenced six people to prison terms for serving toxic and harmful food after 247 preschoolers were found to have abnormally high blood lead levels at a kindergarten in the country's northwest in 2025.
The Intermediate People's Court of Lanzhou City in Gansu sentenced Li Huifang, the person in charge of the kindergarten, to life imprisonment, state-run Xinhua News Agency reported.
Li and Zhu Jinglin, the executive principal of Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Maiji District, instructed and organized the addition of toxic substances to food served to children and staff to make it more colorful and attractive for marketing, the report said.
Li was also deprived of political rights for life and had 500,000 yuan ($74,000) in personal property confiscated, according to the verdict.
Zhu was sentenced to 15 years in prison and fined 300,000 yuan.
Four kitchen workers who carried out the instructions received prison sentences of six to eight years and were also fined.
According to a provincial investigation report in July 2025, the contaminated pastries had been served to children and staff monthly since May 2024.
Of 251 children tested, 247 had abnormally high blood lead levels.
All affected children received hospital treatment or home-based nutritional intervention, and by July 20, 2025, most had completed their first course of treatment and been discharged from the hospital.

Russia Hits 15 Energy Sites in Massive Strike, Zelensky Says
Unknown

2026-10-17
09:14:00 UTC
18:14:00 KST

Russian forces launched one of their largest coordinated assaults against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, striking more than 15 critical electricity generation and transmission facilities across multiple provinces, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Oct. 17.
The president reported that emergency restoration operations are underway across the country, mobilizing municipal utility workers and specialized engineering crews from domestic power companies to restore severed power supplies.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“On the eve, the Russians delivered one of their largest strikes against Ukrainian energy: more than 15 critical electricity generation and energy transmission facilities in various regions of Ukraine were attacked,” Zelensky stated.
“Restoration work is ongoing, involving all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies. I thank everyone working virtually non-stop to restore power.”
Regional impact and grid dispersion tactics
Zelensky highlighted that the most severe disruptions to municipal electricity networks were recorded in northwestern and central urban centers, specifically identifying Lutsk, Rivne, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, Shepetivka, Slavuta, and Netishyn.
Additional kinetic strikes and falling debris damaged energy installations across Kharkiv region, Kyiv region, and Dnipropetrovsk region alongside other administrative jurisdictions.
According to the president, the operational breadth of the assault reflects an intentional Russian doctrine engineered to exhaust municipal repair reserves and disperse domestic technical response teams ahead of freezing winter temperatures.
EU Tasks Commission to Bridge Ukraine’s €70B Funding Gap
“The Russians scaled up their anti-energy operation and are trying to disperse our reserves and recovery capacity to the maximum,” Zelensky said.
Between 7:00 p.m. on Friday and 7:00 a.m. on Saturday, Russian forces deployed more than 320 strike drones against Ukraine’s civil power networks, municipal infrastructure, and residential settlements.
The wave comprised a mix of turbojet-powered and conventional piston-engine Shahed loitering munitions, loitering compact cruise weapons, alongside cruise and ballistic missiles.
“And although our warriors manage to shoot down a significant portion, the scale and continuity of Russian strikes – specifically against energy – unfortunately has many negative consequences,” Zelensky noted.
Push for European support
Zelensky confirmed that European partner nations have assembled new military and energy assistance packages to reinforce Ukrainian defenses, expressing gratitude for European solidarity following high-level summits in Brussels.
Concurrently, the president addressed policymakers and the public in the US, criticizing recent decisions in Washington to waive statutory economic sanctions and tariffs targeting the Russia.
“It is important that everyone in America also sees what is actually happening,” Zelensky emphasized.
“At a time when the Russians delivered such a massive strike against our energy, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to introduce truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war.”
The presidential statement referred to the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which US President Donald Trump signed into law on Sept. 18 but waived via executive order on Friday, Oct. 16, just 48 hours before mandatory 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent duties on third-party petroleum buyers were set to take effect.
“This law could – and still can! – help greatly. But the law needs to actually work, and every vote for this matters,” Zelensky urged, noting that relieving economic pressure incentivizes further aggression.
“Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating,” Zelensky stated.
“Pressure is needed to stop this. An American sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, monetary rewards for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin – all of this only encourages him to strike further. We must not surrender positions; we must try to end the war. End it, rather than give Putin every reason to prolong it indefinitely.”

EU leaders call on all countries to stop aiding Russia in its war against Ukraine – European Council meeting
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:13:03 EEST
18:13:03 KST

European Union leaders have called on all countries to immediately cease any assistance to Russia in its war against Ukraine.
"The European Council reiterates its call on all countries to immediately cease any assistance to Russia in its war of aggression against Ukraine, whether direct or indirect, and notably through the provision of dual-use goods and components," according to the conclusions adopted following the European Council meeting held on October 15-16 in Brussels.
In particular, the European Council strongly condemns the deployment of DPRK military forces in the war against Ukraine, as well as the ongoing military support provided to Russia by, among others, Iran, Belarus, and the DPRK.
In addition, the leaders affirmed that the EU "remains committed to ensuring full accountability for war crimes and the other most serious crimes committed in connection with Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and fully supports ongoing efforts within the framework of the Council of Europe towards the operationalisation of the International Claims Commission for Ukraine and the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine," the conclusions state.
The European Council also called on Russia and Belarus "to immediately ensure the safe and unconditional return to Ukraine of all unlawfully deported and transferred Ukrainian children and other civilians."
At the same time, the European Council acknowledged "the importance of the extension of temporary protection for displaced persons from Ukraine until March 2028."
"The European Union remains committed to supporting Ukraine's repair, recovery and reconstruction, in coordination with international partners, including in the areas of demining assistance and psychological and psychosocial rehabilitation," the document reads.

Israeli settlers burn olive trees, attack 8 farmers in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:12:00 UTC
18:12:00 KST

Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank on Friday, burning olive trees, throwing stones and injuring residents and an American photojournalist as violence escalated during the annual harvest season.
About 80 settlers dressed in black descended on a terraced olive grove above the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, where Palestinian residents had gathered to pick olives, according to Reuters witnesses. Some carried gas canisters, while others used slingshots to hurl stones at the farmers.
The villagers retreated down the hillside before some threw stones back at the attackers. Olive harvesting is an important annual tradition for Palestinian families and a vital source of income for many farming communities.
“The settlers want to attack us and force us from our homes,” said Moutaz Abdelhadi, 42, a farmer who witnessed the assault.
At least two Israeli military jeeps later sped through the area as villagers moved out of their path. Soldiers fired tear gas toward Palestinians, while the sound of live gunfire echoed across the area. A Reuters photographer saw at least one armed settler fire a gun.
The Israeli military said soldiers and border police officers deployed to the scene fired warning shots. It also acknowledged that troops fired toward a person they believed posed a threat.
“Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable,” the military said, adding that attempts to provoke tensions between communities undermined security.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the incident was under investigation.
Heidi Levine, an American photojournalist working for The Washington Post, was among those injured in Abu Falah. Palestinian medics said at least two people were taken to hospitals in the Ramallah area.
Video of the attack showed Levine lying on a dirt path with her hands covering her face as at least three settlers stood around her.
Speaking from a hospital bed, Levine said the attackers pushed her to the ground and repeatedly kicked her.
“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me,” she said.
Levine said her Palestinian colleagues intervened before medics transported her by ambulance to a clinic in Abu Falah and then to a hospital in Ramallah.
The Washington Post later reported that she had suffered lacerations across her body and a broken rib. She also required surgery on one hand after a finger was torn open, exposing bone.
Matt Murray, the newspaper's executive editor, condemned the attack and called for a thorough investigation.
“This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank,” Murray said.
He said Levine had been wearing visible markings identifying her as a journalist and urged authorities to investigate the assault and ensure accountability.
The U.S. State Department said it was deeply concerned about the harm suffered by an American citizen overseas and had contacted The Washington Post to offer consular assistance.
The department also condemned criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and supported holding those responsible accountable.
The assault in Abu Falah was part of a wider wave of settler violence reported across the occupied West Bank as Palestinians began their annual olive harvest.
Local officials and the Palestine Red Crescent Society reported attacks in at least eight villages in the northern West Bank, where many of the territory's olive groves are concentrated.
The Red Crescent said its medics had treated 14 injured people, while local officials reported at least four injuries.
Palestinian officials said at least four Palestinians had been killed and more than 100 injured since the harvest season began earlier in October. They also reported damage to thousands of olive trees.
In Turmus Ayya, another village near Ramallah, settlers attacked farmers harvesting olives and burned three cars, according to local accounts.
Salah Abu Niswa, who witnessed the attack, said the assailants approached the farmers before targeting someone who was alone.
“They snuck up like thieves, they caught someone by himself and began to beat him,” he said.
Yesh Din, an Israeli organization that monitors settlement activity and settler violence, reported at least 170 attacks against Palestinians since Sept. 27, around the beginning of the olive harvest.
The organization’s figures highlight the risks facing Palestinian farmers during a season that is central to their livelihoods and cultural traditions. Attacks on farmers, damage to trees and restrictions on access to groves can threaten both current harvests and future income.
Residents and rights groups have accused Israeli authorities of failing to adequately prevent the assaults or hold perpetrators accountable. Settler violence has intensified this year, with a further increase reported in the weeks leading up to Israel's Oct. 27 election.
Netanyahu has criticized settler violence, but his government has faced international criticism over its response. His right-wing coalition has overseen an expansion of Israeli settlements and smaller outposts across the West Bank.
The attacks have also drawn condemnation from some of Israel's longtime allies, including Britain, which has considered sanctions over settler violence.
About 500,000 Israeli settlers live alongside at least 3 million Palestinians in the West Bank. The United Nations and most countries consider Israeli settlements in the territory illegal under international law. Israel disputes that position and regards the territory as disputed rather than occupied.

Russia suspected of an online influence campaign ahead of important elections in the United States
Kyiv • UNN
Researchers say that a Russian government-backed influence operation is stepping up its efforts to sow division in the United States ahead of the congressional elections. X blocked 13,000 related accounts.
The Russian online influence operation "Doppelgänger" has intensified the dissemination of social media posts addressing the issue of the United States’ support for Israel, in an effort to deepen divisions in American society ahead of the midterm elections to Congress. This was reported by The New York Times on October 16, citing the relevant study, UNN reports.
Details
"Less than three weeks before elections that could change the balance of power in Congress, there are growing signs that Russia and other foreign governments are again trying to influence American voters. An online influence operation backed by the Russian government is stepping up its efforts to sow division in the United States and inflame tensions surrounding Israel as a political wedge, according to a new study by an independent company that tracks digital threats and foreign propaganda campaigns," reads a NYT article titled "Russia Appears to Step Up Efforts to Influence U.S. Voters."
According to a study by Alethea, a company that tracks digital threats and foreign propaganda campaigns, the "Doppelgänger" operation is spreading posts on social media claiming that bipartisan support for Israel in the United States is weakening. Researchers believe that in this way the campaign is attempting to intensify political disputes surrounding the issue.
As the publication writes, the operation is linked to the Russian company "Agency for Social Design," which operates in the public relations sector. The U.S. government and the European Union have imposed sanctions on it.
"On Wednesday, the social network X announced that it had blocked 13,000 accounts linked to three separate influence operations associated with Iran, Russia, and China. The platform said that the fake accounts had distributed ‘content about U.S. politics targeting candidates and public figures across the political spectrum,’" the publication says.
According to people familiar with the matter, "on Thursday, U.S. intelligence officials attempted to hold a secret briefing for some government officials on threats related to the midterm elections." "However, the initiative encountered an obstacle when intelligence officials were unable to establish a secure virtual connection with election personnel, sources said. Although such briefings were commonplace in previous election cycles, Thursday’s would have been the first of its kind in more than two years," the publication writes.
According to available information, a U.S. official confirmed that the call had to be postponed due to a technical problem. He expressed hope that the briefing would take place next week. Current and former officials explained that such meetings usually involve providing background materials and information about possible threats. They are not intended to transmit intelligence requiring immediate action by local or state authorities.

Spain’s far left fails to unite ahead of November vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:11:05 UTC
18:11:05 KST

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez during a press conference following a government cabinet meeting at the Moncloa Palace, one day after announcing a snap general election, in Madrid on October 6, 2026. | Thomas COEX / AFP via Getty Images
MADRID – Parties on Spain’s far left have failed to reach an agreement to run on a joint ticket in the November 29 election, in a setback to Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who would need their support to form a new governing majority.
The Frente Amplio (or Broad Front), an alliance of several parties to the left of Sánchez’s Socialist Party, had hoped to recruit Podemos, which was a junior partner in government from 2020 to 2023. But with the deadline for electoral coalitions falling at midnight on Friday, the parties were unable to reach a nationwide accord.
Instead, the Broad Front and Podemos will run together only in the Canary Islands and the Valencia region.
Advertisement
The Broad Front is made up of Sumar, the current junior partner in the Socialist-led government, the Catalan Comuns, the Communist-led United Left and Más Madrid. Some smaller local parties have also joined the ticket. The lead candidate for prime minister will be Ada Colau, the former mayor of Barcelona.
Sumar, the dominant force in the alliance, has seen its vote share more than halve since 2023, to 5%, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.
Although Podemos has only been polling at 3%, its full involvement in the Broad Front would have meant a greater overall share of seats for the far left, according to analysts.
The PSOE has been trailing the conservative People’s Party and would need a strong performance by parties to its left in order to keep Sánchez in office. The more likely scenario, polls show, is that the PP will be able to form a majority with the far-right Vox, whose support has been rising.
“The Spanish left is caught up in a game of thrones that demobilizes [voters],” said Irene de Miguel, coordinator of Podemos in the western region of Extremadura, as the deadline loomed.

NEW DELHI: Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) president Sukhbir Singh Badal on Saturday held Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann directly responsible for the murder of anti-drug activist Parwinder Singh alias Jhota in Mansa, accusing the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) government of failing to maintain law and order in the state.According to news agency ANI, Badal alleged that the chief minister had neglected policing and failed to control crime.“The situation is such that law and order simply does not exist. Anger over Kyiv's winter preparations fuels calls for Mayor Klitschko to resign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:10:00 UTC
18:10:00 KST

Anger over Kyiv's winter preparations fuels calls for Mayor Klitschko to resign
Local residents gathered on Oct. 17 in front of the city council to demand that Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko step down from the post he has occupied for over 12 years.
"Kyiv without Klitschko," hundreds of protesters chanted as they took to the streets in central Kyiv, according to Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground.
Kyiv's failure to prepare for the coming winter amid Russian attacks on critical infrastructure, coupled with broader mismanagement, were the main factors that brought people to protest.
The protest comes as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure and Kyiv struggles to ensure reliable access to basic utilities and adequate shelter.
The cardboard signs read "Where are the shelters?" "Resign" and "12 years of irresponsibility." Others mockingly called on Klitschko to "leave Kyiv," turning his recent advice that residents consider relocating ahead of a difficult winter back on the mayor himself.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticized Kyiv's preparations for winter, saying other cities are significantly better prepared. But despite growing public frustration, Klitschko's removal remains unlikely, as the city's complex governance structure limits the options for dismissing him during wartime.
The dispute also raises a broader question: who is ultimately responsible for ensuring Kyiv can withstand another winter?
Kyiv is less prepared than other cities
Zelensky said on Oct. 13 that "In almost all regions of Ukraine, including border and front-line areas, resilience plans have been implemented more effectively than in the capital."
Emergency power and water outages, triggering the hum of generators on almost every street, returned to Kyiv as Russia renewed its campaign against energy infrastructure as early as Sept. 30.
Power outages are not new to Kyiv, but near-daily water loss is unprecedented.
Serhii Gorkutsenko, deputy head of Kyivvodokanal, the capital's city-owned water supply company, explained the problem in an interview with Ukrainska Pravda.
"The entire electrical water utility system dates back to the 1970s. With such (voltage) fluctuations, it simply can't hold up — it burns out," he said.
This year's issue is not merely about restoring water supply but also about the sewage system, without which Gorkutsenko said there will be "an epidemiological disaster in three days, because no one will stop using the sewers."
Besides the lack of basic amenities, Kyiv also suffers from a deficiency in safety infrastructure, despite the full-scale war continuing for over 4.5 years.
The lack of shelters and the state of existing ones has been an echoing concern for months, if not years.
Klitschko told reporters on Sept. 11 that mobile shelters have been purchased and "within a month, the first batch — about 40 or 50 of them, as far as I recall — will be installed at public transit stops where there are no permanent shelters."
That promised number suddenly diminished. The Kyiv City State Administration (KMDA) told the media outlet Slidstvo.info on Oct. 6 that far fewer will arrive over a much longer timescale.
The first and so far the only new public mobile shelter appeared on Oct. 15, more than a month after Klitschko's claims.
The protest
The overarching message of the Oct. 17 protest was simple — Klitschko should resign.
However, the issues outlined by the organizers were plentiful. They addressed everything from safety to public transport issues, and the neglect of cultural heritage sites.
Corruption and the city's financial mismanagement was also on the list of protestors' grievances.
Klitschko has been in power since 2014 and was decisively reelected as Kyiv's Mayor twice, in 2015 and 2020.
During these terms, Klitschko has been widely criticized for failing to address the city's urgent needs, instead focusing on building developments that demolish "cultural heritage, green zones, and public spaces," wrote activist and veteran Dmytro Koziatynskyi on social media prior to the protest.
This is the second time in October that a protest has been held at the City State Administration's doorstep. In the evening of Oct. 7, people gathered in protest of the mass felling of trees during the construction of a heating pipeline in Teremky, a district fiercely targeted by Russian attacks.
"I just go around all week and tell people at work, and my foreign friends, and everyone about how Kyiv is an incredibly uncomfortable place to live," Kyiv resident Nadiia told the Kyiv Independent during the Oct. 7 protest.
read also
Likelihood of Klitschko's removal
Klitschko's ousting remains unlikely, however.
Kyiv is run in a convoluted manner, with numerous administrative bodies whose duties either overlap or omit certain areas entirely.
Klitschko is currently Kyiv's mayor and, due to the city's special status as the country's capital, is also the head of the Kyiv City State Administration, a post equivalent to a regional governor. According to the law, the elected mayor is usually appointed as the head of the city administration.
The city is also governed by the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA), a structure created by Zelensky following the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. Andrii Tkachov currently leads it and is responsible for "preparing the city for defense, maintaining public order and ensuring the safety of the civilian population, enforcing the legal framework of martial law, and ensuring the city's essential functions," as written on its website.
Only the heads of KMDA and KMVA can be appointed by the president, while the mayor is elected by popular vote.
Considering this, Klitschko cannot be fully dismissed by Zelensky, but can only resign on his own will. What Ukraine's president can do is strip Klitschko of his title as head of the administration, thus limiting his power over decisions in Kyiv.
Following Zelensky's latest criticism, the city's mayor had five minutes in Ukraine's parliament to address the growing issues.
"We, as the city government, are doing everything in our power to ensure the city's functioning, despite the setbacks the central government is constantly trying to inflict on us; unfortunately, this is what their so-called 'cooperation' looks like," he said on Oct. 14.
He also revealed that, so far this year, Kyiv's power grid has been struck nearly 50 times by missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), an increase since last year.
"Where is the capital's air defense? Where is the protection for Ukrenergo's (energy operator) facilities? Where are the billions you allocated for this?" Klitschko appealed, pointing the finger at the government.
In 2026, Kyiv was allocated over $2.3 billion for winter preparation, but only 51.1% had been used as of Sept. 1, according to the Finance Ministry.
The Kyiv Independent reached out to the Kyiv City State Administration and Klitschko with a request for comment, but has not received a response at the time of publication.

Morocco forms new government under 1st ever female prime minister

Morocco announced a new cabinet on Friday, ushering in a historic era with the country’s first female prime minister leading a four-party coalition, Anadolu reports.
According to state-run Maghreb Arabe Presse (MAP), King Mohammed VI received members of the new cabinet, led by Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, and presided over their appointment ceremony at the Royal Palace in the capital Rabat.
El Mansouri is the first Moroccan woman to hold the country’s top government post.
She will lead a new government formed by a four-party coalition comprising her Authenticity and Modernity Party, the Istiqlal Party, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces and the Party of Progress and Socialism.
The new government includes seven women, including El Mansouri, compared with six in the previous government led by Aziz Akhannouch.
READ: Moroccan opposition leader: We are not Israelis; we support Palestine, King, government and people
The new government comprises 32 members, including ministers and ministers-delegate, according to official figures.
Abdelouafi Laftit kept his post as interior minister, alongside Nasser Bourita as foreign minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi as justice minister and Ahmed Toufiq as minister of Islamic affairs and endowments.
The new cabinet also established a Ministry of Artificial Intelligence, Digital Transformation and Administrative Reform, headed by Ahmed Rahhou.

Independent Scotland would leave UK forces their kit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:01:16 BST
18:01:16 KST

EXCLUSIVE – An independent Scotland would, the Scottish National Party believe, have a legitimate claim on its proportionate share of British military equipment but would decline to exercise it if taking the kit caused serious problems for what remained of the United Kingdom, the SNP Westminster leader told me when I sat down with him to chat all things defence.
Dave Doogan, the member for Angus and Perthshire Glens, said the ownership position is clear even if the practical answer is not: “It’s important to remember that we own the assets, all of them proportionately, at the disposal of the UK defence forces, and so we’ve got a call on them. But why would we make problems for the UK by taking our share?”
He set that against the state of the British inventory, where he argues the margin for giving anything away has long since gone: “You know as well as I do that there is very little redundancy in any platform in the United Kingdom. You know, just look at what they were trying to do to get a functioning Type 45 out to the Mediterranean recently. If we think that there are squadrons of Typhoons up and down these islands ready to go at a moment’s notice, that’s not how it is.”
On that basis he ruled out pressing a claim that damaged the rest of the UK, telling me “So if we were to claim our share of eight per cent or whatever of UK assets, and that caused major difficulties for the UK, well, we just wouldn’t do it because it’s not intelligent.”
Division of assets has been one of the hardest parts of the independence argument to pin down since 2014, when the Scottish Government’s white paper assumed Scotland would inherit a share of equipment and the then British government declined to negotiate before a vote. The eight per cent figure Doogan uses reflects Scotland’s rough share of the British population, which was the basis the 2014 prospectus worked from.
Indeed, his point about redundancy lands on a fleet that has been audited repeatedly on exactly that question. The Royal Navy’s six Type 45 destroyers have spent much of the past decade affected by the propulsion problems now addressed through the Power Improvement Project.
Doogan expects the negotiation to be conducted without rancour once the constitutional question is settled, and said the hostility between the two governments is a product of the constitutional argument itself: “That’s the world that we will actually enter after independence. It will be about constructive and mature discussion about here’s where we were, here’s where we are, where do we want to get to, and how do we do that in the best interests of an independent Scotland and the rest of the UK. Because this enmity that exists just now is a function of trying to keep the UK together. Once Scotland’s out of the UK, that enmity has no purpose anymore, and we’ll work together like grown-up and respectful states.”
He argued that cooperation would follow from self-interest on both sides, and that the rest of the UK would deal with Scotland as it deals with everywhere else it once governed: “Let’s not pretend for one minute that the United Kingdom, once all the heat has gone out of an independence debate and Scotland has chosen to be independent, the rest of the UK will cooperate with Scotland just in the same way it cooperates with every other entity and jurisdiction that used to be governed from London. It’s entirely predictable, because it’s to England’s and the rest of the UK’s self interest to cooperate with Scotland, and it’s in Scotland’s interest to cooperate with the rest of the UK.”
The loss of jurisdiction over the northern half of the island would present a problem, he accepted, and one he does not expect to be handled adversarially: “If the SNP or I have got anything to do with that, that won’t be a challenge because we’ll approach it in a cooperative way. How we do that is up for discussion. A brand new independent Scotland would not want to be undefended, but the rest of the UK would not wish a brand new independent Scotland to be undefended either.”
On the deterrent, Doogan said an independent Scotland would have no further locus once the system left Scottish waters, and would take no view on what Westminster did with it afterwards: “It’s not a Scottish asset or system, it’s a UK asset or system. And so what they choose to do with it, where they choose to berth it, whether they choose to sustain and renew it going forward into the future, that’s entirely up to the rest of the UK. Scotland will have no role in that. We’ll respect their sovereignty and their freedom of decision, and they’ll respect ours.”
The kit Scotland would be declining to take is itself under question in his view, and he turned to the surface fleet while discussing the Type 32 frigate, the conceptual class folded into the Future Cruiser Combat Vessel programme without a commitment on where it would be built: “If I’m being honest and being fair, there is now a serious question mark about how many big grey ships you put on the surface of the sea, and how expensive and challenging it is to defend these assets now.”
He went on to set out the arithmetic that worries him, with the air defence destroyers tied to the carriers and the frigates left to look after themselves: “I don’t doubt the capabilities of Type 45, old as it is. It’s still a very potent warship, assuming it’s actually able to move itself, which is not guaranteed with 45. But it’s going to be busy defending two hulking great aircraft carriers, and so 31 and 26 are going to have to do a job defending themselves. That looks increasingly expensive against a volley, literally volley, of inexpensive, very hard to intercept drones.”
That point about escorts protecting themselves runs into an arithmetic problem the whole alliance is grappling with, because a Sea Ceptor round costs a great deal more than the one-way attack drones now being fired in salvoes at ships in the Red Sea and the Black Sea, and the Royal Navy has been working through directed energy and gun-based answers, including DragonFire, for exactly that reason. The Type 45s carry Sea Viper and Aster for area air defence, the capability the carriers depend on, and the fleet has six of them.
Doogan was also blunt about the policy architecture that was supposed to keep the yards busy into the next decade, recalling the ministerial appointments and slogans that have come and gone during his time in the Commons: “I’ve only been in Parliament seven years, and I remember when there was a shipbuilding czar. It was actually Ben Wallace, the Secretary of State for Defence. Not heard much about a shipbuilding czar recently. I remember when it was all about a shipbuilding pipeline. It was an end to boom and bust was what it was going to be. Well, it just goes to show you that those words are easy. What’s difficult is putting the resource in place to make sure that that happens.”
Doogan accepted that competing orders internationally is the straightforward part of the problem, “An anti-boom and bust and an actual pipeline of work, especially when you’re building grey ships, you have to compete it. Unfortunately, you have to compete it internationally. That’s easy. Let’s have, like, a no-brainer. What’s harder is to find the budget.”
On the wider state of conventional forces, he described a force he believes is being hollowed out around the edges, and listed what he sees when he looks at it: “If our soldiers were delighted, if our airmen felt that they had a purpose and that they could get more than a couple of flying hours a month, if our combat aircraft were properly armed, if we stopped buying systems that are fitted for but not with, because we can’t afford to put the missiles in the launch tubes that these systems have, if we weren’t practising launching artillery with two shells a day or a session, because there isn’t enough.”
He acknowledged where some of the ammunition has gone, while arguing that the replenishment should have followed: “Some of that, of course, is because we’ve sent so much artillery to Ukraine. But shells aren’t complex. We should be replenishing them, and it’s unfortunate that that money is just not there.”
Doogan put a figure on the shortfall he believes the Chancellor is facing, and drew a line around the nuclear enterprise while doing it: “You’ll need to find an extra fifteen to twenty billion for defence, and that’s going to be a real challenge. And that’s fifteen, twenty billion for the whole of defence outside the nuclear enterprise.”
The Type 32 was announced by Boris Johnson in November 2020 as a fifth-generation class of general purpose frigates intended to follow Type 31, and it never progressed beyond concept before being absorbed into the Future Cruiser Combat Vessel work that is now running alongside the Type 83 destroyer replacement for Type 45. Rosyth has gone from assembling the Queen Elizabeth class carriers to building the five Type 31 frigates in the Venturer Building, and the sustainability of that drumbeat after the Type 31 order runs out has been a persistent concern in Fife.
Talking about British kit and Scottish yards at this length is itself a change, and Doogan has been pushing his own party in that direction for years against a habit he describes as widespread across Scotland: “Within the SNP more generally, there is a kind of tacit reluctance to engage with defence issues, for a lot of people in Scotland, not just in the SNP. Defence in Scotland begins and ends with the deterrent. There’s an awful lot more to defence in Scotland than the deterrent. But conventional defence is really important, and I’ve worked really hard to try and get that up the SNP’s agenda.”
He called the shift a positive thing and cited the First Minister’s recent visit to Babcock at Rosyth, along with a run of further visits by SNP elected members to defence establishments in Scotland, both completed and upcoming. He traced the argument back to the party’s NATO policy and what he thinks it obliges a government to do: “SNP policy is to be part of NATO. If you want to be part of NATO, you have to accept that peace and security doesn’t land at your feet. And if you don’t ensure by your own words, deeds and resources that you can do everything you possibly can to secure your peace and security, well then you’re not much use as a government to your people, and you’re not much use to your allies as a partner in peace and security.”
He said the case lands with colleagues when it is put to them directly, and that it follows from something the party already accepts about the armed forces: “When you speak to people about it, that’s not a controversial view in the SNP, and I think that’s a good thing, and it’s a work in progress, and people I think are accepting of it because actually it’s an extrapolation of, if we hold our men and women in uniform in the highest of regard, then we must hold what they do in the highest of regard, and if we do that, then we have to accept that they need to be equipped, and that allows us to hold defence manufacturers in high regard too.”
Doogan spent his career in defence engineering, working on Ministry of Defence helicopters, before entering Parliament in 2019. Asked what he would say to a young person in Scotland weighing up a career in the sector, he was unequivocal: “Any young person looking at possibly taking a job in engineering, do it. And getting a job in engineering and defence, do it, because if for no other reason, in defence you’re operating to the highest of standards in the best of conditions often, and those skills are in huge demand globally and domestically. So it’s a very good employment opportunity.”
He had made a related point at an industry event the previous evening, taking issue with the way politicians talk about employment: “Politicians have a habit of just talking about jobs in abstract, as though all jobs are equal. All jobs are not equal. Engineering jobs are an extremely attractive career proposition, and defence engineering jobs in particular are an extremely attractive employment proposition. So anybody thinking about that, I would say go on ahead and do it, because the more people that repopulate our defence sector in Scotland, the better.”
The same session covered the sub-threshold threats facing Britain and Scotland, which he put in terms of the damage they do to ordinary economic life: “Talking about the range of sub-threshold grey zone threats that we face, which aren’t in themselves the end of the world, but are a serious impediment. See Jaguar Land Rover, serious impediment to our freedom and liberty and our economy and people’s jobs.”
Doogan’s comments come a day after the Scottish Government confirmed it will match the ten million pounds offered by the Ministry of Defence to establish two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges in Scotland, ending a wait of seven months since the offer was made in March. Alyn Smith, the Innovation Minister, wrote jointly with Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn to confirm the money, with sites to be allocated in the east and west of the country covering defence engineering, advanced manufacturing and maritime technology.
The sector Doogan wants repopulated employs a substantial number of people across Scotland. BAE Systems builds the Type 26 frigates at Govan and Scotstoun, Babcock assembles the Type 31 at Rosyth, Leonardo produces radar and electronic warfare equipment in Edinburgh, Thales builds optronics and missile systems at Govan, and Raytheon operates at Glenrothes. All of them compete for the same welders, electrical technicians and systems engineers, and all of them have warned about the pipeline.
The SNP’s position on defence has moved considerably over the past two years, with the Programme for Government committing to a responsible defence industrial growth programme, a formulation that keeps public money away from munitions while backing the wider sector. Doogan describes the shift inside his own party as unfinished work.

All the president’s women: a familiar downward trajectory in Trump’s cabinet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:00:28 UTC
18:00:28 KST

Donald Trump is not, by any measure, a feminist. He has said so himself. But the president has often pointed to his hiring and promoting of women in an attempt to stave off criticism of both his policies and personal conduct over the years.
During his second term, however, there is one common characteristic among most of those who have departed the Trump administration.
In the space of just a few months, half of his eight female cabinet officials have either resigned or been fired. All have been replaced by men. Several other women in his administration have also departed, whether voluntarily or involuntarily.
On Friday, Trump was forced to deny reports that he was considering replacing Susie Wiles, his White House chief of staff, and the first woman to do the job. “She’s gonna be here for a long time,” he claimed.
Numerous top male officials, meanwhile, from Trump’s defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who has on multiple occasions courted global condemnation, to the widely ridiculed FBI director Kash Patel, have survived intense scrutiny and repeated calls for their resignation – and yet remain in post.
Katie Zacharia
The latest female casualty was White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, who was fired on Friday just five days into the role. After a rocky start to her tenure, sparked by a widely panned first White House press briefing on Tuesday, she had also faced questions over her legal credentials after admitting she did not pass the bar exam. The ensuing semantics battle over whether or not she is a lawyer, or an attorney, placed her in a pickle – even with the rightwing cable network Fox News.
Zacharia had taken over from Karoline Leavitt, who said in August that she had chosen to resign from the role after 20 months so she could spend more time with her young family.
Kristi Noem
In terms of firings, the first domino to fall was former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem, who was the face of Trump’s mass deportation campaign until she was unceremoniously sacked on 5 March. Her tenure was plagued by controversy, in large part amid national uproar over federal immigration enforcement operations that killed two US citizens in Minneapolis (one of whom Noem called a “domestic terrorist”, with no evidence), and coincided with a sharp decline in national support for Trump’s immigration agenda.
Her suggestion at a congressional hearing in March that Trump had known about her decision to approve a contract for a $220m ad campaign to encourage immigrants to “self-deport” – which prominently featured Noem on horseback – reportedly left Trump “pissed” and appeared to be the straw that broke the camel’s back. There had also been scrutiny of general leadership failures under Noem, as well as questions the influence of her adviser, Corey Lewandowski, who also left his role when she was ousted.
Noem was repurposed as special envoy to the so-called “Shield of the Americas” coalition and, after that arrangement expired last month, is now serving in a vaguely defined advisory role. She was succeeded as DHS secretary by Markwayne Mullin.
Pam Bondi
Next fell former attorney general and Trump loyalist Pam Bondi, who was pushed out in April after a turbulent 14 months that saw the president increasingly frustrated over her mishandling of the Department of Justice’s long-awaited release of the Epstein files. The Epstein issue became a huge political liability for Trump and infuriated his Maga base, and he also felt that Bondi had failed to sufficiently prosecute his political enemies.
Bondi revealed a month after she was ousted that she had been diagnosed with thyroid cancer. Her deputy, Todd Blanche, assumed the role in August.
It’s worth noting that commerce secretary Howard Lutnick faced public scrutiny after details emerged surrounding his past ties to Jeffrey Epstein and visits to his private island emerged. By contrast, the White House supported him after Democrats called for his resignation.
Lori Chavez-DeRemer
Also in April, former labor secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer stepped down after a Department of Labor inspector general investigation led to a series of allegations of misconduct, including having an affair with a subordinate and drinking alcohol on the job. She was replaced by Keith Sonderling.
Kash Patel has also been alleged to have been intoxicated or absent on the job. He has denied these allegations, and remains FBI director.
Tulsi Gabbard
A month later, in May, Tulsi Gabbard resigned from her position as Trump’s national intelligence director.
While she officially cited her husband’s rare cancer diagnosis, Gabbard was reportedly forced out after a tumultuous stint in which she was largely sidelined as Trump launched attacks on Venezuela and Iran. She had previously testified to Congress that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon.
Gabbard was replaced on an acting basis by Bill Pulte, a Trump loyalist with no previous experience in the intelligence sphere, and eventually by Jay Clayton.
Kimberly Guilfoyle
Earlier this week, the Trump administration asked longtime Trump ally Kimberly Guilfoyle to step down from her position as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials.
The only senior male official to have been somewhat punished by Trump since his return to office is Mike Waltz. The then-national security adviser was fired in May last year after inadvertently adding a journalist to a Signal group chat in which Hegseth disclosed secret war plans.
Waltz had been on thin ice with Trump for a while, and the president was reportedly annoyed by Waltz’s hawkish stance on Iran. Signalgate merely sealed his fate.
But he didn’t disappear to some obscure advisory role; Waltz was nominated to the position of US ambassador to the United Nations. Hegseth, meanwhile, was allowed to ride out the controversy and – several controversies later, including allegations of war crimes – remains in post.
Democrats have highlighted the double standard that Trump only seems to fire women in his administration – even those who are ultra-loyal to him, and decidedly less incompetent than some of their male colleagues.
“If you’re a man in the Trump administration, it seems that they reward misconduct,” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the Democratic congresswoman, observed in April.
“I wouldn’t say I’m a feminist,” Trump said in a 2018 interview. “I mean, I think that would be, maybe, going too far. I’m for women. I’m for men. I’m for everyone.”
But not everyone gets to stick around.

Honeybees are barging aside wild pollinators in hunt for pollen and nectar, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:00:27 UTC
18:00:27 KST

Honeybees are outcompeting wild pollinators for resources by aggressively bumping into them and chasing them away from flowers, research has shown.
The study, by researchers from Anglia Ruskin University, found that areas where there were higher concentrations of honeybees had fewer wild pollinators, such as bumblebees, solitary bees and hoverflies.
Honeybees were also most likely to instigate, and win, competitive interactions, pushing out rivals to collect more pollen and nectar.
The number of managed bees has risen in the UK, as campaigns to “save the bees” resonate with the public, leading to a boom in hobbyists setting up beehives. The number of registered beekeepers has more than doubled, from 19,000 in 2010 to 47,000 in 2025, according to the National Bee Unit.
However, there are growing concerns that this growth in managed honeybees is harming other, wild, pollinators including bumblebees, by increasing competition for food and passing on diseases, especially in areas where there are fewer flowers or an especially high density of hives.
To better understand the nature of this competition, the study in Cambridgeshire observed pollinators over a two-year period as they foraged on bramble and ivy in areas close to honeybee colonies. The study documented the outcomes of 300 interactions between flower visitors from five groups: honeybees, bumblebees, solitary bees, hoverflies and “other”, which included types of flower-visiting and pollinating flies, butterflies, beetles and wasps.
In each interaction, the study noted where an individual “won”, by gaining access to a resource, “lost”, or if a resource was shared. Honeybees won in most of the encounters across both plant species.
Past research has suggested that honeybees outcompete other pollinators indirectly, by taking up resources. However, the Cambridgeshire study provides evidence that they are posing a more direct form of competition, known as “interference competition”, where a species might attack or chase others away.
“That’s important because, of course, it means that the wild pollinators are facing a challenge from both those types of competition from honeybees,” said Victoria Buckle, lead author of the study and a PhD researcher at Anglia Ruskin University.
Honeybees were actively avoided by other flower visitors in 28.4% of interactions on bramble and 35.6% on ivy.
In competitive interactions won by a honeybee, the honeybee either displaced other flower visitors – for example, by landing on them or pushing them off flowers – or chased them away, in about 20% of cases.
Bumblebees were also observed displacing other pollinators, though Buckle believes this was probably not intentional, and was instead a reflection of their less coordinated movements as they fly through confined spaces.
“They bumble along the patch and then they’ll mistakenly bump into another pollinator and it just falls off a flower,” Buckle said. “With the honeybees, the aggression was more overt. You could tell that they’re specifically trying to move the other one off the flower.”
The reasons for honeybees’ aggressive behaviour is likely to relate to the way in which they organise their social groups, said Buckle, adding: “Some castes of bees can be guard bees, so they have that capacity within them to show threat and aggression, to guard their hives and to look after the brood.”
The only pollinator able to hold its own against honeybees was the ivy bee, which was first recorded in the UK in 2001 and feeds mainly on the nectar of ivy flowers. It was seen displacing and chasing honeybees.
The study also found that higher temperatures led to an increased number of competitive interactions, probably because nectar was drying up and plants were going into heat stress. Given that mean summer temperatures are predicted to rise by up to 4C in the UK by 2080, such competition is likely to become more frequent, said Buckle.
More research is needed to examine how wild pollinators can be better protected, she added.
“A lot of beekeepers are environmentally minded and they want to make sure that they’re not impinging or having an impact on other pollinators,” Buckle said. “This research is important because it helps guide our planning and best practices for conservation.”
