Squash down: smaller pumpkins expected this Halloween after drought in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:00:26 UTC
18:00:26 KST

In the lead-up to Halloween, front porches across the country feature fat, proudly carved pumpkins, lit from within by tea lights.
But this year there is likely to be a shortage due to drought, experts have warned, with the squashes much smaller than usual.
Mini pumpkins will have to be used, and some have suggested that those celebrating the spooky festival draw faces on vegetables instead of carving them.
England has faced a punishing drought for most of this year, which has dramatically affected harvests. Data has found that this year could be the worst harvest on record as farmers struggled to irrigate their crops.
Pumpkins are 90% water, and need a lot of it to grow. The vegetables are native to the Americas and were brought over in the Tudor period, during the 16th century.
Guy Singh-Watson, the founder of organic veg box company Riverford, said: “After such an extraordinarily hot, dry summer, it’s not surprising that Halloween pumpkins are smaller than usual as they are mostly water. But perhaps it’s time we questioned our obsession with giant carving pumpkins in the first place.”
Shunning pumpkins would go some way to bringing the carving of vegetables tradition back to its roots. The custom began in 17th-century Britain while marking the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain, which was when spirits were thought to roam the Earth.
Rather than pumpkins, root vegetables such as celeriac, turnips and mangelwurzels were carved into grotesque faces, and some believed they could ward off evil spirits.
Guy Barter, the chief horticulturalist at the Royal Horticultural Society, said: “Pumpkins are on the small side this year unless heavily watered. Such drought makes watering sufficiently very difficult to accomplish in practice. Pumpkins are relatively drought-tolerant but this year the weather stretched their tolerance to the limit.
“The heat later and some drought stress caused fruits to ripen earlier than usual. Their dry matter content and rind hardness are both excellent so the crop should store well, although commercial pumpkins become worthless the day after Halloween. That’s a pity as they make lovely soups until the new year when the much tastier winter squashes take over.”
Singh-Watson said the growing of a large, watery squash simply to throw it away after Halloween was wasteful, adding: “I’ve enjoyed growing pumpkins before, they’re a lovely crop, but the idea of growing something that’s going to be thrown away has become increasingly difficult to justify. Growing any crop comes with an environmental cost, and generating a mountain of waste without feeding anyone makes little sense.”
The vegetable entrepreneur has been growing a selection of small, colourful squashes and is now selling a box containing a selection including crown prince, red onion, sweet lightning, futsu and stripetti. He said: “This time of the year should be a celebration of the wonderful abundance of seasonal vegetables that see us through autumn and winter. Squash come in an extraordinary variety of shapes, sizes and colours, and offer just as much decorative potential, with considerably more flavour. Let’s paint a face on a squash instead … and then eat it.”
Some gardeners have been trying novel methods to try to get the size of pumpkins up.
Ali Goding, the garden manager at RHS Harlow Carr in North Yorkshire, said: “Pumpkins struggle to grow in heavy clay soil during drought conditions, so the team at RHS garden Harlow Carr have trialled a new, novel way to grow pumpkins this year – in a compost cake which helps retain moisture, humidity and warmth and the results have been fantastic while also benefiting wildlife.
“They have set with hard skins in the heat so should store well and they will also have a good flavour with all that sun.
“Normally we are a bit cool, damp and too far north for them to develop a full flavour – so the extra heat worked out well for us. A good year!”

Stinky business: south London bike shop hit by ‘unbearable’ stench from Thames Water sewer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:00:26 UTC
18:00:26 KST

The leafy south London neighbourhood of Herne Hill is a haven for cyclists who can often be seen lapping the local parks and refuelling at the many cafes that line the suburban streets. But there is something foul in the air of this corner of the capital – and for once it’s not the traffic fumes hitting bicycle riders.
A toxic stench thought to be caused by untreated sewage stuck in Thames Water drains has been emanating from the subterranean depths for months, most likely caused by the summer’s lack of rain.
The stink is so acrid that the Bicycle Nation shop has had to bar some customers and its mechanics have been forced to work on the pavement outside.
The owner of the shop, Tamas Polocz, has repeatedly complained to Thames Water since the smell first hit the shop in June and caused his colleague Nick to vomit.
Last week the troubled water company told Polocz it accepted that a mains sewer directly beneath the shop was to blame, but it has yet to offer him and his team of 11 any date for resolving the problem.
Polocz and his colleagues have been left fearing for their physical and mental health after repeated exposure to the gassy stench. And the outlook for the business is bleak.
The odour comes in putrid wafts that occur at least five times a day, according to a “smell chart” used to log the time and duration of each incident with a description. The words used include “cabbage”, “teargas”, “onions”, “spicy BBQ” and repeated references to “shit”.
When the Guardian first arrived at the shop there was a whiff of rotten eggs but not enough to stop mechanics working inside and customers milling about. But within minutes we were overpowered by a repulsive gas that hit the back of the throat and left us scurrying outside, gagging for air.
“It’s unbearable,” said Polocz. “You can’t be in the shop when it comes.”
He added: “It has a really strong physical presence. This is a smell you take home with you. It’s in your hair, on your skin, sometimes it feels it’s inside your skin. When you go home and cough, you taste it again.”
The ordeal comes after record-breaking temperatures and drought prompted calls for a radical overhaul of an outdated sewage system, just as the Great Stink ushered in new sanitation in the Victorian era.
Thames Water initially suggested the Herne Hill smell was due to a gas leak. But extensive tests by the local gas supplier ruled that out.
Polocz said he had been battling the company every week. “Thames Water have always tried to push me away, or blame others. When they finally accepted liability last week I just broke down. But we still don’t have a date for fixing it.”
The exact cause of the stench remains unknown, but a Thames Water engineer told Polocz it was likely to be linked to the lack of rain. The engineer also told him that a cast-iron ventilation pipe that had previously drawn odours away from the shop had not been replaced.
Experts warn that during dry periods, untreated sewage builds up in pipes with no rainwater to flush it out. Microbial activity in the sewage causes foul-smelling gas to be emitted in wafts, in a similar process to the one that causes flatulence in human digestion.
Prof Barbara Evans, the chair of public health engineering at Leeds University, said: “It sounds like methane and it’s probably unsafe working conditions. Biological processes are cyclical just like in your digestive system, which is why sewer smells come in wafts.”
When Polocz woke up to rainfall, he was hopeful it would flush away the stench. “I looked out through the window at home and thought, oh good, but it didn’t make any difference. Even after the rain there was still the smell. Maybe the rain will eventually clear it, but we don’t know. Something is happening down there that is pushing the smell up.”
Evans said: “The first flushes of rain will probably make things smell worse because it just stirs things up. It needs a lot of rain to clear. There might be some blockage there but it’s impossible to know without a proper inspection.”
Harriet Talbot, a board member of Bicycle Nation, said: “You can’t run a business relying on the weather.” She helped set up a webpage asking for customers to sign up for a collect and repair service to help the shop survive.
Polocz said the shop was currently unsustainable because staff had to evacuate so frequently. “We have to do half a day in the shop and half outside on the pavement. But now the cold weather is coming, we can’t keep doing that.”
And the stress from the stink is taking its toll. Polocz said: “I’m 49, but today I feel 62-ish. We have guys calling in sick. It affects you both physically and mentally.”
Polocz said he laid in bed at night worrying how he would be able to keep the shop going. “The last thought of the day and the first thought of the day are now both the same,” he said. “And I wake up at night thinking: what are we going to do about it? I try to listen to a podcast, but I still keep thinking about the smell. Somehow I’m going to get through this and change back to normal.”
Polocz’s plight is likely to add to calls for an overhaul of London’s Victorian sewage system. Evans said: “This underlines the need for a rethink of our sewers. The system was designed for a climate that we just don’t currently have any more.”
The Guardian asked Thames Water when the problem would be fixed, why it had taken so long to resolve, and whether the company would apologise to Polocz.
A spokesperson replied: “Our teams are investigating the source of an odour reported at a bike shop. Initial investigations have confirmed there are no blockages in the sewers surrounding the property. Odour monitors are to be installed, which will enable engineers to detect, measure and track odorous gases in real time and help determine the exact cause.”

Shisha smoking will cause 1 million new lung cancer cases globally by 2050: WHO study

Shisha smoking will cause 1 million new lung cancer cases globally by 2050: WHO study
Western Pacific region will bear the brunt of such cases, says Dr Mahdi Sheikh of International Agency for Research on Cancer
Water pipe smoking will contribute to about 1 million new lung cancer cases globally by 2050, with the Western Pacific region bearing the brunt, according to a study led by a World Health Organization (WHO) research agency that was recently presented in Hong Kong.
The study, which is yet to be published, was headed by Dr Mahdi Sheikh, a scientist of the early detection, prevention and infections branch at the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). It estimated that there would be 82 million new lung cancer cases around the world between 2025 and 2050, with 944,700 or 1.1 per cent of them caused by water pipe smoking.
“One per cent does not seem a lot, but when you translate it into numbers, it’s 1 million cases – when we want to save lives, every life matters,” Sheikh told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of the World Cancer Congress, which was held in Hong Kong for the first time in late September.
“Most of these countries have a low or medium human development index … it means that the burden is going to cluster in the countries with the least resources, which could bear the least burden of cancer.”

Microplastics React With Water, a New Study Says. That’s a Problem for Biology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

One of the reasons plastic has become so ubiquitous is that, generally, it’s very chemically stable, meaning it does not readily react with the substances around it. That’s why this material is so often used for food packaging and water bottles.
The same was thought to be true of microplastics—those tiny pieces of debris that break off from larger plastic objects and which, according to numerous studies, have spread to virtually every ecosystem on the planet. But scientists at Columbia University and UC Berkeley have just discovered that water can make the surfaces of microplastics chemically active and turn them into a potential hazard.
According to the findings of the article published in Nature, this activity can trigger the spontaneous formation of chemicals capable of altering other molecules, like those that are essential for living organisms. The phenomenon, the authors note, occurs even under normal environmental conditions, without the need for sunlight or other agents that cause plastic degradation.
So how can microplastics be so reactive when bigger plastics generally aren’t? The scientists suggest this has to do with the greater available surface area for these reactions to occur.
“As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously,” Wei Min, a professor of chemistry and biomedical engineering at Columbia University, said in a press release. “Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure.”
Among these potentially dangerous chemical products—called reactive oxygen species—a variety known as hydroxyl radicals stands out. They are particularly dangerous because they can snatch electrons from the proteins and fats that make up cell membranes, disrupting their structure and function. These “are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue,” added Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Min’s lab who helped lead the research.
Our body has some defenses against this kind of damage. This is the biological function of the buzzy molecules known as antioxidants. These neutralize the reactive chemicals, but if the reactive compounds greatly outnumber antioxidants, this line of defense can be overwhelmed.
This can develop into a scenario called oxidative stress, leading to the damage of cells. Previous research had already identified oxidative stress among the cellular responses associated with exposure to microplastics, although the mechanisms responsible for this damage are not yet fully understood.
The extent to which microplastics have pervaded our bodies remains an open debate, with some of the more sensational findings having been called into question. But if even a small amount of microplastics are present in our tissues, they could be reacting with the water in our bodies.
The researchers were particularly concerned with the potential effects on blood, which is largely composed of water. If contact with this fluid can chemically activate the surfaces of microplastics, their presence inside the body could pose an additional danger beyond that of the pollutants they carry or release.
When the researchers exposed red blood cells extracted from mice to different types of microplastics, the cells became deformed and ruptured—a phenomenon known as hemolysis. The effects were greater with plastics that were more reactive with water, indicating that this activity was the cause of cellular damage.
Research into the effects of microplastics has long focused on other chemicals leaching from the particles or on their physical effects, often considering the plastic itself chemically inert. The larger pieces generally are, but these findings challenge the assumption that what is true of plastic on a grand scale is also true of the microscopic pieces it breaks down into.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Why AI Isn’t Ready to Tackle Our Convoluted Genomes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
Since its molecular structure was deduced in the 1950s, DNA has been hailed by many biologists as the secret of life. They’ve read and studied the information stored in the DNA found in the cells of living organisms, known as their genomes, and claimed that this genetic database must be some kind of blueprint, code script, or computer. But if DNA really does harbor some greater secret about how life works, biologists have yet to find it.
In fact, the human genome is less a script than a puzzle that gets harder the closer they look. Knowing the entire sequence—the order of all 3 billion or so of our DNA’s chemical building blocks, nearly fully deduced by the international Human Genome Project between 1990 and 2003—hasn’t helped much. That investigation showed that barely 2 percent of the human genome consists of actual genes, the information-coding sequences of DNA.
It’s now clear that understanding the human genome is no longer a matter of figuring out what each gene does. The deeper and much harder question is how those genes are used, or regulated, a question that seems to involve some and perhaps much of the rest of the genome. By switching suites of genes on and off, the many different cell types in our bodies can all be created from the same material. Cells also regulate their genes from moment to moment in response to a constant inflow of signals from their neighbors and surroundings. But the processes that govern gene regulation are proving so complex that some biologists wonder whether a full understanding of it—of how the genome really works—will ever be within the grasp of our puny minds.
Some are counting on outsourcing the analysis to artificial intelligence. Genomic “foundation models” such as Evo 2, Genos, and Google DeepMind’s AlphaGenome are trained on vast quantities of genomic data, which biologists use to make predictions about how differences in DNA sequence affect biological processes and ultimately the traits (including disease risk) of a whole organism. These algorithms don’t worry about the complicated regulatory stuff going on. All of that is supposedly subsumed by the algorithm’s “training,” through which it deduces correlations from cases we already know about.
This approach is likely to be useful, but for those who crave real understanding of how the genome, and ultimately life itself, works, a computational black box will never suffice. And perhaps more to the point, the genome might not submit to the kind of straightforward input-output approach that such AI models ultimately assume.
That’s because the genome is no blueprint or algorithm. It’s something else.
Given that it’s the product of around 4 billion years of evolution, perhaps it’s not surprising that our genome is complicated. The surprise has been what those complications are. “Our genome is not what we might make it if we sat down at the drawing board,” said the biologist Karen Adelman, who studies gene regulation at Harvard Medical School.
The traditional view posits that a small proportion of our DNA holds the code for making the protein molecules that orchestrate our cells’ chemistry. Each instruction for a protein is held in a corresponding gene—we have around 20,000 of these—and gene sequences can range in length from a couple of dozen to almost 3 million DNA “letters” (representing molecules called nucleotides).
Making a protein from its gene is a two-stage affair. First the DNA is read, letter by letter, by an enzyme called a polymerase, which creates a copy of that code in a related molecule called messenger RNA (mRNA). This is called transcription. The mRNA is then read by a piece of molecular machinery called the ribosome, which constructs the protein—a process called translation. The proteins made by the ribosome then go off to do their jobs in making and sustaining the organism.
This picture is still more or less correct. But it turns out that “the genes are probably not the most interesting part of the genome,” Adelman said.
What matters more is how our genes, many of which we share with simpler organisms, are regulated—turned on and off. Which proteins a cell needs changes over time and according to cell type: muscle, brain, skin, and so on. How the genes that encode those proteins are regulated depends on some of the genome that doesn’t code for proteins.
Biologists have known about gene regulation, and the involvement of “noncoding” DNA, since the 1960s. But for many years, most of what they understood about this came from studies of simple organisms like bacteria, where the principles are generally straightforward. It has gradually become clear, though, that in complex eukaryotic organisms like us, gene regulation is far more complicated, involving overlapping systems of oversight and control, each with its own intricacies.
Transcription gets started by proteins called transcription factors, which are like the operations managers of gene regulation. These proteins stick to sections of DNA (typically close to the target gene) and recruit the polymerase enzyme to make an mRNA copy. In bacteria, transcription factors are rather like keys that fit the locks of unique binding sites on DNA. But that’s not how they work in complex organisms. In us, the logic of transcription factors is more difficult to parse.
For one thing, our transcription factors don’t show strong preferences for particular DNA binding sites. What’s more, they tend to work in pairs or groups. And a given transcription factor might have different effects in different contexts, such as activating gene transcription in one cell type but suppressing it in another, depending on which other transcription factors are around.
In bacteria, regulation tends to have an “OR” logic, Adelman said, whereby a particular signal turns a gene on or off: It’s either this or that. But in the human genome the logic is more like what computer scientists designate “AND.” Many signals are integrated to reach a regulatory decision: This and that and also that other thing. In this case, regulation can be more responsive to nuances of context, and the regulatory knobs are tunable rather than being just on or off. “This is part of the beauty” of our regulatory complexity, Adelman said.
When they interact with the genome, transcription factors bind to pieces of DNA called enhancers—which present a puzzle of their own.
Enhancers are gathering points for transcription factors, and they are thought to be the decisive influence on transcription: They deliver the “go” signal for a waiting polymerase to make an mRNA version of the DNA sequence. Seems simple enough, but mapping enhancers to their respective genes is far from straightforward. Our genome has hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions, of enhancers. That means we have many more of them than we have genes. Each gene might be influenced by many enhancers, and each enhancer might influence multiple genes.
“It’s embarrassing that 25 years after the Human Genome Project, we don’t know where all the enhancers are in the genome, let alone what they do when they act and which genes they control,” said Wendy Bickmore, a genome biologist at the University of Edinburgh.
Biologists do know that most enhancers won’t respond to a single transcription factor. Their activation “requires a cocktail,” Bickmore said. “That’s what gives [an enhancer] that exquisite specificity—because it’s only in a particular cell at a particular time that you have the right combination of factors to bind and activate that enhancer.”
Some enhancers are, as you’d expect, close to the genes they regulate, or even sit on DNA inside a gene. But others sit far away from the gene—perhaps millions of nucleotides away, with more genes in between.
The existence of such so-called “distal” enhancers “seems bonkers,” Bickmore said. “How do you get that information from over there to over here, to the gene that needs to be activated? That’s a largely unanswered question.”
One of the answers comes in the form of a loop.
Distal enhancers are brought to the gene they regulate on great loops of DNA or, more strictly, of chromatin, the combination of DNA and its packaging proteins that are unraveled as if from a ball of wool. The loops are created by a protein motor called cohesin, which runs up and down the DNA strand and extrudes it as needed.
Once cohesin has formed a loop to bring elements together, what then? It was once thought that they then stick together or assemble into a molecular machine, but they don’t. Rather, the components appear to form a loose but dense blob in which they interact rather weakly, fleetingly, and indiscriminately—a sort of committee, sometimes called a condensate.
These transcription hubs are extremely fluid and differ from one cell to another. “There’ll be a bit of loop extrusion going on over here, in the next cell it might be over here, and the whole thing is turning over incredibly fast,” Bickmore said. Even if the cells are notionally identical—both skin cells, say—exactly what the gene-regulatory machinery is up to at any moment is never quite the same in any two of them.
Chromatin loops are just one reason why a gene’s transcription depends on the shape and structure of the chromatin around it.
The textbook image of a chromosome—one of the 46 units into which our genomes are divided—is of a compact, X-shaped cluster of chromatin. But any time a cell is not actively dividing, its chromatin is unwound into what looks like a tangled mess. There is order to the chaos, however. Some parts of chromatin are densely packed into a form called heterochromatin. The compacted DNA there is relatively inaccessible to transcription factors; the genes it contains are typically silenced. Meanwhile, other parts are relatively loose, open, and accessible: This is called euchromatin.
There are special enzymes involved in packaging and repackaging chromatin, thereby controlling transcription. In other words, what matters is not just the encoded information in the DNA but also how it exists physically and dynamically in space. “We’ve stopped thinking about the genome as a linear piece of DNA code,” Bickmore said. “Thinking about this incredibly dynamic three-dimensional folding as absolutely inherent to regulation is a very exciting change.”
One aspect of this 3D organization is the clustering of segments of chromatin into compartments called topologically associating domains (TADs). Within a TAD, the genes seem to be coregulated: switched on or off in groups. Such groups keep suites of genes active or silent together to form and provide function in different cell types. Cohesin is also involved in the shuffling of chromatin to construct TADs—a dynamic process in which the chromatin is constantly rearranged in our cells.
Chromatin shape can also be influenced by chemical modifications called epigenetic marks: small molecules attached to DNA packaging proteins called histones or stuck directly to DNA. Some of these epigenetic modifications can alter the electrical charges on histones, which changes how the proteins attract or repel one another and so rejigs the chromatin packing. Epigenetic modifications to chromatin are like annotations of the DNA script that change its meaning in a given context. When cells divide, the epigenetic annotations are copied, too.
How and when the marks get added and changed, and what each type of mark means for gene activity, are complex questions with no simple answers. Some researchers talk of an “epigenetic code” governing this aspect of gene regulation, but it’s far from clear if anything so systematic really exists.
All of these processes and others can determine whether a gene gets transcribed into mRNA. But there are further layers of regulation that determine whether the mRNA is then translated into a corresponding protein—and which protein arises.
This post-transcriptional regulation is often controlled by RNA molecules that are said to be noncoding. These short-lived molecules aren’t templates for proteins, as mRNA is, but have other jobs of their own. While mRNA is produced from the protein-coding areas of DNA (so-called “coding genes”), noncoding RNAs are transcribed from other DNA regions now generally described as noncoding genes. These noncoding RNAs are versatile, taking on varied roles in a cell. Researchers are learning more about what they can do every day, and many if not most of them seem to be involved in gene regulation.
Small noncoding RNAs called microRNAs, for example, can silence mRNAs before they can be translated into proteins. They do this by guiding special enzymes to a particular mRNA to degrade or chemically modify it. The microRNAs don’t do this job alone but, not unlike transcription factors, act combinatorially, in groups, and in a rather promiscuous manner: A given microRNA might regulate many mRNAs, and a given mRNA might be regulated by many microRNAs.
Why make an mRNA only to stop it getting translated in a protein? This sort of post-transcriptional regulation is like having another checkpoint: Does the cell really need this protein? MicroRNAs can be mobilized to allow cells to adjust gene expression depending on the immediate context. In this way, the workings of the genome are less like a program’s inevitable progression and more like an adaptive and responsive process.
Another post-transcriptional complication is that mRNAs get translated to protein only after they have been reorganized. Fresh from transcription, an mRNA contains sequences that encode bits of protein, called exons, as well as sequences that shouldn’t be translated and need to be snipped out, called introns. (Strictly speaking, this pre-edited RNA is called pre-mRNA.) The job of editing introns out and splicing exons together is done by a molecular assembly called the spliceosome, which is made from several proteins together with various noncoding RNAs.
The spliceosome too can be sensitive to context, so that it might splice the pre-mRNA to encode one protein in one cell type and a slightly different protein in another. Sometimes these different protein “isoforms” can have very different roles. Transcription factors, for example, are often alternatively spliced in this way, and their isoforms can take on different regulatory tasks—some might activate gene expression, for instance, while others repress it.
All told, these and other regulatory mechanisms show that the genome is far from some automated program running in the background to build us and keep us alive. Our cells are, in effect, making complex decisions about how to use their genes—both the information they contain and the structure they assume.
Thus, cells need to assemble a rather loose and fuzzy committee of components, such as transcription factors and enhancers, to get transcription underway, which also depends on how the chromatin strand is shaped and molded at that moment. Then there are further layers of decisionmaking and action-taking in between mRNA and the final, functional protein.
Remember, too, that all the players—from transcription factors to noncoding RNAs—are themselves produced from the genome in the same kind of context-dependent process. That makes the genome rather like a recursive, self-referential system that the computer scientist Douglas Hofstadter dubbed “a strange loop.” It acts on itself, mindful of its own history—which determines chromatin conformation and epigenetic markings, say—and heedful of messages from inside and outside the cell. Not, then, a blueprint.
And for that reason, not at all easy to understand. “I wouldn’t have designed it this way if I was God,” Bickmore said. “But here we are!”
Why is gene regulation in animals like us so darned complicated? One potential answer is that evolution doesn’t have the foresight to design with efficiency and transparent logic, but merely tinkers with what it has already available. Maybe so—but eukaryotic gene regulation isn’t just a messy version of what happens in bacteria. It has different principles, and there’s surely a reason for them.
Bickmore suspects that the complexity of regulation and of genome organization might have been the only means of generating complexity in the organism. For example, organisms with many tissue types and varied lifestyles required more control over which genes were on or off in a given cell. One thing this demanded was more and more noncoding regulatory sequences in DNA. But then they couldn’t all fit close to the gene itself.
“As you get more complexity, you need to add more and more enhancers,” Bickmore said. “But where are you going to put them? You start to put them farther and farther away. Once they are [far enough], you start to need TADs and three-dimensional [chromatin] folding to allow those things to work.”
We also need regulatory complexity because, over evolutionary time, the human genome has accumulated DNA from parasitic viruses in the form of jumping genetic material called transposable elements. These sequences have inserted themselves all over our chromosomes and are good at replicating themselves. To sift the good DNA from the bad, we needed additional layers of regulation to ensure that cells weren’t translating RNAs they don’t really need or that could be actively harmful.
With so many context-dependent checks and balances in the workings of our genome, it is evidently not a program or algorithm that predictably generates the same outcome in every situation. It’s an open informational system that responds to external inputs and the genome’s dynamic internal conditions. This poses a challenge if AI relies solely on the genetic sequences within genomes to predict what genomes will do.
Researchers Developing AI-based genomic foundation models, such as AlphaGenome, hope that all these layers of regulation—transcription factors, splicing, epigenetic marks, loops, chromatin packing, and so on—will be implicitly included in the correlations that the algorithms learn between genetic sequence and organismal traits. They’re content for the complexity described above to be in a black box, so long as the model generates accurate predictions. But will that work?
“I’m sure [AlphaGenome] is going to be useful, but with limitations,” Bickmore said. “To me the big gap is in the complexity of the human body—in all the cell types and how they change over time in development. And all that data is missing.”
Fundamentally, the challenge is that the genome is not a set of static, linear instructions. It is highly dynamic, and it uses its information contextually, with combinatorial and promiscuous logic. “Whether we’ll ever be able to capture that aspect” in algorithms like AlphaGenome, “I don’t know,” she said.
Yet the problem goes even deeper because the functioning of specific organisms, including each of us, doesn’t just depend on genomes. Other factors, such as diet, environment, microbiome, and, for us at least, culture, can matter hugely, too—not just in terms of how we act and how healthy we are but also in the state of our genome itself. The biologist Adrian Woolfson, cofounder of California-based biotech company Genyro, which aims to use AI systems for so-called “generative biology,” calls this information cloud the “informiome.”
“While the human genome forms the foundation of the human informiome, other layers of extra-genetic information are equally important,” Woolfson wrote in his book On the Future of Species, published in April 2026. Genomic foundation models won’t even be able to predict all the consequences of genetic mutations, he argued, because the relevant information is not in the genome sequence in the first place.
So how should we think about the genome? Maybe the only metaphors that can capture the way the genome really works must come from biology itself. In 2020, the biological historian Evelyn Fox compared the genome to “an exquisitely sensitive reactive system.” Rather than a sequence of genes leading to the formation of traits, she said, it’s more of “a device for regulating the production of specific proteins in response to constantly changing signals it receives from its environment.”
That sounds close to the picture painted by the geneticist Barbara McClintock in the address she delivered upon being awarded the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for her discovery of transposons. The genome, she declared, is “a highly sensitive organ of the cell, monitoring genomic activities and correcting common errors, sensing the unusual and unexpected events and responding to them, often by restructuring the genome.”
Research since that time has fleshed out this image, revealing how the shape of chromatin can matter as much as the information its DNA sequences encode and how an army of molecules collaborates to reorganize it and make collective decisions about how to use its genetic information in context-dependent ways. There is no human technology that works this way, so metaphors such as blueprints, programs, or computers will always fall short.
Bickmore is optimistic that the workings of the genome are understandable, despite its complexity. “We’ve got a handle on it now,” she said. “We might not know the details, but I think the whole field is coalescing now into a framework where we’re thinking along similar lines.” AI can surely help with this sense-making, but in the end, human reasoning will be needed to discern the fundamental principles.
“McClintock was far more on point than people realized at the time,” Adelman said. “What she said was that the genome isn’t static—it’s living.”

Trump Suspends Sanctions Against Buyers of Russian Oil Under the Graham Act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:59:47 UTC
17:59:47 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump has suspended the tariffs and sanctions provided for in the Lindsey Graham Act, which was passed in September.
This is stated in an executive order published on the White House website on October 16.
Trump invoked a provision of the law that allows the president to waive the restrictions it imposes. In Section 4 of the executive order, he waived a number of tariffs, sanctions, and other measures of pressure against Russia. The president also stated that he had provided Congress with the relevant justification.
“I hereby waive the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and tariffs provided for in the Graham Act,” the executive order states.
Trump noted that lifting the sanctions is in the national interest of the United States.
The document he signed formally establishes the tariffs provided for by law but simultaneously suspends their implementation.
The law provided for the imposition of 100-percent tariffs for 30 days on all goods from the five countries that purchase the largest volumes of Russian oil. The document also provides for sanctions against Russian officials, financial institutions, and other individuals associated with the Russian government. Certain provisions are aimed at preventing circumvention of the restrictions already in place.
The Graham Act also provided for sanctions against a number of Russian entities and 500 percent tariffs on all Russian energy imports to the United States. The deadline for implementing these provisions expired on October 18.
At the same time, Section 115 of the Act grants the president the authority to waive the sanctions, restrictions, and tariffs provided for therein. The Act does not allow for the revocation of sanctions that have already been imposed.
The law contradicts Trump’s agreement with Russian President Putin on the export of Russian diesel fuel to global markets.
Waiving tariffs and sanctions risks sparking new opposition from members of Congress, including many Republicans who are outraged by this agreement. This week, a group of senators from both parties already signed a letter demanding that Trump terminate the agreement with Russia and ensure compliance with the provisions of the Graham Act.

Bangladesh struggles to contain world’s worst measles outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:59:00 UTC
17:59:00 KST

Bangladesh is struggling to contain the world’s largest measles outbreak this year, with more than 1,100 deaths exposing serious gaps in vaccination coverage, emergency planning and efforts to reach vulnerable children.
The country reported 202,000 suspected measles cases, including 22,000 laboratory-confirmed infections, between mid-March and Oct. 9, according to the World Health Organization. Of the 1,147 reported deaths, 94% were children younger than 5.
The outbreak follows a decline in routine immunization coverage in 2025, reversing years of progress against a highly contagious disease that vaccines can prevent. Experts say unreliable data, inadequate preparation and failures to reach parents have further weakened the response.
A Reuters review of WHO documents, combined with interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials, found that millions of children may have been missed by an emergency vaccination campaign launched in April.
The crisis offers a warning to other countries about the consequences of declining vaccination rates and underprepared health systems.
“This is a real warning to every country,” said Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at New York University’s School of Global Public Health.
Preventing an outbreak through vaccination is easier, cheaper and safer than responding after infections spread, Jit said.
“The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died,” he said.
Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters in September that the government was doing everything possible to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October.
In northeastern Sylhet, one of the hardest-hit regions of the country of 178 million people, families say they received no timely warning or access to vaccination services.
Two-year-old Arman Hossain died in July, about 24 hours after being admitted to a hospital for measles treatment. His family sold its three-wheeled auto rickshaw to pay for his care. Arman had not been vaccinated, although his unvaccinated 4-year-old sister survived.
His father, Amin Mia, 26, said health workers had not visited their remote village to offer vaccinations before his son became ill.
“They came only after I buried my son,” he said.
In Chhatak, also in Sylhet, 9-month-old Labiba Akter died of measles in June. Her father, Humayun Rashid, a 30-year-old carpenter, said no health worker had informed the family about the vaccination campaign.
Labiba could have received a dose in April, when an emergency drive lowered the minimum vaccination age from 9 months to 6 months.
“No health worker came to tell us,” Rashid said.
Measles typically kills two or three people for every 1,000 infections, according to the WHO, but the risk can be higher in poorer countries, where malnutrition and limited access to medical care worsen outcomes.
In May, Health Minister Sardar Md. Sakhawat Husain said cases in the worst-affected areas had fallen “almost to zero.” But the decline did not last. Bangladesh recorded an average of 1,198 new cases a day in September, its highest daily average since May.
Bangladesh was once considered a vaccination success story.
The WHO and UNICEF estimated that 96% of eligible children received their first measles vaccine dose in 2024, while 93% received the second. The second dose protects children who do not develop sufficient immunity after the first.
The WHO recommends coverage of at least 95% to prevent measles outbreaks. Bangladesh had approached that threshold before immunization rates fell.
Political turmoil following the 2024 protests that ended Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s 15-year rule disrupted health services. Health workers went on strike, vaccine orders were delayed and follow-up vaccinations were interrupted.
A WHO and UNICEF report published in July estimated that first-dose coverage fell to 90% in 2025, while second-dose coverage dropped to 86%.
The report also questioned the reliability of official vaccination figures from 2023 to 2025. Preliminary data sometimes suggested that the number of children vaccinated exceeded 100% of the target population, pointing to possible errors in counting doses or estimating the number of eligible children.
Those weaknesses made it harder to identify communities being missed and determine where additional resources were needed.
In Bangladesh, experts said, access to vaccines and a lack of awareness have been greater obstacles than vaccine hesitancy, which has gained attention in wealthier countries amid skepticism promoted by figures including U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Bangladesh initially appeared to be making progress after launching an emergency vaccination campaign in April. Nearly 20 million children received vaccinations in April and May, and new infections slowed.
The government said it had reached every child in the target group, covering those aged 6 months to 5 years.
But a comparison with another health intervention in June raised questions about that claim. The June program, which targeted the same age group, had a list of eligible children containing 4 million more names than the measles campaign.
The discrepancy suggested the emergency drive had failed to reach a substantial number of children.
“There is a gap,” Hyder told Reuters on Sept. 14, as cases rose again. He attributed missed vaccinations partly to parental reluctance and children being ill when vaccination teams visited.
Documents reviewed by Reuters also revealed concerns about preparation. Minutes from an April 19 meeting between the government, the WHO and other health partners showed that officials conducted only one round of readiness checks before launching the campaign, citing time constraints. Such campaigns typically involve four rounds.
The checks cover vaccine refrigeration, staffing and estimates of how many children need immunization. The minutes indicated that most, but not all, districts appeared ready.
Hyder said the campaign was organized within four weeks. Tajul Islam Abdul Bari, who led Bangladesh’s immunization program until 2017, said vaccination drives normally require months of preparation.
“When preparedness checks are not done properly, it is often the poorest and hardest-to-reach children who miss out on vaccination and pay the price,” said Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and chair of Bangladesh’s National Verification Committee for Measles and Rubella Elimination.
By August, officials were confronting evidence that the campaign had failed to close major gaps. Meeting minutes showed that the share of children with confirmed measles who had not been vaccinated stood at 82% before the campaign and 85% afterward.
The figures suggested that the campaign had done little to reduce the proportion of unvaccinated children among confirmed cases.
The WHO did not respond to questions about the April and August meetings. Its deputy representative in Bangladesh, Rajesh Narwal, said the organization remained committed to helping the government vaccinate every child at risk.
“Routine immunisation must become more effective and resilient so that these gaps do not develop again,” he said.
In Sylhet, official records show 180 children have died. Of the 16 families Reuters interviewed in September, eight said they had not seen health workers offering vaccinations. At least six said vaccination teams arrived only after a child in their community had died of measles.
The government launched another campaign at the end of September, targeting 3.4 million children who had previously been missed.
“We will involve people across villages so that no child is left behind,” the health minister said at a news conference.
Reaching every child remains difficult. UNICEF and the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics estimate that as many as 40% of children are not registered, complicating efforts to identify eligible recipients and track vaccination coverage. Government data also show that about one-third of health worker positions are vacant.
Experts have urged the government to extend vaccination efforts to children older than 5, who account for about one-third of measles cases, according to the WHO.
Scientists in Bangladesh are also investigating why immunity appears to be waning faster than expected in babies up to around 6 months old. Infants in that age group are generally expected to retain some protection from antibodies passed on by their mothers.
Prompt diagnosis and treatment are also essential to reducing deaths, the WHO says. But Bangladesh is simultaneously fighting a dengue epidemic that is putting additional pressure on its health services.
In September, Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital in Sylhet, a 100-bed facility treating measles patients, appeared overwhelmed in every ward during a Reuters visit. The hospital had 178 patients admitted that day.

Economic Watch: How excavators from China's inland city reach global markets smarter and faster
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:57:27 CST
17:57:27 KST

NANNING, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Two clicks ring out as a robot precisely positions a tightening tool over a bolt on an electric excavator and secures it in place. Every 12.5 minutes, another bright-green excavator rolls off the assembly line, ready to be shipped to markets around the world.
The scene unfolds at the LiuGong Excavator Intelligent Factory in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Guangxi Liugong Machinery Co., Ltd., a leading Chinese machinery manufacturer, now offers over 100 electric product models, which are sold in more than 60 countries and regions.
LiuGong is headquartered in Liuzhou City, an inland industrial city in Guangxi. Built on a strong foundation in automobile manufacturing, steel and machinery, the city has been accelerating the digital and intelligent transformation of its traditional industries.
LiuGong's Excavator Intelligent Factory began operation in November 2023. Inside the bustling workshop, automated guided vehicles (AGVs) carrying components of various sizes glide through the aisles, delivering them to workstations where workers have placed orders.
For Zhao Qifeng, production manager at the factory's assembly line, one of the toughest challenges addressed by intelligent transformation is product inspection.
"Previously, workers used steel rulers, tape measures and stopwatches to carry out tests. Nowadays, we can obtain key parameters through an AI-powered robotic system in about 10 minutes," Zhao said. The resulting "health report" for each excavator is then uploaded to the company's digital system.
With an annual production capacity of more than 20,000 excavators, the factory has achieved an automation rate of 65 percent through its smart upgrade. Overall production capacity has increased by 45 percent, order response time has been cut by 45 percent, and production efficiency has improved by 25 percent.
In the first half of this year, LiuGong's overseas revenue exceeded 10 billion yuan (about 1.49 billion U.S. dollars) for the first time, up more than 20 percent year-on-year, according to Liu Shuangfeng, director of business operations at the company's international business division. LiuGong's footprint now extends to 180 countries and regions worldwide.
Liu said that the company's connection with global markets is expected to improve further thanks to the Pinglu Canal, which just opened to navigation in September.
The 134.2-kilometer canal links Guangxi's capital Nanning with the Beibu Gulf, opening to sea at Guangxi's Qinzhou Port. The closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China is also offering companies in Liuzhou a more efficient export route.
LiuGong plans to increase exports through Qinzhou Port, where more ocean-going vessels are expected to call following the opening of the new canal, according to Liu.
"Compared with shipping through ports in Guangdong, the route via Qinzhou can reduce the company's inland transportation costs by around 15 to 18 percent and shorten transit times by seven to 10 days," he said.
With an established railway network, Liuzhou now features two access routes to the sea: goods can either travel by rail directly to Qinzhou Port, or by rail to Nanning, where they can then reach the port at Beibu Gulf via the Pinglu Canal.
The routes complement each other, giving businesses more options and helping strengthen supply chain resilience, said Qi Jianfeng, director of the development and reform bureau of Liunan District, where Liuzhou Railway Port lies.
To speed up export procedures, a customs-supervised facility at the railway port conducted its first rail-sea intermodal transport customs clearance in May, allowing exporters to complete customs procedures in Liuzhou, said Luo Qiaofeng, chief of Liuzhou Customs.
By streamlining declaration, inspection and release procedures, Liuzhou's new one-stop clearance process has cut customs clearance time by about 48 hours per shipment. A digital system also enables automated checks of container and seal numbers, speeding up cargo release, Luo added.
Liuzhou's official data shows that the city's railway port handled 17,000 TEUs from January to September this year, 22 times the total for all of 2025.
Both the Pinglu Canal and Liuzhou Railway Port are part of China's efforts to develop the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a trade route connecting China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets. The corridor is designated as one of China's strategic backbone passages in the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). Its construction is expected to be fully completed by 2035.
For Liuzhou, the corridor brings the city's increasingly smart manufacturing sector closer to the global market at a faster pace. Though the city lies inland, the sea is no longer that far away.
As Qi put it, "Liuzhou may not be by the sea, but the sea has always been in its people's hearts." ■

Russia on Saturday welcomed U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to waive new sanctions targeting Moscow, calling it a historic move as Ukraine warned that easing economic pressure would encourage Russian President Vladimir Putin to continue the war.
Trump signed an executive order Friday suspending the application of sanctions provisions under the Lindsey Graham Act, a law designed to increase pressure on Russia’s energy and defense sectors, its officials and the network of tankers Moscow uses to circumvent Western restrictions.
The decision comes as Russian forces intensify attacks on Ukrainian cities and diplomatic efforts led by Washington remain deadlocked, raising concerns among Kyiv and its European allies that the Trump administration is easing pressure on Moscow without securing meaningful concessions.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy for investment and economic cooperation, praised the decision on social media, describing the suspension of the law as an “important and truly historic moment.”
Dmitriev argued that the sanctions would have caused serious damage to the U.S. economy and global markets. The Kremlin and Putin had not publicly commented on the decision as of Saturday.
The waiver followed an arrangement between Trump and Putin under which Moscow agreed to release substantial quantities of diesel onto global markets amid mounting pressure on fuel prices. Trump’s decision to suspend the new measures marks a diplomatic gain for Russia as Washington struggles to broker an end to the war.
The Graham Act, named after the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, was designed to tighten restrictions on Russia’s energy and defense industries, officials linked to Putin and its so-called shadow fleet of tankers. It also included provisions targeting countries that continue to buy Russian oil and gas.
Trump’s order suspends the application of the new measures under a national-interest waiver. It does not automatically remove sanctions imposed on Russia under earlier U.S. measures.
The decision has intensified concerns in Kyiv that Washington could weaken its leverage over Moscow while Russian forces continue their offensive.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the waiver Saturday, arguing that easing sanctions would reward Russia despite its continued attacks.
“A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin, all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” Zelenskyy said on social media, urging Ukraine’s allies to maintain pressure on Moscow.
The sanctions decision came as Russia stepped up its attacks on Ukraine, including repeated strikes on the capital, Kyiv, as the war enters its fifth year.
Russian forces struck the southern city of Kherson on Saturday, killing one person and wounding 22, local officials said. The attack underscored the continuing toll of the war even as Washington pursues negotiations.
The conflict, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. Russian forces occupy large areas of eastern and southern Ukraine, and Putin has repeatedly vowed to seize the remaining territory Moscow claims in eastern Ukraine.
Speaking to military leaders Friday while wearing military uniform, Putin said he saw a positive trend in the operations of Russian forces and reiterated that capturing the rest of the Donetsk region remained a major objective.
“Undoubtedly, one of the main objectives remains the liberation of the Donetsk People’s Republic,” Putin said, using the Kremlin’s term for the Ukrainian region.
Russian strikes have intensified in recent weeks, putting additional pressure on Ukrainian air defenses as the country prepares for another winter of war. Kyiv has struggled to intercept incoming missiles and drones while seeking additional defensive systems from its allies.
Putin’s remarks signaled that Moscow intends to continue its military campaign despite diplomatic efforts to secure a ceasefire.
European leaders responded to the growing uncertainty over Washington’s approach by reaffirming their support for Ukraine and calling for continued economic pressure on Russia.
Zelenskyy met European leaders in Brussels on Friday during a European Union summit, seeking sustained financial and military assistance as relations between Kyiv and Washington deteriorated.
European Council President António Costa warned against easing pressure on Moscow while Russian forces continued their attacks.
“This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” Costa said. “Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”
European leaders have argued that maintaining sanctions and strengthening Ukraine’s defenses are necessary to persuade Russia to accept a meaningful ceasefire and negotiate an end to the war.
The EU has also signaled that it intends to maintain its restrictions on Moscow while preparing further measures.
Zelenskyy has sought additional air defense systems, support for Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and continued funding to sustain the country’s defense effort. His appeal came as European governments weighed how to maintain assistance amid uncertainty over the future direction of U.S. policy.
The European response reflects growing concern that Washington’s willingness to ease sanctions could undermine the pressure intended to bring Putin to the negotiating table.
U.S.-led negotiations have yet to produce a breakthrough, with disputes over territory, security guarantees and the terms of a possible ceasefire continuing to obstruct progress.
Trump has expressed frustration with both Putin and Zelenskyy over the lack of progress toward ending the conflict. His increasingly strained relationship with the Ukrainian leader has added to concerns in Kyiv that Washington could press Ukraine to make concessions while offering Moscow economic relief.
The sanctions waiver has heightened those fears, particularly as Ukraine faces intensified Russian bombardments and questions over the reliability of some U.S.-provided military and intelligence support.
For Ukraine, the immediate concern is that easing economic pressure could give Russia greater room to sustain its military campaign. For European governments, the decision raises questions about how to maintain a unified strategy if Washington takes a more conciliatory approach toward Moscow.
Russia’s public celebration of the waiver reflects the potential diplomatic value of the move for Putin, even as the Kremlin continues to pursue its territorial objectives by force.

Switzerland advances bid to host 2038 Winter Olympics

2026-10-17

17:52:23 KST

Switzerland advances bid to host 2038 Winter Olympics
Switzerland is preparing a bid to host the 2038 Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games. Following approval by the Swiss House of Representatives, the relevant committee of the Senate has backed the proposal, which provides for federal financial support of up to CHF200 million ($242 million).
The Senate’s Committee on Science, Education and Culture has given the green light by 10 votes to 0, with 2 abstentions. It has made a number of clarifications to the House of Representative’s draft regarding funding and cantonal participation, according to a statement issued by parliament on Friday.
The privileged dialogue between the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and Switzerland allows the country to prepare a bid to host the Games without competition until the end of 2027. If the bid meets the IOC’s requirements, Switzerland will be awarded the right to host the Games. The IOC is expected to make its decision at its spring session in 2027.
The Games must meet the highest national and international standards of sustainability, transparency and governance. They will be held in a decentralised manner across the four linguistic regions. No new construction projects will be undertaken. The plan does not envisage putting the bid to a referendum of the Swiss people.
+ Switzerland names venues for 2038 Winter Olympics bid
It envisages a total budget of CHF2.2 billion over the next ten years, from the awarding of the Games until they take place. While the Games will be primarily funded by private sources, federal support will amount to CHF200 million. The cantons will be required to contribute at least the same amount.
Additional funds will be used to co-finance the Paralympic Games, reduce public transport costs and make competition venues available throughout Switzerland. The federal government will also be responsible for security measures, estimated to cost between CHF40 and 80 million.

“We agreed that it is necessary to address Ukraine’s additional financing needs for 2027,” Costa told reporters. “And we asked the European Commission to present a concrete proposal for discussion and adoption.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reaffirmed the funding requirement, stressing that Ukraine’s international partners must coordinate to eliminate the looming fiscal shortfall.
“Now it is clear that we have a gap of €70 billion that has to be covered,” von der Leyen stated following the summit, urging allied nations to mobilize financial commitments.
A senior EU official familiar with the leaders’ discussions told European Pravda that the proposal remains in an exploratory stage, noting that formal adoption is not bound to a rigid year-end deadline.
The official explained that deliberations on sourcing fresh capital can progress while disbursements continue under the existing €90 billion ($102 billion) loan facility, which allocates €45 billion ($50 billion) for 2027.

The official added that it remains undetermined whether the forthcoming Commission proposal will incorporate recommendations to leverage Russian sovereign assets immobilized across the EU.
Allied coordination
French President Emmanuel Macron confirmed that international allies – including the Group of Seven (G7), European governments, and broader partner coalition – will review Kyiv’s €70 billion funding request.
“We will indeed be looking at the funding,” Macron told France 24.
“The funding that will be provided by the G7 countries, by our partners and, of course, by the Europeans.”
Macron also disclosed that European defense planners are accelerating programs to supply Ukraine with sovereign satellite imagery and early-warning architectures, noting that friction with Washington has highlighted Kyiv’s acute reliance on American technical capabilities.
“We are working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed,” Macron said.
Addressing recent diplomatic developments, Macron criticized the bilateral commercial diesel agreement reached between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, warning that granting Moscow market access harms allied cohesion.
“This decision is not good for anyone. It sends a negative signal. It is an element of division and doubt,” Macron stated.
Pre-winter air defense shortfalls
The drive to secure 2027 budgetary commitments unfolds as President Zelensky delivered an urgent appeal to European Union leaders in Brussels, requesting 300 Patriot surface-to-air interceptors alongside the multi-billion-euro financial package to shield municipal utilities ahead of winter.
Zelensky warned European leaders that Russian forces have expanded long-range standoff bombardments against civilian power grids, leaving municipal centers exposed as domestic interceptor stockpiles reach depletion.
“I ask you to really focus on helping us get PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors,” Zelensky said in his address to the European Council.
“Ukraine can’t get by on just two or four missiles from a country every few months. We need a winter package – we always spoke about it between us – of missiles: 300 Patriot interceptors specifically against ballistic missiles.”
The appeal coincides with reports that Ukrainian forces have nearly exhausted their inventories of US-manufactured Patriot interceptors, with supply strains compounded by production backlogs and high operational expenditures during US military operations in the Middle East.
While European defense coordinators have lobbied member states possessing Patriot systems – including Greece and Spain – to transfer aging interceptors approaching statutory shelf limits, southern European governments have expressed reluctance to release batteries, citing their own regional defense commitments.

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained about 70% below pre-conflict levels as attacks on commercial vessels continued, a UK maritime agency said Friday.
In its weekly overview, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) reported 125 outbound and 129 inbound transits over the past seven days.
The figures marked a decline from 129 outbound and 146 inbound transits recorded the previous week, according to the agency.
UKMTO reported 12 attacks on vessels during the week, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz, one in the Gulf and one in the Gulf of Oman. Six vessels continued or reached port, one was lost, two were disabled or not under command, and three have unconfirmed outcomes.
Container ship sinks after projectile strike
UKMTO said a container ship was struck by an unidentified projectile near Ras Shaykh Masud on Oct. 13.
READ: Iran says container ship sank after striking naval mine in Strait of Hormuz
The vessel caught fire and sank the following day, according to the agency.
All crew members were evacuated, UKMTO said.
The agency warned that it was struggling to establish the actual number of attacks because most targeted vessels declined to report incidents.
UKMTO said it had recorded 84 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began in late February.
The reported attacks came amid continued tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
The waterway is a major route for global energy and commodity shipments and remains a key issue in negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
The conflict began with US and Israeli attacks against Iran on Feb. 28, followed by a ceasefire in April.
Clashes between Washington and Tehran later resumed as negotiations stalled, although the two sides signed a framework agreement in June.

EU backs just peace in Ukraine, calls on Russia to cease fire, enter negotiations – summit conclusions
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:49:10 EEST
17:49:10 KST

European Union leaders have declared their support for a just peace for Ukraine, based on the principles of the UN Charter, and called on Russia to agree to a ceasefire and begin peace talks.
This position of EU leaders is set forth in the conclusions adopted following the European Council meeting held on October 15-16 in Brussels. "The European Union supports a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law and underpinned by robust and credible security guarantees for Ukraine. Only a solution that respects Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity can bring about a just and lasting peace," the document states.
EU leaders are convinced that "the path to peace in Ukraine cannot be decided without Ukraine," while the EU "will decide on matters of its competence or affecting its security."
"Borders must not be changed by force, the aggressor cannot be rewarded and Ukraine's long-term security and ability to defend itself must be guaranteed," the conclusions read.
The European Council reaffirmed its support for diplomatic efforts aimed at ending Russia's war of aggression and emphasized the EU's readiness to step up its involvement in this process.
EU leaders also stressed that Europe will play "a key role to play in a future settlement and will defend its interests." "The European Council urges Russia to show genuine willingness regarding peace, agree to a full, unconditional and immediate ceasefire and engage in meaningful negotiations towards a just and lasting peace," the document states.

Trump blocks new Russia sanctions days before they take effect
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:47:45 EEST
17:47:45 KST

US President Donald Trump has suspended a sweeping package of sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia just days before the measures were due to take effect, citing American national interests. The decision has drawn criticism from US lawmakers and praise from Moscow, further intensifying tensions between Washington and Kyiv.
Trump issued an executive order on Friday waiving several provisions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Congress passed with bipartisan support and the president signed into law in September.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The legislation was designed to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine by targeting Russian officials, financial institutions and the country's so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to transport oil despite Western restrictions.
It also authorised tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported from major purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas, potentially affecting countries including China and India.
The new restrictions were scheduled to take effect on Sunday, 18 October, but Trump's order suspends their implementation until the administration determines that further action is appropriate.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," Trump stated in the order.
The decision comes amid concerns that additional restrictions on Russian energy exports could drive global oil prices higher ahead of November's US midterm elections. Energy costs have already risen sharply amid the ongoing US-Israeli conflict with Iran, placing political pressure on the Trump administration.
The move was welcomed by Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's investment envoy, who described the suspension as an "important and truly historic moment".
Dmitriev argued that implementing the sanctions would have severely damaged international markets and economic relations between Russia and the United States.
In Washington, Democratic Representative Don Beyer accused Trump of undermining congressional efforts to hold Moscow accountable.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer said in a statement.
The suspension follows another controversial decision by Washington to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports in a claimed effort to reduce American and global fuel prices.
That agreement prompted criticism from a bipartisan group of US senators, including six Republicans, who warned that renewed energy revenues could help finance Russia's military operations in Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has similarly condemned the diesel arrangement, warning that additional revenue would flow into Russia while its invasion continues.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv have deteriorated further over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Trump has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine halt the strikes, arguing that they contribute to higher international energy prices.
Following the collapse of a proposed energy ceasefire, Ukraine resumed refinery attacks on Thursday after Russian forces continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Trump subsequently described the Ukrainian operations as a "disgrace" and renewed his criticism of Zelenskyy.
Ukrainian officials have reported disruptions to satellite communications used for drone operations, while Reuters reported, citing unnamed US and Western officials, that an order to restrict the Starshield system originated inside the White House.
Trump has denied personally ordering the restrictions and has rejected claims that Washington halted intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
