How Switzerland became an organic farming pioneer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

How Switzerland became an organic farming pioneer
A visit to a supermarket in Switzerland leaves many visitors from abroad amazed. With a higher proportion of organic products on the shelves than elsewhere, organic food has become part of everyday shopping in the country.
Almost one in three eggs sold in Swiss shops is organically produced. For vegetables, lettuce and potatoes, the proportion stands at around 27%.
With organic products accounting for 12.3% of all food sold, Switzerland tops the international rankings. It is followed by Denmark (11.6%) and Austria (11.4%).
‘Organic’ is not clearly defined
However, international data is inconsistent. Countries use different survey methods, and terms such as ‘food retail’ and ‘total food market’ are not always defined in the same way.
Furthermore, even the definition of ‘organic’ is not standardised worldwide. A product bearing an organic label in one place often meets different standards to those in other countries. For instance, Swiss certification requirements are stricter than the European Union’s Organic Regulation or the US Organic Standard.
Bio Suisse, the umbrella organisation for Swiss organic farms certified under the Knospe label,External link also points out that Swiss figures have been based on a new dataset since 2024. Some earlier figures have been recalculated.
Despite these limitations, the overall picture remains clear: organic products account for a larger share of Swiss consumers’ shopping baskets than those of shoppers in other countries.
Furthermore, Switzerland has for years topped the rankings when it comes to per capita spending on organic products, at the equivalent of €494 (CHF461) per person per year.
“However, the general price level [in Switzerland] is high in any case,” states the 2026 industry report by the German Federation for Organic Food and AgricultureExternal link (BÖLW).
From niche market to political recognition
Switzerland’s success story did not begin with the sustainability boom. Local organic farming developed into an organised movement during the 20th century.
In 1981, five organisations founded the umbrella organisation for Swiss organic farming, which became Bio Suisse in 1997.
With its ‘Knospe’ (in the form of a bud), the association also created a common certification label. It is not simply the Swiss equivalent of the EU organic logo, but a private label with its own guidelines, which in several areas go beyond statutory minimum standards. The aim is to build trust in production methods and inspections.
Political recognition followed in 1992. At that time, organic farming was included in the Agriculture Act alongside integrated productionExternal link (IP label) as a form of production eligible for support.
Organic farming thus became an integral part of state agricultural policy. In Switzerland, organically produced products therefore moved out of the niche market and into the mainstream food system at a relatively early stage.
Supermarkets enter the fray
The market received perhaps its most significant boost in the early 1990s. Coop launched its own organic brand, ‘Naturaplan’, in close collaboration with Bio Suisse. From then on, the products carried the ‘Knospe’ logo. Organic produce was thus no longer available only in specialist shops, but also in supermarkets.
Later, Switzerland’s second retail giant, Migros, also entered the organic market. The two cooperatives have long dominated the Swiss food retail sector and have an extensive network of stores.
This made organic produce easily accessible and part of everyday shopping. Today, no retailer can afford to ignore organic products.
While organic products accounted for 7.1% of the total food market in 2007, this figure had risen to 10.8% by 2020. By 2024, it reached its record high of 12.3%.
Sales of organic food amounted to CHF4.266 billion.
Organic products accounted for 12.3% of the food market.
Consumers spend CHF468 per capita on organic food.
52% of all consumers buy organic products daily or several times a week.
7,467 organic farms, market gardens and beekeepers in Switzerland and Liechtenstein produce in accordance with Bio Suisse guidelines.
18.4% of Switzerland’s agricultural land is farmed organically.
Source: Bio Suisse
Trust and purchasing power as reasons for success
One reason for the success of organic products in shopping baskets is likely to be the high level of trust that Swiss consumers place in organic labels.
After all, when shopping, nobody can personally check how a field is farmed or how animals are reared. Customers therefore rely on inspections and credible labelling.
However, ‘organic’ does not automatically mean that products were produced in Switzerland. As not everything can be produced domestically, Switzerland also has to import organic raw materials and foodstuffs. Care is taken to ensure that foreign producers comply with the Knospe guidelines.
Another reason is likely to be the high purchasing power of Swiss consumers. Organic products are expensive, and price is one of the main barriers. Higher-income households are more likely to buy organic products; education and place of residence also influence consumer behaviour.
Taste is less important
According to a 2022 study by the Federal Office for Agriculture and the Research Institute of Organic AgricultureExternal link (FiBL), taste is not the primary factor influencing purchasing decisions.
Instead, for 85% of those surveyed, animal welfare and the avoidance of pesticide residues are key considerations. These are followed by environmentally friendly production and the avoidance of preventive antibiotic use in animal husbandry.
Liechtenstein has the highest proportion of organic production
According to figures from Bio SuisseExternal link, in 2025 almost 7,500 farms and market gardens in Switzerland and the Principality of Liechtenstein were producing in accordance with the organisation’s guidelines.
Although Switzerland is the world leader in organic consumption, it does not lead in production. In terms of the proportion of land farmed organically, Liechtenstein leads the worldExternal link at 43.5%. Spain, France and Italy have the largest areas of organic farmland in Europe in absolute terms.
Room for improvement in the catering sector
However, Switzerland’s leading position in terms of market share for organic products is by no means guaranteed. Market share is currently stagnating, prices are high, and some demand has to be met by imports.
The next challenge is to make organic produce more widely available outside supermarkets and affordable to broader sections of the population.
This also includes the catering sector: the aforementioned study by the federal government and FiBL identified strong demand among respondents for organic food in restaurants, canteens and takeaways.
For many people, organic food is less readily available when eating out than it is in supermarkets. Rising living costs can also lead even committed organic shoppers to opt for cheaper products.

Rubio’s Uzbekistan trip underlines Central Asia’s hunt for diverse partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:27:28 UTC
17:27:28 KST

Rubio’s Uzbekistan trip underlines Central Asia’s hunt for diverse partners
Can the United States reassert influence with pragmatic, transactional approach to Central Asia as C5+1 summit gets under way?
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is arriving in Samarkand, the fabled Silk Road city in what is now central Uzbekistan, for talks with key regional ministers on Saturday.
The C5+1 – Central Asia plus the US – summit to be held from Saturday to Tuesday heralds Washington’s new approach to the ex-Soviet region – pragmatic, purely transactional and devoid of speeches about democratisation and human rights.
At the dawn of Central Asia’s independence, Americans used to show up in the mostly Muslim region strategically stretched between Russia, China and Iran, bearing gifts – and giving lectures.
After the 1991 Soviet collapse, amid the region’s economic degradation, joblessness and poverty, US and European diplomats and businessmen were seen as ambassadors of the brave new world of capitalist prosperity.
They wanted reforms – and not just the economic ones.
Western diplomats made sure that former Communist apparatchiks-turned-new regional leaders understood that they’d get investments, technologies and international recognition only in exchange for abandoning the Soviet-era totalitarian ways of governing and building the economy.
The West held forums and workshops on human rights, democracy and decentralisation of governance, and sent thousands of students and officials to Western schools.
And the West accused regional leaders of losing their moral compass and threatened sanctions when they began to amend their nation’s constitutions to extend their presidential terms, appoint their family members and friends to key government jobs and help them create business empires that often competed with Western investors.
“When the West began moralising, teaching them about democracy, human rights, they immediately turned towards China or Russia,” Galiya Ibragimova, Uzbekistan-born, Moldova-based regional expert, told Al Jazeera.
Uzbekistan, the region’s most populous nation of 37 million, offers a perfect example.
Its iron-fisted President Islam Karimov was the first ex-Soviet leader to allow a US military base on its soil in 2001.
But four years later, he kicked it out after Washington lambasted his brutal suppression of a popular revolt in the eastern city of Andijan that killed hundreds of unarmed civilians.
In 2005, a leaked US diplomatic cable called Karimov’s daughter, Gulnara, a “robber baron” who forcibly took over lucrative businesses and was seen as her father’s successor.
Turning to Russia
As to moralising and lecturing, the tables have turned since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, observers say.
Moscow still has plenty of soft power in Central Asia – from movies and pop music to theatre festivals and propagandist TV shows that constantly lie about the war.
The Kremlin also uses its economic clout to promote the imperialist concept of the “Russian World”, where the region is seen as Moscow’s “near abroad”, and its pre-Russian heritage is snubbed as backwards and insignificant.
In 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed that Kazakhstan had “never had statehood”, and his ideological allies repeatedly threatened to annex its Russian-speaking northern part.
This year, Kazakhstan began extraditing Kremlin critics and supplying gas to Russia amid Ukrainian drone attacks on its oil refineries.
In January, Kremlin propagandist Vladimir Solovyov said Moscow should launch a “special military operation” – a term reserved for the war in Ukraine – in Central Asia and Armenia.
Critical remarks from minor political figures followed – but no rebukes from the halls of real power.
Meanwhile, Central Asian labour migrants have been duped or forced into enlisting to fight in Ukraine in droves, while Moscow uses Central Asian companies to import microchips, communications equipment and machine tools to build drones and missiles.
“These days, the US and Russia have switched roles. Today, it’s Russia that began building ties through moralising,” Ibragimova, the regional expert, said.
Return of the White House?
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump’s administration has abandoned the pro-democracy stance and now advocates a utilitarian, transactional approach to foreign policy.
“Under Trump, the American policy in Central Asia is all about ‘just business and nothing more’, without being nosy about human rights, reforms. They are content with everything,” Ibragimova said.
Earlier this month, Trump received Saida Mirziyoyeva, the daughter of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.
A year earlier, Mirziyoyev pledged to invest up to $100bn in the US economy, buy Boeing aircraft and even US-grown cotton, even though Uzbekistan is one of the world’s largest cotton growers.
Washington did not say a word about Mirziyoyev’s crackdown on critics or his daughter’s growing domestic clout.
After largely ignoring Central Asia during Trump’s first term, the White House wants to resume its presence.
“The interest is mostly geopolitical and military-strategic, considering the region’s location in the zone of Russia’s and China’s interests,” Alisher Ilkhamov, head of the London-based Central Asia Due Diligence think tank, told Al Jazeera.
“In the future, Washington apparently wants to have a military base here as a deterrent measure against China,” he said.
The economic interests seem to be focused on rare-earth minerals – crucial for manufacturing a wide array of technology – and other critical elements, especially since China uses them as a political cudgel in its ties with Washington.
The deposits are abundant, but need development, technologies and investment.
Meanwhile, the White House shows little interest in human rights violations in Central Asia, such as the jailing of political opponents and independent journalists.
“An interest in these issues, unfortunately, is absent from Rubio’s agenda, because these problems went missing from US foreign policy priorities since Trump returned to the White House,” Ilkhamov said.
A Norwegian human rights advocate echoes his concerns.
“There are uncomfortable similarities between Trump’s worldview and established authoritarian regimes like Tajikistan and Turkmenistan,” Ivar Dale, a senior policy adviser with the Norwegian Helsinki Committee, a rights watchdog, told Al Jazeera.
“However, Marco Rubio probably has a better understanding of Central Asia and the challenges there than does [Vice President] JD Vance and [Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth,” he said.
The US State Department “should bring back the focus [on human rights] if the C5+1 format is to be taken seriously going forward”, he said.

Yagera woman Jayda Allen Bonner remembered at Melbourne vigil

'We're living with wars behind our doors': Jayda Allen Bonner remembered at Melbourne vigil
In short:
Hundreds of mourners have gathered in Melbourne to pay tribute to a young Indigenous woman one week after she was killed in an inner-suburban apartment.
Jayda Allen Bonner was remembered as "a beautiful soul" by her mother and aunt, who have called for Australians to do more to prevent violence against women.
What's next?
Police investigations are continuing.
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.
Hundreds have gathered in Melbourne to pay tribute to a young Indigenous woman killed at an inner-suburban apartment complex last weekend.
A smoking ceremony was held in honour of 21-year-old Jayda Allen Bonner, who was remembered as "a beautiful soul" by her mother and aunt.
This week, a 31-year-old man was charged with murder and appeared briefly in the Melbourne Magistrates Court.
Police say he was known to Ms Allen Bonner.
Supporters of the Bonner family then marched to Victoria's Parliament to demand changes to domestic violence procedures and reform to better prevent violence against women.
Ms Allen Bonner's mother, Jade Allen, took part in the vigil, wearing a t-shirt emblazoned with an image of her daughter and the phrase 'Justice for Jayda'.
"Jayda loved her family fiercely. She had a heart of gold — she would do anything for anybody," Ms Allen said.
"I want everyone to stand up and stop keeping all of this quiet.
"I want to make sure Jayda's name isn't forgotten. She was one-of-a-kind."
Ms Allen Bonner's aunt Kellie Carter Bell said all Australians need to do more to speak out against violence against women.
"We're living with wars behind our doors,"
she said.
"We need recognition, we need people to understand what this stuff looks like.
"The question should be: What can I do to help (victim-survivors) get out safely?"
Questions raised over police response
Antoinette Braybrook, chief executive of Melbourne-based Aboriginal family violence service Djirra, said the 21-year-old's death was "devastating".
She said it was "outrageous" and "shocking" that Ms Allen Bonner could "fall through the cracks".
Ms Allen Bonner's family has previously said the young woman had made a complaint to police about her safety which she later withdrew.
Her family has also said they tried to contact police themselves, but were told that because Ms Allen Bonner was an adult, there was nothing they could do.
Ms Braybrook said that wasn't true.
"They have the power to investigate violence in the home and initiate their own intervention orders and charge people; my question is, why didn't they do that?"
Ms Braybrook added that it was not uncommon for women experiencing violence to withdraw their complaints to police, even if they were still in danger.
Speaking generally, she said women experiencing violence might be pressured into doing so or be threatened with further violence by their abusers.
"The perpetrator has absolute control, power and control over her in that situation,"
Ms Braybrook said.
"It's a consistent issue in our work."
While Djirra was now in contact with the young Yagera woman's family, Ms Braybrook said given the history of concern for Ms Allen Bonner's safety, it was "extremely disappointing" police or other authorities had not connected her with the service before her death.
"That's one of the concerns that we have as a specialist Aboriginal community-controlled organisation working on the frontline of Aboriginal women and children's safety," she said.
"I am just at a loss — I sit at the table, many tables, with police, with corrections, with courts and others, talking about how we can improve the safety of women.
"When things like this happen to women, it just makes those talks that we participate in all of the time seem like a joke."
A Victoria Police spokesperson said the death of a young woman in Carlton on October 10 was suspicious.
"The investigation is being led by the Homicide Squad," the police spokesperson said.
"As part of investigations, Victoria Police will thoroughly examine any interactions between police and the victim in the lead-up to her death.
"We are unable to comment further while the investigation remains ongoing."

Italy launches probe against Israeli defense minister
Italy has expended its probe into the alleged torture and sexual abuse of activists from the Gaza-bound aid flotilla by Israel’s security forces to include Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz and twelve other high-ranking military, police and prison officials, the Rome Public Prosecutor’s Office has said.
Israel intercepted dozens of yachts in international waters and arrested more than 800 volunteers from various countries in October 2025 and May 2026, who were attempting to break West Jerusalem’s naval blockade of the Palestinian enclave. They were held for days before being deported.
The investigation was launched by Rome earlier this year after some 50 Italian nationals, who were part of the Global Sumud Flotilla missions, complained about being mistreated in Israeli detention, among other things reporting at least 15 cases of sexual abuse and rape. The probe had initially beeen centered on the country’s far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. A similar inquiry was initiated by France.
The Rome prosecutor's office said in a statement on Friday that the case against the Israeli officials concerns suspected torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage.
The activists detained after the 2025 mission reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism, the statement read. The participants of the second mission claimed to have been subject to even harsher treatment by Israeli security forces, including beatings in the dark and the use of tasers and rubber bullets, it added.
Prosecutors said they had sent a request for judicial assistance in the investigation to Israel in June, but it remains unclear if they received a response from West Jerusalem.
Italian law allows crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens to be prosecuted by Rome. If the probe finds the charges warranted, the country could formally request a trial of the Israeli officials.
Katz and Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir, who is now also under investigation, haven’t yet commented on the development. Ben-Gvir brushed off the Italian probe in June, saying that he would “continue to stand proudly alongside our fighters.”
West Jerusalem has repeatedly rejected accusations of mistreating the activists and described the flotilla missions as political provocations designed to aid the Palestinian armed group Hamas. The Israeli prison service said that the detainees were held “in accordance with the law, with full regard for their basic rights.”
Israel claims the blockade of Gaza is necessary to prevent weapons from getting into the enclave. It also denies withholding supplies for Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, almost 2 million of whom have been displaced since the outbreak of the conflict in October 2023, according to UN figures.
West Jerusalem sent its forces into Gaza in retaliation for a Hamas-led incursion in which some 1,200 people lost their lives and 250 others were taken hostage.
Israel’s airstrikes and ground offensive have cost the lives of more than 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, in Gaza over the past three years, the local health ministry has said. Over 1,500 deaths happened despite a US-brokered ceasefire being in effect in the enclave since October 2025.

Canceled school trips abroad leave dozens of families chasing refunds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:24:00 UTC
17:24:00 KST

Canceled school trips abroad leave dozens of families chasing refunds
Dozens of families in Estonia say they are out thousands of euros for canceled school language-learning trips abroad, with one organizer still owing about €50,000 in refunds.
Twelve students from Jüri School were due to travel to Spain this fall through organizer Gerri Vihman and his company Keeleõppereisid OÜ. Each family paid €1,260 for flights, host-family accommodation, language classes in Madrid and insurance.
According to one parent, everything seemed fine until their latest meeting with Vihman, where concerns were raised about his previous issues organizing trips, including a canceled trip to England for Lagedi School.
Asked whether the same thing could happen to them, Vihman replied that he had learned from his mistakes. Concerns grew, however, when Vihman failed to send the families their plane tickets and then canceled the trip.
When teachers inquired whether parents could book the kids' flights themselves, Vihman reportedly said he could not refund them because the money was gone. The parents later learned that he had made no payments in Spain either.
"We realized he had probably planned from the start to steal our money, or that this was fraud," one parent told ERR.
In all, Vihman had collected €15,120 from the Jüri School students' families.
Organizer: All but last two trips paid back
Vihman told ERR that he has organized language trips for nearly 20 years and has never deliberately canceled a trip to keep customers' money.
Every business, he said, has its ups and downs, and most trips have gone smoothly. Over the years, he has canceled seven organized trips for various reasons.
"Sometimes people have canceled by choice, sometimes I've had to cancel myself," Vihman said, admitting that there have certainly also been shortcomings in financial management involved.
Even so, he said he has refunded all but the two most recent canceled trips.
"I am working on the refund process, but everything takes time," the organizer said, adding that he has already been in touch with the Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority (TTJA).
About 40 students' families are still waiting for refunds totaling roughly €50,000.
Vihman also confirmed "in the interest of honesty and transparency" that a Tartu school's trip had been canceled under similar circumstances.
"Lessons learned, and we need to address the situation and work with the parties involved, whether that's the TTJA or the police," he said.
No stranger to consumer regulator
The TTJA's Consumer Disputes Committee has received four complaints this year involving Keeleõppereisid OÜ, said Margot Leen, a consumer rights adviser at the authority. Two consumers received refunds, one withdrew their complaint and one case remains under review.
In 2024, the committee received 10 complaints involving another Vihman-owned company, Keelereisid Eesti OÜ. Five consumers received refunds, four withdrew their complaints and one case was closed because the consumer did not provide the information missing from their complaint.
"Consumers are entitled to a refund if they have paid for a trip and then the organizer confirms it has been canceled," Leen said.
Consumers should first submit a written complaint clearly stating what they want. If the company fails to respond within 15 days or the consumer is dissatisfied with the response, they can turn to the Consumer Disputes Committee.
In contractual disputes, final decisions can be made either by the committee or in court.
Two troubled companies
Before buying anything or signing a contract, consumers can check whether a company is listed as noncompliant with the Consumer Disputes Committee.
Business register records show that Vihman owns both Keeleõppereisid OÜ, registered in 2013, and Keelereisid Eesti OÜ, registered in 2024. Neither company has submitted all required annual reports, and Keelereisid Eesti OÜ's latest filed report showed no sales revenue and a loss of €124,022 in 2023.
Under the Tourism Act, travel companies must not only register their activity with the register of economic activities but also maintain sufficient financial security to cover obligations such as customer refunds if they become insolvent, said Diana Lints, head of the TTJA's Services Supervision Office.
The authority launched supervisory proceedings against Keeleõppereisid OÜ on April 30, issued a precept over its failure to meet the financial security requirement and issued the company a penalty fine.
Schools say earlier trips went smoothly
Jüri School principal Triinu Luiga said the school had acted only as an intermediary for the planned Spain trip, with teachers recommending the organizer to parents who paid the company directly.
"The school had previously taken five successful language trips with companies run by the same person," she said, adding that the teacher involved had also run a background check on the organizer and found no obvious warning signs.
Luiga said the teacher eventually contacted the Madrid school directly to confirm whether the arrangements were still in place, only to learn that Vihman had not been in touch with them at all.
She said the company sent parents a letter on October 14 promising refunds within 14 days.
he school is seeking help from a municipal lawyer but has not filed a police report; because parents paid the company directly, they must file any reports themselves.
Lagedi School principal Oliver Hoole said his school had taken six trips with Vihman without any issues, however a trip planned for this spring was canceled about a week before departure. Vihman told the school that the host language school could no longer accommodate the students.
"Sixteen students were supposed to go, and so far, half of them have gotten their money back," Hoole said, adding that one parent had paid more than €1,000 for the trip.

Repeated displacement leaves Gaza shelters deteriorating ahead of winter: IOM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:21:13 UTC
17:21:13 KST

Sahin Demir
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
Repeated displacement during three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has left shelters across the enclave increasingly deteriorated, while restrictions and funding shortages are hampering preparations for winter, a senior UN migration official said late Friday.
Karl Baker, regional crisis coordinator for the Gaza response at the International Organization for Migration (IOM), said some Palestinians have been displaced as many as eight times, damaging or destroying tents and other temporary shelters each time families are forced to move.
“When they move, all those goods that they currently have or did have either get destroyed, or they have to seek new shelter,” Baker told UN News.
Even basic materials such as tarpaulins need to be replaced roughly every six months, but humanitarian agencies have been unable to bring replacements into Gaza at the required scale, he said.
Baker said agencies now need to move beyond temporary solutions toward more durable transitional shelters.
Materials needed for stronger roofing, concrete floors, and more substantial walls, however, are affected by Israel’s “dual-use” restrictions over security concerns.
“After three years of war, we do need to improve the level of shelter which is inside, and move further away from temporary and more toward transitional type of shelter,” he said.
Baker said IOM remains in constant contact with Israeli authorities, but some durable materials continue to be denied entry over security concerns.
He also cited funding shortages and disruptions to international shipping as obstacles, saying IOM relies on suppliers in countries including China, India, and Pakistan.
Although funding has begun to arrive, it remains insufficient to meet the needs of an estimated 1.8 million to 1.9 million people requiring shelter assistance, he added.
Baker said only around 30% of Gaza is currently accessible to most of the population, forcing displaced Palestinians into increasingly crowded and often flood-prone areas.
“The 30% in which they currently live is a very large displacement camp,” he said.
With winter rains already beginning, humanitarian organizations are working to address flood-prone areas and deploy water pumps, but Baker warned that getting displaced Palestinians through the winter would be the biggest challenge.
Earlier this month, IOM said available and incoming shelter supplies covered only 17% of Gaza’s winter needs, while more than half of tents and makeshift shelters were in poor condition.
A ceasefire has been in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, but Israeli attacks and restrictions on the entry of humanitarian and shelter supplies have continued.

Frontline soldiers will receive a new field ration: what it will contain
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:20:47 EEST

Frontline soldiers will receive a new field ration: what it will contain
Kyiv • UNN
The updated field ration was developed based on suggestions from more than 60,000 service members. It will contain heaters, ready-to-eat meals, and water purification tablets.
Ukrainian military personnel carrying out combat missions directly on the line of contact will be able to receive an updated field food pack. The new field ration was developed taking into account proposals from the service members themselves. The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine reports this, according to UNN.
Details
"Ukrainian soldiers on the front line will receive a new field ration developed taking their proposals into account. The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine approved the relevant amendments to the standards for the daily field food pack on the initiative of the Ministry of Defence," the post reads.
Which military personnel will receive the new field ration
According to the available information, the alternative field food pack is intended for certain categories of military personnel of the Armed Forces and the State Special Transport Service who participate in combat operations directly on the line of contact.
During the development of the new ration, the results of a survey in the "Army+" app were taken into account. More than 60,000 military personnel took part in the survey and expressed their preferences regarding the composition of the field ration, ready-made meals and other food products for use in field conditions.
"Together with my team, we processed the requests and implemented the most popular proposals from the service members. The rations have become more comprehensive: more ready-made meals and fewer small individual items," said Deputy Minister of Defence Mstyslav Banik.
What the alternative daily field ration contains
The updated field ration will not replace but rather serve as an alternative to the daily field food pack — Standard No. 15.
The enhanced field ration for defenders includes:
-  two separate rations instead of one daily field food pack; 
-  flameless heaters; 
-  ready-made meals in retort packaging; 
-  water purification tablets. 
In addition to the rations, bottled drinking water will be issued at a rate of 1.5 litres per day, and from 1 June to 1 September — 3 litres.
"We removed the biscuits and added special flameless heaters, water purification tablets, as well as dried fruit, chocolate and nuts. This increased the calorie content by almost 15%," Mstyslav Banik noted.
According to available data, the combined calorie content of the first and second rations is 4,100 kcal, while the difference in calorie content compared with standard field rations is 600 kcal. The Defence Procurement Agency of the DOT of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine will purchase the alternative food packs in accordance with the new standards.
Reminder
In Ukraine, military personnel who observe Islamic or Jewish dietary laws now have access to halal and kosher field rations. The new specifications take religious requirements and product quality into account.

Majidi denounces US war on Iran as his film wins top prize at 31st Busan International Film Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:20:10 UTC
17:20:10 KST

Majidi denounces US war on Iran as his film wins top prize at 31st Busan International Film Festival
TEHRAN – Majid Majidi received the Best Film Award at the 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) on Thursday for his latest film “Midday Meal”.
Winning the award, the renowned director secured a direct entry for his film, which had its world premiere at the festival, for consideration at the upcoming Academy Awards, Honaronline reported.
Starting this year, the grand prize winner under the Busan Award competition section automatically gains qualification to submit for the Best International Feature Film category at the Academy Awards. The Best Film Award also comes with a cash prize of 50 million won ($37,180).
Iran has already chosen Babak Khajehpasha’s “Land of Angels,” a drama about children enduring the war in Gaza, as its official submission for the 99th Academy Awards. But “Midday Meal” now has an open, alternate route to the race.
At the closing ceremony of the festival, jury president Zhang Yimou, Chinese filmmaking legend, praised “Midday Meal” as the ideal film and noted that all seven jury members agreed unanimously on the selection. Buzz around Majidi’s movie had been building on the ground in Busan all week, with many predicting — correctly — that it would take home the top prize.
Receiving the award, Majidi expressed his gratitude to the festival. He said it was an honor to receive such a huge prize on his first visit to Busan, adding that the energy came from the love of his late mother.
He dedicated the award to the “brave people of Iran” who are “still resisting oppression” and “never give up”.
Referring to economic sanctions imposed on Iran, the Iranian filmmaker said, “For 48 years, our people have been subjected to the harshest economic sanctions, to the extent that even access to medical assistance for treating children with cancer has been denied. Despite this, they have not surrendered.”
Majidi also referred to military attacks on Iran, saying, “You have all witnessed how, when they realized that the Iranian people would not surrender, they repeatedly subjected our country and cities to the most intense and brutal bombardments.”
He went on to describe the killing of children on the first day of the attacks, saying, “On the first day of the attack, 168 innocent children were torn apart, and the bodies of some of them were never found.”
Referring to attacks on homes, universities and residential areas, as well as the deaths of thousands of people, Majidi questioned why the Iranian people should have to pay such a price.
“What do you think our people’s crime is? They simply want to be independent, and we will stand firm to the very end,” he said. “I wish for a future with no more war, full of peace, love, and friendship,” he concluded.
Earlier in the festival, Majidi spoke at length at a press conference about how he had nearly declined the invitation to travel to South Korea because he felt depressed and exhausted by the dire situation at home. He ultimately decided that the trip would allow him and his film to convey “some kind of small message from my people to the people of other nations and other places.”
“Midday Meal” dazzled critics in Busan with its powerful, parable-like storytelling and assured visual style. The film follows Davoud Soulan (Mohammad Rahimi), a contract teacher in a remote village in southeastern Iran whose hopes of securing a permanent government job are jeopardized when a wealthy benefactor dies and the free lunches that keep his impoverished pupils coming to school disappear. Determined to save both his school and his future, Soulan resorts to increasingly desperate measures, including dangerous cross-border fuel smuggling, as his natural decency comes into conflict with his modest ambitions.
The film continues Majidi’s longstanding thematic preoccupation with the moral pressures faced by people on society’s margins, as seen in earlier festival-winning works like “The Color of Paradise” (1999) and “Baran” (2001).
For “Midday Meal,” he assembled an entirely nonprofessional cast through street casting in the region, setting their performances against the stark, otherworldly landscape of Iran’s so-called Martian Mountains.
Majidi and cinematographer Houman Behmanesh capture much of the drama with a gliding camera, often placing their protagonist against the region’s rugged, otherworldly landscape. The film gradually takes on the quality of an enigmatic existentialist parable.
The film marks the first time Majidi has been invited to Busan, having previously played Cannes, Berlin and Venice over the past 35 years. He is Iran’s most submitted filmmaker to the international category of the Academy Awards, landing a nomination in 1999 with “Children of Heaven” and making the shortlist in 2021 with “Sun Children”.
With its humanist approach to social realism and its particular focus on child welfare, “Midday Meal” is of a piece with Majidi’s oeuvre, which includes such films as “The Color of Paradise” and the 2020 Venice competition entry “Sun Children”; he remains best known internationally for his 1998 film “Children of Heaven,” the first Iranian production ever to be nominated in the category today named Best International Feature.

Mexico: Killers of US, Australian surfers jailed for 158 years each
October 17, 2026
A court in Mexico sentenced three men to more than 158 years each in prison on Friday for murdering two Australian surfers and their American friend in 2024.
The court also ordered the defendants to pay compensation to the victims' families, an official said.
The three defendants, Jesus Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were convicted a week ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
What was the case about?
In 2024, the three victims were on a surfing trip to Mexico's Pacific coast.
Brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their American friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were shot dead in Baja California state during an attempted robbery.
The three were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on April 27, 2024.
Days later, their search, assisted by the FBI, led to their bodies dumped in a cliff-top well, with gunshot wounds to their heads.
Their killings sent shockwaves through Ensenada, the hotspot for surfing that attracts people from around the world.
While Mexico has long struggled with widespread insecurity, the area where the murders were committed was considered safe for tourists.
What did the families of the victims say?
"There will never be justice for the loss of a child, but these men will never hurt anyone else again,” said Page Rhoad, mother of the slain American, via Zoom after the sentencing.
The Robinsons' parents traveled to Mexico from Australia for the month-long trial and left after the initial guilty verdict.
"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin Robinson said.
Debra Robinson said what hurt the most was that her sons "were treated with such cruelty" in their final hours.

OPINION: The policing of Muslim women’s bodies, from West Asia to Europe and beyond

Strike on Yandex Data Center: Five of Nine Buildings Damaged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:16:53 UTC
17:16:53 KST

Satellite images revealed that the strike on the Yandex data center in the Vladimir region damaged five of the nine buildings located on the site.
The images were published by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.
The attack took place on the night of October 11. A fire broke out on the facility’s grounds as a result of the drone strikes.
Judging by the satellite images, both of the company’s data centers located at this site were damaged. In the first data center, all four buildings were hit and sustained numerous impacts, while in the second data center, satellite images recorded a single impact.
This and other Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers caused serious disruptions to the Russian segment of the internet and popular services, including the Yandex Pay payment system.
The Yandex data center in Vladimir is one of the largest in the company’s network. Its rated capacity is approximately 56 MW.
The first phase of the data center began operations in September 2017. The capacity of the first phase was 10 MW; the initial project called for a gradual expansion of IT capacity to 40 MW and the installation of 2,880 server racks.
This data center houses one of the company’s three supercomputers—the Galushkin, which was commissioned in June 2021. It consisted of 136 computing nodes equipped with AMD EPYC 7702 processors and 1,088 NVIDIA A100 graphics accelerators with 80 GB of memory. The system had 136 TB of RAM, and its nodes were connected via a high-speed InfiniBand HDR network.
Its theoretical peak performance reached 20.64 petaflops. In November 2021, the system ranked 36th on the global TOP500 list and second among Russian supercomputers.
According to the Russian opposition publication T-invariant, it, like Yandex’s other two supercomputers, was likely damaged as a result of Ukrainian attacks. All of Yandex’s supercomputers were used primarily for training neural networks.
“It will not be possible to restore the operation of supercomputers of this caliber. And the issue isn’t even about having the money. The main problem isn’t even the sanctions, but the shortage of chips and other components: there’s a huge waiting list for them worldwide. However, the costs of gray and black market imports are also very high,” says a supercomputer expert interviewed by the publication.
In March 2026, Yandex launched a new data center with a stated capacity of 40 MW and space for 2,800 server racks, as well as independent power and communications systems.

Expert Insights: Meet the Danes with wind in your hair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:14:31 UTC
17:14:31 KST

The author: Vivienne McKee is a British actor and director who has lived in Denmark for decades. Her shows are among the most popular with Danish audiences. She also writes a column for The Copenhagen Post, where she offers guidance to internationals on navigating life in Danish society.
I am often asked by my non-dane friends: how do I meet danes? It’s true that danes are often difficult to connect with . They spend their leisure hours mainly with their families, less frequently, with colleagues, and rarely with strangers. In the UK, people catch up with their neighbours and any passing stranger over a pint of beer at the pub. In Denmark this tradition does not exist. Possibly because pubs do not exist here, just cafes or late night bars.
How about a drink?
If you think Copenhagen is quiet, try the provinces. I once worked for a few months at a theatre in a provincial town in Jutland. We actors were all in temporary accommodation, so I asked my danish colleagues where we could go for a drink after rehearsals. They looked aghast and told me they spent their evenings learning their lines, making dinner and training at the fitness centre. The idea of meeting for an after-work drink was apparently not on their agenda. Fortunately a local shop owner told me that, as it was Friday, I could join her and her friends at the local pub. I couldn’t believe my ears – a pub? She told me to come at 4.00 pm to “The English Pub“ by the harbour. Although I thought that 4.00 pm was rather early for a drink, to my astonishment, the place was simply heaving with people. There were so many that I had to push my way through a boisterous crowd to reach my new friend. We chatted happily over the clamour, and then suddenly, everyone got up and left. Within minutes the pub was empty. She told me that at 6.00 pm everyone went home for dinner. As she left, she shouted – see you next Friday !
And now the good news!
Yes, meeting Danes is not easy, and it’s easy to complain. But there is a fantastic opportunity for meeting Danes right here in Copenhagen. In addition, you get a sight-seeing tour of the city, free of charge and, as a bonus – wind in your hair ! A cool dane, Ole Kassow, started an NGO called “Cycling without Age .” Their slogan is “Ret til vind I håren, uanset alder“ (“The right to wind in your hair, whatever your age“).
The story goes that he lived opposite an old people’s home and, noticing an old fellow sitting alone outside, he asked him if he’d like to go for a bike ride. With the agreement of the matron, he hired a trishaw bike and took the old man out . When they returned the man couldn’t stop smiling . The idea grew in Ole’s mind to make his bike rides available to everybody. Now, 15 years later, his brilliant idea is working all over the world. In 56 countries including – most of Europe, North America, South America, Australia, Africa and Asia and with its 62,000 volunteer riders, Kassow’s “Cycling Without Age” has become an international phenomenon.
Practice your Danish
These bike rides use volunteers to pedal the bikes and chat to the wide selection of people who ride on them. On my first ride I collected a 89 year old fellow called Carl. It was the day after Børsen, the Stock Exchange with the dragon-tailed spire, burnt down, and when we cycled up to the charred ruin, tears filled his eyes, but soon he was entertaining me with stories of a Copenhagen when trams filled the streets and beer cost one kroner. We had a great bike ride together checking out all the sights, and I had a useful time practising my Danish with a helpful listener. So if you want to meet Danes, get to know the city and practise your Danish at the same time, I cannot recommend a better activity. You meet Ole and other volunteers when you collect your trishaw, get involved in fun activities , and at the end of each ride you feel good because you’ve improved yours and someone else’s, life – even if the wind has made a mess of your hair!

Romania is a recommended destination by National Geographic for October 2026
Saturday 17 October 2026 09:38

Transfăgărășan in the Carpathian Mountains
PHOTO Mariana Chiriță, Radio Romania International
Font size
National Geographic’ magazine has included Romania in its list of the most beautiful vacation destinations for October 2026, following New York, Madagascar, Argentina, Scotland, and Egypt. Ranked sixth, the country is recommended especially for culturally-focused road trips. The magazine highlighted the stunning landscapes along the Transfăgărășan and in Transylvania in general.
According to the publication, October is the last month the Transfăgărășan is open to tourists, and the fall scenery offers some of the most spectacular views in the Southern Carpathians. “October is the last month in which the Transfăgărășan - a 56-mile highway that winds through the peaks and valleys of the southern Carpathian Mountains - is fully open to visitors (for the rest of the year the sheep and brown bears have it all to themselves). It’s at its most scenic in autumn when the landscape is awash with amber foliage” the magazine notes. Tourists are invited to discover Transylvania, Bran Castle, and the Black Church in Brașov, or to explore the mysterious Hoia-Baciu Forest, known for its tales of paranormal phenomena.
Bran Castle
PHOTO Ştefan Baciu, RRI
“For those seeking full immersion into Romania’s more mystical history and culture, Transylvania is the ideal roaming ground. Follow in Count Dracula’s footsteps on a tour of the region’s famed Bran Castle, nicknamed Dracula’s Castle due to its resemblance to the home of the fictional Transylvanian vampire, before heading to nearby Brașov to see its gothic Black Church” the article adds.
“Or follow the Transfăgărășan to the country’s eastern reaches for a stroll through the Hoia-Baciu Forest, which is known for its abundance of rugged hiking paths, crooked trees and paranormal tales.” National Geographic writes adding that: “Kürtőskalács, or chimney cake, is a must-try delicacy that’s served year-round but best enjoyed on chilly autumn afternoons. They can be bought at street-food markets and from carts parked by popular attractions,” wrote National Geographic.
Brasov
PHOTO romania-insider.com
Romania has also been included in other prestigious rankings and lists compiled by National Geographic, focusing on conservation, ecotourism, and global attractions. In March 2026, the country ranked second worldwide in the list of the most spectacular nature conservation projects worth traveling for. The publication highlighted the massive reforestation efforts, biodiversity, and rewilding initiatives (such as the reintroduction of aurochs). Romania was described as one of the last destinations in Europe offering truly wild, vibrant, and unspoiled nature.
Furthermore, the Făgăraș Mountains in the Southern Carpathians, nicknamed “Europe’s Yellowstone,” ranked second worldwide in a list compiled by the magazine of the most spectacular nature conservation projects, surpassed only by Ecuador’s Cloud Forests.
Over the years, various regions and attractions in Romania have been selected for the prestigious annual “Best of the World” list or recommended as destinations by National Geographic experts, including Maramureș, the Danube Delta, and Transylvania.

The Iron Church of St Stephen – a symbol of Bulgarian identity in Istanbul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:12:07 UTC
17:12:07 KST

From Radio Bulgaria's best collection
The Iron Church of St Stephen – a symbol of Bulgarian identity in Istanbul
The foundation stone was laid by Prince Nikola Bogoridi on October 25, 1859, construction began 32 years later, and the church was officially consecrated on September 8, 1898
Saturday 17 October 2026 10:25
Saturday, 17 October 2026, 10:25
PHOTO nationalgeographic.bg
Font size
The Bulgarian Church of St Stephen in Istanbul (also known as the Bulgarian Iron Church), associated with the struggle for church independence which began in the 1930’s and the 1940’s, is the world’s only iron Orthodox Church. It is 20 meters tall, including the bell tower. The Bulgarian Orthodox temple was built on a site covering 500 square metres. It is a three-nave cross-shaped basilica. It was made of pre-fabricated cast iron elements. The altar faces the Golden Horn and a 40-meter-high beautiful belfry.
The Bulgarian Iron Church was built at the end of the 19th century when the Bulgarian community in Istanbul (then Tsarigrad) amounted to 50,000 people. In 1849 statesman Stefan Bogoridi donated a plot of land with several buildings-a wooden and two stone houses situated in Fener district in Istanbul. The wooden house was later reorganized as wooden church.
The wooden building used as a Bulgarian church in Tsarigrad before being replaced by the iron church in 1898
PHOTO archive
On October 17, 1849, an Ottoman royal decree allowing the Bulgarians to have their own religious temple was issued. Then, the ground floor of the wooden house donated by Stefan Bogoridi was turned into a temporary chapel. Later, it became a separate church named after First Martyr and Archdeacon St Stephen in honor of benefactor Stefan Bogoridi. The temple was known at that time as the Wooden Church.
In 1850 the stone buildings in the church yard were demolished and later a three-story building, known as the Convent, was built instead. It became headquarters of the Bulgarian Exarchate, established on February 27, 1870. The Bulgarian Exarchate functioned in Istanbul even after Bulgaria’s liberation- until the Balkan War in 1912.
PHOTO nationalgeographic.bg
On June 25, 1890 an Ottoman royal decree allowed the Bulgarian Exarchate to build a new church on these premises. The new church was inaugurated by Exarch Joseph. An iron frame was preferred to concrete reinforcement due to weak ground conditions. The construction plans of the Iron Church were prepared by the Ottoman Armenian Architect Hovsep Aznavur. The pre-fabricated iron elements weighing 500 tons were made in Vienna and transported to Istanbul (Tsaribrod) by ship through the Danube and the Black Sea. The main skeleton of the Iron Church was made of steel and covered by metal sheets. It was completed on July 14, 1896. In terms of architecture, the Iron Church combines Neo-Gothic and Neo-Baroque influences. The icons were painted by a Russian artist and the six church bells were also cast in Russia. Two of them are still in use.
PHOTO St. Stephen Bulgarian Orthodox Church Foundation
The official inauguration of the new St Stephen Church was made by Exarch Joseph on the Nativity of Mary feast on September 8, 1898. Today, the St Stephen church is one of the world’s few metal churches.
Bulgarian church figures such as Hilarion of Makariopolis, Avksentiy Veleshki, Maletiy Veleshki and Paisius of Plovdiv were buried in the church yard.
The St Stephen Church which marked its 120 anniversary in 2018 is regarded the most-valuable monument of the Bulgarian historical and cultural heritage in Türkiye and abroad.
PHOTO BTA
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov

China Focus: From potato capital to token city: Ulanqab rises as China's AI hub
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:11:19 CST
17:11:19 KST

HOHHOT, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Ulanqab, in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, has long been known as the home of the potato. Now the grassland city has become a factory for AI tokens, which stream along an invisible "information superhighway" to Beijing.
An advanced optical cable runs directly to the capital, with a measured one-way data transmission latency of just 2.1 milliseconds, making several hundred kilometers in between almost imperceptible.
A Goldman Sachs report says that Ulanqab has emerged as one of the largest and fastest-growing AI computing clusters in the Asia-Pacific region, with a number of leading companies setting up operations here.
The appeal is partly geographic. Inner Mongolia enjoys a climate that allows natural cooling for nearly 10 months a year, vast land that can support gigawatt-scale computing projects, abundant green power, and proximity to the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, with network latency within 5 milliseconds.
COMPUTING LEAP
"When I came here to scout a site in 2022, the area was relatively desolate," recalled Zhou Yiguang, director of the resource development department at the Ulanqab base of VNET Group, a cyberspace infrastructure service provider.
Today, VNET's projects in Ulanqab have a planned total land area of 1,100 mu (about 73.3 hectares), the equivalent of more than 100 football fields, and a total IT capacity of about 1.3 gigawatts, capable of supporting computing cluster deployment at the million-card scale.
In November 2025, Ulanqab launched a three-year action plan to build a "token city," aiming to create a complete industrial chain of "wind and solar power generation, green computing power and token value output."
The city has now taken on 75,000 petaflops of computing workloads from Beijing, supporting large-model training for leading companies such as ByteDance, DeepSeek and Baidu. These resources power applications across cutting-edge fields such as computer vision, autonomous driving, and film and television rendering.
The city's operational computing capacity has reached 190,000 petaflops, with intelligent computing accounting for more than 90 percent of the total.
In the first half of 2026, Ulanqab's fixed-asset investment, electricity consumption and revenue in the computing power industry grew by 39 percent, 90 percent and 12 percent year- on-year, respectively, according to the official data.
Inner Mongolia has rolled out a package of policies to support the development of data and AI, the token economy, and the green computing power industry.
By June, 20 of China's 30 leading private companies in the computing power industry had established a presence in Inner Mongolia, with total investment exceeding 200 billion yuan (about 30 billion U.S. dollars). By August, the total computing power of Inner Mongolia had reached 363,000 petaflops, nearly quadrupling in less than two years.
BROAD TALENT DEMAND
Ulanqab has attracted more than 100 data center projects, and the computing boom has created strong demand for professionals in infrastructure operations and maintenance.
Chen Gang, 23, is a local of Ulanqab and works as a technician at a data center, handling cutting-edge equipment every day. But two years ago, he was still uncertain about his future.
For generations, a lot of locals made a living by growing potatoes. Many young people left to find work elsewhere, and Chen once worked as a hotel waiter in Qingdao, east China's Shandong Province.
Watching the data industry take off in his hometown, Chen decided to seize the opportunity. He quit his job and returned to Ulanqab, enrolled in a local training program and then got hired by a data center.
Chen's core work is routine inspection, to ensure that power supply, cooling and server room equipment are running safely. That requires a solid command of electrical systems, heating, ventilation and air conditioning, low-voltage systems and fire protection.
In 2026, more than 20 computing power companies have set up operations in Ulanqab, drawing more young people back home.
The industry-education integration base for computing power and AI in Inner Mongolia, which pairs computing power centers with vocational training, has trained more than 2,000 AI professionals.
By March 2026, China's average daily AI token calls had surged from about 100 billion in early 2024 to 140 trillion. These young people, like Chen, are stepping into a new stage of the computing power industry, where value is measured in AI tokens. ■

China calls for joint efforts to address risks, challenges in nuclear field
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:11:14 CST
17:11:14 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- China's ambassador for disarmament affairs, Li Chijiang, on Friday called on the international community to work together to address the risks and challenges in the nuclear field.
Li made the appeal at the thematic debate on nuclear weapons at the Disarmament and International Security Committee of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.
Over the past year, confrontation within multilateral nuclear arms control mechanisms has further intensified. The international community is increasingly concerned about the risks of a nuclear arms race and nuclear war, he said.
The Cold War mentality is the primary source of deterioration of the international strategic security environment, the envoy noted.
Double standards are the greatest challenge to the international nuclear non-proliferation regime, and unilateralism is the greatest obstacle to global governance in the nuclear field, he added.
"The international community should work together to address the risks and challenges in the nuclear field following the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security," said Li.
Relevant nuclear-weapon states should abandon their policy of nuclear deterrence based on winning a nuclear war and the first use of nuclear weapons, he said.
The international consensus on the nuclear test ban must not be challenged, Li said, adding that the commitments on "moratorium on nuclear testing" must be honored.
The state with the largest nuclear arsenal should effectively fulfill the special and primary responsibility for nuclear disarmament by making drastic and substantive reductions in its nuclear arsenal, rather than pursuing "the world's most robust, credible and modern nuclear deterrent," Li said.
Efforts to prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons should not undermine the right of developing countries to the peaceful use of nuclear energy. The peaceful use of nuclear energy must not be used as a cover for nuclear proliferation, he said.
A certain non-nuclear-weapon state accumulates large amounts of plutonium of no credible civilian use, promotes the revision of the "Three Non-Nuclear Principles," and openly advocates the possession of nuclear weapons. The international community must be vigilant and exercise strict constraint, Li said.
The Three Non-Nuclear Principles, formally adopted by the Japanese parliament in 1971, refer to not possessing, not producing, and not permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons into the country.
China's position of advocating the complete prohibition and thorough destruction of nuclear weapons remains firm, its policy of no-first-use of nuclear weapons is consistent, and its efforts to maintain global strategic security and stability have never ceased, he said. ■

IOC replaces commissions with working groups under "Fit for the Future" reforms
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:10:38 CST
17:10:38 KST

LAUSANNE, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- The International Olympic Committee (IOC) on Friday announced that it will transition its stakeholder engagement model from a commission-based approach to a working group approach.
Over the past 15 months, several working groups have already been established to address key "Fit for the Future" topics, demonstrating the value of the approach. As part of the review, the IOC paused its non-institutional commissions in February while assessing future engagement models.
Following that assessment, the IOC has decided to discontinue 12 commissions: Athletes' Entourage; Culture and Olympic Heritage; Digital Engagement and Marketing Communications; Gender Equality, Diversity and Inclusion; the IOC Advisory Committee on Human Rights; Olympic Education; Olympic Programme; Olympism365; Public Affairs and Corporate Communications; Revenues and Commercial Partnerships; Sustainability and Legacy; and Technology and Technical Innovation.
The change stems from the ongoing "Fit for the Future" reform process and follows more than a year of consultation and review, including discussions with commission members, the IOC said. The organization concluded that working groups with clearly defined mandates offer a more effective and flexible mechanism for shaping policy and supporting decision-making.
The IOC says the shift will enable more targeted engagement on key strategic priorities and policy development across the Olympic Movement.
A number of institutional bodies will continue their work unchanged. These include the Athletes' Commission, the Audit Committee, the Coordination Commissions for the Olympic Games and Youth Olympic Games, the Ethics Commission, the Finance Commission, the Future Host Commissions for both the Summer and Winter Games, the Health, Medicine and Science Commission, the Human Resources Committee, the IOC Members Election Commission, the IOC Television and Marketing Services Board of Directors, the Legal Affairs Commission, the Olympic Broadcasting Services Board of Directors, the Olympic Channel Services Board of Directors, the Olympic Refuge Foundation Board and the Olympic Solidarity Commission.
The IOC said the transition "is designed to provide greater flexibility in engaging subject-matter expertise while strengthening its ability to address specific opportunities and challenges through focused, purpose-driven collaboration." ■

From a marriage proposal to a fight for survival: Israeli couple recounts flydubai terror
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:08:07 UTC
17:08:07 KST

"I told her, 'Baby, I love you.' I couldn't believe this was how I was going to die." That is how Adar Hayut, one of the passengers who subdued the terrorist pilot on a flydubai flight, described the terror he experienced about two weeks ago when the plane went into a steep dive and he began thinking about saying goodbye to his family and his fiancée, Michal, to whom he had proposed during their trip to Japan.
"We weren't supposed to be on that flight," Hayut told ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth. "We had flown to Japan for a monthlong trip, during which I proposed to Michal. We had originally been booked on a different flight, but were switched to this one. We were sitting on the plane, and I was reading an article on my iPad and taking notes while Michal was looking at the flight map on the screen, going through the cities displayed and checking what there was to do in each one. Suddenly, the plane started going crazy, making random turns in every direction."
At that point, he said, he was focused on calming the panicked passengers.
"Someone shouted to fasten our seat belts. I hadn’t fastened my seat belt yet, and very quickly I found myself floating between my seat and the ceiling for two full seconds. I saw people around me panicking and shouted, 'Breathe deeply into your stomachs. Everything is OK. Fasten your seat belts.'"
Hayut buckled up. At that stage, he had no idea it was an attempted terrorist attack. He said he was convinced there was a mechanical problem, possibly causing the plane to stall, and that the pilot was trying unsuccessfully to regain control.
"I was certain we were going to die. I thought that if I got up, Michal and I would die apart, and I couldn't bear not being with her in our final moments."
But as the dive grew steeper and the plane went into a spin, Hayut realized there was no way out.
"I understood that we were going to crash," he said. "So many thoughts were racing through my head. I thought about people in similar situations who chose to say goodbye to their loved ones. I looked at Michal and told her, 'Baby, I love you.' I repeated it several times. I couldn't believe this was how I was going to die, that my family would have to go on living without me and that I wouldn't get to see the AI bubble burst."
Michal said she, too, wondered whether this was really how their story would end.
"We had been talking about starting a family and were excited to begin planning the wedding," she said. "I was terrified and felt we were going to die. I thought maybe I should record something for my parents."
It was then that Hayut heard the screams of Tali Manes, the wife of Tzvika Manes, who also helped subdue the terrorist. According to witness accounts, she was the first to alert passengers to what was happening and call for help.
"Someone shouted, 'We need people up front. We need people to help,'" Hayut continued. "Meanwhile, one of the flight attendants was moving toward the front of the plane, shouting for everyone to fasten their seat belts. When he reached the front, he turned back. His face fell, as though he had just seen death itself. As he headed toward the back of the plane, apparently to get a first-aid kit, he shouted, 'I can't believe it.'
"When I saw his face, I realized something else was probably happening. But what went through my mind was that one of the passengers had stabbed both pilots and that death was certain. I thought that if I got up, Michal and I would die apart, and I couldn't bear not being with her in our final moments."
After the plane stabilized, Hayut heard people shouting that they needed a doctor and decided to get up and help.
"I turned to Michal and asked, 'Is it OK if I get up?' She said, 'Go.' I ran toward the front, and when people tried to stop me, I told them I was a medical student," he recalled.
"I squeezed past people and entered the passageway leading to the cockpit, where a chaotic scene was unfolding amid a lot of shouting. Slightly to my left, I saw the Indian pilot lying on the floor, bleeding. The terrorist was curled up over the Indian pilot's legs, with Assaf Rajuan and Yaniv [Hayun] on top of him.
"I asked them who was flying the plane, and they told me, 'The pilot.' I could see a pilot sitting in the left seat of the cockpit, with blood smeared across his right shoulder."
Hayut initially went to help the injured Indian pilot but realized the terrorist had not yet been fully subdued. He left the pilot and moved to restrain the attacker. Then people began shouting that the terrorist had a knife.
"The terrorist was struck several more times. A flight attendant lowered a set of plastic restraints onto his exposed hand, and I tightened one. Without hesitating, I grabbed the hand that posed the threat, secured it with the second restraint and tightened it. I tightened it so much that it could cause tissue necrosis because, as far as I was concerned, there could be absolutely no chance of him breaking free," he said.
'We're picking up the pieces'
But then, according to Hayut, the flight attendants asked the passengers to loosen the terrorist's restraints.
"The flight attendants started arguing with us. They wanted to loosen the restraints a little, which made us suspicious that they might be against us."
Hayut described a confrontation with the crew that continued until the flight attendants began listening to the passengers.
At that point, Hayut again went to reassure the other passengers.
"I told them, 'Everyone, there has been a terrorist attack. The situation is under control. There's a pilot flying the plane,'" he said.
"I felt I had succeeded, but when I returned to the cockpit, I realized the issue of loosening the restraints hadn't been resolved, and things were heating up again.
"During the argument, Yaniv [Hayun] said, 'Guys, if we don't take charge here, I don't know how this is going to end.' I started pulling one of the flight attendants away. We struggled while standing, and I decided to calm things down. When I calmed down, he calmed down too, and they began to come around."
Michal said that even after the plane stabilized and the situation was brought under control, she and the other passengers remained terrified.
"At that point, we thought the terrorist was one of the passengers, and we didn't know whether he had accomplices. I felt I needed to arm myself with something to defend myself, and I was afraid he had brought some kind of explosive on board.
"Everyone was suspicious of the flight attendants. We didn't know who was cooperating with whom. There was a lot of tension until the plane landed."
About two weeks later, the couple is still struggling with the trauma.
"I still haven't processed it, and I feel like my body is still in shock. I haven't cried yet or fully let it all out," Michal said.
"I'm having a very hard time concentrating, and I have nightmares at night. I'm taking sleeping pills. I've always had trouble falling asleep, so now it's even more overwhelming. Physically, I still feel the tension from what happened on the plane, and it's affecting me."
The couple returned home safely but have yet to celebrate their engagement.
"No one asks us about Japan or the engagement. They ask about what we went through on the plane," they said.
"Fortunately, it ended well. We're trying to pick up the pieces because we need to start planning the wedding, but we still haven't fully recovered."

Russia rebuilt its Blackjack bomber on a new tech base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:05:01 UTC
17:05:01 KST

- Tupolev’s chief said 80% of the Tu-160M bomber’s systems and equipment were modernized, including avionics, navigation and engines.
- He said the bomber’s modular avionics will allow newer systems to replace outdated ones without redesigning the whole suite.
Russia’s Tupolev says about 80% of the systems and equipment on its new Tu-160M strategic bomber have been modernized, and that the aircraft’s onboard electronics were designed as a modular architecture so newer systems can be swapped in later without rebuilding the whole suite.
Tupolev General Director Yuri Abrosimov made the claims in comments published by Russian state defense conglomerate Rostec and Tupolev’s parent, United Aircraft Corporation. The Tu-160M keeps the outward look of the Soviet-era Tu-160 supersonic bomber, known in NATO as the Blackjack, but most of its systems, including avionics, navigation and engines, have been upgraded, he said.
“Outside, the Tu-160M has kept that same recognizable silhouette, but inside it was created on an entirely new technological base with active use of digital technologies. 80% of the systems and equipment were modernized,” said Abrosimov, in remarks translated from Russian.
According to Abrosimov, the modular avionics will let Russia integrate newer equipment over time in place of outdated systems, which he said would allow the bomber to keep up with emerging requirements and take on a wider range of missions. He did not specify which systems are new or name any planned additions.
The Tu-160 is a four-engine, variable-sweep-wing bomber that can carry up to 12 long-range cruise missiles in internal rotary launchers and serves in the air leg of Russia’s nuclear triad. Under the Tu-160M program, Kazan Aviation Plant is both upgrading older Tu-160s and building new aircraft, and earlier upgrade phases have added a new radar, a digital glass cockpit, new navigation and communication equipment, and NK-32-02 engines.
Russia signed a contract in January 2018 for 10 new Tu-160M bombers worth a reported 160 billion rubles. The first newly built aircraft flew in January 2022, but deliveries slipped repeatedly, and Russia’s Aerospace Forces received two Tu-160M bombers in late 2025, The Defence Blog reported.
The bombers have been used to launch cruise missiles at Ukraine. Analysis by the Ukrainian aviation monitoring channel AviVector, published in May, found that only seven of Russia’s 18 Tu-160M bombers were flying combat missions, while seven to nine aircraft were at the Kazan plant at any given time for modernization, maintenance or construction, The Defence Blog reported.

The fire broke out at a wooden resort and restaurant at Inani Sea Beach in Cox's Bazar, the fire service said in a statement, adding that the blaze was completely extinguished after two firefighting units responded alongside local authorities and police.
The Border Guard said in a statement that its personnel also joined the rescue operation.
At least nine people were injured when the fire broke out early in the morning while they were asleep, Jamuna TV reported. Their identities have not yet been confirmed.
All those affected are believed to be tourists, as the area is a popular tourist destination, the report said.
The fire may have originated from a stove in the resort's kitchen or an electrical short circuit, the report noted, while the cause has not yet been verified.
The district authorities have formed a committee to investigate the incident.

France braces for nationwide protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:02:00 UTC
17:02:00 KST

France: Protesters rally nationwide amid rising social polarization
October 17, 2026
Mass rallies are taking place across France on Saturday, with protesters airing grievances ranging from high prices and social inequalities to a dilapidated education system.
The protests come on the heels of a initial wave of demonstrations that began last month over the situation at schools in the country, with pupils complaining about teacher absences and run-down facilities.
President Emmanuel Macron has called "for calm and respect" ahead of the protests, saying that the right to protest went hand in hand with "respect for people and property."
In Paris and Marseille, police have fired tear gas at protesters during clashes.
What do we know about the protests in France?
More than 600 demonstrations are planned across France, according to protest organizers.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told France 2 television that "a pretty big turnout" was expected, while a police source told the French AFP news agency that authorities estimate nearly 200,000 people will attend.
However, the Paris demonstrators will face restrictions, with police banning rallies around the Elysee presidential palace, the prime minister's office and the Champs-Elysee avenue, along with other key locations.
A march through the center of the city has also been banned.
The main Paris demonstration is due to begin at 2 p.m. (1200 GMT) at the Place de la Republique and head to the north of the city.
Reports began emerging late on Saturday morning of riot police clashing with protesters in the Saint-Denis area on the outskirts of the capital, as well as near the Gare du Nord train station, among other areas.
Fears of violence at the French protests
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Thursday that authorities fear there could be violence during the protests.
"This is a moment of fatigue in the country," Lecornu said. "We are in an atmosphere of perma-crisis: wars, inflation, and issues surrounding purchasing power."
Jordan Bardella, the head of the far-right National Rally, which is leading the polls ahead of next year's presidential election, said he expected clashes.
"I'm extremely concerned," he said during a visit to the Paris car show. "It will be a day of chaos for France."
The school protests that have rocked France in recent weeks have already seen considerable violence, with several protesters and more than 900 police injured.
In one notable incident, an adolescent school pupil had one hand blown off and several fingers on the other hand injured by a stun grenade.
The internal police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen cases of alleged police violence.
Who is taking part in the protests?
Students are to be joined by trade unionists and remnants of the Yellow Vests ("Gilets jaunes") movement, which staged mass weekly protests from November 2018 to June 2020, initially against rising fuel prices. They later morphed into protests against the high cost of living and economic inequality in general.
The student protests over the past weeks have been backed by Jean-Luc Melanchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed ("La France insoumise", or LFI), who marched in one demonstration on Tuesday.
The government has blamed the LFI for pouring fuel on the fire of widespread public discontent, an allegation the party has denied.
