Hanged, electrocuted and poisoned: The killers who survived execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:39:11 UTC
16:39:11 KST

"Take it off! Take it off! Let me breathe!" cried Willie Francis, a 17-year-old boy from Louisiana, after an electric current intended to kill him passed through his body. The year was 1946. Francis was strapped into the electric chair and prison officials had already thrown the switch. But instead of dying, his body convulsed, the chair shook — and he remained alive. Prison officials were forced to release him from his restraints and return him to his cell. A year later, they tried again. This time, they succeeded.
Francis' case became one of the most famous episodes in the history of capital punishment in the United States, but it was far from the only one. Throughout history, there have been documented cases of death row inmates surviving hanging, electrocution or attempts to kill them by lethal injection. Some survived because of technical malfunctions, others because of mistakes by execution teams. In exceptionally rare cases, prisoners survived even after the execution method itself had been administered.
These stories have returned to the headlines following the extraordinary case of Christa Pike, the Tennessee killer who survived two doses of execution drugs last month. But behind these remarkable stories lies a far more troubling question: What happens when a state sentences someone to death, attempts to carry out the punishment — and fails?
Hanged, declared dead — and revived before her autopsy
One of the earliest and most astonishing cases occurred in England in 1650. Anne Greene, a 22-year-old servant from the Oxford area, was convicted of infanticide after becoming pregnant by the grandson of the man who employed her and suffering a miscarriage. At a time when unmarried women who concealed pregnancies could be regarded as murderers if they could not prove the circumstances of their babies' deaths, she was sentenced to death by hanging.
In December of that year, Greene was taken to the gallows in Oxford. A rope was placed around her neck and she was hanged before a crowd of onlookers. According to historical records, she remained suspended for about half an hour, and people at the scene even pulled on her legs in an attempt to hasten her death.
She was then cut down and delivered in a coffin to doctors at the University of Oxford, who intended to dissect her body. But it emerged that Greene was still alive. The doctors detected signs of breathing and a pulse and began trying to revive her. They warmed her body, treated her and monitored her condition. Against all expectations, she gradually regained consciousness and recovered.
Her extraordinary survival caused a sensation. Some saw it as divine intervention, and the doctors who treated her helped secure a pardon. Greene was not returned to the gallows. She was released, married and had three children. According to a study published in the Journal of Medical Biography, she lived until 1659 — nine years after her supposed execution.
Her case became a local legend, and pamphlets and poems describing the woman who survived hanging circulated in England for years. Centuries later, her story continues to be examined in medical studies, including efforts to understand how she managed to survive for so long after being hanged.
'The man they could not hang'
More than 200 years later, in February 1885, another extraordinary incident occurred in England. John "Babbacombe" Lee was convicted of murdering his employer, Emma Keyse, and sentenced to death by hanging.
He was brought to the gallows at Exeter Prison, where executioner James Berry prepared to carry out the sentence. Lee was positioned on a wooden trapdoor designed to open beneath his feet, dropping him through the gallows.
But when the mechanism was activated, the trapdoor failed to open. Prison officials attempted to repair the malfunction and operate the gallows again, but the second attempt also failed. The same thing happened a third time.
Eventually, officials decided to halt the execution. The case attracted widespread attention across Britain, and Lee became known as "the man they could not hang." The British home secretary commuted his death sentence to life imprisonment.
Although Lee escaped the gallows, he was not immediately freed. He spent another 22 years in prison before being released in 1907. His subsequent fate remains uncertain, but his story is one of the best-known cases of an execution thwarted by a mechanical failure.
The teenager who survived the electric chair
The case of Willie Francis, more than 60 years after the failed attempts to hang Lee, ended very differently.
Francis, a Black teenager from Louisiana, was convicted of murdering Andrew Thomas, a white pharmacy owner who had previously employed him. He was sentenced to death in 1945, when he was 16, and on May 3, 1946, he was taken to the electric chair.
According to official testimony later presented to the U.S. Supreme Court, Francis was strapped into the chair, a hood was placed over his face and the operator threw the switch. The teenager's body convulsed violently and he jerked in his seat. One witness described how officials demanded that the electrical current be increased after it became clear that the boy was not dead, but the operator replied that he was already delivering the maximum possible power.
Francis continued breathing. He cried out for officials to remove the hood and let him breathe. After the attempt failed, prison officials released him and returned him to custody.
It later emerged that a malfunction in the chair's electrical system had prevented a sufficiently powerful current from passing through his body to kill him.
His lawyers argued that Louisiana had no right to execute him a second time. They maintained that another attempt would constitute cruel and unusual punishment, prohibited under the U.S. Constitution, and would expose him to the risk of death a second time under the same sentence.
The case reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which rejected Francis' arguments in January 1947. The majority held that the unintentional malfunction during the first attempt did not make a second attempt a violation of his constitutional rights.
On May 9 of that year, Francis was returned to the electric chair. This time, the system worked and he died at age 18.
His case became a significant legal precedent that continues to shape legal battles involving death row inmates who have survived execution attempts.
Eighteen needle punctures, two hours of pain — and a return to death row
In recent decades, most botched executions in the United States have involved the very method intended to replace the electric chair: lethal injection.
One prominent case was that of Romell Broom, who was convicted of kidnapping, rape and murder in Ohio and sentenced to death in 1985.
On September 15, 2009, Broom was taken to the execution chamber, placed on a gurney and restrained. The execution team began searching for a vein into which they could insert an IV line to administer the lethal drugs.
But the task proved exceptionally difficult. Time after time, team members inserted needles into Broom's arms and legs but were unable to find a suitable vein.
A total of 18 needle punctures were documented over approximately two hours. In one instance, a needle even struck bone. Broom cried and complained of pain as the team continued its attempts.
Eventually, officials decided to halt the execution. Broom was returned to his cell, with his death sentence still in effect.
He subsequently launched a legal battle to prevent the state from attempting to execute him again, arguing that the suffering he had already endured should rule out another attempt.
In 2016, however, the Ohio Supreme Court rejected his arguments in a 4-3 decision, allowing the state to set a new execution date.
Broom was never subjected to another execution attempt. In December 2020, more than 11 years after surviving the first attempt, he died in prison from complications of COVID-19. He was 64.
Cancer patient warned of the risks — and his execution attempt failed
In February 2018, Alabama attempted to execute Doyle Lee Hamm, a 60-year-old prisoner convicted of murder. But Hamm had advanced cancer, and his lawyers had warned before the execution that his medical condition would make it extremely difficult to find suitable veins for a lethal injection.
Despite the warnings, the state decided to proceed.
For approximately two and a half hours, members of the execution team attempted to insert needles into his body, including his legs and groin.
According to a medical report subsequently submitted to the court, at least 11 puncture marks were found on his body, along with bruising and other injuries.
Eventually, prison officials were forced to abandon the attempt. According to reports, Hamm was in such severe pain that staff had to carry him back to his cell.
Unlike Francis and other condemned prisoners, Hamm did not have to face the execution team again. A subsequent legal settlement stipulated that Alabama would not make another attempt to execute him, and he remained in prison. He died of cancer in November 2021 at age 64.
A year before the failed attempt to execute Hamm, a similar incident occurred in Ohio.
Alva Campbell, a 69-year-old prisoner suffering from lung cancer and other serious illnesses, was taken to the execution chamber in November 2017. The team made four attempts to establish an IV line but failed.
Campbell was returned to his cell and a new execution date was set for 2019. However, he died of natural causes in March 2018, before the state could try again.
They survived lethal injection — but the state found another way to kill them
Not everyone who survived an execution attempt managed to escape the death penalty indefinitely.
Kenneth Eugene Smith, convicted of involvement in a contract killing in Alabama, was taken to the execution chamber on November 17, 2022.
For hours, the execution team attempted to establish an IV line but failed to complete the procedure before the execution warrant expired at midnight.
Smith was returned to his cell alive. His lawyers later argued that the failed attempt had caused him severe psychological trauma, but Alabama remained determined to carry out his sentence.
In January 2024, Smith became the first person in the United States to be executed by nitrogen hypoxia, a method in which the oxygen a person breathes is replaced with nitrogen gas.
Alabama presented the method as an alternative to lethal injection, but the execution drew fierce criticism. Witnesses said Smith shook and writhed for several minutes, contradicting authorities' claims that he would lose consciousness quickly.
A similar case involved Alan Eugene Miller, who was convicted of murdering three people.
In September 2022, Alabama authorities attempted to execute him by lethal injection but were also unable to establish an IV line. The procedure was halted after more than an hour.
Miller's obesity, with his weight reaching 159 kilograms (350 pounds), significantly complicated efforts to locate suitable veins.
Two years later, in September 2024, Miller was executed using nitrogen gas. He became the second person in the United States to be executed by that method, after Smith.
Both condemned prisoners who survived their initial lethal injection attempts ultimately died when the state used a different execution method.
Eight needle attempts — and a prisoner still awaiting his fate
In February 2024, Thomas Eugene Creech, one of the longest-serving death row inmates in the United States, was taken to the execution chamber in Idaho.
Creech, who was convicted of multiple murders, had spent decades in prison and was set to become the first person executed by the state in 12 years.
For about an hour, the execution team attempted to insert an IV line into his arms and legs. Eight attempts were made, but each time, the vein located proved unsuitable or the team was unable to insert the needle properly.
. (Tennessee Department of Correction)
Eventually, the prison warden decided to halt the procedure. Creech was returned to his cell, and Idaho began examining changes to its execution protocol.
His subsequent legal argument that another attempt would constitute prohibited punishment was also rejected.
He remains alive under a death sentence.
In May 2026, a similar incident occurred in Tennessee.
Tony Carruthers, convicted of murdering three people, was taken to the execution chamber. The team successfully established an initial IV line but was unable to insert the additional line required under the state's procedures.
After more than an hour of attempts, the procedure was halted.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee announced that he was granting Carruthers a reprieve of at least one year.
Four months later, the same state would find itself at the center of a far more extraordinary case.
Seven needles, two doses of lethal drugs — and Christa survived
On September 30, 2026, Christa Pike, 50, was taken to the execution chamber in Tennessee.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
Despite difficulties inserting the needles, the execution team administered two doses of pentobarbital, a drug intended to cause her death.
But Pike continued breathing.
She was rushed to a hospital unconscious and in critical condition, and doctors and her lawyers feared she would not survive.
Emergency call recordings released afterward revealed that efforts to save her life were also marred by failures.
After the execution attempt failed, more than half an hour passed before emergency responders were allowed into the prison, partly because dispatchers initially suspected the call was a hoax.
Witnesses continued to hear Pike breathing heavily even after the curtain in the execution chamber was closed. It remains unclear what medical treatment she received during those minutes.
On October 10, Pike was discharged from the hospital and returned to prison, where she continues to receive medical care.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, she is the first known person to survive an execution attempt after lethal drugs were administered.
Experts believe the drugs may not have properly entered her bloodstream, but the official cause of the failed execution has yet to be determined.
Following the incident, Tennessee's governor ordered a suspension of further executions pending an investigation into the failures, and the state's corrections commissioner resigned.
The question of whether the state will attempt to execute Pike again remains unresolved.
Can a person be executed twice?
Pike's case brings the American legal system back to a question considered nearly 80 years ago following Willie Francis' survival: Does a failed execution attempt effectively constitute the carrying out of a person's sentence, and would another attempt violate the constitutional prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment?
The ruling in Francis' case established that the mere failure of an execution attempt does not necessarily prevent a second attempt.
However, legal experts point to the distinction between a case in which equipment fails before the punishment is administered and one in which a lethal substance has already been injected into a person's body, causing suffering and other consequences.
The issue becomes even more pressing in light of data on botched executions.
A study by Amherst College professor Austin Sarat, which examined 8,776 executions in the United States between 1890 and 2010, found that 276 had gone wrong in some way — approximately 3.15%.
The highest failure rate was recorded in lethal injections, long considered a more advanced and humane method of execution: approximately 7.2%.
The stories of Francis, Greene, Broom, Smith and Pike differ greatly.
Some took place centuries ago, others in recent years. Some of the condemned prisoners were convicted of particularly brutal crimes, and victims' families waited years for their sentences to be carried out.
Yet all these cases point to a single reality: Even a procedure designed to end a human life is not immune to mistakes, malfunctions and unexpected failures. For some condemned prisoners, survival meant genuine salvation. For others, it was merely a temporary postponement of death.
Willie Francis survived the electric chair but died in it a year later. Kenneth Smith and Alan Miller survived lethal injection attempts but were ultimately executed using nitrogen gas. Others died in prison without the state ever succeeding in carrying out their death sentences.
Now, nearly 80 years after Francis cried out to be allowed to breathe, the United States once again faces the same question: What happens when a person the state has decided to kill refuses, against all expectations, to die?

Poor urban planning blamed for Istanbul flood damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:37:00 UTC
16:37:00 KST

Experts have attributed extensive flood damage in Türkiye’s largest city to poor urban planning, saying construction along creek beds and concrete surfaces blocking rainwater from reaching the soil have increased the city’s vulnerability.
Former Environment Ministry Undersecretary Mustafa Öztürk said narrowing and covering waterways leaves surrounding buildings exposed to floods. “Rainwater always finds its way,” he said.
He called for wider creek protection zones, mandatory rainwater harvesting, roadside green spaces that collect runoff and rain gardens that let water soak into the soil. He urged checks on flooded buildings’ load-bearing systems, as water corrodes internal steel over time.
Landscape architect Hülya Dinç said 100-meter creek protection strips became 10-meter maintenance strips in 2013. She called for protection zones tailored to each creek’s basin, slope, geology and flood behavior.
“Urban planning decisions cannot be made without considering the integrity of creek systems,” she said.
Istanbul Water and Sewerage Administration (ISKI) 2023 data lists 2,772 creeks totaling 3,919 kilometers. Dinç’s research, based on 2007 maps, found 108 of 168 main creeks outside drinking water basins had lost their natural structure. Only 60 remained intact, while 33 of the 168 lay outside residential areas.
Dinç noted 31 percent of creeks flowing into the Golden Horn are encased in concrete. Waterways such as Ihlamur in Beşiktaş and Fulya in Şişli now lie beneath roads, as does Bayrampaşa beneath Fatih’s Vatan Avenue.
Urbanization accelerated after 1950, spreading to valley floors in the 1980s. Former industrial land along the Cendere creek gave way to housing, offices and malls.

Mysterious drones spotted twice by the British Air Force during exercises - report
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:35:36 EEST
16:35:36 KST

Mysterious drones spotted twice by the British Air Force during exercises - report
Kyiv • UNN
During exercises over the North Sea, British military pilots twice came dangerously close to unidentified drones. One object was flying at an altitude of more than 5,000 meters.
This year, British military pilots reported two dangerous close encounters with unidentified drones during exercises over the North Sea. One of the objects was spotted at an altitude of more than 5,000 m, while the pilot of a tanker aircraft said it was so close that he instinctively ducked. The Telegraph reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
"This year, Royal Air Force fighter jets reported close encounters with two unidentified drones in British airspace. The near-collisions occurred within a few days of each other during exercises simulating aerial combat and mid-air refuelling over the North Sea. One of the mysterious objects was spotted at an altitude of 17,000 feet (more than 5,000 m), which is more than 40 times the permitted altitude for commercial drones," the publication says.
According to the information available, "numerous separate external investigations" are currently under way. As the publication writes, the incidents occurred amid growing concerns that hostile states are using drones to spy on the West.
"Several weeks after the drones were detected by the Royal Air Force in February, the US armed forces were placed on heightened alert after unidentified drones were spotted at Fort McNair, a military outpost in Washington, DC, where senior US government officials reside. Earlier this year, defence experts said that drones spotted over US airbases in Norfolk and Suffolk were linked to a Russian vessel based off the coast. The encounters with the Royal Air Force also occurred several days before the start of the US war with Iran," the publication writes.
According to the publication, the first incident occurred on 18 February near Cromer in Norfolk. A Royal Air Force Airbus Voyager tanker was refuelling a Typhoon fighter jet when an unidentified object flew over them. According to audio recordings reviewed by investigators, the Voyager commander reported what he had seen to military air traffic controllers and suggested that it might have been a small drone travelling from east to west.
"Er, something just flew over us – probably a drone at flight level one seven zero – do you have anything on the screen?" the pilot asked the Royal Air Force radar controller who was overseeing the refuelling.
"One seven zero" is aviation code for an altitude of 17,000 feet (more than 5,000 m), the altitude at which the aircraft was flying.
The controller said he could not see the drone on radar, prompting the pilot to reply: "Okay, understood, it was, er, quite small, er, I would say about the size of a drone, and travelling from east to west, it literally passed directly overhead. It made me instinctively duck. Yes, just, er, talking to [the Typhoon being refuelled], because they saw it as well, er, approximately between us, about 100–150 feet (approximately 30–45 m) above us, directly overhead."
In a subsequent report, the pilot said: "The proximity was such that I instinctively ducked, and it was reported to air traffic control (ATC) that it was a drone."
Recall
Over the course of a year, about 340 unidentified drones were detected near British military facilities. Experts are calling for stronger infrastructure protection.

Trump Waives Graham Act Sanctions On Russia Before They Take Effect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:33:35 UTC
16:33:35 KST

WASHINGTON -- US President Donald Trump has waived nearly all substantive sanctions, tariffs, and restrictions included in a bipartisan law aimed at pressuring Russia to end its war against Ukraine, prompting sharp criticism from Ukraine advocates and lawmakers from both parties who say the move undermines efforts to force Moscow to negotiate.
In an executive order signed late on October 16, Trump said withholding the measures was in the national interest of the United States. The order came just two days before the sanctions package was due to take effect on October 18.
The legislation, known as the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, was signed into law by Trump in September. It was named posthumously for Republican Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, a prominent congressional supporter of Ukraine who died on July 11.
The law was designed to give the administration additional leverage over Russian President Vladimir Putin by authorizing tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India, and providing for sanctions targeting Russian officials, financial institutions, and the country's so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent existing restrictions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy responded on October 17 by saying that it was an unfortunate decision to backtrack on the sanctions at a time when "pressure is needed"
"At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "This Act could have helped enormously -- and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters."
"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine -- right before winter," he said. "Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this. A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin -- all of this only encourages him to keep attacking."
Trump's decision to waive the measures has raised questions about whether his administration intends to use the economic pressure Congress sought to place on Moscow to compel an end to the war.
In the order, Trump said the legislation authorized him to waive the application of sanctions provisions against foreign individuals. He said he had submitted a certification to Congress that issuing the waiver was in the national interest.
The law also requires the administration to provide a report explaining the basis for that certification. The report must be submitted in unclassified form, although it may include a classified annex.
The White House has not publicly detailed, in the material provided for this report, the substantive justification for waiving the law's major provisions.
'A Cruel Policy Choice'
Mykola Murskyj, director of advocacy at Razom for Ukraine, a US-based nonprofit supporting Ukraine, told RFE/RL that Trump had squandered an opportunity to increase pressure on Putin.
"Trump squandered a golden opportunity to bring peace to Ukraine," Murskyj said.
He said lawmakers had spent months building bipartisan support for the legislation, which included tariffs on countries buying Russian oil, restrictions on purchases of Russian sovereign debt, and limits on new investments in Russia.
"All that has been erased in a late-night order Friday from the White House," Murskyj said.
He also questioned the duration of the waivers. "Shockingly, these waivers don't even have an expiration date," he said.
Razom condemned the decision in a separate statement, saying that refusing to use the tools available to pressure Russia was a deliberate policy choice.
"Lacking the tools to end this war would be a tragedy. Having them and refusing to use them is a cruel policy choice," said Daniel Balson, Razom's director of advocacy.
Balson said the legislation had been painstakingly negotiated by a bipartisan group of senators working with White House officials over several months before winning substantial support in both chambers of Congress.
"Today's implementation order signals to the Kremlin that it can continue its invasion," he said, adding that Ukrainians would continue fighting despite mounting humanitarian and energy challenges.
In the week before the waiver, Russia reportedly launched more than 700 drones, along with ballistic and cruise missiles, against Ukrainian cities and power plants.
Questions Over Justification, Deadlines
The decision has also raised questions about what explanation the Trump administration provided to Congress for setting aside the sanctions and tariff provisions.
Max Meizlish, a former official at the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control who is now deputy director of the Center on Economic and Financial Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told RFE/RL that the administration's justification was now a central issue.
"The question now is what substantive justification the administration provided Congress for waiving virtually every major sanctions and tariff provision of legislation that passed with bipartisan support," Meizlish said.
Under the law, the administration must submit a written certification that the waiver is in the national interest, along with a report explaining the basis for that determination. The reporting requirements are intended to provide Congress with an account of the reasoning behind the administration's decision.
Separately, Section 113 of the law sets out requirements for providing written justification to relevant congressional committees in connection with the imposition of tariffs. Sources familiar with the matter told RFE/RL that the administration had missed an October 8 deadline related to those requirements.
The waiver also follows a separate decision by Trump to permit Russian diesel sales amid concerns over rising fuel prices and global supply shortages.
Trump said last week that Russia could immediately supply 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and then 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
The waiver comes as the administration seeks to bring down US fuel prices ahead of November's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. Energy prices have also been affected by the US war in Iran.
It has drawn criticism from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers who had supported the Graham legislation and urged the president to implement it fully, as well as from Ukraine and its European allies. Zelenskyy called it "a gift" for Putin.
Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat and co-author of the bill, accused Trump of siding with Putin and the networks that sustain Russia's war effort.
"Donald Trump confirms again that he stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug and the enablers of Russia's war machine," Blumenthal wrote on social media, arguing the decision ran counter to the views of most Americans, members of Congress, and European allies.
"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," he added.
Republican Representative Don Bacon also criticized the president's move, saying: "The President is prolonging the war, not ending it."
On October 16, Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, introduced bipartisan legislation to block Trump's proposed deal to buy diesel from Russia.
The deal "will hand Putin millions of dollars to continue slaughtering Ukrainian civilians with impunity," Meeks said, urging Congress to pass the legislation.

Canada’s Calian wins $33M deal to script NATO war games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:31:19 UTC
16:31:19 KST

- Calian won a five-year contract worth about CA$47 million ($33.2 million) to develop training scenarios for NATO’s Joint Warfare Centre in Stavanger, Norway.
- The scenarios support NATO’s strategic and operational-level exercises, simulating political, military, economic, civil and information factors that change during training.
Canadian defense contractor Calian Group has won a five-year contract worth about CA$47 million ($33.2 million) to keep writing the scenarios behind NATO’s major command exercises at the alliance’s Joint Warfare Centre in Stavanger, Norway.
The Ottawa-based company said it won the contract after a competitive procurement and will continue an existing role as a prime contractor supporting the center. Under the deal, Calian will design, build and maintain the training scenarios used in NATO’s strategic and operational-level exercises.
Those scenarios are the fictional but detailed worlds in which NATO headquarters staff train. Calian’s teams build in political, military, economic, civil and information factors that shift as an exercise runs, so commanders and staff have to make decisions, coordinate across land, sea, air, cyber and space and respond as the situation changes, much as they would in a real crisis.
“The security environment is changing quickly and NATO forces need training that reflects the complexity, uncertainty and pace of modern operations,” said Roch Pelletier, Calian’s regional vice president of defence.
The Joint Warfare Centre, which reports to NATO’s Allied Command Transformation, runs the alliance’s large computer-assisted command post exercises, in which headquarters staffs work through a simulated campaign without moving troops in the field. It prepares NATO commands and forces for current and future operations through exercises and experimentation, and Calian also provides subject matter experts for those events.
“The award reflects NATO’s continued confidence in our people and our expertise. We are proud to continue working alongside the Joint Warfare Centre to deliver the realistic, demanding training environments that help commanders and staff prepare to operate and succeed together,” said Pelletier.
Calian, which has more than 6,000 employees worldwide and works across defense, space, health care and critical infrastructure, runs a training and simulation business serving Canada, Europe and allied militaries, and the new award keeps it working with the Joint Warfare Centre for the next five years.

U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Oct. 16 waiving most penalties under a new Russia sanctions law, two days before the measures were due to take effect.
The legislation, which Trump signed on Sept. 18, targets Russian officials, state companies and banks and provides for tariffs on major importers of Russian oil and gas.
The Lindsey Graham Act - named after the deceased U.S. senator who sponsored the bill - targeted Russia's energy and defense sectors as well as Putin and other senior officials.
"The Trump administration's suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin, said on social media.
Trump said the waivers were “in the national interests of the United States.” They will remain in effect until the president or secretary of state determines that further action is appropriate.
Washington had already eased sanctions on Russian diesel on Oct. 9 after Trump agreed with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase supplies in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of November’s U.S. midterm elections.
Trump has also criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries, accusing Kiev of driving up global energy prices.
“Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” he told Newsmax in an interview aired on Oct. 15, saying Ukraine could strike other targets.
He said he found Zelensky “more difficult to deal with than Putin” and accused him of resisting a settlement.
Trump also compared him to P.T. Barnum, the 19th-century American showman.
Speaking at the White House on Oct. 16, Trump said he had a good relationship with Zelensky, while again urging him to settle the war.
Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” on Oct. 11, but Zelensky said Moscow continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Kiev subsequently resumed strikes on Russian refineries.
Speaking in Brussels earlier on Oct. 16, Zelensky warned that the diesel deal would provide Moscow with more money to fund its war and could lead to further sanctions relief.

Anthropic proposes law regulating AI to US lawmakers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:29:00 UTC
16:29:00 KST

Anthropic proposes law regulating AI to US lawmakers
SAN FRANCISCO – Anthropic, the creator of the AI assistant Claude, confirmed on Oct 16 that it is circulating a draft Bill among US lawmakers aimed at regulating artificial intelligence to address the lack of federal legislation on the risks posed by the new technology.
According to the draft, first reported by Politico on Oct 16, Washington could block a model’s release or use if there is an imminent risk of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, or causing more than US$1 billion (S$1.28 billion) in damage, but only with a judge’s approval.
A company spokesperson told AFP that the proposal “grants the federal government the ability to block or deter dangerous deployments of the most powerful models”.
“It requires frontier developers to test the most powerful models, be transparent to the public about their findings, submit them to independent evaluation, and maintain a robust security programme,” the spokesperson said.
AI policy in the US under President Donald Trump has relied primarily on voluntary industry pledges and executive orders intended to sustain an AI boom that tech leaders say is driving the country’s economy.
Congress, politically divided and heavily lobbied by Big Tech, has yet to pass a federal AI law, and is out of session until after November’s midterm elections.
Security became a hot topic after recent revelations of security incidents caused by AI agents – autonomous software that operates without constant human supervision – that escaped the control of their developers.
Anthropic, which was banned from the Pentagon by the Trump administration in February, was forced by Washington in June to suspend its most advanced models for nearly three weeks.
Its chief executive officer Dario Amodei in September called on the industry to slow down development, fearing that a group of AI agents could take control of “the entire internet” within six to 12 months.
Trump has dismissed the numerous calls to slow down the technology as “negative forces”.
The proposed legislation would also override certain state laws, such as those in force in California.
Anthropic wrote in June that “absent a strong federal law, states should retain full authority to legislate”.
Charlie Bullock of the Institute for Law & AI think-tank praised the proposal as “pretty reasonable”, and “more than other frontier labs have done”.
But he said on social media platform X that he considers it “weaker” than the FRONTIER Act, a competing Bill introduced in the House of Representatives this summer. AFP

Behind the lights and grandeur: What it takes and costs to build a Durga Pujo pandal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:28:03 UTC
16:28:03 KST

Before the dhak begins: The money and machinery behind a Durga pujo
Long before the first beat of the dhak, a Durga Pujo has already been decided, priced and partly built. The goddess arrives in autumn, but the people who bring her to a neighbourhood start months earlier, with a theme, a budget and a list of permissions that must be collected one office at a time.To the crowds who walk through a pandal's gates, a pujo is a few days of colour, light and sound. To the club that puts it up, it is a yearly project that runs on money raised from the neighbourhood, a small circle of skilled craftsmen and a large number of people who all have to be in the right place on the right day. In West Bengal that project is repeated in locality after locality, each with its own ledger.
The quiet work before the dhak
The ledger is not small. A medium-scale pujo costs several lakh rupees, and the biggest share does not go to the idol at the centre of it all. It goes to the structure built around her. Most visitors never see the figures, the deadlines or the people behind them, and that is exactly how the organisers want it. A pujo is meant to arrive as a finished thing.The budgetNirmal, a pujo organiser from West Bengal who has run one for the past 10 years, knows that ledger well. "A medium scale pujo in West Bengal would cost somewhere between 10 to 15 lakhs," he says. "Every year the budget increases as per the market inflation."
That second sentence matters as much as the first. A committee that spent a certain amount last year should expect to spend more this year on the same pujo, before it adds a single new ambition. For a club working with money collected from its neighbours, the target keeps moving upward, and the neighbours are asked to keep up with it.
The pandal takes the biggest share
Ask him what costs the most and the answer is immediate. "The pandal costs the most," he says. Not the lighting, not the idol, not the food. He puts the pandal at around Rs 3 lakh to Rs 5 lakh for a medium-scale pujo, which makes it the line the rest of the budget has to work around.The idol costs a fifthNext to the pandal, the idol is a modest line. "Whatever the pandal costs, the idol costs its one-fifth," Nirmal says. For a medium-scale pujo, that works out to around Rs 80,000.It is a striking ratio. The figure at the heart of the festival, the one every visitor has come to see, costs a fraction of the structure that shelters her.Within the idol's cost, the most expensive element is gold. Certain gold items are designated for it, among them an ornament that is given by the club organising the pujo. The ornament comes from the organisers themselves, which makes it a different kind of expense from the rest.A theme, decided half a year earlyA pandal needs a theme, and the theme needs time. "The theme is decided at least six months ago," Nirmal says, meaning at least six months before the pujo. That is a long lead for a festival that lasts only days.Who decides it varies. In some committees, he says, there is a specific person whose sole job is deciding the theme. In others, the pandal makers can decide it too. The choice matters for more than looks, because the budget is also decided through the theme. Once the idea is fixed, the cost of building it can be worked out, and the money follows.This is why the calendar starts so early. A theme chosen six months out leaves room to price the work, find the right artisan and settle the budget before construction begins. By the time the neighbourhood sees the first bamboo go up, the important decisions have already been made.Two months, or moreConstruction is where the calendar turns uncertain. Asked how long a medium-scale pandal takes to build, Nirmal is candid. "It depends on the workers, to be honest," he says. "Some can build the same pandal in two months, whereas some will require more time."
Six months, one theme, lakhs of rupees
The reason, as he describes it, is a shortage of skill. "The skilled pandal makers are not a lot in number. Mostly there is just one skilled artisan and a lot of people work under him."That structure explains a good deal. The quality of the pandal and the speed at which it rises rest heavily on one person, with a large crew following his lead. For an organiser, choosing a pandal maker is therefore as much a scheduling decision as a financial one. A maker who is slow, or one who is booked elsewhere, can put the whole timeline at risk.Where the money comes fromThe funding model is local. "Every area or colony has a designated club which builds a pandal," Nirmal explains. "And then they get chanda, donations, advertisements that ultimately make the pujo what it is."There is also help from the state. This year, he says, the West Bengal government is providing Rs 1 lakh to small-scale pujos, and electricity is completely free. Free power removes a bill that would otherwise sit beside the lighting and the pandal. The Rs 1 lakh grant, though, is meant for small-scale pujos. Set against a medium-scale budget of Rs 10 lakh to Rs 15 lakh, most of the money still has to come from the neighbourhood, from donors and from advertisers.The people who are paidSome costs are smaller but just as fixed. The priest's expenditure, Nirmal says, is around Rs 30,000 to Rs 40,000. The dhaki, whose drumming is as much a part of the pujo as the idol, is paid around Rs 10,000. On top of that, he gets free food, lodging and clothes.
What it costs to raise a Durga Pujo
Those extras are part of the arrangement. A dhaki who is housed and fed for the duration of the pujo is a cost the committee carries beyond the headline fee. Nirmal was also asked about bhog expenditure, but his answer covered only the priest and the dhaki.What the numbers leave outAdd up the lines Nirmal named, the pandal, the idol, the priest and the dhaki, and the total lands somewhere between roughly Rs 4.2 lakh and Rs 6.3 lakh. His estimate for the whole pujo is Rs 10 lakh to Rs 15 lakh.The gap is considerable. It covers everything else a pujo needs, including the lighting and food he named only to rule them out as the biggest expense. Nirmal did not break down how that money is divided.
Everything, from beginning to endAsked about the biggest challenge organisers face, Nirmal does not name a single expense. "The biggest challenge is that everything from the beginning to the end is completed properly," he says.
That includes permissions. "You have to get proper permissions like the police and the fire department," he says, "and it takes a lot of people to complete a pujo and to make a pujo what it is."The pandal maker and his crew, the artisan working on the idol, the priest, the dhaki and the club members collecting funds are all working towards the same date. Seen this way, the Rs 10 lakh to Rs 15 lakh is only part of what a pujo demands. The rest is coordination, and much of Nirmal's decade in the job has gone into it.For the people who walk through the gates, the pujo arrives as a finished thing. For the club behind it, it began at least six months earlier with a decision about a theme, and it will begin again next year at a higher cost.

Did Chinese cars squeal on Norway’s military?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:28:00 UTC
16:28:00 KST

Did Chinese cars squeal on Norway’s military?
- Chinese-made rental cars recorded sensitive data during a Norwegian military exercise at Oslo airport, including access codes, routes and officials’ movements.
- The army confirmed the videos were found on vehicle systems, but kept using the cars because there were no alternatives; it later deleted the files and chose site-specific security rules.
- The case has raised wider fears about connected vehicles and foreign dependence, as Norway warns modern cars are “rolling computers” that may collect and send sensitive information.
AI generated
OSLO – Chinese-made cars filmed sensitive information during a Norwegian military exercise, including access codes at secure sites and officials’ comings and goings, raising concerns about the risks posed by connected vehicles.
During a security exercise at Oslo airport from Sept 14 to 18, waiting soldiers tapping on their vehicle’s screen discovered videos recorded by the on-board cameras, the Dagens Naeringsliv (DN) newspaper revealed.
The recordings showed who was getting in and out of the cars, the routes taken and even the codes used to open gates or doors to military facilities.
In its report three weeks after the exercise, DN said the recordings came from rental vehicles – at least two of them Deepal cars, made by Chinese state-controlled automaker Changan.
They were supplied to the army by Hertz Norge, which is indirectly owned by the Chinese auto group Geely.
“Yes, soldiers from the Home Guard found videos from the vehicles’ sensors stored in their systems,” Lieutenant-Colonel Per Gunnar Grosberghaugen, Norwegian Home Guard spokesperson, confirmed to AFP.
It was not known if the recordings were shared with a third party, notably in China, but the officer could not rule out the possibility.
The case highlights a paradox: While Europe’s armies are bolstering their protection against espionage and hybrid threats, the vehicles they use can collect sensitive information.
Even after discovering the leaks, the military continued to use the vehicles until the end of the exercise due to a lack of alternatives and the soldiers deleted the videos, DN reported.
Judging that the impact of a general ban on Chinese-made vehicles would be disproportionate to the potential security gain, the military said it preferred security procedures tailored to each site, with possible local bans on vehicles equipped with cameras and sensors, regardless of their origin.
Hertz Norge stressed that it complies with Norwegian and European regulations.
“Our customers’ data is safe with us,” Hallvard Nerbovik, its marketing and communications director, told AFP.
“No personal data related to our rentals is shared with car manufacturers, our owners or other third parties without explicit legal grounds,” he added, without specifying whether the on-board videos may have been transferred.
Changan group did not respond to AFP’s questions.
App spies
In 2025, tests carried out for Oslo’s Ruter public transport authority revealed that Chinese manufacturer Yutong could theoretically remotely immobilise its electric buses with their “over-the-air” update system.
Norway could use the buses one day to evacuate the population in the event of an emergency.
Ruter has since introduced mechanisms enabling it to monitor and delay incoming signals to control updates, it said.
Modern vehicles are not the only potential Trojan horses.
Smartwatches and fitness apps such as Strava, popular with joggers, can also expose sensitive military information.
In 2018, data published by Strava made it possible to identify military sites and soldiers’ routes, notably in Afghanistan and Syria.
In March, French newspaper Le Monde was able to locate the French aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle in almost real time in the eastern Mediterranean, thanks to a sailor on board using the app.
The Norwegian National Security Authority (NSM) said modern vehicles are “rolling computers that collect information”.
“We don’t know for sure where the information is sent or what it’s used for,” NSM official Andreas Skjold-Lorange told AFP.
The organisation, which is responsible for minimising strategic risks including digital, said that beyond the data collected, Norway should be wary of excessive dependence on a single country – especially if that country does not cooperate with Norway on security matters.
“If we become too dependent on services or products from a given country, that makes us vulnerable, whatever that country may be,” Skjold-Lorange warned. AFP

British Army wants quiet power to replace noisy generators
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:25:42 UTC
16:25:42 KST

- UK Defence Innovation launched a £2.45 million Tactical Power Challenge for the British Army to find better battlefield power generation, storage and charging technologies.
- The competition, run with Australia’s ASCA, closes for first-stage bids on Nov. 10, 2026, with funded demonstrations due by March 2028.
The British Army is looking for new ways to power its troops in the field, offering £2.45 million ($3.26 million) to companies that can develop better batteries, faster chargers and quieter alternatives to the diesel generators units rely on today.
UK Defence Innovation, the Ministry of Defence’s innovation arm, launched the Tactical Power Challenge on Oct. 15 on behalf of the British Army, with support from the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory, known as Dstl. The competition is being run alongside Australia’s Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator, which has its own parallel effort on distributed tactical power, and first-stage bids are due by noon GMT on Nov. 10, 2026, according to the UK government announcement.
The push stems from how much more electricity armies now use. Radios, drones, sensors, electronic warfare kit, counter-drone systems and battlefield computers all need power, and research and experimentation by the British and Australian armies found a sharp rise in power demand driven by digital and autonomous systems. Most of that power still comes from fuel-burning generators, which are noisy, hard to move and depend on regular fuel deliveries.
“Reliable and deployable power is fundamental to maintaining operational advantage,” said John Cunningham, director of innovation responsible for UK Defence Innovation.
The challenge has two parts. The funded strand, called Innovative Tactical Power, is a two-stage competition for technologies at an early-to-middle stage of development, roughly from lab prototypes to systems tested in a relevant environment, which winners would mature and demonstrate by March 2028. A separate, unfunded strand called Immediate Power is aimed at more mature products that could meet current needs quickly, and companies with promising systems may be invited to join British Army trials and experiments in the UK.
The Army’s wish list includes safer battery chemistries that hold at least as much energy as lithium-ion cells, high-speed charging, new types of power generation, and equipment to store, manage and distribute electricity across dispersed units. It also wants technology that lets troops operate silently, cuts the fuel they need to haul, supports uncrewed and robotic systems, and includes power sources soldiers can carry themselves. Both complete systems and individual components are eligible.
“British industry is central to delivering the capabilities our Armed Forces need for the future. This challenge will help identify and develop sovereign technologies that can improve operational energy resilience, support deployed personnel and strengthen the UK defence innovation ecosystem,” said Cunningham.
The British Army has a requirement for more than 4,000 Lightweight Field Generators and is studying how to modernize its tactical power as current systems near replacement, giving companies that perform well a possible route into future procurement.
Bids may be shared with Australia’s Department of Defence for assessment, and results from funded projects may be passed to Australian and U.S. defense partners under information-sharing arrangements. Second-stage submissions will be by invitation only, with demonstration work due to finish by March 2028.

Sweden Extradited Russian National Who Supplied Microelectronics to Russia in Circumvention of Sanctions to USA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:22:18 UTC
16:22:18 KST

Sweden extradited 52-year-old Russian citizen Alexandr Suvorov to the U.S., where he is accused of illegally supplying American microelectronics to Russia in circumvention of sanctions.
This was reported by the U.S. Department of Justice.
According to the U.S. investigation, from March 2022 to April 2023, he ran a procurement network that supplied dual-use electronic components to Russia through GS Group Limited, a company registered in Hong Kong. According to the investigation, some of these components can be used in military communications and radar systems, as well as in high-precision positioning systems.
“According to the charges, Alexandr Suvorov organized an international procurement network that illegally supplied U.S.-manufactured electronic components with military applications to buyers in Russia,” said Roman Rozhavsky!, assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division.
Suvorov was extradited to the Northern District of New York on October 15. The next day, he was scheduled to make his first court appearance in Albany.
He faces three charges: conspiracy to launder money in international transactions, illegally exporting goods from the United States, and violating the Export Control Reform Act.
Under the first and third counts, Suvorov faces up to 20 years in prison; under the second, up to five years. He may also face a fine.
More than three-quarters of the onboard computer in Russian Geran-4 drones consists of electronic components manufactured by American companies.
Products from Texas Instruments account for the largest share, along with components from National Semiconductor, which it acquired—more than half.
In early October, the U.S. Department of the Treasury imposed sanctions against the A7 shadow banking network, which is linked to Russia and Iran.
A7 developed a large-scale network of front companies that allows Russia to circumvent Western sanctions and purchase goods for its military-industrial complex.

Türkiye seeks inclusion as France, Germany agree on car rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:22:16 UTC
16:22:16 KST

Türkiye has been left outside a Franco-German automotive proposal announced on Oct. 16 that would give Britain conditional access to the EU’s planned “Made in EU” support scheme.
The agreement brings France and Germany closer on rules governing which vehicles qualify for public procurement and financial support. For Türkiye, a major production base supplying European markets, the concern extends to future model allocations and factory investment.
The proposal still needs support from other EU member states and the European Parliament before becoming law.
Under the Franco-German plan, the automotive provisions would cover the EU’s 27 members and allow European partners that were part of the single market on Jan. 1, 2020, to opt in.
That definition provides a route for Britain, which left the single market at the end of 2020, but does not include Türkiye.
Participation would require reciprocal treatment and continuing alignment with EU rules on investment from third countries and trade protection.
For Britain, this could mean adopting the bloc’s measures restricting imports of Chinese-made electric and hybrid vehicles.
The agreement narrows a longstanding difference between Paris and Berlin.
France had sought to reserve support for production within the EU, while Germany favored including trading partners closely integrated into European automotive supply chains.
The wider rules are being negotiated under the Industrial Accelerator Act, which would introduce European-content requirements for vehicles benefiting from public purchasing and support schemes.
A joint statement released by French President Emmanuel Macron’s office said the aim was to reduce emissions while strengthening Europe’s capacity to develop and manufacture the next generation of electric vehicles.
It linked that transition to investment, research and production in France, Germany and across Europe.
Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa had advocated a similar approach at the Paris Motor Show, calling for incentives for companies investing in European design, research and development, factories and suppliers.
He also urged a swift agreement on emissions rules and measures supporting European production.
The Franco-German compromise combines that industrial preference with concessions on emissions.
It would retain the European Commission’s proposed 90 percent reduction in CO2 emissions from new cars by 2035, compared with 2021 levels, while removing the requirement to offset the remaining emissions through measures such as low-carbon steel and alternative fuels.
That change would give manufacturers greater flexibility to continue selling combustion-engine and hybrid vehicles beyond 2035, in line with German industry demands.
For Türkiye, the debate concerns its largest automotive export market. The sector exported $41.5 billion in 2025, with EU countries accounting for $30.1 billion, or 72.5 percent, according to the Uludağ Automotive Industry Exporters’ Association.
Trade Minister Ömer Bolat pressed Türkiye’s case during talks in Brussels earlier in the week.
“Türkiye must be accepted from the very beginning as an equal partner within the framework of the ‘Made with Europe’ concept,” he said on Oct. 14.
Bolat said European companies accounted for nearly 75 percent of Türkiye’s automotive production.
He warned that excluding the country could disrupt the production and supply relationships established through its three-decade customs union with the EU, harming investment, employment and exports on both sides.
The Commission’s March draft already provides for content from customs-union and free-trade partners to receive equivalent treatment in certain procurement and support schemes, subject to conditions.
Bolat said that restrictive automotive provisions nevertheless remained and that Ankara was seeking changes through talks with EU institutions and manufacturers.
Toyota also called for a broader agreement on Oct. 16.
Its European division welcomed discussion of Britain’s inclusion but said the arrangement should extend to other trusted partners, including Türkiye and Japan, whose cooperation could support European competitiveness.
The company said wider inclusion would also benefit future investment decisions, including a battery production study.

France rolls out fifth new nuclear attack submarine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:22:01 UTC
16:22:01 KST

- Naval Group rolled out Rubis, the fifth of six Barracuda nuclear attack submarines for the French Navy, at Cherbourg on Oct. 16, 2026.
- Four boats have already been delivered since November 2020, and France plans to receive all six by 2030.
Naval Group has rolled out Rubis, the fifth of six Barracuda nuclear-powered attack submarines it is building for the French Navy, moving the boat out of its construction hall at the company’s shipyard in Cherbourg on Oct. 16, 2026.
The submarine was transferred onto the yard’s floating shiplift platform in the presence of Catherine Vautrin, France’s minister for the armed forces and veterans. Naval Group will now finish outfitting the boat and run a series of trials alongside the quay and then at sea before handing it over to the French Navy.
“It is with great pride and a deep sense of responsibility that we today transferred the Rubis, the fifth Suffren-class nuclear attack submarine, to its launch platform. This crucial milestone comes just 17 months after that of the nuclear attack submarine De Grasse, a symbol of our commitment to our customers,” said Pierre Éric Pommellet, chairman and CEO of Naval Group.
The program is known as Barracuda, and the boats themselves are called the Suffren class after the first submarine in the series. It is replacing the six Rubis-class attack submarines France put into service from the 1980s, and the new Rubis takes the name of the boat that led that older class. France’s defense procurement agency, the DGA, runs the program with the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission, which handles the nuclear reactors, and the plan calls for all six submarines to be delivered by 2030.
Four are already in service or delivered. Suffren was handed over in November 2020, followed by Duguay-Trouin and Tourville, and De Grasse was delivered in June 2026, about 13 months after its own rollout in May 2025 and four months after it first went to sea. If Rubis follows a similar path, it will spend the coming months on quayside testing, reactor startup and sea trials. The sixth and final boat, Casabianca, is also under construction.
The Suffren-class boats are about 99 meters (325 feet) long and displace roughly 5,300 tonnes submerged. They carry F21 heavyweight torpedoes, Exocet SM39 anti-ship missiles and MBDA’s naval cruise missiles, which give the French Navy the ability to strike targets on land from a submerged submarine, and they can carry and deploy special forces.
Naval Group designs and builds the submarines and produces the main components of their nuclear propulsion plants with TechnicAtome. It also provides logistical support and maintenance for the boats in Toulon, the home port of France’s attack submarine force on the Mediterranean.
About 3,000 people are working on the design and construction of the submarines, including around 800 from Naval Group subcontractors, up from the 2,500 the company cited when De Grasse rolled out last year.

Australia's first Vietnamese heritage museum opens in Melbourne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:21:12 UTC
16:21:12 KST

Australia's first Vietnamese heritage museum opens in Melbourne after decade-long push
In short:
The first Australian museum dedicated to the Vietnamese refugee experience has opened Melbourne.
Vietnamese-Australians are one of the country's largest migrant groups and many fled after the country's civil war ended.
A community campaign helped galvanise interest in the museum concept, with bipartisan support for the new centre.
Before the days of bánh mì takeaways and discount flight holidays, to most Australians Vietnam was known only for the horrors of conflict and conscription.
That was to change with the end of the Vietnam War.
Thousands of Vietnamese refugees made the perilous journey to Australia in the mid-1970s, saying an abrupt goodbye to Saigon and an apprehensive hello to Melbourne's Sunshine and St Albans or Sydney's Cabramatta and Canley Vale.
Five decades on, refugee beginnings and generational achievement were recognised with the opening of the nation's first museum dedicated to Vietnamese-Australian history.
Constructed on a council car park in Sunshine, the unveiling of Vietnamese Museum Australia marked the culmination of a decade-long campaign to establish a permanent monument to the community's pioneering generation.
The parents of the museum's chief executive, Tammy Nguyen, escaped Vietnam on a perilous six-day, seven-night boat journey.
"There are more than 350,000 people of Vietnamese-origin living in Australia and everyone has their own unique story to tell," Ms Nguyen said.
"This museum is a living monument to all those who courageously left their homeland behind — often as refugees on overcrowded and unseaworthy boats — seeking freedom and a better future."
The project has received bipartisan support, with Victorian Premier Ben Carroll officially opening the centre on Saturday alongside MPs from across the political divide.
Both the federal and Victorian governments contributed millions to the project, alongside grassroots community contributions.
Liberal MP Trung Luu, who represents the Western Metropolitan Region in the state's upper house, said the museum's opening was a significant day for the Vietnamese community.
"As someone who came to Australia as a refugee from Vietnam, today is deeply personal for me," he said.
"This museum honours the courage of every family who made that journey."
University of Melbourne development studies professor Lan Anh Hoang said public attitudes towards Vietnamese refugees in the 1970s and 1980s were mixed as the nation adjusted to life post-White Australia policy.
"In the immediate aftermath of the fall of Saigon, there was a great deal of sympathy and compassion, particularly because of Australia's own involvement in the war,"
she said.
"But as boat arrivals continued towards the end of the 1970s, concerns grew about uncontrolled migration, and the legacy of the White Australia policy meant that racial anxieties still lingered."
Professor Hoang said Vietnamese migrants to Australia who relocate in 2026 find themselves in a more welcoming environment.
But she added that they also tended to be more educated or skilled, with better English proficiency than the refugees who came in the 1970s.
"Many describe the kindness and generous support of churches and community organisations (in the 1970s)," she said.
"At the same time, Vietnamese families and their children faced more than their fair share of racism in the community and at school.
"It was not easy to be a Vietnamese kid growing up in Australia at that time."
University of Technology Sydney sociology professor Andrew Jakubowicz said the mid-1970s intake of Vietnamese-Australians under the Fraser Government was the first real test of the post-White Australia policy consensus.
Malcolm Fraser became a champion of the Vietnamese-Australian diaspora and members of the community paid tribute to the ex-PM at his 2015 funeral.
"(Vietnamese-Australians) were admitted as the first big group of refugees from a group that had almost no prior presence," Professor Jakubowicz said.
"Initially, most were Catholic southerners and pro-Saigon. Their actual travel to Australia was traumatic — they were the first modern boat people.
"They arrived in the shadow of the end of White Australia into a country that was trepidatiously ready to accept Asians.
"Before then, most Asians admitted after 1967 were English-speaking professionals."

Estonia's Soviet-era summer cottage culture to become museum exhibit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:19:00 UTC
16:19:00 KST

Estonia's Soviet-era summer cottage culture to become museum exhibit
Estonian researchers are mapping the country's fading garden-cottage heritage — the suvila built across the Soviet era.
Built to strict Soviet rules, they stand apart from what came before and after, embodying both state leisure and private dreams.
Nearly 50,000 were built between 1950 and 1980. Now art historians from the Estonian Academy of Arts and ethnologists from the University of Tartu have joined forces to understand this heritage — what people built, and how they spent their time there.
"The privately owned summer cottage is a type of building constructed en masse during the Soviet era that shows how the state sought to create opportunities for working citizens to enjoy leisure time," said Epp Lankots, dean of EKA, on "Tähelepanu! Tegemist on teadusega."
Dagmar Ingi, head of rural architecture at the Estonian Open Air Museum, stressed the human-centered approach. "For me as an ethnologist, it is extremely important that we study the person and their relationship with their summer cottage," she said.
The researchers spend their summers across Estonia, talking to owners and documenting history. Interviews are free-form, closer to conversation than survey. They examine the whole property — garden beds, small structures, interiors — and spatial specialists measure and draw up plans. "We photograph them if people allow us to, inspect the interiors and draw up site plans so that, at some point, if someone wants to study this subject, all this material will have been properly preserved," Ingi said.
They also dig into archives for rare types, like terraced summer cottages. Owners bring out old photo albums, receipts and construction plans kept for decades — insight into everyday building practices and people's ingenuity.
The researchers approach every participant without prejudice. "For us, it does not matter what work they do or what kind of life they have lived. Every person's story is important, significant and interesting precisely as they have lived it," Ingi said.
The work is limited by time and the subjectivity of memory. Decades-old events arrive filtered through nostalgia, lending emotional color but diminishing factual accuracy.
The knowledge won't gather dust. "The aim of this project is actually to find a Soviet-era summer cottage that can be relocated to the Open Air Museum, where we can tell the story of a summer cottage built in the 1960s or 1970s, together with the story of the person who owned it, what they dreamed of and what they needed the summer cottage for," Ingi concluded.

US To Make Investment, Counterterrorism Push As Rubio Heads To Central Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:18:51 UTC
16:18:51 KST

WASHINGTON -- As Secretary of State Marco Rubio heads to Uzbekistan this weekend, Washington is hoping the high-level diplomatic engagement translates into concrete economic and security cooperation.
Speaking to reporters on a background call on October 16 Rubio's visit, a State Department official said more than 200 American companies would accompany the secretary to Samarkand, where he is expected to meet with the foreign ministers of all five Central Asian countries.
The tour reflects the Trump administration's effort to combine diplomacy with trade, investment, and security cooperation across South and Central Asia, regions Washington views as increasingly important to its economic and strategic interests.
"For too long, the United States has focused on the Middle East and the East, and this area in the middle, Central Asia, has not gotten the attention that it deserves," the senior official said.
The American delegation will include representatives of major companies such as Boeing, Citibank, and Franklin Templeton, as well as businesses operating in critical minerals and other strategic sectors.
Officials from the US International Development Finance Corporation, the Export-Import Bank of the United States, the National Security Council, and the State Department will also participate in meetings designed to connect American businesses with potential partners across Central Asia.
The senior State Department official said Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan alone had generated more than $30 billion in new investments into the United States over the past year.
Republican Senator John Curtis, who has supported closer US engagement with Central Asia, says the region's stability is essential to American interests at a time of heightened uncertainty elsewhere in the world.
"A stable Central Asian region, with so much uncertainty in other parts of the globe, is just essential for us," he told RFE/RL.
"It's up to them, but to partner with us could be an incredibly important part of a relationship. As everybody knows, critical minerals are very important, not just to the United States but to the world. And I think that's a great asset they have that could be very important."
Samarkand, a historic trading center on the Silk Road, will serve as the main venue for the Central Asian portion of Rubio's trip.
The visit will include bilateral meetings and the C5+1 format meeting, as well as direct engagement between American companies, regional businesses, and government representatives.
Kazakhstan's announced intention to join the Abraham Accords was another key development highlighted during the briefing. The senior official said Washington was working toward a potential signing ceremony but did not provide a date.
“Stay tuned," the official said, adding that the sides hoped to complete the process "sooner than later.”
The Abraham Accords were originally established to normalize relations between Israel and several Arab and Muslim-majority countries.
Kazakhstan's potential participation would extend the framework's reach, although the official did not provide details about the terms or timing of the country's formal accession.
The official also said Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan had been invited to attend the Group of 20 summit as observers for the first time.
The invitations were presented as part of Washington's broader effort to raise Central Asia's international profile and deepen ties with its governments.
All five Central Asian presidents have publicly invited US President Donald Trump to visit their countries, the official said, adding that regional governments had welcomed Washington's increased engagement.
Trade and investment are not the only priorities. The United States is also looking to strengthen counterterrorism cooperation with some Central Asian countries.
The official did not identify the countries involved or provide details of the initiatives but described security cooperation as an important element of Washington's expanding regional relationships.
The renewed outreach comes as Central Asian governments maintain complex relationships with Russia and China while seeking to broaden their international partnerships.
The official did not describe the initiative as an effort to displace either power, instead emphasizing commercial opportunities, stronger diplomatic contacts, and cooperation on shared security concerns.
Rubio's visit is intended to turn the outcomes of that high-level engagement into practical cooperation.
Following the Uzbekistan visit, Rubio is scheduled to travel to Mumbai and Jamnagar, India, to advance economic and diplomatic ties with New Delhi.

U.S. Navy destroyer sails all the way around Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:18:08 UTC
16:18:08 KST

- USS McFaul completed a transit around Africa, refueling and resupplying with help from Kenya, Ghana and Cabo Verde.
- The destroyer moved from Middle East operations into the U.S. 6th Fleet area, making its last stop in Mindelo, Cabo Verde, on Oct. 10.
The U.S. Navy destroyer USS McFaul (DDG 74) has sailed all the way around Africa, stopping in Kenya, Ghana and Cabo Verde for fuel and supplies on a voyage of thousands of nautical miles from the Indian Ocean to the Atlantic.
U.S. Naval Forces Europe-Africa announced the completed transit on Oct. 14 in a release. The Arleigh Burke-class destroyer relied on the three countries for refueling, anchorages and other logistics support along Africa’s eastern, southern and western coasts, the U.S. Navy said, with the final stop a refueling visit to Mindelo, Cabo Verde, on Oct. 10.
The voyage capped a long deployment. McFaul, homeported at Naval Station Norfolk, Virginia, operated in the Middle East with the U.S. 5th Fleet from at least January 2026, sailing in the Arabian Sea alongside carrier strike groups. By Sept. 21 the destroyer was in the Indian Ocean, and on Sept. 23 it took on fuel from the cargo and ammunition ship USNS Oscar V. Peterson (T-AKE 9) before heading south around the continent and moving into the U.S. 6th Fleet area, which covers Europe and Africa.
“The execution of this transit is a testament to the strength of our maritime partnerships across the African continent and the professionalism of the McFaul team,” said Vice Adm. J.T. Anderson, commander of U.S. 6th Fleet. “Operating alongside our partners ensures the safety and security of vital sea lines of communication and reinforces our shared commitment to regional stability.”
A destroyer like McFaul cannot carry enough fuel for a trip of that length on its own, so the voyage depended on finding fuel along the way, either from U.S. Navy supply ships at sea or from ports in friendly countries. Rounding southern Africa instead of using the Red Sea and Suez Canal adds thousands of miles to a trip between the Middle East and the Atlantic, and the U.S. Navy did not say why McFaul took that route.
“Voyages of this scale are sustained by the trust and teamwork of our global allies and maritime partners,” said Cmdr. Adam Samson, McFaul’s commanding officer. “We extend our sincere gratitude to our host partners across Africa. Their responsiveness and professionalism demonstrated our mutual dedication to maritime safety.”
Commissioned in 1998, McFaul carries the Aegis combat system and SPY-1D radar, vertical launch cells for air defense, strike and anti-submarine missiles, and a flight deck for helicopters. The ship is named for Navy SEAL Chief Petty Officer Donald L. McFaul, who was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for his actions during Operation Just Cause in Panama in 1989.
McFaul remains on a scheduled deployment in the U.S. 6th Fleet area of operations, which is headquartered in Naples, Italy.
