Lidl has Denmark’s cheapest basket of organic groceries, analysis finds
Lidl offers the lowest prices on a selected basket of organic groceries among seven Danish supermarket chains, according to an analysis by price-monitoring service Madprisluppen.
A basket containing 22 organic products cost 355.20 DKK at Lidl. The same basket cost 449.60 DKK at Meny, the most expensive chain in the comparison.
Madprisluppen said the Lidl basket was 26 percent cheaper than the one at Meny.
“We want to make it easier for Danes to make room for organics in everyday life, and here price plays an important role,” Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said.
Rema 1000 was the second-cheapest supermarket, with its basket costing only 5 DKK more than Lidl’s.
SuperBrugsen was the second-most expensive, though its total was almost 35 DKK below Meny’s.
The analysis also included Netto, 365discount and Føtex. Prices were recorded from October 9 through October 12.
Products included milk, eggs, vegetables and dry goods. Meat was excluded because Madprisluppen found it difficult to identify comparable products across the chains.
The monitoring service also found that supermarkets carry fewer organic products than they did six years ago. Organic prices have increased, and such products appear in special offers less frequently than non-organic groceries.
Norway to lend 10-meter Viking boat to Danish museum for 10 years
A Norwegian Viking boat will be displayed at Moesgaard Museum near Aarhus under an unusual 10-year loan agreement.
The oak boat is almost 10 meters long and nearly two meters wide. It was among three smaller vessels discovered when archaeologists excavated Norway’s Gokstad ship in 1880.
The Gokstad ship is Norway’s largest preserved Viking ship.
“The boat is a very important cultural treasure from the Viking Age, and it is not an everyday occurrence that we grant permission for such a boat to be taken out of the country,” Kaare Stang of Riksantikvaren, Norway’s cultural heritage authority, said.
The three smaller boats had been chopped into pieces, possibly as part of a burial ritual, according to archaeologists.
The Museum of Cultural History in Norway owns the boat and applied for permission to lend it to Moesgaard Museum for a new exhibition.
Norwegian authorities normally approve loans for no more than three years. Moesgaard Museum must therefore submit a report on the boat’s condition every three years during the loan period.
Stang said Norwegian authorities trusted the Danish museum to protect the boat but emphasized that it must eventually return to Norway.
No arrival date has been announced.
Moesgaard Museum already displays a 6.5-meter Gokstad boat that was used to transport crews and exchange orders between warships.
Copenhagen establishes support groups for parents of children missing school
A new parents’ association has signed a four-year agreement with the City of Copenhagen to establish support groups for families whose children experience prolonged, involuntary school absence.
Such absence is often connected to poor well-being and is considered concerning when a pupil misses at least 20 percent of school for two consecutive quarters. That corresponds to about 10 days per quarter.
The first groups will be funded by Copenhagen and include eight to nine parents who meet approximately once a month, education news outlet Folkeskolen.dk reported.
A family therapist will lead the meetings, with a parent from Forældrekommissionen, or the Parents’ Commission, also participating.
Louise Gielov and Jens Langorn helped establish the association after their family appeared in the Danish public broadcaster DR documentary “Skolens tabte børn,” which showed daily life with children unable to attend school.
The couple received more than 1,000 messages from parents in similar situations after the documentary aired.
The association now has 2,545 members and aims to establish parent groups across Denmark. It also plans to use families’ experiences to promote earlier intervention and broader changes to prevent school absence.
The proportion of pupils with prolonged concerning absence increased from 2.4 percent in the 2019-2020 school year to 5.1 percent in 2024-2025.
The association has also secured 7 million DKK from foundations.
Dane becomes first European participant to receive combined flu and Covid vaccine
A 65-year-old Dane will become the first person in Europe to receive a new combined influenza and Covid-19 vaccine as part of a clinical trial Friday.
The trial will examine whether one injection can protect against both diseases as effectively as, or better than, the two separate vaccines currently used, Danish public broadcaster DR reported.
The first participant will receive the vaccine at Gentofte Hospital.
“We are investigating whether one shot with this new vaccine is just as effective or potentially better than the two shots given today at preventing hospitalizations with influenza and Covid-19,” said Tor Biering-Sørensen, a professor and senior physician at Herlev and Gentofte Hospital who is leading the trial.
About 165,000 Danes have agreed to participate. More than 300,000 people are expected to join over the next two years.
Half of the participants will receive one dose of the combined vaccine. The other half will receive separate influenza and Covid-19 vaccinations.
People age 65 and older in Denmark are automatically invited to receive free vaccinations against both diseases. The Danish Health Authority said about 1.3 million residents received invitations in September.
People with chronic illnesses or other conditions placing them at increased risk are also eligible for the free program.
The vaccines are intended to reduce the risk of severe illness and hospitalization during the winter respiratory infection season.

Archaeologists uncover more than 1,000 graves in Copenhagen park
Archaeologists have excavated more than 1,000 graves containing human remains beneath Hans Tavsens Park in Copenhagen’s Nørrebro district.
The park, located next to Assistens Cemetery, was previously used as a burial ground for Copenhagen’s poorest residents. Victims of the city’s 1853 cholera epidemic are among those buried there.
“We can use it to gain insight into the poor population from this period and Copenhagen’s history,” Museum of Copenhagen archaeologist Olivia Persson told Danish public broadcaster DR.
The excavation is taking place before Hans Tavsens Park and the neighboring Hans Tavsens Gade are redeveloped into a connected green space.
The project will also allow the park to collect water during cloudbursts, helping prevent flooding of nearby roads and basements as Denmark experiences wetter weather.
Construction began in autumn 2025 as part of the City of Copenhagen’s plan for managing extreme rainfall. The redevelopment is expected to be completed in spring 2028.
Most of the remains will be transferred to the University of Copenhagen’s Anthropological Laboratory for storage and examination. Some will undergo additional analysis, while the remainder will be reburied in the park.
Researchers will examine the health of selected individuals. They will also study how the graves were arranged to better understand religious and cultural attitudes toward death among Copenhagen’s poorer population at the time.

Greenland’s parliament unanimously adopted a resolution Thursday directing the government to draft legislation temporarily banning deep-sea mining.
The proposed ban would remain in effect through December 31, 2029, with the possibility of two-year extensions.
Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government, supported the considerations behind the resolution. It said it would introduce a bill for the temporary ban during parliament’s spring 2027 session.
The ban must therefore pass as legislation before taking effect.
WWF Greenland, the local branch of the World Wide Fund for Nature, called the decision “an important step in the right direction,” according to AFP.
“With this decision, Greenland has the opportunity to send a strong signal that the protection of the ocean, nature and the Greenlanders’ livelihood must be taken seriously when we face new forms of exploitation of marine resources,” the organization said.
WWF Greenland says deep-sea mining can damage marine ecosystems and biodiversity.
Fishing is the main driver of Greenland’s economy, while hunting remains important to local communities.
The vote came one day after US President Donald Trump said oil, gas and mineral exploration was beginning in Greenland. Greenland’s government subsequently denied the claim. Trump did not mention deep-sea mining.
Greenland suspended new oil and gas exploration permits in 2021. Industrial oil drilling and gas extraction have never been conducted there, according to AFP.
Denmark considers lower temperature rule to allow electric cremation ovens
Denmark’s 20 crematoria could replace oil- and gas-powered ovens with electric models if authorities approve a lower minimum temperature requirement.
The Danish Environmental Protection Agency has proposed reducing the required temperature in cremation ovens’ post-combustion chambers from 800 to 750 degrees Celsius, engineering publication Ingeniøren reported.
The proposed change has been submitted for public consultation.
Electric ovens are expected to reduce both environmental effects and the financial cost of cremations.
Michael Smidemann, chair of the Danish Crematoria Association, said crematoria were interested in replacing their existing ovens.
“The background is a desire to sharpen the green profile, even though it is somewhat mixed how green the electricity we receive actually is,” he told Ingeniøren.
Electric cremation ovens can reach 750 degrees. Requiring them to reach 800 degrees would demand additional heating elements, increasing electricity use and causing heavy wear on the ovens’ brickwork, according to Ingeniøren.
Denmark recorded 58,185 deaths in 2025, according to the Danish Crematoria Association.
Of those who died, 51,252 were cremated, corresponding to 88.1 percent of all deaths.
A cremation typically takes about 90 minutes, according to information from the City of Copenhagen and other sources.
Specialized services received 61 percent of growth in municipal spending
Denmark’s specialized social and education services received 61 percent of the inflation-adjusted growth in municipal service spending from 2018 through 2025.
The finding comes from an analysis by Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd, or AE, an economic policy institute linked to the Danish labor movement, according to Dagbladet Information.
Specialized services include support for children, young people and adults with particular needs, along with special classes and special education.
Municipalities spent approximately 80 billion DKK on these areas in 2018. By 2025, spending had risen to 93 billion DKK.
Residential facilities accounted for 40 percent of the increase. Municipal spending on those facilities now totals about 27 billion DKK, according to AE.
“When expenditures in the specialized areas grow, there is less money for the general areas, which also need investments,” AE director Lars Andersen said.
However, the analysis does not establish that the increased specialized spending directly caused cuts elsewhere.
Municipal service funding also covers daycare centers, public schools and elderly care.
The government and Local Government Denmark, the association representing Denmark’s municipalities, have increased the overall spending limit annually since 2018. Their latest agreement raises it by 3.3 billion DKK for 2027.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats has previously acknowledged that rapidly rising specialized social service costs continue to create financial difficulties for some municipalities.

Through its existing model, retailers sell unsold food in discounted surprise bags, with Too Good To Go receiving a percentage of each transaction.
The company says its expansion will help businesses recover value from unsold merchandise while giving customers access to a wider selection of discounted products.
“Our partners are increasingly approaching us with challenges regarding surplus goods that extend beyond food and asking if we can help. Surplus exists in all parts of the store,” Lykke said.
Surplus stock can include seasonal products, discontinued items, outdated packaging and gift sets that are no longer in demand.

Tiny parasitic wasp discovered in Denmark for the first time
A nature enthusiast searching beneath ferns in a North Zealand forest has identified an insect species never previously recorded in the country.
The discovery was made in mid-September at Gribskov National Nature Park during a bioblitz, a 24-hour event in which participants search for and document wildlife.
Around 70 people took part in the event, organized in collaboration with the Vores Vilde Natur project and biodiversity platform Arter.dk.
Nature educator Lars Holm Hansen discovered the wasp, measuring just a few millimeters, while shaking bracken ferns to examine the insects hiding underneath.
He collected several specimens using an insect aspirator but could not immediately identify them.
After posting a photograph on Arter.dk, he received help from experts who identified the species as Hemiptarsenus ornatus.
“It shows that if you put in a little effort out in the field, you can get lucky, and it is simply worth the effort,” Hansen said.
The Natural History Museum of Denmark confirmed the finding in a press release.
Museum insect curator Lars Vilhelmsen explained that the species has previously been recorded in Germany, Sweden and Norway.
“It has probably been here all along. It is already known from several countries around us, but it is so small that you do not just easily spot it,” Vilhelmsen said.
He added that relatively few people in Denmark study parasitic wasps, meaning many species may remain undocumented.
Hansen, who had participated in six bioblitz events this year, also suggested the insect’s Danish name: smykket dværgsnyltehveps.
He believes Danish names make unfamiliar species easier to discuss and remember.

Three Danish films shortlisted for Europe’s Oscars
Three Danish films have been shortlisted for the European Film Awards, often described as Europe’s equivalent of the Oscars.
The films are the dramas Kvinde ukendt by May el-Toukhy and Gæsten by Mads Mengel, and Sine Plambech’s documentary Rescue, the Danish Film Institute announced on Instagram.
A total of 45 films have been shortlisted in the fiction category.
May el-Toukhy’s Kvinde ukendt has already received international recognition. The drama was selected for the Venice Film Festival in September, where it won the main prize, the Golden Lion. Its lead actress, Mathilde Arcel, was named best actress.
The film has also been selected as Denmark’s entry for the Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category.
Set during the liberation of Denmark in May 1945, the drama follows a woman who has worked as a maid in the home of an elderly, respected widower she is now preparing to marry. She struggles to hide the fact that she has had a relationship with a German soldier.
Mads Mengel’s Gæsten has also attracted international attention. In July, the film received two awards at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in the Czech Republic.
It won the Special Jury Prize in the festival’s main competition, known as the Crystal Globe Competition, while Mengel was named best director.
The film follows Karl and Emilie, a couple preparing to host a naming ceremony for their son. Their plans are disrupted when an uninvited guest arrives: Karl’s mother, played by Trine Dyrholm, with whom he has not spoken for years.
The third Danish film on the shortlist is Rescue, a documentary by anthropologist Sine Plambech. It had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.
The documentary follows people fleeing across the Mediterranean and examines how the European Union’s border policies affect the lives and conditions of refugees.
Rescue is one of 15 films shortlisted in the documentary category.
Producers, distributors and other rights holders can submit films for consideration by the European Film Academy. The academy’s board and invited European experts then select films for the shortlist.
Members of the academy, which includes professionals from across the European film industry, watch the shortlisted films and vote to determine the final nominations. They vote again to select the winners once the nominations have been announced.
The final nominations will be announced on November 14. The awards ceremony will take place in Athens, the Greek capital, on January 16.

International trains, along with InterCity and InterCityLyn express trains, are running on their normal schedules, but they must move at lower speeds on parts of the route.

Liberal Alliance wants mindset interview for citizenship applicant
A debate in Denmark over a proposed law granting citizenship to 2,055 people has centered on whether the applicants have been checked well enough for anti-democratic opinions.
Liberal Alliance, a political party in Denmark, carried out its own check of the people listed in the citizenship bill. During this review, the party found a woman who had repeatedly praised Hamas and former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh.
Following the discovery, Liberal Alliance wants the woman called in for an interview with Indfødsretsudvalget, the Naturalization Committee of the Danish parliament.
Alex Vanopslagh, the leader of Liberal Alliance, spoke about the matter to the Danish newspaper Politiken.
“As we see it, it just emphasizes the need to wait to grant more citizenships until a proper screening model is in place, so that we can specifically catch some types who, based on what we can see so far, appear strongly anti-democratic,” he told the newspaper.
Every six months, a new bill is introduced in Folketinget, the Danish parliament, to give people Danish citizenship. This happens after an application process that is often long and detailed. This process was also followed under the previous coalition government in Denmark.
The most recent round of citizenships was scheduled at the same time a parliamentary election was called in the spring. Because of the election, the bill that included citizenship for the 2,055 people was delayed.
The delay gave momentum to demands from opposition parties. They argued that officials must carry out a more thorough review of the people on the list to find out if any of them hold anti-democratic views. Socialdemokratiet, the Danish Social Democratic Party, supported this demand as well.
However, the new government decided to present the citizenship bill before a new screening system was ready. This choice led to a larger debate during the opening of the Danish parliament.
During that debate, Rasmus Stoklund, the political spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, said that if opposition parties found a person on the bill who had anti-democratic views, they could inform the Naturalization Committee. Liberal Alliance has now acted on that suggestion.
Politiken also spoke with the woman identified by the party. She denied that she supports Hamas or any killings.
“I do not support anyone who kills anyone. Because I do not like anyone killing anyone, regardless of whether they are Israeli, Russian or anything else,” the woman told the newspaper.
She stated that she is ready to attend an interview with the committee to explain her position.
Other political parties have reacted differently to the proposal. Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, supports calling the woman in for an interview.
However, Enhedslisten, the Danish left-wing Red-Green Alliance party, strongly opposes the idea.
“It is deeply concerning that Liberal Alliance now to such an extent wants to begin exercising thought control,” Peder Hvelplund, the citizenship spokesperson for Enhedslisten, told Politiken.

Kirsten Schwalbe becomes Denmark’s oldest person ever at 112
A woman from Struer has set a national longevity record, reaching 112 years and 218 days on Wednesday and surpassing the previous record held by Karla Lindholm Jensen.
Schwalbe also joins the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people. The world’s oldest living person is Britain’s Ethel Caterham, who is 117.
The previous Danish record holder, Karla Lindholm Jensen from Herning, died in 2020.
Ahead of the milestone, Jyllands-Posten attempted to interview Schwalbe, but she needed a day of rest. Instead, the newspaper spoke with two of her three daughters.
Her daughter Hanne Jensen, 86, described how her mother sometimes struggles to understand that her children are now elderly themselves.
“She knows well enough that we are getting older, but she forgets that we can no longer withstand everything,” Jensen told the newspaper.
Schwalbe was born in Salling in 1914, just months before World War I began, and grew up alongside nine siblings.
She married her first husband in 1938, and the couple had three children.
Despite her age, Schwalbe continues to live in her own home in Struer.
Her life has previously been documented by regional broadcaster TV Midtvest in the television series “Kirstens vilde år,” which airs on TV 2.
Schwalbe has attributed her longevity partly to genetics. Four of her nine siblings also lived beyond 100, she told Berlingske in 2024.
She has also emphasized the importance of maintaining a positive outlook, previously telling TV Midtvest that a person’s mood plays an important role in living a long life.
Government party proposes mandatory helmets for e-bike riders
Rising numbers of serious traffic injuries have prompted Moderaterne, the Moderates, to call for stricter safety rules for people using electric bicycles.
Sten Larsen, the party’s health spokesperson, told regional broadcaster TV2 Østjylland that helmets should become a legal requirement for e-bike riders.
“E-bikes are both heavier and faster than regular bicycles,” Larsen said.
He pointed to an increase in serious injuries and deaths involving electric bicycles as justification for the proposal.
Currently, Denmark does not require helmets for ordinary bicycles or standard e-bikes, whose motors provide assistance at speeds of up to 25 kilometers per hour.
However, helmets are already mandatory for speed pedelecs, which can provide motor assistance up to 45 kilometers per hour.
According to the Danish Road Directorate, 200 e-bike riders were injured in traffic accidents in 2025, including 133 who suffered serious injuries. Another 11 riders died.
The number of seriously injured e-bike riders was the highest recorded in six years.
Larsen wants to discuss the proposed legislation with Transport Minister Signe Munk of Socialistisk Folkeparti, the Socialist People’s Party.
Ritzau sought a comment from Munk, but her ministry said she was unavailable.
Cyklistforbundet, the Danish Cyclists’ Federation, opposes making helmets compulsory, arguing that such a measure could discourage cycling.
“Our purpose is to get more people to cycle. So every measure that pulls in the opposite direction, we will oppose. But we warmly recommend that people use a bicycle helmet,” federation chair Jens Peter Hansen told TV2 Østjylland.
The proposal would introduce a helmet requirement for standard e-bikes, bringing their rules closer to those already applying to faster electric bicycles.

Greenland moves closer to restoring former time zone and ending daylight saving time
Greenland’s three governing parties have agreed to support a proposal that would move the territory back to UTC-3 in 2028, reversing a decision made just a few years ago.
The parties, which hold a majority in Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, announced their position during a debate Tuesday, according to Sermitsiaq.
The proposal would also abolish daylight saving time starting next year.
“We have decided that we should return to UTC-3 on the basis of the many people who have submitted a consultation response,” the governing parties said.
In 2022, Greenland’s parliament approved a move from UTC-3 to UTC-2 to balance the time difference with Europe and the United States. The change took effect in March 2023.
However, the decision has remained controversial, with 4,142 residents signing a petition calling for the previous time zone to return.
Opposition parties Naleraq and Siumut proposed reversing the change in May. The government initially opposed the move but supported ending daylight saving time.
Despite the government’s changed position, Greenlandic leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen of Demokraatit, the Democrats party, warned about potential consequences.
He said the change would increase the time difference with Europe by one hour in winter and two hours in summer.
Nielsen argued that reduced overlap with Danish medical specialists could lead to longer patient waiting times.
He also warned of higher costs for businesses, weaker flight connections with Europe and financial expenses associated with changing the time zone.
The proposal is scheduled for a final parliamentary vote October 21.

Greenland’s government has cancelled repayment claims totaling 39.8 million DKK against more than 19,000 residents who received excessive employment benefits because of government IT errors.
Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government, announced Saturday that recipients would not have to return the overpayments from the Suila-tapit program.
Suila-tapit is an employment tax allowance of up to 1,313 DKK a month for workers earning between 70,000 and 500,000 DKK annually.
The program was introduced on January 1, 2025, to encourage employment and reduce economic inequality.
Errors in the Greenlandic Self-Government’s IT systems caused some residents to receive excessive payments during 2025. The government initially demanded that the money be repaid.
“Some citizens were paid too much without having done anything wrong themselves, and that responsibility does not lie with the individual citizen,” Finance Minister Aqqaluaq B. Egede of Inuit Ataqatigiit said.
Residents who have already repaid the money will receive refunds.
“We cannot turn back time, but we can take responsibility and ensure that citizens do not have to pay for the mistakes made in the system,” Egede said.
The repayment demands had faced public opposition. A large demonstration was planned in Nuuk on Saturday but was cancelled shortly after the government announced it would withdraw the claims.

Copenhagen has far more municipal savings per resident than poorer municipalities
Danish municipalities differ significantly in how much readily available money they hold, according to an analysis by CEPOS, a Danish liberal think tank.
Copenhagen Municipality has the largest liquid holdings per resident, with savings equivalent to 31,685 DKK for each person.
At the other end of the ranking are Hjørring, Sorø, Thisted, Lolland and Aalborg municipalities. Their liquid holdings range from 3,127 DKK to 4,354 DKK per resident.
Liquid holdings can be viewed as municipal savings that have not been allocated to a specific purpose. Municipalities typically use the money to manage ongoing incoming and outgoing payments.
CEPOS said municipalities must always maintain a certain level of liquidity to cover their regular financial obligations.
Local authorities may also build up savings to finance future projects.
More than 500 marine mammals stranded along Danish coasts in 2025
A total of 538 marine mammals were recorded as stranded along Denmark’s coasts in 2025, according to a report from the Danish Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency service for stranded marine mammals.
The animals included 363 harbor seals, 38 grey seals and 137 harbor porpoises.
Most were found dead. Of the harbor seals, 310 were dead when discovered, while 136 of the 137 harbor porpoises were found dead.
The report identified disease, parasites, injuries and weakness as possible reasons for the strandings.
One animal from each of the three groups was recorded as having stranded after becoming caught unintentionally in fishing nets.
More unusual marine mammals were also found along the Danish coastline during 2025. These included a humpback whale and a striped dolphin.
Ambulances get deer whistles to avoid hitting animals
Ambulances and emergency medical vehicles in the North Denmark Region will be equipped with wildlife whistles to reduce the risk of collisions with animals.
The small plastic whistles are mounted outside vehicles and produce a high-frequency sound when air passes through them. The sound is intended to frighten animals away from the road.
“Unfortunately, we have a number of collisions with animals when we drive with emergency signals in forests and natural areas,” the region’s Prehospital Services wrote on Facebook.
“It is dangerous for the people in the car, it delays the driving, and is dangerous for the animals.”
The decision comes as Denmark faces a possible record year for deer collisions.
Dyrenes Beskyttelse, Denmark’s largest animal welfare organization, recorded 8,739 deer collisions during the first nine months of 2026. That compares with 7,994 during the same period in 2025.
The previous annual record was 11,870 collisions in 2025.
The risk of encountering deer is particularly high during autumn and around sunrise and sunset.
However, it remains unclear whether wildlife whistles effectively keep animals away from roads.
Two insurance companies previously gave the devices to motorists as part of separate trials. According to FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ association, the companies could not reach a clear conclusion about whether the whistles reduced collisions.

Apartment prices in Copenhagen fell for the second consecutive month in September, while prices in Aarhus rose sharply.
The average sales price for owner-occupied apartments in Copenhagen Municipality declined by 1.0 percent from August to September, according to housing platform Boligsiden. Prices fell by 0.5 percent the previous month.

In Aarhus Municipality, apartment prices rose by 3.7 percent in September, the third-largest monthly increase since records began in 2011.

Prices in Aarhus have increased by 23.3 percent over the past year. Nordea housing economist Lise Nytoft Bergmann called the development “extraordinary” but warned that prices would eventually reach a limit.
Nationwide apartment prices were unchanged in September. Prices for houses and holiday homes increased by 0.3 percent overall.

NEW YORK, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday, waiving major energy tariffs and sanctions on Russia mandated by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, just days before the act takes effect.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States," Trump said in the order.
The action freezes upcoming tariffs of up to 100 percent that were slated to hit the top five importers of Russian crude oil and gas, as well as restrictions aimed at Russia's "shadow fleet" of oil tankers and energy and defense sectors.
The move came after Trump struck an agreement with Russia to release more Russian diesel into global markets and announced an energy infrastructure ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.
Under the agreement, Russia could "immediately" begin supplying 300,000 tons of diesel, an additional 500,000 tons in November and then 1 million tons "immediately thereafter," local media quoted Trump as saying on Friday. Meanwhile, Washington has agreed to purchase diesel fuel from Russia to help lower global energy prices.
The move also marks Trump's efforts to lower fuel prices before the U.S. midterm election in early November.
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September. The act was named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
The legislation has authorized up to 100 percent tariffs on goods imported into the United States from the top five buyers of Russian crude oil or gas, and broader financial sanctions and energy restrictions targeting Russia. ■

Jakarta-Bandung High-Speed Railway handles over 18 mln passenger trips in 3 years

JAKARTA, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- The Jakarta-Bandung High-Speed Railway, locally known as Whoosh, has operated safely for three full years as of Saturday, handling over 18 million passenger trips since it entered commercial service, according to China Railway International Co., Ltd.
During the three-year period, the first high-speed rail line in Indonesia operated a total of 58,666 bullet train trips, safely traveling over 8.9 million kilometers with an on-time performance rate of 99.4 percent, said the company.
The number of daily train services has increased from 14 at the initial stage of operation to a peak of 62 trips, with the highest single-day passenger volume reaching 26,770, official data showed.
In terms of service enhancements, the Whoosh team has tailored ticketing options and service models to cater to various travel habits and budgets. Flexible dynamic pricing, multi-channel ticketing, frequent-flyer-style loyalty cards, and ticket modification services have been introduced to provide passengers with more versatile travel options.
Since entering operation, the railway has reshaped urban transportation along the route, attracting businesses in tourism, catering, and retail to cluster around railway stations, thereby creating job opportunities and boosting income for local residents.
To date, stations along the route host 117 commercial vendors, including 29 micro, small, and medium enterprises, offering local food, beverages, souvenirs, and creative cultural products.
While boosting local consumption, the railway has also attracted an increasing number of international travelers. The operation team has improved station facilities, commercial amenities, and last-mile transport connectivity.
According to data from operator PT Kereta Cepat Indonesia China, Whoosh has transported and served over 960,000 international travelers, giving a strong boost to local tourism and related industries.
To ensure safety, the team tailored China's high-speed rail management to Indonesia's weather and seismic conditions through advanced real-time monitoring and emergency response systems.
Whoosh, also the first high-speed rail line in Southeast Asia, now operates at speeds of up to 350 km per hour, reducing travel time between Jakarta and Bandung from around four hours to about 45 minutes. ■

Interview: IMF official highlights mounting global fiscal challenges
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:25:43 CST
15:25:43 KST

Rodrigo Valdes, director of the Fiscal Affairs Department of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), speaks in an interview with Xinhua in Washington, D.C., the United States, on Oct. 8, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Rui)
WASHINGTON, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Governments in almost all economies face pressing fiscal challenges, with high debt levels, higher interest rates and growing demands for public spending, an International Monetary Fund (IMF) official has said.
"It's a reality that debt is high. The debt-to-GDP ratio is increasing for the world economy. We have higher interest rates than a few years ago, and there are a lot of demand for more spending," Rodrigo Valdes, director of the Fiscal Affairs Department of the IMF, told Xinhua in a recent interview in Washington D.C., ahead of the 2026 Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group, being held in Bangkok, Thailand.
"All those things together make us think that the challenge for fiscal policy is very important," Valdes said.
According to the newly released Fiscal Monitor, global public debt is historically high and is projected to exceed 100 percent of global GDP before 2030, real interest rates on government debt remain above pre-pandemic levels, and spending pressures continue to mount across advanced economies and emerging market and developing economies.
New IMF research shows that when debt is already high, rising policy rates lead to a larger deterioration in fiscal deficits and debt, and high debt also makes market interest rates more sensitive to fiscal developments, according to an IMF blog posted Wednesday.
Higher interest rates "have worsened the scenario for everybody because at the end of the day, interest affects everybody," Valdes told Xinhua.
"Higher interest means that the cost of carrying debt is higher, and therefore is a global phenomenon that implies that we need more efforts, a bigger primary result, just to stabilize debt," he said.
Valdes also noted that defense spending, in particular, has contributed to mounting fiscal pressures. "I would say new defense spending in some countries, particularly in Europe, but also some demand for more spending in the U.S.," he said.
Beyond defense spending, population aging is driving up healthcare and pension costs, while climate change is creating additional investment needs, both of which add to fiscal pressures, Valdes noted.
"We have many sources of more spending pressures," he said.
The IMF official noted that for low-income countries, oil price shocks and extreme weather events are particularly concerning, as they can exacerbate food insecurity. "They have to prepare for that."
On oil shocks, Valdes said that governments worldwide have so far provided subsidies or tax cuts equivalent to an average of around 0.5 percent of GDP to contain oil prices, although the figures vary widely across countries.
If the governments don't allow oil-price increases to pass through to consumers, the cost could be even higher, between 1 and 1.5 percent of GDP, he added, stressing that preventing such price adjustments can affect global prices.
"If prices in some parts of the world do not adjust, that means that consumption doesn't adjust," and the only way to bring global demand and supply back into balance is through higher global prices, he said.
Such policies also have significant spillover effects, Valdes said, underscoring the need to move away from "inefficient and costly" interventions toward measures that are "targeted, temporary and transparent."
He urged policymakers to take a holistic approach in policy design and implementation, recognizing that no single policy instrument can achieve all objectives.
"A holistic approach means that you have to look at revenues and the spending side together," Valdes said. "We recognize fully that conducting fiscal policy is not easy -- it requires a combination of art, politics and techniques."
Building confidence across all stakeholders is essential, he added.
Commenting on China's fiscal picture, the IMF official said China has several characteristics that make it less vulnerable than other countries with comparable debt levels.
"In particular, China has many assets, some of them that are liquid. The financial account or the balance of payments is not fully open, and that also cautions for big movements of capital," Valdes said.
China pays a relatively low interest rate compared with other countries and has a high savings rate, he said. "All these factors, I would say, help reduce the risks."
China is already taking actions to tackle the economic challenges, he said, noting that expenditure should be used carefully to support the economy's ongoing shift toward greater consumption. ■
Rodrigo Valdes, director of the Fiscal Affairs Department of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), speaks in an interview with Xinhua in Washington, D.C., the United States, on Oct. 8, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Rui)

TASHKENT, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- From electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing to green energy and regional railway, Uzbekistan's cooperation with China is increasingly translating high-level political trust into tangible economic gains, an Uzbek expert has said.
Eldor Tulyakov, executive director of the Development Strategy Center of Uzbekistan, a think tank, made the remarks in an interview with Xinhua.
As bilateral engagement enters a broader and deeper stage, Tulyakov highlighted that cooperation with China has worked to advance the Central Asian country's national development goals.
"Political trust creates favorable conditions, and practical work gives it substance," he said.
"The tangible results of cooperation are most visible where enterprises are already operating, infrastructure has been built, and new professions have emerged," he added.
Trade, investment and joint ventures, he said, have all grown substantially in recent years, with both sides setting more ambitious targets ahead.
Tulyakov said investment delivers the greatest long-term value when it strengthens local capacity.
"The significance of such projects goes beyond the finished product," he said, pointing to the demand they create for engineering expertise, maintenance, components and services.
He applied the same logic to connectivity, citing the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, which is under construction.
Its strategic value extends far beyond logistics. "For businesses, it means easier access to markets. For regions, it creates opportunities for auxiliary industries," he said.
In his eyes, the railway's true value "lies in terminals, streamlined customs procedures and coordinated action among neighboring countries."
On people-to-people exchanges, Tulyakov highlighted the role of vocational education and the bilateral mutual visa-free regime.
Educational exchanges, he noted, should be seen both as an investment in trust and as the cultivation of talent for joint projects.
"A student who learns the language and gains cross-cultural experience better understands the business environment," he said. "Those skills will directly serve research, entrepreneurship, diplomacy and industry."
Tulyakov highlighted the Treaty on Eternal Good-Neighborliness, Friendship and Cooperation signed at the second China-Central Asia Summit, as well as joint efforts within the Shanghai Cooperation Organization framework.
"This sends a clear signal to society and businesses alike that the parties intend to develop relations consistently and with a long-term perspective," he said. ■

Wife of abducted Lebanese Jewish leader dies after 42 years of waiting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:22:54 UTC
15:22:54 KST

In early September, it was reported that Israel was seeking to advance efforts to locate and repatriate the remains of leaders of Lebanon's Jewish community as part of negotiations with Lebanon. The men, regarded as Jewish martyrs, were abducted and murdered by terrorist organizations in the neighboring country in the mid-1980s.
Behind the names of the 12 community members are families who have waited decades to learn the fate of their loved ones and are closely following the slow-moving negotiations.
One of those families is the Jamous family. Miriam (Maro) Jamous, wife of Salim Mourad Jamous, a leader of Lebanon's Jewish community, will never learn what happened to her husband. Miriam lived with him and their three children in Lebanon until his abduction in August 1984. She later immigrated to Israel, where she eagerly awaited any developments in the case. She died on Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement.
Speaking to ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth, their son Moshe Jamous says his mother's life story and courage deserve recognition in their own right.
Miriam was born in Damascus, Syria, and grew up in a synagogue in one of the city's neighborhoods. The Jewish community allowed her family to live there on the condition that all family members help maintain the building. Over the years, she grew close to Rabbi Nissim Indibo, the chief rabbi of Damascus.
According to her son, Miriam worked several jobs in Damascus, including as a nurse who visited people's homes to administer injections. That work gave her special permission to move around at night.
Jamous says she eventually became an operative who helped smuggle young Jewish women out of Syria and into Israel.
"She would go out at night under the cover of being a nurse and work as a seamstress during the day," he recalls. "She became deeply involved in smuggling Jewish women out of Syria and persuading them to immigrate to Israel."
Jamous says his mother tried twice to immigrate to Israel herself but was caught and imprisoned in Syria for several months each time.
The smuggling operations took a turn after a tragedy in which a group of Jewish girls was murdered while being smuggled out of the country.
"It caused profound grief and led members of the Jewish community to blame the leadership responsible for the smuggling operations," he says. "A decision was made to continue the mission, but this time to try something different: Send the daughters of prominent families out of Syria to restore the community's trust."
Escape from Syria and love in Lebanon
That group of young women, which now included Miriam Jamous, managed to reach Lebanon, from where they were supposed to continue to Israel. But Miriam and a handful of others remained in Lebanon.
"My father fell in love with her, and she decided to stay," her son says. "From that point, my mother's life took a glamorous turn. She met a man who was one of the leaders of the Jewish community, someone who was supposed to take care of her, and he did. She had a lavish wedding and rose in social status. All of this happened during Lebanon's civil war, a bloody conflict that spared no community."
The couple married in Lebanon in 1975. They later lived in Beirut with their three children, Moshe, Moti and Shalom, all of whom were born at the American University Hospital in the city.
"When their eldest son was born, my parents made sure to bring him to Israel for his brit milah," Jamous says, referring to the Jewish circumcision ceremony. "It was my mother's first visit to Israel. They crossed through Rosh Hanikra and then returned to Lebanon. My younger brother's circumcision and mine were held at the Magen Abraham Synagogue in Beirut."
The family says Miriam also played a role in smuggling Torah scrolls from Lebanon to Israel.
According to published reports, Shlomo was a textile and real estate merchant who maintained an office inside the synagogue in the Wadi al-Yahoud quarter of western Beirut. After his abduction, his office was set on fire and the word "Jew" was spray-painted on its walls.
"My father was one of the leaders of the Jewish community in Lebanon and was involved in smuggling operations," his son says. "My mother accepted my father's instructions: Don't ask what I'm doing, don't ask where the money comes from and don't ask when I'll be home. She didn't understand it at the time, but over the years, after his abduction, she came to understand what he meant. From the moment he was abducted, she took charge of everything connected to Lebanon's Jewish community."
'They would dump bodies near our house'
"When my father was abducted, my mother immediately stepped into his shoes because she was the wife of the last chairman of the Jewish community," Jamous says.
"Everyone turned to her, including terrorist organizations. Whenever a body was dumped near our house, my mother was the one who had to arrange the burial and determine whether the person was Jewish. During the civil war, if people thought someone who had been killed was Jewish, they would leave the body near our home in Lebanon because everyone knew where we lived. She became consumed by this responsibility. She had no choice."
Jamous says his mother eventually realized that she had to get him and his brothers to Israel. According to him, they were smuggled into the country in October 1986, two years after their father's abduction, and lived in various institutions in Israel.
The family says Miriam entered Israel with the children, left the two older brothers there and returned to Lebanon with the youngest.
"She was far away, but she always made sure to call," her son recalls. "Who connected her to a telephone? There are so many unanswered questions. What telephone was she calling from?"
Why was it so urgent to smuggle you out that year?
"First, there was the situation in Lebanon. The second reason was a telephone call from the kidnappers saying they wanted the eldest son. They were willing to release my father in exchange for him," he says.
According to Jamous, his mother immediately understood that her children were now in danger.
"Mom came to Israel every few months and then returned to Lebanon. We lived in various institutions and boarding schools in Israel. Questions arose about who gave her permission to go back. Everything went through Rosh Hanikra. What's more, she received money so she could continue supporting herself there."
According to a publication by Israel's National Insurance Institute, Miriam immigrated to Israel in 1989.
Jamous says that when his mother finally settled in Israel and decided to close the chapter of her life in Lebanon, she lost her identity and social standing.
He believes she never received the recognition and support she deserved.
"She lived a hard life, without financial assistance. She could not afford to raise us at home. We lived in boarding schools and would go out to visit her. She worked manual labor jobs," he recalls.
And throughout all those years, what was happening with your father's abduction case?
"It came up several times over the years, but not much in the Israeli media," he says. "It didn't receive attention. They told my mother, 'Stay home, and if there's any news, we'll let you know.' But my mother was involved in the entire process, including the preliminary contacts concerning negotiations."
Israel and Lebanon are approaching an eighth round of talks in the current negotiations. At what point did your family become involved?
"At first, it wasn't discussed, but we had also asked that it not be discussed. My father is at the top of the list. We were involved throughout these rounds of talks. My mother met many times with Gal Hirsch, the Prime Minister's Office coordinator for hostages and missing persons.
"When I told her that the issue had officially been placed on the negotiating table with Lebanon, she began to fade. She withdrew into herself. She kept saying, 'My husband will come back to me.'"
Jamous says that when his mother began seeing media reports confirming that the fate of the missing Jews was among the issues being negotiated, she became overwhelmed by longing for her husband.
“Some time later, she fell ill and asked her children to come to the hospital. She died on Yom Kippur.
"In her final moments, she received special attention at the hospital once the staff understood the significance of the situation. I encouraged her, spoke to her and told her the negotiations were progressing.
"She would ask me every time, ‘Have they held talks yet?’ And I would tell her, ‘Yes, they have, but there’s been a slight delay.’
"She kept asking to see Dad, to see his belongings and touch them.
"In her final moments, when I was with her, she said something for the first time: 'Moshe, I can let go now. I'm tired.'"

AI fears are being weaponised
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:21:39 UTC
15:21:39 KST

AI fears are being weaponised
Tech giants are fighting to protect their monopolies from cheap open-source models. Fear is their weapon.
As the growth of artificial intelligence accelerates, it is already posing significant challenges to society. Companies have started laying off workers whose jobs AI models can now perform. The expansion of data centres has spiked energy consumption and increased the carbon footprint. AI agents are being used by malicious actors to automate the spread of disinformation. Algorithms are demonstrating bias, raising concerns about flawed application and discrimination by human-related technologies that use them. AI is being used to identify targets in warfare, leading to greater loss of human life.
These are complex problems that demand serious regulatory attention. Yet, today’s dominant AI policy conversations are rarely grounded in these immediate challenges.
Instead, the global discourse has been swept by apocalyptic prophecies. We see this doomsday narrative promoted by some within the AI industry and echoed at the highest levels of decision-making: from lawmakers like Senator Bernie Sanders championing bans on superintelligence, to cautionary messages from the Vatican, to former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton calling open-source AI a real threat.
It is entirely reasonable for global leaders to take these industry-amplified warnings seriously. However, this chorus of influential voices sounding the alarm about AI “existential risk” has inadvertently pulled our focus away from the multiple crises AI has caused, already affecting labour, the environment and communications.
Worse still, the public panic is being weaponised to enforce a modern regime of digital colonisation – the concentration of power in the hands of a few AI corporations in a handful of countries.
The doomsday narrative provides the perfect justification for regulations that would target open-source AI models, which are free or cheaper to use and allow users to modify them to fit their needs. The logic presented to lawmakers is simple and seductive: if advanced AI is a potential weapon of mass destruction, it can only be developed by a trusted few.
Under the banner of “safety”, tech giants are attempting to write the rules to protect their monopolies by shutting down competition from smaller, cheaper open-source AI models.
This directly mirrors historical colonial tactics: preventing local industry from developing to force total reliance on the “empire’s” exports.
Currently, the entire globe is dependent on these frontier AI systems developed by tech giants, especially the Global South, which lacks the resources to create its own AI models from scratch, now costing upwards of $100m in compute power alone.
The problem with using the dominant AI models is not only that they are costly, but also that they often fail in local contexts. Consider Kenya’s recent rollout of the AI-driven Social Health Authority (SHA) system. Because the imported model was built on assumptions that did not accurately capture the reality of Kenya’s vast informal economy, the system failed spectacularly, systematically overestimating incomes and overcharging the poorest citizens for healthcare premiums.
To be effective, frontier AI systems must be adapted to local data. Since building them from scratch is financially impossible for most, open-source AI serves as the only viable bridge for local innovators. More importantly, preserving open-source AI allows the Global South to step off the West’s treadmill of human-mimicking chatbots.
Developing nations do not necessarily need conversational AI systems; they need AI that can help tackle development challenges in areas such as energy, healthcare, agriculture, manufacturing and climate mitigation.
If we crush open-source AI out of a disproportionate fear of AI agents, developing nations lose the main mechanism they have to build their own sovereign tech ecosystems for development.
Furthermore, AI monopolies lock in users in a cycle of data extraction and severe cognitive dependency. We are already witnessing the early stages of cognitive degradation as users increasingly outsource their critical thinking, creativity, and agency to frontier AI systems.
This dependency creates a feedback loop where our growing reliance fuels more data extraction, which in turn builds even more capable systems that strip away human agency and centralise absolute control.
While the Global South is uniquely vulnerable due to historical inequities, this dependency traps anyone not at the frontier. Even wealthy nations in the Global North face the exact same threat of lock-in and extraction.
So what is the solution? Calls for AI bans are certainly not. Abandoning AI would mean letting go of a technology uniquely positioned to accelerate the discovery of new drugs and new solutions to the energy and climate crises. There is already evidence of this with the development of tools such as AlphaFold and MOFSeq.
Banning open-source AI models is also a bad choice. Safety does not negate equitable access to AI. We can, and must, fund robust safety research and implement rigorous testing for near-term breaches. But we cannot allow the fear of hypothetical futures to justify the deliberate consolidation of power in the present.
Safeguarding the future of AI means ensuring that its development is decentralised, transparent, and globally distributed. It means defending open-source innovation as a public good and a fundamental weapon against digital colonisation. It means proactively addressing the human cognitive toll of the technology, ensuring that AI serves to augment human intelligence rather than erode it. It means anchoring absolute accountability in humans, instead of anthropomorphising AI agents that possess no humanity.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

"This directly conflicts with local government autonomy, which is enshrined in the constitution."

Here is our rolling coverage from India on Saturday, October 17:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
WATCH — Indians in Germany protest as voter roll controversy goes global
India's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party is challenging the Indian Election Commission over alleged electoral irregularities.
The controversy is spilling beyond India's borders. Indians in Berlin are joining calls for accountability over controversial voter list revisions.
Supreme Court says access to internet fundamental right for children, calls blanket bans 'disproportionate'
India's top court declared that access to and use of the internet is a fundamental right of every individual, including children, legal news outlet LiveLaw reported Saturday.
It said that a blanket ban on children's internet activity could make them vulnerable to greater risks rather than protect them from online abuse and exploitation.
The Supreme Court also issued directions to bolster the processes for detecting and removing child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) from social media and other online platforms, the report said.
The court stressed that the right to freedom of speech and expression also incorporates the right to know, receive and impart information and ideas, LiveLaw reported.
The two-judge bench described the internet as a "marketplace of ideas, creative expression and information" and said that its value went beyond the material it contains, as it provides opportunities for children in remote areas and those with disabilities.
"For many children, particularly in remote areas, it is often the only source of learning and information," the court said, according to LiveLaw.
For children with special needs, the internet is often the only platform where they can find company with others like them, the court said.
The court acknowledged that the internet, in its current form, poses safety risks to children. But it said that keeping children away from the internet because of failures by platforms and the relevant authorities to detect and remove harmful content would amount to mistaking the victim for the problem, LiveLaw reported.
What did the court say on blanket restrictions on internet use for children?
The Supreme Court said that a legal ban would not stop children from using the internet, and that they could move to other unregulated platforms.
"Any blanket restriction on the access of internet by children is nothing more than unproven measures of proven disproportionality," LiveLaw cited the court as saying.
The Supreme Court called for safeguards to ensure online child safety and the regulation of content accessible to children.
It suggested measures such as a "child mode" for social media accounts, LiveLaw said.
Saturday's Supreme Court judgement comes amid a global debate on the ban of social media for children over risks from harmful content. Australia declared the world's first social media ban for under-16s last year.
France followed suit this summer, before its Constitutional Court blocked the move.
US lawmakers urge Marco Rubio to bring up India protest crackdown
Six lawmakers from the United States' Democratic Party have called on US Secretary of State Marco Rubioto raise India's handling of the youth protests during his visit next week.
The US representatives include Pramila Jayapal, Ilhan Omar, Jim McGovern, Rashida Tlaib, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Jesus Garcia.
"As the world's largest democracies, the US and India have an obligation to promote and defend the rights to freedom of assembly and expression," Jayapal wrote on X, sharing a letter addressed to Rubio.
The letter alleges a "pattern of repression, wrongful detention, and excessive use of force by security forces" during the student protests in Delhi and other parts of the country.
The lawmakers also highlight incidents of "apparent surveillance," saying that they had received reports that the Indian diplomatic missions in the US "hired photographers to surveil protesters on American soil."
"These incidents raise particular alarm in light of India's documented pattern of engaging in transnational repression, including through the weaponization of consular services, harassment, intimidation, and physical violence," the letter said.
The group urged Rubio to prioritize the issues in his discussion with Indian officials.
The US Secretary of State is visiting India early next week, after traveling to Uzbekistan.
He is slated to meet Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar in Mumbai. His agenda also shows a trip to Jamnagar in the western state of Gujarat.
Student leader Neha Bora released from detention
All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora, who was also detained during the latest protest in New Delhi on Friday was released later in the night.
Bora has emerged as a prominent face in the protests against India's top poll official.
Speaking to the media after her release, Bora called for Dipke and other protesters to be released, saying that they had been "illegally detained".
"They are ordinary citizens demanding accountability and their right to vote. Carrying out such illegal detentions and keeping people at the police station overnight makes no sense at all," Bora said.
A widespread review exercise — called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — has struck off over 130 million names from India's electoral rolls since it began last year.
Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large proportion of minority voters. They accuse Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains.
The neutrality of the Election Commission of India (ECI) is being questioned.
The ECI denies favoring any party. It says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also helps in preventing the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Youth being made 'pawns' — BJP
Modi's party has slammed its opponents for undermining democracy and has denounced the protests as attempts to create "anarchy".
BJP's Rajnath Singh — who is also India's defense minister — addressed the protests at a press conference on Friday.
Singh accused the opposition, led by the Congress party, of wanting to bring a "regime change along the lines of Bangladesh" and using Indian youth as "pawns in the politics of disorder."
"It appears that the Congress and its political allies, both directly and through their affiliated organisations, are attempting to channel the energy of young people not into constructive activities and nation-building, but into instruments of political confrontation and the spread of chaos," he said.
CJP's Dipke arrested after detention — reports
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke has been arrested, following his detention on Friday when he stepped out to participate in a rally he had called in New Delhi, media reports said.
Dipke was arrested to prevent a breach of the peace and will be taken before a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court later today, news agencies ANI and PTI reported.
CJP legal affairs head Ratna Singh also said that Dipke had been arrested, adding that he would appear before the SEM court in central Delhi's Mandir Marg at 12 p.m. (630 UTC).
Singh claimed that Dipke's lawyers had not met him.
The 'Cockroach' movement said early on Saturday that they did not know where their founder had been detained, calling his detention a "kidnapping."
"Until now, neither his parents nor his lawyers and not the CJP team have been given any updates about his location," the CJP said on X, as it published a video of CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde asking about Dipke's whereabouts.
Dipke was detained publicly on Friday as he left the house in Jhandewalan where he was staying to take part in CJP's 'Lehra Do Tiranga' (Wave the tricolor) protest rally in Connaught Place.
Videos of his detention showed the CJP founder being told by a police official that he was being placed under "preventive detention" before he was taken to a police car.
Dipke was seen displaying India's flag as police and media personnel surrounded him. Some supporters were seen trying to block the police vehicle from driving away with Dipke.
Just hours earlier, a group of Delhi Police officials had visited the 31-year-old at the Jhandewalan residence and served him a notice barring the Friday protest.
The Delhi Police had previously reiterated that Section 163 of India's criminal procedure law, which prohibits any form of assembly or protest, was in force in the Connaught Place area.
"The manner in which he was picked up from right outside his residence, no information about his whereabouts, and the fact that even his lawyers have been unable to meet him raise serious concerns about due process and fundamental rights," Singh wrote on X.
Even after Dipke's detention, hundreds of protesters turned up in Connaught Place defying the heavy security deployment. The protesters were seen waving the Indian national flag as part of the CJP's 'Tricolor' rally. According to police, some 150 protesters were detained during the demonstrations.
The fresh protests came after CJP co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were sent to a five-day detention in jail on Wednesday for alleged violation of prohibitory orders and breach of a peace bond after they attempted a demonstration. They too were carrying the Indian tricolor and the flag has since been at the center of CJP's campaign.
The Indian flag "belongs to the 1.3 billion people of this country and not the Delhi police. We will wave it where we want!" the movement has said.
Dipke, Das and Ranka were earlier detained on October 10 from a plane as they arrived in the capital for a protest march calling for the resignation of India's Chief Election Commionser Gyanesh Kumar over alleged manipulation of voter lists.
They were released after nearly 24 hours.

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you the weekend edition of the India blog, where we break down all the biggest headlines that are creating a buzz in the country.
The world's largest democracy has seen almost daily protests since the start of October. The youth-led 'Cockroach' movement, opposition parties, student organizations and civil society members are calling for India's election chief to step down over a sweeping revision of voter rolls that they say benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke was taken away in a police car even before he could get to the protest location. It was the second time that Dipke was detained in less than a week.

US, Israeli business groups unite to strengthen economic ties amid growing anti-Israel backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:20:17 UTC
15:20:17 KST

On paper, they were all competitors: Dozens of regional groups, many funded by their respective local governments, each one hoping to recruit Israeli businesses to grow their own economies.
But this week in Michigan, at the first-ever US-Israel Innovation Exchange Summit, they all united with the common goal of promoting broader American business ties with Israel, in a political climate in which scaling back support for Israel is moving into the mainstream.
By the conference’s end, the attendees had signed a memorandum of understanding pledging “to establish a framework for cooperation, information sharing, relationship development, and coordinated activities designed to strengthen economic, innovation, investment, and commercial relationships between the United States and Israel.”
The collaboration made sense to the Israeli officials on hand.
“So many states want Israeli businesses to come to their territory, because they understand that will lead to economic growth in their state,” Elad Strohmayer, consul general of Israel to the Midwest, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency at the summit on Wednesday. “That’s the win-win that we’re trying to promote.”
US-Israel economic ties face growing boycott pressure
He said the US is also a dream destination for many Israeli businesses. “If you’re an Israeli entrepreneur and you want to expand, the market in Israel is limited. Where do you want to expand? Of course, it’s the United States.”
After decades of largely unfettered growth in the US-Israel business relationship, cracks are forming in several places. As the Michigan conference was unfolding, New York City’s Jewish and pro-Israel comptroller, Mark Levine, announced he would stop buying Israel bonds, citing the country’s declining credit ratings following the war in Gaza. Anti-Zionist groups, including Jewish Voice for Peace, trumpeted the move as a victory for the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions movement, though Levine has denied that politics played a role.
Around 50 people had gathered from across the country and Israel for the summit, which organizers hope to become an annual event. In so doing, they seek to turn the tide on a trend that concerns many in the pro-Israel community: increased scrutiny and protest of American business ties to the country.
“This is, I think, a long time in coming,” Mark Davidoff, CEO of the Michigan Israel Business Accelerator, told JTA at the summit.
American business groups seek to expand Israeli investment
Overlooking sweeping views of the city’s skyline, presenter Zineb Riboua, a research fellow with the conservative Hudson Institute think tank, boasted that “Israeli companies sustain tens of thousands of jobs on US soil.” Other speakers were particularly bullish on Israeli involvement in data centers, which have attracted immense controversy in the United States over environmental concerns as well as a brewing backlash to the technology companies they sustain. Many in the room, though, saw data center investments as a prime business opportunity.
Davidoff said that the Paul E. Singer Foundation, run by the pro-Israel hedge fund manager, approached MIBA to spearhead a collaborative effort “to share best practices” on attracting Israeli business.
Prominent Jewish and business leaders in Michigan and beyond also back the summit. Gary Torgow, chair of the Jewish Federations of North America, welcomed attendees to the conference held at the downtown Detroit headquarters of Huntington Bank, which he also chairs.
Detroit’s federation was another sponsor, along with several local economic development groups, Israeli universities and Israel’s Midwest consulate general. Chaim Martin, Israel’s economic attaché to the US and an appointee of far-right finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, was also in attendance.
Michigan protests target public funding for Israeli business ties
Mounting a stand for pro-Israel business interests took on an especially defiant character in Michigan. Here, Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and other figures have mobilized a sizeable pro-Palestinian movement on multiple fronts—including the state’s economic interests. In the weeks leading up to the summit, MIBA itself had been the target of local protests.
A campaign called “MI Money Out Of MIBA,” whose member organizations include the Detroit chapter of JVP, has objected to the more than $5 million in public funds the group has received since 2018 to help bring business to the state. The protesters have particularly objected to MIBA’s connections to the defense industry.
“Our state should not be using any public funds to subsidize business with a country carrying out a genocide, apartheid, and occupation,” a petition backed by the anti-MIBA campaign and signed by more than 2,400 people to date reads. The effort was amplified by Palestinian-American US Rep. Rashida Tlaib, of Michigan, a strident Israel critic, who posted to social media earlier this month that the group “should not be receiving a dime of public funds.”
“When small businesses, many of them Black- and women-owned, are struggling in our state, there never seems to be money for them, but Governor [Gretchen] Whitmer has funding for bombs that kill children,” Tlaib wrote. “These weapons have been used to commit genocide and murder the family members and loved ones of so many of our neighbors.”
Business leaders push back against anti-Israel accusations
Davidoff fought back against Tlaib’s accusation. He told the Detroit News this week that the accelerator-connected Israeli company in question doesn’t deal in weaponry. Instead, he said, the business works in “counter-drone technology designed to protect critical infrastructure, first responders, and US service members against hostile drone threats.”
That strategy, a direct response to critics and misinformation, proved controversial among the rest of the pro-Israel business crowd at the summit. During one session, panelists sang the virtues of flying “under the radar.” Asked by a moderator how many members of the summit publicize the location of their events ahead of time, only two hands in the room went up.
In contrast, Davidoff hopes that, by being clearer about their investments and aims, pro-Israel business accelerators can set the record straight. MIBA does not invest directly in the Israeli government, he said, adding that others should understand that.
“I think at some point, you don’t have a choice but to move a chess piece,” he told JTA. “Being silent too long is misinterpreted.” He declined to comment on the prospects for Michigan’s pro-Israel business community should El-Sayed win his Senate race.
Strohmayer, for his part, claimed during his session that “Israel is much stronger economically than it was before the war.” Partnerships with American interests are more about “fostering the relationship” than boosting Israel’s economy, he told the room — though his pitch wasn’t without a different kind of existential urgency.
“We need, with the rise of antisemitism, to remind people that Israel is a valuable partner to the United States,” he said.
