'The emotional cost has been unbelievable': How three years of war have changed Israelis - study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:19:59 UTC
15:19:59 KST

Since the Israeli voluntary organization ERAN (Emotional First Aid) was founded in 1971, it has never received so many calls for help as during the past three years.
The devastating psychological trauma, fears, and chronic anxiety resulting from the vicious Hamas terrorist onslaught down south elicited 928,911 calls for help: 316,514 in the first year, 320,486 in the second year, and 291,911 in the third year.
The shock of the terrorist incursion, the murders, hostage taking, rapes, and destruction of homes in the Gaza border communities made ERAN an emotional refuge for Israelis of all ages.
Trained ERAN counselors are available at no cost, around the clock, and just a phone call away, while the number of public mental health professionals for counseling was and remains minimal.
Of the total inquiries, 21,829 involved suicidal thoughts, intentions, or actions. The average rate of such calls over the three years stood at 2.35%.
Understanding the mental health crisis
Suicidal distress stems from a combination of factors, so the trend should not be attributed solely to the war or any single cause, said ERAN CEO David Koren in an interview with The Jerusalem Post.
Among young people and adolescents, the subject of suicide was very prominent; it nearly doubled over the three years of the war, rising from 2.6% in the first year to 4.4% of total inquiries in the third year.
Among soldiers, the rate of calls regarding violence and sexual abuse rose from 5% to 10% in the second year, and stood at 8% of total inquiries in the third year of the war.
The rate of calls involving loneliness among the general population rose from 28% in the first year of the war to 41% of total inquiries by the third year, continued Koren, who served as CEO from 1998 to 2005 and then returned to the job in 2011.
He brought impressive credentials to the post – he was certified in mediation and crisis management, earned a bachelor’s degree in social work from the University of Haifa, and is an active board member of the Israeli Trauma Coalition.
Maria Berta Zaslany established the association in Jerusalem in memory of her husband, Dr. Arieh Zaslany, who served for over 18 years as director of mental health services for schools in Jerusalem and as a psychiatric consultant for the Jerusalem Municipality.
He specialized in treating suicidal individuals and successfully dissuaded many from taking their own lives. After he passed away in 1968 at the age of 57, the first branch was at Mrs. Zaslany’s Jerusalem home, and it gradually grew into a national association.
“We are like a seismograph of society. For over five decades, we worked devotedly to provide psychological first aid to anyone in need of a listening ear and support,” Koren said.
“Over the years, we have faced numerous challenges and periods of crisis and uncertainty; from these experiences, a deep commitment has grown to serve as an available, humane, and accessible resource for the people of Israel – at any hour, on any day,” he continued.
“The three years of war have presented us with a harsh and ongoing reality. Behind every call for help stands a person grappling with pain, loss, anxiety, loneliness, or burnout, and sometimes a combination of these.”
A rise in distress
Asked what the single biggest change the organization has seen in the kind of distress Israelis discussed was, Koren responded: “As time passed, the population felt that the war was endless. They had thought it would be won in a few months, not three years. The emotional cost has been unbelievable. It affects everybody; it has made us a people with much less patience and connection with our environment. We constantly have to be alert.”
Reserve soldiers suffer from a lot of stress because they and their families haven’t returned to normal life. Many lost their jobs and businesses. Having to “re-enter” reserve duty time after time is very hard on them, he stated.
“Uncertainty is very difficult for children and teens, who are showing a significant rise in distress. Adults over 25 are suffering from tension and emotional fatigue, which had already worsened during COVID. It’s a normal reaction to an abnormal situation.”
Young people who tell ERAN about their problems relating to school, university studies, military service, disrupted education, and uncertainty about the future are all under stress because their routine has fallen apart, Koren continued.
“We have heard from callers about plans to emigrate from Israel out of fear or hopelessness, but we have no data on how many,” he said.
ERAN can’t know how many people have called for help multiple times, or whether they called several times about different problems.
“In addition, some people call from numbers that are hidden. We have to provide absolute numbers,” the organization’s CEO explained. “We also don’t have demographic information about specific sectors, such as various immigrant groups, that call more, because all the calls are made anonymously.”
Supporting the volunteers
He said the organization’s 1,800 volunteers around the country also need emotional support.
“We don’t have enough. We have branches in Australia with 50 volunteers and one in North America with 150, who answer most queries when it’s late at night in Israel.
“The Aliyah and Integration Ministry covers the cost of professional counselors in Russian, Amharic, Arabic, French, and Spanish who are on duty for five hours in the afternoons and evenings.”
Becoming an ERAN volunteer family is open to every Israeli person over the age of 25, from all backgrounds, who can listen, understand, and empathize.
They need to be able to speak, read, and write Hebrew. Some work from ERAN’s 15 branches, while others take calls from their home on a designated phone.
It also has a professional staff of 50 dedicated employees, ranging from headquarters and management to branch managers and coordinators.
ERAN is hearing from Israelis who never entered the formal mental-health system but are desperate for help, said Koren.
“Some are consulting AI-based conversations like ChatGPT and Gemini, and these can help, but they’re not the same as ERAN, which provides a human voice,” he said.
Dr. Shiri Daniels, ERAN’s national professional director, concluded: “In the daily routine, it’s important to notice those who are struggling, identify signs of distress, ask directly about suicidal thoughts when concerns arise, listen, and ensure that help is accessible before the distress deepens.
“We’re living in a state of ‘pseudo-routine.’ Most of us continue to work, study, raise children, and function, but functioning is not necessarily an indication of mental well-being.
“Amidst ongoing uncertainty and threats, distress can gradually accumulate, manifesting as burnout, loneliness, relationship difficulties, and a compromised sense of stability and security.”
For mental health support, call 1201 at any time of the day or night; visit the ERAN website (eran.org.il) or contact it via WhatsApp (052-8451201).

Many of the recent drone and missile attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi terrorists on Saudi Arabia are based on targeting intelligence provided by the Islamic regime, The Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday.
The report cited a former Israeli official, Danny Citrinowicz, who described the intelligence connection between Iran and the Houthis as "very, very strong on the operational level."
“Iran has a major interest in the Houthis’ success," said Citrinowicz, who previously served as head of the Iran branch for Israeli defense intelligence. "It harms Saudi Arabia; it raises the oil prices. Therefore, there is a shared strategic interest that isn’t based on a client-patron relationship, but rather on strategic cooperation."
The report comes as the Houthis have intensified attacks against Saudi Arabia, striking the country's presidential palace complex on Thursday, killing five, and in a separate attack striking Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, killing 17 and injuring over 300.
The Iranian interest in the Houthis' attacks on the Saudis was also highlighted by New York-based security think tank the Soufan Center, which told the WSJ that the strikes are "helping Iran project power."
Iranian officials deny being involved with Yemen's Houthis
Iranian officials have previously denied involvement with the Houthis, with the report citing Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei as saying in September that the Houthis are “entirely independent actors who make their decisions based on their own interests.”
Despite Baghaei's claim, members of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) have commended the recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-led coalition in the region.
Adam Baron, a Yemen expert and fellow with Washington-based policy institute New America, told the WSJ that the recent Houthi military gains were "undeniably" based on external Iranian assistance.
“The support the Houthis received from Iran and other Axis actors undeniably paved the way for the rapid-fire gains they’ve made over the past few months,” he said.

Now-ousted US general warned of defense munition shortage months before Iran war - report

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:19:43 UTC
15:19:43 KST

A now-ousted US general warned that the American military was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage could last for at least five years in the months before the war with Iran began, according to a CBS News report on Thursday.
Multiple US officials familiar with the matter told CBS that Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George’s risk analysis was included in the Pentagon's Global Force Management Allocation Plan in late December.
George was ousted by US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in April in the midst of the war with Iran.
According to CBS, George warned that both Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) battery and Patriot missile stockpiles would stay strategically low until at least 2030.
Anonymous US officials explained that George’s assessment stemmed from multiple factors, including the transfer of Patriot systems to Ukraine, munitions expended while defending Israel, and reduced defense industry production.
Officials told CBS that the US military does possess a significant stockpile of some offensive munitions, such as Joint Direct Attack Munitions (JDAM) and Small Diameter Bombs.
Over 50% of Patriot, THAAD interceptor stockpiles reportedly expended
Among the arms at critically low stock levels is the Patriot Advanced Capability-3 interceptor, a surface-to-air munition designed to destroy ballistic and cruise missiles mid-air.
Patriot PAC-3 orders have an average delivery time of over three years, CBS cited the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) as estimating in April. Defense contractors can take over four years to deliver a new shipment of THAAD interceptors.
CSIS estimated that prior to the Iran war, when George made his assessment, the US may have had around 2,300 Patriot interceptors. Between 1,050 and 1,430 interceptors, or up to 61% of prewar inventory, may have been expended during the war with Iran.
According to CSIS, pre-war THAAD stockpiles included about 355 interceptors. Between 190 and 290 of the munitions were allegedly used in the war, potentially using up 82% of the inventory.
Stockpiles could take four years to replenish, US official says
While American defense contractors have made moves to increase production of THAAD and Patriot interceptors, a US official told CBS that even if no more munitions were used, it could take until 2030 for the stockpiles to be fully replenished.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell denied the reports of munitions shortages in a statement to CBS, stating that the US has "everything required to strike at the time and place of the president's choosing."

====================================================================================================

Israeli startup 'Ciconia' lands California helicopter safety deal to prevent midair collisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:19:40 UTC
15:19:40 KST

California-based helicopter operator HeliStream is expected to equip its aircraft with collision avoidance systems developed by Israeli startup Ciconia, following a successful demonstration held in August 2026 in San Bernardino County, California, before firefighting representatives from across the United States.
The demonstration, conducted in the largest county in the US by area, tested the Israeli company's Collision and Conflict Avoidance System (CCAS) in scenarios involving helicopters and drones operating in congested airspace, particularly during firefighting and emergency response missions.
As airspace becomes increasingly crowded with helicopters, drones, and other unmanned aircraft operating in confined areas, aviation safety has become a growing concern for emergency services. Ciconia, based in Ness Ziona, has developed a decentralized collision avoidance system designed not only to identify potential threats but also to calculate safe evasive maneuvers for aircraft.
"Multiple aircraft, sometimes belonging to different organizations, operating together over a small, concentrated area is a recipe for disaster," said Col. (res.) Moshe Cohen, Ciconia's CEO and co-founder.
Cohen, a former Israeli Air Force attack helicopter pilot, assembled a team of aviation and technology specialists following his military service. The company's leadership includes Lt.-Col. (res.) Dr. Ilan Zohar, chief technology officer and an expert in drone control, and Lt.-Col. (res.) Gil Yanai, a former IAF test pilot and commander of its Flight Test Center who also serves as an El Al Boeing 787 captain and Ciconia's vice president of business development.
The team also includes Lt.-Col. (res.) Eran Bar-On, a former test pilot who heads algorithms and flight testing; Lt.-Col. (res.) Eran Nir, a former IAF Yasur helicopter captain, military technology specialist, and El Al Boeing 787 captain; operations manager and systems engineer Ronen Stofman, a former IAF flight test engineer; and software engineer Misha Poyarkov.
California helicopter pilot tests Israeli collision avoidance technology
Among those who tested the system in Southern California was Andreas Moser, HeliStream's chief pilot, who has worked at the company for 34 years.
HeliStream operates a diverse helicopter fleet used for pilot training, utility operations, high-voltage power line infrastructure work, and aerial firefighting. These missions increasingly involve multiple aircraft sharing restricted airspace, including firefighting helicopters, reconnaissance aircraft, water-dropping planes, and observation drones.
Moser describes his extensive flying experience with humor, saying he pilots "everything from a small Robinson R22 to a Sikorsky Black Hawk."
More than 200 civilian Black Hawk helicopters operate in the United States, according to the figures cited in the original report, primarily supporting firefighting operations using specialized water tanks or buckets suspended beneath the aircraft. Israel's National Security Ministry has also pursued the acquisition of three such helicopters to reinforce the country's existing aerial firefighting fleet.
For Moser, who regularly operates in Southern California's crowded skies, collision avoidance presents a significant operational challenge.
"We fly in one of the busiest airspaces in the world," he said. "Helicopters operate under visual flight rules, and you are responsible for avoiding collisions yourself. In a single-pilot crew, that consumes an enormous amount of energy and attention from the pilot, who is supposed to be flying the helicopter and carrying out the mission."
Drones pose growing threat to aerial firefighting operations
According to Moser, the increasing presence of drones around wildfires has created an additional safety risk for emergency aircraft.
Some drones are operated by emergency agencies to map fires and assess conditions on the ground, while others are flown by unauthorized civilian operators seeking to observe the scene.
"All it takes is for someone to think they have seen a drone in the air, and all firefighting operations are stopped until its location is confirmed or it has left the area," Moser said.
"There have been fires, even in the Los Angeles area, where structures were threatened and flights were suspended because of drones. We have even had a collision between a firefighting aircraft and a drone in our area."
Moser warned that a similar collision involving a helicopter could have serious consequences.
"A collision like that with a Robinson or even a Black Hawk could bring you down or cause severe damage that immediately ends the flight," he said.
The danger was underscored on August 2, 2026, when two firefighting helicopters collided while battling wildfires near Athens, Greece. One helicopter crashed, killing its two crew members, while the crew of the other aircraft survived.
Why conventional aircraft warning systems fall short
For decades, aviation has relied on technologies such as Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) and Traffic Collision Avoidance Systems (TCAS) to improve aircraft situational awareness and reduce the risk of midair collisions.
However, Moser said conventional traffic alert systems do not always provide helicopter pilots with the information needed during low-altitude missions involving numerous nearby aircraft.
"ADS-B is excellent, but all it tells me is that there is a target out there," he said. "It doesn't tell me whether that traffic is actually a threat to me, and it doesn't tell me where to fly if there is a collision risk."
"If I have four or five other aircraft around me, ADS-B doesn't tell me which one is the immediate problem."
The volume of alerts can itself become a distraction, particularly during training exercises or firefighting missions involving several helicopters operating close together.
"Sometimes, during training or in crowded airspace with seven or eight aircraft, we have no choice but to turn off the warning system," Moser said. "It keeps beeping nonstop, you can't distinguish one target from another, and you end up going back to the old method of looking outside with your own eyes."
He added that conventional ground-based traffic monitoring and air traffic control services can also be limited by radar coverage, particularly during wildfires in mountainous or remote regions.
Israeli-developed CCAS provides pilots with evasive maneuvers
Ciconia's system is designed to address these limitations through decentralized conflict detection and collision avoidance algorithms that do not depend on centralized air traffic management.
"The strength of Ciconia is that it doesn't rely on centralized management," Moser explained. "You can be in the middle of nowhere, and if another aircraft is equipped with ADS-B, the system will detect it."
More importantly, he said, the technology is designed to distinguish between nearby aircraft that pose no immediate danger and those whose flight paths could result in a collision.
"Ciconia tells you: 'You have all these targets around you, but none of them matters except this one, because it is climbing toward you, approaching head-on, or descending in your direction.'"
Unlike systems that primarily provide traffic information or alerts, Ciconia's CCAS is designed to generate a specific evasive maneuver while taking surrounding aircraft into account.
"Many systems can tell you there is a problem, but they also identify collision risks when there is no real danger," Moser said.
"Identifying a problem isn't difficult. Identifying only the dangerous situations, identifying all of them, and generating a practical, safe solution is the real challenge."
"Ciconia doesn't just provide a warning. It provides a maneuvering solution and makes sure that avoiding one collision doesn't put you in danger of another."
California flight demonstration exceeds pilot's expectations
During the August demonstration, Moser tested the technology in flight scenarios simulating aerial firefighting and congested helicopter operations.
"In the test, the system exceeded all my expectations," he said.
"There was one case where, because of a misunderstanding over the radio, one of the aircraft turned in a direction it wasn't supposed to. The system immediately detected the change, recalculated the solution, and presented us with a safer route."
"The speed with which it reacted to changes in proximity and flight direction was simply impressive."
Gil Yanai, Ciconia's chief test pilot, said the demonstration included police aviation and firefighting scenarios in which helicopters and drones operated together. The team also recreated a scenario resembling the fatal helicopter collision in Greece.
"The system allowed the pilots to operate freely," Yanai said. "As long as the airspace was safe, they continued working normally. The moment a real threat emerged, the system immediately displayed the required evasive maneuver."
The demonstration also included a large drone supplied by the San Bernardino County Fire Department, equipped with a CCAS unit, while another unit was installed on the Robinson helicopter flown by Moser.
"We demonstrated that helicopters and drones can operate safely together when CCAS ensures that they do not approach each other dangerously," Yanai said.
"When a collision threat develops, CCAS alerts the drone operator. If necessary, the system then takes control of the drone and diverts it. If the situation remains dangerous, CCAS provides flight instructions to the helicopter pilot."
The instructions are delivered through the aircraft's intercom system and displayed on a cockpit screen, allowing pilots to respond without diverting excessive attention from their primary mission.
Pilot workload remains a major factor in deadly helicopter accidents
The need for improved collision avoidance technology has become increasingly apparent following fatal aerial firefighting accidents in recent years.
Moser pointed to a previous collision in the United States involving a Sikorsky Skycrane heavy helicopter and a Bell 407, which killed the crew members aboard the smaller aircraft, as well as the August accident in Greece.
"These pilots are excellent pilots. They are good people who want to do their jobs and return home safely," he said.
"So why does this happen? It happens because of overload."
According to Moser, helicopter crews conducting firefighting missions must simultaneously manage smoke, strong winds, turbulence, water drops, and the movements of nearby aircraft.
"The human brain becomes so occupied with fighting the fire, dealing with smoke, wind, and turbulence, that you become accustomed to other aircraft being close to you, and your brain stops recognizing them as a threat," he explained.
He compared the phenomenon to helicopter accidents involving power lines, where pilots may be aware of an obstacle but fail to react in time because of excessive workload.
"When you go out to fight a fire, your primary mission should be fighting the fire," Moser said. "But once avoiding collisions becomes your main concern instead of putting out the fire, you become ineffective."
HeliStream expected to adopt Ciconia system for helicopter safety
Following the successful California demonstration, HeliStream is expected to equip its aircraft with Ciconia's CCAS technology, although the companies have not disclosed a purchase value, number of systems, or delivery schedule.
Moser said that as firefighting operations become increasingly complex, the risk of midair collisions remains his greatest concern, surpassing even mechanical or engine failures.
"I stand behind this 100%," he said. "My biggest concern is not an engine failure or a complex mechanical malfunction."
"My number one concern, both now and in the future, as there are more fires and more helicopters and drones in the air, is coming dangerously close to another aircraft."
"That is the greatest threat. Ciconia's CCAS system offers a real solution to a critical problem at an affordable price. We at HeliStream are eagerly awaiting it."

Israel faces a nationwide mental health crisis post-October 7, Clalit experts warn - study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:19:37 UTC
15:19:37 KST

The outrageous massacre committed by Hamas terrorists on October 7, 2023, inflicted many hidden wounds – traumas almost as painful as being stabbed with a knife or shot with a gun.
Haim Ben-Arye was one of these undetected victims. A longtime school-bus driver who was deeply devoted to his young passengers, Haim was happily married to Irit for 30 years and a loving father of six adult children.
Not long before the attack, Haim’s daughter had shared joyous news: she was pregnant with his first grandchild. He had so much to look forward to.
Yet on October 25, just 18 days after the massacre, Haim drove to a remote location and ended his life.
“He loved his job and his passengers,” his wife, Irit, recalled. “On the morning of October 7, our son, a first responder, told us, ‘Something terrible has happened.’
“Haim went to shul to be with the children whose fathers had gone to fight. He played with them and sang songs. But after Shabbat, we sat in front of the TV, and he just wept.”
Later that evening, Haim’s boss asked if he could drive his bus to evacuate children from Kibbutz Be’eri to safety. He agreed immediately. He returned home at 5 a.m., devastated and in shock.
“I couldn’t help them,” he told Irit. “My passengers were in total silence for over two hours.”
While Irit returned to her job at Clalit Health Services on October 8, Haim stayed home and watched horrific scenes on television. He hardly turned it on before.
On October 25, schools reopened for half-days, and Haim was scheduled to return to his bus route. When Irit called him later that day, he didn’t answer. Shortly after, a friend messaged that someone had died by suicide.
“I knew it was Haim,” Irit said. “I rushed home and saw people gathered in front of our house. My instincts were right. Haim was all heart.”
During the shiva mourning period, a man came to pay his respects and shared how Haim had once saved his child’s life.
The man’s son had seemed withdrawn on the bus, and Haim was the only person – including family and teachers – who noticed the boy felt profoundly alone, ensuring he got the help he needed.
“I told my children that their father shouldn’t have taken his life, but his heart simply broke,” Irit shared. “To me, he is still a hero.”
Irit shared her family’s tragic story with about 100 English-speaking journalists worldwide during a recent online seminar (webinar) hosted by the Clalit Research Institute, titled Israel’s Mental Health Front: Three Years Since October 7.
The event highlighted how personal grief reflects a widespread psychological emergency across the country.
The scale of the challenge
Prof. Amir Krivoy of the Geha Mental Health Center emphasized the scale of the challenge. Clalit, Israel’s largest public health insurer, serves five million members, half the nation’s population, and maintains comprehensive electronic data on their mental health.
“The population has endured cumulative stress since 2020, from coronavirus lockdowns and social tension over judicial reforms to the Hamas incursion, the war in Gaza, and Iranian missile attacks,” Prof. Krivoy explained.
“This sequence generated immense acute and chronic stress. While the peak occurred on October 7, Israelis were already in a fragile state.”
According to Clalit’s findings, the last baseline “normal” years were 2018 and 2019. Since then, chronic stress and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) have surged, particularly along the southern and northern borders.
Evacuated residents experienced a tenfold increase in psychological distress compared to those who remained in their homes. Furthermore, health professionals have observed an unprecedented rise in PTSD among children and adolescents, who usually suffer rarely from it.
All four public health funds have estimated that there are 60,000 Israelis who developed clinical PTSD between October 2023 and December 2025; half were Clalit members.
Krivoy recalled that he ran a clinic in the southern city of Sderot, where during the Hamas attacks and the subsequent battles, 53 people – including 37 residents of and visitors to Sderot, 11 police officers, three IDF soldiers, and two firefighters – were murdered or killed.
“I learned that 90% of the population didn’t sleep at night. They were afraid there would be another attack. Even two years afterward, many didn’t go for diagnosis because they were afraid to leave their homes.
“There will be more like them in the coming years unless they get relief. There must be follow-up. We know from experience that Israelis are resilient, but we have to be able to detect crises early and treat them in time.
“Israeli society will recover, but we have to help them.”
Living in a traumatic reality
Nufar Bar-Lipshatz, a developmental psychologist in a Clalit clinic in Beit She’an, told the Webinar audience that “we still live in a traumatic reality. My own husband has done a lot of reserve duty during summers and the High Holy Days, and the war isn’t over.”
She continued, saying that “delegations of Clalit therapists were sent to evacuated families who spent months in Eilat after the massacre.
“For some, it was the first time that they met a therapist. They were living in hotels, and they didn’t know when they could return. We encouraged them to talk; we encouraged their children to build toy houses so we could better understand their problems.
“In 20 years, these children will help run our society. Some of their family members were murdered, injured, and taken hostage. When the siren sounded, the difficulty continued. The child still struggles to feel safe. Some parents didn’t talk about it, but the kids can ‘read’ the stress in their parents’ faces and voices.”
Saying everything is fine doesn’t work, continued Bar-Lipshatz.
“They may develop fears that someone will kidnap them when they’re asleep or that their father could die in the army, but they won’t tell their parents, so they keep these fears to themselves.
“It can cause aggression and a hard time in preschool and school. Parents must give honest explanations, even though it’s hard.
“We can give the child a sense of meaning, recall their moments of bravery, that they went to the safe room fast; that they called the police or a relative even if they cried on the phone.”
Toddlers who are not yet verbal have difficulty expressing their experiences.
“We observe how they play and function every day,” the psychologist continued. “They may have nightmares, show aggression and withdrawal, play soldiers, hide, run to the shelter. Not every difficulty began in war. Some had problems before, but war can intensify it.”
A growing number of children who were emotionally affected by it all began to stutter.
“We didn’t have the personnel to treat each one individually, so we decided to organize a group of three- and four-year-olds with their parents,” recalled Bar-Lipshatz. “A siren sounded during the session, so we took them all to a shelter and did yoga, encouraging movement, play, and laughing.”
Challenges faced by health funds over the past decade
Prof. Ran Balicer, the founder and director of the research institute, Clalit’s chief innovation officer, and deputy director-general who also teaches at Ben-Gurion University in Beersheba, noted that mental health reform was added to the “basket” that insurers must pay for only in 2015.
Then COVID came and created a big burden. With the massacre, the health funds found that the mental-health care they were supposed to provide was underbudgeted, understaffed, and had long waiting times.
The 9/11 attacks on New York and Washington caused emotional harm in only 4% of Americans. In comparison, 15% of Israelis were directly affected. Not a single family wasn’t shocked by the barbarity.
When Iranian and other terrorist groups’ missiles fell, some Israelis took knives to the “safe” room. They felt nowhere was safe.
Clalit conducted a nationwide study with the Myers-JDC-Brookdale Institute that included 2,500 respondents. In January 2024, depression had affected 34%, and even today, it is clinically high.
Anxiety was 27%, and today it affects 20%. PTSD was 32% and has declined to 20%. One in five adults continue to report severe impairment in their daily functions, Balicer reported.
“We retrained primary care doctors so they could help treat patients. We added mental-health coaches, digital innovation, and used an AI tool to screen patients. Digital data helps us know who has a problem and predict future illness.
“Instead of waiting for patients to come in sick, doctors call and tell them they may have a medical problem. Not all doctors were willing to use them, but now they like the preventive-medicine technique because it can save lives.
“So many patients had been silent after October 7 that we created proactive preventive mental-health outreach and followed up treatment for 1,500 per week out of 8,000. We will continue to do this.”

Exclusive: Watchdog lists ships carrying Russian gas, blasts Trump sanctions waiver
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:13:18 UTC
15:13:18 KST

Exclusive: Watchdog lists ships carrying Russian gas, blasts Trump sanctions waiver
The NGO Urgewald has identified what it says are all the 134 vessels involved in Russian gas trade since 2022, which have carried over 150 million metric tons of cargo since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to data shared with the Kyiv Independent.
As of Oct. 15, around 1.5 million metric tons more were in transit.
The news comes as U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 16 issued a broad waiver of Russia sanctions that were set to take effect two days later under a law championed by the late U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham.
The law authorized the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five countries buying Russian gas and oil, and also provided for extensive sanctions against Russian officials, banks, and the energy sector, including ships involved in the Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) trade.
"Republicans and Democrats passed this law in Lindsey Graham's name to squeeze Russia's war revenues. Trump has now hollowed it out before its main sanctions could bite," said Alexander Kirk, a sanctions campaigner at Urgewald, on Oct. 17.
"That is a betrayal of the bipartisan effort behind this law and a lifeline to (Russian President Vladimir) Putin."
Between the law's signing on Sept. 18 and Oct. 15, 42 tankers had transported Russian gas, according to the analysis.
These include Boris Davydov, an Arc7 tanker that departed Russia's Yamal terminal on Oct. 6; Konstantin Posiet, which departed Arctic LNG 2 on Sept. 21; and Clean Horizon, which left Yamal the same day with a cargo later delivered to the French port of Dunkerque.
U.S. lawmakers from both parties have urged the White House to impose sanctions under Graham's law in order to pressure Moscow toward ending the war in Ukraine. For LNG tankers, this would enable Washington to target those ships and restrict their access to international shipping services.
Instead, Trump has taken increasingly accommodating steps toward Russia, announcing a deal earlier in October to purchase Russian diesel.
"Congress must challenge this retreat and demand that the administration explain whose interests are served by shielding Russia's energy trade from the pressure this law was designed to impose. Ukraine should not have to pay the price for Washington's unwillingness to act," Kirk said.
The list of 134 ships carrying Russian gas between Feb. 24, 2022, and Oct. 15, 2026, includes 17 Arc7-class LNG carriers, an advanced tanker type designed to export product from the Russian Yamal LNG terminal in the Arctic.
The EU paid 7.88 billion euros (about $8.9 billion) worth of gas from the Arctic project in the first nine months of 2026, Urgewald reported earlier.
While the U.S. has never been a major buyer of Russian fossil fuels and banned all imports in 2022, the EU remains the leading buyer of Russian LNG, followed by China, Japan, and South Korea, according to the CREA think tank.
But the EU has been phasing out Russian LNG imports, with a full import ban to take effect in January 2027.
Urgewald's latest findings underscore how much Russian LNG trade continues to rely on Western services.
Of more than 2700 voyages undertaken since February 2022, about a third were taken by ships owned by either the Greek shipping company Dynagas or the U.K.-based, U.S.-owned company Seapeak, according to data.
Both account for roughly 17% of the voyages each, with the Dutch Anthony Veder gas shipping company coming in third.
Greece has secured a sanctions exemption for Dynagas, allowing the company to continue shipping Russian LNG to non-EU countries even after the EU ban takes effect.
Other operators include Russian companies such as Gazprom and Novatek, as well as China's Cosco.
LNG trade has faced weaker sanctions pressure than Russia's oil exports, which have been constrained by an EU- and G7-imposed price cap, forcing the country to rely increasingly on its shadow fleet to ship its oil.
"Europe must now act with urgency. Sanction the tankers, cut off the services that keep them operating, and close the loopholes sustaining Russia's LNG exports," Kirk said.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,562,970 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:10:00 UTC
15:10:00 KST

Russia has lost 1,562,970 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 17.
The number includes 1,950 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,415 tanks, 25,554 armored combat vehicles, 163,883 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,266 artillery systems, 2,221 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,710 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,962 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Our industry will become more resilient and independent which improves deterrence and boosts overall national security,” says Minister of National Defence Robertas Kaunas.
Pekkla UAB designs and manufactures UAV and unmanned terrestrial vehicles. The company is established in Lithuania commercially and has the required infrastructure. Ukraine’s December One RND yields expertise and experience in Research and Development (R&D).
December One RND brings R&D insights, technical expertise, production capabilities and product concepts it plans to test on the Lithuanian market. Pekkla UAB makes available its infrastructure and business contacts in Lithuania, advises on regulation and shares its commercial platform.

Trump Says He Would Like to See Putin at G20 Summit

15:08:00 KST

US President Donald Trump said he is uncertain whether Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami this December, but stated that he “would love to have him” at the gathering.
Responding to questions from journalists regarding Putin’s prospective participation, Trump confirmed that the Russian leader’s attendance remains unconfirmed, Forbes TV News reported on Saturday, Oct. 17.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I don’t know if he’s coming. I would love to have him, certainly,” Trump told reporters.
The remarks follow earlier statements from the White House indicating an openness to hosting the Russian leader at the multilateral summit, which is scheduled to convene in Florida in December.
The prospective invitation has emerged as a point of contention among Western allies and European institutions, who have maintained an international diplomatic boycott of the Russian head of state since the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
President Trump:
"I don't know" if Putin will be attending G-20 Summit in Miami pic.twitter.com/aT4FTQ8dVZ
— Forbes Breaking News (@ForbesTVNews) October 16, 2026
European pushback
Trump’s openness to hosting Putin in Miami has drawn sharp criticism from European officials.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas previously condemned the diplomatic invitation, pointing to state-sponsored security threats and criminal indictments unsealed in the US involving Russian intelligence operations.
Kallas highlighted a September indictment by the US Department of Justice charging individuals linked to Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) with plotting the contract assassination of a prominent Russian dissident on American soil.
Trump Denies Role in Slowing Ukraine’s Military Starlink
“Trump’s inviting Putin to the G20 was very hard to hear,” Kallas stated, arguing that hostile intelligence activities operate under direct instructions from the Kremlin.
The European Commission confirmed that the EU will use the Miami summit to condemn Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine, regardless of whether Putin travels to the event.
Commission deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill emphasized that the 27-nation bloc has utilized every G20 platform since 2022 to demand the cessation of hostilities, reiterating that the stance will continue “irrespective of the participants at any G20 meeting.”
Any potential international travel by Putin also intersects with legal obligations surrounding the International Criminal Court (ICC), which issued an arrest warrant for the Russian president in March 2023 over unlawful deportations of Ukrainian children.
While the US is not a state party to the Rome Statute of the ICC and is not legally obligated under treaty law to execute ICC warrants, an in-person appearance by Putin would mark his first visit to a Western nation since the full-scale war began.
Kremlin positioning
The Kremlin has responded cautiously to public discussions regarding the Florida summit, sending mixed signals regarding whether Putin would accept an official US invitation.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov previously described speculation regarding Putin’s travel as “premature,” noting that an official determination has not yet been finalized by the presidential administration.
Peskov also dismissed prospects for a prospective bilateral encounter between Putin and President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the Miami meeting, reiterating Moscow’s stance that any substantive leader-level consultations could occur only in the Russian capital.

US: Homes burned in California as wildfires rage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:08:00 UTC
15:08:00 KST

US: California wildfires destroy homes, force evacuations
October 17, 2026
At least six expensive properties have been engulfed by fast-spreading wildfires on the southern coast of California, prompting thousands of people to evacuate.
The Orange County Fire Authority said on X that the so-called Norte fire had scorched about 465 acres (188 hectares) and that at least four homes had been impacted in the affluent San Juan Capistrano municipality.
Black smoke billowing from the hills was visible for miles as firefighters tried to contain the fast-moving blaze.
The agency said firefighters were "aggressively attacking the fire from ground and air" and repeatedly requested people to stay away from the area.
Danger of fire spreading remains as thousands without power
The Norte fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente and wind drove it into San Juan Capistrano.
The National Weather Service warned of "high risk for large fires and rapid fire growth," especially over Los Angeles and Ventura counties, as well as the mountains and foothills of San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties
The wildfires have continued to worsen due to the intense Santa Ana winds, low humidity and unseasonably high temperatures.
According to forecasters, wind gusts of up to 50-70 miles (80-110 kilometers) per hour were recorded in the mountains, with coastal and valley areas seeing gusts between 35 and 55 miles per hour.
Authorities have turned off the electricity supply to reduce the risk of electrical sparks that the heavy wind gusts could carry, leaving thousands of people in the state without power.

Hyundai recalls more than 94,000 vehicles in U.S. over fire risk
Hyundai Motor America is recalling more than 94,000 Hyundai and Genesis vehicles in the United States due to a potential fire hazard linked to overheating power seat motors, Qazinform News Agency cites Yonhap.
According to the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the recall affects 94,622 vehicles, including certain 2015-2016 Hyundai Genesis and 2017-2020 Genesis G80 models.
The agency said a faulty power seat control switch could become stuck, causing the front power seat motor to overheat and potentially ignite a fire while the vehicle is either parked or in operation.
As a precaution, owners of affected vehicles have been advised to park outdoors and away from buildings or other vehicles until repairs are completed, as the defect increases the risk of fire-related injuries.
Hyundai is currently developing a remedy for the issue. Notification letters are expected to be mailed to affected vehicle owners beginning Dec. 7, according to U.S. transportation authorities.
Earlier, German automaker Volkswagen is recalling 208,724 vehicles in the US due to a steering system defect, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA).

Oregon school shooting: Police praise 'heroism' of those who intervened to stop more killing

Oregon school shooting: Police hail 'heroism' of those who stepped in
October 17, 2026
Police in the northwestern US state of Oregon have identified a teenage gunman who shot dead four people at a school as a former special needs student there, while praising people who stepped in to stop more killings.
Three children aged 5, 8 and 11 lost their lives in Thursday's rampage, along with a 25-year-old female teacher, before the shooter was shot dead by a father of two pupils at the school, located in the town of Bend.
Another young child and a teacher were also injured in the attack.
Who intervened to prevent more deaths in Oregon?
A man in a vehicle outside the school who was shot at and missed by the 16-year-old gunman was the first to alert police to the danger.
Before they arrived, however, a female teacher tackled the shooter after he had already killed the victims with a pump-action 12-gauge shotgun in the school's special needs classroom.
While the two wrestled with each other, a man identified by family as Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old father of two girls at the school, rushed in with his legally held weapon and shot the gunman dead.
"He heard shooting and saw a teacher involved in a physical altercation with the suspect ... and fired his weapon, striking the suspect multiple times," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters.
"When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. The teacher who is willing to stand and fight for her children ... incredible. That is true heroism, and we don't see that a lot in society," he said.
Praise from Trump as gun control debate revived
Giamanco's mother told the local branch of Fox News that she was "very proud" and that her son was "an absolute hero."
US President Donald Trump also hailed Giamanco's actions.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he told reporters.
The shooting in Bend has triggered the usual responses from both sides in the everlasting debate about gun control laws in the US.
The National Rifle Association (NRA), one of the main and most powerful opponents of tighter laws on the possession of weapons by civilians, hailed the actions of the armed bystander.
"Yesterday's terrible act of violence in Oregon serves as another reminder of the importance of a law-abiding armed citizenry," the NRA said in a post on X.
Gun control advocates, however, once more condemned the relative ease with which firearms can be procured in the US, which they see as the main factor in the country's high rate of gun-related deaths compared with most other developed countries.
"America's gun violence crisis is killing our babies. Enough is enough," gun-control group GIFFORDS said.
According to an analysis by the education information portal Education Week, there have been 26 shootings at US schools so far this year that have resulted in injuries or deaths.
More than 360 mass shootings have been recorded across the country this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive.
It defines mass shootings as incidents in which at least four people are shot, excluding the shooter.

National Taiwan University plans AI subscription aid for lower-income students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:03:11 UTC
15:03:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — National Taiwan University plans to provide financial assistance to students from low- and middle-income households to cover AI service subscriptions, with the program potentially launching next semester.
As AI becomes more widely used in education, students and faculty face the growing cost of subscription-based tools. Academic research also requires substantial computing resources, according to CNA and Ettoday.
At a university meeting, geography professor Chien Shiuh-shen (簡旭伸) raised concerns about unequal access. He noted that students’ ability to pay for advanced services varies, calling for university-wide licenses to ensure all students can access AI tools regardless of their financial circumstances.
In response, NTU President Chen Wen-chang (陳文章) said AI subscriptions cost about NT$8,000 (US$247) per person annually. With approximately 400 students from low- and middle-income households eligible for assistance, the program is expected to require more than NT$3 million a year.
The university plans to cover the cost through financial aid or a sustainability fund supported by donations from alumni and the public, Chen said. It could begin as early as next semester, once implementation guidelines are finalized.
Separately, Vice President Liao Wan-jiun (廖婉君) proposed a university-wide system for purchasing AI software licenses and subscriptions to improve access for faculty and students.
She added that NTU plans to treat computing resources as basic campus infrastructure because of their importance to academic research. Under the proposed system, the university would allocate computing quotas to individuals and research projects.

France braces for tense day of protests as security concerns take centre stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:00:58 UTC
15:00:58 KST

The French government stepped up security measures ahead of Saturday’s nationwide protests over the cost-of-living crisis, with student groups also expected to join demonstrations amid fears of potential clashes.
France is bracing for a major day of protests on Saturday, as hundreds of demonstrations and other actions are set to take place across the country.
Trade unions and citizens branding themselves as "yellow vests" are protesting against the cost-of-living crisis and rising fuel prices, with large numbers of students also expected to join.
Authorities are on high alert amid concerns over potential clashes and public disorder.
In Marseille in southern France, protesters had already set bins and electric scooters alight on Saturday morning, prompting intervention by riot police.
Meanwhile, shops across the country have boarded up their storefronts in a bid to avoid potential looting or vandalism.
According to a source close to France's Interior Ministry, 500 actions are anticipated across the country on Saturday, as well as around 90 protests, with authorities preparing for possible violence in Paris and other major cities.
The protests follow four weeks of student demonstrations over a range of issues, including teacher absences, overcrowded classrooms, and outdated facilities.
Most student protests have been peaceful, but there have been clashes involving rioters and widespread criticism of alleged police brutality and violence.
The source told Euronews that the far-left movement could seek to provoke confrontations with law enforcement and attempt to breach security perimeters along protest routes. They also warned that blockades of key transportation routes and essential infrastructure would "not be tolerated."
Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron said on Friday that whilst the right to protest "is fully respected," it "must be accompanied by respect for people and property."
"That is why I call for calm and respect: these rights must be preserved," he said.
Mounting scrutiny of police actions
French law enforcement authorities have faced increasing scrutiny in recent weeks amid several allegations of police violence.
In one case, a 15-year-old schoolboy allegedly lost an eye after being struck by a police rubber bullet. In a separate incident, a 14-year-old reportedly lost his hand after picking up a police stun grenade. The circumstances surrounding both cases remain under investigation.
Following the latter case, France suspended the use of certain types of stun grenades.
Yet, in an interview on Friday, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that the use of stun grenades would be allowed on 17 October should "serious urban violence" occur on the sidelines of demonstrations, cautioning that stun grenades were "never used when things are going well."
Nuñez told France's Senate on Tuesday that 36 investigations into alleged police violence during student protests had been opened. He said that four of these cases related to mutilating injuries and six to significant injuries, whilst the others were related to alleged blows, insults and reported sexual violence.
One man who had flown into Paris from the US on Friday told Euronews he was "supportive" of peaceful protests.
"Hopefully nobody gets hurt and people's voices are heard," he said.
A taxi driver in the capital called the situation "very delicate."
"People have the right to protest, but peacefully," he said, adding that the "people in charge need to find some solutions."
Yellow vest movement
There has been speculation that the 17 October demonstration could mark the return of the yellow vest grassroots movement, which emerged in 2018 in reaction to a planned government fuel and diesel tax hike.
For months, yellow vest protestors gathered every weekend to block roundabouts, motorways, and fuel depots across the country, with tense police clashes also occurring.
It comes as the French government also grapples with a major public debt crisis as it attempts to pass a budget containing austerity measures through a hung parliament.
Police union lodges complaint against state for 'endangering lives of others'
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Thursday that 937 police officers and gendarmes had been injured since the start of the protests. He also reported injuries among 248 students and 149 teaching staff members, which he said was the highest number of injuries ever recorded by France's Education Ministry.
Lecornu warned that the “secondary school student movement” was transforming into a “wave of urban violence."
Meanwhile, Alliance Police Nationale, one of France's largest police unions, announced in a statement on Tuesday that it would lodge a complaint against the state "for endangering the lives of others."
The union denounced what it qualified as "contradictory orders" given to police officers, who have been "exposed to violence and left at the mercy of public hostility" over the course of secondary school protests.
“After the president’s [French President Emmanuel Macron] expressions of empathy towards rioters and emphasis on dialogue, we are now faced with vague instructions, contradictory orders and superficial public statements!"
"The discrepancy between Laurent Nuñez’s public statements and the verbal instructions passed down through the chain of command has become unbearable," the union said.
The hard-left France Unbowed party has been accused by the government and political opponents of encouraging violence and stoking unrest through inflammatory language.
In a speech delivered on 30 September, the party's leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, urged his supporters to "stand up to police brutality," adding that "there will be neither forgetting nor forgiveness for anyone."
He later qualified his comments, stating that he backed peaceful protest methods.

Yemen's Houthis claim responsibility for fresh missile strike on Aden airport
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group claimed responsibility after two missiles struck Aden International Airport on Friday, saying they had targeted a weapons depot as well as a military command headquarters. The Aden Security Department said a Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo had been preparing for takeoff when the attack took place.
Missiles apparently launched by the Iran-aligned Houthi group struck Yemen's Aden International Airport on Friday, while a Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile headed for the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz.
The coalition said it had also destroyed two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and three drones in Saudi Arabia's Southern and Riyadh regions. It did not identify the attackers.
Read moreHouthis deny targeting holy city of Medina after Saudi Arabia says it intercepted missile
In Aden in southern Yemen, two missiles landed on the airport grounds, the Aden Security Department said, blaming the Houthis. It said the incident was the second attack on the facility in less than a week.
In a statement attributed to a military source, the Houthis said an attack targeted "the Saudi forces' command headquarters in the Badr camp in Aden province" as well as a weapons depot.
No casualties were reported. A Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for takeoff when the missiles landed, the security department said.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Yanbu is a key outlet for Saudi oil exports, allowing the kingdom to ship crude to international markets via the Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. The vital waterway has been largely throttled by Iran since the US and Israel launched attacks on the country in February.
With regional tensions and security threats raising concerns over the safety of shipping and tighter global energy supplies, Brent crude oil briefly touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May.
Saudi Civil Defence authorities issued an alert early on Saturday for Abha in southwestern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border before sending an all-clear. Earlier they had issued alerts in the Jazan region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, where such warnings have become frequent since fighting resumed last month.
Also early on Saturday, Houthi-affiliated media reported strikes east of Yemen's northwestern city of Saada. The Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in the area.
Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has raised fears of a further deterioration in the country's humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions are worsening rapidly.
The Yemen conflict has become another front as the Iran war has widened into a regional conflict. The Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014 and forced the internationally recognised government south. A Saudi-led intervention began the following year, leading to years of stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.
The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since the conflict reignited following a Saudi strike on Sanaa International Airport in July, with the Iran-allied group targeting airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure.
The group has also targeted sites in government-held parts of Yemen in recent days, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital.
A spokesperson for the Houthi-run health ministry said on Friday that 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what he described as "Saudi aggression" since the escalation began on September 3. Reuters could not independently verify the figures.

====================================================================================================

Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

NHS organisations that care for millions of people in England are rejecting Palantir’s patient data technology, according to freedom of information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases.
Some health bodies said the £330m federated data platform (FDP) operated by the controversial US company had made it easier to manage waiting lists and has improved surgery scheduling. But, from Gateshead to Truro, others said they were declining to use it or had carried out trials and reverted to old systems. A Suffolk trust said other systems “supercede” the FDP’s functionality, while Greater Manchester’s care board called the Palantir system “duplicative” and “retrograde”.
The responses come as Andy Burnham’s government faces a crunch decision about whether to exercise a break clause in the seven-year NHS-Palantir deal, which was intended to better integrate the health system’s data to improve clinical accuracy and efficiency. Protests against the US firm’s role have also focused on its other contracts with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security forces. There is also dispute over evidence for the system’s effectiveness and public concern about the involvement in the NHS of a company cofounded by the tech billionaire Peter Thiel, who said in 2023: “The NHS makes people sick.”
According to more than two dozen FOI responses reviewed by the Guardian, 16 trusts and health boards declared they do not use it, following its introduction in March 2024. They include the University hospitals of North Midlands NHS trust, which said it will not use it primarily because “it does not appear to provide functionality over and above what we have already” and Dorset HealthCare university trust said it “will not be adopting or going live with the FDP”. Humber Teaching NHS foundation trust said: “We have no plans to use it.”
Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS foundation trust said it has used the system but it has “not offered significant improvements on local systems”. Avon and Wiltshire mental health partnership NHS trust said it had yet to find an FDP tool that offered significantly more than its existing capabilities and University hospitals Birmingham NHS foundation trust, which cares for more than 2 million people, said it had no plans to use it, citing “limited expected benefit over existing solutions”. The FOIs were gathered by Medact, a health campaign that opposes Palantir’s role in the NHS, and posted to a public transparency website, WhatDoTheyKnow.
Palantir has previously challenged claims that other software could be just as effective, with its senior vice-president, the former Labour MP Tom Watson, saying last week: “If there are companies that can do it, they would have taken part in free and open competition” to run the FDP.
Watson, a Labour peer and former minister alongside Burnham, was appointed as Palantir’s chief lobbyist last month amid a wave of opposition to the Palantir deal. He warned his former colleagues in Labour not to let “mob rule … lead procurement practices”.
But two parliamentary select committees have urged the government to end Palantir’s contract, including the Commons’ science and technology committee. Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat member of the committee, said the NHS boards’ responses “justify what I have been saying for the last year, which is that Palantir’s system is just not that good”.
“Once again we have proven that centrally dictating a solution to the NHS can’t work,” he said. “We have to get back to developing interoperability so each trust has its own software but with a set of standards for how they interact. Palantir are great sales people but they over-promise and under-deliver.”
Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne, a spokesperson for Medact, said the FOIs showed alternatives existed, a safe transition away from Palantir was possible and “the government has no excuse to extend the contract”.
“Instead of outsourcing key NHS functions to big tech companies, the government must back NHS innovation and the highly skilled NHS data professionals who work alongside doctors and nurses to deliver care in the public interest,” she said.
Palantir accused Medact of “slanted analysis” and of “misleading the public”.
“The FDP is, objectively, a successful programme,” a spokesperson said, adding that its purpose was to provide trusts with tools to draw on depending on their existing capabilities and needs. “It is one of just 20% of major government programmes with a green delivery rating, with ministers stating that it ‘is significantly exceeding its benefits forecast and has exceeded every target’.”
It said NHS trusts, including Chelsea and Westminster, Leicester, Northampton, Bath, North Cumbria, Croydon, Great Western, Dorset, Chesterfield, Ashford and St Peters and Norfolk have publicly praised the FDP.
Palantir also points to NHS data that shows trusts using the FDP have carried out 117,000 additional operations and a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients. NHS England has, however, had to add a caveat to its statistics, making clear it cannot draw conclusions about cause and effect as other variables have not been controlled for.
The government’s national data guardian for health and social care, Dr Nicola Byrne, this week urged ministers to give substantial weight to the “trust factor” when deciding on Palantir’s fate. More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the FDP. Byrne, a government-appointed watchdog, said there was evidence “a significant number of local organisations” were reluctant to adopt the FDP including due to concerns about Palantir and “a preference for other solutions”.
Sophie Don, the chief executive of Voror, a patient data company that bid unsuccessfully against Palantir, said: “Of course Palantir isn’t the only company that can do this. It doesn’t surprise me that it is making things harder … If NHS staff are choosing not to use it, it’s a clear sign it’s not creating value. There are many home-grown systems that would release much more value to the NHS than the [Palantir] platform.”
A spokesperson for NHS England said: “137 NHS trusts have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform – helping staff join-up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.”

A Greece for all seasons: my autumn roadtrip through the Peloponnese
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:00:23 UTC
15:00:23 KST

As I drove across the causeway which links the tiny fortress island of Monemvasia to the south-eastern coast of the Peloponnese, the Aegean sparkling on all sides, I recalled a line by Yiannis Ritsos, one of Greece’s greatest 20th-century poets. Ritsos lived in Monemvasia, in a house that is today a museum on a cobble-stretch by the tawny castle walls. A favourite passage goes: “The voyage is neither a leave-taking nor a home-coming – an ethereal bridge …”
The excuse for my trip to the Peloponnese’s deep south – Messinia, the Mani, and Laconia – fell between those two ideas. My mother has roots in the Peloponnese – a sort-of homecoming that I’ve long wanted to explore – and with the summer over and greedy for an adventure to myself, I set out by car, leaving Kalamata, the leafy port city and gateway to the area, on a coastal road circuit.
Autumn in the Peloponnese is another Greece. Forget the Cycladic white and blue; mountain valleys are carpeted in pine forests and wildflowers, a great stretch of green studded with rustic limestone houses. These villages, relieved by the end of a scorching summer, celebrate boisterous harvest festivals for wines, oranges and chestnuts in Laconia, figs in Messinia, and olives near Kalamata. This is the Greece the diaspora yearns for: the chorio – a word that snaps us back to our relatives and Greek rural life, villages where the air is healthy, eating depends on what is grown metres away, and tavernas are alive with locals rather than tourists. In the shoulder season, the weather is cool enough for long walks along the region’s spectacular trails but, at about 25C, is also still good for swimming.
The two-hour drive to Monemvasia began with the Taygetus pass, winding through villages and cliffside tunnels as golden eagles soared above the firs. On the far side of the Taygetus, the road opened to Mystras, an archaeological Byzantine site stacked up its hillside. I climbed to the Paleologian Palace and its chapels, then descended, hungry, to the village of Parori, where Taverna Ores was serving syglino, the local cured pork, and an okra stew. I practised my flimsy Greek with the waitress and her mother, who kept one eye on a television gameshow while stirring the stew pots.
After lunch I stopped at Sparta – site of the ancient city state and modern metropolis. Beneath the Taygetus, in the spectral hush of the olive groves, there is an acropolis, an agora and little else. Yet the air carries something over the ruins, and it’s a short but necessary stop. A statue of Leonidas, hero of Thermopylae, stands facing the new city with the ruins at his back.
This is still the Greece of the Spartans: locals remain fiercely attached to their ancient ancestry. Monemvasia has a thrilling connection: in AD600, a bishop is said to have led the Spartan population to the rock to fortify themselves against invading tribes. Set on to a slope inside the castle walls is a town of tight passages and medieval Orthodox churches. It is a vivid encounter with Byzantine Greek architecture, as well as traces of Venetian trade: the sweet, fortified wine malvasia was once a prized export. Even my guesthouse, Kelia (rooms from €70), began as a monks’ residence on the sea-facing Chryssafitissa Square.
Leaving Monemvasia, I took a detour south for the golden sand dune beaches in Elafonisos. Reaching this island requires taking a 10-minute ferry ride from Pounta. The turquoise waters of Simos beach are deserted in the off-season – a necessary respite before my hour drive north-west to spend a night in Gythio. This working harbour town has neoclassical pastel mansions and waterfront restaurants provisioned by local fishers. Here the Mani begins.
“Victory or death” reads the Maniot banner, above the Spartan motto “With the shield, or on the shield”. The region has a reputation for a conservative way of life that might seem unfashionable in modern Greece, but I find it seductive. The Mani’s beauty comes partly from its insularity. Driving an hour to Vathia, rugged mountains are crowned by labyrinthine stone tower villages that Maniot clans built to protect themselves during periods of vendetta or skirmishes with the Ottomans. Some are now ghost towns. Others have been converted into guesthouses.
But it was in Gerolimenas that a Greek friend suggested I stay for a few nights. The seaside village is an easy base for touring both western and eastern coasts. Along the latter, I hiked to mainland Greece’s southernmost point, Cape Tainaron lighthouse and went for an impromptu dip. The Mani’s water is so gin-clear the boats appear to hover above the surface.
The Akroyiali hotel (doubles from €80 B&B) opened in the 1970s, before most of the region’s roads. It is built on Gerolimenas’s shore, so I dozed to the pulse of waves and chatter from the hotel’s taverna below, where owner Mr Theodorakakis and his family entertained guests.
“The Mani is changing at its own rhythm,” Theodorakakis told me. “This is a special place. We can’t keep hiding from the world.” Most Greeks prefer to visit off-season, he said. “You can actually explore the region without burning. But be careful of the north-eastern wind. It cuts through!”
Leaving Gerolimenas, I drove 30 minutes up the western coastal route, entering the busy town of Areopoli, where I shopped for hand-harvested sea salt and wild oregano. Pretty Limeni and Kardamyli – the home of British writer Patrick Leigh Fermor (who popularised the region) – get the Mani day-trip overspill from Kalamata. Regardless, it’s quieter in autumn. Every hairpin bend opens on to sea views, flowers and limestone.
I was lunching over one such view of a grassy cape when the taverna owner mentioned a woman in the village who knew miralogia. These are wailing Maniot lamentations sung at funerals, which are heard rarely these days. After two days of asking around, I found Kaiti Braimi in a small chapel where she agreed to sing. “In a way, they’re less necessary,” the octogenarian told me. “No more vendettas.”
The haunting rhythms of the miralogia were in mind as I left the Mani to enter Messinia – cutting through Kalamata again, but this time heading west. Here, the villagers were celebrating. Clarinets hummed in taverna gardens at Sunday family parties and relatives joined hands in circles to dance the kalamatianos. Passersby stood and clapped before being dragged in.
On the hour drive from Kalamata to Pylos – which would be my base – the Maniot mountains flattened into lush forests. Wildflowers bloomed on the roadside. Yet in Messinia’s expansive green are traces of ancient civilisations, including the bronze age palace of Nestor, north of Pylos.
My route sidetracked to the Polylimnio waterfalls. You can sidetrack easily in Messinia; there are unspoiled beaches (like Tsapi on the south coast, where mountains tumble into the sea), as well as areas for canyoning, cycling and kayaking. After a small hike, I bathed in clear pools surrounded by pines, alone mostly, apart from an Athenian couple. “We’re here for my birthday,” the man said. “Messinia is the best place in Greece for outdoor activities.” They pointed me to a canyoning trail north of the Bay of Navarino – a tip for my next visit.
That evening in Pylos’s port, only an hour from where I began my voyage in Kalamata, I paused for an ouzo at a kafenion. A group of lads were watching Greece play Germany at football on the television. They wailed their own miralogia with every missed shot, but when the game ended in a win the cafes along the harbour roared.
I thought back on my drive through the Peloponnese’s deep south, a journey that revealed a rural Greece I’d grown up romanticising from family, and believed was slowly disappearing. But not here. In the mountains and shores of Messinia, the Mani and Laconia, I found a Greece for all seasons.
