The Israeli politicians seeking to replace Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:00:58 UTC
14:00:58 KST

The Israeli politicians seeking to replace Netanyahu
A look at Israel’s main opposition leaders, their parties and their largely shared positions on Gaza and other wars before October 27 election.
Do any of these Israeli candidates support a Palestinian state?
On September 26, five leading members of Israel’s self-styled Zionist opposition signed a non-aggression pact, seeking to oust incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in the October 27 election.
Gathered at the Tel Aviv home of opposition leader Yair Lapid were his co-runner, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, leader of Beyachad; former Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the new Yashar party; Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party; and Avigdor Liberman, head of the Yisrael Beiteinu party.
In the statement of principles published after the hours-long meeting, the leaders said, “Despite ideological differences among us, the formation of a Zionist, statesmanlike government dedicated to repair and reconstruction is our shared overarching goal.”
However, how long that pact might last — Liberman has already accused frontrunner Eisenkot of seeking a deal with Netanyahu — how meaningful a change in substance as well as style they offer, and which of them might lead a future coalition, remain open to question.
With the exception of Golan, all take a fundamentally right-wing approach to Israel’s challenges.
None is committed to establishing a Palestinian state, with only the Democrats acknowledging it as a distant, unspecified goal. None, Golan included, accepts that Israel’s war on Gaza amounts to genocide or that it has committed war crimes in killing more than 74,000 people there. Nor has any questioned Israeli military actions against Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Qatar and Iran, instead reserving criticism mostly for how those actions have allowed Israel to be perceived internationally.
“The dominant forces in the opposition such as Bennett, Liberman or Eisenkot represent right-wing politics,” said Ahron Bregman, an Israeli analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London. “They are not willing to touch the real, fundamental issue which is at the heart of everything: the Palestinian issue, and the Palestinian aspirations for independence.” He likened them to Netanyahu, but without the corruption allegations and support of far-right figures, such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. “Israel as a whole is a right-wing nation,” he added.
So, who are the main opposition figures and what do their parties stand for?
Gadi Eisenkot – Yashar
Credited with originating the Dahiyeh Doctrine in 2008, involving “disproportionate force” and large-scale destruction of civilian infrastructure against groups such as Hezbollah and Hamas, Eisenkot served as Israeli military chief from 2015 to 2019.
The 66-year-old entered politics in 2022 with former Defence Minister Benny Gantz’s National Unity alliance and later joined the war cabinet assembled by Netanyahu after the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on October 7, 2023. In December that year, his son Gal, 25, and two nephews were killed while participating in the genocide in Gaza, losses commentators say have helped forge a connection with an electorate that has come to see itself as scarred by war.
In June 2024, he quit the war cabinet alongside Gantz, accusing Netanyahu of lacking a strategy to end the war. A year later, Eisenkot founded the centrist Yashar (Straight/Honest), advocating for professional government, military service for all – including ultra-Orthodox Jews – and a state commission of inquiry into the failings before October 7.
While notoriously ambiguous on many of Israel’s foreign policy positions, he has been critical of the government’s reliance upon the United States in achieving its war aims, while not questioning those aims themselves. In June, he characterised Washington’s mediated negotiations with Tehran to end the war against Iran that Washington had embarked upon with Israel as “a deal taking shape far from here and far from Israeli interests” and, the same month, railed against US restrictions on Israel’s freedom of action in Lebanon.
Eisenkot has ruled out including the United Arab List, or Ra’am party, in a post-election coalition. In a September 26 Channel 12 interview, he said no Arab party would accept his conditions, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state.
Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid – Beyachad
Beyachad (Together) is the joint list announced in April 2026 by former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, who served for a combined 18 months in 2021-2022 between Netanyahu governments.
Bennett, a 54-year-old longtime supporter of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, leads the list, with Lapid, the 62-year-old founder of the centrist Yesh Atid party, in second place.
Lapid has called his partner “a right-wing politician, but an honest one”. Neither has prioritised resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict or supported a Palestinian state. Though their 2021 coalition included Ra’am, Bennett has acknowledged that this broke an electoral promise.
Lapid has been one of Israel’s most outspoken critics of how its genocide and multiple strikes upon its neighbours are perceived internationally, while rarely questioning the rationale behind those actions. Bennett, in contrast, is more outspoken in his hawkish views. A full-throated supporter of the country’s war on Iran, he also congratulated Israel’s military and security services for a September 2025 attack on Qatar’s capital, Doha, that targeted senior Hamas leaders as they met to consider a Gaza ceasefire proposal put forth by the US. A Qatari security official was killed in the attack, which drew condemnation from across the region and beyond.
They now seek a government composed solely of Zionist parties, also ruling out reliance on Arab parties.
Avigdor Lieberman – Yisrael Beiteinu
The most hawkish voice at Lapid’s table, Lieberman, 68, founded Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) in 1999 to represent right-leaning Russian-speaking immigrants.
Once Netanyahu’s protege, Lieberman has ruled out serving under him or joining a coalition that includes the ultra-Orthodox or relies on Arab parties, which he calls anti-Zionist. He has also rejected a minority government, reportedly making him a principal obstacle to Eisenkot becoming the bloc’s prime ministerial candidate.
In November 2023, Lieberman repeated his 2018 assertion, made then as defence minister, that there were “no innocents in Gaza”. In February, he visited the Karem Abu Salem crossing, known as Kerem Shalom to Israelis, and accused Netanyahu’s government of funding Hamas by allowing the minimal humanitarian aid that has been permitted into Gaza.
The Yisrael Beiteinu leader has been a consistent supporter of Israel’s genocide and subsequent military actions. In September 2025, he joined other Israeli politicians in criticising Netanyahu for the apology to Doha that he had been forced to make by the Trump administration for that month’s strike, saying the apology was instead owed to the Israeli public. Equally, he has argued against any restraint in its invasion of Lebanon, telling the Jerusalem Post in March: “If once again we go for a limited operation, some manoeuvre near the border, maybe talk about a security zone, it’s complete madness.”
“Lieberman does not belong in this bloc,” said Shaiel Ben-Ephraim, an Israeli analyst with Atlas Global Strategies, arguing that his main motivation was hatred of Netanyahu.
However, Ben-Ephraim said, Lieberman “maintains a loyal base and is a crucial force in Israeli politics”. His core constituency is the former Soviet electorate, but he has gained wider trust through his perceived independence.
Observers say he could potentially return to Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc.
Yair Golan – Democrats
The only leader at Lapid’s table from the Zionist left and the only one open to working with Palestinian parties, Golan heads the Democrats, a liberal party that was formed in 2024 through the merger of Labor and the social democratic, secular Meretz.
A retired major-general and former deputy chief of staff, Golan, 64, earned domestic plaudits for driving south during the 2023 Hamas-led attack and helping repel it.
Golan is alone among many in the anti-Netanyahu bloc in his criticism of the government’s war aims, arguing that military achievements are being squandered without a coherent diplomatic and political strategy
In May 2025, two years into the genocide in Gaza, Golan sparked controversy when he told a news conference that a “sane country does not kill babies as a hobby”, accusing ministers of celebrating the starvation of Palestinian children in the territory. He later walked back the comments after widespread criticism in Israel. In October, while praising the achievements of the previous year’s 12-day war against Iran, he told party members that the assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei at the beginning of the conflict was a “mistake”. “Not because he didn’t deserve to die,” he caveated, “only because it doesn’t serve the interests of the State of Israel.”
Despite his openness to working with Palestinian parties, in September, Golan backed the disqualification of Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Arab Balad party, over an article about October 7, drawing criticism from the Joint List – an alliance of the Arab-led Hadash, Ta’al and Balad parties – and commentators.
Roi Zur, a University of Essex specialist in Israeli politics, said that despite Golan and Lieberman’s ideological differences on security and conflict, there will be “no winning coalition without these two”. He added that concerns about a clash between them miss the point, noting that both oppose Netanyahu, favour secularisation and strongly oppose exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews.

Jackson Boxer’s vegan recipe for poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:00:25 UTC
14:00:25 KST

I have a great respect for the leek, which is possibly the most demanding vegetable in its need to be freshly cooked before consumption. A warm leek, fresh from the pot, is an ethereal, collapsing sigh of diaphanous veils, whereas cold it can all too easily become a slippery and almost slimy mess of hopelessness.
Poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnuts
All the various elements can be made ahead of time except the leeks, which should be just warm from their poaching, and the dressing, which should be made at the last minute. Vegetable bouillon may seem a bit of a faff to make just to poach some leeks (if you prefer, simply cook them in two litres of seasoned water with a dash of white wine instead), but a good, light vegetable broth is a useful thing to have around, and a batch will keep happily in the fridge for three or four days. To toast nuts successfully, cook them on a tray in an even layer in a 170C (150C fan)/335F/gas 3½ oven for 15-20 minutes, which will toast them evenly to the core without scorching.
Prep 25 min
  
Soak and chill Overnight
  
Cook 1 hr, plus cooling
  
Serves 4
For the hazelnut miso
 
250g hazelnuts
  
40g white miso paste
 
25ml olive oil
 
5g flaky sea salt (about 1 tsp)
For the vegetable bouillon (optional; see recipe introduction)
 
1 medium carrot, peeled and quartered
 
1 medium onion, peeled and quartered
 
1 medium shallot, peeled and left whole
 
2 garlic cloves, peeled
 
4 leek tops (from trimming the leeks below)
 
1 bay leaf
  
5 thyme sprigs
  
2 parsley sprigs
  
1 star anise 
  
150
 ml white wine
  
2 litres filtered water
  
40g flaky sea salt
For the pickled pears
 
2 conference pears
  
150ml white-wine vinegar
  
50g sugar
For the leeks
  
4 leeks
 , trimmed, roots removed and thoroughly cleaned, then cut in half across the middle
 
2 litres vegetable bouillon (see above and method)
 
Minced chives and chopped chervil, to finish (optional)
For the dressing
 
200g pear pickling liquor (see above and method)
 
100ml extra-virgin olive oil
  
5g flaky sea salt (about 1 tsp)
  
2g ground black pepper
  (about ½ tsp) 
  
50g minced shallot
  
10g minced garlic
  
100g toasted hazelnuts
 , chopped
The day before, put the nuts in a container or bowl, add a litre of water and leave overnight to soften. Next day, strain the nuts, reserving the soaking liquid.
Put all the bouillon ingredients in a large pot (again, you can do this a day before), bring to a low simmer and cook gently on a medium heat for 25 minutes. Take off the heat, leave to rest and cool for four hours, then strain.
Peel, quarter and core the pears, then cut each quarter in half lengthways and put in a container, for which you have a lid. Put the vinegar, sugar and 75ml water in a saucepan, bring to a simmer, then pour the pickling liquor over the pears, cover and chill for 12 hours.
Put the drained nuts, miso, olive oil and salt in a food processor, dribble in just enough of the soaking liquid to lubricate, then blitz to a smooth, rich puree the consistency of mayonnaise; add a drop more liquid to loosen, if need be.
Submerge the leeks in the bouillon, bring it to a low simmer and cook for 15 minutes, until the leeks show only gentle resistance to the tip of a sharp knife. Take off the heat and leave to cool to room temperature for about half an hour.
Meanwhile, make the dressing. In a stainless-steel bowl, whisk the pickling liquor and oil to a smooth and coherent emulsion, then stir in all the other dressing ingredients.
Lift the just-warm leeks out of the poaching liquid and cut lengthways into quarters. Spoon some hazelnut miso on each plate, then arrange the leeks on top. Dot pieces of pickled pear between them, spoon over the dressing and garnish with minced chives and, if you’re lucky enough to have some, chopped chervil.
- Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House, Vesper and Dove, all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London

- 1. ‘Indiscriminate and voracious’: the prosecution sets out its case Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty. Jury selection began on Monday but the prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC opened the case on Wednesday. She told the court that Brand, 51, was a ruthless, calculated and manipulative predator with an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact. His methods varied, she argued, and women were just a means to an end for him. “Sometimes he might tell women what they wanted to hear, be nice, be kind. Sometimes he might have appeared interested in their cause, sometimes he might even have made sexual advances within minutes of meeting them, identified someone young and impressionable where he was performing – but every time he had identified his target, he was intent on trying to fulfil his sexual desire,” Karmy-Jones said.
- 2. ‘I was like a zombie’: court hears first women’s accounts The court has so far heard from two of the six women who have made allegations against Brand. Both women have given evidence from behind a screen, and the trial judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, has told the jury that the measure was quite standard, saying: “Don’t hold it against anyone.” The earliest allegation Brand faces is from a woman who claims the TV personality raped her after a fringe cabaret show at the 1999 Labour party conference in Bournemouth. She broke down in tears in the witness box on Thursday as she told how Brand was “monster-like” when he pushed her on to a bed in a hotel room in an attack that left her feeling as if she couldn’t breathe. “I was like a zombie on the bed. All I could think was he’s inside me and the quicker the better,” she said. Brand is accused of indecently assaulting the second alleged victim, who told the court on Friday that he transformed into a “wild-eyed maniac” when he tried to drag her into a men’s toilets for a sexual encounter. The woman, who was working for MTV at the time, alleged she “wrenched” herself free, saying: “I emerged relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me.”
- 3. 'No power imbalance': Brand sets out his defence The court heard that in prepared statements in police interviews, Brand denied all the allegations. He said he had never engaged in nonconsensual sexual activity, and suggested some accounts may have been reinvented or imagined after a 2023 documentary about his alleged sexual misconduct. His defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, suggested to the first complainant that Brand was a “very young-looking boy” and there was “no power imbalance” during their alleged encounter in 1999. He suggested to the second complainant that Brand had “invited” her into the toilet for a consensual sexual encounter and that it had been a “short-lived, very, very minor incident”.
- 4. 'I pray for everybody': Brand puts faith in Christian image Brand has arrived at court with his wife, Laura, on three of the five days the case has been sitting. His security guard and members of his entourage have sat in the public gallery each day. Arriving at Southwark crown court on Friday in his signature dark suit, cross necklace and long scarf, the actor said: “Obviously it’s an extraordinary and stressful situation, but it is also an exploration of truth and justice and, as I’ve said before, I pray for everybody involved. “It’s in a way very, very sad but hopefully it can bring about some conclusions that are beneficial.” In court, Brand has sat upright with his hands in his lap, appearing to listen intently to the evidence. Journalists sitting in the press gallery, directly behind the glass dock, have caught glimpses of his reflection as he stares ahead. Occasionally, he has been spotted clutching prayer beads.
- 5. The court case as content Brand has arrived at court each morning to a large crowd of photographers and journalists from across the world. There has been widespread international coverage of the case, including in the US, where Brand now lives with his wife and children. Each day there have been at least 20 journalists crammed into court 3 where the trial is taking place, and about 30 more have been watching on a screen in another courtroom in the building. Some have accessed the case remotely via CVP link. There are at least five daily podcasts covering the trial, and several journalists from the same outlets have been angling to get into court.

The Letby case inquiry will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS – and patients will be less safe | Mark McDonald
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

I have been Lucy Letby’s barrister for the past two years. I have spent thousands of hours going through the evidence, speaking to experts and examining what happened to the babies who died or became seriously unwell on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital. I have worked with nearly 30 experts, including internationally recognised specialists in neonatology, pathology, insulin, statistics and other fields. It may be to some an inconvenient truth, but I am convinced that Letby is innocent, and her convictions represent one of the most serious miscarriages of justice in modern British legal history. That means she was failed by the police, the NHS, the criminal justice system and, importantly, a plethora of experts who simply got it wrong.
My work on the case has also raised wider concerns about the evidence and conclusions surrounding the deaths on the neonatal unit, and what the lessons being drawn from this case will mean for doctors and nurses in neonatal medicine.
Neonatal units are among the most demanding environments in the NHS. These are tiny, desperately ill babies. Their condition can change within minutes, and doctors and nurses make difficult decisions under enormous pressure, often with incomplete information.
Sometimes, despite the best care, babies die. That is an uncomfortable truth, but any serious discussion about neonatal safety has to acknowledge it. What worries me is that we risk creating a culture in which clinicians become frightened to work in these environments.
Imagine being a doctor working a night shift in a neonatal unit. A baby’s condition suddenly deteriorates and you have to make decisions quickly, but despite your efforts they die. Then, years later, the circumstances of those decisions are reconstructed with the benefit of hindsight. Every action is examined. Every decision is questioned. And the possibility of a criminal investigation hangs over the process. Who would still want to work in neonatal medicine?
This is not only a theoretical question. The NHS already faces enormous challenges in recruiting and retaining staff. We need people who do take on this challenging work to feel confident enough to make decisions. We need them to be able to say: “I don’t know”. We need them to admit mistakes, report near misses and challenge colleagues and managers. Above all, we need them to tell the truth.
For many years, the NHS has tried to develop what is often described as a learning or “no-blame” culture. The idea behind this was never that there should be no accountability. What it means is that when something goes wrong, the first questions should be: what happened? Why did it happen? And what can we learn?
A public inquiry set up after Letby’s convictions, chaired by Lady Justice Thirlwall, delivered its report in mid-September. The report placed great emphasis on monitoring and surveillance, and specifically stated a need to move away from the no-blame culture. These recommendations risk creating a surveillance society within the NHS, where clinicians fear that every adverse outcome may lead to scrutiny and blame. Patient safety depends on openness, trust and learning from mistakes, not a culture of suspicion in which clinical error, systemic failure and deliberate criminal conduct become dangerously blurred.
That would be a terrible unintended consequence. The safest NHS is not one in which staff are frightened of making mistakes and practise defensively. It is one in which staff feel safe enough to admit mistakes.
Thirlwall’s is not the first major inquiry into failures in maternity and neonatal care. Over the past two decades, there have been major investigations into trusts in Morecambe Bay, Shrewsbury and Telford, East Kent and Nottingham, among others. Again and again, inquiries have found problems with leadership, communication, escalation, teamwork and listening. Again and again, recommendations have been made and promises given that the NHS will learn. So perhaps we need to ask a more difficult question: why hasn’t it?
The answer cannot simply be that we need another set of rules, another layer of monitoring, or another system for identifying individual responsibility. We need to listen to the people who actually work in these units. This is where I am particularly critical of the government, of successive governments.
Who is asking what these changes will feel like to a nurse working a 12-hour shift in an understaffed neonatal intensive care unit? Who is asking what it will feel like to a doctor knowing that an unexpected clinical outcome could result in years of scrutiny? The government has a responsibility to protect patients. But it also has a responsibility to protect the workforce on whom patient safety depends. The two things are inseparable.
I think trade unions also have a responsibility here. They should defend patients, but they should also defend their members. This does not mean defending wrongdoing. It means defending fairness, and making sure that a doctor or nurse is judged in the circumstances in which they actually made a decision, rather than simply with the benefit of hindsight. It means recognising that an adverse clinical outcome is not evidence of criminal conduct.
There has been remarkably little public debate about the possibility that the response to Thirlwall’s inquiry could create fear among NHS workers. Furthermore, no Labour MP has spoken up, and that silence matters.
The Thirlwall recommendations risk creating an environment in which a disgruntled healthcare professional can point the finger at another, triggering investigations that can quickly become criminal investigations.
The doctors and nurses caring for vulnerable newborns deserve protection from unfair hindsight, disproportionate suspicion and a culture in which every adverse outcome becomes a potential question of individual blame. Because if the lesson we take from the Thirlwall inquiry is that we need more blame, more surveillance and more fear, then I worry that we will have learned the wrong lesson.
We will not have made the NHS safer. We will simply have made it harder for the NHS to care for the babies who need it most.
- Mark McDonald is a criminal defence and human rights barrister specialising in miscarriages of justice

Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

In February 2016, days after David Cameron announced the UK would hold a referendum on leaving the EU, he told workers in Slough not to imagine they could change their minds a few years down the line if they did not like how things panned out. Voting to stay in or leave was a once in a generation thing, he said. “This is a decision that lasts for life.”
Well times change, as the last prime minister but five could testify. A decade after Britain told Brussels where to go, Brexit is back on the political agenda. After years in which many politicians avoided any mention of the B-word, Andy Burnham broke the omertà in his party conference speech last month, saying he would look again at Britain’s relationship with Europe.
This week he went further, insisting the current arrangement must change: “Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain.” Among a range of options on the table, he has been clear, is the possibility of going “all the way” and rejoining the EU.
There are pressing economic reasons Burnham has been talking up closer alignment, as the EU works out its position on the UK’s access to its protectionist “Made in Europe” legislation, which the prime minister has said could hurt British manufacturing.
But after years of bitter division and political dysfunction in the fallout from the vote, are the British public really ready to talk about Brexit again – and even to contemplate reversing it?
Polling evidence may suggest so. A “megapoll” of more than 11,000 people published this month found that half of Britons now support rejoining the EU, with only 28% opposed, and the remainder undecided. Almost 60% think it was wrong to leave.
Sliced some ways, the numbers are even more striking: a More in Common survey in June to mark a decade since the vote found that if another referendum was held today across Britain’s 632 constituencies, just 11 would vote to leave (even in Clacton, Nigel Farage’s constituency, 52% supported rejoining).
What changed? To the polling expert Rob Ford, a professor of political science at the University of Manchester, there are several key reasons, from demographic change to buyers’ remorse. Brexiters are fewer in number – “a lot of leave voters have died, bluntly” – and both young people entering the electorate and those who did not vote in 2016 skew heavily in favour of Europe. And with the project widely considered a disappointment at best, a proportion of those who opted to leave have switched positions.
“Although each is a relatively slow moving and relatively small incremental force, add them together over a decade and it adds up to quite a lot of change,” said Ford.
Given the divisiveness and turbulence of the past decade – and the fact many Labour MPs represent constituencies that voted to leave – it is little wonder that some senior Labour figures have expressed nervousness about reopening the debate. “[Burnham] definitely needs to proceed with caution because we don’t want to restoke division,” one cabinet minister told the Guardian.
But the view from formerly Brexit-supporting areas is not necessarily what it was. “Hull East voted 74% leave in the referendum, however I believe the mood has changed,” said Karl Turner, the Labour MP for the constituency since 2010 (he now sits as an independent after having the whip withdrawn).
“Constituents tell me they expected Brexit to improve their lives; instead many face higher costs and fewer opportunities.” As a result, he said, they were “increasingly ready to consider the practical benefits of rejoining the EU”.
Ford added: “Andy Burnham looks at the data and says, well, I’ve got an electoral coalition that’s 80% remain and becoming more so. The parties to my left that I need to squeeze have a [position] that is even more remain than that.
“And the overall balance of opinion in the country is now nudging up towards 60% in favour of remain, sometimes even higher in terms of how many think Brexit is a mistake. Why wouldn’t I move in a pro-remain direction? It’s the direction of travel of the country. The art of leadership is getting out ahead of the trends that are happening and using them to your advantage.”
Sara Hobolt, a professor in the department of government at London School of Economics, agrees that the polling data today suggests Brexit could be an effective general election rallying cry for Labour. “This is an issue that a lot of people were quite upset with Keir Starmer and his government for not talking about it. It is something that definitely mobilises the base.”
While Labour supporters and those the party wants to win back from other progressive parties overwhelmingly support remain, she points out, the Conservative party is now much more divided on the issue, having lost many of its hardline Brexiters to Reform. “That means that [by putting Brexit back on the agenda] you can potentially do more damage to the right than the left.
“But I think probably the main thing for Andy Burnham is that this has been seen in his electoral base as something [that has been overlooked]. ‘You talk about growth? Why are you not talking about Brexit?’ Because overwhelmingly remainers think that a lot of the economic problems we’ve faced over the last decade are due to Brexit.”
But if uniting the left before a Westminster election is one thing, winning a future Brexit referendum is a whole other challenge, as the experience of 2016 showed. “There clearly is support for rejoining the EU,” says the More in Commondirector, Luke Tryl, “the question is, how resilient would that be in the face of a referendum campaign?”
One factor is, inevitably, Brexit weariness, he says. “The British public are tired. They’ve lurched from crisis to crisis, from row to row, and I think, for some, just the idea of reopening the wounds [is unwelcome]. I think in a campaign rejoin, if it got to that, would start ahead, but I don’t think the headline polling we are seeing now would remain where it is once it was subject to a full back and forth.”
Ford agrees – noting that the EU will be resistant to serious discussions so long as there is the prospect of a wholesale reversal under a future Reform government. The risk of bringing up Brexit is not just because the subject is neuralgic to many, he says. “One of the problems during the Brexit years was it was just simply impossible to get a conversation going about all the other pressing issues that mattered.
“There is a risk for Burnham, if this thing starts to take life of its own yet again, that the big difficult conversations he wants to have about some of the longstanding structural problems in British society will be harder to have because for a lot of people in the political conversation, Brexit is like catnip – they’ll run straight to it. And then you’re not able to get them to pay attention to the issues you want them to pay attention to.”

Data centres are the new front line and Europe’s AI factories should slow down, says UN adviser
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:00:22 UTC
14:00:22 KST

Data centres have become prime military targets and the drone strikes in Ukraine should force Europe to rethink where it builds its AI infrastructure, one expert says.
Data centres in Ukraine, Russia and the Middle East have become crucial targets in conflict that can temporarily bring down a country’s economy and public facilities such as banks and hospitals.
Russia has struck data centres in Kyiv and Ukrainian drones hit back at multiple data centres in Russia in recent weeks, in attacks Kyiv has described as aimed at places that provide revenue streams for Moscow’s war machine.
The military targeting of data centres should prompt Europe to rethink where it builds its AI infrastructure, said Mehdi Paryavi, an adviser to the United Nations and founder of the International Data Center Authority (IDCA) think tank.
“When you hit enough important targets, you can take down the entire economy,” he told Euronews Next.
As societies digitise, taking down a data centre can mean “paralysing the functions of military, healthcare and finance”.
Data centres are the physical facilities where a company can house its servers and data. They are also crucial to artificial intelligence as they supply the massive amounts of energy it needs.
They become especially important in warfare as Ukraine uses AI for drone targeting as well as other military uses.
The new target on data centres should make countries consider more where they build them, Paryavi said, but he argued the industry’s long-standing advice to choose sites carefully and keep their locations quiet may no longer be enough.
“Maybe you need iron domes, maybe you need to build them underground, or you need to build bunkers,” he said without getting to specifics due to national security reasons.
But “the days that you would just build data centres in random locations are over,” he said.
He also acknowledged that no country has a solid answer to how to do that without slowing the race to build AI capacity.
A European hub
Asked whether the strikes will make European governments rethink their plans for AI gigafactories, a type of data centre, Paryavi said: “100%”.
When asked about Europe’s plans for data centres, a spokesperson from the European Commission told Euronews Next that it launched a tender to establish up to seven AI gigafactories across Europe.
“The call is still open. Once closed, the proposals will be evaluated and then the award decisions will be taken,” it added. The call will close on November 12.
However, there was no specific comment about whether the targeting of data centres in warfare would change any data centre plans.
The economic cost to data centre damage can also be astronomical and “almost irreversible” to replace for many countries, including Europe, said Paryavi.
Data centres can cost up to $25 billion each and take up to three years to build.
“Europe cannot afford to finance hundreds of billions of dollars of assets and then somebody takes them out,” Paryavi said. “I project that the whole thing [the building of data centres] has to slow down.”
He urged European states to act as a bloc, saying no single country could do it alone, as combined with the security risks are global energy shortfalls as well as a lack of trained workers.
Rather than having scattered data centres, he advised building them in concentrated areas so you could build an iron dome to protect them.
“Building data centres and digital hubs is the only way a nation or a hub or data centre companies can secure themselves,” he said.

The Home Office has denied a great-grandfather from Lancashire the chance of meeting his five-month-old British great-grandson, who lives abroad.
William Cross was born in Thailand on 30 April to parents Matthew Cross, 31, who is from Burnley in Lancashire, and Khin Thant Zin, known as Jue Jue, also 31, a refugee who fled persecution in Myanmar to Thailand.
The family live on the island of Koh Tao, famous for its diving schools and a centre for turtle conservation. It is a popular tourism spot and Cross, a mechanical engineer, opened a steakhouse restaurant there 15 months ago. He met Zin on the island and the couple are now engaged. She works in the restaurant managing social media and human resources.
Cross’s parents have visited the family in Thailand and have met their grandson. But William’s great-grandfather George Kerr, 74, who lives in Clayton-le-Moors in Lancashire, has multiple health problems and so is unable to fly out to Thailand to meet the baby. Instead, a large family gathering was planned in Burnley for Christmas.
Cross said: “My grandfather suffers from ill health and sadly he is unable to travel. He and I have been extremely close all my life and I’m desperate for him to meet his grandchild.”
The family have just signed a lease on a new home and have bought some land on the island for later development.
They assumed that organising a short trip to the UK for a family Christmas would be straightforward. But the Home Office refused Zin’s visitor visa application, which means the family will be unable to travel.
Officials said they were not satisfied she was a “genuine visitor”, and that there was no evidence Zin would return to Thailand because she had not shown evidence of significant family ties there, and she was unable to show sufficient evidence of her income.
“Jue Jue has never had a bank account,” Cross said. “Her brother and sister both live on Koh Tao and her mum is planning to move here when her younger sister has finished school in Myanmar.”
The visitor visa application process is expensive and cumbersome. “They required documentation from my family to be financial guarantors while we’re in the UK. Passport photos of my grandfather, my mum and dad and me, a typed letter from each of us confirming our commitment to sponsorship, a formal letter of invitation from my parents saying they would be comfortable with my partner being in my home,” Cross said.
“We had to travel to Phuket, a journey of two nights and three days from Koh Tao on a ferry and buses, which cost us £400, to complete biometric screening required for the visitor visa application.”
There is no right of appeal against this visa refusal so the couple are preparing a new application, although the Home Office refusal letter warns that future applications are likely to be refused “unless the circumstances of your application change”.
They also need to buy and provide evidence of return flight tickets even though they don’t know whether the new visa application will be granted. They have to make the long journey from the island on ferry and buses a second time to repeat the biometrics.
“By the time we send our next application, the whole thing will have cost us £3,000 with no guarantee of it being accepted,” Cross said.
The family are still hoping that baby William will be able to meet his great-grandfather at Christmas. Temperatures on the island rarely fall below 25C, so back in Burnley his relatives have bought warm baby clothes in the hope he will get a chance to wear them.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “We do not routinely comment on individual cases. All visa applications are carefully considered on their individual merits, in line with the immigration rules and based on the information and evidence provided by the applicant.”

As King Charles heads to the Caribbean, he should know that Winston Churchill admitted to imperial plunder 90 years ago | Kenneth Mohammed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:00:21 UTC
14:00:21 KST

For us in the Caribbean, there is something surreal about Britain’s renewed nostalgia over empire. As Britain’s monarch prepares to visit the Caribbean, and at a time when we in the former colonies are demanding to have a serious reckoning with slavery and reparations, UK politicians are invoking a dumbed-down distortion of history.
Rewriting the facts: the Reform MP Robert Jenrick has argued that colonies owed Britain a “debt of gratitude” for the institutions empire bequeathed them. Jacob Rees-Mogg, a former minister in a Conservative government, has described British colonialism as “one of the greatest civilising, prosperity-creating forces the world has ever seen”. The opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, has disputed colonialism’s contribution to Britain’s prosperity. Then there is Suella Braverman. The Reform MP suggested in July that rather than Britain paying reparations, former colonies should repay Britain for the investment and infrastructure provided under empire. This prompted Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, to call that proposition “asinine”. At best it is historical amnesia. At its worse it is an insidious misrepresentation of facts.
The question from a global development perspective is: who developed whom? We can ask Eric Williams, Walter Rodney, George Padmore or generations of African, Caribbean and Indian scholars. But there is one inconvenient witness that stands as a testimony to the truth. Winston Churchill.
On 20 July 1937, Churchill addressed the West India committee dinner at London’s Dorchester Hotel. Peter Hulme, emeritus professor of literature at the University of Essex, painstakingly reconstructed the provenance of that speech.
In it, Churchill reflected on how Britain became a global economic power. His words stark when placed alongside today’s politically sanitised recounts of empire. Britain’s possession of the West Indies and India, Churchill explained, provided “the strength, the support, but especially the capital, the wealth” that allowed Britain to survive its wars, dominate international commerce and establish its global commercial and financial leadership. Churchill was acknowledging that colonial wealth had financed the development of Britain.
Churchill’s surviving notes contained an even more revealing phrase: Britain’s Caribbean possessions had provided “that unexpected margin of capital”, an advantage Hulme describes as arising from two centuries of Caribbean slavery.
The conventional imperial story begins with what Britain left behind: railways, ports, courts, schools, parliamentary institutions, the English language and Christianity. It rarely begins with what Britain and Europe took away, or rather extracted, through exploitation and genocide. Railways and ports were integral to transporting colonial commodities to overseas markets. Colonialism was an exploitative and violent system designed solely for the benefit of the coloniser.
The Caribbean provides the clearest illustration. For generations, extraordinary wealth was produced through sugar by enslaved Africans and their descendants. Yet when slavery was abolished, Britain compensated not the enslaved but the enslavers.
Hulme’s reconstruction of Churchill’s dinner provides an almost grotesquely appropriate snapshot of that political economy. Among those present was Lord Hailsham, whose family fortune was connected to Caribbean sugar and enslavement; his ancestor Charles McGarel received £129,464 in compensation following abolition for 2,489 enslaved people. About £101m in today’s money, by Hulme’s calculation. The Register of British Slave Traders presents data on the 13,000 investors in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. It reveals the impact on Britain’s development during its formative era. So, while the slave trade built generational wealth in Europe, it kidnapped and displaced about 13 million Africans, stealing and destroying their generational wealth.
While Churchill celebrated imperial achievement at the Dorchester, Caribbean workers were rebelling against their economic conditions. The 1930s saw strikes and disturbances across the British Caribbean. Movements demanding political representation and self-government were gathering strength. These must seem strange expressions of gratitude to the rehabilitators of colonialism. They ask what Britain built rather than what Britain extracted. They count railways but not resources. They celebrate institutions while ignoring who those institutions were originally designed to govern and whose interests they protected. That is the part of the “gratitude” argument that is so troubling. It asks us to judge colonialism through the eyes of the coloniser.
Most importantly, they treat development as something Britain bestowed upon the rest of humanity rather than a global historical process in which the labour, resources and markets of colonised peoples contributed heavily to Britain’s transformation. That is why the question of who developed who is consequential.
Which brings us to King Charles. From 27 October to 4 November, he will visit the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda, culminating in the Commonwealth heads of government meeting. Buckingham Palace describes the visit in terms of community and a shared future. But is this royal diplomacy an attempt to contain or dissuade Caribbean demands for reparatory justice and constitutional independence?
Britain faces growing demands to confront its colonial responsibilities. Jamaica is pursuing a legal route now. However, in 2014, several Caribbean countries attempted to sue the British government for reparations. Britain then used jurisdiction issues arising from the Commonwealth to block the claim. Caribbean and some African governments continue to press for dialogue yet several, seemingly suffering from Stockholm syndrome, persist in retaining the British monarch as head of state: Antigua and Barbuda, Bahamas, Belize, Grenada, Jamaica, St Kitts and Nevis, St Lucia, and St Vincent and the Grenadines.
Buckingham Palace has already confirmed that Charles will not formally apologise for Britain’s involvement in slavery. Apparently, apologies and reparations are matters for government, which opposes paying reparations. Charles has expressed personal sorrow over slavery and described it as an atrocity. But sorrow without accountability is a meaningless attempt at appeasing the “natives”.
The Commonwealth presents itself as an association of equal, independent nations, committed to democracy, development and cooperation. Its supporters point to diplomatic access, technical assistance, educational opportunities, election observation and collective influence on the climate crisis, debt and development. But membership must be judged by outcomes, not colonial sentiment.
If Commonwealth countries cannot secure meaningful engagement from Britain on one of their most consequential historical grievances, how equal is the relationship in practice? What influence do smaller members genuinely exercise over the priorities of the organisation’s wealthiest and most powerful states? And does membership provide sufficient economic and diplomatic benefits to justify its continued symbolic association with an empire whose historical injustices remain unresolved?
These questions are particularly relevant to Caribbean states confronting climate vulnerability, high debt burdens and persistent structural economic disadvantage. The Commonwealth cannot remain an instrument of British soft power, where royal receptions and appeals to shared history substitute for substantive economic justice. Therefore, proposals on reparations warrant serious negotiation, even where governments disagree about legal liability and historical responsibility.
As King Charles arrives in the Caribbean, there will be welcoming ceremonies and speeches about friendship and solidarity. But these crucial questions remain unanswered.
Churchill concluded, on that now-forgotten evening in London: “We could never forget the patriotism and loyalty of the West Indies in those historic times to the mother country.”
The Caribbean should welcome genuine partnership. It need not accept neocolonialism and historical amnesia as its price.

Trip designers, wellness and privacy: What's trending in luxury travel for 2027?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:00:05 UTC
14:00:05 KST

Next year, the luxury travel sector is set to be less about grand displays of opulence, and more about being intentional. From slower itineraries to privacy and dining experiences, here’s what the discerning traveller should know.
What will luxury travel look like when more no longer necessarily means more? In 2027, travellers could place a greater emphasis on what money can’t buy, like quiet surroundings and experiences that are truly worth the journey.
From swapping airport rushes for a private lounge away from the terminal to slower rail holidays, wellness escapes and allocating when to spend, luxury is becoming less about excess and more about being intentional.
“Luxury today is completely different than what it was,” Marie-France Perrel, Head of Business Development, Hotels at Michelin Guide, said during the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 in Brussels.
“It’s no longer the sort of standards of opulence that we had in mind,” she added, as travellers’ focus has shifted to properties that “offer a sense of place”.
If luxury travel is on your agenda for 2027, here’s some of the trends that might just shape your experience.
Where to go?
Next year, Europe is set to dominate the luxury travel map. Virtuoso’s 2027 Luxe Report, which surveyed more than 3,100 travel advisors across more than 50 countries, cited that seven of the top 10 most popular global destinations will be on the continent.
Following Japan in first place, Italy, France, Greece and Spain make up the top five, while Croatia, South Africa, Portugal, the UK and the US are in the top 10.
Meanwhile, luxury travel company Abercrombie & Kent (A&K) recommends holidaymakers add Chile’s Easter Island to their 2027 bucket list to discover its “open air museum”. Sights include the 1,000 moai statues, and for set-jetters, many of the filming locations for Martin McDonagh's "Wild Horse Nine" are on the island, too.
A&K also picks out “iconic” destinations such as China, which is “firmly back on the radar”, and Egypt, thanks to a “renewed interest” that shows little sign of slowing.
Booking a holiday? Speak to a 'trip designer'
AI might be able to generate an itinerary in seconds, but the travel agent is making a comeback and has become “chic again”, according to Elle magazine.
Rebranded as a “travel advisor” or “trip designer”, they are found “across Instagram, posting a never-ending stream of curated travel content, often with a caption insinuating that all of this could be yours”.
The magazine also highlighted that today’s luxury travel advisors cover fixing, negotiating and at times, perform “miracles”.
Rather than relying on algorithms, the wealthy value the human touch of knowing when to go, which room to request, and which restaurants live up to the hype – something that automation simply can't replicate.
Is privacy the ultimate luxury?
In an era of hyper-connectivity, private travel experiences are a sought-after element among affluent holidaymakers.
Virtuoso’s Luxe Report also highlighted that in a time when social media is turning destinations into overcrowded spots overnight, privacy is all about “avoiding the queues and camera clicks, while being able to move through the world with minimal friction”.
Writing on A Luxury Travel Blog, Sherif Khalil describes privacy as “the new luxury” and that wealthy travellers now want it “more than prestige”.
Khalil added: “Nowadays privacy might just mean having a museum to yourself before the doors officially open. Sailing out quietly instead of queueing on a dock. Taking your time over breakfast instead of clock-watching for whatever’s next on the schedule. Honestly, it might be the rarest thing money can buy.”
Another natural fit here would be checking into a holiday villa rather than a hotel for added privacy. Unlike at a hotel, guests won’t have to share amenities or communal areas, nor would they have to worry about an 11am cut off to have breakfast, or any other meal, for that matter.
An airport lounge… but not inside the airport
Privacy also matters for airline passengers who would rather skip the airport rush.
Announced recently, DiamondAir has launched a private, remote check-in area minutes away from London Heathrow. It offers travellers “an intimate space” replete with á la carte dining and a wellness area – all at the backdrop of runway views.
“The Lounge” is designed around both sides of the flight. For departures, guests arrive to relax and are able to check-in with their luggage being pre-collected and transported through the airline's baggage system. While those arriving at Heathrow can also go to the lounge to relax then transfer for the concierge service at the airport.
Elevated in-flight dining
No longer confined to just the restaurant floor, airlines have made food an integral part of the journey, with carriers “elevating” their menus at 30,000 feet.
Singapore Airlines is set to unveil its latest in-flight dining experience across its Suites, First and Business Class cabin classes this November.
The new menu, developed by the carrier's in-house and guest chefs, features more than 100 new and revamped appetisers, main courses and dessert dishes. The meals will be served on new serviceware, incorporating the brand's signature batik motif.
Slow luxury
Needless to say, 2026 has been an anxiety-inducing year – least of all for the travel industry. So, with that in mind, nervous system-regulating getaways may just be the ticket in 2027.
Rather than chasing the fast lane and convenience, travellers will seek slow luxury travel experiences that connect deeply with a destination's culture and people, without sacrificing exceptional hospitality.
This approach prioritises quality, depth and privacy over packed itineraries and visible displays of opulence.
In search of balance, travellers can opt for luxury rail instead of boarding a plane.
The Northern Belle, a luxury restored train that has preserved the glamour of the 1930s, will offer a new programme of day trips paired with caviar blinis and afternoon tea in 2027, all at the backdrop of the UK’s sweeping views.
Meanwhile, Italy can be explored onboard La Dolce Vita Orient Express, including a two-night trip along the "truffle route" from Rome to Alba and back.
River cruises
Unlike ocean cruise ships, river cruise vessels can navigate directly through inland cities and towns, combining scenic journeys with stops along major cities or hidden gem towns – all with the luxury fittings of a boutique hotel floating on water. And they often accommodate just a fraction of their ocean-going counterparts.
A new river ship that’s set to enter the global fleet is the Viking Sekhmet. Launching in November, it is specifically built to cruise the Nile and hosts as few as 82 guests. Highlights in 2027 include the signature Pharaohs & Pyramids journey and a new Total Eclipse on the Nile itinerary spanning 12 days.
In Europe, a 27-day Scenic Cruises’ river and land journey set for 2027 will include a 13-day tour of Switzerland, with dining woven into the experience. The itinerary includes risotto making, 29 breakfasts, 15 lunches and 19 dinners, alongside a scenic stay in Interlaken.
Why hotels are ‘rethinking wellness’
Hotels are “rethinking wellbeing”, according to the Lemongrass Annual Travel Trend Report 2027.
And the successful luxury properties “won’t be the ones adding more treatment options, diagnostics, or feel-good interventions”, Lemongrass said. “Instead, they’ll remove sources of stress, focus on restorative lighting and acoustics, reduce sensory overload, and integrate nature and biophilic elements throughout the guest experience. They will still be beautiful, but they won’t simply impress guests; they will also help them regulate and restore their whole selves.”
Highlighted by the report, Estonia’s Eha Retreat places an emphasis on wellness, with each stay beginning with a consultation to create a personalised wellbeing programme and in-room elements including guided sleep meditations.
Less is more (sometimes)
All this doesn’t have to mean splurging at every stage of the journey. In what Lemongrass called the "great trade-off" within luxury travel, more tourists are becoming intentional and deliberate about their spending.
This could look like pairing pricier purchases with inexpensive alternatives. For example, by choosing an economy or premium economy ticket instead of business or first, there’s more that can be put towards an indulgent stay.
The extra funds could also go towards tailor-made experiences. Signature Travel Network‘s trend watch report found that there is now a growing demand for holidays that are “genuinely personal and difficult to replicate”. Here, itineraries could include private cultural encounters and travelling to witness once-in-a-lifetime natural phenomena.

Vytautas the Great invited Muslims to Lithuania ‘not because he was a leftist’ – interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Paulius Abdulhakimas Bergaudas from Klaipėda converted to Islam on his own initiative while finishing school and later completed a PhD in the subject at Cambridge. In an interview with LRT.lt, he talks about the myths surrounding Muslims in Lithuania and what the country’s politicians should avoid doing.
What do you think we fail to understand about Islam in Lithuania?
Knowledge of Islam is very limited, not only in Lithuania but throughout Europe. For example, people do not know what sharia is. Many say it should be banned, but one of its teachings says you should smile at your neighbours, friends and other people.
A good example is a 2020 study by the Lithuanian Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson on which neighbours people would not want to live alongside. According to the study, 41% of Lithuanians would not want to live next door to a Muslim, but only 11% would not want to live next door to a Turk. Yet almost all Turks are Muslims.
This means that, statistically, 30% of people in Lithuania do not even know what a Muslim is. They probably imagine an Arab wearing a turban, even though Arabs make up a minority of Muslims worldwide. The vast majority of the world's Muslim population lives in south-east Asia, particularly Malaysia and Indonesia.
We often hear claims that there is a clash of civilisations, that Christian identity is under threat and that Islam will sweep away our culture.
There are two possible answers. First, the arrival of Muslims in Europe is good for Christianity because it reminds Europeans that they are Christians. People often forget this and remember it only when their neighbour becomes Muslim, even though they themselves may never have set foot in a church.
From an academic perspective, I believe the Clash of Civilisations theory was developed not to explain reality, but to justify US hegemony and control in the Middle East.
When violence in the Middle East is met with violence in response, it is described as a clash of civilisations, even though that violence would not have occurred had the US not struck first. This rhetoric is now being applied to domestic politics to stir up fear. Vytautas Sinica is among those trying to use it.
Muslims are a minority in Europe and the West. Comment sections often feature remarks such as: “If you like Muslim countries so much, go and live there.” But that is precisely where most Muslim migrants go – to Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.
While Muslims may account for around 10% of the population in Europe, immigrants make up about 80% of Qatar's population, most of them from South Asia, including Pakistan and India.
Lithuania’s Conservatives (TS-LKD), for example, claim their numbers are growing and that things will soon get worse.
The number of immigrants will continue to grow as long as the relevant immigration policies remain in place, but Muslims still account for a minority of all arrivals. We need to decide where to draw the line and what proportion of immigrants people are willing to accept.
In reality, all the percentages being discussed are plucked out of thin air. Successful integration and peaceful coexistence depend directly on trust in state institutions, including the police, the armed forces and healthcare services.
If immigrants do not trust these institutions, they are more likely to isolate themselves from society and take no part in its activities. When problems arise, they will be less likely to seek help and more likely to try to resolve matters on their own terms.
That is precisely how ghettos emerge. If politicians do not undermine trust through their rhetoric, integration will be successful.
In the UK, protests and riots broke out this summer following a knife attack carried out by a migrant. What is the mood there?
A horrific crime took place in Belfast when someone was attacked with a knife in a public place. But it was neither the only nor the first horrific crime. Ironically, and tragically, the same victim had been set on fire by another local man, probably a Christian, 20 years earlier. There were no protests then.
In Belfast alone, local men – husbands, brothers and sons – have killed 30 women over the past six years, but nobody organised protests over that.
If we genuinely care about crime, we should be equally concerned about all offences, not just those committed by immigrants. We could deport every immigrant, and women would still suffer violence. The hypocrisy becomes clear: people are not really concerned about crime; it is an excuse to express racism under the guise of civic concern.
Fear makes it harder to integrate migrants and increases the likelihood that they will commit crimes. The demographic group most likely to commit crime is young men from disadvantaged backgrounds.
If integration goes badly, newly arrived migrants will struggle to escape poverty. They will remain in disadvantaged environments and become more likely to commit crimes. Then people will say: “Look, immigrants commit more crimes”, even though this will be explained purely by demographics and economics, rather than by the fact that they are immigrants.
In the UK, Lithuanians account for 2% of the foreign population but 4% of the prison population. Does that mean Lithuanians are twice as likely to commit crimes?
What does the Muslim community in Lithuania look like?
Most people who have arrived over the past five to 10 years are here temporarily. The number planning to stay long-term is growing, but much more slowly. If immigration to Lithuania suddenly stopped, most would leave within a few years. It would be similar to Lithuanians who emigrated when EU borders opened.
One important detail is that the vast majority are men who have come to earn money to support their families. That is another reason why it would be strange to assume they are more likely to commit crimes. Although most immigrants from Muslim-majority countries are men, they still [proportionately] commit far fewer crimes than Lithuanian citizens.
Lithuania ranks ahead of Latvia and Poland in terms of tolerance and acceptance of other people. As a result, some immigrants decide to stay once they have learned the language.
What constitutes a good integration policy?
Trust in state institutions goes beyond integration policy. Do communities – not just migrants – trust the police, the armed forces and healthcare services?
During the pandemic, for example, many people refused to be vaccinated. The same applies to migrants: if they do not trust institutions, they will become isolated and will not take part in community activities. If they become victims of crime, they will not turn to the authorities but will try to resolve matters in their own way.
When there is no trust, people take matters into their own hands, and ghettos emerge. [...] If someone knows that they can go to the police if they are attacked because of their skin colour, they will integrate.
If politicians undermine trust through their rhetoric, they pave the way for a lack of integration. Where there is trust, there is integration.
How does the community react to Lithuanian politicians' anti-migrant statements?
Of course, it is unpleasant, and there is a lot of misinformation. Lithuania is still not like some other countries where migrants can be said to distrust the state.
There are only a handful of politicians who use populism to attract voters. If you ask people what they think of the mayor of Vilnius, you will not get the most flattering answers.
Is it because he supports introducing stricter language requirements, or because he associates migration with ghettos?
Learning the language is very welcome and a good thing. Unless there is an absolute necessity to learn such a difficult language, people will not learn it [...]. Moreover, this could deter some immigrants, so immigration would automatically decrease. It is already declining.
Incidentally, immigration is also falling elsewhere in Europe, yet people continue to talk about the need to reduce it. This shows that the issue of migrants is merely a smokescreen.
The emergence of ghettos is nothing more than fearmongering. Many people, not just Muslims but also people of other skin colours, face difficulties when trying to rent a flat: “You're from India? Next.”
In our community, we often encounter people who come to us and say: “Help me find a flat, because nobody will rent to me because of stereotypes.” This is precisely what can lead to ghettos. If we cannot integrate into society, who will support us? Other members of the community. They will all try to live together, in isolation. That is how a ghetto emerges.
On the other hand, is it necessarily a bad thing if a place is simply home to members of one demographic group? If we look at how the Tatars lived in Lithuania for centuries, the village of Keturiasdešimt Totorių could also be described as a ghetto.
We can look at the UK, for example. Migrants speak English and participate in community life. The prime minister was a Hindu, and the mayor of London is a Muslim. He recently performed the Hajj pilgrimage and, on returning, posted his support for an LGBT Pride event on social media and defended the hospitality industry against restrictions.
These things might be seen as unbecoming of a Muslim. If we want an example of the highest level of integration, we have one here. But are there still people who oppose Muslim migrants? Yes. This shows that there will always be something people claim is missing.
Are we simply racist?
There are genuine problems that need to be addressed. For example, a large proportion of Muslims live below the poverty line. Refugees, too, are often young men fleeing war zones. This means they may have psychological problems.
We can imagine that young men in such circumstances, as refugees, might be more likely to commit crimes. We need to talk about this and ensure that the people we accept do not belong to demographic groups that are more prone to crime. But they make up such a small proportion of all immigrants, and the benefits migrants bring are far greater.
Even if we got rid of all immigrants, those who dislike having a Muslim neighbour would continue to feel that way. London has a Muslim mayor who supports the LGBT community and the alcohol industry, yet people still say: “The mayor of London is a Muslim – sharia is coming.”
Have you considered the reasons behind this? Could historical trauma play a part?
Perhaps it is human nature to look for a scapegoat. In the past, Europe's Jewish communities were blamed for supposedly causing all its problems. Today, it is Muslim migrants who, in reality, make up only a small proportion of the population.
You mentioned Lithuania's Tatars earlier. How did Lithuania, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Lithuanian people receive Muslims in the past?
The Grand Duchy of Lithuania was a very diverse land, where rulers were concerned not with religion or ethnicity but with realpolitik: if you were useful, they liked you. Vytautas the Great did not invite the Tatars because he was a leftist who wanted to destroy national identity, but because he needed reliable, loyal soldiers. That was how he viewed Muslims.
[...] Lithuania is unique and, I would say, an example for Western Europe of how to live alongside people of different religions, because our Muslim community is incomparably older than those in other European countries.
In my opinion, Lithuania's integration mechanisms today are also much better than those in other European countries. It is therefore disappointing to see ideas imported from populists in Western Europe, who are not Lithuanian, taking root here and turning into attacks on Muslims.
It is clear to everyone that such attacks benefit hostile forces in the East that have nothing to do with Islam. I hope Lithuanians will follow the path of their ancestors and refuse to be intimidated by a caricature of Islam as a bogeyman – one that has nothing to do with the reality around us.

Dmitriev calls suspension of Graham Act historic moment
Unknown

MOSCOW, October 17. /TASS/. The suspension of the law of the deceased Senator Lindsey Graham (recognized in Russia as a terrorist and extremist) is a historic moment, said Kirill Dmitriev, special representative of the Russian president for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries, head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund.
"Suspension of the Graham Act by the administration of President [Donald] Trump is an important and truly historic moment. Instead of sanctions and confrontation, we have dialogue, mutually beneficial cooperation, and shared responsibility for global stability," Dmitriev wrote on Telegram.
According to him, the Graham Act could have completely halted economic cooperation between Russia and the United States and caused serious damage to the American economy and global markets.

Trump puts on hold new Russia sanctions he signed into law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
04:45:03 UTC
13:45:03 KST

Trump puts on hold new Russia sanctions he signed into law
US president’s executive order comes two days before sanctions deadline and a week after diesel deal with Putin.
United States President Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia that he signed into law last month, telling Congress the pause is in the national interest.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday, two days before a deadline in the law that would put the sanctions into effect.
The law – named after Lindsey Graham, the Republican senator who died unexpectedly in July after returning from Ukraine – passed in the House of Representatives and the Senate by large margins. The bipartisan legislation was drafted by Graham and Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal.
It seeks to starve Moscow of money for its war on Ukraine by sanctioning Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers carrying its energy exports.
It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the five biggest importers of Russian oil or gas with an exception for countries that import less than 15 percent of Russia’s natural gas exports and are taking steps to cut them.
Kirill Dmitriev, special envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin, said on social media that Trump’s move was “an important and truly historic moment”.
“The US-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue,” he added.
Diesel deal and criticism
The decision to suspend the sanctions came a week after Trump said the US signed a deal to buy diesel from Russia to try to lower global fuel prices.
Both Republicans and Democrats criticised the deal, saying it would help Russia’s war effort without affecting fuel prices.
Democratic Representative Don Beyer said he and other politicians had “warned” that Trump might do this, referring to Trump’s deal with Moscow.
Beyer called on Congress to “fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine”.
Trump recently has also increasingly criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to reach a deal with Russia.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Oleksandr Merezhko, the chairman of the Ukrainian parliament’s Committee on Foreign Policy and Interparliamentary Cooperation, linked Trump’s latest moves, which put Ukraine at a disadvantage, to next month’s midterm elections in the US and predicted an improvement in relations after the voting.
“President Trump is a difficult partner, but we are dependent on the United States, and we need to have constructive, respectful relations even with Trump, no matter how difficult it might be,” he said.
“I believe that after the midterm elections, the situation will be better, the emotions will subside and we will be able to return to constructive dialogue with President Trump,” Merezhko added.
Polls have suggested that Trump’s Republican Party will have a hard time keeping its majorities in Congress in the November 3 elections due to voters disapproving of Trump’s handling of the US-Israel war on Iran and blaming him for higher prices.

Country diary: The challenge of making a thatched roof pine-marten proof | Tom Allan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
04:30:20 UTC
13:30:20 KST

That the thatch is thick with moss and crusted with the brittle fronds of lichen is not unusual for a roof of this age. What’s puzzling me is the hole in its centre. It is about 10in wide – a dark scoop, as if someone has taken a giant ladle to the roof.
When I climb the ladder for a closer look, I can see toothmarks on the reed. I also see that the hole does not go all the way through – the animal obviously gave up after an exploratory burrow.
“It was probably the pine marten,” says Pam Aitchison, the owner of this thatched roundhouse in a glen just south of the Cairngorms, which I am here to re-thatch. She fed it peanut butter and jam sandwiches for a while, but stopped when she became concerned that it might be damaging the roof.
This is a first for me in 14 years working on thatched roofs. Damage by squirrels is fairly common. They can chew through reed, wire netting, roof battens and even lead chimney flashings. Rats and jackdaws are familiar culprits too, but pine martens – less so.
They are a regular presence in this glen, though. Bruce, a semi-retired plumber who lives up the track, had a pair of martens nesting in the roof of his garage for a few summers. Initially, he tried various ways of keeping them out, but in the end he decided to live with them. “They’ll squeeze through anything,” he said. “You cannae blame them wanting somewhere to live.”
The tightly packed new thatch I am laying should, I hope, be less inviting to the mustelids than the soft surface of the old reed.
I set to work fixing in place the bundles of water reed, which has come from just down the road, in Tayside (unlike the majority of thatching reed in the UK, which is imported from overseas). It was harvested from Britain’s largest continuous reedbed – an 11-mile-long arc of Phragmites planted in the early 19th century.
Originally intended as a flood defence, it is now managed by the RSPB, and contains a quarter of Britain’s population of bearded tits, as well as marsh harriers and water rails. Thatch can be a home for wildlife before it goes on the roof, too.

Three sentenced to 158 years in Mexico for murder of Australian, US surfers

- Families called the deaths “hell” and “incredibly difficult”. The US State Department later warned Americans to reconsider travel to Baja California because of crime and kidnapping risks.
AI generated
MEXICO CITY – A Mexican judge on Oct 16 sentenced three men to 158 years and nine months in prison each for the killings of two Australian brothers and their American friend during a 2024 surf trip to the state of Baja California, a judicial official said.
The defendants, identified by the authorities simply as Jesus Gerardo, known as El Kekas, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were found guilty a week ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
The victims were Australian brothers Jake Robinson, 33, and Callum Robinson, 30, and their American friend Jack Rhoad, 30.
The judge also ordered the defendants to pay compensation to the victims’ families, said an official from the Baja California state judiciary.
In November, Gisell Silva was sentenced to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to aggravated robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence, in a fast-track proceeding.
The woman, then 23, was arrested a few days after the foreigners’ bodies were found in a water well.
The Robinson brothers and Rhoad were camping and surfing near Punta San Jose, about 80km south of Ensenada, when they were reported missing in late April 2024.
After a days-long search, aided by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, their bodies were found on May 3 at the bottom of a well.
The victims were each found with gunshot wounds to the head, and the pickup truck they were travelling in was found, burnt, several kilometres away, the authorities said.
“There will never be justice for the loss of a child, but these men will never hurt anyone else again,” said Page Rhoad, mother of the dead American, via Zoom after the sentencing.
Martin and Debra Robinson, parents of Jake and Callum, followed the sentencing hearing remotely after returning to Australia last week, following the initial guilty verdict.
In an interview as they left one of the 24 hearings that made up the trial, they described their sons’ deaths as “hell” and an “incredibly difficult” experience.
While the Ensenada area is considered relatively safe, Baja California ranks among Mexico’s most violent states.

Trump imposed &quot;hellish&quot; sanctions on Russia and immediately suspended their implementation – BBC
