How Culver City is quietly emerging as a new mecca for AI filmmaking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
02:33:28 UTC
11:33:28 KST

How Culver City is quietly emerging as a new mecca for AI filmmaking
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Culver City’s mix of Hollywood studios, tech companies and available office space is drawing a growing cluster of AI filmmaking startups eager to reshape the industry.
- The companies tout new creative possibilities, using generative tools for everything from short-form crime shows to commercials and film effects.
- But unions and many Hollywood workers fear AI will take jobs, even as studios explore hybrid productions and secure protections against fully synthetic performers.
The heart of Screenland is cozying up to artificial intelligence.
The open space in Culver Steps typically hosts community events and movie nights. But on Wednesday, it turned into a job fair for companies looking to hire talent for AI studios.
Companies showed off their life-like AI videos, urging emerging talent — and out-of-work creatives — to join them as they worked to reinvent traditional filmmaking.
“It’s a great breeding ground for this new filmmaking,” Dave Clark, cofounder of AI film production studio Promise, said about Culver City. “To the independent filmmakers here, it’s time to take back power.”
The event was part of LA Tech Week, a citywide event organized by venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.
Culver City has emerged as a magnet for companies and consumers.
Culver City is already home to big names in Hollywood and technology like Amazon MGM Studios, TikTok, Apple, and Sony Pictures Entertainment. Recently, a growing cluster of AI studios, including Promise, TrueShort, Native Foreign, and PhantomX, are expanding in the neighborhood.
Luma AI, a $4-billion Palo Alto startup that makes generative AI video software, opened a facility in Culver City last year. The company’s Dream Lab occupies a 7,000 square feet space and employs a team of 13.
“Culver City is the future of AI and filmmaking,” Caroline Ingeborn, Luma AI’s chief operating officer, said in a statement.
The companies said they are drawn by the legacy studios they hope to rival. The fact that space is available and affordable thanks to the general decline of the entertainment business in L.A. also helps.
Proponents of AI see it as an antidote to high production costs and say it allows creatives to make films that otherwise would never be made. However, many in Hollywood, its unions, and the public at large are suspicious of the surge in AI use, worried it is stealing the work of human creatives and taking people’s jobs.
The new wave of AI filmmakers have accepted the rise of AI as inevitable, and are forging ahead, increasingly in Culver City.
The city is not opposed to it.
“We’re a hub for the creative economy that is continuing to evolve,” said Adam Troy, Culver City assistant city manager, in a statement. “We look forward to what’s next in the space and what businesses see their future here in Culver City.”
Job postings reveal studios are quietly adopting AI.
TrueShort moved into Culver City last month, taking over most of a 5,000-square-foot office space near Amazon’s studio. The AI studio has raised $17 million and employs about 45 people. Around 75% of them are creatives: filmmakers, editors, sound designers and composers.
Its streaming app hosts short-form true crime audio and video shows that are fully AI-generated. On average, a 10-minute episode costs about $10,000 to make and takes about 10 days to go from idea to release.
“The next Netflix or the next Disney is going to come out of AI this time,” said Nate Tepper, cofounder of TrueShort. “And, in a way, it kind of needs to be a startup because the big incumbents are not going to move as fast. They’re going to be afraid of backlash.”
The company outgrew its Santa Monica office and is now located near Culver Theater.
“It is cool being next to the other bigger lots like Sony and Amazon, only because it’s inspiring,” Tepper said. “We want the lot. We want to become the big studio.”
A California e-commerce platform is fueling the rise of live shopping in the United States, taking on giants such as TikTok and tackling concerns that the app is draining people’s bank accounts.
Culver City-based creative studio Native Foreign makes AI commercials for brands that are more open than Hollywood about AI use. It has done ads for Virgin and Toys R Us.
It made one of the first AI-animated shorts, “Critterz,” using OpenAI’s software and planned to help make a movie based on it, but OpenAI pulled out of the project and canceled its video-making AI model.
“We don’t have the kind of opportunities that maybe some huge huge studios and companies have, so we are able to bag above our weight with these tools,” Nik Kleverov, co-founder of the company, said on a panel at LA Tech Week.
Amid rapid technological change, a growing number of filmmakers and companies in Southern California are using AI tools to radically rethink how films and TV shows are made.
Google-backed Promise is another Culver City-adjacent AI studio that’s a proponent of hybrid productions, where human actors work with AI specialists. The company uses AI to generate backgrounds, visual effects, and synthetic humans for its slate of films, but a lot of the performances are shot on soundstages across L.A. using actors.
In late 2024, the studio acquired Curious Refuge, an online AI school that teaches traditional artists and newbies to use generative AI tools for filmmaking. Promise moved close to Culver from Venice in June.
Excitement about AI grows even as the industry puts up guardrails to contain it. The actors’ guild SAG-AFTRA has secured special protection against fully synthetic performers in the union contract signed this year.
However, some Hollywood veterans point out that the industry has fought over technology before. Alex Cancado, who spent years in visual effects and has worked on over 80 movies, now works in the AI Studios division of Amazon MGM Studios.
Tech giant Google has been quietly making overtures to major studios as it tries to find ways to get Hollywood to use its AI technology.
Pitching the crowd of creatives on Wednesday, he said the transition from practical effects to computer graphics was equally fraught.
“It was a challenge getting CG to be accepted by directors and producers,” Cancado said.
Much of the buzz around AI use for big productions started with a conference in Culver City called “AI on the Lot,” which started in 2023. It has since grown to thousands of attendees.
The organization also sponsored the job fair on Culver Steps and a networking happy hour for media AI companies in Culver City. It estimates that AI media companies with $2 billion in backing have converged on the city.
Mike Gioia, a founder of AI on the Lot, attends City Hall meetings and is trying to build momentum around the concept of a “Culver cluster” — bringing more companies and individuals working in AI to the neighborhood.
“We want to make Culver City the capital of AI media,” said Gioia.

US records 4,410 measles cases as outbreak grows

US records 4,410 measles cases as outbreak grows
The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has recorded 4,410 measles cases so far in 2026, an increase of 330 in a week, and has dispatched an investigator to the state of Pennsylvania to help contain the country’s largest outbreak, Al Jazeera reports.
CDC figures also show 451 measles-related hospitalisations nationwide this year. Children and teenagers aged five to 19 account for 42 percent of cases, followed by adults aged 20 and older, who make up 41 percent. Seventeen percent of cases were among children under the age of five.
Pennsylvania reported 1,222 cases across 42 counties as of Wednesday, including 86 new infections since October 9, according to the state health department. The outbreak has led to 225 hospitalisations and five confirmed measles-associated deaths. State officials are actively investigating a sixth reported death.
The CDC is sending a so-called “disease detective” from its Epidemic Intelligence Service to work with state health officials on the Pennsylvania outbreak. The deployment follows Pennsylvania’s request for federal assistance, known as an Epi-Aid.
Pennsylvania has expanded vaccination efforts in affected communities. State health centre staff have administered more than 5,900 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine doses at 202 pop-up clinics since the outbreak began in late April.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on October 5 as measles cases rose in nearby Pennsylvania. The order is effective until November 4 and expands the number of healthcare professionals authorised to administer vaccines and allows nurses greater flexibility to order measles testing.
Measles vaccination coverage among US kindergarteners fell from 95.2 percent in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4 percent in 2025–2026, according to data from the CDC. The agency estimates that about 280,000 kindergarteners are at risk because of gaps in vaccination coverage.

Wind-whipped flames have scorched multi-million dollar homes south of Los Angeles as a wildfire quickly ravaged hundreds of acres.
Dramatic footage on Friday showed burning homes and thick smoke billowing from the tinder-dry bushy hills, where the quick-spreading fire is fuelled by intense Santa Ana winds, low humidity and unseasonably high temperatures.
The Orange County Fire Authority said on X that the so-called Norte fire had scorched about 465 acres and that at least four homes had been impacted in the affluent San Juan Capistrano municipality.
The agency said firefighters were "aggressively attacking the fire from ground and air" and issued repeated pleas for people to stay clear of the area.
The fast-moving blaze prompted widespread evacuation orders as multiple helicopters vied to douse the flames.
Officials also warned of poor air quality for residents nearby.
The National Weather Service warned of "high risk for large fires and rapid fire growth" especially over Los Angeles and Ventura counties, as well as the mountains and foothills of San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties.
Firefighters were also busy battling the Bryson fire, which broke out overnight on the outskirts of the famed Malibu beach community. As of Friday afternoon that conflagration was at 147 acres and 17 percent contained, according to the state's Cal Fire agency.
And the Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton was impacted by the Henderson Fire, which prompted freeway closures and had burned at least 2,070 acres by Friday, according to Cal Fire.
Residents told to be ready for emergency evacuations
Tens of thousands of customers in Los Angeles county alone were without power, as authorities de-energised power lines in a bid to lessen the possibility of electrical sparks that the heavy wind gusts could carry.
The fierce winds were set to peak on Friday across Los Angeles County but the high heat and low humidity meant the high fire danger would continue into the weekend.
Forecasters said winds roared between 80 and 110 kilometres per hour in the mountains, with coastal and valley areas seeing gusts between 55 and 90 kilometres per hour.
In some areas temperatures soared as high as 38 degrees Celsius, the National Weather Service said.
The weather authority said fire danger would remain through much of the day on Saturday, warning residents to be prepared for emergency evacuations.
They also cautioned drivers about dangerous crosswinds, particularly on elevated roadways.

North Korea says it tested AI-assisted precision-guided torpedo system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
02:00:21 UTC
11:00:21 KST

North Korea has tested a "new-type" precision-guided torpedo system that uses artificial intelligence for target detection and guidance, state media said, as the nuclear-armed country steps up weapons testing.
The announcement on Saturday came days after Pyongyang said it had test-fired two types of cruise missiles from a submarine after weeks of friction with Seoul over a landmine explosion along their border.
Analysts say North Korea could be rapidly advancing its missile and weapons technology with support from Russia received in exchange for sending troops to support its war against Ukraine.
The underwater test-fire of the "super-speed" Zam-2.0 torpedo system took place on Thursday "to confirm the successful technical updating" of the weapon, the Korean Central News Agency said.
"AI technology was applied to the target detection and the guidance function of the new-type super-speed precisely guided torpedo," KCNA said.
The test proved "the core technology for raising the efficiency of propulsion and the performance of rocket propulsion device", it said, adding it had completed "more than 180 rounds of different tests over the past five years".
Earlier this month, North Korea announced the AI-assisted launch of an intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
Pyongyang said at the time there was "no way to avoid" the hypersonic missile, which was "capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude".
Torpedoes are designed to strike enemy targets underwater at high speed, but the stated introduction of AI could also allow North Korea to carry out evasive manoeuvres and make autonomous decisions to confuse an adversary, analysts say.
"South Korea and the United States deploy decoy targets to divert torpedoes, but AI could potentially help distinguish real targets from decoys," Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University, told AFP news agency.
"From torpedoes to submarine-launched weapons, Pyongyang is pouring resources into demonstrating that US strategic assets can be rendered ineffective."
In September, Pyongyang's leader Kim Jong-un emphasised the need to raise "the level of artificial intelligence" in the country's weapons systems.
'Arms race'
Saturday's announcement came as the two Koreas appear to be intensifying an arms race over hypersonic missiles.
Hypersonic missiles travel at more than five times the speed of sound and can manoeuvre mid-flight, making them significantly harder to track and intercept.
Days after North Korea announced it had tested its AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile, Seoul test-fired its own weapon — a hypersonic glide vehicle it called a "key strategic asset capable of changing the course of the battlefield".
North Korea this week cast doubt on Seoul's test, saying it may have "failed to achieve hypersonic flight", a claim South Korea rejected a day later.
The latest weapons tests come amid growing speculation over a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim, as world leaders prepare to gather for November's APEC summit in China.
After several overtures met with silence from Pyongyang, Trump said again this week he "may" meet North Korean leader Kim during his Asia tour next month.
Ahead of a possible North Korea-US summit, Pyongyang appears to be "playing down South Korea's hypersonic missile programme to portray itself as ahead of Seoul — Washington's ally — in the arms race", Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AFP.
But North Korea may need more time to advance its torpedo system, particularly in reducing the noise it generates underwater, he said.
"At high speeds underwater, a torpedo generates significant noise, making it easier to detect," Yang said.
"Reducing that noise is a major technical challenge requiring advanced technology — and North Korea does not yet appear to have reached that level."

WASHINGTON, October 17. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has issued a decree according to which he will not impose several sanctions based on the law on tightening restrictions against Russia.
"I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act. I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," the document published on the White House website states.
Under Article 115, the president has the right to waive the application of sanctions and duties provided for in the law. To do so, he must submit to Congress a justification that such a decision is in the national interests of the United States.
On September 18, Trump signed into law a bill passed by Congress that provides for sanctions against Russia’s top political and military leadership, state·owned companies, as well as secondary sanctions against Russia’s trading partners. According to the document, within 30 days after signing — or by October 18 — the Washington administration must determine which companies and individuals may be subject to restrictions, or determine that such new restrictive measures do not align with US interests, and notify Congress accordingly.

Trump signs order suspending Russia sanctions under Graham Act
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
04:36:00 EEST
10:36:00 KST

Trump signs order suspending Russia sanctions under Graham Act
US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order suspending certain sanctions, restrictions and tariffs on Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
Source: Trump's executive order on the White House website; Bloomberg
Quote from the order: "I hereby waive the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Graham Act or this order. I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States."
Details: According to Bloomberg, Trump has suspended sweeping tariffs linked to Russian energy exports that were provided for under legislation he signed last month. The measures had complicated his efforts to bring down diesel prices ahead of the US midterm elections.
Trump invoked an exemption provision in the Act, which was introduced by the late Senator Lindsey Graham in response to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The legislation also codified and expanded sanctions targeting Moscow.
The executive order formally establishes the tariffs while suspending their application, meaning Trump could bring them into force later if he chooses to do so.
The move gave Trump 30 days to impose 100% tariffs on all goods from the five largest buyers of Russian oil. It also provided for sanctions against numerous Russian legal entities and 500% tariffs on all imports of Russian energy products into the US. The 30-day period was due to expire on 18 October.
These provisions conflicted with Trump's plan, announced last week, to work with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to bring the country's diesel supplies onto global markets. Trump is seeking to lower diesel prices in the US, which have been hovering at record highs just weeks before the 3 November elections.
Waiving the tariffs risks provoking renewed opposition from members of Congress, including many Republicans angered by his decision on Russian diesel fuel.
Suspending the law's application also allows Trump to avoid a potential conflict with the largest buyers of Russian energy products: China, India and Türkiye.
Background:
- On 17 September, the US Congress passed bill H.R. 5334, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The legislation authorises 500% tariffs on Russian goods, secondary tariffs of up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, and mandatory sanctions against key sectors of the Russian economy.
- On 19 September, Trump signed the Graham Act into law, setting the first 30-day deadline for the implementation of its provisions for 18 October.
- On 9 October, the US Department of the Treasury, through the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), issued General Licence No. 135, allowing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel fuel.
- On 14 October, a bipartisan group of 12 US senators sent a strongly worded letter to Trump, calling the diesel deal with Moscow a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and urging him to immediately revoke the licence and move to full implementation of the Graham Act.
- Twenty-two Democrat and Republican members of the US House of Representatives wrote to Trump demanding the full and immediate implementation of the sanctions against Russia provided for under the Graham Act.

US coastguard rescues 16 after boat sinks off Mexico’s Baja coast
Unknown

US coastguard rescues 16 after boat sinks off Mexico’s Baja coast
At least 11 people believed to still be missing, with rescue operations underway.
The US coastguard has said it rescued 16 people from the Pacific Ocean after a boat sank off Mexico’s Baja California coast.
The coastguard said on Friday it responded to a Mayday call reporting that a boat was sinking. The search is ongoing for 11 people believed to be still missing.
The boat went down about 225km (140 miles) west of Ensenada, Mexico.
A rescue helicopter reached the site about two hours after someone on the boat transmitted the Mayday call at about 1am (08:00 GMT) on Friday, said coastguard Lieutenant Santiago Tamburini.
It took about 90 minutes for the coastguard crew, which included a rescue swimmer, to pull the 16 people from the water, Tamburini said.
The people rescued were Mexican nationals, according to the Mexican consulate.
One survivor was being treated for a suspected shark bite and two were in critical condition, authorities said.
The rescued were flown by helicopter to San Diego, California, and transported to hospitals. The Mexican consulate in San Diego said it offered consular assistance.
The coastguard and US Navy are continuing to search the area with two helicopters, a fixed-wing plane, a cutter and a navy combat ship.
The boat sank in an area frequented by smugglers transporting migrants to the US. It is also popular with fishing and leisure boats.
Details about the boat’s origin, destination and what it was doing are not clear. No vessel, only debris, was found, and it was unclear what type of boat was involved, the coastguard said.
“Boats in that area can be for fishing, leisure, personal recreation. We just don’t know what they were doing out there. We all know it’s a suspected smuggling route,” Tamburini said.

Oregon school shooting: Father of two kills teen gunman as teacher fights back; 4 dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
01:22:40 UTC
10:22:40 KST

Kaylub Giamanco was driving home for lunch on Thursday when he heard gunfire coming from Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, where his two daughters are students. Moments later, the 36-year-old carpenter followed a teenage gunman into the school and shot him dead, ending a rampage that left four people dead, including three young children.
The attacker, identified by police as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, was a former student at the school who had attended special education classes. Armed with a 12-gauge Maverick 88 pump-action shotgun purchased by his mother, he shot his way through locked school doors and opened fire in a special education classroom, killing a teacher and three children aged 5, 8 and 11. A 7-year-old student and another teacher, 54, were also wounded.
At a news conference Friday, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz revealed that another teacher had attempted to stop the gunman before Giamanco intervened. The teacher threw her cellphone at the attacker, tackled him and struggled to take away his weapon. Police said she survived the confrontation without being injured.
"She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Krantz said, praising her actions as heroic.
Investigators said the first confrontation occurred outside the school, when the teenage gunman threw his shotgun over a fence and climbed onto the school grounds. A driver in a red pickup truck shouted at him, prompting the attacker to open fire on the vehicle, striking it three times. The driver escaped unharmed and called 911.
Giamanco, who was passing nearby, witnessed the teenager shooting at the vehicle and heading toward the school. He pulled into the parking lot, took his .40-caliber pistol and pursued the attacker inside. There, he encountered the gunman struggling with the teacher and fired several shots, killing him.
Police said the attack unfolded within minutes. Investigators estimated that the teenager fired as many as 15 shotgun rounds and still had approximately 44 rounds of ammunition when he was killed.
'He doesn't feel like a hero'
Giamanco's brother, Kyle, told NBC News that despite being credited with preventing further bloodshed, his brother does not see himself as a hero. Instead, he is struggling with guilt over the lives he was unable to save. He has declined interview requests while he processes what happened.
Their mother, Kenda Freeman, told the New York Post that she was immensely proud of her son's quick thinking and courage. "He is absolutely a hero," she said, adding that he was going through an extremely difficult time.
Freeman also read a statement on behalf of the family, saying Giamanco was not seeking public recognition and wanted instead to thank first responders, school employees and members of the community for their support. His family, including his two daughters, requested privacy.
According to the New York Post, Giamanco had previously practiced shooting with U.S. military veterans who served in Iraq. In a September 2018 Facebook post, he described participating in shooting exercises with a group of former soldiers, thanking them for sharing their experience and service.
President Donald Trump also praised Giamanco, describing him as a "great hero" who "took care of business." Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said the shooting was a terrible tragedy but suggested the death toll could have been even higher without the father's intervention.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," Trump said.
'The teacher shouted no, please'
Accounts from children who survived the attack have provided a harrowing picture of what unfolded inside the school.
Stacy Green, whose granddaughters, ages 7 and 11, attend Silver Rail Elementary, said the girls heard multiple gunshots coming from a neighboring classroom. They also heard a special education teacher pleading, "No, please," before more gunfire erupted.
Another grandmother, Christine Wenzke, said her 10-year-old grandson, Aizen, heard so many gunshots that he lost count. The boy, who was closest to his classroom door, rushed to lock it before joining his classmates and teacher behind lockers, following emergency procedures they had practiced.
"I locked the door and I went back behind our lockers," Aizen told ABC News. He said the students and their teacher were unharmed, but many children were terrified and crying.
Police identified one of the victims as 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert, remembered by her family as a compassionate educator devoted to children with special needs.
"Meghan was compassionate and had a huge heart," her family said in a statement. "She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs." Relatives also described her as a beloved daughter, sister, niece and granddaughter.
The youngest victim was 5-year-old Rhoam Summer. His aunt, Swan Sheridan, remembered him as a fearless climber, a fast runner and an enthusiastic reader who adored his stuffed animals.
"He never met a stuffie that he didn't think needed to be rescued and cared for," she said. Sheridan described her nephew as a joyful child who had been full of energy since birth.
The names of the other two children killed, aged 8 and 11, were not released by police at their families' request. The two wounded victims, a 7-year-old student and teacher Becky Drury, remained under medical care. Authorities said the child was in serious but stable condition, while Drury's injuries were serious but not life-threatening.
A former student returns with a shotgun
The New York Times reported that the attacker had attended Silver Rail Elementary in 2020, when he was approximately 10 years old. His mother, Shauntai Nickerson, previously told a local news outlet that her son had struggled with remote learning during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Speaking to reporters after the shooting, Nickerson expressed grief for the families of the victims and said she wished she could have prevented the tragedy. Police said they were still investigating how the teenager obtained the shotgun and what motivated the attack.
Outside Silver Rail Elementary, residents of Bend have established a makeshift memorial filled with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals. Families and community members have gathered there to remember the victims and offer support to those affected.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter attends kindergarten at the school, told The Associated Press she was astonished that someone had been willing to pursue the gunman into the building. Fighting back tears, she described the intervention as extraordinary and said she was deeply grateful that more lives had been saved.
Silver Rail Elementary, located roughly 160 kilometers southeast of Portland, serves children from kindergarten through fifth grade and enrolled approximately 459 students last year. Classes across the Bend-La Pine school district were canceled Friday following the shooting.
As the community mourns the four victims, investigators continue trying to determine why a former student returned to his old elementary school armed with a shotgun. For the families of the children and teacher who died, and for the father who ran toward the gunfire, the events of those few minutes will leave a lasting mark.

Sukkot in Florida offers an Israeli family joy, community, and a reminder of war - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
00:56:03 UTC
09:56:03 KST

On the eve of Sukkot, I find myself not in Jerusalem but in Kissimmee, Florida, in a gated vacation home community called Encore at Reunion.
Our youngest grandchild, Ye’ela, now seven, has convinced her family that it’s her turn to visit Disney World. Her older siblings have already been. My son, daughter-in-law, and their four children can all take off the days of Sukkot. My physician son even has a lecture to give for Hadassah in Miami. We decide to go for it.
I admit to having a weakness for Disney World. Walking down Disney’s Main Street, U.S.A., riding through the African savanna on Kilimanjaro Safaris in Animal Kingdom, and watching For the First Time in Forever: A Frozen Sing-Along Celebration in Hollywood Studios when the snow comes down (twice!) offer an invigorating vacation break from the Middle East. I like refilling my Disney popcorn bucket at every stop, eating Mickey Mouse-shaped ice cream, and being silly enough to decorate my hat with a Minnie Mouse headband.
Seven-year-old Ye’ela has spent most of her life either in a pandemic or wartime, and I want to see her pose with those Disney princesses and ride the Slinky Dog Dash roller coaster with her siblings.
So I take on the job of logistics, which has to include Sukkot observance, of course.
Where to stay? We want a house, not a hotel, partly because it’s less expensive, but also because we can prepare kosher food for kids used to Israeli cuisine and celebrate the holiday our own way. There are literally tens of thousands of vacation home rentals in the Orlando area, but only a handful of rental communities allow or tolerate the building of those strange shacks called sukkot on their property. Hence, we decide on Encore at Reunion.
For most of the year, Encore is a regular vacation resort village for American and foreign guests. But on Jewish holidays, particularly Sukkot and Passover, hundreds of observant Jews abandon their already chilly backyards in colder states to erect their sukkot in Florida.
Encore is 18 km. from the Magic Kingdom and closer to the other three Disney parks. It is not only sukkah-friendly but has an eruv, making carrying possible on Shabbat. Over the last decade or so, this has become a popular holiday venue for religious Jews. The resort also includes shuttles to the parks and a large, free water park with impressive waterslides for all ages.
I arrange for an unassembled sukkah to be delivered by one of several local suppliers (Klein’s, if you’re interested). Ironically, we live on a Jerusalem street with a bustling Four Species marketplace, but fear violating import laws by bringing an etrog into the Citrus State. So I order the Four Species from a pop-up Chabad distributor, also at Encore.
We bring some pots and pans and buy others. With 337 km. separating Miami International Airport from Encore, I search for and find a reliable, reasonably priced van service (DNR Limousine Services, in case you’re interested; ask for Vladi) that also stops at a kosher supermarket so we can pick up our large online order of food supplies and sushi lunch.
By the day before the holiday, the nondescript vacation village has been transformed into a Sukkot hub. Thatched-roof booths are ubiquitous, mostly in driveways, but also in backyards beside the private swimming pools.
Nearly all those rental homes also have golf carts in their driveways, not for golfaholics, but for families to use as transportation and entertainment on the resort’s streets. Many of the drivers look dangerously underage.
Despite jet lag, we spend our first two happy days in Disney parks. Then it’s Sukkot eve. Our sukkah is up and, thanks to my daughter-in-law, our holiday food is sizzling on a hotplate delivered by Amazon Prime.
One neighbor insists that we come inside and eat a plate of cholent. Another invites my husband to walk with him to one of the pop-up synagogues for the Mincha prayer. My granddaughter Eliana, 18, and I try to follow them soon after candlelighting, but never find the synagogue.
The air is balmy, with no Florida hurricanes threatening tonight. There are few cars on the street. Passersby wish us “gut Shabbos” and “gut yom tov.”
'Strange and unexpected'
“How strange and unexpected it is to be in Florida and to be surrounded by religious Jews,” Eliana says.
Most of those strolling like us are girls and women, their cooking done, their menfolk off to synagogues. The teenage girls look a lot like Eliana, in holiday dresses, long hair, and welcoming smiles. We stop to chat with a few of them along the way.
Then, when we are alone, Eliana says something that changes the mood.
“I see these girls. In most ways, they’re just like me, but none of them has been through what we teenagers in Israel have gone through. We’ve dodged rockets, cared for families where the father was gone for months, and, worst of all, we’ve gone to so many funerals and shiva calls. We’re all going to national service and the army. How different our lives have been.”
We walk quietly after that, her words bringing us back to Israel, to her hometown of Modi’in.
Modi’in has suffered devastating military losses during the war. So many young residents have fallen that the military cemetery has required expansion. When you’re 18, you know many of the soldiers from school or youth movements. The names on the gravestones are not strangers.
Eliana herself is spending the year at Tzahali, a pre-military preparatory academy for religious young women, founded in 2006. The academy is named in memory of combat navigator Tamar Ariel, whose youth group was led by Eliana’s aunt and uncle. Its program combines Torah study with preparation for meaningful leadership and service in the IDF.
Eliana already has her future army placement.
Our somberness fades as we sit around the holiday table, enjoying the home-cooked food and the novelty of having our own sukkah so far from home. Sukkot is, after all, the holiday of joy, reaffirming our reliance on the Almighty. Through the thatched roof of our Florida sukkah, the same stars we see at home are abundant and reassuring.
Little Ye’ela does get to see the princesses. She turns out to be a roller coaster enthusiast, riding with siblings Matan, 10; Ariel, 16; and Eliana on the famous roller coasters.
By the time we reach the finale, the magnificent fireworks over the Magic Kingdom, no one thinks of comparing them to the Iron Dome squiggles of light that have so often illuminated the heavens over Modi’in. Watching the bursts of light align in the air to create hearts and Disney characters, the children are able to look up at the sky and focus on the beauty.
We, too.
The writer is the Israel director of public relations at Hadassah, the Women’s Zionist Organization of America. Her latest book is A Daughter of Many Mothers, cowritten with Holocaust survivor and premier English-language witness Rena Quint.

Missiles hit Yemen's Aden airport as Saudi-led coalition intercepts missile headed for Yanbu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
00:56:01 UTC
09:56:01 KST

Missiles struck Aden International Airport in southern Yemen on Friday, while a Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile headed for the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz.
The coalition said it had also destroyed two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and three drones in Saudi Arabia's Southern and Riyadh regions. It did not identify those behind the attacks.
In Aden, two missiles landed on the airport grounds, the Aden Security Department said, blaming the Iran-backed Houthi group. It said the incident was the second attack on the facility in less than a week. The Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility.
No casualties were reported. A Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for takeoff when the missiles landed, the security department said.
Yanbu key to Saudi oil exports
Yanbu is a key outlet for Saudi oil exports, allowing the kingdom to ship crude to international markets via the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz, where heightened regional tensions and security threats have raised concerns over the safety of shipping.
Brent crude briefly touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May, as worries over escalating Middle East tensions raised concerns about tighter global supplies.
Saudi Civil Defense authorities earlier issued alerts in the Jazan region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, where such warnings have become frequent since fighting resumed last month.
Houthi attacks raise concerns over deteriorating humanitarian crisis
Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has raised fears of a further deterioration in the country's humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions are worsening rapidly.
The Yemen conflict has become another front in the wider regional war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Yemen's war began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and forced the internationally recognized government south. A Saudi-led intervention began the following year, leading to years of stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.
The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since the conflict reignited, targeting airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure. In recent days, the group has also targeted sites in government-held parts of Yemen, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital.
A spokesperson for the Houthi-run health ministry said on Friday that 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what he described as "Saudi aggression" since the escalation began on September 3. Reuters could not independently verify the figures.

Lawler, Conley battle for Jewish voters in pivotal New York race that could decide House control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
00:55:46 UTC
09:55:46 KST

Two rivals in the pivotal race for New York’s 17th Congressional District are aggressively courting Jewish voters, each seeking to present themselves as a champion of Israel and a defender against antisemitism.
Rep. Mike Lawler, a two-term Republican incumbent, and Democratic challenger Cait Conley are neck and neck in polls, with both within the margin of error, in a race that could help determine which party controls the House in the last two years of President Donald Trump’s second term.
Continued Republican control of Congress would give Trump a more favorable setting for advancing his legislative agenda. A Democratic House majority would give the opposition control of House committees and their investigative powers.
NY-17 comprises Putnam and Rockland counties and parts of Westchester and Dutchess counties. An estimated 19% of the district’s residents are Jewish, according to a 2024 study commissioned by the Jewish Electorate Institute.
Each candidate is trying to tie the other to polarizing figures in their respective parties. Lawler is asserting that Conley refuses to separate herself from New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the increasingly progressive wing of the Democratic Party. Conley is accusing Lawler of being a rubber stamp for Trump’s legislative priorities.
Jewish voters emerge as key constituency in New York House race
For Conley to win, she’ll have to convince Jewish voters that not only is she a staunch Israel ally and determined to protect the Jewish community from antisemitism, but that she can distance herself from the left wing of the Democratic Party and the members of the Democratic Socialists of America, such as Mamdani and others who have been widely critical of Israel.
One reason is that most Orthodox Jews, a major constituency in Rockland County, identified as Republican or leaned Republican, according to a 2020 Pew Research national survey. Another is that a September poll by the Jewish Electorate Institute found that 57% of Jewish voters believe antisemitism is increasing within the Democratic Party, despite about 70% of Jewish voters favoring Democrats. The same national poll found 60% believed antisemitism was increasing in the Republican Party.
When the two candidates squared off in a televised debate hosted by PIX11 on Wednesday night, Lawler brought up the New York City mayor’s statement on Oct. 7, which mourned those killed and abducted on the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks before accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza and saying US tax dollars funded war crimes.
Lawler, noting that Conley repeatedly declined to condemn Mamdani in their previous debate, said the mayor issued “the most vile antisemitic statement on Oct. 7th, blaming Jews for their butchering on Oct. 7th.” Turning to Conley, Lawler asked, “Do you denounce Zohran Mamdani’s recent statement on Oct. 7th, which blamed Jews?”
“Yes, I do denounce Mamdani’s statement on October 7th, a day that we should be honoring and mourning the loss of life, the greatest loss of life to our Jewish community since the Holocaust,” she responded. “I condemn antisemitism from any party or anyone.”
Lawler, Conley clash over Mamdani, support for Israel
Both candidates spoke strongly in support of Israel. Debate moderator Dan Mannarino asked if US taxpayer money should still be used “to send offensive and defensive weapon funding to aid Israel.”
“Israel is our greatest ally in the world,” Lawler replied. “The fact is, they’re the only democracy in the Middle East.”
He then accused the Democratic Party of ambivalence toward Israel. “I am opposed to any effort by the Democrats and the DSA to defund the strategic partnership between the United States and Israel, and I will fight it tooth and nail,” he said.
Conley agreed with Lawler that the US should continue funding offensive and defensive weapons for Israel.
“I believe in Israel’s right to exist,” she said. “It is the only democracy in the Middle East. It is a strategic partner for American national security, and I believe America has a responsibility to help ensure the safety and security of the Israeli people.”
New York House candidates diverge over Netanyahu, Iran war
Even so, she sought to distinguish herself from Lawler by affirming her willingness to chastise the Israeli government when warranted. “I also will criticize the Netanyahu administration when I believe it is doing the wrong thing for Israel and America,” she said.
Conley said that although she supported the Trump administration’s military strikes on targeted locations associated with Iran’s nuclear weapons development program, she believes that the “feckless execution” of the war has drawn the country “into this reckless conflict without clear military objectives or an exit strategy.”
Lawler defended voting against congressional efforts to end the war, while trying to tie Conley to Iran’s ability to fund terrorism. He argued that while Conley served as director for counterterrorism on President Joe Biden’s National Security Council, the US “eased sanctions on the illicit oil trade between China and Iran, allowing them to accumulate hundreds of billions of dollars. That’s what funded Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis. That’s what financed the October 7th terrorist attack.”
Conley defended her record by noting that the head of ISIS was killed during her tenure. She also said that similar attacks on Iran have been on the table for both Democratic and Republican administrations for decades, but they were never carried out because those administrations determined such attacks would threaten national security.

Unknown Publisher

00:55:43 UTC
09:55:43 KST

A Norwegian teenager who flew to Britain to commit murder after being recruited online by a Swedish organized crime group linked to Iran was jailed on Friday for 20 years.
British prosecutors said Johannes Natland, now 19, was recruited by the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish criminal group that pays young people to carry out "violence as a service" on behalf of clients, including the Iranian state.
He was convicted in July of conspiracy to murder. Natland had not been told the identity of the person he had agreed to kill in return for a payment of 270,000 Norwegian kroner, around $28,600, prosecutors said.
The case was one of a number in recent years involving young adults who have stood trial in Britain over serious criminal acts carried out after being recruited online. Britain says some of them have ended up acting as unwitting proxies for foreign states such as Iran or Russia.
Foxtrot has been linked to several murders across Europe, and Britain and the US allege the group was behind attacks against Israeli and Jewish targets on behalf of Iran, which denies the allegation.
Teen said 'it will be cool to kill'
Natland had only just turned 18 when he flew from Norway to Britain, having responded to an advert which offered money to kill and said "nothing can go wrong."
He admitted possessing a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver and ammunition, but denied conspiracy to murder, saying he did not intend to carry out the plan and had considered shooting himself in the foot to get out of it.
But prosecutors said Natland was an enthusiastic recruit, who boasted to a friend that "it will be cool to kill someone."
Judge says she was sure Natland would have carried out attack if not caught
Natland was sentenced at London's Woolwich Crown Court to detention for 20 years by Judge Bobbie Cheema-Grubb, who said she was sure he would have carried out the murder if he had not been arrested by police.
"This was not an impulsive act lasting a few moments ... your conduct demonstrated purpose and persistence," she said, adding that Natland would serve at least 13 years in custody.
Natland's Norwegian lawyer Farid Bouras said in a statement: "Our priority now is to bring him home. We will be working to secure his transfer to Norway as quickly as we possibly can."
Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said there was no evidence of any direct link to Iran in Natland's case, which served as a warning to those who may be recruited to become criminal proxies.
"As Natland found, the people orchestrating these crimes will not protect you from the consequences," she said.

Defense firm Elbit Systems expands operations in Europe with new Swedish facility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
00:55:22 UTC
09:55:22 KST

Elbit Systems Sweden AB announced on Wednesday that it plans to establish the Israeli defense company's first European production and maintenance center for laser warning systems (LWS) in Sweden, as part of efforts to strengthen European defense manufacturing and support the security needs of NATO member states.
The facility, expected to become operational in 2027, will provide local integration, assembly, maintenance, and long-term technical support for laser warning systems supplied to European customers.
The initiative is part of Elbit Systems' long-term strategy to expand its industrial presence across Europe and strengthen local manufacturing and technological capabilities. The company said the facility would help improve system availability, shorten delivery times, and enhance support for European customers.
The establishment of local production capabilities also comes as European countries increase defense spending following Russia's invasion of Ukraine and pressure from US President Donald Trump for NATO allies to raise their military expenditure. Local manufacturing could strengthen Elbit's position in European defense procurement programs that prioritize domestic or regional industrial participation.
Elbit Systems to produce next-generation laser warning technology in Sweden
The planned facility will focus on Elbit Systems' next-generation passive laser warning systems, designed to immediately detect and locate laser threats directed at military platforms. The technology provides crews with additional time and operational flexibility to deploy protective measures.
According to the company, the new systems are designed to integrate seamlessly with existing command-and-control infrastructure. Their decentralized architecture reduces the number of components, minimizes modifications required to military platforms, and is intended to improve reliability and operational durability.
Armed forces worldwide already deploy Elbit's laser warning systems as key components of advanced self-protection suites for military aircraft, vehicles, and other platforms.
Sweden becomes a key hub for Elbit's European defense operations
Established in 2020, Elbit Systems Sweden has become an increasingly important part of the company's European operations, employing more than 100 people across the country. The subsidiary serves as a regional hub for Elbit's activities in Northern Europe and works closely with Sweden's defense industry.
In recent years, Elbit Systems Sweden has supported the Swedish Armed Forces through advanced defense and digitalization programs, strengthening its position as a long-term industrial and technology partner.
The expansion follows other Elbit initiatives in Europe. In June 2026, the company conducted major demonstrations of its digital battlefield networking capabilities in Sweden for representatives of NATO militaries and European defense companies.
Elbit has also expanded its European business through defense contracts involving Greece and Sweden, reflecting growing demand for Israeli-developed military technology and locally supported defense systems.
Elbit Sweden CEO highlights local manufacturing and NATO supply chains
Tobias Wennberg, CEO of Elbit Systems Sweden, said the initiative represents an important step in expanding the subsidiary's industrial capabilities and strengthening its ability to develop, deliver, and manufacture systems locally.
"This initiative represents an important step for us and reflects our commitment to strengthening our capabilities to develop, deliver, and produce locally," Wennberg said. "It also aligns well with our core technologies and enables us to expand our scope going forward."
"Through the establishment of this center and the transfer of advanced technologies, we aim to support Swedish, European, and NATO customers with reliable, long-term, and locally supported self-protection solutions with secure and sovereign supply chains," he added.

Italy names Israeli officials in probe over Gaza flotilla

Breadcrumb
Italy names senior Israelis, Katz in probe over Gaza flotilla activists
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and senior military, police and prison officials have been placed under investigation in Italy over the treatment of Gaza flotilla activists, Italian prosecutors said on Friday.
The move expands an investigation that was previously focused on Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir.
The case concerns suspected torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage when Israeli forces intercepted small fleets of boats headed towards Gaza in 2025 and 2026, the Rome prosecutors' office said in a statement.
Investigators opened the probe after complaints from 50 Italian citizens who were detained by Israeli authorities following two Global Sumud Flotilla missions in September to October 2025 and April to May 2026.
Katz did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Ben-Gvir in June dismissed news that he was under investigation, saying he would "continue to stand proudly alongside our fighters".
DEATH THREATS AND BEATINGS ALLEGED
Prosecutors said activists detained after the first mission had reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism.
Activists involved in the second mission reported even harsher treatment, including beatings in the dark, the use of tasers and rubber bullets, the statement said.
Investigators had identified various individuals forming the military and police chains of command involved in the operations, prosecutors said.
Besides Katz and Ben-Gvir, prosecutors named 12 senior Israeli military, police and prison officials as suspects, including military chief Eyal Zamir.
Zamir also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Prosecutors said they had sent Israel a request for judicial assistance in June, seeking information needed to reconstruct events and establish individual responsibility. They did not say whether Israeli authorities had responded.
The prosecutors said they had also held talks at the European Union's judicial cooperation agency Eurojust because similar investigations into the two flotilla missions were under way in other unnamed European countries.
Under Italian law, crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens can be prosecuted in Rome.
Being placed under investigation in Italy does not imply guilt and does not automatically lead to a trial. However, if the probe determines that charges are warranted, prosecutors could lodge a formal request for trial.
Flotilla organisers say they aimed to break Israel's blockade of Gaza by delivering humanitarian assistance. Israel says its naval blockade on Gaza is lawful.

The 16-year-old who killed three children and a teacher at an elementary school in the US state of Oregon was a former special-needs student at the school, police and school officials have said.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz identified the attacker on Friday, a day after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, as Griffin J. John II.
He said the teenager attacked a classroom of special-needs students, where all the victims were shot.
Steven Cook, superintendent of Bend-La Pine Schools, said John was not enrolled in the local public school system at the time.
“That classroom was a special needs classroom, and the suspect was a special needs student in that school,” Cook told a news conference.
Krantz said John shot his way through locked doors with a 12-gauge shotgun, firing as many as 15 shots, and had about 44 rounds left when he was killed. Police are still trying to determine how he obtained the gun.
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or with a parent’s consent.
The shooter’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, separately told reporters outside her apartment: “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something.”
A teacher threw her phone at the gunman, then tackled and fought him, likely saving lives, Krantz said, calling her actions “heroic”. She was not injured.
A 36-year-old father, Kaylub Giamanco, who has two children at the school, then followed the gunman inside and shot him dead minutes after the first 911 call.
US President Donald Trump called Giamanco a “great hero”. “It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump said.
The children killed were aged five, eight and 11, and the teacher was Meghan Lambert, 25, police said.
A seven-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to hospital in critical condition.
The shooting is the 28th mass killing in the US this year, according to a database by The Associated Press, USA Today and Northeastern University.
The Gun Violence Archive in the US has documented 369 mass shootings in 2026, defined as incidents in which four or more people are shot.
The Everytown for Gun Safety group has counted at least 100 incidents of gunfire on school grounds this year, with 34 deaths.

Russia's Rosatom targets year-end nuclear start-up at Turkey's Akkuyu
Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom expects the first reactor at Turkey's Akkuyu nuclear power plant to achieve its first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction before the end of this year, Rosatom head Alexei Likhachev said on Friday.
"We remain on track for the planned physical start-up in the second half of December... We hope that before the end of the year the Turkish unit will transition from the construction phase to the start-up phase," he said.
Moscow and Ankara signed an agreement in 2010 to build a nuclear power plant with four Russian VVER-1200 reactors, but the project has faced repeated delays and bureaucratic hurdles.
Rosatom began construction of the Akkuyu plant in 2018. The commissioning schedule has been repeatedly pushed back from its original 2023 target.
After Moscow launched military action in Ukraine in 2022, pressure on the project increased. Although Rosatom was not targeted by Western sanctions, risks related to payments and other issues remain.
Physical start-up involves fuel loading and achieving first criticality, the reactor's first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. The next major milestone is grid connection and the start of electricity generation.
Likhachev also reported progress in talks with potential partners for the Akkuyu.
He said he had discussed the matter the previous day with Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar, who attended the Russian Energy Week forum.
"We have developed a menu of possible arrangements for a Turkish investor. The choice is primarily up to the Turkish government. I hope that following our meeting, Mr Bayraktar will brief the country's leadership and that the right decisions will be taken."
The Akkuyu project, costing more than $20 billion, is financed by Russia. Rosatom, its sole owner, can sell up to a 49% stake to a partner to share the investment burden.
In April, Rosatom said it started new talks with Turkish companies on joint ownership of Akkuyu after the Iran war spurred interest in such assets.

In brief

Australians have been warned to postpone any planned travel to Saudi Arabia after the government increased its travel advice amid a "volatile" security situation in the Middle East hub.
The Australian government updated its travel advice for Saudi Arabia and its international airport in Riyadh to "do not travel", after fighting between Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement and a Saudi-led military coalition saw strikes on the airport that killed at least 14 and wounded hundreds last week.
A strike on King Khalid International Airport on Saturday killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, with the Houthis claiming responsibility for the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade.
The following Monday, another strike killed one person and injured 11 others, Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said, as the Houthis said the group had attacked other airports and said the worst was yet to come.
The latest advice on the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade's Smartraveller website said Australians should postpone any planned travel to Saudi Arabia, including for religious purposes, avoid travelling to King Khalid International Airport, and exercise extreme caution travelling to any other airports, amid an "unpredictable" security situation.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Following Houthi threats to target Saudi airports and airspace, "air travel is significantly disrupted at all major airports, with regular airspace closures, flight cancellations and delays", the missive read.
The government warned that "do not travel" also meant "do not transit".
"If you choose to travel despite our advice, ensure you understand the risks," it said.
What to do if you're in Saudi Arabia
The government warned that Australians in Saudi Arabia who wish to leave should do so "while commercial options remain available", and, if it is safe to do so, to consider private car, train or bus options, including to aviation hubs Abu Dhabi, in the UAE and Doha, in Qatar.
Travel warnings for Qatar and the UAE, whose transit hubs see millions of people each year, are currently at Level 2 — "exercise a high degree of caution", due to the threat of terrorism and the unpredictable security situation in the region.
Australians are advised not to travel from any Saudi airports, but if they do choose to do so, they should monitor updates, follow the advice of local authorities and airport staff, and minimise time there.
As flights were postponed or delayed with little to no notice, Smartraveller said: "do not leave for any airport until you have reconfirmed your flight with your airline".
"Military strikes and reprisal attacks have occurred across parts of the Middle East region and tensions remain elevated ... Security conditions can deteriorate quickly, and travel advice levels may change at short notice," it said.
People who choose to remain in Saudi Arabia should be prepared to shelter in place at short notice and ensure they have sufficient food, water and other essential supplies, the government warned.
"If a strike occurs, seek shelter in a substantial building and stay away from windows. Falling debris from intercepted missiles and drones also poses a risk," it said.
On Saturday, Britain's foreign office also issued a warning advising against all but essential travel to Saudi Arabia.

Researchers have identified a specific enzyme that clumps up and damages cellular powerhouses in the brains of mice with Alzheimer’s disease. Developing chemical compounds to prevent or eliminate these clumps slowed memory loss and brain cell death in the animals. The findings were published in Cell Reports Medicine.
Alzheimer’s disease involves the buildup of misfolded proteins in the brain, most notably beta-amyloid plaques and tau tangles. These proteins interfere with brain cell function and eventually lead to memory loss and cognitive decline.
A lesser-known player in cell survival is an enzyme called G-protein-coupled receptor kinase 2, or GRK2. In healthy cells, this enzyme usually operates in the main fluid of the cell, where it helps regulate cellular communication and stress responses.
When modified by a specific chemical tag in a process called phosphorylation, GRK2 changes its behavior. It can migrate to mitochondria, the microscopic structures that generate energy for cells.
A research team led by Joshua Abd Alla and Ursula Quitterer at ETH Zurich in Switzerland investigated whether abnormal regulation of this enzyme contributes to the brain damage seen in Alzheimer’s disease. Mitochondrial dysfunction is a major feature of the condition, and the researchers suspected that modified GRK2 might be interfering with these cellular powerhouses.
The team first examined the brain tissue of genetically modified mice that develop Alzheimer’s-like symptoms. They looked specifically at older mice that already exhibited heavy beta-amyloid buildup.
They found that a massive portion of the GRK2 in these mice had clumped together into large, dysfunctional aggregates. These clumps were highly concentrated on the mitochondria within the brain cells of the animals.
When the researchers looked at brain tissue samples from a small study of four human patients with dementia likely caused by Alzheimer’s, they observed the exact same pattern of clumped GRK2. In both the mice and the human samples, the accumulation of this enzyme was accompanied by mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated oxidative stress.
The researchers noted that the presence of beta-amyloid and toxic tau proteins actually triggered the initial phosphorylation and clumping of GRK2 in laboratory models. This suggests a destructive cycle where Alzheimer’s hallmark proteins damage mitochondria by causing GRK2 to clump, which in turn accelerates the buildup of more Alzheimer’s proteins.
To understand how the clumped enzyme causes damage, the researchers analyzed which other proteins it bound to in the mouse brains. They discovered that it attached to a protein called TOMM6, which normally helps transport materials across the outer membrane of mitochondria.
The researchers then tested the chemical interaction between GRK2 and TOMM6 in laboratory dishes. They observed that active, healthy GRK2 typically adds a chemical tag to TOMM6, keeping it stable and functional.
The clumped, modified version of GRK2 found in the diseased brains was inactive and failed to modify TOMM6. Without this chemical tag, TOMM6 also began to clump up and lose its ability to interact with the mitochondrial pores.
The scientists next bred new strains of mice to genetically force different versions of the GRK2 enzyme into their brains. When they introduced an inactive, clumping version of GRK2, the mice developed severe mitochondrial damage, rapid beta-amyloid accumulation, and died at an accelerated rate.
Conversely, breeding mice to produce extra active, healthy GRK2 protected the animals against these symptoms and improved their survival. In another genetic test, the researchers engineered mice to produce extra TOMM6 to compensate for the amount lost to clumping.
While extra TOMM6 reduced the large plaques of beta-amyloid, it unexpectedly caused a different, soluble form of beta-amyloid to build up. This soluble buildup was highly toxic to the brain cells, leading to an increased mortality rate in the animals.
Because simply adding TOMM6 was harmful, the team tried a pharmacological approach to fix the root of the problem. They developed a small chemical compound called CPD10, designed to stabilize GRK2 and prevent it from adopting the harmful, clumping shape.
Using computer modeling, the researchers found that CPD10 preferentially attaches to the healthy, unphosphorylated form of GRK2. By binding to this active form, the compound shifts the cellular balance, making it much harder for the enzyme to become phosphorylated and clump together.
They administered this compound to aging Alzheimer’s mice over a six-month period. The compound successfully penetrated the brain and prevented the enzyme from clumping on the mitochondria.
The mice treated with CPD10 had healthier mitochondria, fewer beta-amyloid plaques, less toxic tau protein, and experienced less brain cell loss than untreated mice. Behavioral tests in a water maze showed that the treated mice also retained better spatial memory.
The researchers explored a second chemical strategy aimed at removing the existing clumps rather than preventing new ones. They synthesized another molecule, CPD57, designed to boost the activity of the proteasome, which acts as the garbage disposal system of the cell.
Cells naturally use the proteasome to break down damaged or unnecessary proteins, preventing toxic buildups. The CPD57 compound physically binds to the opening of this disposal system, acting like a gate opener to let more waste inside.
They treated older Alzheimer’s mice with this compound for 14 days and evaluated their brain tissue. The compound increased the cellular garbage disposal activity and successfully degraded the clumped GRK2 and TOMM6 proteins.
When given over a six-month period, this molecule also slowed the accumulation of beta-amyloid plaques and reduced signs of cellular aging. The findings demonstrate that targeting these protein clumps from multiple pharmacological angles can offer neurological protection in animal models.
While these chemical compounds showed promising results in mice, animal models of Alzheimer’s disease do not perfectly replicate the human condition. The human tissue analysis in this study relied on a very limited number of brain samples obtained during surgery for brain tumors.
Because these samples were taken during active operations rather than after death, they provided a rare snapshot of the living brain’s chemistry, but the sample size was inherently small. Larger studies involving more human patients are necessary to confirm how widespread this specific enzyme clumping is in the general population.
It remains an open question whether the clumped enzyme on the mitochondria is the primary driver of the brain damage, or if the overall lack of healthy, active GRK2 floating elsewhere in the cell is the real culprit. Future research using organisms entirely deficient in GRK2 will help pinpoint the exact mechanism behind the cellular deterioration.
Extensive safety and efficacy testing will be required before either of the newly developed chemical compounds can be considered for human clinical trials. These findings provide a new pharmacological avenue to protect the aging brain.
The study, “Analysis of GRK2 aggregation in the pathology of Alzheimer disease in animal models,” was authored by Joshua Abd Alla, Alexander Perhal, Xuebin Fu, Andreas Langer, Yasser el Faramawy, and Ursula Quitterer.

TOKYO, October 17. /TASS/. Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has sent an offering to the Yasukuni Shinto shrine, which is considered a symbol of militarism in China and several other Asian countries, according to Kyodo news agency.
Takaichi, as Kyodo notes, refrained from making a personal visit to the shrine not to create diplomatic problems with South Korea and China, which react sharply to such pilgrimages. Before becoming prime minister, Takaichi regularly visited this shrine twice a year, including as a minister. The last time the head of the Japanese government personally made a pilgrimage to Yasukuni was in December 2013, when Shinzo Abe held that position.
The current offering was made on the occasion of the traditional autumn festival celebrated at the shrine. Takaichi’s previous offering on the occasion of the 81st anniversary of the announcement of Tokyo’s surrender in World War II, which was marked on August 15 of this year, was made not as the head of the government, but as the leader of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party.
This Shinto shrine, located in the center of Tokyo, houses lists of names of the Japanese people who died on the battlefield since the second half of the 19th century. The list also includes war criminals who were executed after Tokyo’s surrender in World War II by order of the International Military Tribunal. Visits to Yasukuni by Japanese officials provoke protests and are perceived in China, South Korea, and other Asian countries as a justification of Japanese aggression.

What's next?
The Rugby World Cup will be held in Australia beginning on October 1 next year.
Mark Nawaqanitawase is refusing to rule out turning his back on Australia for next year's home Rugby World Cup as a three-nation tug-of-war for the cross-code super talent escalates.
While Wallabies captain Harry Wilson and coach Les Kiss have no doubts Nawaqanitawase will be wearing the gold jumper at the 2027 global showpiece, the player himself is keeping his options open.
The in-demand winger's manager this week suggested Nawaqanitawase may choose to represent Fiji, to honour his father's heritage, or Italy, who the dual international is also eligible for through his grandmother.
Still only 26, the prospect of Nawaqanitawase defecting from Australia had seemed improbable.
Under World Rugby laws, if he chose to switch allegiances, following 11 Test appearances for Australia in 2022-23 before enjoying a hugely successful two-year stint in the NRL, the dual international would not be allowed to wear the Wallabies jumper ever again.
Representing Fiji or Italy could appear a more appealing scenario in the twilight of his career, but not his pomp.

"My only focus right now is moving to Japan in a couple of weeks and connecting with my new team at Saitama Wild Knights.
"I will weigh up my options and make a decision next year on my international future.
"Love, Marky."
After taking in the Kangaroos' thrilling Rugby League World Cup win over New Zealand on Thursday night with Nawaqanitawase in Sydney, Wilson is confident the free agent will be playing for Australia next year.
"I don't have to convince him," Wilson said ahead of the Wallabies' second Bledisloe Cup clash with the All Blacks in Sydney today.
"I played junior Wallabies with him, played Wallabies with him, saw him last night supporting the Kangaroos, so I think it's pretty obvious who he wants to play for."
Coach Kiss is also optimistic about the 2023 Olympic sevens star opting for a Wallabies return next year.
"I think there's no doubt that he wants to be back in the game for us, that's for sure," Kiss said.
"We'll continue our conversations and go from there. I'm not going to speak on his behalf at all. But we know where he wants to play."

President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man. I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to. It was an honor to work for him. https://t.co/Tp4NizrhE2

from laboratory waste to art, discarded research prototypes transform into sculptural objects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
23:35:50 UTC
08:35:50 KST

from laboratory waste to art, discarded research prototypes transform into sculptural objects
what happens to the physical remains of innovation? the form that remained transforms discarded prototypes, failed experiments, and forgotten fragments of scientific research into unique sculptural objects through a process of fragmenting, layering, and fusing materials.
prefer designboom on google
DISCARDED RESEARCH PROTOTYPES turn into SCULPTURAL OBJECTS
Developed by industrial designer and researcher Ruben Moutinho, THE FORM THAT REMAINED transforms discarded research prototypes, experimental models, and obsolete components into a series of one-of-a-kind sculptural objects. The project establishes its material archive directly from scientific and technological development projects, preserving the technical geometries, surface treatments, and structural forms produced during iterative testing and refinement. Rather than concealing their origins, each sculpture retains the name or acronym of its source research project, such as SHESOIL, AUTONOVA, LIVIA, BRIVA, ACTIVA, and UNIKA, as an independent sculptural identity.
Sculptures act as physical archives of scientific process
Central to the collection is STRATA, a material process involving the cutting, fragmenting, collage, overlapping, and fusion of components harvested from a single research initiative. The assembly method brings together technical structures and organic shapes, exposing diverse colors, textures, and material characteristics without masking the boundaries between individual parts. By shifting discarded prototypes out of their original functional context, the process designer Ruben Moutinho follows produces non-reproducible objects with irregular geometries and layered surfaces, converting temporary experimental remains into permanent sculptural artifacts.
project info:
name: THE FORM THAT REMAINED
designer: Ruben Moutinho
designboom has received this project from our DIY submissions feature, where we welcome our readers to submit their own work for publication. See more project submissions from our readers here.

Albanian PM blames ‘foreign hands’ for unrest as student protests intensify
Riot police clash with protesters for fourth day, as young Albanians protest corruption and poor university conditions
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has blamed “foreign hands” for the increasingly violent student-led protests that are calling on him to resign.
Riot police clashed with protesters outside the education ministry for the fourth day in a row, as thousands of young Albanians marched through the capital, Tirana, on Friday to protest government corruption and poor university conditions.
“This is not a student phenomenon,” Rama said in a video address on Friday. He said there were “foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace”.
Rama insisted that the protest had “absolutely nothing to do with the hardships, problems or legitimate aspirations of anyone who desires a better life”.
Police officers used water cannon and tear gas as demonstrators hurled rocks.
The protests have spread beyond the capital to Elbasan, Shkodra and Korca, where demonstrators broke windows and set fire to rubbish bins, local media reported.
The ongoing escalation follows months of mostly peaceful demonstrations, originally sparked by the sale of part of Albania’s coastline to a luxury resort development linked to Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.
Days of unrest have increasingly targeted banks and government buildings. Protesters hurled bricks and concrete blocks at the education ministry on Tuesday. They also set fire to several buildings across the city, including the prime minister’s office, the finance and justice ministry buildings and branches of several banks.
According to a police statement, 160 people were detained over alleged acts of violence on Thursday evening.
The EU question
Demonstrators are demanding Rama’s resignation, as well as electoral and education reforms.
The prime minister, whose government denies corruption, said he would be ready to discuss rising education costs but rejected the calls to resign.
He said on Thursday, “My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward.”
His dismissal “would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership”, he added.
Corruption scandals have complicated Albania’s efforts to join the EU. Analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking.
Rama won a fourth term last year on promises to take Albania into the EU, aiming for membership as early as 2028.
