US deficit hits $2T in a year, highest level since 2021
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:31:15 UTC
05:31:15 KST

The US budget deficit has grown to almost $2 trillion over the past year, reaching its highest level since 2021.
The expansion comes amid growing worries about the massive $40.3 trillion US debt load, rising inflation, and climbing borrowing costs.
Refunds of the Trump administration's tariffs, after they were overturned, have further widened the budget gap.
The federal deficit, which occurs when government spending exceeds its revenues, rose to $1.99 trillion in fiscal year 2026, the Treasury Department said.
This marked a 12-percent increase from the prior year, when the shortfall came in at $1.78 trillion.
A key driver of expenditures was the rising interest paid on public debt, which jumped $144 billion to a record $1.36 trillion.
Interest costs on around $32 trillion in publicly held US debt have been ballooning in recent years, and climbing bond yields have sparked further concerns.
Treasury bond yields, which influence interest rates for mortgages and auto loans, have jumped this year, with steeper borrowing costs adding to pressures that US voters face ahead of November's midterm elections.
Treasury data released Friday showed $145 billion in customs refunds over the year, primarily from tariffs, erasing significant gains from Trump's duties.
Overall, government revenues climbed by three percent to $5.40 trillion in the latest fiscal year, which ended September 30.
But spending was much higher, rising by six percent to $7.40 trillion.
War risks
The Trump administration has pledged to cut deficits and government spending since it returned to the White House last year.
Besides slashing the federal workforce and foreign aid, the Republican-controlled Congress pushed through cuts to the Medicaid health insurance scheme and moved to shrink the federal food assistance program too.
But they also extended expiring tax cuts and provided fresh funding for administration’s migrant deportation drive.
The latest data released on Friday showed that higher tax collections from individuals and customs revenues were offset by more refunds and lower corporate tax collections.
Among other sectors, spending on defence military programs increased by $48 billion, or six percent, over the year to $917 billion.
Taken together, a Treasury official estimates the US deficit-to-GDP ratio is around 6.2 percent, up from 5.8 percent last year.
This stands in contrast to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's previously stated goal of bringing the deficit down to three percent of GDP, alongside other targets like spurring economic growth of three percent.
The latest budget figures come less than three weeks before US midterm elections, where US President Trump's Republican party is fighting to retain control of Congress.
Ahead of the crucial vote, both Republicans and Democrats have raised ideas that could widen the budget shortfall further.
Democrats say they are looking to reverse Medicaid cuts and revive health care tax breaks.

The Trap Was Only 100 Meters Wide. Russian Troops Kept Walking Into Ukraine’s Kill Zone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:29:46 UTC
05:29:46 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
The Trap Was Only 100 Meters Wide. Russian Troops Kept Walking Into Ukraine’s Kill Zone
Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps has detailed unusually heavy Russian losses during Operation Vivaldi, which its commanders attribute to the tactical isolation of the combat zone, according to the video released on October 16.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In the footage, Kucher, a battalion commander in the 3rd Army Corps, claimed his unit killed more than 250 Russian troops at one location. Another commander, Zhora, explained how Ukrainian forces used the terrain to their advantage against Russian troops.
“This site is interesting because it has a small open area, about 100 meters,” Zhora stated. He noted that Russian troops did not understand Ukrainian maneuvers for a long time and kept sending reinforcements to the same spot. “He had no other option than to constantly send infantry exactly where we needed them,” he explained.
Kucher described a pattern in which Russian commanders, seeing no progress, kept ordering fresh waves forward. He recalled that a Russian soldier would emerge to film the area with his phone, and Ukrainian troops deliberately left him alone.
“The guy comes out, shoots everything on camera, we don’t touch him on purpose, he turns back, the crowd runs for 15 minutes. The crowd dies,” Kucher said of the sequence, according to the footage.
An hour later, he added, the same routine repeated, with the following wave running for 20 minutes before being destroyed. Kucher described the scene as “quite humiliating.” He also stated that Ukrainian forces knowingly avoided striking a nearby checkpoint or capture point in a small forest area, so that Russian commanders would keep feeding troops into the kill zone.
Kucher said the dead came from across Russian ranks. They included:
- artillerymen;
- assault groups;
- pilots who were rotating in or out of the area;
- about a dozen and a half special forces troops from one of the regiments.
The commanders presented isolation as the decisive factor. “We completely hid his infantry maneuvers at the tactical level, which led to additional losses and the inability to build normal defense around the green valley,” Kucher declared. “In terms of enemy losses, this is the biggest result, in fact.”
Zhora outlined the operation’s objective. “The ultimate goal was to take control of all logistical routes, cut off the forces of the enemy, which hold the defense, from possible replenishment, rotation, and some infantry maneuvers,” he wrote. He added that the aim was also to create an encirclement zone.
Zhora concluded that cooperation among all branches of the 3rd Army Corps was highly effective during the operation. In his words, it allowed the corps to work efficiently and “save a large number of our infantrymen’s lives.”
The losses come as Operation Vivaldi continues to push Russian forces back in the Donetsk region. By September 20, the 3rd Army Corps had taken full control of Drobysheve and liberated Shandryholove and Derylove, bringing the territory returned across the operation's first two seasons to 125 square kilometers.
Another 800 Russian troops were killed in that phase, pushing total losses across both seasons above 3,000 personnel. The first season alone cleared 75 square kilometers of the northern Donetsk region and retook Novoselivka, Oleksandrivka, and Yarova.

Morocco's King Mohammed VI appoints new government
Morocco's King Mohammed VI formally appointed on Friday the members of his country's new government, led for the first time in its history by a woman prime minister, Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri.
Her centre-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) came out on top in September elections, and has entered into a coalition with the right-wing Istiqlal party and two smaller left-wing parties. Together they hold 210 of the parliament's 395 seats.
Thirteen out of 31 ministers from the previous government were retained in the incoming cabinet, including Nasser Bourita as Minister of Foreign Affairs and Abdelouafi Laftit as Minister of the Interior.
PAM newcomer Fouzi Lekjaa -- a budget minister in the outgoing government better known as the head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation -- has been promoted to economy minister.
The new government also includes seven women, counting the prime minister, as did the previous one.
Following her royal audience on Friday, Mansouri touted an "ambitious government programme that can meet citizens' expectations".
September's vote, which saw the lowest turnout in nearly 20 years, was marked by concerns about the cost of living, employment and inequality.
The incoming government will have to address those concerns while also preparing for the 2030 World Cup, which will be co-hosted with Spain and Portugal.

AOC transfers $1m to Michigan candidate El-Sayed in progressive push
Progressive stalwart, who is seen as potential 2028 candidate, says she wants to combat ‘smears’ against El-Sayed.
United States Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has transferred $1m to support Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, in a major progressive push for the upstart politician.
Ocasio-Cortez, who has become a progressive stalwart since her surprise 2018 congressional victory, confirmed the donation in a statement on Friday and a speech in Michigan. The transfer was first reported by the New York Times.
The lawmaker pointed to political attacks against El-Sayed, a large portion of which have focused on his Muslim faith, his Egyptian heritage and support for Palestine.
“I’m not waking up on November 4th wishing I did more to combat the smears aimed at Abdul,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement, in reference to the November 3 congressional midterm election. “I’m leaving everything I can on the field.”
Speaking at an event in the Detroit area, Ocasio added that she transferred the money from her own campaign to show “the cavalry is coming”.
“And the only reason I’m doing that is because I see the energy of each and every one of you stepping up to make an effort,” she said.
The move comes as Ocasio-Cortez has been campaigning for El-Sayed in Michigan, joining him on a bus tour of the conservative-leaning Upper Peninsula area before hosting three events on Friday in the state’s largest city, Detroit.
El Sayed’s populist progressive message has gained traction with voters in the state, where he currently leads Republican Mike Rogers by 2.6 percentage points, according to a Real Clear Politics average of high-quality polls.
The support from Ocasio Cortez, who is weighing a potential 2028 presidential candidacy, also underscores a wider effort by progressives to court disaffected Trump voters. The pair highlighted economic issues while on the trail in the midwestern state.
Trump’s approval ratings are at a career low ahead of the midterm vote. A slate of recent polls has shown widespread public disapproval of Trump’s handling of the US economy and the knock-on effects of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Recent polls have also shown an appetite for a more comprehensive change in US government, signalling a potential opening for candidates running outside of the establishment of both major parties.
An AP-NORC poll released this week found that 80 percent of respondents said they supported either a “complete and total upheaval” or “substantial change” in how the country is run.
Speaking alongside Ocasio-Cortez on Friday, progressive House Representative Ayanna Pressley called on the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which raises and allocates funds for Senate candidates, to make “an equitable investment in progressive and diverse candidates” like El-Sayed, Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon and Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom.
El-Sayed, who received an early endorsement from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, has also recently been embraced by a handful of more centrist Democrats, including former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris. Sanders donated $250,000 to El-Sayed’s campaign, CNN reports.
Big spending
The new financial support from Ocasio-Cortez, which was given to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, arrived as the Michigan Senate race has become one of the most expensive in the state’s history, topping $268m as of October 15, according to the Detroit Free Press.
El-Sayed, meanwhile, outpaced Rogers in fundraising from July 1 to September 30, bringing in $30.6m compared to Rogers’ $9.6m. Still, Rogers’ campaign had more cash on hand as of September 30, with $6.5m compared to El-Sayed’s $3.8 million.
Michigan is among the key Senate races that could determine control of the chamber for the final two years of US President Donald Trump’s term.
Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the 100-member body.

Jillaroos lived up to their end of the bargain, but fans need to follow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:06:12 UTC
05:06:12 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
analysis
Jillaroos lived up to their end of the bargain in Rugby League World Cup opener. Now fans need to follow
Seeing the Jillaroos in action is a rare privilege — a collection of the best women's rugby league players in the world, in the sport's global showpiece, on home soil.
The three-time defending champions opened their World Cup at Western Sydney Stadium with a flexing 40-0 win over Samoa, in a campaign that should engage and excite Australians and the vast diaspora of the other competing nations.
While that was the case for the earlier men's game between Samoa and France, with 13,174 fans, mostly representing western Sydney's large Samoan community, they left in large numbers at the end of that game.
And there were very few supporters — Samoan or Australian — left by the end of the women's clash, in a disappointing sight for an event of this stature.
This is not a new dilemma for women's sport. When and where to play, whether to have double headers, how best to engage existing fan bases and draw in new ones?
Women's State of Origin has been a good example of elevating the women's game in its own way, standing separately to the men's series, often in smaller venues, but packing them with passionate fans who are there only to watch the women. And drawing big numbers on TV too.
The World Cup presents a different challenge, with Australia currently in a league of its own on the field and another trophy considered by many as a fait accompli.
But the world is starting to catch up, and as the tournament progresses over the next month, it would be a shame for the event to go under the radar.
Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner summed it up simply afterwards.
"Let's get around women in sport, right? All women in sport, and particularly this Rugby League World Cup. We've got a lot of talented women across all of the teams," she said.
"Stay and support that and the growth. Something really cool is happening in this generation of sport with our ladies, and you're going to miss it.
"There's history making moments over this World Cup, no doubt, and want to see our fans, particularly in the green and gold, to be a part of that. But also just in general, come and have a look."
Samoa coach Frank Pritchard suggested the late 8pm kick off didn't help, and the women were keen to play before the men.
"Our fans and our supporters will always stick through it and and stay there," he said.
"I've seen a lot of blue jerseys out there. We had plenty of support, that's for sure."
Jillaroos captain Isabelle Kelly was less concerned with the crowd, than with ensuring the Jillaroos achieve what they set out to at this tournament. And all signs point to a four-peat.
Jillaroos just warming up
It was a straightforward win for the Australians, who were not at their ruthless, rampaging best, but instead showed they are warming to the task, and will likely ignite as the tournament progresses.
Five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher had an impressive first outing in the green and gold. She was player of the match on debut, continuing the form that saw her guide the Sydney Roosters to the NRLW Premiership.
"Her kicking game was amazing. And she took her opportunities when she had them as well," Skinner said.
"So couldn't get better than that in a World Cup debut for the Jillaroos, become part of a legacy piece, and you get player of the match. So really proud of her."
Olivia Kernick made crucial gains through the middle, Tamika Upton pulled the strings in bursts without being at her fully devastating best, and Jaime Chapman, Julia Robinson, and Jess Sergis surged as needed, with all seven tries scored by different players.
There were scrappy moments though, times where Samoa's defence jolted, and the visitors found ways to cut through the Australians when going direct.
Freedom Crichton Ropati's bone cruncher on Tiana Penitani Gray in the dying minutes was a highlight, epitomising Fetu Samoa's dedication to valiantly protecting their line, even with the result long gone.
Leading 28-0 at half time, the Jillaroos were restricted to just two tries after the break.
Overall, it was an effort that was enough for the Jillaroos to be content, without being complacent, and for Samoa to find light at the end of the tunnel, rather than wallowing in darkness.
"We spoke about pride in the jersey and what it takes to be here, sea of blue, effort on effort, and definitely showed that in the second half," Pritchard said.
"That second half proved to us that competing and staying in the fight is more than just a footy game."
Starting to see it
Athletes often speak of the honour of representing their country and their family on the world stage.
But for many of the Pasifika nations competing at this tournament, filled with players from the diaspora in Australia and New Zealand, it hits a little different.
As with the men, tears streamed down the faces of the Fetu Samoa players during the national anthem.
And they continued afterwards, not of disappointment, but of deep understanding of what it means to be here.
"What our ladies are doing for our young girls at home with sport in general, especially rugby league, is massive," Pritchard said.
"It's something that our girls can gravitate towards."
It was an especially meaningful game for Evania Isa'ako, who has previously represented Australia.
"For me, it was not just coming and playing and putting on this jersey; it was being able to learn [about the culture]," she said.
"So off the field, culturally, everything that we've done. All the work that Frank's put in behind the scenes… outsourced people to come in and teach us, that's the really important stuff behind the scenes that people don't see."
They might not see it yet, but come the end of the tournament, maybe there'll be more eyes watching.

Iran has denied having anything to do with attacks by Yemen's Houthis, a day after Saudi Arabia said Iran had encouraged the militia's recent escalation against the country.
"The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations," Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement on Friday.
Baqaei said the Houthi militias act according to their own interests and assessments, while arguing that claims about Iranian involvement were not credible. He added that Tehran did not view an escalation of tensions as being in the interest of any party.
Since Yemen's civil war flared back to life in July, Iran-allied militant group has repeatedly struck Saudi targets including Red Sea tankers, oil facilities and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last week. Riyadh says 19 people have been killed and over 360 wounded in attacks on its airports.
A Saudi-led military coalition has supported Yemen's internationally recognised government for more than a decade, and reported on Friday having intercepted more missiles and drones as the kingdom comes under sustained attack from the Houthi militia.
A day earlier, a Saudi foreign ministry official said Iran had "encouraged" the escalation, which Tehran denied.
The Saudi official, deputy minister for public diplomacy Rayed Krimly, had said the Houthis rejected an offer to meet in Oman at the outset of the latest round of hostilities.
Baqaei however reiterated an offer to mediate between the two sides, saying Tehran "has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities".
Ballistic missile intercepted
On Friday, a spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition said it had "intercepted and destroyed three drones in the southern area and Riyadh... and two cruise missiles over the Red Sea".
He added that "in the past hours, we intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile over Yanbu", a city home to the terminus of a major oil pipeline on the Red Sea coast.
The Houthi militia attacks have proliferated since the group launched a lightning offensive in Yemen in September, seizing strategic government-held territory along the Red Sea coast overlooking a major chokepoint for global shipping.
The pressure on Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, comes as global energy markets were already rattled by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz at the outset of the wider US-Israeli war on Iran in February.
Krimly, of the Saudi foreign ministry, accused Iran on Thursday of continuing "to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN security council resolutions".
Yemeni government forces have launched a counteroffensive with Saudi air support to retake areas seized by the Houthi militia, but have so far failed to reverse their gains.
On Friday, the local security office in Aden, the government's interim capital, said two missiles landed within the perimetre of the city's airport, "in the second incident of its kind in less than a week", adding that no one was killed.
The day before, the militant group launched a deadly missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden, killing five people and wounding 16 others, according to the health minister.
Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani denounced the "cowardly" act on X, calling it a "continuation of (the Houthis') criminal pattern".
A government minister said on condition of anonymity that the Houthis hit command centres for Yemeni and Saudi coalition forces housed at the palace complex.
Media affiliated with the Houthis said the attack had targeted "the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden".

South African number three David Bedingham has spoken of the need for his team to wear down Australia's bowlers if they are to level the Test series.
Only Aidan Markram made 50 in the first Test, and South Africa have axed two batters for the second game in the three-match series.
What's next?
ABC Sport will live-blog the second Test in Gqeberha, starting on Sunday night.
South Africa have vowed to do better at wearing Australia's bowlers down in the second Test, desperate to rebound after the batters' meek surrender in Durban.
The Proteas are set to welcome back pace ace Kagiso Rabada for Sunday's second Test in Gqeberha, after he terrorised Australia on the last tour in 2018.
But the hosts have pointed to their batting as the biggest bridge that must be mended between the two sides after the series-opening 214-run defeat.
Aiden Markram was the only Protea to pass 50 in the Test, with seven others scoring between 30 and 49 across both innings.
That prompted coach Shukri Conrad to claim he was "pulling the very last strands out of his hair" as he axed both Tristan Stubbs and Kyle Verreynne.
South Africa number three David Bedingham spoke of the relentless nature of Australia's attack on Friday, with Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon offering little reprieve.
But with the three Tests in this series essentially being played back-to-back, he stressed the importance of putting work into the Australian bowlers.
"It's just about trying to take them to 80 overs, 100 overs, 120 overs," Bedingham said.
"And then, I know they're machines, but everyone gets tired eventually. Well, hopefully…
"When Kesh (Maharaj) and Simon (Harmer) were batting around the 68th over in the first innings, I'm not saying they were tiring, but the ball was a lot softer.
"It looked a lot easier. So if we could have maybe been four, five down there, then maybe the game would have a different angle."
Meanwhile, Rabada looks almost certain to play, as the Proteas fight to avoid their first home series defeat since England toured in 2019-20.
Rabada's record of 58 wickets at 21.39 is the second best of any quick against Australia this century, behind only Jasprit Bumrah.
He was the Proteas' arch-villain in the 2018 series, colliding with Steve Smith after taking his wicket in Gbqerha (then Port Elizabeth) and only avoiding a ban on appeal.
Rabada has steamed in at South Africa training this week, showing no signs of the hamstring tear that sidelined him for through the ODIs and first Test.
"He's massive for us," Bedingham said.
"It looks like he's quick again, he's sharp.
"Even if you look back last year in the World Test Championship final, he took nine wickets against Australia.
"Against any team he plays against, he's ready. Hopefully, come this next Test, he takes nine or 10 wickets; that would be quite nice."
Batters Marques Ackerman and Matthew Breetzke are expected to come in at St George's Park, with Ryan Rickelton to take gloves from Verreynne.

Israeli settlers attack US photographer covering West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:48:07 UTC
04:48:07 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli settlers attack US photographer covering West Bank violence
Israeli settlers on Friday attacked an American photojournalist working for The Washington Post while she was covering violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the occupied West Bank.
Heidi Levine, a veteran photographer, was taken to hospital in Ramallah following the attack, with photos showing her lying on a gurney with injuries to her leg and hand.
The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, days ahead of elections in which he is seeking settlers' support, insisted the circumstances behind the incident were unclear, in contrast with the full-throated condemnation offered by his chief rival.
The attack comes 10 days after settlers beat an AFP photographer covering the West Bank olive harvest, Jaafar Ashtiyeh, leaving him also requiring hospital treatment.
Speaking to journalists from her hospital bed, Levine said that "more than 50" masked settlers holding sticks suddenly attacked her while she was working near the Palestinian villages of Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya in the central West Bank.
"All of a sudden they jumped me and I luckily had my helmet and flak jacket on and I... kept my face to the ground to try to protect my face," she said.
"They just kept kicking me and kicking me," she added.
After receiving initial care in Ramallah, Levine was transferred to Israel's Beilinson Hospital in Petah Tikva, where doctors found she had suffered four broken vertebrae and would need surgery.
The Washington Post said Levine had been wearing a flak jacket clearly marked "Press".
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," Matt Murray, the paper's executive editor, said in a statement.
'No mercy'
Netanyahu's office said Levine had been "allegedly assaulted", adding that the circumstances were "unclear and are under investigation".
"Those responsible will be held accountable," it said in an X post, giving a version of events in which "some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths", with both sides throwing objects at the other.
Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main rival in the upcoming polls, blamed Friday's "unacceptable" attack on a "handful of rioters" whose actions, he said, "stain an entire nation".
A US State Department official said it condemned "criminal violence by any party in the West Bank" and called for "legal accountability for those responsible".
The official added the department had "reached out to the Washington Post to offer consular assistance".
AFP news agency reported that a journalist working for the agency reported witnessing Palestinian medics tending to someone in the area and Israeli soldiers pushing away journalists trying to approach.
The Israeli military said troops and border police forces were deployed to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation".
"A female journalist had been injured during the confrontation," it said, adding the circumstances would be examined.
"Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable acts," the military said.
The Israeli police said it had opened an investigation into incidents in Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya.
"We were on our land, picking olives, and suddenly the settlers came down on us and started hitting us, throwing stones," said Mukhlis Zuhdi, a farmer from Abu Falah.
"There was even a foreign journalist whom they beat. These people have no mercy or compassion in their hearts," he told AFP.
'Brazen violence'
The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories, said the settlers stole Levine's passport, phone, wallet and equipment.
"This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank," it said.
Reporters Without Borders said it strongly condemned the attack and called on Israeli authorities to "put an end to this impunity and prosecute the perpetrators of this heinous assault".
"This brazen violence... is evidence of the impunity with which extremist Jewish settlers operate, often under the protection of Israeli armed forces," added the advocacy group, known by its French initials RSF.
Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank, with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.
Excluding east Jerusalem, around three million Palestinians live in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, alongside more than 500,000 Israelis residing in settlements considered illegal under international law.

EU leaders task European Commission with finding €70 billion for Ukraine in 2027
The European Council on 16 October tasked the European Commission with preparing proposals to cover Ukraine's €70 billion budget shortfall for 2027.
Source: a European Pravda correspondent in Brussels, citing a statement by European Council President António Costa following this week's European Council meeting
Details: The European Commission must prepare proposals on where the EU can find the money to cover the gap in Ukraine's funding needs for 2027, as outlined by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"We asked the Commission to come forward with a proposal to address Ukraine's additional financing needs for 2027," Costa said.
He did not provide further details about plans for funding for Ukraine next year.
European Pravda spoke to a senior EU official familiar with the discussion at the 16 October meeting among EU leaders about funding for Ukraine which preceded the decision, and learned more about the plans.
According to the official, the proposal is still at an early stage, so no specific date has been set for its preparation.
"It is too early to talk about dates and timelines. Our counterparts at the European Commission now need to wake up, catch up on the news and realise what they need to do next," the official told European Pravda.
The official noted that it was "not necessarily the case that this proposal needs to be approved by the end of the year".
The idea is that efforts to find additional funding could continue until the entire €90 billion loan has been exhausted, including the €45 billion allocated for 2027.
Asked by European Pravda whether the European Commission's forthcoming proposal might recommend using Russian assets frozen in the EU to fund Ukraine, the official said there was no answer to that question yet.
Previously: The European Commission acknowledged that Ukraine's budget really does face a €70 billion shortfall in 2027, which international partners will have to cover.
European Pravda's sources in the EU explained that Ukraine's stated need for €70 billion in international funding comes on top of the money earmarked for 2027 under the EU's €90 billion loan.
The European Council's decision followed Zelenskyy's address to EU member state leaders on 16 October, in which he said Ukraine would need at least €70 billion in additional financial assistance from international partners in 2027.
Background: EU and Ukrainian representatives concluded during a joint meeting on 1 October that Ukraine currently does not require additional international funding in 2026.

Ukraine Seeks to Scale Up Civilian Protection With Finland’s Support
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held talks with Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on October 16 to address the urgent need for expanded protective infrastructure across Ukrainian cities.
Discussions focused on safeguarding civil energy grids and municipal facilities against ongoing Russian aerial strikes, according to President Zelenskyy.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The discussions focused on speeding up joint defense efforts and deploying additional interceptor assets to protect critical infrastructure.
During the discussion, both leaders prioritized the progress of the Shelter Coalition, a collaborative effort created alongside Helsinki to ensure accessible and secure protective facilities in every local municipality.
President Zelenskyy emphasized the imperative to accelerate civil defense preparations and noted that additional defense decisions and support measures from Finland are anticipated later this month.
"Together with Finland, we established the Shelter Coalition, and now this work needs to be accelerated. Proper shelters must be available in every Ukrainian city and community," President Zelenskyy stated.
"We constantly need weapons to shoot down missiles and drones, to protect human lives and critical infrastructure facilities. There will be new decisions in support of Ukraine this month. Finland always helps us, and we deeply appreciate this," he added.
At the same time, Ukraine is set to receive an additional 15,000 long-range artillery shells from Denmark as part of a new military aid package, with a portion of the ammunition already delivered, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense.
In October 2025, Finland confirmed that its network of more than 50,500 bomb shelters was fully operational and capable of accommodating 4.8 million people, according to government assessments.
The nation's civil defense inventory showed that nearly 91% of the shelters were built to withstand conventional attacks, while 83% included air filtration systems designed to protect against nuclear, biological, or chemical threats.

GTA developer denies firing staff over union activity
A senior executive at Rockstar Games, the developer behind the Grand Theft Auto video game, denied monitoring employees' union membership as an employment tribunal examined the dismissal of 34 workers, Anadolu Agency reports.
Robert Spampinato, the company's vice president of human resources, told the tribunal in Glasgow, Scotland, that allegations he had instructed managers to "keep tabs" on union membership were "categorically not true."
Twenty-three former employees, most previously based at Rockstar North in Edinburgh, are challenging their October 2025 dismissals with support from the Independent Workers' Union of Great Britain (IWGB).
The union alleges the workers were targeted for trade union activities, while Rockstar maintains they were dismissed for sharing confidential company information on a Discord server.
The tribunal heard that an anonymous employee had passed information about union meetings and recruitment activities to Human Resources managers.
Spampinato acknowledged that the information helped management follow workplace grievances but denied any attempt to suppress union activity.
Asked why the dismissals occurred in October 2025 despite some information being available earlier, he said Rockstar was in "crisis mode" because of delays to Grand Theft Auto 6.
"We were in a moment when we knew we were running late on the development," he said.
The game is scheduled for release on Nov. 19 after two delays.
The tribunal proceedings are continuing.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Rockstar Games’ upcoming PS5 lineup includes the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI, scheduled for release on November 19, 2026, while updated versions of Red Dead Redemption 2 and Grand Theft Auto IV were reportedly in development.

Nirit is travelling 14,000km to vote in Israel's election. She's not alone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:38:26 UTC
04:38:26 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Nirit Eylon immigrated to Australia 21 years ago. This month, for the first time, she’s flying back to Israel specifically to vote.
The country does not allow citizens living abroad to vote from outside its borders.
But with an election many view as the most consequential in its history fast approaching, estimates from the US-based Fly&Vote initiative, which helps facilitate their travel, suggest as many as 53,000 Israeli expats are expected to return.
Eylon is among them.
"There is a perception that this election is about right and left. I don't believe it's so. I believe it's between right and wrong," the 52-year-old, who lives in Melbourne, tells SBS News.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Eylon believes Israel is at a crossroads. She views the election as a contest between competing visions of the country’s future: one grounded in liberal democratic values, and another shaped by religious nationalism.
She believes Israel's leaders must be held accountable for failures surrounding the October 7 attacks, and that political change is necessary for Israel to begin to heal.
Eylon is far from alone in viewing this election as pivotal.
Israeli political science expert Shahar Burla, a contributing editor at The Jewish Independent, is one of more than 11,000 Israeli-born people living in Australia.
He tells SBS News he knows around 20 people in his immediate circle who are planning to return to Israel for the election — a circumstance he describes as "very unusual".
"I think that the main motivation is fear," he says.
There is a fear that if the Netanyahu bloc will win again, that will be the end of Israel as we know it as a democratic, liberal, free state.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government has pursued sweeping changes to Israel's institutions, including moves to curb the judiciary’s oversight of government decisions, while pushing increasingly hardline policies towards Palestinians and expanding Israeli military operations across the region, including in Lebanon and Iran.
Ongoing geopolitical tensions and fractured alliances mean the election will be watched closely by many outside Israel too.
SBS News has spoken with nine people from Jewish, Israeli, Palestinian, Lebanese and Iranian communities in Australia about what is at stake for them in this election, as conflict continues to reverberate across the Middle East.
While their views on peace, security and coexistence vary, they share one common belief: that Israel cannot continue on its current path.
For Palestinian Australian academic Shamikh Badra — who lost his father, his brother and his brother’s family to the war in Gaza — a change of government would be welcome, but he cautions it's not a simple fix.
"I am not saying that [the] next government will automatically be better, but removing this government is the first step," he says.
The electoral landscape
Netanyahu, as leader of the Likud party, has served as Israel's prime minister for nearly 20 non-consecutive years since he was first elected in 1996.
In the lead-up to the 27 October election, a relatively new, centrist party called Yashar has been polling neck and neck with Likud.
Former Israel Defense Forces (IDF) chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot leads the party, which takes its name from the Hebrew word for 'straightforward' or 'honest'.
Eisenkot is Netanyahu’s primary challenger to lead the country, and has a personal stake in Israel's ongoing conflicts, having lost both his son and nephew in the Hamas-Israel war.
He's running on a platform of accountability for the October 7 attack, promising to restore trust in Israel's institutions and strengthen national security.
But neither party is close to winning enough seats for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.
That means coalition-building will be crucial to forming government.
Currently, Israel’s parties are divided over their willingness to govern alongside Netanyahu rather than splitting along traditional left-right lines. Two distinct camps remain: those willing to join a Netanyahu-led coalition, and those who may be willing to join one led by Eisenkot.
But neither bloc appears to have a clear path to a parliamentary majority, raising the prospect of political deadlock.
Burla notes that while Eisenkot has positioned himself at the political centre, his prospective coalition spans the political spectrum and includes right-wing parties.
That limits how far a new government could go on issues such as recognising Palestinian statehood and negotiating territorial compromise.
Among Israel's major Jewish-led parties, support for Palestinian statehood remains limited. Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats, is the only major party leader to have endorsed a future two-state solution.
Burla believes changing Israel's leadership could remove a "first obstacle" to peace with Palestinians, but does not expect significant progress in the coming years.
"None of them will speak about a Palestinian state at this stage, or any territorial compromise with the Palestinians.
"But I think that Eisenkot has at least the potential, the political potential, to move forward some kind of a peace process."
High stakes for those with a vote — and those without one
Yasmeen Abu Fraiha is a medical doctor who works with humanitarian missions in the Middle East.
She's one of roughly two million Palestinian citizens of Israel, a group that makes up around 20 per cent of the country’s population.
Fraiha tells SBS News many "feel the urgency in these elections". She believes Palestinian voters will turn out in higher numbers than they have for previous polls.
Palestinian citizens of Israel have historically voted at lower rates than the wider population. In the 2022 election, just over half of Arab and Druze voters cast a ballot, compared with more than 70 per cent nationally, according to the Israel Democracy Institute.
Fraiha, too, feels democracy is at stake. But for Palestinians, she says, the consequences are more fundamental.
"I don't know if it will be necessarily better if [Netanyahu] loses, but it will definitely be worse if they win again," she says.
It’s really a matter of life and death for us as Palestinians, for sure in the West Bank and Gaza, but also inside Israel.
Yet many Palestinians who will be directly affected by the election’s outcome will have no say in it.
Badra, the Sydney-based researcher and community organiser from Gaza, says his family paid the ultimate price under Israel’s current government. His priority is to see it removed from power.
Beyond that, a path to peace will not be easy. But Badra says any lasting solution must address Palestinian rights and security, including an end to occupation and settlement expansion.
"Security for Palestinians means being able to live in your home without fear of bombing. It means children have food, medicine, education. It means people being able to move freely and live with dignity," he says.
"It also means real political and human rights for Palestinians."
On 7 October 2023, Hamas killed 1,200 people and took another 251 captive during its attack on southern Israel.
Israel's retaliatory bombardment of Gaza has decimated much of the strip and killed more than 74,000 people, including more than 1,400 since a ceasefire began last October, according to the local health ministry.
The humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain dire, with critically limited access to food, water and essential services. UNICEF estimates nearly 84 per cent of Gaza’s population continues to live in overcrowded displacement sites or damaged shelters.
Far from Israel, but close to home
The election’s outcome will be felt far beyond Israel. For many Australians like Sam Hoballah, the results will be deeply personal.
Born in southern Lebanon, in a town close to the Israeli border, the Sydney-based interpreter moved to Australia 40 years ago.
However, much of his family still lives in Lebanon, a country scarred by civil war and decades of regional conflict.
As a child, Hoballah says he grew accustomed to periods of recurring war and insecurity. Last August, before Israel launched its ground invasion of southern Lebanon, he returned to his hometown to visit family.
"This time it was different," he tells SBS News of the conflict in recent years.
"While [they] have been living in a difficult, insecure situation in that part of Lebanon, this time it is catastrophic."
Following the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, a new chapter began in the decades-long conflict between Israel and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah.
Despite a ceasefire in November 2024, the conflict flared again in March this year, after Israel and the US initiated war with Iran.
The Iran-backed Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel in support of its ally, triggering a major Israeli air and ground offensive in Lebanon.
More than 4,300 people have since been killed in Lebanon, according to the country’s health ministry, while dozens of Israelis have been killed in the conflict.
Israel’s occupation and bombardment of southern Lebanon has flattened villages and displaced hundreds of thousands of people.
Hoballah says his own siblings are among them; parts of his hometown, Shaqra, have been reduced to rubble.
"It's a total misery there now," he says.
"So you can imagine the psychological impact this has on our community here [in Australia]."
The 66-year-old says he can’t recall a time in his life when people in southern Lebanon felt safe under any Israeli government.
"To be honest, there was some differences, but no major difference."
He has little faith the election will bring meaningful change, but hopes to see Israel led by a more moderate coalition.
I'm a person who believes that people of different nationalities, race, faith, they can live together, and we can live with the people in Israel.
For Australians with ties to Iran, the war has also brought Israel's political future into sharp focus.
Suren Edgar, vice president of the Australian Iranian Community Alliance, says the conflict has affected many in his community very personally.
"You are consistently checking the news, trying to contact people and worrying about what may happen next," he tells SBS News.
He says decisions made by Israel’s next government "could have direct consequences" for his friends, family and the wider region.
"For me, what is at stake is whether the region moves toward another cycle of war, or towards greater stability."
Edgar hopes Israel's next government will balance its security concerns with the need to protect civilians and infrastructure, recognising that long-term security cannot come from permanent regional conflict.
"I hope it understands that weakening the Islamic Republic and weakening Iranian society are not the same thing."
Across different diaspora groups, the election is also being viewed as a vote on the direction the country will take in managing its foreign relationships and conflicts into the future.
Ric Benjamin is chair of the New Israel Fund Australia and a longtime organiser within Australia’s Jewish community.
He says many Jewish Australians feel "strongly connected to Israel" and are passionate about its elections, even if they can’t cast a ballot.
Benjamin points to the work of Jewish and Palestinian Israelis who continue to cooperate despite the conflict, such as those in the health and humanitarian sectors, as a rubric for Australians navigating their own divisions.
"If it's possible for people who are on the ground in the conflict, who have on both sides lost people through war or terror, if they are able to come together, why is it that our communities, 15,000 kilometres away, can't find that when they cry out for help?
Let's focus on the common causes and the common issues we have, and through that build trust and and build an acceptance.
That desire to break the cycle of conflict at the ballot box is one of the reasons Israeli Australian Limor Fayena has extended her trip to Israel. It will be her first time voting in Israel in 20 years.
The Sydney-based 50-year-old software engineer, who is also Burla's partner, says she hopes her vote will help bring about a "more responsible government" — one that will consider the future being created for the nation's children and grandchildren.
"How can we minimise the option of another war and sit down and think about the future — not the current and not the past?"

European Union leaders called on Israel to immediately reverse plans to expand illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and warned businesses against bidding for construction contracts, citing serious legal, economic and reputational risks, according to a statement issued Friday following a two-day summit in Brussels.
In conclusions adopted at the Oct. 15-16 European Council meeting, EU leaders condemned Israel's continued expansion of illegal settlements and escalating violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinian civilians in the occupied West Bank.

The European Union has pledged to help Ukraine reduce its dependence on US-owned satellite communications, while acknowledging that it cannot replace Starlink in the short term.
Speaking at an EU summit in Brussels on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said services were still being restored after disruptions he described as “a very unpleasant and dangerous surprise”.
Ukraine reported restrictions this week on some Starlink internet terminals, saying they had hampered its ability to defend against Russian forces.
The disruption came amid renewed tensions between Kiev and Washington even as US President Donald Trump denied ordering temporary disruption of Starlink service for Ukraine’s military.
EU leaders rallied around Zelenskyy but acknowledged limits to the support Europe could immediately provide.
“We are working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed,” French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters after the talks.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Europe had no readily available replacement.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine, and unfortunately in the short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” she said.
Europe’s satellite plans
EU countries currently pool and share satellite communications capacity through GOVSATCOM, a programme in which the bloc wants to fully include Ukraine, EU spokesperson Thomas Regnier said.
The EU also plans to incorporate commercial services into GOVSATCOM early next year to help meet military needs while it develops its own satellite network.
That network, known as IRIS², is intended to rival Starlink. Launches are planned for 2029, with full operations targeted for 2030.
Ukraine uses SpaceX’s military satellite service, Starshield, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-controlled territory and interceptor drones.
It also uses the company’s civilian Starlink system, though not for offensive operations.
SpaceX owner Elon Musk, whose stance on Ukraine has shifted repeatedly since 2022, said this week that any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his company.
Limited alternatives
European support extends beyond EU programmes. France’s Eutelsat already provides satellite communications services to Ukraine through its OneWeb network, although it has disclosed little about government and military uses.
Its constellation of 648 satellites, however, is far smaller than Starlink’s network of more than 10,000.
According to specialist publication Via Satellite, OneWeb cannot support drone and ground robot operations because of limited capacity and a lack of compact satellite terminals.
Kallas said the European Defence Agency had identified critical capabilities that Europe lacked, stressing that those gaps needed to be filled “as soon as possible”.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also underscored Ukraine’s dependence on the service.
“Starlink is the key for Ukraine, actually, to fight or fight back,” he told reporters. “It takes time for us to have the same capabilities. We do have it, but not enough.”
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said he had discussed Starlink with Macron on Thursday, including how European countries could provide more such services in the near future.

Major lender in Bathla development sells debts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:30:19 UTC
04:30:19 KST

Major Bathla lender La Trobe sells $31.2m loan as private credit firms seek to recover funds
In short:
La Trobe Financial has sold its senior loan facility, tied to a Bathla Group development, to investors through a fund managed by 360 Capital.
The $31.2 million purchase would give 360 Capital greater influence over the Marsden Park project.
What's next?
Morningstar expects private credit fund growth to slow substantially.
The fallout from the collapse of property developer Bathla Group continues to reverberate through Australia's private credit market, with lenders taking matters into their own hands to recover money tied up in the failed construction giant.
In one of the latest deals, property investment and funds management group 360 Capital has revealed it acquired a senior loan facility for about $31.2 million through its private credit fund, funded by private investors and entities within the 360 Capital group.
A senior loan facility is the first mortgage debt in a commercial investment and ranks highest in repayment priority.
The ABC understands the debt was acquired from major private lender La Trobe Financial, relating to a Bathla development at 137 South Street, Marsden Park, in Sydney's north-west.
The Marsden Park project comprises 72 apartments and is nearing completion, according to two sources close to the construction.
Half of the apartments have already been pre-sold under contracts worth $25.8 million (excluding GST), 360 Capital said in a statement.
In August, La Trobe disclosed it had $38.1 million in loans to Bathla, comprising four residential loans and one development loan.
The ABC understands through this deal, La Trobe has sold its development loan, recovering all outstanding principal, interest and late-payment charges and significantly reducing its exposure to the collapsed developer.
Deal gives 360 Capital greater control
360 Capital's ASX-listed mortgage investment trust, the 360 Capital Mortgage REIT, already held an $8.9 million loan secured against the development, which ranked behind La Trobe Financial for repayment.
The trust has invested a further $5.2 million in the deal.
"The step was not taken lightly, but is very important to protect the value of the trust's subordinated position," the company said.
The deal means entities associated with 360 Capital now control both the first and second mortgages over the development, giving them greater influence over how the project is completed and the debts recovered.
Morningstar equity analyst Winky Tan said lenders holding first mortgages were in a much stronger position to recover their money, while mezzanine lenders further down the repayment queue risked losing most, if not all, of their investment.
"When you're able to finish the project, you can sell it as a finished product, which will have a much higher valuation than a half-finished project," she said.
Following the purchase, advisory firm Wexted was appointed as receiver, with a focus on speeding up the process of obtaining occupancy certificates and settling the 36 pre-sold apartments.
360 Capital executive chairman Tony Pitt said the group expected to recover the full amount owed to it under the loan.
Ms Tan cautioned that the ultimate financial outcome for any lender would depend on whether the remaining apartments could be sold and at what price, particularly given the downturn in the property market.
'Perfect storm' unfolding in private credit sector
Lenders including Centuria Bass and CVS Lane suspended withdrawals from some funds in August amid concerns about their exposure to Bathla.
MA Financial, which says it has no exposure to Bathla, also introduced withdrawal limits on some of its funds amid concerns more investors could seek to pull out their money.
Major private credit manager Metrics Credit Partners, which also says it has no exposure to Bathla, suspended withdrawals from some unlisted funds amid scrutiny of asset valuations.
Corporate regulator ASIC has previously warned of poor practices across the private credit sector, including questionable asset valuations, opaque fees and inadequate disclosure.
ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said the Bathla collapse highlighted the need for stronger oversight, warning the industry was now "beyond warnings" and should prepare for enforcement action.
Ms Tan described the sector as facing "a perfect storm" of higher interest rates and falling property prices, with developers potentially struggling to refinance their debts just as nervous investors sought to withdraw their money.
Morningstar expects growth in private credit funds to slow substantially in the near to medium term, potentially make it harder for developers to secure financing and further worsening Australia's housing shortage.

The European Union will develop a new tool to swiftly block access to the bloc’s market in the event of a trade war, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has said.
Her announcement came after France and Germany said on Friday that they wanted to strengthen the EU’s legal armoury in case of a potential trade conflict with China.
"We will develop a new instrument for decisive action by limiting access to the single market where this is in the union’s interests fast and immediately," she told reporters after EU leaders met in Brussels.
Von der Leyen also reiterated calls for Europe to change the way it consumes energy, warning that the bloc’s dependence on imported fossil fuels has increased costs by $119 billion without delivering any additional energy.
Speaking at a press conference after the summit, she said Europe’s reliance on imported oil and gas continues to expose its economy to geopolitical developments beyond its control.
She said gas prices had surged by around 140 percent since late February, while diesel prices had doubled, highlighting the economic consequences of the ongoing energy crisis.
"We must also change the way we consume energy," von der Leyen said, calling for the replacement of foreign fossil fuels with electricity produced in Europe.
Energy transition
She stressed that Europe must remain committed to its energy transition, focusing on affordable, clean and domestically produced energy sources, including nuclear power and renewables.
European Council President Antonio Costa also highlighted the impact of high and volatile energy prices on households and businesses, describing energy costs as a crucial component of Europe’s competitiveness.
He said the bloc was paying the price of its dependence on fossil fuels and the absence of a fully integrated single energy market.
Costa also announced that he would convene another informal meeting of EU leaders in Alden Biesen, Belgium, in February 2027 to assess progress on defence and competitiveness following previous discussions.
Short-term measures
Von der Leyen outlined several short-term measures agreed upon to mitigate the impact of rising energy prices.
These include the release of 100 million barrels of oil and diesel over the next four months, managed by the International Energy Agency, extending the scope and duration of a temporary state aid framework introduced in February, and postponing implementation of the methane regulation by one year.
The EU will also launch a strategic dialogue on European refineries, with the aim of strengthening refining capacity within the bloc and helping bring prices down.
Von der Leyen also addressed concerns over the EU’s trade relationship with China, calling for a substantial and rapid rebalancing of economic ties.
She said the bloc’s trade deficit with China reached €1 billion per day in 2025 and warned that the imbalance was expected to worsen in 2026.
Costa said the bloc’s commitment to Ukraine remained strong and that the EU had identified the means to cover the country’s financial needs for this year. He called on the European Commission to propose measures addressing additional financing needs for 2027.

====================================================================================================

Greece’s violation narrative defends an airspace boundary that does not exist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:59:01 UTC
03:59:01 KST

Above the Aegean lies an imaginary boundary that Athens has imposed for years, treating a line drawn for civil aviation as a unilateral declaration of sovereignty.
On that basis, the Greek General Staff regularly issues “violations and infringements” bulletins, systematically labelling Turkish aircraft activities that comply with international law as “airspace violations”.
Greek media carry the same framing in the same language, and a 10-nautical-mile airspace claim, resting on no international treaty, is planted in the public mind day after day.
This pattern produced its most recent example a few days ago.
On October 5, 2026, two Turkish F-16s came into close contact with Greek fighter jets off Meis.
Greek authorities announced a tally of seven aircraft for that day (two armed F-16s, one maritime patrol aircraft and four unmanned aerial vehicles) and released the figures as “seven FIR infringements and nine violations of national airspace”.
Those figures were released on the eve of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Athens on 6 October, and a fresh “15 violations” bulletin was announced on the day of the visit.
Yet flight information region (FIR) responsibility and sovereignty over national airspace belong to different categories. Turkish aircraft fly within the Athens FIR while remaining in international airspace, and Athens counts that airspace as its own on a legally invalid basis.
Greece thereby merges two separate categories under a single heading of sovereignty violation in its political discourse, keeping its maximalist claim alive.
This is precisely where the real issue surfaces: a flight information region, which carries a technical aviation responsibility, is being turned into a state boundary in political discourse and into propaganda against Türkiye.
Limits drawn by international law
Sovereignty over national airspace finds its legal basis in the 1944 Convention on International Civil Aviation.
Article 1 affirms that every state has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory, and Article 2 defines “territory” as the land areas and the adjacent territorial waters under that state’s sovereignty. The extent of airspace is therefore tied to the extent of territorial waters.
That principle of sovereignty offers no basis for attributing sovereignty to FIRs responsible for providing air traffic services in international airspace.
An official working paper (A35-WP/109) submitted by the United States to the 35th Session of the Assembly of ICAO (International Civil Aviation Organization) states that FIR arrangements bear no direct relation to sovereignty, that delegating air traffic service responsibility to another state does not derogate from national sovereignty, and that the authority of the state providing that service is limited to technical and operational considerations.
The paper grounds these findings in ICAO Annex 11, which governs air traffic services.
Air traffic service responsibility in those parts of the Athens FIR that cover international airspace therefore confers no right on Greece to establish sovereignty over those areas or to require prior flight plans from state aircraft.
This is the legal distinction on which Türkiye’s objection rests: air traffic service responsibility is not equated with sovereign authority, and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs records plainly state that “there is no such concept” as a “FIR violation”.
Türkiye’s refusal to meet the flight plan request also rests on the Convention itself. Article 3 states that the Convention applies to civil aircraft and not to state aircraft, so no flight-plan obligation arises for military aircraft.
That same article establishes the authorisation requirement for flights over another state's territory, and the band between 6 and 10 nautical miles falls outside the definition of territory in Article 2.
As for the provision Greek military authorities invoke, it obliges states, when issuing regulations for their own state aircraft, to have due regard for the safety of civil aircraft navigation.
It gives no state the authority to request another's flight plans.
Athens’ own official statements carry the argument to a more striking point. Greece’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs states plainly on its “Athens FIR” page that the FIR arrangement does not concern sovereignty; it concerns only jurisdiction.
Even so, statements Greek military authorities publish under the heading of FIR violation systematically blur the distinction between air traffic service responsibility and sovereignty over national airspace.
On its own page of terms, the General Staff defines national airspace as 10 nautical miles based on a 1931 decree and states that entry into the Athens FIR without a flight plan counts as an infringement.
Two institutions of the same state tell two different versions of the law on the same question. Through military bulletins, a responsibility officially acknowledged to bear no relation to sovereignty is converted into a stream of data that feeds a claim of sovereignty.
This claim traces back to a decree that entered into force in 1931.
Its title in the United Nations repository of national legislation on the law of the sea reveals the nature of the instrument, which defines the extent of territorial waters for the purposes of aviation and the control thereof and fixes the territorial waters referred to in Civil Aviation Act No. 5017 at 10 nautical miles from the coast.
Greece’s actual territorial waters at that date measured 3 nautical miles.
When Athens extended them to 6 nautical miles in 1936, it retained the 10-mile figure devised for aviation purposes, creating a 4-mile gap between sovereignty at sea and airspace, one that has lasted to this day.
One territorial sea for aviation, another for seafaring…
The Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs recounts how the claim was promulgated on its own website. According to the ministry, the 10-mile limit was entered into aeronautical information publications and maps; the ministry submitted the maps to ICAO in 1955, and the minutes of the 1958 regional meeting referred to them.
Every document offered as the basis of a sovereignty boundary consists of domestic legislation and technical aviation records, and none of them carries the character of a treaty that establishes a boundary.
Türkiye rejects this claim.
Its Ministry of Foreign Affairs records that the band between 6 and 10 nautical miles forms part of international airspace, describes the Greek thesis as arbitrary, and defines it as an attempt to reduce the international airspace of the Aegean by 50 percent.
Indeed, a claim to airspace wider than the territorial waters beneath it finds no basis in the Convention or in general practice.
One of Athens’ closest allies has confirmed this maximalist claim's legal weakness through its official position.
A report prepared under the Eastern Mediterranean Security and Energy Partnership Act of 2019 stated that Washington officially recognises airspace of up to 6 nautical miles in the Aegean and does not share the Greek government’s view.
The report also noted that Congress could not be provided with the list of Turkish violations it requested because the boundaries are disputed.
Airspace coinciding with territorial waters is settled international practice, and Greece’s thesis falls outside it.
A claim resting on a domestic decree and unrecognised internationally amounts to nothing more than a unilateral, maximalist political choice.
Narrative of victimhood
When Athens presents its legal disputes with Türkiye to international opinion, it positions itself as the party whose sovereignty and security are under threat, and it has turned this into something close to a policy.
By framing the Aegean disagreements as a challenge to Greece’s rights, this approach equates Türkiye’s legal objections with threats and places Athens’ theses at the centre of the debate.
Official statements from the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs regarding disputes in Turkish-Greek relations provide clear examples of this approach.
On issues such as Aegean airspace, the demilitarised status of the islands, maritime jurisdiction, and FIR responsibility, Athens presents its own theses as legal facts while characterising Türkiye’s objections as a challenge to Greek sovereignty.
This narrative merges disputes with different legal bases and different historical trajectories into a single discourse of “Turkish pressure”.
This pushes Greece’s own maximalist choices into the background and automatically recasts Türkiye’s objections, grounded in international law, as problematic conduct.
Carrying this discourse to the European Union level is also politically striking. The European Commission’s November 4, 2025 Türkiye report offers a current example of bilateral disputes entering the language of an institutional text.
That report records that Türkiye has conducted no unauthorised flights over Greek islands since 2023. Its overall narrative, however, treats the Aegean disputes through Greece’s claims and lends Athens’ theses an institutional weight they have not earned.
Greece continues to broaden its political support for its theses by bringing bilateral disputes onto the EU agenda. Using EU membership for that purpose does nothing to turn Athens’ claims into theses that international law accepts.
Athens’ avoidance of judicial settlement on this question marks the weakest point in the narrative. Greece’s January 14, 2015 declaration recognising the International Court of Justice's compulsory jurisdiction excludes from the Court’s jurisdiction disputes concerning state boundaries or sovereignty over its territory, and, in framing that exception, expressly lists disputes over the breadth and limits of its territorial sea and airspace.
A party that claims its sovereignty has been violated has, by its own hand, closed off the compulsory judicial route that would determine where that sovereignty's boundary runs.
Confidence in a legal position does not require shielding it from review.
Resolving the Aegean disputes requires a consistent assessment based on the relevant international instruments and the parties' legal grounds.
Athens needs to stop manufacturing tension over imaginary boundaries; otherwise, no genuine ground for dialogue in the Aegean can be established, even in the long term.

Al Jazeera correspondent Kimberly Halkett explained that the appointment and subsequent reversal could create further problems for Trump as Republicans prepare for a pivotal midterm election.
“The fact that there was that major credibility issue as well as a shaky performance is what sealed her fate,” said Halkett. “This makes the president look impulsive at a time when he’s already being criticised for not having a campaign that is really on track to win in November.”

Kenya records third Ebola case, linked to first patient who died
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:57:40 UTC
03:57:40 KST

Kenya records third Ebola case, linked to first patient who died
Nairobi says 65-year-old female patient in quarantine with Bundibugyo strain; no signs of community transmission.
Kenya has recorded its third case of the Bundibugyo virus disease – a strain of Ebola that has killed thousands of people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) – 10 days after reporting its first case and death in Nairobi.
The latest confirmed case – a 65-year-old woman – was a “primary contact and a close relative of the first and second cases”, Kenya’s Health Ministry said in a statement on Friday, adding that the patient has been in quarantine since October 6.
After developing symptoms, she was isolated and then tested positive for the virus, it added in a statement.
“Once she developed fever, sore throat and malaise, she was isolated and specimen collected for testing. She tested positive for Ebola,” the Health Ministry said. “She was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care improving her chances of recovery.”
Kenya’s cases are linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, which is the second-largest on record globally  with more than 9,000 cases and over 4,300 deaths since it was officially detected in May.
Kenya’s first case emerged last week after a Kenyan man, who had been ill in the DRC about a month before travelling by road to Uganda, flew to Nairobi on October 3, where a relative drove him to the hospital. He died on October 5.
In its statement on X, the Health Ministry moved to reassure the public that there was no community spread of the disease and that the risk to the Kenyan public remained low.
Out of 130 contacts listed, 127 had been traced and were in quarantine, it said.
Efforts to control the spread of the Ebola outbreak have been complicated because the Bundibugyo strain has no licensed vaccine. Research is under way to develop one or more vaccines that work against the strain and some of these vaccines are already in the early phases of testing in humans.
Transparency demands over Ebola response funds
The new case in Kenya was reported as Africa’s top public health body and Congolese health authorities called for greater transparency in how Ebola response funds are used.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said financial information provided by aid organisations indicated that more than $700m of donor money was unaccounted for.
Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa CDC, told the Reuters news agency that international donors disbursed about $962m to organisations implementing Ebola response activities in DRC, rather than to the government.
Kaseya said those organisations reported receiving $228m, of which $127m had been spent and roughly $100m remained available.
But he said it was too early to speak of embezzlement.
In a post on X, Congolese Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba warned aid groups were required to provide details on funding sources to his ministry or risk being barred from working in DRC and blacklisted across Africa.
Meanwhile, on the ground in the DRC, Ebola cases have been detected in a new province bordering the Central African Republic, two health officials told Reuters on Thursday.
The two cases were confirmed in North Ubangi, the eighth Congolese province affected by the Bundibugyo outbreak, the officials said. Congolese authorities have not yet officially announced the outbreak has spread to North Ubangi.
