From Terah to today: The many roads that lead Jews home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:56:53 UTC
03:56:53 KST

For thousands of years, Jews lived in exile, far from the land of our ancestors. Scattered across the world, we dreamed of returning to the country we had once inhabited. Wherever Jewish history carried us, our hearts remained attached to the same place.
We lived in countless countries, spoke different languages, and belonged to different cultures. Through centuries of wandering, one truth remained unchanged. There is only one Jewish homeland.
The first Zionist
Though there is only one Jewish homeland, there are many roads that lead home. This was always true. Terah, the father of Abraham, was raised in a world of idolatry. Yet he felt an inner tug to leave Mesopotamia, modern-day Iraq, and journey toward the Land of Israel. He received no Divine command. He did not believe in the one God, yet something stirred within him, drawing him toward a distant land.
Ironically, he was the first Zionist, the first person described by the Torah as setting out for the Land of Israel from his homeland. His motives are unknown. He gathered his son Abraham and other family members and traveled toward Canaan. Along the way, Terah settled in Haran, where he eventually died.
His son Abraham later heard the voice of God commanding him to continue the journey his father had begun. Abraham traveled to the Land of Israel with a religious mission: to spread belief in the one God. Yet his pagan father had begun the journey.
Evidently, God implanted within the Jewish soul an instinctive attachment to its homeland. He gave us the ability to respond to the pull of land, peoplehood, and historical destiny even without religious commitment or prophetic revelation. At history’s dawn, this attachment could awaken even in a heart that had not yet awakened to faith.
The age of “isms”
This ancient echo reemerged millennia later. The 19th century witnessed a dramatic weakening of organized religion. The Enlightenment and the Age of Reason promised to lift humanity out of the ignorance and suffering of the medieval world. Science, discovery, and individualism propelled humanity toward an era of progress.
Organized religion, and Christianity in particular, was increasingly blamed for centuries of human suffering. Its unholy alliance with monarchy and political power had contributed to bloodshed and feudalism. Religion’s walls were crumbling.
Into this widening void emerged new ideologies. Society abhors a vacuum, and ideologies rushed to replace religion. Socialism, utilitarianism, communism, and other movements competed for the hearts and minds of Europeans.
It was the great age of “isms,” as new systems of thought offered competing visions of human identity, social order, and historical progress.
Yet perhaps the most powerful “ism” of all was nationalism. Increasingly, people defined themselves primarily by their nation rather than their religion. “John” was no longer primarily a Protestant who happened to live in England, but a proud Englishman who happened to be Protestant.
“Gustave” was no longer primarily a Catholic who happened to live in France, but a proud Frenchman who happened to be Catholic. National identity swept across a continent long shaped by religion and religious rivalries.
A Jewish awakening
Unfortunately, Judaism did not fare much better than other religions. With Emancipation, for the first time in our long exile, we were invited to become full-fledged members of an enlightened European society.
Many combined these newfound freedoms with traditional Jewish observance, but others abandoned their Jewish roots entirely.
Many Jews look back with reverence upon the great age of the yeshivot, when brilliant young men devoted years, sometimes decades, to intensive Torah study. This remarkable era helped lay the foundations for the phenomenal growth of Torah study in the modern world.
Yet there was another side to this history. Far more Jews were drawn into the universities and intellectual circles of Europe than into its great yeshivot. For many, the door swung in only one direction: away from Jewish religious life.
Millions of Jews faced the threat of losing their Jewish identity and disappearing into the surrounding culture. Traditional religious appeals no longer spoke to them. If Jewish identity depended exclusively upon religious commitment, an enormous portion of the Jewish people was in danger of being lost to history.
As Jewish identity weakened across Europe, God awakened that ancient echo. In the age of nationalism, Jewish nationalism emerged, offering Jews a way to identify with their land, their people, and their history. It captured the hearts of Jews, including many who had drifted away from religious observance.
Secular Zionism was a Divine impulse, awakening an ancient attachment to our land and people that had lain dormant for centuries. As religious commitment weakened, God stirred a different form of Jewish consciousness. Millions of Jews today express their deepest connection to their people through their commitment to our national project of return and to the modern State of Israel.
Oct. 7 demonstrated how deeply the State of Israel stands at the center of contemporary Jewish identity and how much more vulnerable Jewish life would be without it.
This became even more evident in the subsequent eruption of anti-Zionism and its frequent convergence with antisemitism, which further underscored Israel’s centrality to Jewish identity and the Jewish future. Israel has become a powerful anchor of Jewish belonging, even for Jews whose connection to religious observance is limited.
Thousands of years ago, Terah felt the pull of our land without profound religious conviction. Thousands of years later, countless Jews, far less detached from God than Terah had been, followed a similar path. They felt drawn to the same land, the same people, and the same historical destiny.
Across the centuries, Jews have found their way home through countless different journeys, shaped by different convictions, circumstances, dreams, and personal attachments. There is one home, but there are many roads which lead home.
Another road home
The roads leading to our homeland are as varied as the Jewish people themselves. Some are paved with religious conviction, others with national identity and historical consciousness.
Many Jews harbor a lifelong dream of aliyah and eventually fulfill that dream by building their lives and families in Israel. Still other roads emerge unexpectedly, shaped by circumstances, personal attachments, and the bonds of family.
My mother, of blessed memory, passed away this past Sukkot. She took a different road to our one homeland. We were raised in a Zionist home, though not an especially ideological one, and Zionism was not a central part of our upbringing.
Our family grew up in Brooklyn during the 1970s, when it was a thriving center of Modern Orthodox Jewish life, with flourishing synagogues, schools, and communities.
Moving to Israel was never part of her plan. However, her children developed a deep attachment to Israel, and all eventually moved here and built their families.
Wanting to be close to her children, grandchildren, and eventually great-grandchildren, my mother and father moved to Israel at an advanced age.
Their aliyah was not the fulfillment of a lifelong dream. It was not driven primarily by ideology or Zionist conviction. It was driven by a deep love of family.
Yet leaving behind a familiar world and beginning a new life so late in life required enormous courage and determination. I will always be grateful to my Mommy for making that sacrifice and giving us those precious years together. My mother made that journey, and now she is buried just a few minutes from our home in Gush Etzion.
There are many roads that lead home. Some are paved with ideology, conviction, and Zionist dreams. Others are paved with something simpler and more personal: the love of family.
May God bless her soul, and may her love and devotion continue to inspire our family for generations.
The writer is a rabbi and educator at Yeshivat Har Etzion (Gush). Find his latest book, Echoes of Rashi: Bereishit, at mtaraginbooks.com

Thai authorities inspect Chabad House in Chiang Mai, find no violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:56:46 UTC
03:56:46 KST

Thai law enforcement authorities conducted a multi-agency inspection of the Chabad House on Chang Khlan Road in Chiang Mai on Wednesday, led by Deputy Provincial Governor Boonlue Thammatharanurak, finding no legal violations or irregularities at the Jewish community center.
At a press conference after the inspection, the deputy governor said Thai law does not clearly regulate premises that also serve as Jewish places of worship. He noted that gatherings primarily take place on Fridays and Saturdays, attracting approximately 100 to 200 participants, mostly Israelis attending communal meals, and recommended that the center maintain a "low-key" approach to its activities.
The inspection involved representatives from the provincial administration, military, immigration police, provincial cultural authorities, Chiang Mai Municipality, and the Internal Security Operations Command (ISOC). Authorities reported finding no violations, with the deputy governor describing the visit as a "routine inspection" that had not been prompted by any complaint.
Officials examined the legality of the property's lease and operating licenses. According to local media reports, Chabad rents restaurant premises from a local resident under a lease valid until 2028 and holds a food service license covering up to 200 square meters, as well as an alcohol license issued by the Excise Department.
Chiang Mai Chabad inspection follows raids on Jewish institutions in Bangkok
The Chiang Mai inspection differed significantly from the raids carried out in Bangkok on October 8, when Thailand's Department of Special Investigation (DSI) conducted searches under judicial warrants, with the involvement of the justice minister and several government agencies.
The Bangkok operation involved police, tax authorities, immigration officials, the Lands Department, and the Anti-Money Laundering Office, among other agencies.
During searches at the Chabad Foundation, the Jewish Association of Thailand, and related offices, investigators seized documents, identified foreign workers from Myanmar and Laos without valid work permits, and found dozens of companies registered at the same address.
The operation formed part of an investigation into suspected nominee ownership arrangements, property holdings, and financial activities involving Israeli-linked businesses.
Unlike the Bangkok raids, the Chiang Mai inspection was presented by authorities as a routine enforcement visit, with no reports of search warrants or seized materials.
The Chabad House in Chiang Mai has operated since 2004 and has undergone inspections over the years. However, a coordinated inspection involving so many enforcement agencies had never previously taken place at the center in more than two decades of operation.
Thailand expands investigations into Israeli-linked businesses and Chabad centers
The inspection comes amid a broader wave of enforcement operations involving Chabad institutions across Thailand, including Phuket, Bangkok, and other locations.
The operations, expanded partly under instructions from Thailand's deputy interior minister, are linked to investigations into business and property networks associated with Israeli nationals.
Authorities have raised concerns regarding foreign ownership, financing arrangements, and commercial practices, against a backdrop of public tensions involving Israeli tourists.
Israeli Ambassador to Thailand Dr. Alona Fisher-Kamm visited the provincial government building and met with the deputy governor approximately one month ago. She also visited the Chiang Mai Chabad House separately during the same period.
Thai authorities said they would continue monitoring the premises but emphasized that there were currently "no irregularities."
Journalists were not permitted to enter the building during the inspection. According to reporters at the scene, Chabad security personnel prevented them from entering.
Chiang Mai Chabad rabbi says center operates in full compliance with Thai law
Rabbi Yossi Pikel and his wife, Chani, have served as Chabad emissaries in Chiang Mai, northern Thailand, for 17 years.
The couple welcomes Jewish visitors and travelers to the city, providing assistance, guidance, and support throughout their stay.
The Chabad House offers prayer services, Shabbat and holiday meals, and classes on Hasidic teachings and the weekly Torah portion.
The center also operates a synagogue, a kosher meat restaurant offering packaged food for travelers, a women's mikveh (ritual bath), a travelers' shop, and additional services.
Speaking to Walla, Rabbi Pikel said the inspection had been coordinated in advance. He explained that inspections take place periodically but acknowledged that a joint visit involving so many agencies was unusual.
"I'm glad they came to inspect, and I'm glad they saw that everything was in order," Pikel said. "We operate by the book and try to do everything properly."
The rabbi also emphasized his efforts to build positive relations with the local Thai community, noting that the restaurant is open to Thai residents as well as Jewish and Israeli visitors.
He said that all visitors are welcome, subject to the center's security screening procedures.
"The place is open to everyone," Pikel said.

Israeli media's polling obscures the majority opposed to Netanyahu - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:56:16 UTC
03:56:16 KST

Israel’s media is reporting astonishing news this week: in the polls, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc has overtaken that of Gadi Eisenkot.
After all the failures, disasters, scandals, and debacles of recent years, could Netanyahu really be heading for another victory? According to the reports, apparently so. In reality, not so much. We are seeing a misreading of the polls.
According to recent surveys, Netanyahu’s bloc has about 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while Eisenkot’s bloc stands at 51 or 52 – but only because of artificial exclusions.
When all the parties opposed to Netanyahu’s continued rule, meaning the right-wing and haredi (ultra-Orthodox) bloc, are counted together, the total reaches about 67 seats. That is a solid parliamentary majority, six seats above the threshold required, and virtually unprecedented in Israel’s modern political era.
For at least the past half-century, since the end of Mapai’s one-party dominance era, a prime minister whose opponents held 67 seats two weeks before an election would have been described as heading toward defeat.
Instead, the public is being told that Netanyahu is leading.
How does this happen? Quite simply, the political blocs are being counted in a way that serves Netanyahu.
Parties opposed to him are excluded from the change bloc because they are not considered natural coalition partners, prefer a national unity government, or because they have ideological disagreements with other opposition parties.
The result is the false appearance of a close race, or even a right-wing advantage, when the numbers themselves tell a very different story.
Herein lies the fundamental mistake: a solid political bloc and a governing coalition are not the same thing. Elections first determine the balance of power in the Knesset. Only afterward do negotiations over forming a government begin.
A party can oppose Netanyahu without committing to join an Eisenkot government, and it can support a government from outside the coalition without becoming part of it. A recommendation to the president is another matter entirely.
The conflation of these concepts has become a powerful political tool in Netanyahu’s hands.
Three factors illustrate just how misleading the conventional arithmetic has become: the Reservists party, the Arab parties, and Ofer Winter’s party.
Start with the Reservists party. This new outfit, which receives four seats in some polls, is excluded from the change bloc because its leaders favor a national unity government. Fine.
But a preference regarding the composition of a government is hardly equivalent to supporting Netanyahu’s continued rule.
The Reservists’ positions on the judicial overhaul, equality in military service, the political system, and even the Palestinian issue are considerably closer to those of the camp seeking to replace Netanyahu than to his alliance with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the haredi parties.
Even if they are unwilling to commit in advance to an Eisenkot-led coalition, there is no political logic in portraying them as an entirely neutral force.
At the very least, they should be regarded as potential members of the change bloc, even if they would be reluctant partners who set conditions. Their preference for unity does nothing to change the fact that the current government is a long way from the political vision they present.
Arab parties and Ofer Winter
The second distortion is much larger and more consequential: the Arab parties.
This may be Netanyahu’s most impressive political achievement.
For years, he has managed to persuade large sections of the public, including his political opponents, that the votes of Israel’s Arab citizens somehow count for less when determining who has won an election.
The Right is allowed to count all its natural allies, while the Center-Left is expected to behave as though a substantial portion of its potential majority simply does not exist.
There are, of course, profound ideological differences between the Arab parties and the Zionist parties of the Center and Left. Israel’s Jewish character creates discomfort, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and national security present genuine difficulties.
It is also clear that Eisenkot, Avigdor Liberman, and Naftali Bennett are reluctant to form a government dependent on Arab parties, or even to be seen as willing to do so.
But this is where the confusion Netanyahu has so successfully cultivated begins: whether a particular party will join a coalition is a different question from whether its seats can prevent Netanyahu from forming a government.
Israeli history has already provided examples. In 1992, Labor and Meretz won 56 seats, while the five seats held by Hadash and the Arab Democratic Party gave Yitzhak Rabin’s camp a parliamentary majority of 61. Nobody doubted Rabin had won.
Rabin formed a government with Shas, but after its departure he relied on outside support from the Arab parties.
In 2021, Yair Lapid succeeded in assembling the coalition that removed Netanyahu from power, with the four seats of the Islamist Ra’am party forming an essential part of its majority: 61, to which Bennett, much like Shas in Rabin’s day, simply added his seats.
Netanyahu, by contrast, is never required to explain why the haredi parties, which oppose drafting their young men into the military and demand budgets and privileges that provoke widespread public resentment, are legitimate partners in his bloc. Their seats are counted automatically.
But when it comes to Arab parties, ideological disagreements suddenly become grounds for excluding them from the calculation. Suddenly, unlike in years past, they have disappeared from the opposition bloc in the media’s pie charts.
Netanyahu has managed to turn this double standard into a political convention.
The third factor, and perhaps the most intriguing of all, is a new party led by firebrand Brig.-Gen. (res.) Ofer Winter.
Winter has declared that he will recommend to the president that Netanyahu be tasked with forming the next government, so it is natural to count him initially with the Right.
Although Winter is an unmistakably right-wing figure, he also supports drafting haredi men into the military, a position that puts him on a collision course with Netanyahu’s haredi partners.
How can he sit in a government dependent on parties that oppose one of the central reforms he wants to advance?
Suppose Winter recommends Netanyahu, as promised. Even with Winter, however, Netanyahu reaches only 53 seats, according to the numbers under discussion. He is eight short.
A presidential recommendation cannot manufacture parliamentary seats that do not exist, and if Netanyahu cannot recruit additional partners, he cannot form a government.
At that point, another possibility could open up for Winter: joining a government of change focused on rebuilding the country.
There is no guarantee he would choose that path. But there is also no reason to assume that a declaration of loyalty to Netanyahu during an election campaign necessarily determines his behavior under every possible post-election scenario.
Urgent national tasks
The next government of change would face an enormous agenda, much of which would not require agreement on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
It would need to repair Israel’s foreign relations, address the military draft crisis and relations with the haredim, restore basic standards of good governance, combat rampant crime, and establish an independent state commission of inquiry into the failures of October 7.
These are urgent national tasks on which broad agreement could emerge, even among people with radically different views about the future of the territories.
Winter would not be a natural partner for a major diplomatic initiative with the Palestinians. But such an initiative is unlikely to get underway in the first year or two of the next government anyway.
During that period, simply preventing further damage would be an important achievement: curbing Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, halting the establishment of illegal outposts, and avoiding measures that would deepen Israel’s international isolation.
Agreement with Winter on some of these issues would be difficult, but there is no reason to assume in advance that every compromise is impossible.
Eisenkot, Bennett, and Lapid are projecting growing confidence that they can form a government based on a Jewish parliamentary majority, without relying on the Arab parties. Clearly, that confidence rests on precisely the scenarios described above.
And with the addition of outside support from the Arab factions, something they have already promised free of charge, such a government could conceivably enjoy an enormous parliamentary majority.
The coming election could therefore very well bring Netanyahu’s rule to an end.
That possibility may be considerably closer than the public realizes, simply because the media continues to present the political landscape according to rules that Netanyahu himself has managed to establish.
Caution is necessary, of course, because polls are not votes cast at the ballot box. But it is equally important to read the polls correctly. That matters if the change bloc is to find the fighting spirit needed to bring masses of voters to the polls.
And there is room for hope. As Theodor Herzl famously put it, “If you will it, it is no dream.”
Especially when the alternative is failure and Netanyahu somehow remaining in power, which would be a catastrophe threatening the very future of the state.
The writer is a former Cairo-based Middle East editor and London-based Europe/Africa editor of the Associated Press. He served as chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem and authored two books about Israel.

Kindergarten head gets life sentence for poisoning 247 children in NW China
A court in northwest China’s Gansu Province has sentenced six people for producing and selling toxic food that poisoned 247 preschool children at a kindergarten in Tianshui City, with the facility's person in charge receiving a life sentence, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Xinhua.
According to a verdict issued by the Intermediate People's Court of Lanzhou City on Friday, Li Huifang, head of the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Tianshui's Maiji District, was sentenced to life imprisonment, stripped of political rights for life and had 500,000 yuan ($74,000) in personal assets confiscated. A provincial investigation report released in July 2025 found that contaminated pastries had been served to children and staff monthly since May 2024. Tests showed that 247 of 251 children examined had abnormal blood lead levels.
All affected children received hospital treatment or nutritional interventions at home. By July 20, 2025, most had completed their first round of treatment and had been discharged from hospital. Medical experts reported an average 40.21% reduction in blood lead levels, meeting projected treatment targets.
The investigation also led to disciplinary probes involving 10 local officials, including the provincial health commission director and senior leaders in Tianshui. The Gansu provincial government has pledged continued support for the children's medical care and recovery.

Lukashenko Orders “People’s Militia” Units in Every Belarusian Village Council
Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko has ordered the creation of “people’s militia” units in every village council across the country, expanding a defense structure introduced after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, The Moscow Times reported on October 16.
Lukashenko announced the move while observing training by one such unit in Belarus’s Verkhnedvinsk district, according to the report.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Moscow has sought to draw Belarus more directly into Russia’s war against Ukraine. It was previously reported by The Wall Street Journal that the Kremlin threatened to reduce financial support for Minsk if Lukashenko resisted deeper involvement.
“We need to expand. We need to create more such basic units somewhere. They must be connected to each other,” Lukashenko stated.
The Moscow Times reported that Lukashenko described the militia as the first level of Belarus’s defense system. Territorial defense forces responsible for protecting infrastructure would form the next layer, followed by the regular army.
“When creating this structure, I meant that every village council should have a people’s militia unit. This is the core,” Lukashenko said. “In the event of hostilities, this core can expand.”
He added that weapons had already been prepared for the units.
“You will have an assault rifle, grenades, a machine gun,” Lukashenko stated.
Lukashenko had previously instructed the Belarusian Society of Hunters and Fishermen to recruit people with experience handling weapons into the militia, The Moscow Times noted.
Belarus began creating the “people’s militia” after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Defense Minister Viktor Khrenin previously linked the decision to the “military-political situation” and presented the force as a deterrent against a potential attack.
Since the beginning of 2026, Belarusian authorities have intensified military and security exercises, The Moscow Times reported. The drills have included mobilization scenarios, responses to missile strikes involving mass casualties, and wartime civil-defense measures.
Exercises involving both territorial defense forces and the “people’s militia” were also held in the Vitebsk region over the summer.
The militia expansion comes amid broader signs of Belarusian military preparations near NATO borders. A recent report found that Belarus is modernizing railways, communications networks, and defense production with Russian support, with some facilities expected to reach full capacity by spring or mid-2027.

In Burham, near Birzeit north of Ramallah, the Red Crescent said its teams treated a 70-year-old man injured in an assault by Israeli occupiers.
Three other Palestinians were injured in a similar attack in Deir Jarir, east of Ramallah, and taken to a medical center for treatment, the organization added.
The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said its teams in Ramallah treated a 63-year-old woman and a 40-year-old man injured during an attack on farmers harvesting olives in Abu Falah.
Both were taken to a hospital, the group said.
In Burqa, east of Ramallah, the Red Crescent reported four injuries after Israeli occupiers attacked Palestinian farmers.
Al-Baydar said the victims sustained injuries to their heads, backs and hands, while a foreign journalist was pepper-sprayed during the assault.
In Turmus Ayya, north of Ramallah, local sources told Anadolu Agency that occupiers attacked olive pickers and torched three Palestinian vehicles in the Al-Nabaat area.

Warning sirens sounded in the town to alert residents to the attacks, the sources added.
Al-Baydar said American journalist and international solidarity activist Heidi Levine was injured when Israeli occupiers assaulted her in the presence of Israeli troops.
Levine was taken to Al-Istishari Hospital for treatment, the organization added.The Palestinian Civil Defense said one of its members sustained bruises when Israeli occupiers attacked an emergency crew responding to the burning vehicles in Turmus Ayya.
The occupiers assaulted firefighters after they arrived at the scene and set fire to a Civil Defense vehicle, the agency said.
Civil Defense volunteers from Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya also helped extinguish the fires, according to the agency.
The Civil Defense warned that targeting emergency personnel and vehicles posed a direct threat to efforts to protect lives and property and respond to emergencies.
Elsewhere, in Rammun, east of Ramallah, Israeli occupiers assaulted Palestinian farmers and forced them off their land during the olive harvest, according to Al-Baydar.
In Qabalan, south of Nablus, occupiers chased and physically assaulted a Palestinian woman before stealing her olive harvest, the organization said.
Similar attacks targeted farmers and olive pickers in the eastern part of Burin village and the town of Majdal Bani Fadil, also south of Nablus.
In Arraba, southwest of Jenin, Israeli occupiers attacked homes belonging to the Al-Rahhal family, Al-Baydar reported.
On Monday, the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said it had documented 136 attacks linked to the olive harvest season carried out by Israeli forces and occupiers since the beginning of October.
According to the commission, the incidents included beatings, expulsions, intimidation, gunfire, tear gas and arrests.
They also included the theft of olives and harvesting equipment and damage to trees, causing losses to farmers and restricting their access to agricultural land.
The olive harvest is a vital source of income for thousands of Palestinian families in the occupied West Bank, where farmers face growing attacks and restrictions on access to their land during the season.
Attacks by Israeli forces and occupiers against Palestinians and their property across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, have intensified since the start of Israel’s genocide in Gaza in October 2023.

Trump’s first attorney general pick accused of sex trafficking
Two women have filed a federal lawsuit accusing former US Representative Matt Gaetz, President Donald Trump’s first pick for attorney general, of participating in a sex trafficking ring while serving in Congress. Gaetz has faced similar allegations for years, and has denied any wrongdoing.
The lawsuit, filed in Florida on Thursday, alleges that Gaetz and several other men, including former Seminole County Tax Collector Joel Greenberg and former Florida legislator Christopher Dorworth, sexually exploited the plaintiffs between 2017 and 2019.
The women, identified as Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2, are seeking unspecified damages under the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act.
According to the complaint, Greenberg recruited financially vulnerable young women through the dating website SeekingArrangement.com and introduced them to Gaetz.
The lawsuit alleges that Gaetz had sex with Jane Doe 1 and a 17-year-old girl at a July 2017 party where narcotics were distributed. He allegedly paid the minor $400 in cash and transferred $500 to Jane Doe 1 three days later.
Gaetz and Greenberg subsequently made at least 19 payments to Jane Doe 1, ranging from $150 to $1,000, the complaint claims. Jane Doe 2 alleged that she first had sex with Gaetz in exchange for money in October 2017.
The plaintiffs also accused the defendants of providing drugs and financing trips to Miami, Las Vegas, the Bahamas and other destinations in exchange for sex.
The men allegedly used “their public office, power, and wealth to prey on the economic vulnerability of Plaintiffs,” the lawsuit states. Both women were in their early twenties when they met Gaetz.
Greenberg pleaded guilty to federal charges, including sex trafficking of a minor, in 2021 and was sentenced to 11 years in prison.
Responding on X on Thursday, Gaetz appeared to mock the lawsuit, posting a photo of three women in swimsuits overlooking the ocean in the Bahamas.
“Jane Doe Strikes Again!” he wrote, sarcastically questioning why nobody had responded to the women’s supposed cries for help on Instagram. He later told reporters he looked forward to disproving the allegations.
Jane Doe Strikes Again! Two adult women sued me today alleging they were sex trafficked to the Bahamas. I’m shocked nobody responded to their repeated cries for help, posted to instagram. https://t.co/HPvX2xypzs
— Matt Gaetz (@mattgaetz) October 15, 2026
In December 2024, the House Ethics Committee reported finding “substantial evidence” that Gaetz had paid women for sex, including a 17-year-old girl, and used illegal drugs while in office.

Gaetz withdrew from consideration to be Trump’s attorney general in November 2024 after several Republican senators signaled opposition to his nomination over the allegations.

Tatarstan interested in IT professionals, medical personnel, welders from India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:29:29 UTC
03:29:29 KST

KAZAN, October 16. /TASS/. Tatarstan is interested in English-speaking engineering and technical professionals, IT specialists, medical personnel, and highly skilled welders from India, the republic’s Labor, Employment, and Social Protection Minister Elmira Zaripova stated.
“Today, our needs align in terms of qualifications. India is not only a source of labor, but also of English-speaking engineering, technical, and IT professionals, medical personnel, and highly skilled welders. I would like to point out that welders from India are familiar with Russian federal standards, particularly those on manual submerged-arc welding. In other words, they are familiar with our standards, and this also brings us closer together,” she noted during “The Labor Market: Challenges and Prospects” session held within the framework of the second Russian-Indian Business Forum "TIME: Tatarstan Initiative Mutual Efficiency."
According to Zaripova, unemployment in Tatarstan is practically nonexistent. There are nearly 3,000 unemployed citizens, accounting for less than 0.2% of the economically active population. At the same time, there are 14-25 job openings for every unemployed person.
The regional minister also noted that Tatarstan received a quota in 2026 to recruit more than 3,000 Indian citizens and that more than 600 work permits were issued to Indian citizens in the republic in 2025. Currently, more than 1,000 Indian citizens are officially employed in the region. The average age of an Indian worker is 29, an age at which people focus on long-term career prospects. In addition, nearly 1,300 Indian students are enrolled in Tatarstan universities, primarily in medical and technical programs.
“The key to future progress lies in harmonizing standards for the recognition of professional qualifications. Without this, workers trained in their home countries will not be hired here, especially in fields such as welding, engineering, medicine, and IT. This is a priority that is now being addressed at the federal level as well,” Zaripova concluded.
The second Russian-Indian Business Forum "TIME: Tatarstan Initiative Mutual Efficiency" is taking place on October 14–17 at the Center for Unique Craftsmanship in Kazan. TASS is the forum’s general information partner.

UK PM adviser’s wife expresses ‘support’ for Palestine Action
Police reviewing social media post by writer Sarah Helm, wife of Burnham’s National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell.
British police are reviewing a social media post by the wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell in which she appears to endorse Palestine Action, a group proscribed in the country as a “terrorist” organisation.
“God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action,” Sarah Helm, a writer who is married to Powell – Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s national security adviser – wrote on X on Thursday.
She was responding to a post defending Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who this week announced her books would no longer be sold in the United Kingdom over her plans to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.
A Metropolitan Police spokesperson on Friday said Helm’s post is “being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required”.
A government spokesperson cited by the Reuters news agency said the views expressed in Helm’s post “are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity”.
‘Absurdly authoritarian ban’
UK-based activist group Defend Our Juries defended Helm for defying what it called an “absurdly authoritarian ban on Palestine Action”.
“We know of 36 people who have been arrested and had their homes raided for similarly expressing support for Palestine Action on social media,” said a spokesperson for the group.
“We hope Sarah will not face the same treatment for standing up for free speech and Palestinian lives.”
The UK government outlawed Palestine Action in July 2025, after activists from the group broke into a Royal Air Force base and sprayed red paint on two aircraft to protest against UK military support for Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Being a member or a supporter is punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
Since the ban went into effect, police have arrested more than 3,500 people in the UK for alleged support of the group, many of them for holding up placards, according to rights group Amnesty International.
Palestine Action has contested its proscription, but the Court of Appeal upheld it in June.
The UK’s new Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband last month said the government was “looking at” the Palestine Action ban, adding that he did not believe mass arrests resulting from its proscription were “anyone’s intent”.

How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:21:43 UTC
03:21:43 KST

How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm elections
Through statements in English, Iranian officials are emphasising gas prices and issues with the US economy.
In messages that appear to be directed at the American public, Iran has been highlighting the cost of the war that the United States and Israel launched against the country ahead of the United States midterm elections.
Iranian officials have published articles in state-affiliated outlets stressing the disastrous impact of the war on oil prices and the US economy, while Iran’s chief negotiator and Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has actively targeted US officials about rising costs and military spending.
Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said Tehran is looking to increase the political cost of the war for Trump by trying to talk directly to the American public.
“It’s not necessarily that they’re trying to get Democrats in power or manipulate US politics in a certain direction, other than just overall increasing the costs on this issue of the Iran war, and just playing that game of information warfare and getting out their own narrative and propaganda as well,” Toossi told Al Jazeera.
Trump’s Republican Party is looking to retain control of the Senate and House of Representatives in next month’s midterm vote. But the Democratic Party, which largely opposes the war with Iran, is mounting a strong challenge across the congressional electoral map, including in areas that have been conservative strongholds for decades, such as Texas.
On Wednesday, Ghalibaf shared a news story on inflation rising to 3.7 percent last month along with a collage of negative headlines on the US economy.
The social media post also featured a comic strip from the Road Runner cartoon showing Wile E Coyote building a catapult that misfires and launches a boulder at him.
“Let’s ‘play the percentages’. Not in odds, but in the % increases,” Ghalibaf wrote in a message to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has been leading the sanctions campaign against Iran.
Bessent said last month that he represents “the house”, likening the economy to a casino while addressing the national debt and bond market.
Ghalibaf’s remark referred to the increase in inflation, underscoring that the cost of living keeps rising due to the war despite Bessent’s assertions.
Days earlier, he shared an image of a ghost shaped like a bell curve, with diesel prices rising and housing affordability and consumer confidence falling.
Since the start of the war on February 28, Iran has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, sending energy prices soaring. In the US, the price of diesel is at an all-time record of $6.33 per gallon (3.8 litres), according to the American Automobile Association, and gas is $4.33, up from less than $3 before the war.
Iran has intensified its attacks on vessels around the strait in recent days after Trump and his aides repeatedly stressed that the waterway is under US control.
The uptick in energy prices has fuelled overall inflation in the economy, leading the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates last month at a time when Trump has been calling for them to be cut to stimulate economic activity.
In a letter to the American public on September 29, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) accused Trump of lying about the cost of the war and the state of the US economy, dismissing the president’s claims that oil prices would soon nosedive.
“Countries around the world have lost their faith in the US economy. Demand for American bonds has plummeted. In fact, countries are starting to offload their US bonds. Soon, the dam will break, and the economy will implode, causing, unfortunately, great pain for Americans for many many years,” the IRGC said.
“Americans need to wake up. They need to wrest control back from corrupt politicians. Now is the time, as the American political system is at its weakest.”
The US midterm elections are seen as a turning point in the conflict – not because of their potential outcome, but because of what Trump might do after the vote.
Trump has suggested that he would either strike a deal with Iran or return to a full-scale war after the November 3 legislative elections. He has also dismissed the idea that the vote will have any impact on his Iran policy.
“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realise is that I’m not running,” Trump said at the United Nations General Assembly last month.
“I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election. When it comes to Iran, it doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
If the Democrats gain control of Congress, they can push for measures to curb Trump’s ability to continue the war, including through withholding funding for the military campaign.
But Toossi said there is a debate within Iran on the potential impact of a Democratic victory in November.
While some point to foreign policy hawks among the Democrats to argue that little would change, others say a midterm defeat would make him politically vulnerable and likely constrain his war powers.
“I don’t think they’re hedging their bets either way, and I don’t think it necessarily affects their overall strategy of increasing the costs [of war] regardless of whatever happens in November,” Toossi told Al Jazeera.

Trump fires White House press secretary Katie Zacharia after just five days on the job
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:11:20 UTC
03:11:20 KST

President Donald Trump has fired his newly appointed White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, after just five days on the job, U.S. media reported Friday, following a troubled debut and growing controversy over her claims about her legal career. The reports came shortly after Trump publicly suggested she should reconsider remaining in the position, saying she had been treated unfairly by the media. Trump later said he was in no rush to appoint a new White House press secretary to replace Zacharia, Fox News reported.
Speaking to reporters on the White House lawn before departing for a campaign rally in Georgia, Trump said he had spoken with Zacharia about the intense criticism she faced since taking the job.
"I told Katie, in my opinion, she was treated very unfairly," Trump said, adding that she had been "brutalized by the media."
Recounting their conversation, Trump said: "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy.'" He added: "I want her to have a good life. I don't want her to have a life like she's led the last three days."
The president also addressed Zacharia directly through reporters, saying: "Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this."
At the time, Trump stopped short of announcing her dismissal, saying he would make a final decision after returning from his campaign trip. "When I get back, we're gonna talk," he said.
CNN reported, citing a source familiar with Trump's private conversations, that the president had been more decisive behind closed doors, telling advisers that Zacharia "wasn't ready for prime time," According to the report, Trump initially believed her first briefing had gone better than his advisers thought, but changed his assessment following her interview with Sean Hannity.
White House communications director Steven Cheung confirmed Zacharia's departure, telling The New York Times that she was "transitioning into a new role that will be announced at a later date."
Zacharia later responded to her dismissal in a post on X, sharing a photograph of herself with Trump. "President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic and hardworking man," she wrote. "I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to." She concluded: "It was an honor to work for him."
The Wall Street Journal reported that it had interviewed Zacharia in her office shortly before she was dismissed. Just before 1 p.m., as she discussed her plans for the position, senior Trump adviser Jason Miller knocked on her door. "JD wanted to chat with us real quick," he said, referring to Vice President JD Vance. According to the newspaper, Zacharia never returned to the interview or to her position.
Before her dismissal became public, Zacharia appeared calm and spoke enthusiastically about her close relationship with Trump. "That's what matters," she said. Discussing her plans for the press team, she added: "There are no staffing changes that are happening. I'm trying to keep everyone cohesive." Less than an hour later, she was out of the job.
Asked how she was holding up, Zacharia told the Journal: "I'm just running on no sleep and high adrenaline and probably too much caffeine and no food." The newspaper noted that she had less than 24 hours to prepare for her first White House briefing.
Zacharia said she found it difficult to turn down the assignment because she wanted to be a team player, describing how she scrambled to gather the necessary information and prepare for the briefing on short notice.
Nevertheless, Zacharia told The Wall Street Journal that she did not believe Trump had made a mistake by sending her into the briefing room on such short notice and stressed that she did not blame the White House.
Zacharia, who replaced Karoline Leavitt, began her new position Monday and held her first White House press briefing Tuesday. The briefing lasted just 14 minutes, during which she read extensively from prepared talking points and took questions from only three news organizations, all considered friendly to Trump. Critics said she appeared nervous and stumbled over some of her answers, although Trump initially defended her performance.
During the briefing, Zacharia mistakenly referred to her husband as the president before correcting herself. She also said her role was to highlight Trump's accomplishments, emphasizing that the president was best equipped to speak for himself.
When she abruptly ended the briefing, Zacharia told reporters they could direct further questions to Trump on the White House's South Lawn before his departure for a campaign event in Alaska.
Zacharia's five-day tenure was the shortest in White House press secretary history, surpassing Stephen Early, who served as acting press secretary for 14 days in 1950.
Her brief stint also drew comparisons to Anthony Scaramucci, whom Trump fired as White House communications director after just 11 days in 2017. Scaramucci, who later became a Trump critic, expressed solidarity with Zacharia in a post on X.
"Dear Katie — speaking as the world's leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family. In time you’ll realize that the Universe did you a major favor," he wrote.
The controversy intensified over questions about Zacharia's legal qualifications. She had previously described herself as having practiced law, and Trump himself had referred to her as an attorney. However, during an interview Thursday with Fox News host Sean Hannity, she acknowledged that she had failed the bar examination and had never retaken it.
Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University's law school in 2011. While a law degree is generally required to become an attorney in the United States, graduates must also be admitted to a state bar before they can practice law.
The watchdog group Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California, calling for an investigation into whether Zacharia had violated the law by repeatedly presenting herself as an attorney despite lacking a license to practice law.
The organization's executive director, Michelle Kuppersmith, said Zacharia had described herself as an attorney during appearances on Fox News, CNN and Newsmax and had identified herself as chief legal counsel for a California-based conservative nonprofit.
"Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility," Kuppersmith said. "The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has."
The California bar confirmed to U.S. media outlets that it had no record of Zacharia holding a license under either her married or maiden name.
Before joining the White House, Zacharia had worked as a conservative media commentator and communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group, the parent company of Truth Social. Trump announced her appointment on October 9, praising her loyalty and predicting she would do an excellent job representing his administration.
Zacharia, 41, previously worked at a law firm in Beijing after moving to China with her husband. Foreign nationals are not permitted to take China's bar examination, although they may perform certain legal work at local law firms.
Asked Tuesday where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia replied: "When I moved to China." In a subsequent statement, she said she had "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," but did not clarify whether she held a U.S. law license or where, if anywhere, she had been admitted to practice.
Zacharia told The New York Times that when she began appearing on cable news, she consulted Pepperdine University's president about how to describe her legal qualifications. She said she was advised that she could call herself a "lawyer" but should not use the terms "attorney" or "esquire." However, legal experts have questioned whether someone who has not passed the bar exam can properly describe themselves as a lawyer.

On Friday, during a Fox News interview on Thursday, Zacharia said she did not pass the bar. Anthony Scaramucci served director of communications for 10 days during Trump's first administration.

Control of Congress: How past midterms shine a light on Republican challenge in November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:04:39 UTC
03:04:39 KST

The US midterm elections, scheduled for November 3, will determine control of Congress and shape the last two years of President Donald Trump’s final term.
All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives, the lower chamber of Congress, will be up for grabs in the midterms – the informal term for the nationwide polls held in the middle of every four-year presidential term.
Elections will also be held for 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate, the upper chamber of Congress, on the same day.
Currently, the Republican Party has a slim majority in both chambers.
Without a majority in Congress, the incumbent president finds it difficult to pass legislation or make key appointments.
But historical patterns show that the party of the sitting president usually loses House seats in midterms. That has been the case in roughly 20 of the last 22 midterm cycles.
Experts say the trend is likely to continue, even though rising polarisation in US society, along with other factors, complicates any major shift in voting patterns.
“During the past 10 years with Trump dominating the political scene, many of the old rules and historical traditions have been defied,” John Zogby, a public opinion pollster and co-founder of the Arab American Institute, tells TRT World.
Since 1982, every first-term president – with the sole exception of George W Bush in 2002 – has lost seats in the first congressional election after his ascendancy, he notes.
Presidents Ronald Reagan, Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Trump himself in 2018 “lost a huge number of seats” in the midterms.
“As things stand right now, all of the ingredients appear to be in place for the opposition Democratic Party to continue this legacy,” Zogby says.
Trump’s approval ratings are at a low point. They are particularly low on affordability, the economy, and the war in Iran, which are issues that “matter most to American voters”.
Barely a fortnight before the election, “the president’s party appears to be in trouble,” he says.
According to David Schultz, a professor of political science at Hamline University and editor of Presidential Swing States: Why Only Ten Matter, the historical pattern of the president's party losing House seats in midterms should be treated only as a “strong tendency”, and not a law.
The exceptions of 1998 when backlash to Clinton’s impeachment helped Democrats – and 2002 when the September 11 attacks created support for George W Bush – show that “unusual external events” can override the ordinary midterm referendum dynamic.
“As of (now), the major polling averages put Trump’s approval between about 36 and 38 percent,” Schultz tells TRT World.
He points out that the share of swing voters in the electorate has shrunk from 10-15 percent in earlier decades to closer to 0-5 percent.
Meanwhile, the number of truly competitive House seats has fallen from around 120 to about 30.
With fewer voters available to switch sides, outcomes depend more heavily on who turns out on the day of election.
“Detachment from Trump is not the same as attachment to Democrats,” Schultz says.
He expects Republicans to lose House seats, but the size of their seat losses is “far less certain” at this point.
Trump’s name on the ballot?
Presidential approval among voters in midterms ranks among the strongest single predictors of the outcome, experts say.
Zogby points to past cycles in which weak presidential approval, paired with economic stress or unpopular policies, produced large losses: Reagan amid a recession in 1982, Clinton in 1994, and Obama after the Affordable Care Act in 2010.
Trump has reinforced the personal nature of the contest, telling supporters to “vote like his name is on the ballot”, Zogby notes.
Schultz cautions that the relationship between the presidential approval and midterm outcomes is not automatic.
Presidential approval works better when paired with economic perceptions, he says.
Both signals are negative for Republicans this year: voters are sour on the economy and the country’s direction, he adds.
A survey by Quinnipiac University, a non-partisan polling service, has shown only about 32 percent approving of Trump’s handling of the economy against 65 percent disapproving.
But Schultz notes many reasons why poll numbers may overstate Democratic gains.
Roughly 79 percent of Republicans still approve of Trump, according to Quinnipiac polling.
Disapproval does not automatically translate into a vote for the other party, he insists, adding that independent voters now make up a smaller, more disengaged share of the electorate than in earlier eras.
Issues that matter
Zogby describes the top concerns among the electorate as having “melded into one super issue”, as affordability, the war in the Middle East, and inflation.
This goes against Republicans because they currently hold power at House, Senate, and presidential levels.
Even on issues long favourable to Republicans – such as immigration and crime – the Republican Party’s ratings have slipped, he says.
For Schultz, core concerns among the US electorate are grocery and gas prices, housing, and the cost of health care.
Other than immigration and tariffs – which have contributed to the overall affordability problem – another important issue for the electorate is the war against Iran.
The so-called war of choice – now in its eighth month – remains unpopular among voters. Polls show only 29 percent approving of Trump’s handling and 65 percent disapproving.
What distinguishes 2026 from past midterms is that a “small set of issues is nearly inseparable from President Trump himself”, Schultz notes.
“The election, therefore, functions as a referendum on a person more than a contest between issue platforms,” he says.
“Because Democrats have not offered a clear alternative economic message, affordability may produce disengagement as often as it produces Democratic votes,” he adds.
The wild cards
Several conditions can possibly allow Republicans to limit losses or retain at least one chamber of Congress, experts say.
Zogby identifies Democratic vulnerabilities as a major wild card.
“Voter trust for the Democrats is at the lowest point ever,” he says.
Overall, the Democratic Party has a 26 percent positive rating, which includes about 65 percent of Democratic voters – down from 85 percent who trusted their own party in November 2024, Zogby says.
“Democrats also lack an agenda going forward. Those that do have an agenda for action are the progressive wing, and even moderate Democrats are attacking them for being too radical,” he says.
This leaves open the possibility of “last-minute revulsion” by late-deciding voters, he says.
Trump himself remains a wild card who has “rewritten the rule book many times”, he adds.
Schultz outlines a number of factors that can possibly affect the midterm outcomes.
One, partisan loyalty can outlast disappointment with the president, he says.
Many unhappy Republicans will still support their candidate for Congress when they think the alternative offers no clear programme.
Two, the “Democratic brand” imposes a ceiling: only about 21 percent of voters approve of Democrats in Congress, but more than three-fourths of Democratic voters describe their vote primarily as “opposition to Trump”, he says.
Three, a change in the news, such as a durable settlement of the Iran war, falling gas prices, or easing inflation, can improve Trump’s standing by a few points in key places, Schultz says.
Schultz also points to the structure of the Senate. It favours Republicans, while Democrats must defend all their seats and gain a net four, several of them in states Trump carried comfortably.
Finally, polling and turnout error can be consequential if low-propensity voters who dislike Trump decide to stay home on the day of the election.
“Taken together, my judgement is that Republicans are far better positioned to hold the Senate than the House,” he says, adding that maintaining the majority in the House would require a combination of strong Democratic abstention and durable Republican loyalty – something the current polling does not show.

Saudi Arabia’s biggest problem may be its enemy’s smallest weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:03:43 UTC
03:03:43 KST

Saudi Arabia’s biggest problem may be its enemy’s smallest weapons
The Houthis continue to strike Saudi Arabia despite Riyadh’s threats of a forceful response and promises to enlist outside partners to defend the kingdom.
By targeting airports and oil infrastructure, Ansar Allah is seeking to raise the cost of Saudi involvement in Yemen’s conflict and force the kingdom’s leadership to reconsider the terms of a settlement.
The latest wave of Houthi attacks has targeted facilities of particular importance to Saudi Arabia. On the evening of October 13, a strike hit Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, home to the company’s key management operations. The Saudi Energy Ministry reported a fire, though miraculously no one was killed.
Ansar Allah also claimed strikes on an oil refinery in Riyadh and King Khalid International Airport. The choice of targets suggests the Houthis want to put virtually all of the kingdom’s oil revenue at risk and disrupt its international air connections.
These targets also suggest that the movement is trying to influence Saudi leaders’ decisions directly. Oil infrastructure generates government revenue, airports connect the country to the outside world, and confidence in the kingdom depends on the security of both. Even limited damage can therefore produce an impact far greater than the cost of the weapons used.
What is driving the conflict?
The Houthis have their own history of confrontation with Saudi Arabia. The movement emerged in northern Yemen, fought a series of wars against the central government between 2004 and 2010, and seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Its rise was rooted in Yemen’s political system, local conflicts, and the collapse of state institutions. Iranian support strengthened an already established force with its own social base and political objectives.
The Saudi intervention in 2015 cemented Riyadh’s position as the movement’s principal foreign adversary. For the kingdom, the aim was to prevent a hostile force from consolidating power along its southern border and to support Yemen’s internationally recognized government. For the Houthi leadership, the war became both a threat to its survival and a rallying cause. Invoking foreign aggression allowed the movement to portray its struggle for domestic supremacy as a defense of national sovereignty.
That logic remains relevant to the current escalation. Saudi support for an offensive by Yemeni government forces threatens the Houthis’ territorial gains and bargaining position. Striking deep inside the kingdom allows them to raise the price of that support. Their apparent calculation is to make continued Saudi involvement in the war carry a recurring cost on Saudi soil.
The movement’s demands are concrete: an end to strikes, limits on assistance to its Yemeni adversaries, the lifting of transportation and trade restrictions, and agreements on revenues and payments. These issues were under discussion long before the latest escalation. The framework for a roadmap presented by the UN in December 2023 included a nationwide ceasefire, payment of public-sector salaries, the resumption of oil exports, and an easing of restrictions on Sanaa airport and the port of Hodeidah.
By increasing Riyadh’s costs, Ansar Allah hopes to extract concessions and retain control of the territory it has seized. A ceasefire on those terms, however, would consolidate the movement’s position without resolving how power should be shared in Yemen.
Attacks on Saudi Arabia also serve Ansar Allah’s domestic political interests. The movement uses its ability to strike deep inside the kingdom to bolster its standing among supporters. Confrontation with Riyadh also allows the Houthis to cast themselves as Yemen’s defenders against foreign intervention and use that claim to justify their bid for power.
Iranian military and technological assistance has undoubtedly expanded Houthi capabilities considerably. But the relationship with Tehran does not erase Ansar Allah’s own interests in Yemen’s power struggle or its confrontation with Saudi Arabia. Reducing the movement’s actions to the execution of Iranian orders fails to explain either the conflict’s local roots or the Houthi leadership’s objectives.
A more accurate description would be a partnership with unequal resources in which the Yemeni side retains substantial autonomy. Weakening Saudi Arabia may serve both partners’ interests, but their preferred terms for ending the war may differ. Ansar Allah must consider conditions on Yemen’s battlefields and the survival of its own rule. Agreements between Iran and outside powers therefore do not guarantee an automatic halt to Houthi operations.
The economics of war
The development of domestic missile production and an expanding network for procuring components make it harder for Riyadh to bring Houthi attacks to an end. If the movement can replenish its arsenal from several sources, restricting Iranian supplies will have only a partial effect. An agreement with Tehran alone would therefore be insufficient to secure Saudi facilities. Much will depend on whether the Houthis themselves believe continued strikes serve their interests.
Nor do the Houthis need to match Saudi Arabia in the quantity or quality of their weapons. They can choose their targets and pause between attacks, while the kingdom must continuously defend airports, oil facilities, and cities across a vast territory. Even a single hit can disrupt a facility’s operations, trigger flight cancellations, or bring business activity to a halt. Purchases of American air defense systems reduce that threat but do not eliminate it. Riyadh’s problem is that military superiority has yet to deprive its adversary of the ability to inflict economically painful blows. That is precisely the capability the Houthis are trying to turn into negotiating leverage.
Saudi military spending exceeds $82 billion per year, yet the kingdom still struggles to protect its infrastructure from Houthi attacks. This exposes the gap between the cost of the weapons it has purchased and their effectiveness in this particular war. Advanced fighter jets and missile defense systems give Riyadh a considerable advantage, but detecting small drones and low-flying cruise missiles requires extensive radar coverage and rapid information sharing between units. Without those capabilities, expensive equipment cannot reliably detect and engage targets in time.
In a prolonged confrontation, the disparity in weapons costs also becomes significant. According to cited estimates, a Patriot interceptor costs more than $3 million, while some Houthi drones cost just $15,000–25,000. Defenders have to use such interceptors against cheap aircraft to protect far more valuable assets. But sustained defensive operations deplete stocks that cannot be replenished quickly, particularly amid strong global demand for air defense systems. This gives the Houthis an opportunity to wear down the kingdom’s defenses even when most of the aircraft they launch fail to reach their targets.
Technical difficulties are compounded by the structure of the Saudi armed forces. The separation of the regular military and the National Guard has historically served, in part, to protect the monarchy against a coup. But separate chains of command and highly centralized decision-making can hinder coordination and limit commanders’ initiative. Another weapons purchase, then, will not solve the problem on its own. Even additional detection and interception systems will deliver limited results if information arrives late and coordinating a response takes too long.
The Houthis can reasonably expect these shortcomings to take time to address, leaving them able to continue inflicting painful blows in the meantime. Domestic production and broader supply networks help sustain that campaign. The movement does not need to destroy major industrial facilities or shut down air travel altogether; a recurring threat is enough to make airlines reconsider routes, investors postpone decisions, and Saudi leaders spend more on protecting infrastructure.
Will help come from abroad?
Statements by Türkiye and Pakistan expressing their readiness to defend Saudi Arabia do not yet provide grounds to expect either country to enter the war fully, much less fight the Houthis inside Yemen. At an October 5 meeting, the parties to the Mecca Agreement announced that they would provide forces and equipment for the kingdom’s defense. The political weight of those promises, however, will depend on whether the allies can actually reduce the number of attacks and the damage they cause. As long as the strikes continue, Houthi leaders may view such declarations as rhetoric unlikely to be followed by a dangerous expansion of the war.
Ankara’s position reinforces that calculation. Turkish Foreign Affairs Minister Hakan Fidan outlined possible assistance with air defense, electronic warfare, and technical support, while explicitly ruling out Turkish troops taking part in offensive operations on foreign soil. Türkiye has thus set clear limits on its role from the outset.
Pakistan also has reasons to avoid direct intervention. Joining the war in Yemen would mean additional military spending and the risk of worsening relations with neighboring Iran. It would therefore be premature to expect Islamabad to take on the task of defeating the Houthis on Riyadh’s behalf. Its commitments to the kingdom leave room for a role limited to defending specific facilities and providing military assistance.
A similar distinction applies to the American position. Intelligence sharing and targeting assistance support Saudi operations, but they do not mean Washington is willing to stop the attacks at any cost. The Houthis appear to be counting on precisely these limits to outside involvement. Their bet is that the kingdom’s allies will help it defend itself but will be reluctant to become embroiled in a prolonged war to achieve Saudi objectives in Yemen.
Until that support produces a substantial reduction in attacks, threats to bring in allies may carry little weight with Ansar Allah.
***
The Houthis are seeking to demonstrate that continued Saudi intervention will bring losses that neither a vast defense budget nor foreign partners can prevent. If that pressure prompts Riyadh to scale back assistance to their adversaries or accept settlement terms favorable to them, the movement will have an opportunity to translate its battlefield gains into lasting political advantages.
Such an outcome would also benefit Iran by weakening Saudi Arabia’s position. Its most immediate consequence, however, would be to strengthen Ansar Allah itself in the struggle for power in Yemen.

North Kazakhstan receives first shipment of pedigree livestock from Australia
North Kazakhstan region has received its first shipment of pedigree cattle from Australia, with 305 Aberdeen Angus animals arriving via a special cargo flight through Astana International Airport, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The imports are being carried out under Kazakhstan's 2026-2030 Comprehensive Livestock Development Plan, which aims to strengthen the national breeding base, improve herd genetics, boost domestic breeding capacity, and increase output of competitive livestock products.
The plan envisions the purchase of 50,000 head of breeding livestock, including 40,000 head of cattle and 10,000 head of small ruminants. Kazakhstan has already imported approximately 9,500 head of cattle.
Those participating in the herd renewal program are Shal Akyn AGRO-2020 LLP and Asyl Farms LLP. According to Gabiden Balginbekov, director of Asyl Farms, the company selected the Aberdeen Angus breed because of its strong fattening performance and high-quality meat.
"The import of Australian livestock will allow us to establish our own highly productive herd and further develop pedigree breeding directly in the North Kazakhstan Region," he said.
The region has compiled a portfolio of 23 projects for the purchase of pedigree livestock with a total value of 15 billion tenge.
Since the beginning of the year, the region has imported more than 3,000 head of breeding livestock from Germany and Denmark. By the end of the year, another 10 cargo flights carrying pedigree livestock from Australia are expected to arrive. The total number of imported animals in the region is projected to reach around 11,000 head of cattle and more than 1,500 head of small ruminants.
At the same time, the North Kazakhstan region is expanding infrastructure required for the livestock industry development. The region currently operates 118 dairy farms, including 50 modern facilities. 57 veterinary stations are under construction, with total funding of 1.5 billion tenge.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Kazakhstan exports wheat to 29 countries, with shipments worth 1.6 billion US dollars.
