Did Egypt's Sisi hint at stepping down in 2030?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:22:37 UTC
01:22:37 KST

Breadcrumb
Did Egypt's Sisi hint at stepping down in 2030?
A series of statements by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has raised questions over whether the former military general will step down when his current term ends in 2030.
Speaking at the 44th Armed Forces Educational Symposium on Wednesday, Sisi reaffirmed that Egypt's constitution would remain protected and unchanged, remarks that were welcomed by supporters but also drew scepticism.
The president said the constitution would remain untouched, and warned against attempts to incite unrest in Egypt.
“There is a constitution for this state, there is a constitution that we approved for this state, no one will touch it … no one will touch it," Sisi reiterated.
The remarks have sparked debate in Egypt, with some interpreting them as a sign that he does not plan to pursue constitutional changes that would allow him to remain in power for longer.
Here, The New Arab takes a closer look at what the constitution states and what his comments could be hinting at.
What does the constitution say?
Egypt's 2014 constitution, prior to being amended in 2019, stipulated in Article 140 that the country's president is elected to serve a four-year term, with the possibility of re-election only once.
In 2019, an amendment that maintained the two-term limit but extended each term to six years forwarded by a pro-government bloc, was approved by parliament.
The amendment was later approved in a public referendum which saw 88.8 percent of voters vote in favour and 11.1 percent against, with a turnout of 44 percent.
Rights groups and monitors warned at the time that the moves would entrench repression in Egypt, with reports of intimidation of referendum voters and journalists, arrests of opponents of the amendments, and vote buying by state-aligned entities.
Why is Sisi making these statements now?
Sisi's latest statements come amid calls from supporters for him to extend his rule over the country, including the launch of an online petition calling for the president to stay in his post until 2050.
This, however, has prompted widespread backlash, as many have decried it as undemocratic and have cited Sisi's crackdown on dissent.
Saeed Sadek, a professor of political sociology, told The New Arab that the president's statements appear to be aimed at closing the door to speculation about his political future.
The comments also come at a time when Egypt is facing several challenges, particularly from upheaval in the region and a sustained domestic economic crisis.
Sadek added, however, that the statement raises the political cost of any attempt to amend the constitution in the near future, though it does not completely shut the door to changes.
The constitution, he highlighted, contains mechanisms for amendments which can be activated with the necessary political will and backing of parliament.
Sadek notes that Sisi had made similar statements prior to the 2019 amendments.
What has been the response?
While Sisi did not explicitly say he would step down or rule out standing for re-election in 2030, his words have sparked some optimism for many.
Hamdeen Sabahi, Karama Party founder and former presidential candidate who stood against Sisi in 2014, described the president's comments as the "best of words", and expressed his hope that they would be followed up by the "best of actions".
In statements to the press, Sabahi expressed hope that Sisi would hand over power in 2030, paving the way for a new era in Egypt.
Amr Hashem Rabie, an expert at the Al-Ahram Center for Political and Strategic Studies, also told The New Arab that Sisi's statements indicate that Egypt is heading towards the election of a new president in 2030, unless unforeseen circumstances alter this course.
He added that some political parties, such as Nation's Future Party, Homeland Protectors, and the National Front Party, might push for street rallies to demand the president's continued rule, in addition to the role of some media figures who might promote the idea that there is no viable alternative to the president.
Sisi's remarks were also welcomed by Justice Party leader Abdel Moneim Imam, who similarly expressed hope for a peaceful transfer of power.
Egypt's Civil Democratic Movement was among those who welcomed the remarks, though cautioned that the constitution should not be subject to amendment according to circumstances or individuals.
Many Arabic-language reports from outside of Egypt have further expressed skepticism about the president's remarks, given that he holds such a tight grip on the state's institutions.
Sisi took power after removing Egypt's first democratically elected president, Mohamad Morsi, in 2013, and has led a crackdown on dissent within Egypt. By 2030, the former military general would have served as Egypt's president for 16 years.

Andy Lord appointed Interim Chair of NAD Group Advisory Board
The Board provides independent support and challenge, helping to ensure the Group is well run and manages its strategy, performance and risks effectively.
Andy Lord has been appointed Interim Chair of the National Armaments Director (NAD) Group Advisory Board.
Andy is currently Commissioner of Transport for London, responsible for the delivery of safe and reliable transport services across the capital.
He joined TfL in 2019 as Managing Director of London Underground, subsequently becoming Chief Operating Officer before his appointment as Commissioner. Throughout his career, he has held several senior engineering, operational and customer-service roles.
Andy also served as a Non-Executive Director and Board member for Defence Equipment & Support from 2018 until March this year.
Andy has been appointed by Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, until April 30, 2027.
The appointment comes as the NAD Group continues to establish a simpler, more integrated governance model designed to support effective decision-making, clearer accountability and stronger management of performance and risk across the Group.
National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce said of the appointment:
  I am delighted to welcome Andy as Interim Chair of the NAD Group Advisory Board. Andy brings extensive experience both within our organisation, having served as a DE&S Board member and trusted critical friend for eight years, and in leading large, complex organisations.
His insight, challenge and independent perspective will be invaluable as we continue to build the NAD Group into an integrated, mission-focused organisation.
The new Advisory Board’s role is to provide independent support and challenge to the NAD and senior leadership, helping to ensure that the Group is well run and manages its strategy, performance and risks effectively.
On taking up the role, Andy said:
  I am delighted to be appointed the Interim Advisory Board Chair. I have seen first-hand the expertise and commitment that exists across the organisations that now make up the NAD Group, and the vital contribution they make to Defence.
The opportunity now is to build on those strengths, bringing together expertise from across the Group to deliver even greater impact. I look forward to supporting the leadership team as it continues to drive integration, transformation and operational excellence in support of its mission.
The Board provides a strategic, Group-wide perspective, testing whether the organisation is moving in the right direction and identifying where further support, challenge or intervention may be valuable.
These contributions support the NAD Group’s ambition to create a high-support, high-challenge environment, in which leaders are empowered to deliver while remaining accountable for results.
Alongside Andy, the NAD Group’s Non-Executive Members (NEMs) are Robert MacLeod, Tony Meggs, Tracy Sheedy, Carolyn Battersby, Claire Hawkings and Sarah Albon (Safety & Security Committee only).
NEMs are not part of the NAD Group’s executive management structure. Their value comes from their independence and the breadth of experience they bring.
The Board will be supported by three specialist committees covering nominations and remuneration; audit and risk assurance; and safety and security.

Drones Reach Russia’s Siberian Energy Heartland, Spark Fire 3,000 Kilometers From Ukraine
Drones attacked an industrial facility in Russia’s Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug on October 16, triggering a fire roughly 3,000 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.
Ukrinform reported the attack, citing Radio Liberty and Russian regional authorities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Khanty-Mansi Governor Ruslan Kukharuk confirmed that drones struck an industrial facility in the Surgut district, causing a fire. He added that specialists were assessing the extent and nature of the damage but did not identify the affected enterprise.
The Ukrainian OSINT monitoring channel Supernova+ claimed the target was the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant named after Viktor Chernomyrdin, who served as Russia’s prime minister from 1992 to 1998 and previously headed the Soviet gas industry. The facility's identification has not been independently confirmed.
The plant, operated by Gazprom Pererabotka, is Russia's largest facility for processing oil and gas condensate mixtures. It is located near Surgut in Western Siberia, approximately 3,000 kilometers from Ukraine.
The Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug is one of Russia's major oil and natural gas production centers, making its industrial infrastructure significant to the country's energy sector.
The attack followed a series of drone alerts across Russia's remote Siberian energy-producing regions. Earlier on October 16, authorities declared drone threats in the Khanty-Mansi and neighboring Yamalo-Nenets autonomous districts, as well as the Tyumen, Chelyabinsk, and Sverdlovsk regions.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Starlink Speeds Rise Again in Ukraine—but Key Frontline Missions Are Still Disrupted, Zelenskyy Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:17:34 UTC
01:17:34 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Starlink Speeds Rise Again in Ukraine—but Key Frontline Missions Are Still Disrupted, Zelenskyy Says
Starlink connectivity has improved in Ukraine following reported signals from the White House to restore higher operating speeds, but the system remains restricted, and Ukrainian forces still cannot carry out some frontline missions as before, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said during a briefing in Brussels on October 16.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s partners said there had been signals from the White House regarding the restoration of Starlink’s higher-speed capabilities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Have they returned to the previous speed? No. But has the speed increased? Yes,” Zelenskyy said.
The restrictions have become a significant battlefield issue because Ukraine uses high-speed Starlink connectivity on rapidly moving unmanned systems. Zelenskyy stressed that Ukrainian forces do not currently use Starlink for deep strikes inside Russia.
“No, we do not use Starlink for attacks or retaliatory strikes on the territory of the Russian Federation. That is precisely why we appealed to SpaceX and the White House to open up such a capability for us. If we had it, we obviously would not be asking,” he said.
Zelenskyy described the sudden restrictions as an unpleasant and dangerous “surprise,” particularly because Starlink is used in operations intended to intercept Russia’s new jet-powered Shahed-type drones.
“We use Starlink to intercept jet-powered ‘Shaheds’ that fly in and strike our civilians, killing our families. We use special interceptors—drones that move at high speed and use Starlink,” Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that the service was not completely switched off. Instead, its effective speed limit was sharply reduced, which prevented some Ukrainian interceptor drones from keeping their satellite connection while pursuing fast-moving Russian targets.
“And when the speed was reduced, we were unable to shoot down a certain number of these ‘Shaheds.’ That is very painful and unpleasant. In other words, we were unable to provide protection for the population. The ‘Shaheds’ were flying at more than 400 kilometers per hour, while our speed was reduced to 78 km/h,” he said.
That means Russian jet-powered drones were traveling at more than 249 mph, while Ukrainian Starlink-equipped systems reportedly faced connectivity restrictions at around 48 mph.
The restrictions have also affected Ukrainian middle-strike operations against Russian military targets in occupied Ukrainian territory. Zelenskyy said Starlink connectivity had previously supported those missions, but the new limits made some of them impossible.
“And we can no longer do this,” he said.
Beyond combat missions, Zelenskyy emphasized that the restrictions have also complicated battlefield logistics. Ukrainian units use drones connected through Starlink to deliver food and water to troops holding isolated or difficult positions.
“Many people are within reach of enemy drones; we use UAVs to deliver water and food to people who have been holding positions for a long time. We use drones and Starlink. So this affected our ability to protect the population,” Zelenskyy said.
Previously, Germany called for speed restrictions affecting Starlink service in Ukraine to be lifted, stressing that Berlin itself finances part of the satellite communications equipment used by the country.

IN BRIEF: Key statements by Deputy PM Novak at Russian Energy Week plenary session

01:16:46 KST

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. The Russia-US diesel deal is beneficial to all parties, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told a plenary session of Russian Energy Week.
He stressed that EU criticism of the agreement goes against the interests of European consumers.
Novak stressed that Russia has been and remains a reliable energy supplier to global markets, including the West.
TASS has summarized the key takeaways from the deputy prime minister's speech.
Russia-US diesel deal
"I view this deal as a pragmatic solution that is advantageous for all market participants."
"As for criticism from our European partners, we have grown accustomed to their political decisions and statements running counter to the pragmatic demands of the market and consumers. It is European consumers who suffer first and foremost."
"The market is currently experiencing a significant shortage - we estimate it at about 25% of global trade. This is primarily due to supply disruptions from the Persian Gulf to external markets. Furthermore, Russia banned exports in July to supply its domestic market."
"On a per-barrel basis, the current diesel price is roughly $200 per barrel against a crude oil price of $120. Crack spreads for diesel relative to crude oil have widened."
Russia’s reliability and Europe’s costs
"The key factor for reliability today is physical access throughout the entire supply chain - from production and processing to delivery. In this regard, Russia has always been a reliable supplier of energy resources - both to Western Europe, where long-term infrastructure projects for oil and gas have been built since the 1960s, and to global markets today."
Europe's costs have risen since it began shifting away from affordable and stable Russian supplies: "Many industrial operations have relocated to other countries; there are bankruptcies and business closures. Yet, today, politics takes precedence over rational decisions that would benefit consumers. In my view, everything they do regarding energy policy is to the detriment of their own economies and consumers."
Russia is prepared to boost energy supplies to Europe, including under existing long-term contracts: "We are ready to provide larger supply volumes [to Europe]. It was not us who rejected affordable and stable energy supplies from Russia; Europe made that decision for political reasons."
"We remain committed to fulfilling our contracts, including long-term agreements - some of which, for gas, run until 2035-2040. A refusal to take supplies under these contracts is a unilateral decision that has no basis in the existing legal and regulatory framework."
Russia has supplied energy resources to Europe worth $320 billion since 2022, including $21.3 billion in the first nine months of 2026.
Situation in global energy markets
Energy consumers are seeking alternatives to hydrocarbons as global demand declines: "Today, consumers are exploring options for accelerated energy substitution, reducing energy expenditures, and improving energy efficiency," Novak stated.
"We are witnessing a decline in global demand for energy resources this year, which also impacts consumer costs. Amid this structural transformation - and particularly the fallout from geopolitical events in the Strait of Hormuz - we are seeing a sharp price shock. This affects not only insurance and freight but also the overall cost of oil and petroleum products, which have nearly doubled since the beginning of the year."
Russia is "ready to balance energy markets and maintain our role in ensuring energy security based on long-term partnerships."
Russia advocates for closer international cooperation in the energy sector: "It is clear that the shock we experienced this year - as well as other shocks over the past 15 years - has prompted countries to take more unilateral approaches to safeguarding their own energy security," the deputy prime minister noted. "In my view, this is a misguided trend, because global energy security can only be ensured through cooperation and joint action.

Trump backs Israel unity plan keeping Netanyahu PM for two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:16:22 UTC
01:16:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump backs Israel unity plan keeping Netanyahu PM for two years after election: Report
The Trump administration is backing efforts to form a broad Israeli unity government after this month's election that could keep Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister for up to two years before handing power to opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, according to an Israeli media report.
The proposal would exclude far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and bring together Netanyahu's Likud party with Eisenkot's Yashar party, Israel Hayom reported on Friday.
The newspaper cited unnamed US and foreign political officials familiar with the discussions. Neither Washington nor the Israeli parties involved have publicly confirmed an agreed plan.
Israel is due to hold a Knesset election on 27 October.
Polls have suggested neither Netanyahu's right-wing bloc nor the fragmented opposition is guaranteed a stable governing majority, raising the possibility of prolonged coalition negotiations.
According to Israel Hayom, the US and regional governments believe a broad coalition would be better placed to make major decisions on ending regional conflicts and advancing President Donald Trump's wider Middle East agenda.
One unnamed foreign official quoted in the report said a fragile minority government would be unable to make the "major and decisive political decisions" the region required.
The proposed arrangement would allow Netanyahu to remain prime minister for up to two years before Eisenkot succeeded him, according to the report.
During that period, the government would be expected to work towards ending wars on multiple fronts and reaching political agreements with regional states, particularly Saudi Arabia.
The Trump administration has been pushing Riyadh to join the Abraham Accords and normalise relations with Israel.
Washington has linked that effort to other parts of the US-Saudi relationship, including F-35 fighter jets and a civilian nuclear programme.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said, however, that normalisation with Israel would require meaningful progress towards Palestinian statehood.
The issue has also become entangled with Washington's proposed nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, which Trump has said would depend on Riyadh joining the Abraham Accords.
According to Israel Hayom, Saudi Arabia is also seeking a different political configuration in Israel before moving forward.
US Ambassador Mike Huckabee has recently met several senior Israeli politicians, including Eisenkot, the report said.
The contacts were said to have been handled carefully because of concerns over perceptions of US interference in the election.
But Israeli politicians were reportedly told that Washington and other governments would welcome a broad and stable coalition without far-right parties.
Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, has emerged as one of Netanyahu's principal challengers in the election and leads the centrist Yashar party.
The proposed government would also seek to address domestic issues that have deeply divided Israeli politics.
These include demands for an official inquiry into the failures surrounding the 7 October 2023 attacks, disputes over the judiciary and the continuing row over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has denied reports that he is directly involved in efforts to engineer a unity government.
He has nevertheless said he wants to avoid repeated elections and see a stable government formed after the vote.
The reported US effort comes as Israel's election remains highly fragmented, with Palestinian parties potentially playing a decisive role if neither major bloc secures a governing majority.

Division in Lebanon over Hezbollah’s confiscated explosives
Hezbollah said the explosives were to be used against Israel, though political figures and some analysts fear assassinations.
Beirut, Lebanon – On October 5, a minivan was stopped at a checkpoint in Dahr el-Baydar between the Bekaa Valley and Mount Lebanon region.
Lebanese security forces discovered the car was carrying hundreds of kilos of explosive materials, including TNT and C-4, according to Lebanese officials.
On Thursday, Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah released a statement saying that the explosives belonged to Hezbollah which had demanded their return, along with the release of the two people detained in the vehicle.
“From the moment the vehicle was detained, the relevant bodies within [Hezbollah] immediately contacted the security and judicial agencies and informed them that the vehicle and its cargo belonged to the resistance,” Fadlallah said in his statement. “They demanded the immediate release of those detained and the return of the vehicle and everything inside it, as these are capabilities used by the resistance to confront the Israeli occupation of our land in the south [of Lebanon].”
Fadlallah indicated that the explosives were for use against Israel, which continues to occupy large parts of southern Lebanon, and not internally against the Lebanese government or other factions, as some political figures and analysts had suggested.
“We therefore warn the [Lebanese] authorities of the consequences of continuing to escalate their measures,” he said. “[Hezbollah] will defend its people’s rights and the capabilities it uses to confront the Israeli enemy and it will not tolerate any targeting by any party implementing American demands against our resistance.”
But many of Hezbollah’s political opponents, who blame the Iranian-backed group for targeting political opponents in assassinations in the past, fear that smuggled explosives will be turned against Hezbollah’s detractors.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam pointed out that C-4 explosives had been used in previous assassinations, although investigators have not established that the seized shipment was intended for such an attack.
Hezbollah has never admitted carrying out assassinations, despite repeated accusations against it, including the killing of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri in 2005.
Regional implications
On March 2, when Hezbollah responded to ongoing Israeli attacks for the first time in over a year in retaliation for the killing of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Salam and his government banned the group’s military activities. Salam’s coalition government includes two Hezbollah ministers who opposed the decision and the group has repeatedly defied the government’s declaration by continuing to fight Israel.
Fighting has largely subsided since June, when Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-administered trilateral framework agreement. Under the deal, pilot zones would be established as part of a phased process in which Israel would eventually withdraw its troops and the Lebanese Army would enter to disarm Hezbollah. However, the programme has had complications from the start as Israel never had a presence in some of the areas included in the pilot zones, according to locals, and Israeli demolitions continue in the areas under its occupation.
In recent weeks, Lebanese security forces have uncovered a number of operations aimed at smuggling explosives.
Lebanese officials have condemned the smuggling operations and Salam has vowed to investigate the incidents, particularly the Dahr el-Baydar incident.
“We will not be lenient in following up and expanding the investigation in order to identify all those involved in this criminal operation and those behind them,” Salam wrote on social media. “We will deal with weapons outside the legal framework with the required firmness.”
But the issue also points to growing disagreements between Lebanon’s government and Hezbollah’s leadership over the role of armed resistance.
Explosive concerns
Since the end of Lebanon’s civil war in 1990, Hezbollah has been the principal Lebanese force to keep its weapons. This was ostensibly part of a national security formula of “the army, the people and the resistance” aimed at opposing Israeli occupation – which continued until 2000 before resuming in 2024 – and aggression, while the country was also under Syrian hegemony.
That changed last year when President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Salam came to power. The Hezbollah allied al-Assad regime in Damascus had just fallen, cutting off a powerful land route of weapons and financing from Tehran. The regional power dynamic appeared to be shifting towards a decrease in Iranian power and more influence from the United States and Israel, leading Lebanon’s leaders to announce that all non-state weapons would come under control of the state.
Despite Hezbollah’s opposition to the new leaders’ decrees, the Lebanese Army went about disarming Hezbollah sites in southern Lebanon. Some Hezbollah opponents have declared the group weak and defeated, though analysts say the group still retains some fighting power and that Lebanon’s regional alliances could largely be determined by regional events.
Still, the group’s domestic influence has been challenged at times by the new Lebanese leadership, including in the Dahr el-Baydar incident.
Marcel Baloukji, a former brigadier general who oversaw the Lebanese Army’s border committee with Syria, told Al Jazeera that the recent busts, and particularly the Dahr el-Baydar incident, were connected to the security situation in the wider region, particularly concerning the US-Israeli war on Iran and the recent intensification of violence between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
He suggested that Hezbollah could be looking to follow the lead of other pro-Iranian actors in the region and intensify attacks against adversaries. But he also added that Hezbollah may need explosives for drones to attack Israeli forces occupying southern Lebanon.
Government difficulties
Despite the promises by Lebanese officials to investigate, analysts said concerns remain about how effective the investigations might be.
Issam Kayssi, a Beirut-based analyst at the Carnegie Middle East Center, raised questions over Salam’s relationship with the Lebanese security apparatus. Lebanon has multiple security agencies, some of which have competing loyalties to different political figures or parties.
“We are more than a year on from the Raouche incident,” he said, referring to a Hezbollah event held on Beirut’s seafront in 2025 to commemorate the assassination of the group’s late leaders Hassan Nasrallah and Hashem Safieddine. Hezbollah projected the likeness of the two slain leaders on Pigeon Rock in Beirut’s Raouche seafront district, despite the projections being prohibited by authorities, prompting Salam to call for the arrest of those responsible. Security agents on site failed to act to prevent the projections and observers fear that elements of the security agencies may not be fully cooperative with Salam in the explosives investigations he ordered.
Baloukji described Salam’s relationship with the security agencies as “somewhat strained.” He added that it could be the latest file in a series of difficulties facing the Lebanese government, as Israel’s occupation and ongoing demolition of southern infrastructure continue.
“Our situation remains in a state of prolonged limbo, with no solutions in sight,” Baloukji said. “The framework agreement is stalled and there is no resolution to de-escalate the situation in the south.”

16:03:38 UTC

An Israeli opinion poll published on Friday showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition tied, with neither reaching the majority needed to form a government, while 55% of respondents favored a unity government if the upcoming election produces no decisive result, Anadolu reports.
The Maariv poll, published 11 days before the Oct. 27 general election, showed that if voting were held today, both Netanyahu’s bloc and the Jewish opposition would win 51 seats each in the 120-member Knesset.
Arab lawmakers, meanwhile, were projected to win 14 seats, while the Reservists Party would secure four, without indicating which bloc it would support.
A government requires the backing of at least 61 lawmakers. Otherwise, Israel could face another election.
Both Netanyahu’s camp and the main Jewish opposition parties reject relying on Arab parties to form a government.
According to the poll, Netanyahu’s bloc would be divided among Likud with 18 seats, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power eight, the religious United Torah Judaism party eight, Shas seven, Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism six and Ofer Winter’s Amcha Yisrael four.
The Jewish opposition would include Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party with 21 seats, Naftali Bennett’s Together 13, Yair Golan’s Democrats nine and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu eight.
READ: Israel elections: Palestinian state caught between Netanyahu’s incitement, Eisenkot’s rejection
Among Arab parties, the Joint List led by Yousef Jabareen was projected to win eight seats, while Mansour Abbas’ United Arab List, or Ra’am, would receive six.
The Reservists Party, headed by Yoaz Hendel, is projected to win four seats, with the poll not determining which camp it would support.
On the preferred candidate for prime minister, Eisenkot, a former Israeli army chief of staff, remained ahead of Netanyahu with 48% support compared with 41% for the incumbent.
Israelis do not directly elect their prime minister. The post goes to the politician able to form a coalition backed by at least 61 lawmakers.
If the political deadlock continues, Israel could face another election unless a unity government is formed.
The poll found that 55% of Israelis prefer a national unity government over another election if the Oct. 27 vote fails to produce a clear outcome.
Another 27% said they favor holding a new election, while 18% were undecided.
The results showed differences between the two camps.
Among opposition voters, 54% said they support a unity government provided it is headed by a leader from their bloc.
Among coalition voters, 36% backed a unity government led by Netanyahu, while 32% preferred another election if no clear result emerged.
Maariv said the poll was conducted by the private Lazar Research Institute among a random sample of 700 Israelis, with a margin of error of 3.7 percentage points.

EU rallies in support of Ukraine amid Trump standoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:02:13 UTC
01:02:13 KST

EU rallies in support of Ukraine amid Trump standoff
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy asks EU leaders for extra $79bn to help fight Russia next year.
European Union leaders have urged continued support for Ukraine amid a deepening rift between Washington and Kyiv that has raised fears the country could be left more exposed to Russian attacks heading into the winter.
Top EU officials stressed the need to keep arming Ukraine and sanctioning Russia on Friday, the second and final day of an EU summit in Brussels attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
“This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine,” said European Council President Antonio Costa, standing beside the Ukrainian leader. “This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions. Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”
The EU is hosting Zelenskyy at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine, four-and-a-half years after neighbouring Russia invaded it.
Russian missiles and drones have rained down on Ukrainian cities daily, and Kyiv’s souring relationship with the United States has sparked fears that Washington could pull back crucial intelligence sharing and weapons support.
Arriving at the summit, Zelenskyy thanked EU leaders for their support and pointedly referred to them as “real leaders”.
That remark appeared to be a dig at US President Donald Trump, who last weekend blindsided the Ukrainian president by announcing that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities.
Zelenskyy abandoned that deal on Thursday, saying Russia had failed to live up to it, a move Trump called “a disgrace”.
Trump has also angered Ukraine by suspending sanctions on Russian oil products and striking a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow to supply large quantities of diesel to global markets.
“This diesel deal will never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets,” Zelenskyy said on the sidelines of the summit. “But it will put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war.”
He also accused the Russian leader of having no real interest in peace talks.
“Putin does not want peace talks at the moment, in any form,” Zelenskyy said. “He’s playing with words … Quite simply, it looks like a parody of a genuine desire to end the war.”
Zelenskyy asks EU for $79bn
Bracing for expected winter-time attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Zelenskyy asked EU leaders for an additional 70bn euros ($79 billion) in funding next year to keep up the fight against Russia.
“The war will cost 155 billion euros [$174bn] next year. And we need at least 70 billion euros more from you – for defence, for weapons and for our resilience,” the Ukrainian president said.
“This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.”
Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard, reporting from the summit in Brussels, said Zelenskyy made an “emotional plea” for European support, with air defence systems at the top of his “wish list”.
Zelenskyy appealed to European countries to dig into their own stocks to help cover Ukraine’s needs in the colder winter months, said Birchard. “But of course, that would mean some European countries potentially compromising their own national security.”
‘We stand by your side’
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told the Reuters news agency that the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for next year.
“Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell,” Michal said.
European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen pledged continued EU support for Ukraine through the winter.
“Russia is trying everything to destroy the energy and water infrastructure. But we stand by your side. We will support you as we did in the other winters,” she said.
Austria, however, urged caution in the debate over new, far-reaching financial commitments to Ukraine.
“There are so many figures being bandied about that we now need to put them into context, explain them and make it clear where this shortfall is coming from,” said Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.
Al Jazeera’s Birchard said the general European solidarity for Zelenskyy was a stark difference from recent messages coming from Washington. “He is once again, at least, among friends,” she said.
However, Birchard added that some European officials were said to be appealing to Zelenskyy behind closed doors to “kind of dial down” his public criticism of Trump, which they fear could put Europeans in a tough position.
“Of course, they [European officials] want to show that they are close to Ukraine, that they are supporting Zelenskyy, but they also don’t want to antagonise the US,” she said.
Friday’s summit came as Russian strikes killed three people in Kharkiv and left hundreds of thousands of people without power in Ukraine.
The Kremlin last week said Ukraine had undermined the possibility of an immediate resumption of peace talks after hitting Moscow with drones during last month’s election.

15:57:41 UTC

Democratic candidates have outraised Republican rivals by huge margins in key US congressional races, new campaign finance filings show, even as tech billionaire Elon Musk pumped record sums into efforts to keep the GOP in power.
The figures emerged after candidates and political groups submitted their third-quarter fundraising reports to the Federal Election Commission (FEC) by Thursday's deadline, the last quarterly disclosure before the November 3 midterm elections.
In six states viewed as pivotal to Senate control, Texas, Alaska, Ohio, Maine, Michigan and Iowa, Democrats collected between three and six times as much as their Republican opponents in the July-September quarter, according to an analysis of the figures by Punchbowl News.
The reports revealed a striking contrast between Democrats' strong fundraising at the candidate level and Republicans' advantage in money flowing through wealthy donors and outside political groups.
In Texas, Democrat James Talarico raised a record $64 million, compared with $10.2 million for Republican Ken Paxton's campaign.
In Ohio, former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown raised $23.1 million against $4.8 million for Republican incumbent Jon Husted. And in Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson collected $20.4 million compared with $5.2 million for Republican Senator Susan Collins.
Democrats also outpaced Republicans in crucial House races, with at least 47 Republican incumbents outraised by Democratic or independent challengers, compared with only about six Democratic incumbents outraised by Republicans.
At least 27 Democratic candidates in competitive House districts raised more than $2 million each, against just four Republicans.
Massive advertising campaign
Yet Republicans have an enormous financial counterweight in Musk, the world's richest person, whose third-quarter donations of at least $276 million were confirmed in filings, making him the election cycle's largest known political donor.
Of that, $158 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Senate fundraising group, which is spending the entire sum on bankrolling a massive advertising campaign in Texas supporting Paxton.
Another $20 million went to an organisation backing Republican House candidates.
Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief, has contributed some $366 million during this election cycle, according to US media analyses.
Outside groups can spend enormous amounts independently of campaigns, but candidates get cheaper advertising rates, meaning their dollars can stretch further in the final weeks before the November 3 vote.
Republicans retain sizeable cash reserves in several districts, and fundraising alone cannot determine electoral outcomes.
But the figures underscore the financial resources available to Democrats as they seek to overturn Republican majorities in both chambers of Congress.

More than 1.4 million people are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026, the ministry added.
Starvation as a weapon
Israeli authorities have used starvation as a weapon during the genocide in Gaza since October 2023, according to Palestinian government bodies and rights organizations.
Israel tightened restrictions on crossings in March 2025, preventing thousands of aid trucks waiting at border crossings from entering the enclave.
The restrictions followed widespread hunger in northern Gaza caused by the blockade and limits on food and relief supplies, forcing some residents to eat animal feed and wild plants.
In late May 2025, Israel allowed 87 aid trucks to enter Gaza for the first time after 81 days, according to Gaza’s government media office.
Aid later continued to enter on a limited and intermittent basis under strict restrictions until February 2026, when Israel allowed a limited increase in the number of trucks entering the enclave under a ceasefire agreement.
Palestinian officials said the shipments still lacked sufficient quantities of essential food items.
According to Gaza’s government media office, Israel has allowed in only about 34% of the humanitarian aid trucks agreed upon.
OPINION: The ceasefire that keeps killing children: Gaza one year on
Malnutrition reaches ‘catastrophic levels’
“Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached catastrophic levels that are killing children, the elderly and vulnerable groups,” the Health Ministry said.
More than 1.4 million Palestinians, around 67% of Gaza’s population, are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026.
More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition were recorded among children under 5 from 2024 through August 2026, the ministry added.
Of them, 18% of children were suffering from severe acute malnutrition that threatened their lives, while 12.2% of children were affected by stunting, indicating the impact of food shortages on their development.
The mortality rate among children under 5 rose from 13.6 to 33.4 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2022 and 2025, the ministry said.
It estimated that 74,200 children will need treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027.
Pregnant women
Among pregnant women, the ministry said the prevalence of anemia rose to 61% in 2026, compared with 41% before the war.
“Around 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded during the first half of 2026, more than three times the number recorded during the previous six months,” it added.
“One in three pregnancies in Gaza is now classified as high-risk,” the ministry continued.
“The figures show that the health consequences of the food crisis are increasingly affecting mothers and unborn children, in addition to children,” it said.
Calls for urgent international action
“The right to food is a fundamental human right that does not cease to exist during war,” the ministry said.
It called on the international community and the UN to take immediate action to ensure the safe, sustained and unrestricted entry of food, therapeutic nutritional supplements and medicines into Gaza.
The ministry urged that children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and the elderly be given priority as the groups most vulnerable to malnutrition.
It also called for support to revive local food production to help curb the worsening humanitarian crisis.
The figures come amid the humanitarian consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, which has caused widespread destruction to infrastructure, health facilities and food production sources.
The war has also damaged farmland, food production facilities and water networks, undermining residents’ ability to meet their basic needs locally.
Repeated displacement, loss of income and soaring prices have further increased families’ dependence on humanitarian aid, while access remains irregular.

The UK government has cleared the way for Axel Springer’s planned purchase of Telegraph Media Group after deciding not to refer the deal for a more detailed competition investigation.
Culture Minister Lisa Nandy said Friday that she would not refer the proposed acquisition to a Phase 2 investigation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), the UK’s competition regulator.
“I will not be referring this matter to a more in-depth ‘Phase 2’ investigation by the Competition and Markets Authority,” Nandy said in a written statement.
She also said the Public Interest Intervention Notice (PIIN), issued in January 2024, and the related public interest merger reference order had ceased to be in force following her decision.
The decision reduces regulatory uncertainty surrounding one of the UK media industry’s high-profile ownership transactions and allows Axel Springer to proceed with its planned purchase without a more detailed competition investigation at this stage.
Axel Springer is one of Europe’s largest media groups. It owns major German newspapers, including Bild and Die Welt, as well as international digital outlets Politico and Business Insider.
The acquisition would bring one of Britain’s most prominent newspaper groups under the ownership of the Berlin-based company, marking a significant change in the UK media landscape.
The Telegraph Group was placed under receivership in 2023 after its former owners, the Barclay family, accumulated substantial debts to banks. Since then, the newspaper’s future has remained highly uncertain.
Before Axel Springer entered the picture, the UAE-backed RedBird IMI consortium had sought to acquire the newspaper.
However, the prospect of a long-established conservative British newspaper coming under the control of Gulf capital — and, indirectly, a foreign state — triggered a major political controversy in the UK.
The British government subsequently introduced legislation banning foreign state ownership of newspapers, prompting RedBird IMI to step back and transfer its acquisition rights to Axel Springer.

The move expands an investigation that was previously focused on far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
The case concerns suspected torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage when Israeli forces intercepted small fleets of boats headed towards Gaza in 2025 and 2026, the Rome prosecutors' office said in a statement.
Investigators opened the probe after complaints from 50 Italian citizens who were detained by Israeli authorities following two Global Sumud Flotilla missions in September to October 2025 and April to May 2026.
Katz did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Ben-Gvir in June dismissed news that he was under investigation, saying he would "continue to stand proudly alongside our fighters."
Death threats and beatings
Prosecutors said activists detained after the first mission had reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism.
Activists involved in the second mission reported even harsher treatment, including beatings in the dark, the use of tasers and rubber bullets, the statement said.
Investigators had identified various individuals forming the military and police chains of command involved in the operations, prosecutors said.
Besides Katz and Ben-Gvir, prosecutors named 12 senior Israeli military, police and prison officials as suspects, including military chief Eyal Zamir.
Zamir also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Prosecutors said they had sent Israel a request for judicial assistance in June, seeking information needed to reconstruct events and establish individual responsibility. They did not say whether Israeli authorities had responded.
The prosecutors said they also held talks with the European Union's judicial cooperation agency, Eurojust, because similar investigations into the two flotilla missions were underway in other unnamed European countries.
Under Italian law, crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens can be prosecuted in Rome.
Being placed under investigation in Italy does not imply guilt and does not automatically lead to a trial. However, if the probe determines that charges are warranted, prosecutors could lodge a formal request for trial.
Flotilla organizers say they aimed to break Israel's blockade of Gaza by delivering humanitarian assistance. Israel says its naval blockade on Gaza is lawful.

The vote that could redraw Canada: Everything you need to know about Alberta's referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:33:58 UTC
00:33:58 KST

Alberta is holding a nonbinding referendum on Monday to ask residents if they want to remain part of Canada, marking the first time the oil-rich province has ever put the question of separation to the public.
Polls have consistently shown most Albertans — about 70% — want to stay in Canada, with roughly a quarter of residents supporting an independent Alberta.
What’s on ballot for Albertans?
The ballot has 10 questions, each with its own colour-coded option.
The last ballot question voters see is question 10: whether Alberta should remain a Canadian province or start the legal process required to hold a binding referendum on separation.
A simple majority in favour of separation could trigger that process.
There are nine other nonbinding questions about immigration, access to provincial services — including education, social care and healthcare — and voter identification requirements.
Why is Alberta putting its future to a vote?
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said in May it was “time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject, and move on,” when she announced the government would add a question on separation.
Smith’s decision followed months of campaigning by a small but vocal group of separatists, who argue Alberta’s energy wealth subsidises poorer parts of the country and that Ottawa's bureaucracy has stifled the province’s economy.
Some members of the group had backed Smith's candidacy for premier. Smith says she voted to keep Alberta in Canada in advance polling, according to a video she posted on social media on Wednesday.
Has Canada faced break-up vote before?
Yes, but not in Alberta. The majority-French-speaking province of Quebec has held two referendums, in 1980 and 1995.
Quebecers voted to remain in Canada both times, but by the slimmest of margins in 1995.
The separatist Parti Quebecois (PQ) won a provincial election earlier this month and has pledged to hold a third referendum, but only after US President Donald Trump has left office and if the party holds a majority.
The PQ won a minority government on October 5, meaning it will rely on smaller parties to pass legislation.
Canada is a federation of 10 provinces and three territories.
While Ottawa handles matters of national interest, such as defence, trade and foreign policy, the provinces and territories hold significant power over medical care, education and land rights.
When will the verdict be in?
Polls are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. on Monday (0200 GMT on Tuesday).
Elections Alberta says it will count ballots by hand and count the separation question first.
Elections Alberta will publish results on its website as they arrive, and unofficial results are expected within 48 hours after voting ends.
What comes next if Alberta votes to leave?
Smith has said she will respect the result and quickly begin the process to hold a legally binding referendum. But separation would not happen imminently.
After the 1995 Quebec referendum, Canada's Parliament passed the Clarity Act in 2000, which says talks about secession can be triggered only if a clear majority of the public supports it, without specifying the necessary threshold.
The act also states provinces and territories have no unilateral right to leave Canada and that a constitutional amendment negotiated by provincial, territorial and federal governments is required.
First Nations groups have objected to an independent Alberta, as their land treaties with Canada predate Alberta's entry into Confederation.
In May, an Alberta court judge ruled the province’s chief electoral officer was wrong to allow separatists to collect signatures requesting a referendum, because the process should have prompted a consultation with Indigenous peoples whose rights might be violated by separation.
Alberta has appealed the decision.
Where does Carney stand on referendum?
Mark Carney, Canada’s Prime Minister, was largely raised in Alberta and has previously said “the best place for Alberta is in Canada” and that the country cannot succeed if it's divided.
He released a video on Canadian Thanksgiving, October 12, saying national unity is critical as Canada fights threats from abroad, including a trade war with the US.
Carney has campaigned to keep Alberta in Canada.
Would Quebec referendum pass based on current polls?
Current opinion polls indicate that a Quebec sovereignty referendum may fail, with support for independence stuck in the 25–35% range and opposition often reaching 60–70% among decided voters.
Aggregators such as 338Canada show roughly 70% No versus 30% Yes once undecided respondents are excluded, while individual surveys from Léger, Pallas Data and others consistently place the No side well ahead.
Even among francophones, Yes support is not high enough to carry a province-wide majority.
While campaign events, question wording or external shocks could still move the numbers, nothing in the present data suggests a competitive race.
A Yes victory would require a dramatic and sustained shift that current polling does not forecast.

Zelenskyy stated that after speed restrictions were introduced, Ukraine temporarily lost the ability to use the system effectively for those interceptions, and the limits have still not been fully lifted for the Defense Forces.
The Ukrainian president also addressed frozen Russian assets, emphasizing that Kyiv wants access to the funds before Moscow can regain control over them.
“We know clearly that they very much want them back. This is one of Russia’s goals. Ukraine wants to receive this money before Russia is able to do so,” Zelenskyy stated.
On intelligence sharing, Zelenskyy noted that Ukraine receives data from dozens of countries, while the US continues providing information on ballistic missile launches.
“There are many challenges with ballistic missiles. We are working on every possible option so that Ukraine can be as independent as possible,” he added.
At the same EU summit, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated that Brussels was preparing a 22nd sanctions package against Russia and would not lift existing restrictions until Moscow ends the war. She also accused Russia of violating the energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump “not a single minute” after it was announced.

Ukraine Develops Full-Body Protective Armor That NATO Armies Do Not Currently Field
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:31:40 UTC
00:31:40 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Develops Full-Body Protective Armor That NATO Armies Do Not Currently Field
Ukraine is introducing a new layer of body protection for frontline troops, centrally procuring 4,700 fragmentation-resistant suits for the first time, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense on October 15.
The roughly two-kilogram protective system consists of a specialized jacket, trousers, and pteruges designed to shield the pelvis and upper thighs.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The pteruges include an adjustable belt and seven sections containing soft ballistic inserts: two frontal, four lateral, and one rear.
Unlike rigid armor plates, the soft ballistic packages are designed to conform to the soldier’s body while providing protection against fragments and bullets. The sections can be repositioned for fit, while the rear section includes additional padding for troops operating while seated. The suit can also be worn with a standard body armor vest, extending protection to areas that are normally left exposed.
“Our task at the Ministry of Defense is to listen to the needs of the troops and supply exactly what our warriors really need,” Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik stated. The design underwent military testing among personnel whose combat duties require high mobility before the final model was approved.
The armor is intended primarily for assault troops, medics, and other personnel operating near the line of contact, where artillery shells and drones create persistent fragmentation threats. The Ministry noted that comparable protective suits are not currently fielded by NATO countries and that a prototype of the Ukrainian design was provided to Western partners for evaluation.
Ukraine's pace of battlefield adaptation has drawn growing attention from its Western partners. Earlier in October, former US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll called it “humiliating” to watch Ukraine field better weapons despite a far smaller budget.
He argued that the US procurement system was too slow to keep pace. In May 2025, Driscoll created the 600-soldier Unmanned Assault Battalion, an experimental drones-first unit in Italy that worked alongside Ukrainian advisers.

Uzbekistan's 2 ancient canals added to World Heritage Irrigation Structures List
Uzbekistan’s Dargom and Shohrud canals were recognized as World Heritage Irrigation Structures in 2026 and added to the International Commission on Irrigation and Drainage (ICID) register, UzA reports.
The award ceremony took place on October 14 during an international congress in Marseille, France. Officials received certificates and commemorative plaques recognizing the canals.
The Dargom Canal, which supplies water to the Samarkand oasis, is believed to have been built between the 5th and 4th centuries BC. Nearly 102 kilometers long, the canal still irrigates almost 178,000 hectares of land today.
The Shohrud Canal is believed to have been dug in the 3rd-4th centuries AD. For centuries, it has played a key role in the development of Bukhara and the surrounding oasis.
Uzbekistan’s Dustlik and Eski Tuyatortar canals were also added to the World Heritage Irrigation Structures list in 2025.

Italian intelligence suggest link between Palestinian terrorists, Sicilian mafia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:19:27 UTC
00:19:27 KST

Previously classified Italian intelligence documents reveal suspected connections between Palestinian terrorist organizations and the Sicilian Mafia during the 1980s, including possible cooperation in weapons trafficking, narcotics smuggling, and explosives expertise, according to an investigation published Thursday by the Italian newspaper Il Giornale.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The investigation, by journalist Giulia Sorrentino, draws on intelligence reports, judicial records, and historical documents describing networks extending from Lebanon and Syria to Sicily and Rome. The material also includes an intelligence warning about a possible terrorist attack against the US Embassy in Rome.
Drug trafficking and Palestinian terrorism
One of the central documents, dated November 9, 1983, contains information gathered by Italy’s Carabinieri, the country's military police force, concerning international drug trafficking and Palestinian terrorist operations.
According to the intelligence report, members of Sicilian Mafia networks associated with the Greco and Gambino families were operating in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, then under strong Syrian influence. The area reportedly contained narcotics-processing facilities near Baalbek.
The source alleged that six AK-47 assault rifles had reached Mafia associates and been used in attacks in Sicily. It also described a shipment of approximately 900 kilograms of morphine base reportedly sent from Lebanon toward the Sicilian city of Catania in October 1983.
The same intelligence material warned that Palestinian terrorist organizations might attack Western targets if the multinational military force stationed in Lebanon intervened against Palestinian positions. The source specifically reported knowledge of a planned attack against the American Embassy in Rome.
Sorrentino's investigation also revisits the July 29, 1983, assassination of Rocco Chinnici, an Italian magistrate who played a leading role in the campaign against organized crime.
Chinnici and three other people were killed when a car bomb containing approximately 75 kilograms of explosives detonated in Palermo. The attack's use of a remotely detonated explosive device resembled techniques employed by terrorist organizations during Lebanon's civil war.
Judicial records describe how Bou Chebel Ghassan, a Lebanese police informant, had provided information about contacts with Mafia figures and efforts to obtain weapons and morphine. Days before Chinnici's assassination, Ghassan reportedly described methods of killing investigators remotely, comparing them to those used by Palestinian terrorists in Lebanon.
No record that Palestinian operatives participated in assassinating Chinnici
Although the testimony raised questions about possible foreign connections, Italian judicial proceedings established Cosa Nostra's responsibility for Chinnici's murder. The records do not demonstrate that Palestinian operatives planned or participated in the assassination.
The investigation also revisits allegations published by Corriere della Sera on June 22, 1993. In a report from Beirut, correspondent Antonio Ferrari quoted Zeid Wehbe, a Palestine Liberation Organization representative, alleging that operatives associated with Abu Nidal had infiltrated Mafia networks.
According to those allegations, Abu Nidal's organization supplied expertise in explosives and sophisticated killing devices in exchange for assistance with criminal operations.
Abu Nidal, whose real name was Sabri al-Banna, led a Palestinian terrorist faction that broke with Yasser Arafat's PLO. His organization was responsible for attacks against Israeli, Jewish, Western, and Palestinian targets.
An Italian military intelligence report dated January 13, 1986, also described connections between Abu Nidal and circles associated with the family of Syrian President Hafez Assad. The document, identified through research by Italian historian Giordana Terracina, referred to the international terrorist known as Carlos the Jackal.
The assessment followed the December 27, 1985, coordinated attacks against airports in Rome and Vienna by Abu Nidal's Palestinian terrorist organization. The assaults killed 16 civilians and injured approximately 120 others.
Sorrentino also cites an October 1990 memorandum attributed to Italian General Demetrio Cogliandro. The document raised allegations concerning Arab banks operating in Italy, financial transactions involving Middle Eastern governments, and funds allegedly reaching Italian organized crime groups for narcotics purchases.
The intelligence records became accessible through a broader Italian government initiative launched in 2014 to declassify historical documentation relating to terrorism and political violence.
The newly published investigation does not establish that Abu Nidal's organization maintained a formal operational alliance with Cosa Nostra or participated in Mafia assassinations. The allegations in the intelligence reports have not all been independently corroborated.
However, the documents demonstrate that Italian intelligence agencies were examining possible connections between Palestinian terrorism, organized crime, and Middle Eastern trafficking networks years before allegations of an Abu Nidal–Mafia partnership became public in 1993.

The readout outlined a French-German proposal for a comprehensive package combining an "ambitious European decarbonisation pathway" with regulatory flexibility to reflect different market realities and technological conditions.
The package also provides incentives for investment, research and development, European production, and resilient supply chains.
"This balanced approach will enable the European Union to pursue its climate objectives while strengthening the technological sovereignty, industrial base and international competitiveness of its automotive industry," the statement added.
"Our objective is clear: a competitive, innovative and decarbonised European automotive industry, producing in Europe and creating the jobs of tomorrow."
French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz welcomed the agreement.
"We hope that this Franco-German dynamic can swiftly lead to an agreement with our partners, for our jobs and our industry," Macron said.
Merz said they agreed on the package "for freedom of choice, technological openness, and upholding climate goals." "This is an investment signal to industry," he added.

The Bedouin shepherd who claimed he was a kidnapped Jewish child
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:17:01 UTC
00:17:01 KST

Had this been a TV drama, someone would probably have asked the writers to tone it down. In 1956, a little boy disappeared from Tirosh, a farming community between Beit Shemesh and Kiryat Malachi. His mother had left him playing in the yard with a neighbor while she went to the clinic. When she returned, he was gone.
The boy was Yitzhak Gabay, 2. His brother David was 7 and his sister Aliza was 4. “We were going for tetanus shots,” David, now 78, recalled this week. “Mom told the neighbor, ‘I’m taking David and Aliza to get vaccinated. Keep an eye on Yitzhak.’ We were gone seven minutes. When we came back, Yitzhak wasn’t there. We asked the neighbor where he was. She said, ‘I gave him a tomato, and he headed back toward the house.’”
Relatives, neighbors and police searched for the child, but found no trace of him. “There were dozens of police officers and even a tracking dog, which died after a snake bit it,” David said. His parents spent years looking. “There wasn’t a rabbi, a sorcerer or a medium we didn’t go to.”
Of all those visits, David remembers one in particular, to the rabbi known as the Baba Sali. “We went to him right after the kidnapping,” he said. “He told us exactly when we would find Yitzhak. How many years, how many months, how many days. Even how many hours.” David remains convinced that the prediction came true.
Their mother, Zohara, had been pregnant 16 times; only David, Aliza and Yitzhak had survived. Nine years after her youngest son vanished, she died at 32. The family says she died of a broken heart. Her husband, Yisrael, stayed in Tirosh while David and Aliza married and moved to Tel Aviv. As the years passed, the family kept hoping someone would come forward with information, or recognize the boy and bring him home.
About two decades after the disappearance, an argument broke out in a Bedouin family. A young shepherd named Abdullah was quarreling with a relative when the relative snapped: “Who asked you? You’re not even Bedouin. Your mother is Jewish.” Abdullah could not forget it. He began to wonder whether the people who had raised him were his parents, and whether they had kept something from him.
He later said he began dreaming of an elderly Jewish man who told him he was Jewish. Eventually, Abdullah left his family and went to the home of Rabbi Yitzhak David Grossman in Migdal HaEmek, in northern Israel. He told Grossman he believed he was Jewish and had grown up with a family that was not his own. He wanted the rabbi’s help finding out who he was.
Word spread, and the story appeared in Yedioth Ahronoth. Families with missing children began arriving at Grossman’s door. Among those who heard about the shepherd was Yisrael Gabay. Twenty-one years had passed since his son’s disappearance.
David was then serving as an army personnel officer in Sharm el-Sheikh. “One day I got a call from the police: ‘Where are you? Get on the first flight. We need you back in Israel,’” he recalled. “As soon as I landed, Dad said, ‘We need to go to Migdal HaEmek.’” His father told him about the newspaper report and the shepherd who claimed his mother was Jewish.
“Thousands came to the rabbi, all saying he was their son,” David said. “The line stretched from Tel Aviv to Petah Tikva. Everyone had identifying marks. We arrived on Thursday, almost at the end, and we had the clearest signs. My brother had had treatments on his back as a child, and they’d left scars.” Abdullah had scars on his back, too.
Grossman had invited Yisrael to come with two friends from Tirosh. The family stayed through the Sabbath, and on Saturday night the rabbi arranged an informal identification lineup. David remembers a larger group taking part. “They brought in six or 10 men who looked more or less like Dad, but this young man went straight to him. He didn’t even look at the others. And I said, ‘That’s my brother.’ He was huge, like Dad.”
For Yisrael and Abdullah, that settled it. Abdullah began calling himself Yitzhak and moved into Yisrael’s home in Tirosh. He was also known as Abdullah-Yitzhak or Ovadia Ben Yisrael. “I remember we had a party, and Bedouin families came carrying weapons,” David said. “Then he stayed with us in Tirosh, where my father lived.”
Newspaper reports from 1977, however, said a police investigation had found no family connection. They cited a new blood test that had ruled out a biological relationship between Abdullah and the Gabays. Nearly half a century later, relatives interviewed this week dispute those reports. The story is still vividly remembered by the family and by Grossman’s assistant, who first brought it to public attention.
Abdullah tried to adjust to Jewish life with the Gabays, and they tried to help him settle in. But living together was difficult. “Abdullah was bored at Yisrael’s,” said Bracha, David’s wife. “He spoke only Arabic, and the father spoke only Hebrew. There was nothing for them to do at home in Tirosh. Back in his village, there were horses and sheep.”
David said Abdullah’s Bedouin family never explained how he had come to live with them, and the Gabays never asked. “My father died knowing he had found his son, and that this was the right child,” he said. Abdullah began spending time with the people he now regarded as his brother and sister. After a serious argument with David, he moved in with Aliza, who was raising five children.
Aliza has since died, but her son, Shimon Ben Khalifa, remembers Abdullah-Yitzhak well. To him, he was simply his uncle. “I was a baby when they found him, so I grew up with the whole story,” he said. “My mother was sure he was her brother. Nobody ever thought otherwise.”
Asked about the blood-test reports, Ben Khalifa said: “I never heard of a test like that. On the contrary, I think they did another test that showed he was my mother’s brother. There was also an older aunt, his mother’s sister, who always said that was the child. That was Yitzhak.”
Life in Tel Aviv did not suit Abdullah. By then, he had married a woman from the village where he had grown up. Relatives say she was a teacher and had even considered converting to Judaism for him. The couple tried living in Tirosh, but they were far from the families who had raised them. They eventually returned to Zarzir, where Abdullah did well raising calves and tending olive groves.
He stayed in touch with Aliza’s family. “We visited his home several times,” Ben Khalifa said. “His son was at my house two months ago. My younger brother got married two years ago, and he was at the wedding.”
“To this day, I’m sure he’s my brother,” David said. “He named his eldest daughter after our mother. Once he told me he lived between two worlds, Jewish and Bedouin.” Yisrael died 12 years ago, still carrying a childhood photograph of Yitzhak in his wallet. “Until the day he died,” David said, “he believed he had found his child.”

Ousted US general warned before Iran war of missile defense shortages lasting until 2030: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:15:38 UTC
00:15:38 KST

Ousted US Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned months before the US-Israeli war against Iran that American missile defense stockpiles were critically low and could take until 2030 to recover, CBS News reported Thursday.
George raised the warning in late December, two months before the conflict began, according to US officials familiar with his assessment. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed him from his post in April as the war was underway.
The general’s assessment, included in the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 force allocation planning, identified shortages of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors and Patriot missiles, with supplies expected to remain at strategically low levels until 2030.
The officials reportedly attributed the shortfall to weapons transfers to Ukraine, US military support for Israel, and limited defense industry production capacity.
The war with Iran has further strained supplies, according to the report. A Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimate found that US forces entered 2026 with approximately 2,300 Patriot interceptors and used between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict.
READ: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran: Report
The country’s prewar THAAD inventory stood at around 355 interceptors, of which an estimated 190 to 290 were expended.
Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, told CBS News that these systems would be crucial in a potential conflict with China.
“Air defense — missile defense — that will be huge,” he said, explaining that a major confrontation with Beijing would demand substantial interceptor supplies.
Replenishing the stockpiles remains a lengthy process, the report said. The CSIS estimates that new THAAD interceptor contracts take over four years to fulfill, while Patriot PAC-3 orders take an average of 3 1/2 years.
The Pentagon rejected claims of a shortage. Chief spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: “Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false.”
He added that Washington retains “everything required to strike at the time and place of the President’s choosing.”

The governor of Yemen’s Taiz province announced Friday that electricity and water stations, as well as the city’s waste collection services, had shut down because the Houthis were preventing fuel from entering the city.
“Houthi militias are besieging Taiz and have closed all roads leading to it for the past 15 days,” Nabil Shamsan said in a statement on the US social media company Facebook.
Hospitals in Taiz are unable to provide medical care to patients due to shortages of medicines and medical supplies, Shamsan said.

Tensions have escalated since July, with Taiz remaining a major front line in Yemen’s conflict as government forces and the Houthis engage in repeated clashes around the city.
Since Oct. 5, government forces have been leading a military offensive, known as Dawn of Yemen, aimed at restoring state institutions from Houthi control and retaking the capital Sanaa.
