How Israeli firm’s ‘zero-click’ malware attack poses global security risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:12:13 UTC
23:12:13 KST

How Israeli firm’s ‘zero-click’ malware attack poses global security risk
A new ‘zero-click’ hack uses ads to target victims without any action needed on their part.
Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found. You are not even required to “click” on anything.
An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims.
In June 2025, 45 devices used by Al Jazeera staff – including several who reported on sensitive subjects – were targeted with spyware which installed itself without the need to open or download any files.
An investigation by the Canada-based academic research unit Citizen Lab, prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe into the issue, discovered that the Israeli company Candiru was behind the attacks.
Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat. “We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera.
“This is the next level, because people are being microtargeted,” he said. “This is the point we’ve come to when it comes to surveillance.”
How ‘zero-click’ malware works
Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed.
Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners.
Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru. The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists, journalists and political activists across 10 countries.
Al Jazeera Media Network has condemned the targeting of its staff members’ devices and called for those responsible to be held accountable.
Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance. “Executing code inside the browser does not automatically give an attacker full control over the computer,” Willems told Al Jazeera.
“To escape the browser’s isolated environment – the ‘sandbox’ – the attacker may need a second vulnerability,” Willems said, adding that an advanced spyware operation can combine several vulnerabilities.
“The attacker attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to bypass security boundaries. This is precisely what makes this type of attack so dangerous,” the analyst said.
Once the device is infected, the malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials.
It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms. To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time.
Advertising: A new global security threat?
Analysts say Citizen Lab’s findings point to the escalation of an existing threat, which expands the scale and reach of traditional cyberattacks and makes them much harder to detect.
While “zero-click” attacks are not completely new, the findings outline a new technique through which online advertisements are used as a route to infection.
Stephen O’Shaughnessy, a lecturer in cybersecurity at the TU Dublin Blanchardstown campus in Ireland, explained that when a user opens a website or app, an automated auction sells the advertisement space in a fraction of a second. That auction shares data about the victim, including the device ID, IP address, rough location and the app or site they are on.
“Discover-Tech posed as an ordinary advertiser, used that data to find their target and win the auction for that person’s screen,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera. “Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.”
“Because no message or link is involved, there is almost nothing for the victim to notice,” he added.
Discover-Tech appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served advertisements via major networks such as Google, Yandex and Beeswax.
In its report, Citizen Lab said this illustrates the structural flaws in the online advertising system, which essentially failed to detect or prevent the abuse.
Discover-Tech advertisements have popped up on devices used by personnel in national-security-sensitive networks around the world, including those of various ministries of defence, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organisations and media outlets, Citizen Lab found.
The research unit said these advertisements have also appeared on networks used by the United Nations, NATO, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union’s General Secretariat.
‘Almost nobody was watching’
Government networks have also been targeted in at least 24 countries, including the United States, Italy, Denmark, Norway, Australia, Russia, Mexico and Israel itself. Networks of media organisations have also been targeted, mainly in Australia, Denmark and Sweden, according to Citizen Lab.
In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.
O’Shaughnessy said infection has not been confirmed there – only profiling of users. “But that alone is concerning, he said. “The ad system was built to send code from strangers to billions of screens with pinpoint targeting. Almost nobody was watching it from a security angle.”
The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets. “For individuals at high risk, like journalists and officials, the best first defence is to install an ad blocker, switch off their advertising ID through their phone’s privacy settings, keep everything updated, and turn on Lockdown Mode or Android’s Advanced Protection,” he said.
Precautions also need to be taken within the industry and at government level. “To combat this, the ad industry needs to properly vet who’s buying ads,” O’Shaughnessy said, while “regulators need to stop personal data being sprayed out to thousands of unknown bidders in every auction.”

Netanyahu, opposition blocs tied as 55% back unity government if election inconclusive: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:12:02 UTC
23:12:02 KST

Abdul Raouf Arnaout, Mohammad Sio
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
An Israeli opinion poll published on Friday showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition tied, with neither reaching the majority needed to form a government, while 55% of respondents favored a unity government if the upcoming election produces no decisive result.
The Maariv poll, published 11 days before the Oct. 27 general election, showed that if voting were held today, both Netanyahu’s bloc and the Jewish opposition would win 51 seats each in the 120-member Knesset.
Arab lawmakers, meanwhile, were projected to win 14 seats, while the Reservists Party would secure four, without indicating which bloc it would support.
A government requires the backing of at least 61 lawmakers. Otherwise, Israel could face another election.
Both Netanyahu’s camp and the main Jewish opposition parties reject relying on Arab parties to form a government.
According to the poll, Netanyahu’s bloc would be divided among Likud with 18 seats, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power eight, the religious United Torah Judaism party eight, Shas seven, Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism six and Ofer Winter’s Amcha Yisrael four.
The Jewish opposition would include Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party with 21 seats, Naftali Bennett’s Together 13, Yair Golan’s Democrats nine and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu eight.
Among Arab parties, the Joint List led by Yousef Jabareen was projected to win eight seats, while Mansour Abbas’ United Arab List, or Ra’am, would receive six.
The Reservists Party, headed by Yoaz Hendel, is projected to win four seats, with the poll not determining which camp it would support.
On the preferred candidate for prime minister, Eisenkot, a former Israeli army chief of staff, remained ahead of Netanyahu with 48% support compared with 41% for the incumbent.
Israelis do not directly elect their prime minister. The post goes to the politician able to form a coalition backed by at least 61 lawmakers.
If the political deadlock continues, Israel could face another election unless a unity government is formed.
The poll found that 55% of Israelis prefer a national unity government over another election if the Oct. 27 vote fails to produce a clear outcome.
Another 27% said they favor holding a new election, while 18% were undecided.
The results showed differences between the two camps.
Among opposition voters, 54% said they support a unity government provided it is headed by a leader from their bloc.
Among coalition voters, 36% backed a unity government led by Netanyahu, while 32% preferred another election if no clear result emerged.
Maariv said the poll was conducted by the private Lazar Research Institute among a random sample of 700 Israelis, with a margin of error of 3.7 percentage points.

The Philippines and China have traded sharp remarks over the Chinese ambassador’s comments on the use of force.
Manila on Thursday rebuked China’s ambassador over remarks that Beijing could “easily win” a confrontation between the two countries, calling them a “thinly veiled threat” of force.
Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan told reporters Thursday that China “may easily win” if it wanted to use force, but stressed that Beijing would not do so because “we love peace.”
He was responding to Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.’s description of China as a regional “troublemaker.”
The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs said Jing showed a “poor choice of words” that was “hardly helpful” given complicated bilateral relations, according to the state-run Philippine News Agency (PNA).
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said Friday that Jing’s remarks “sound very much like a threat” and warranted a discussion with the ambassador.
Responding at a regular Foreign Ministry briefing Friday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Beijing’s position remained unchanged.
“China’s position on improving and growing its ties with the Philippines is clear,” Mao said, adding that Beijing hoped Manila would have a “full and accurate understanding” of it.
The Chinese Embassy in Manila said Jing had been selectively quoted and described the Philippine response as an “over-interpretation.”
China and the Philippines have repeatedly clashed over disputed reefs and waters in the South China Sea, including areas Manila says fall within its exclusive economic zone.

Türkiye raises defense equipment procurement by 229% in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:58:29 UTC
22:58:29 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Türkiye increased allocations for weapons, ammunition and other defense equipment purchases by 229% in its 2027 budget, Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said Friday.
Speaking at a ceremony marking the finalization of the central government budget proposal at the presidential complex in Ankara, Yilmaz outlined spending priorities spanning defense, education, health and infrastructure.
“Allocations for purchases of weapons, ammunition, weapons systems and other defense equipment, which constitute a significant portion of defense spending in the National Defense Ministry's budget, have been increased by 229%,” he said.
Including other defense expenditures, the proposed budget earmarks 2.206 trillion Turkish liras ($44.5 billion) for defense and a separate $25.2 billion for internal security.
The 229% increase applies specifically to the procurement allocations identified by Yilmaz, rather than total defense spending.
Yilmaz said Türkiye had reduced its defense industry's dependence on foreign suppliers, describing developments over the past quarter-century as a revolution.
Current global conditions demonstrated the importance of the country's earlier decision to strengthen its domestic defense industry, he added.
Beyond defense, the government proposes allocating $57.5 billion to investment, equivalent to 10.4% of the 2027 budget.
Yilmaz said investment would continue across irrigation, railways, maritime transport, oil and natural gas exploration, and mining.
Education, including higher education, would receive $75.6 billion, retaining the largest share of central government spending at 13.7%.
The proposal also provides $17.5 billion to address earthquake damage and strengthen resilience against disasters.
Yilmaz said the budget proposal had been submitted to parliament within the constitutional deadline. He will provide further details during a presentation to parliament's Planning and Budget Committee next week.

Can Russia help ease tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:56:43 UTC
22:56:43 KST

Can Russia help ease tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan?
Russia has close ties with the Taliban and is courting Islamabad, but analysts say its leverage remains uncertain.
Islamabad, Pakistan – Sitting with his elbows on his knees, Russia’s Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev leaned towards Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, for talks in Rawalpindi on October 14.
While Kolokoltsev was in Pakistan, Sergey Naryshkin, director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), flew into Kabul to meet the Taliban’s intelligence chief, Abdul Haq Wasiq.
Officially, Russia, Pakistan and Afghanistan have issued little beyond standard statements about the meetings. But the signs are clear: Pakistan and Afghanistan have spent the past year exchanging fire and public threats. Qatar and Turkiye brokered a ceasefire in Doha last October and China hosted talks in Urumqi in April, but attacks inside Pakistan continued. Islamabad again struck Afghan territory in June, September and this month.
Russia now appears to be stepping in as a mediator.
Moscow’s special representative for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, told Russia’s TASS news agency earlier this month that his country was ready to play peace broker between Kabul and Islamabad if both sides requested it.
Pakistan’s ambassador to Russia, Faisal Niaz Tirmizi, said in March that Islamabad had approached Moscow. The Taliban, though, have not publicly requested Russian mediation, raising questions about how much and in what capacity Moscow can push Pakistan and Afghanistan to talks when other mediators have struggled.
A complicated history adds to the challenge Russia faces.
A diplomatic opening
Pakistan’s military media wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), said the Rawalpindi meeting discussed issues of “mutual interest and the regional security environment, with particular emphasis on strengthening bilateral security cooperation.”
The statement did not mention Afghanistan and neither Russian officials nor the Taliban have disclosed what the intelligence chiefs discussed. Moscow has, however, voiced concern about the fighting.
“We are seriously concerned about the ongoing military confrontation between Pakistan and Afghanistan, which affects civilians, including children,” the Russian embassy in Kabul posted on X earlier this month.
The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said Pakistani strikes between September 30 and October 1 killed at least 10 civilians, mostly children.
In decades past, the idea of Russia mediating between Pakistan and the Taliban might have been unthinkable. Throughout the Cold War and even after the collapse of the Soviet Union, Russia was – and remains in many ways – one of the closest strategic and military partners of India, the neighbour Pakistan has fought multiple wars against. While in Afghanistan, Russia backed the Northern Alliance against the Taliban throughout the 1990s.
But in recent years, Russia has significantly strengthened relations with both Pakistan and the Taliban. Then Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan was in Moscow when Russian forces invaded Ukraine in 2022. Last year, Russia became the first country in the world to officially recognise the Taliban government in Afghanistan.
Those shifts have been driven by Russia’s desire to broaden its options in South Asia, at a time when India has embraced the United States and to counter the rise of the Afghan branch of ISIL, also known as the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or ISKP. While the Taliban are concerned with ruling Afghanistan, ISKP has broader territorial ambitions and carried out an attack in Moscow in 2024 that killed nearly 150 people. The Taliban and the ISKP are sworn enemies.
Fighting between Pakistan and the Taliban created regional instability and Moscow was worried that could make it easier for armed groups to spill into Central Asia, said Taimur Khan, a research associate at the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad (ISSI).
“Mediation also helps Moscow preserve its regional influence and avoid a vacuum that could invite renewed extra-regional involvement,” he told Al Jazeera.
Why mediation stalled
Qatar and Turkiye brokered a ceasefire between Pakistan and the Taliban in Doha last October, but talks in Istanbul collapsed the following month and skirmishes resumed. Islamabad also launched air raids inside Afghanistan. China hosted talks in Urumqi in April.
In mid-September, Turkiye’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin, met Taliban officials in Kabul and Kandahar before travelling to Islamabad.
An attack in Kohat followed on September 18, with Pakistan striking Afghanistan on September 24 and October 1.
“Other actors have so far achieved more tangible mediation results in this conflict,” Eldaniz Gusseinov, a Central Asia analyst and head of research at the geopolitical foresight agency, Nightingale Int, told Al Jazeera.
Russia’s own effort stalled at a Moscow meeting on October 5.
Kabulov told TASS that the Afghan delegation objected to Afghanistan being mentioned too often in connection with “terrorism”.
“For Pakistan, this is a substantive security issue, not merely a matter of wording,” Pakistan’s Foreign Office spokesperson, Sajjad Haider Khan, said on October 9 at a weekly media briefing.
Kabul-based security analyst Tameem Bahiss said the objection reflected Kabul’s longstanding position.
“Accepting language that repeatedly associates Afghanistan with terrorism could be seen as an acknowledgement of the very allegations Kabul has consistently denied,” he told Al Jazeera.
The TTP problem
At the Moscow meeting, Pakistan’s special representative for Afghanistan, Mohammad Sadiq, said “terrorism” remained at the core of Afghanistan’s problems.
Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi said the two countries’ problems could be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, according to Afghan media.
Pakistan says the Pakistani Taliban and other armed groups shelter in Afghanistan.
Kabul rejects the allegation, saying it does not allow its territory to be used against other countries and that Pakistan’s security problems are largely internal, Bahiss said.
Moscow’s public warnings have focused on the ISKP.
“There is no visible public pressure from Russia on the Taliban over Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), and Moscow is unlikely to exert such pressure,” Gusseinov said. TTP is the official name of the Pakistani Taliban, which is behind dozens of the deadliest attacks Pakistan has suffered in recent years.
He argued that pressing the Taliban hard on Pakistan’s behalf would undermine Moscow’s standing as a neutral mediator and its partnership with the Taliban against ISKP.
“Russia’s primary concern is ISKP and it appears satisfied with the Taliban’s efforts to counter the group,” Abdul Sayed, a Sweden-based analyst specialising in armed groups and security dynamics in Afghanistan and Pakistan, told Al Jazeera.
What Moscow brings
Still, Russia has something earlier mediators did not. In July 2025, it became the only country to recognise the Taliban government.
Taimur Khan said that could give Moscow another source of influence.
“The Taliban authorities’ interest in preserving that recognition and expanding cooperation with Moscow could give Russia additional influence in seeking action against the TTP and other terrorist groups operating from Afghanistan,” he said.
In May, the two sides signed an unpublished military-technical agreement covering, according to Kabulov, the repair and maintenance of equipment the Taliban already hold, mostly Soviet and Russian-made.
Three days after the signing, the Taliban’s Defence Minister, Mohammad Yaqoob, said Pakistan would soon no longer dare to launch strikes.
On June 9 and 10, Pakistani aircraft struck Kunar, Khost and Paktika provinces, killing 13 civilians, according to the Afghan government.
“Russia has greater access to the Taliban than any other major power, but its actual leverage is considerably more limited than is often assumed,” analyst Gusseinov said.
Sayed said senior Taliban leaders continued visiting Russia and India as fighting escalated, seemingly signalling they could offset Pakistan’s military superiority through new alignments.
“While the military and political significance of these ties remains unclear, the Taliban present such diplomatic developments to the Afghan public, particularly their supporters, as political achievements that reinforce their image of strength,” he said.
Why the SCO matters
Pakistan chairs the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) for 2026-27 and will host the 10-member bloc’s summit in Islamabad next year.
The Taliban were not invited to this year’s summit in Bishkek, where members called for an inclusive government in Kabul.
On July 16, then-Foreign Office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said Afghanistan first needed diplomatic relations with member states, when asked whether Pakistan was blocking its inclusion in the SCO.
In September, Tirmizi, the Pakistani envoy in Moscow, said he did not see full SCO membership for Afghanistan as an option under the current Taliban government.
“The chairmanship strengthens Moscow’s reasons to invest in its relationship with Pakistan and manage differences over Afghanistan constructively,” Taimur Khan said.
The Foreign Office did not answer Al Jazeera’s questions about whether the Taliban would be invited next year.
“I cannot recall an instance where Kabul has explicitly requested Moscow to mediate between the two countries,” Bahiss said. “Nevertheless, Kabul’s repeated calls for diplomacy and its relatively close relations with Russia suggest that it would likely welcome Russian mediation if Moscow offered to play such a role.”

Russia’s Remote Siberian Oil Regions Face Renewed Drone Alerts 2,500 Kilometers From Ukraine
Russian authorities declared a drone threat across the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug in western Siberia, approximately 2,500 kilometers from Ukraine’s border, according to Interfax on October 16.
Khanty-Mansi Governor Ruslan Kukharuk confirmed the warning, announcing that emergency services and relevant government agencies had been placed on heightened readiness.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Russian Telegram monitor channel Supernova+ also reported a drone threat in the neighboring Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, commonly known as Yamal. Similar alerts were issued in Russia’s Tyumen, Chelyabinsk, and Sverdlovsk regions, Interfax reported.
"Responsible services and agencies have been placed on heightened alert and are taking all necessary measures to ensure security," Kukharuk wrote on Russia’s Max messaging platform, as quoted by Interfax. Russian aviation authorities also introduced temporary flight restrictions at Sovetsky and Uray airports, according to local media.
Khanty-Mansi and Yamal are major centers of Russia’s oil and natural gas industry, situated thousands of kilometers from Ukraine. The October 16 warnings highlight security concerns extending into western Siberia, although the available reports do not establish that drones entered either autonomous district or struck any facilities that day.
The October 16 warning was not the first drone-related alert in either region. Authorities in Khanty-Mansi had announced a drone danger warning on June 25, while Yamal introduced its first such alert on July 6.
On September 9, Khanty-Mansi authorities escalated their warning to a more serious drone attack threat for the first time, prompting restrictions at six airports and the introduction of remote learning in schools, according to Kommersant and 86.ru.
Further drone alerts were issued in both autonomous districts on September 21 and October 8, demonstrating that warnings have become increasingly recurrent in Russia’s remote northern territories. On October 8, authorities confirmed that alerts had been lifted across Khanty-Mansi, Yamal, and Tyumen after precautionary measures were introduced.

Britain Is Taking Too Long to Blame Russia for Sabotage, Labour MP Warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

22:55:44 KST

- Category
- World
Britain Is Taking Too Long to Blame Russia for Sabotage, Labour MP Warns
Britain is taking too long to publicly attribute sabotage and arson to Russia, leaving businesses supporting Ukraine without timely warnings that they may themselves become targets, Labour MP Graeme Downie told UK Defence Journal on October 16.
Downie, author of The Putin Tax report, contrasted Britain with countries such as Estonia, which recently blamed Russia within days of an arson attack on a drone manufacturer.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We’ve seen other NATO countries like Estonia blaming Russia and attributing blame within days without the need to publish all of the raw intelligence,” he said.
Downie argued that Britain effectively applies a criminal standard—“beyond reasonable doubt”—when deciding whether to attribute hostile-state activity, when a lower civil standard could allow the government to act faster.
“Rather than apply the criminal bar of beyond reasonable doubt, you probably apply a civil legal bar of overwhelming evidence, and on the balance of probabilities,” he said, adding that the current approach “delays it.”
That delay can have practical consequences for British companies supplying Ukraine. Downie said firms should not necessarily be afraid, but they need to understand that they could be targeted and receive better guidance on protecting themselves.
“I think it’s not they should be worried, but they should be aware,” he said. Publicly identifying attacks more quickly, he argued, would signal to companies supporting Ukraine “that they need to get protection.”
He also warned that Britain’s subsea energy and communications infrastructure faces a serious threat from hostile activity.
“The threat to subsea infrastructure is entirely real,” Downie said, warning that even short disruptions to internet cables or energy networks could inflict major economic damage.
His comments follow the March 2024 arson attack on a warehouse in Leyton linked to aid for Ukraine. Men were later convicted over the fire, which prosecutors said had been organized on behalf of Russia’s Wagner Group.
Earlier, reports emerged that British warships and helicopters spent significantly more time tracking Russian naval activity in July as Moscow maintained an elevated presence around UK waters and across the North Atlantic.
Royal Navy patrol ships and aircraft devoted 21 days to monitoring Russian vessels during the month, up 25% from July 2025, according to figures released by the British Navy.

Ukraine Tests First Aerial Drone Designed to Evacuate Wounded Soldiers From the Front
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:55:41 UTC
22:55:41 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Tests First Aerial Drone Designed to Evacuate Wounded Soldiers From the Front
Ukraine has begun front-line testing of StarGate, its first aerial drone designed to evacuate wounded soldiers from areas too dangerous for conventional vehicles or evacuation teams, the Associated Press (AP) reported on Octobe 16.
Ukraine is increasingly using unmanned ground vehicles to evacuate wounded troops from areas where Russian FPV drones make conventional rescue missions too dangerous. In April, the First Separate Medical Battalion completed six casualty evacuations with ground robots in a single day under constant drone threat.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
AP received exclusive access to a field demonstration of the system before StarGate was handed to a Ukrainian combat brigade for testing under front-line conditions.
“The idea came directly from the front line, from the trenches,” a SkyFall spokesperson told AP.
The drone was developed over the past year by Ukrainian defense technology company SkyFall after a request from the commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, known as Code 9.2.
In some sectors, the battlefield “kill zone” under constant drone and artillery threat extends 10 to 15 kilometers or farther, AP reported. StarGate has a one-way range of 15 kilometers and is designed to reach wounded troops inside those areas without exposing an evacuation crew.
“Covering 10 kilometers in minutes would be a drastic change on the front line,” KVN, a commander with Code 9.2, told AP.
StarGate can carry up to 150 kilograms, enough for a wounded soldier wearing body armor and combat equipment. Its evacuation compartment is built around a medical-grade stretcher.
According to AP, the drone cruises at 65 kilometers per hour and can reach 105 kilometers per hour. SkyFall states that it can be prepared for flight in about 10 minutes.
The system uses Starlink and SkyFall’s proprietary L-Link communications system, alongside AI-assisted navigation designed for environments where GPS is unavailable, spoofed, or jammed.
During the demonstration observed by AP, FPV drones simulated attacks on StarGate while electronic jamming was active. The evacuation drone deployed a net against one approaching FPV, knocking it off course.
SkyFall also states that StarGate can return toward a safe area if communications are completely lost. The drone is equipped with thermal cameras for night operations and is designed to fly in rain and snow.
The company has demonstrated that the aircraft can continue flying after losing one of its arms, although AP noted that SkyFall has not released data showing how reliably it can survive damage under combat conditions.
Each system is expected to cost at least $50,000, depending on its configuration. SkyFall aims to produce up to 1,000 StarGate drones per month by the end of 2026.
“It’s a completely new method of evacuation,” KVN told AP. “It’s difficult to talk in depth about the pros and cons right now. We need to work with it more.”
Unmanned systems already play an expanding role in Ukrainian casualty evacuation, particularly where ground vehicles face mines, craters, destroyed roads, rivers, and drone attacks. AP reported that ground robots can take two to three hours to reach some positions, while StarGate is designed to cover comparable distances in minutes.
The StarGate tests build on Ukraine’s growing use of unmanned systems for casualty evacuation. In June, the Third Army Corps reported that its ground robots had evacuated more than 600 wounded soldiers during their first year of operations, while completing more than 18,000 missions overall.

Bulgaria Asks NATO for Aircraft, Air Defenses and Counter-Drone Systems as Black Sea Attacks Intensify
Bulgaria has requested additional aircraft, air defense systems, counter-drone equipment, and air patrols from NATO as attacks on vessels in the Black Sea intensify, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said, according to Novinite on October 16.
Speaking to journalists, Stoyanov warned that the security situation in the Black Sea was deteriorating, with attacks becoming increasingly frequent. He pointed to recent strikes in Romanian territorial waters as evidence of the growing threats facing countries in the region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We have requested aviation, surface-to-air missile systems, counter-drone systems, and air patrols—essentially, the entire spectrum of available assets,” Stoyanov said, adding that the deployment of additional allied resources would also help demonstrate a stronger NATO presence in the region.
However, the minister acknowledged that it remained unclear which capabilities Bulgaria would ultimately receive. He noted that Romania and the Baltic states were facing similar security challenges, while European partners were paying increasing attention to threats in the Black Sea.
“I hope for a swift response and a strengthening of our capabilities,” Stoyanov said.
To improve regional coordination, Bulgaria is also seeking closer cooperation with neighboring NATO members. According to the minister, a meeting involving the defense ministers of Bulgaria, Türkiye, and Romania, alongside the chiefs of defense of all three countries, is expected to take place soon.
The discussions are intended to support the development of a coordinated response to emerging threats and strengthen cooperation among the three Black Sea NATO members.
Despite the requested assistance, Stoyanov cautioned that deploying additional allied forces and equipment would not eliminate all security risks in the region.
“100% security is impossible,” the defense minister said, emphasizing that the objective was to minimize potential threats rather than guarantee complete protection.
Meanwhile, Bulgaria continues to rely on its existing military resources to monitor its maritime territory and respond to potential threats.
According to Stoyanov, the country currently operates two reconnaissance systems dedicated to maritime surveillance, with a third expected to become operational by the end of the year.
The minister said the additional system would introduce technology that had not previously been deployed elsewhere.
The calls for additional security measures follow a series of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, including an incident near Bulgaria’s coast on October 13.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev reported that two commercial vessels had been struck by drones overnight, leaving one ship sunk and forcing the evacuation of the entire crew of another after three drones hit its deck and hull.
One of the vessels was the Chelsea 3, a Ukrainian-owned cargo ship sailing under the Maltese flag, which came under attack approximately 18 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian coastal town of Byala.

Timelines for Ukrainian settlement, US interference: Lukashenko’s statements

MINSK, October 16. /TASS/. Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko said he is convinced that peace in Ukraine will be achieved either this year or next.

TASS has compiled the Belarusian president’s key statements.
Ukrainian settlement
Peace in Ukraine will be reached this or next year: "This peace will be achieved. If not this year, then next year. I am absolutely sure of that."
"Russia is stronger, sturdier" and "is able to fight for a long time," but "the economic impact is tremendous": "Who can like and want this? Russians understand this, they are ready for peace."
"If Ukrainians do not agree to a peaceful settlement this year, it will be even more difficult for them next year, and eventually it will become impossible."
Belarus wants the conflict in Ukraine to end as soon as possible and is ready to do its best to help achieve that: "Peace is not only possible but necessary. There will be peace; it will be achieved. "Various factors are affecting both Russia and Ukraine. But these factors are clearly pushing both Ukraine and Russia toward peace, due to the impossibility of continuing such military operations. For these humanitarian and human reasons, peace is needed there. And it will be achieved."
Importance of elections in Ukraine
Vladimir Zelensky once promised to remain in office for one presidential term: "Promises should be kept."
Zelensky must hold a presidential election in Ukraine: "He needs to organize an election."
The US’ attempts to dictate its terms
US President Donald Trump "should not dictate to Ukraine what to do."

Ethiopia announces instalment of interim government in Tigray
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:54:06 UTC
22:54:06 KST

Ethiopia announces instalment of interim government in Tigray
After military pushed back TPLF uprising, PM Abiy Ahmed promises free elections within six months.
Ethiopia has announced that an interim government will take control of the state of Tigray, after its armed forces retook control of the northern region.
The installation of the six-month administration was announced in a statement by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Friday. He pledged that free elections would then be held in the state.
The move comes after the Ethiopian military pushed back an uprising launched last month by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Tigray’s main political party had launched the insurrection after announcing in April that it was retaking control of the region, effectively ending a peace deal with Ethiopia’s federal government.
The government promised that the interim government would create “a stable political situation” in Tigray so that free elections could be held. It has appointed five officials to run the state, including the mayor of the capital, Mekelle.
The officials will carry out “directives and instructions” delivered directly from the federal government.
The TPLF has yet to respond to the announcement. The rebel group launched an ambitious offensive in September in alliance with several other armed groups aimed at toppling the Abiy government. The Ethiopian government has accused the breakaway state of Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, accusations that Eritrea has denied.
After some early gains in the Afar region, its fighters were defeated and lost Tigray’s major cities. They surrendered in Mekelle in early October. Eritrean troops who had entered Tigray withdrew after heavy drone strikes from the Ethiopian armed forces.
The TPLF governed Ethiopia for nearly 30 years until 2018, when Abiy’s party came to power. Tigray, in response, boycotted national elections and rejected the central government, creating a severe rift.
The region remains scarred by the 2020-2022 war between federal forces, backed at that time by Eritrea, and the TPLF, which resulted in the killing of almost 600,000 people.
A peace deal ended the fighting, but key promises were not kept, including the return of displaced people and the disarmament of the TPLF.
Since the recent escalation, Ethiopia and Eritrea have accused each other of inciting war, raising fears of a wider conflict.
On Wednesday, the United States urged both sides to “de-escalate” during a phone call between Abiy and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

UK threatens African state with blanket visa ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:48:43 UTC
22:48:43 KST

UK threatens African state with blanket visa ban
Britain has threatened to ban all Eritrean nationals from obtaining visas over their government’s alleged refusal to take back rejected asylum seekers and convicted criminals, prompting the East African country to accuse London of political manipulation.
The Home Office said on Thursday that Eritrea had “abruptly” withdrawn returns cooperation earlier this year and refused to engage constructively despite months of private talks.
The department removed fast-track visa processing for Eritrean officials and VIPs and required its diplomats to obtain permission to travel more than 60 km (37 miles) outside of London. It said the measures were intended to increase “pressure on countries refusing to take back illegal immigrants.” The travel curbs mirror Eritrea’s longstanding restrictions requiring British diplomats to obtain permission to travel outside the capital, Asmara, the Home Office said in a statement.
“My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK,” Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood warned.
Eritrea’s embassy dismissed the measures as a “perfunctory political gimmick,” saying Asmara had repeatedly rejected forced returns and sought dialogue that London refused. It accused Britain of offering “blanket asylum to anyone who claims to be Eritrean in a bid to undermine” the Eritrean government.
The embassy said Asmara suspended escorted returns after British authorities allegedly passed off forced repatriations as voluntary and failed to disclose that some deportees were still serving prison sentences. It said no Eritrean official had received a UK visa since 2023.
The dispute reflects Britain’s drive to curb irregular migration. Eritreans accounted for 18% of approximately 33,000 small-boat arrivals across the English Channel in the year to June 2026, the largest nationality group, according to Home Office figures.
Around 84% of Eritrean asylum claims received positive initial decisions, according to Home Office figures, while UN reporting has documented indefinite national service, arbitrary detention and risks facing people forcibly returned. Britain has used similar pressure against Angola, Namibia and DR Congo to secure greater cooperation on migrant returns.
The British government’s migration policies have also triggered a separate dispute with Rwanda after then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer abandoned a previous Conservative government’s asylum relocation scheme in July 2024. The plan would have sent some asylum seekers who arrived in Britain irregularly to Rwanda for their claims to be processed, with successful applicants settling there.
The policy cost £700 million (about $930 million) and sent only four volunteers to Rwanda, according to British ministers. Kigali pursued arbitration over unpaid commitments, but a tribunal rejected its claims, including two £50 million payments, in a ruling announced in June.

'Wake-up call for retailers': How cyberattacks threaten supermarket food supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:46:04 UTC
22:46:04 KST

Empty supermarket shelves usually suggest a shopping frenzy, panic buying ahead of a disaster or a disruption to deliveries. A cyberattack on refrigeration systems is a far less obvious explanation.
Yet that is what happened in France, where refrigerated shelves were left empty after hackers targeted systems used by several major supermarket chains.
During the attack, hackers remotely manipulated the systems, using their defrost function to raise temperatures to around 50C (122F), threatening fresh and frozen food stocks.
Systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss, as well as those from US company Copeland and Italian company Dixell, were targeted.
Affected stores disconnected their equipment from the network, while the incident raised concerns over potential food losses and disruption to supermarket operations.
French Economy Minister Roland Lescure told parliament Tuesday that around 700 food distribution centers had been affected, while initial estimates put the number of targeted stores at around 500.
As France assessed the consequences of the attack, a separate incident was reported in the Netherlands.
Albert Heijn, the country's largest supermarket chain, announced Monday that operations at several distribution centers had come to a standstill after systems were shut down "preventively" following an attempted cyberattack.
While no link has been established between the two incidents, both highlight how cyberattacks can disrupt the infrastructure that supermarkets rely on to keep food fresh and supplies moving.
Dominique Schelcher, head of French supermarket group Cooperative U, described the refrigeration attack as “unprecedented, extremely serious and unacceptable.”
Targeting equipment essential to preserving fresh products constituted “an attack on the French food supply chain,” he wrote on US social media platform X.
The incident has drawn attention from cybersecurity specialists because of its direct impact on physical operations.
"This is one of the first large-scale cyber-attack affecting directly the daily life of French people," Kevin Tellier, a cybersecurity engineer at French cybersecurity firm Synacktiv, told Anadolu.
Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at cybersecurity company Sophos, said the French and Dutch incidents illustrated "two different but equally important" risks facing retailers.
The French attacks showed "how a cyber intrusion can have direct physical consequences, disrupting refrigeration and destroying stock," he said.
The Dutch incident, meanwhile, demonstrated "how a cybersecurity event can disrupt digital services and business operations."
"Together, they reinforce that cyber risk in retail is now a business continuity issue, not just an IT issue," Pilling said.
Tellier said the French incident demonstrated how a cyberattack could disrupt everyday life, even without particularly sophisticated methods.
“A 15-year-old kid could have done this as it was not very sophisticated,” he said.
He also warned that artificial intelligence could increase attackers' capabilities, including those with limited experience.
“I don't really believe in rogue AI scenarios ... but rather in attackers using AI to augment their potential,” he noted.
Pilling said the French incident was not an outlier, although attacks with direct physical consequences were not the dominant form of cyber impact observed across Europe.
“Across Europe we're seeing increased legislative and regulatory attention to operational technology and other connected systems that were never originally designed to face today's threat landscape,” he said.
"Governments understand that this is a significant resilience issue both now and into the future," he added.
What made the French incident unusual was the visibility of its real-world consequences, Pilling said.
“Attacks that deliberately cross that cyber-physical threshold are relatively rare," he said.
Asked whether the incidents pointed to a deliberate strategy of targeting food security, Pilling said it was too early to draw such a conclusion.
“We do not yet know who was responsible or what their motive was,” he said.
Food supply chains and retail operations contribute to civilian resilience, meaning disruptions can have consequences beyond the companies directly affected, he added.
One reason such attacks can have consequences beyond the digital world is their potential to compromise operational technology (OT), the hardware and software used to monitor and control physical processes, including refrigeration and industrial machinery.
"From my technical perspective, OT is often forgotten and has been largely underestimated during the last decades," Tellier said.
OT systems are designed to operate continuously, meaning updates and security measures are often seen as potential sources of disruption, he explained. The diversity of such equipment can also make security audits and improvements difficult.
Tellier said the attack did not surprise his company, which had previously reported vulnerabilities affecting Danfoss refrigeration systems and other brands.
“I remember well my colleagues logged on the control panel three years ago while they reported the vulnerability to Danfoss,” he added.
According to Tellier, Danfoss cooperated with Synacktiv and deployed a patch after three months. However, he said it remained unclear why the same vulnerability appeared again in 2025 and could have been exploited in France again this year.
Tellier said Danfoss had described the affected models as obsolete and no longer eligible for security updates, although some were still functioning properly.
Updating OT equipment can also be time-consuming, he said, because some systems require technicians to connect a USB stick to each device to install updates manually.
Tellier also pointed to management interfaces accessible through the internet, saying their exposure could have been identified through a security audit.
“Individual Supermarkets were not aware until today that they could lose money on a cyberattack,” he added.
"Centralized management is useful to cut costs, it was implemented for this purpose. However, centralizing means introducing single points of failure that must be audited regularly," Tellier said.
Pilling said modern supermarkets rely on equipment vendors, maintenance providers, remote management platforms and connected equipment.
“Those dependencies improve efficiency, but they can also create shared points of failure if security isn't managed consistently across the ecosystem,” he said.
Centralized management software allows organizations to manage thousands of devices, but can also amplify the impact of an attack if a central platform is compromised, Pilling explained.
“The same technology that improves operational efficiency can rapidly magnify the impact of a security incident,” he said.
Food distribution systems could also be targeted to cause disruption without directly attacking traditional critical infrastructure, such as power or water networks, he added.
“A relatively small technical compromise can translate into spoiled stock, supply-chain disruption and public concern,” Pilling said.
The incident also demonstrated the potential consequences of attacks on widely deployed platforms and shared services, he said.
“The more interconnected these systems become, the greater the potential impact when something goes wrong,” he said.
Preventing similar attacks will require supermarkets to look beyond software updates and strengthen the security of the systems that keep their operations running, according to Pilling.
“This is a resilience issue as much as a patching issue,” Pilling said.
He recommended that retailers identify their refrigeration systems, check whether they remain supported by manufacturers and secure their remote-access interfaces.
“Where remote access is operationally necessary, it should be limited to trusted management networks or secured remote-access services, with strong authentication and appropriate network segmentation,” he said.
Pilling also recommended updating supported equipment, isolating obsolete controllers and monitoring systems for unexpected changes.
"Regardless of who is ultimately responsible, the French refrigeration attack should be a wake-up call for retailers and operators of connected infrastructure," he said.
Systems supporting food supplies, safety and day-to-day services are now part of the "cyber battlefield" and need to be secured accordingly, he added.

Türkiye expects 4.2% economic growth in 2027
Presenting the government's 2027 budget proposal at the presidential complex in Ankara, Yilmaz said stronger growth among Türkiye's trading partners would create opportunities for exports and support balanced economic expansion.
The Turkish economy grew 3.7% in 2025, he said, adding that investment outpacing private consumption had strengthened production capacity and improved the composition of growth.
“In 2027, we expect our growth to rise to 4.2%, supported by the anticipated improvement in the global outlook and the recovery in external demand,” Yilmaz said.
The government aims to gradually accelerate growth to 5% by the end of its medium-term program through policies focused on productivity, technological transformation, and innovation, he said.
Employment is expected to increase by 657,000 people next year, with labor force participation reaching 53.4% and unemployment declining to 8%, from a projected 8.1% in 2026.
Yilmaz said annual inflation, which fell below 30% in September, was expected to reach 28.4% by the end of this year before declining to 21% by the end of 2027.
“Price stability is the fundamental priority of our program,” he said.
He said the current account deficit was expected to fall below 2% of gross domestic product next year from a projected 2.6% in 2026.
Türkiye will continue policies to boost exports, strengthen energy supply security, and reduce dependence on energy imports, he added.
Goods exports this January-September rose 5.2% year-on-year to $211 billion, bringing the rolling annual total to a record $283.7 billion, Yilmaz said.
The share of medium-high- and high-technology products in exports reached 44%, compared with around 28% in the early 2000s, he added.
Earlier, it was reported that Türkiye introduced new regulations prohibiting social media platforms from providing services to children under the age of 15.

The European Council’s conclusions on Montenegro were amended following an intervention by Croatia, with references to deadlines for the provisional closure of negotiating chapters removed, Croatian public broadcaster HRT reported Friday.
The earlier draft called for an agreement on the provisional closure of all negotiating chapters by the end of 2026, provided Montenegro implemented the necessary reforms, and for work on its accession treaty to be completed as soon as possible.
The revised conclusions welcome ongoing work on drafting an accession treaty with Montenegro and take note of the Irish Council presidency’s intention to work toward the provisional closure of negotiating chapters, provided Montenegro implements the appropriate reforms.

“We amended the conclusions at our initiative, sending a realistic message to our colleagues in Montenegro that they should get down to talks with Croatia,” he said.
Plenkovic said Zagreb had raised outstanding issues with Montenegro related to Chapter 23, covering the judiciary and fundamental rights, and Chapter 31, covering foreign, security and defense policy.
Croatia has presented eight demands to Montenegro, six concerning Chapter 23 and two related to Chapter 31.

Israeli diplomats and embassy staff vote in record numbers as election turnout abroad hits 86.7%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:38:13 UTC
22:38:13 KST

Voter turnout among Israeli diplomats, government personnel stationed overseas and eligible family members reached 86.7%, according to figures released Friday after voting concluded at 99 Israeli diplomatic missions worldwide ahead of the October 27 general election. 
Of 4,863 eligible voters, 4,218 cast ballots, compared with turnout of 69.6% in the November 2022 election, an increase of 17.1 percentage points.
Voting began Thursday under a longstanding arrangement allowing Israeli diplomatic and government personnel serving abroad, along with eligible family members, to vote before polling stations open in Israel. Unlike diplomats and other authorized personnel, ordinary Israeli citizens living or traveling abroad cannot vote overseas. The Foreign Ministry and Central Elections Committee operated 101 polling stations at 99 missions, serving embassy and consulate employees, government representatives, attachés and their eligible relatives.
Because of time zone differences, voting began at Israel's embassy in Wellington, New Zealand, at 11 p.m. Israel time on October 14, followed by the embassy in Suva, Fiji, Israel's newest diplomatic mission, at 12:01 a.m. Voting then moved westward across the globe over approximately 30 hours, with the final polling stations closing at Israeli missions in Los Angeles and San Francisco at 6 a.m. Friday. The largest polling station was at Israel's consulate in New York, where more than 700 people were eligible to vote.

Qatar pledges a lifeline for Lebanon's economy and reconstruction in the south
Qatar will help Lebanon revive its struggling economy, including supporting the future reconstruction of the country’s south, the Qatari prime minister said Friday.
Qatar will continue to support the Lebanese army "as a national institution that safeguards the country's security, unity and stability," Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said after meeting in Beirut with his Lebanese counterpart Nawaf Salam.
For years, Qatar has been a friendly country to Lebanon and a mediator for domestic and international political crises in the region. Qatar has also given tens of millions of dollars to the Lebanese army since Lebanon’s economic meltdown began in 2019.
The Qatari official said that QatarEnergy has reached an agreement with French company TotalEnergies to jointly develop a solar power plant in Lebanon as an initial project. He said that the aim is to develop a major investment project "that would benefit the Lebanese economy, as well as the Qatari companies and entities participating in it."
Salam said that he will put the plans for Lebanon’s electricity sector to the Lebanese Cabinet soon.
"The Qatari side will fund, implement and activate the project without any cost on the Lebanese state," Salam said, adding that such a move is important because of Lebanon's financial crisis.
Lebanon's state electricity company is one of the country's biggest sources of debt, hemorrhaging about $40 billion over the past decades with a bloated workforce and outdated infrastructure. The company provides only a few hours of electricity each day, and the state, until a year ago, had taken advances from the Central Bank when diesel fuel ran out.
Earlier in the day, Qatar's prime minister met with Lebanon’s president and parliamentary speaker and discussed with them the situation in southern Lebanon, where Israel captured dozens of villages and towns earlier this year during the latest Israel-Hezbollah war. Over the past several months, Israel has carried out large-scale demolitions in villages that its troops occupy.
The latest Israel-Hezbollah war began in early March, with Israel killing more than 4,300 people and occupied large parts of southern Lebanon.
The Qatari official said that Israel should withdraw from Lebanon and cease its attacks in the country. He said that Qatar is working in coordination with the United States to help lay the groundwork for future reconstruction in southern Lebanon, in a manner that would allow displaced people to return to their homes.
About 1.2 million people were displaced in Lebanon at the height of the war. Most have returned home since a June ceasefire, but more than 300,000 remain displaced, according to the International Organisation for Migration.

Israeli-enforced starvation persists in Gaza despite ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:36:54 UTC
22:36:54 KST

At least 466 Palestinians, including 157 children, have died from malnutrition and starvation since 2024, Gaza's health ministry has said, as the UN confirms acute malnutrition remains a risk.
The figures were released on World Food Day, observed annually on October 16.
At least 189 elderly people died of starvation, representing 40.5 percent of the deaths, it said.
In August 2025, the UN declared famine in Gaza. More than 1.4 million Palestinians are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026, the ministry added.
Meanwhile, a new UNICEF report has confirmed that while the ceasefire since October has allowed more humanitarian aid and commercial supplies to enter, acute malnutrition remains a risk.
The report said progress in pushing back the threat of famine, confirmed by a global food security monitor in August last year, had been achieved through a scaled-up food and nutrition response, the easing of restrictions on the entry of food and nutrition supplies, and the ceasefire.
However, those gains remain fragile, it said.
“Acute malnutrition rates have fallen, but only one in three children under the age of two is currently achieving minimum dietary diversity,” the report stated.
“We can't go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods, and services that they require,” UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires told reporters in Geneva.
Starvation as a weapon
Israel has used starvation as a weapon during the genocide in Gaza since October 2023, according to Palestinians and rights organisations.
Israel tightened restrictions on crossings in March 2025, preventing thousands of aid trucks waiting at border crossings from entering the enclave.
The restrictions followed widespread hunger in northern Gaza caused by the blockade and limits on food and relief supplies, forcing some residents to eat animal feed and wild plants.
In late May 2025, Israel allowed 87 aid trucks to enter Gaza for the first time after 81 days, according to Gaza’s government media office.
Aid later continued to enter on a limited and intermittent basis under strict restrictions until February 2026, when Israel allowed a limited increase in the number of trucks entering the enclave under a ceasefire agreement.
Palestinian officials said the shipments still lacked sufficient quantities of essential food items.
According to Gaza’s government media office, Israel has allowed in only about 34 percent of the humanitarian aid trucks agreed upon.
Malnutrition reaches 'catastrophic levels'
“Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached catastrophic levels that are killing children, the elderly and vulnerable groups,” the health Ministry said.
More than 1.4 million Palestinians, around 67 percent of Gaza’s population, are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026.
More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition were recorded among children under 5 from 2024 through August 2026, the ministry added.
Of them, 18 percent of children were suffering from severe acute malnutrition that threatened their lives, while 12.2 percent of children were affected by stunting, indicating the impact of food shortages on their development.
The mortality rate among children under 5 rose from 13.6 to 33.4 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2022 and 2025, the ministry said.
It estimated that 74,200 children will need treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027.
Pregnant women
Among pregnant women, the ministry said the prevalence of anaemia rose to 61% in 2026, compared with 41 percent before the war.
“Around 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded during the first half of 2026, more than three times the number recorded during the previous six months,” it added.
“One in three pregnancies in Gaza is now classified as high-risk,” the ministry continued.
“The figures show that the health consequences of the food crisis are increasingly affecting mothers and unborn children, in addition to children,” it said.
The figures come amid the humanitarian consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, which has caused widespread destruction to infrastructure, health facilities and food production sources.
The war has also damaged farmland, food production facilities and water networks, undermining residents’ ability to meet their basic needs locally.
Repeated displacement, loss of income and soaring prices have further increased families’ dependence on humanitarian aid, while access remains irregular.

"The Jewish people are not foreign occupiers in the land of our forefathers," Netanyahu said in a video posted to X/Twitter. "Our history is not a colonial enterprise. Our land is not stolen land. This is our homeland."

"That's where Jews come from," he said. "And we've been attached to it for thousands of years."
The prime minister differentiated Israel from European nations with colonial pasts, saying that the Jews in Israel are not "the Dutch in Indonesia... the Belgians in the Congo, we're Jews in Judea."
Obstacle to peace lies with Israel's, America's enemies, Netanyahu says
Regarding the path to a peace agreement, Netanyahu said that the obstacle to peace is not Israel, but rather the enemies in the region shared by Israel and the United States.
Specifically, Netanyahu noted the enemies' "refusal to recognize the Jewish people's right to a state of our own, in any boundary."
He cited chants of "Death to Israel" and "Death to America," which are common in states like Iran, a shared enemy of the US and Israel.
"We are the 'Little Satan,' you are the 'Great Satan,'" he said, referencing how such states often refer to Israel and the US, respectively, saying that both countries are "defending our common civilization."
"A peace built on illusions will crash against the rocks of Middle Eastern reality," said Netanyahu. "Israel will not gamble with its survival to accommodate those who refuse to accept the facts of history, to accept our right to exist, or who wish to appease terror.

Obama: Palestinians 'understandably' want their 'land back'

"If the attitude of Israel is, now that we are the strongest, the most technologically advanced in the region, then our security will depend on us simply doing whatever we need and taking whatever we want, and not making any concessions to anyone," he added. "That may work short-term... but you have ceded moral ground if that is the position you take."
Obama did introduce nuance into the conversation, according to The Irish Times, saying that the millions of Jews and Palestinians in the region "aren't going anywhere."
"The citizenry of Israel has to rethink, to reimagine, how your children and grandchildren are going to live in this region," he said. "Are you just going to be behind walls and wipe out everybody around you, or are you going to find some just way of defending yourself while still acting in an ethical, moral way?"
Obama added that the Palestinians must come to understand that they will not "outkill" or "outweaponize the Israelis."
"We have to look to other examples of how change comes about," he said, pointing toward "nonviolent strategies." "That's going to take some time."

EU decision could drive more Sika deer to Zurich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:31:31 UTC
22:31:31 KST

EU decision could drive more Sika deer to Zurich
The spotted Sika deer from Japan could soon be migrating to the Swiss canton of Zurich in greater numbers. This is due to a European Union directive for member states to cull the animals.
In Germany and Austria, the EU decision announced in the summer of 2025 caused quite a stir. The media were already referring to an “extermination and culling plan”. The EU had classified the spotted sika deer as an “invasive alien species”.
Private ownership of these deer will therefore only be permitted until August 2027. Furthermore, wild populations are to be “intensively hunted”. In this way, the EU aims to prevent damage to native forests and to stop the Asian deer from interbreeding with native red deer.
More
How Switzerland is battling invasive species
Around 40 Swiss Sika deer
The decision from Brussels could have implications for the canton of Zurich. “We will notice the increasing hunting pressure in Baden-Württemberg,” says Reto Muggler, co-head of the cantonal Fisheries and Hunting Administration. This means that more sika deer could migrate into the area.
This Asian deer species already lives in the canton of Zurich, albeit only in a small area of just over 2,300 hectares. The animals can be observed north of the Rhine in the Rafzerfeld in the canton of Zurich and in the canton of Schaffhausen. This population numbers just over 40 animals.
Unlike in the EU, where culling plans are a recent development, sika deer have, however, been hunted in the canton of Zurich for years. Last year, 19 animals were shot to prevent the population from spreading. “If more sika deer were to enter the canton of Zurich, they would continue to be hunted as part of normal management,” said Muggler.
The canton does not currently fear any significant geographical spread. According to Muggler, the sika deer remains within its territory. As such, it has not yet swum across the Rhine.
Nor does Zurich regard the possibility of Sika deer interbreeding with red deer as a threat. This is because the species live far apart and are unlikely to cross paths.
Gift from Japanese Emperor
The Zurich sika deer population descends from a population in the Black Forest that has lived there since 1939. The spotted deer actually originate from South-East Asia and the Far East. They arrived in Europe – more specifically, in France – in 1890 as a gift from the Japanese Emperor. There, they managed to escape from the grounds of Rambouillet Castle near Paris.
Around 1900, sika deer were brought to Germany because it was fashionable to ‘enrich’ the native wildlife with non-native species. Many sika deer lived in parks, where – as had happened in France – they once again managed to escape. There are now five populations in Germany.
Sika deer are related to red deer but are significantly smaller. From May to September, they have a summer coat with white patches.

The military said all circumstances surrounding the incident would be examined.
The Binyamin Regional Council disputed the Palestinian account, describing the incident as a "planned provocation" organized by the Palestinian Authority. It claimed that hundreds of "terrorists and anarchists" had confronted Israelis, throwing stones and firing fireworks directly at them while journalists filmed the violence. The council also alleged that Palestinian Authority vehicles were present in the area and that left-wing activists had planned confrontations during the olive harvest to promote allegations of settler violence. These claims were not independently verified.
Israeli police said they had opened an investigation into violence in Abu Falah and nearby Turmus Ayya, including suspected stone-throwing and vehicle arson. Investigators and forensic teams were sent to collect evidence and witness statements under military escort. "The Israel Police and the IDF view any manifestation of violence gravely, particularly when it involves journalists carrying out their work," police said, pledging to bring those responsible to justice.
In Turmus Ayya, Palestinian reports said settlers set fire to olive trees and several vehicles, including one belonging to the Palestinian Civil Defense. The organization said one of its members was attacked while trying to extinguish a burning vehicle. Additional violence was reported near Burqa and Birzeit, where Palestinians said olive harvesters had been assaulted. The Palestinian Red Crescent reported treating four injured people near Burqa, while Palestinian media said a 70-year-old man was injured in the Birzeit area. The incidents come amid heightened tensions across the West Bank during the olive harvest, which has repeatedly been disrupted by attacks on Palestinian farmers and their property.
The U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack on American photojournalist Heidi Levine and was monitoring the situation. "The Trump administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans," an embassy spokesperson said, adding that the State Department provides appropriate consular assistance to Americans facing difficulties abroad. "We are in regular dialogue with partners about improving stability and security in the West Bank. We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests and convictions of those responsible." The embassy declined further comment, citing privacy and other considerations.
The Washington Post also condemned the attack and called for a full investigation. "This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank," said Matt Murray, the newspaper's executive editor. "She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist." Murray said the newspaper was relieved that Levine had received medical care and was safe, but was "outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job," urging authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and take appropriate follow-up action.

Israel picks between 'secular democracy or theocracy' in election, chess master Garry Kasparov says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:27:27 UTC
22:27:27 KST

When Israelis head to vote on October 27, they won't just be picking the next government; they will be deciding whether Israel becomes "a secular Hebrew democracy, or a rigid, rabbinical theocracy," Garry Kasparov, a Russian chess grandmaster, political activist, and writer, wrote in an op-ed for the New York Times published on Thursday.
"Just as Abraham Lincoln observed that the government could not persist 'half slave and half free,' Israel cannot go on half theocratic and half secular," Kasparov, whose father was Jewish, argued.
"Americans resolved that contradiction over four years of brutal civil war. Israel’s election on Oct. 27 offers a bloodless way out of this morass," he wrote.
"Democracies are built on compromise," Kasparov said. "But sometimes a compromise can turn dangerous."
Growing up in the Soviet Union shaped Kasparov's view of Israeli democracy
He explained that his upbringing in the Soviet Union shaped his perception of both the US and Israeli democracies. "I see this dynamic at play in two democracies with which I closely identify: the United States and Israel."
"As a young Soviet with a Jewish father, I grew up to become a staunch supporter of Israel, an outpost of liberalism surrounded by illiberal, Moscow-backed Arab states," Kasparov wrote.
"While I rejected the anti-Americanism and anti-Zionism of the Communist regime under which I was raised, I also sought a textured understanding of the United States and Israel."
Israel faces a breaking point, risk of permanent rupture
"I learned early on that the United States had reached a breaking point just 84 years after independence. America’s founders included men who owned slaves and men who did not. They could not both midwife the union and challenge the 'peculiar institution.' This guaranteed the birth of the United States but cursed the young nation with an affliction that nearly caused a permanent rupture."
Kasparov believes that Israel is also facing this affliction and risk of permanent rupture. Rather than the divisive issue being slavery, the divisive issue that Kasparov says has placed Israel at this crossroad is the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) draft to the IDF. He clarified in the NYT that "There is, of course, no moral equivalence between the haredim, as the ultra-Orthodox are called in Israel, and slave owners."
He cites then-prime minister David Ben-Gurion's original agreement with the haredim as the thing that set in motion the aforementioned split. In 1948 Ben-Gurion approved a temporary agreement with haredi yeshiva students, granting 400 people an exemption from army service to study Torah. Today, upwards of 50,000 people evade IDF draft to study Torah.
"The pact haunted their descendants and today is sustained by a nationalist far right and an unscrupulous prime minister willing to bend the law to stay in power," Kasparov said.
Haredi draft is 'corroding' Israel's social compact
"In Israel today, ultra-Orthodox political power is corroding the social compact that holds the country together."
"Israelis of Ben-Gurion’s generation may not have understood the kind of foundation they were laying," Kasparov argued. "They may have presumed they were simply handing out draft exemptions to a few hundred young men. Many of the American founders similarly expected slavery to peter out over time."
"Instead, slavery expanded significantly after 1776, just as religious influence in Israel exploded in the decades following 1948. The draft exemption became especially infuriating to secular Israeli Jews after Oct. 7 and the war in Gaza."
The haredi draft is not the only way Kasparov thinks that religious influence is corruptive to Israel. He argues that their power over Israeli law, from marriages, divorces, and funerals to transportation and public services on Shabbat, is "toxic" and unfair to the millions of Israelis who do not observe Shabbat.
"The ultra-Orthodox parties in the Knesset are so single-minded that it seems they will support anyone, no matter how clouded by accusations of misdeeds, who preserves their special privileges," Kasparov wrote in the NYT. "This is how the haredim have become indispensable accomplices and supporters to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition."
Netanyahu's relationship with the haredim in Knesset
"Without the ultra-Orthodox, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would not have backing for many of his authoritarian endeavors," he argued, and similarly, "Without Mr. Netanyahu, the ultra-Orthodox would lose their protected status."
Despite his comments that Israel is choosing between secular democracy or rigid theocracy, Kasparov added that he does not want religion and culture to be suppressed. "When I was growing up in the Soviet Union, Communist thugs enforced atheism and suppressed Jewish culture. This is not what I want for Israel."
"I simply believe in equality before the law and an Israel that embodies its founders’ aspirations of being a 'light unto the nations,' rather than an international pariah held back by far-right and religious special interests," Kasparov wrote.
"Israel’s election on Oct. 27 offers a bloodless way out of this morass."
