EXPLAINER – Israel elections: What do main parties say about Palestinians?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:39:57 UTC
21:39:57 KST

Growing international recognition of Palestinian statehood and a UN inquiry’s finding that Israel committed genocide in Gaza have not stopped leading candidates in Israel’s Oct. 27 election from campaigning against Palestinian independence and promising further military action.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition pledge to double down on their policies in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. However, key opposition figures also reject Palestinian statehood, criticizing Netanyahu more for failing to dismantle Hamas than for the devastation of Gaza.
The parties differ over annexation, settlement expansion and who should govern parts of Palestinian territory. But their positions suggest that replacing Netanyahu would not necessarily break with policies that have prolonged the occupation and denied Palestinians sovereignty.
Here is where the main parties stand on Gaza, settlements and Palestinian self-government. All seat projections come from an Oct. 14 Madad poll, which put the four coordinating opposition lists at 50 seats and Netanyahu’s existing coalition parties at 47 – both short of a 61-seat majority.
Netanyahu’s Likud leads the government that took office in December 2022 and oversaw the military campaign that devastated Gaza and killed nearly 75,000 people.
Netanyahu faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, including starvation as a method of warfare.
Still his party is polling second, with 18 projected seats.
On Gaza, he insists Hamas must fully disarm before Israeli forces end their occupation.
Likud portrays Palestinian statehood as a security threat, accusing opposition leaders of enabling it even when they explicitly reject it.
Its government has accelerated settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, with ministers presenting construction as a means of preventing Palestinian independence. Occupier violence against Palestinians has also increased.
At his September UN General Assembly speech, Netanyahu dismissed reports of record Israeli occupier violence against Palestinians in the West Bank as a “handful of young juvenile delinquents.”
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism, a far-right coalition partner, received six projected seats and could again help Netanyahu govern.
Speaking on a Ynet podcast in September, Smotrich called for dismantling the Palestinian Authority and extending Israel’s genocidal war to the West Bank: “do there what we did in Gaza.”
He also demanded annexation of territory Israel occupies in Gaza.
His West Bank agenda includes annexing approximately 82% of the territory, under a proposal presented in September 2025. That would leave Palestinians in fragmented areas rather than a territorially connected state.
Under this strategy, the primary stated goal is to permanently eliminate the possibility of an independent Palestinian state.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power, another far-right coalition partner, received eight projected seats.
At a September campaign news conference, Ben-Gvir presented a plan to displace 1.86 million Palestinians from Gaza over seven years under what he calls “voluntary emigration.”
Ben-Gvir advocates restoring Israeli settlements in Gaza rather than Palestinian self-government.
He has also defended extreme measures such as reducing food for Palestinian detainees.
In August 2026, he called for Israeli forces to kill “30 to 40” people in Gaza every night, while declaring that “all of Gaza” belonged to Israel.
Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar led the poll with 20 projected seats, making him a leading contender to head an opposition government.
Speaking near Gaza on Thursday, Eisenkot pledged to end Hamas’s rule within 18 months of becoming prime minister, either through US President Donald Trump’s framework or military action, leaving open the prospect of further Israeli military operations in the enclave.
Eisenkot told a Channel 7 podcast on Oct. 11 that “the principle of two states for two peoples is a mistake,” rejecting the two-state solution.
He also opposes incorporating millions of Palestinians into Israel, saying he wants to preserve a strong Jewish majority.
Former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s Together alliance received 12 projected seats and could emerge as a key partner in an opposition coalition. Despite differences over Gaza’s future, both have opposed Palestinian statehood in the near term.
Bennett rejects Palestinian statehood and has called for continued Israeli military operation in Gaza until Hamas is disarmed.
Although Lapid has expressed support for a two-state solution in the longer term and occupier settler violence, he has not committed to reversing settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank.
Bennett, meanwhile, supports settlement expansion, which further entrenches Israeli control over Palestinian land and undermines prospects for an independent Palestinian state.
Avigdor Lieberman’s secular nationalist Yisrael Beytenu received nine projected seats and joined the opposition campaign pact.
Lieberman proposes dismantling the Palestinian Authority and canceling the Oslo agreements, replacing Palestinian self-rule in Areas A and B of the occupied West Bank with Jordanian administration while Israel retains control over Area C, which accounts for around 60% of the territory.
He openly presents the proposal as a way to prevent an internationally recognized Palestinian state, denying Palestinians a sovereign future while preserving Israeli control over much of the occupied territory.
For Gaza, Lieberman has advocated cutting off water, electricity and fuel supplies while backing continued Israeli military operations.
Ofer Winter’s new Amcha Israel received four projected seats. It opposes Palestinian statehood and promotes Palestinian displacement from Gaza. A potential Netanyahu partner, it also supports ultra-Orthodox enlistment, creating possible friction with his religious allies.
Those allies, United Torah Judaism and Shas, received eight and seven seats respectively. Their priorities center on religious institutions and military-service exemptions.
Shas supports dismantling Hamas and demilitarizing Gaza while opposing indefinite Israeli control. United Torah Judaism has no comparably detailed independent Gaza policy, according to the Jerusalem Post.
The poll also gives four seats to the separate Reservists list led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, adding another potential factor in coalition negotiations.
The Joint List received nine projected seats and Ra’am six. Their votes could be decisive, but Netanyahu and leading opposition figures reject governing partnerships with Arab-led parties.
Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas has called for recognition of an independent Palestinian state and an end to occupation. His party previously joined the Bennett-Lapid government in 2021.
Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen has made progress toward Palestinian statehood a condition for negotiating support for a new government.
Their demands also challenge continued Israeli control of Palestinian territory. In its July 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found Israel’s continued presence unlawful and said it must end new settlement activity and evacuate settlers.

Olivia from Spain was just 13 when she developed the Jelly Cleaner – a simple filtering device made from two plastic bottles and a pair of tights to trap microplastics and clean the ocean. Now a European Climate Pact Ambassador, Olivia has gone on to give numerous presentations on the Jelly Cleaner, climate change and the health of the oceans to schools, universities, and international organisations.
She is fired up by her mission: “Climate change is a global problem that is affecting everyone. We are the ones who have caused climate change, but we are also the ones who have the power and obligation to fix it.”
If you’re committed to informing and inspiring climate action in your community, now is your chance to become a European Climate Pact Ambassador, too. You can be young or old - all you need to demonstrate is that you’re ready to inspire and motivate others to take climate action and be a changemaker.
You have until 31 October 2026 to submit your European Climate Pact Ambassador application. Applications are assessed on a rolling basis – so early applications are welcome!
What is the Climate Pact?
It’s a movement of people who are each taking action to help build a cleaner and more resilient Europe. Launched by the European Commission, it supports the EU's goal to become climate-neutral by 2050.
If you’re chosen as a climate pact ambassador, you will get involved in community building, share your own climate actions and solutions, and organise practical activities such as tree planting days or car-free initiatives. You will also get the opportunity to join high-level events and exchanges at local, regional and EU levels.
You will become part of a growing and diverse community of over 1,000 Climate Pact Ambassadors and dozens of partner organisations.
Take inspiration from Olivia: “Any person can start by creating change in their own home, or even at school or at work. And this creates a ripple effect. The future will be ours – it’s in our hands right now. We need to act before it’s too late, for us and for all future generations.”

Iran issues post-war tourism recovery and competitiveness strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Iran issues post-war tourism recovery and competitiveness strategy
TEHRAN – Iran’s tourism ministry has issued a strategic and operational plan to revive the country’s tourism industry during the transition and post-war periods, with a focus on rebuilding its international tourism brand, improving competitiveness and coordinating recovery measures nationwide.
Anoushirvan Mohseni-Bandpey, deputy tourism minister, said the document had been approved by the minister of cultural heritage, tourism and handicrafts and sent to provincial departments for implementation, according to a report published by the ministry and carried by IRNA.
The plan aims to establish a common framework for decision-making, prioritize practical measures and coordinate tourism recovery efforts at national and provincial levels. It also seeks to move beyond simply restoring conditions that existed before the crisis by redefining Iran’s competitive advantages and aligning its tourism offerings with emerging global trends.
The document identifies three priority tourism product groups: nature-based tourism, ecotourism and community-based tourism; health tourism, including medical services, wellness and mental and psychological recovery; and cultural and historical tourism.
According to the deputy minister, these sectors could help strengthen Iran’s position in international tourism markets by drawing on the country’s geographical diversity, cultural heritage and specialized services.
He said the strategy was designed not only to set priorities and outline a long-term vision but also to establish mechanisms for implementing, monitoring and evaluating recovery measures.
Mohseni-Bandpey said regular monitoring would help identify implementation obstacles, enable timely adjustments and provide a clearer assessment of progress toward the strategy’s objectives.
He stressed that successful tourism recovery would depend on linking strategic policymaking with practical implementation, institutional coordination and continuous evaluation. Consistent implementation, he said, could help strengthen the country’s competitive position, rebuild its tourism brand and support a more sustainable industry aligned with global developments.
The strategy comes as Iran’s tourism industry faces severe disruption following the outbreak of war on Feb. 28, when the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran. The conflict prompted widespread airspace closures and flight suspensions across the region, disrupting international travel and undermining visitor confidence.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Turkish Airlines and CFM International signed a memorandum of understanding Friday for the purchase of more than 300 aircraft engines and long-term maintenance services covering a fleet of over 600 engines, the companies announced.
The new engines, including spares, will power up to 150 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft under an order announced in late September comprising 100 firm orders and 50 options, according to a press release.
The service agreement will cover the entire LEAP-1B engine fleet of Turkish Airlines and its subsidiary AJet, including engines previously ordered or delivered, spare engines, those powering leased aircraft and potential options.
The memorandum also includes a material services agreement supporting the establishment of an engine maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) facility in Türkiye.
The agreement was signed at a ceremony in Istanbul by Turkish Airlines Chairman Murat Seker, Turkish Technic CEO Mikail Akbulut and Olivier Andries, CEO of Safran, one of CFM's two parent companies.
Seker said the agreement would support the airline's expanding fleet, flight network and operational efficiency.
"We are pleased to strengthen our partnership with CFM, with whom we have worked for many years, through a comprehensive service package," he said.
"This cooperation will provide the expertise, reliability and support needed to develop our maintenance, repair and overhaul capabilities for LEAP engines," he added.
Akbulut said Turkish Technic would expand its engine maintenance capabilities by providing comprehensive services for LEAP engines, while continuing investments alongside its established aircraft and component maintenance operations.
Andries described the agreement as another milestone in a partnership spanning nearly four decades, saying it would support Turkish Airlines' growth and fleet expansion.
GE Aerospace Chairman and CEO H. Lawrence Culp Jr. said the cooperation would support the expansion of the airline's Istanbul-based network and the development of its engine maintenance capabilities.
Including AJet's fleet, Turkish Airlines currently operates 96 Boeing 737 Next Generation aircraft powered by CFM56-7B engines and 79 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft equipped with LEAP-1B engines.
CFM has delivered more than 10,000 LEAP engines since the engine family entered service a decade ago, with the fleet accumulating over 100 million flight hours, the statement said.

Tesla unveiled a new version of its Roadster sports car on Oct. 15, demonstrating a prototype that used compressed-air thrusters to jump over parked vehicles at a test site in Texas.
The car uses 10 nozzles and ultra-high-pressure air tanks to propel itself in the air and accelerate on the ground, CEO Elon Musk said.
During the demonstration at a SpaceX facility, the vehicle climbed a steep ramp and hung upside down using suction underneath it, before launching off the ramp, flipping in midair and landing with the help of air jets.
Tesla said the car, which had no driver during the demonstration, accelerated from zero to 60 miles (97 kilometers) per hour in less than a second.
Musk told spectators he needed a live audience to confirm that the demonstration was not generated by artificial intelligence.
He said production was expected to begin in 2028, but cautioned that the vehicle might not be legal in all markets.
The demonstration did not show sustained flight.
Roger Connor, curator for vertical flight at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum, told CNN before the event that aircraft need to be lightweight, while road vehicles require bumpers and other crash protection.
Such a hybrid would be “a poor performing aircraft and a poor performing vehicle, and also quite expensive,” he said.

EU unveils new strategy to step up fight against human trafficking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:31:02 UTC
21:31:02 KST

Melike Pala
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The European Commission unveiled a new strategy to combat human trafficking on Friday, setting out six priorities, including the use of technology, cooperation with the private sector, tackling organized crime, and plans to strengthen partnerships with non-EU countries.
More than 20,000 victims of human trafficking were registered across the European Union in 2023 and 2024, marking a 16.1% increase, according to a Commission statement.
Women and girls accounted for 63% of registered victims, most of whom were trafficked for sexual exploitation, while children represented 15% of the total.
Men made up 74% of victims trafficked for labour exploitation.
The first priority focuses on harnessing modern technology to improve the prevention, detection and investigation of human trafficking.
The second priority aims to strengthen cooperation with the private sector to reduce exploitation risks and improve early detection.
Under the third priority, the EU will step up efforts to disrupt transnational trafficking networks linked to organized crime through cross-border cooperation, intelligence-led policing, financial investigations and asset recovery.
The bloc also called on member states to expand cross-border operational cooperation through joint investigation teams, with support from Europol and Eurojust.
The fourth priority addresses trafficking risks linked to migration by strengthening screening procedures, border processes and safeguards in reception conditions.
The fifth priority focuses on improving preparedness and rapid responses during crises, while the sixth priority aims to strengthen the protection of people vulnerable to trafficking.
The strategy will be discussed by the European Parliament and the European Council.

Iran win U23 World Greco-Roman team title
TEHRAN - Iran U23 Greco-Roman team managed to win the team title of the U23 World Championships in Las Vegas, United States.
Iran finished with 119 points, five more than Kazakhstan which finished a surprising second with 114 points. Russia was third with 105 points.
Asian silver medalist Erfan Jarkani held on to a 1-1 criteria lead against Manato Nakamura (JPN) to win the 63kg gold. Nakamura challenged at the end of the bout but there was no foul or fleeing from Jarkani, who won with a final score of 2-1.
At 87kg, Yasin Yazdi, also a Asian Championships silver medalist, won his career first-ever gold medal with a 4-0 victory over Temirlan Turdakyn from Kazakhstan in the final. He got the par terre position in the first period but did not score any points.
However, he began the second period with a takedown and that eliminated any chances of him being put in par terre. Yazdi was awarded the second passivity as well which extended his lead to 4-0.
"I’d been waiting for this gold for about two or three years," Yazdi said. "I was able to win it here, and I hope I can keep winning gold medals in the future."
Yazdi said that before the final, he was aware of the Turdakyn's shortcoming and prepared more for exchanges in standing than par terre.
"Before the final, I knew I could win the match because I felt my opponent wasn’t as well-prepared as I was," he said. "My opponent was tall and I may have trouble taking him down and controlling him on the mat. So, I focused most of my effort on the standing exchanges. I could tell that my opponent was starting to get tired in the last 30 seconds of the first period, so in the second period I put even more pressure on him."

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated 12 communities in the Kharkov and Zaporozhye Regions and the Donetsk People’s Republic over the week of October 10-16, including two communities during the past 24 hours in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Last week, Battlegroup North units took control of the settlements of Lukashovo, Lobanovka, Reznikovo, Kupino, Nefyodovka and Chernoye and yesterday they established control of the settlements of Varvarovka and Nikolayevka in the Kharkov Region through active and decisive operations. <…> During the week, Battlegroup Center units liberated the settlements of Novotroitskoye, Petrovskoye and Lidino in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said in a statement.
"Over the past week, Battlegroup East units continued their advance deep into the enemy’s defenses and liberated the settlement of Nikolskoye in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry reported.
Russian troops deliver eight precision strikes on Ukrainian military sites over week
Russian troops delivered one massive and seven combined strikes by precision weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles on Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, logistics and telecommunications centers and ammunition depots over the week, the ministry reported.
"On October 10-16, 2026, the Russian Armed Forces delivered one massive and seven combined strikes, hitting military-industrial enterprises, logistics and telecommunications centers, transport infrastructure facilities used to support the Ukrainian army’s operations, sites producing and storing unmanned aerial vehicles, ammunition and materiel depots, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries," the ministry said.
Russian troops delivered strikes over the week, degrading some infrastructure facilities of Ukrainian ports used to receive and store military supplies, it said.
"In addition, some infrastructure facilities of Ukraine’s ports used to receive, store and distribute military cargo were degraded," the ministry said.
Russian troops struck 15 dry cargo ships involved in the delivery of Western weapons and military hardware to the Ukrainian army over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the week, 15 dry cargo ships involved in the delivery of Western weapons, military hardware, fuel and equipment for the needs of the Ukrainian army were hit," the ministry said.

Russia’s Battlegroup North thwarted all the Ukrainian army’s attempts during the past week to break out of the encirclement in the Kharkov Region, the ministry reported.

Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicts over 1,675 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted more than 1,675 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed five enemy armored combat vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the past week in the Kharkov and Sumy Regions, Battlegroup North units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of six mechanized brigades, two motorized infantry brigades, two airmobile brigades, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army, four territorial defense brigades and a National Guard brigade," the ministry said.

"During the past week, Battlegroup West units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on formations of two mechanized brigades, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and two territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.

Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted more than 1,155 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed nine enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Over the past week, Battlegroup South units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, a mountain assault brigade, an airmobile brigade, an unmanned systems brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and a territorial defense brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,155 personnel, nine armored combat vehicles, 198 motor vehicles, 13 field artillery guns and two electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts over 2,740 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 2,740 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 37 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
Over the past week, Battlegroup Center units "inflicted losses on formations of four mechanized brigades, a jaeger brigade, an airborne brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and three National Guard brigades," the ministry said.
Overall, the Ukrainian army lost more than 2,740 personnel, 37 armored combat vehicles, 76 motor vehicles, 11 field artillery guns and 11 electronic warfare stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 1,695 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 1,695 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed seven enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the past week, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of a mechanized brigade, an assault brigade, three air assault brigades, three assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and two marine infantry brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,695 personnel, seven armored combat vehicles, 53 motor vehicles, three field artillery guns and two electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 240 Ukrainian troops in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 240 Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Last week, Battlegroup Dnepr units improved their tactical position and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade," the ministry said.
"As many as 240 [Ukrainian] military personnel, an armored combat vehicle, 116 motor vehicles, five artillery guns and nine electronic warfare stations were destroyed," the ministry reported.
Russian air defenses intercept 5,695 Ukrainian UAVs, four cruise missiles over week
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 5,695 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and four Flamingo cruise missiles over the week, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down seven guided aerial bombs, two rockets of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system, four Flamingo long-range cruise missiles, a Neptune long-range missile and 5,695 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Tally of Ukrainian army’s losses
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 263,235 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,251 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,790 multiple rocket launchers, 36,738 field artillery guns and mortars and 74,686 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

Pakistan orders school inspections following deadly roof collapse
Families demand justice for the 35 people killed; relatives say they had warned that the roof was leaking.
Authorities in Pakistan have ordered inspections of regional schools after the collapse of a classroom roof killed at least 34 children and a teacher.
Reports on Friday said that the government has ordered the administration of the northeastern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to launch the checks after the deadly incident at Al-Khair school on Thursday.
At least 34 students aged 13 or younger, as well as a teacher, were killed in the roof collapse.
There are conflicting reports about whether the inspections will cover both public and private schools or only private schools. The province’s education department has been given three days to report its findings, according to The Associated Press news agency.
Schools are to be classified as safe, in need of repairs or improvements, or potentially unsafe. Various structures will be assessed, including roofs, ceilings, walls and staircases.
Police arrested Mohammad Khan, the owner of Al-Khair school, shortly after the roof of mud and bricks collapsed.
The building was structurally weak, according to Peshawar Police Chief Saeed Ahmed, who also said that Khan had told officers that recent rains had weakened the structure.
Bereaved families are demanding justice, with some of the victims’ relatives maintaining that they had warned Khan about rainwater repeatedly seeping into classrooms.
Dozens of mourners gathered outside the school on Friday to remember those who died.
Pakistan’s construction standards are widely reported to be poor and builders commonly use substandard materials.
The roof of a private tutoring centre in the eastern city of Lahore collapsed in June, killing 14 people.

Ukraine exports gas for first time since start of full-scale war
Companies sold about 12.75 million cubic metres of natural gas at the first export auction held by the Ukrainian Energy Exchange (UEEX) on 15 October.
Source: the auction results published by the UEEX
Details: The sale prices ranged from €69 to €69.03 per MWh.
The largest volume was sold by Naftogazvydobuvannia PrJSC, at about 7.78 million cubic metres. The remaining gas was sold by Naftohazdiia LLC, Naftohazheorozvidka LLC and Kosul LLC. All four companies belong to the DTEK Group, Ukraine's largest private energy company.
In total, they sold about 12.31 million cubic metres of gas.
All four companies initially offered the gas at €87 per MWh. The final prices were about 21% lower. They were also 19% below the last recorded price at the Dutch TTF hub, which stood at €85.5 per MWh.
The export price was 89% higher than the domestic price.
Deliveries are scheduled to take place at the Polish border between 26 October and 31 December. Full prepayment is required for all lots. Deliveries will proceed subject to the sellers obtaining the relevant export licences from the Ministry of Economy.
For reference: Following the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, the government banned gas exports. A government decision on 7 October 2026 reintroduced permission to export gas.
Background:
- In late August, Ukraine accumulated enough gas to meet the basic scenario for getting through the winter.
- The export sales limit stands at 15% of the volume of gas delivered by a producer to the gas transmission system in the previous month. Gas exports are prohibited during winter.

TikTok’s Career Ladder Creator Max Klymenko and Etnodim Turn Ukraine’s Fading Traditional Crafts Into Charity Shirt
Ukrainian embroidered clothing brand Etnodim has partnered with British content creator of Ukrainian origin Max Klymenko to launch a charity shirt inspired by his popular TikTok series Career Ladder, with profits from sales going toward supporting Ukrainian children affected by Russia’s war.
The collaboration brings together Klymenko’s internationally recognized social media project, which has helped him attract nearly 10 million TikTok followers, and traditional Ukrainian craftsmanship.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In his Career Ladder series, Klymenko interviews people from a wide range of professions, including public figures such as Will Smith, Gordon Ramsay, French President Emmanuel Macron, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The concept of exploring different careers inspired Klymenko and the Etnodim team to highlight traditional Ukrainian occupations, some of which are gradually disappearing.
The resulting shirt features embroidered representations of historic crafts and professions, including blacksmithing, pottery, harvesting, and milling, reflecting the importance of preserving Ukraine’s cultural heritage.
“We wanted to convey the idea of equal opportunities without stereotypes and remind people that every profession has its own value. The embroidery features traditional Ukrainian crafts that are gradually disappearing, including blacksmithing, pottery, harvesting and milling. The composition on the shirt’s side panel is inspired by Apple Picker, a work by Ukrainian artist Oleksandr Saienko,” the Etnodim team explains.
Beyond its connection to the TikTok series, the design also draws on Klymenko’s personal memories of growing up in Ukraine, particularly his childhood experiences with his grandmother.
According to the press release, conversations about his upbringing, family memories, and current work helped shape the creative direction of the collaboration.
“When I think about my childhood, I immediately think of my grandmother: the time I spent with her, the little forts made of yarn I used to build when visiting her, and all the wonderful things in her house that have stayed in my memory. Decorative plates, a large wooden spoon with classic red and colourful Ukrainian patterns, and a knitted picture of Mykolaiv landscapes hanging on the wall—that picture is probably the most vivid work of art I remember from childhood,” Klymenko said.
The partnership also reflects Klymenko’s continued involvement in charitable initiatives supporting Ukraine and his efforts to introduce Ukrainian culture and experiences to international audiences.
As part of the initiative, profits from sales of the Career Ladder shirt will be donated to Kids of Ukraine to support its SviTY programme, which assists teenagers affected by the war.
The programme focuses on emotional recovery, education, and personal development, helping young people acquire new skills, identify their strengths, and explore future career opportunities.
Through the collaboration, Etnodim and Klymenko aim to combine the promotion of traditional Ukrainian crafts with practical support for children and teenagers navigating their futures amid the ongoing war.
In another recent collaboration, German sportswear brand PUMA joined forces with Ukrainian fashion label CHER’17, marking its first partnership with a local fashion brand in Ukraine.
According to a press release, the CHER’17 x PUMA collection explores the unpredictability of everyday life under the campaign slogan “No plan is a plan.” The collection reinterprets PUMA’s signature designs through details inspired by unexpected mishaps and everyday imperfections.

Ukraine Could Get Starlink Deep Inside Russia in Exchange for 100-Day Oil Strike Pause, WSJ Says
Unknown

2026-10-16

21:10:35 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Could Get Starlink Deep Inside Russia in Exchange for 100-Day Oil Strike Pause, WSJ Says
Two Republican US senators have proposed expanding Starlink coverage roughly 300 kilometers, or 186 miles, inside Russia in exchange for Ukraine suspending strikes on Russian oil refineries for 100 days, The Wall Street Journal reported on October 15, citing people familiar with the discussions.
Senators Roger Wicker and Kevin Cramer presented the proposal to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during an October 9 visit to Kyiv as part of a bipartisan congressional delegation, according to the report.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Zelenskyy indicated that he was prepared to accept such an arrangement, the sources said.
The expanded coverage could give Ukrainian forces reliable satellite connectivity during operations against Russian ballistic missile launchers located deeper behind the border.
That would potentially allow Ukraine to target the systems before they launch missiles rather than relying solely on air defenses to intercept incoming weapons after they are fired.
Zelenskyy has publicly said Ukraine could also consider halting strikes on Russian refineries in return for additional US-made Patriot interceptors. The Starlink proposal would offer a different form of protection by helping Ukrainian forces target the launch platforms themselves.
According to the WSJ, the senators viewed the proposed arrangement as a possible first step toward reviving a stalled diplomatic process.
The discussions come amid growing pressure from Washington for Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil infrastructure. US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on October 11, after which Ukraine temporarily suspended strikes on Russian energy facilities.
Despite Kyiv observing the pause, Ukrainian forces subsequently stopped receiving US early warnings about Russian ballistic missile launches, according to Ukrainian officials. The military version of Starlink, Starshield, was also restricted, complicating frontline operations and middle-strike missions against Russian military targets.
Reuters separately reported that the instruction to restrict Starshield came from the White House, although its sources did not identify who specifically ordered the measure. A senior US official said Trump personally had not issued the order.
Previously, Ukraine lifted restrictions on strikes against Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure after observing a three-day pause requested by Washington, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated.
“The ban has been lifted. We’ve had enough,” Zelenskyy said.

"We have gathered here to expand international cooperation aimed at preserving our shared natural heritage. For millions, water shortages and land degradation have already become an everyday reality. Most concerning is that these processes transcend national borders, undermining sustainable development and threatening global stability.
Environmental agenda, based on a balanced approach and concrete action, must take precedence over political differences. Our shared priority should be international cooperation based on true partnership, impartiality, and, above all, a commitment to achieve practical results," the President said.

12:07:46 UTC
21:07:46 KST

Tokayev highlights Kazakhstan's success in restoring rare animal populations
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Kazakhstan has achieved significant progress in biodiversity conservation, citing the recovery of populations of the saiga antelope, snow leopard, Turan tiger, Przewalski's horse and Caspian seal, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of Akorda.
The President described the revival of the saiga population as one of the country's greatest conservation achievements.
“This ancient animal survived the last Ice Age and remains very essential to the natural balance of our steppes. Today Kazakhstan is home to around 98 percent of the world’s saiga population. In 2003, just 21,000 species remained in our country. By the spring of this year, their numbers had reached an estimated 4.7 million,” Tokayev said.
He also noted encouraging signs in the recovery of the snow leopard, “a proud symbol of our mountain heritage.”
“Around 70 percent of its range in our country are within protected areas. Reliable and sustained protection and systematic scientific monitoring have helped its population grow from critically low levels of 90s last century to nearly 190 animals today. Behind all these recoveries are years of hard and dedicated, determined work by the authorities, scientists and international partners,” he noted.
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev expressed his gratitude to the Russian Federation and its President, as well as the United Nations Development Programme, the World Wildlife Fund, and other international partners, including NGOs, for their assistance in restoring the population of the Turan tiger.
He emphasized that in July this year, a tiger was released into the wild for the first time in 70 years, marking a milestone for Kazakhstan.
The Head of State also noted that efforts are underway, in cooperation with Czech, German and Hungarian partners, to reintroduce the Przewalski’s horse to Kazakhstan.
The President also highlighted the need to protect the Caspian Sea and its unique biodiversity.
“At the recent first Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan, I called for urgent, coordinated action to prevent fatal damage to this fragile ecosystem. The future of Caspian seals causes a particular concern. Its population has fallen from one million to 270,000 over the past century. In Kazakhstan, the Caspian seal has been officially listed as a rare and endangered animal. We urge all five littoral states and international community to increase efforts to protect these species. The tragedy of the Aral Sea is a stark reminder of the devastating cost of reckless exploitation of nature and we must not allow the Caspian Sea to suffer the same fate,” Kassym-Jomart Tokayev emphasized
Earlier, it was reported that Kassym-Jomart Tokayev arrived at the Meridian Expo and Event Center in Yerevan, Armenia, to attend the COP17 Leaders' Summit on Biodiversity.
Addressing the summit, the President called for greater international cooperation to preserve biodiversity and presented the Taza Qazaqstan initiative.

Starvation killed 466 Palestinians since 2024, says Gaza Health Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:05:11 UTC
21:05:11 KST

- More than 1.4M people are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through end of 2026.
- More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition recorded among children under 5
At least 466 Palestinians, including 157 children, have died from malnutrition and starvation since 2024, Gaza's Health Ministry said Friday.
The figures were released on World Food Day, observed annually on Oct. 16.
At least 189 elderly people died of starvation, representing 40.5% of the deaths, it said.
In August 2025, the UN declared famine in Gaza.
More than 1.4 million people are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026, the ministry added.
 
Starvation as a weapon
Israeli authorities have used starvation as a weapon during the genocide in Gaza since October 2023, according to Palestinian government bodies and rights organizations.
Israel tightened restrictions on crossings in March 2025, preventing thousands of aid trucks waiting at border crossings from entering the enclave.
The restrictions followed widespread hunger in northern Gaza caused by the blockade and limits on food and relief supplies, forcing some residents to eat animal feed and wild plants.
In late May 2025, Israel allowed 87 aid trucks to enter Gaza for the first time after 81 days, according to Gaza’s government media office.
Aid later continued to enter on a limited and intermittent basis under strict restrictions until February 2026, when Israel allowed a limited increase in the number of trucks entering the enclave under a ceasefire agreement.
Palestinian officials said the shipments still lacked sufficient quantities of essential food items.
According to Gaza’s government media office, Israel has allowed in only about 34% of the humanitarian aid trucks agreed upon.
 
Malnutrition reaches 'catastrophic levels'
“Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached catastrophic levels that are killing children, the elderly and vulnerable groups,” the Health Ministry said.
More than 1.4 million Palestinians, around 67% of Gaza’s population, are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026.
More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition were recorded among children under 5 from 2024 through August 2026, the ministry added.
Of them, 18% of children were suffering from severe acute malnutrition that threatened their lives, while 12.2% of children were affected by stunting, indicating the impact of food shortages on their development.
The mortality rate among children under 5 rose from 13.6 to 33.4 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2022 and 2025, the ministry said.
It estimated that 74,200 children will need treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027.
 
Pregnant women
Among pregnant women, the ministry said the prevalence of anemia rose to 61% in 2026, compared with 41% before the war.
“Around 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded during the first half of 2026, more than three times the number recorded during the previous six months,” it added.
“One in three pregnancies in Gaza is now classified as high-risk,” the ministry continued.
“The figures show that the health consequences of the food crisis are increasingly affecting mothers and unborn children, in addition to children,” it said.
 
Calls for urgent international action
“The right to food is a fundamental human right that does not cease to exist during war,” the ministry said.
It called on the international community and the UN to take immediate action to ensure the safe, sustained and unrestricted entry of food, therapeutic nutritional supplements and medicines into Gaza.
The ministry urged that children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and the elderly be given priority as the groups most vulnerable to malnutrition.
It also called for support to revive local food production to help curb the worsening humanitarian crisis.
The figures come amid the humanitarian consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, which has caused widespread destruction to infrastructure, health facilities and food production sources.
The war has also damaged farmland, food production facilities and water networks, undermining residents’ ability to meet their basic needs locally.
Repeated displacement, loss of income and soaring prices have further increased families’ dependence on humanitarian aid, while access remains irregular.

Somalia sets date for delayed presidential election

Somalia sets date for delayed presidential election
Somalia has scheduled its presidential election for May 15, 2027, following constitutional changes that extended President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s term by one year, the country’s electoral commission announced on Thursday. The decision comes amid opposition criticism of the amendments adopted earlier this year.
The announcement was made by Abdikarim Ahmed Hassan, chairman of the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission, during an appearance on state television. Elections for both chambers of parliament will take place on April 15, one month before the presidential vote, he said.
The commission also released a timetable for preparations, with voter and political party registration set to begin on November 1, 2026, according to the Somali National News Agency (SONNA).
Mohamud’s presidential term was originally due to expire in May 2026. However, constitutional amendments approved by parliament in March extended the presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years, pushing elections back to 2027. Opposition leaders, including former presidents and prime ministers, rejected the changes and called for elections to be held as originally scheduled.
Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed has challenged the constitutional amendments in the Supreme Court, arguing that they were adopted without proper legal procedures or broad political agreement. He also rejected the new election timetable, warning that it could lead to “parallel elections, political divisions, internal conflict and a threat to Somalia’s statehood,” Somalia Today reported on Thursday.
Somalia last held a presidential election in 2022, when lawmakers elected Hassan Sheikh Mohamud for a second term, defeating Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed. The vote followed months of delays and was conducted through an indirect system in which members of parliament chose the president.
The country also faces continuing security challenges from Al-Shabaab, an armed group affiliated with Al-Qaeda that has fought Somalia’s federal government since 2007. The terrorist group conducts raids, bombings, and targeted assassinations in an effort to destabilize the Somali government and regional security structures, and also establish its own rule based on a hardline interpretation of Sharia law.

Heavy cost for US to return to confrontation with Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

The experience of recent conflicts has demonstrated that possessing advanced weaponry and massive firepower does not necessarily equate to achieving strategic objectives. Factors such as depletion of military stockpiles, damage to military equipment, need to procure replacement ammunition, and Iran’s capacity to restore its defensive capabilities all serve to complicate the White House’s calculations regarding a potential re-engagement in military confrontation with powerful Iran.
In a report citing the financial and military costs of past US strikes against Iran, the British newspaper “The Times” highlights the significant strain this conflict has placed on Washington’s military resources. According to the report, US expenditures have exceeded $43 billion in this war, dozens of American aircraft have sustained damage, and the US stockpiles of interceptor missiles have come under pressure. Regardless of the final assessment of the conflict's military outcomes, these figures indicate that sustaining large-scale operations against Iran requires substantial financial and material resources, the resources that cannot be replaced or replenishment in the short term is impossible.
The significance of this issue becomes even greater when the direct costs of military operations are weighed alongside their strategic consequences. In military calculations, the number of attacks carried out or the volume of ammunition expended is not, in itself, the definitive measure of victory. What truly matters is the ratio between the costs incurred and the objectives intended to be achieved through those expenditures. If a military operation entails the extensive use of ammunition and damage to equipment, yet fails to eliminate the adversary’s capacity to continue their resistance, persisting with the same approach may simply lead to mounting costs with no guarantee that the desired outcome will ever be attained.
Erosion of Military Stockpiles: Washington’s Hidden Challenge
One of the most significant consequences of a military conflict is the strain placed on stockpiles of weapons and ammunition. The extensive use of interceptor missiles to counter threats from missiles and drones, particularly when attacks are sustained, can deplete ready-to-use stockpiles, thereby increasing the need for production and resupply. This issue is of particular importance to the United States. In addition to its military commitments in West Asia, Washington must also ensure its forces remain prepared to address potential crises in other parts of the world.
Replenishing arms stockpiles is not merely a matter of securing funding. The production of certain advanced systems and the ammunition they utilize requires complex supply chains, specialized raw materials, and specialized industrial capacity. However, even if new budget allocations are made, rapidly replacing expended stocks is not necessarily feasible. The higher the rate of ammunition consumption in a conflict, the greater pressure placed on production schedules, the prioritization of arms deliveries, and the allocation of resources toward other military missions.
Under such circumstances, Washington’s decision to launch a new round of strikes is not limited merely to an assessment of operational capability; rather, it must also account for the opportunity cost of expending munitions and the subsequent impact on US military readiness. In other words, every missile used in an operation must be evaluated within the context of the United States’ broader defense requirements.
Iran’s Capacity for Recovery and Difficulty of Achieving a Definitive Outcome
On the other side of this equation lies Iran’s capacity to maintain and restore its defensive capabilities. In a report, “The Times” notes that, despite military attacks and pressures, Iran has managed to recover a portion of its missile and drone capabilities. This is significant from the perspective of military calculations, as the effectiveness of an offensive operation depends, to a large extent, on the degree of its lasting impact on the adversary’s capabilities.
If military strikes fail to permanently dismantle a nation’s defensive capacity, inflicting damage at a specific point in time does not necessarily equate to eliminating that nation’s ability to continue its resistance. The potential to repair equipment, restore certain operational capabilities, and maintain the capacity to produce or deploy weaponry can alter the conflict’s equation over time. In such a scenario, the aggressor may be compelled to repeatedly expend further munitions and equipment to sustain military pressure—all while the ultimate outcome of this process remains uncertain. The strategic implication is clear: as long as the adversary retains the ability to continue resisting, one cannot conclude that their defensive capacity has been exhausted based solely on the volume of attacks carried out.
Why could a renewed attack be more costly?
The United States re-engaging in a confrontation with Iran could trigger a repeat of that same costly cycle. New operations would require ammunition, logistics equipment, fuel supplies, the movement of troops, and the protection of military bases and facilities. Should equipment sustain damage or the scope of the conflict expand, costs would rise accordingly. Furthermore, a prolonged crisis could impact energy markets and economic expectations, extending the repercussions well beyond the military battlefield.
On the other hand, the United States must also consider the possibility of a prolonged conflict and the need to remain prepared for unforeseen scenarios. Military operations might begin with limited objectives, but reciprocal responses and shifting conditions could expand their scope. Under such circumstances, the final cost will not necessarily align with initial estimates.
The fundamental question for the White House is whether the costs of a new confrontation would yield commensurate gains. If the objective is to durably weaken Iran’s defensive capabilities, the persistence of its missile and drone capacities could make achieving this goal more difficult. Furthermore, if the aim is to compel Tehran to accede to Washington’s demands, it remains to be seen whether military pressure would truly lead to such an outcome, or if it would merely generate additional costs.
The White House’s Strategic Calculus Test
A report by “The Times” once again draws attention to the gap between military superiority and the achievement of strategic outcomes. Possessing extensive military capabilities enables the infliction of damage, but it does not, in itself, guarantee that the adversary will cease resistance or that the aggressor’s political objectives will be realized. When assessing a conflict, one must simultaneously consider the costs incurred, the resilience of the parties involved, and the extent to which objectives have been achieved.
For Washington, returning to a confrontation with Iran—without regard for the lessons of past costs—means re-entering a path with a predetermined outcome. The strain on U.S. military stockpiles, combined with Iran’s ability to restore parts of its defensive capabilities, suggests that repeating such attacks will not necessarily shift the equation in favor of the aggressor.
Ultimately, the primary challenge for the United States is not merely the capacity to launch a new operation, but the ability to achieve a sustainable outcome at a manageable cost. If previous strikes failed to realize Washington’s intended objectives, any decision to follow the same path requires a clear answer to the question: what will be different this time? Absent such an answer, a renewed attack risks becoming less of a solution to the crisis and more the beginning of another phase of resource depletion and escalating strategic costs for the United States.

"You can say anything, and you can even compare the prime minister to Shabbetai Zevi. That sounds absurd to me," he added.
Bismuth said Netanyahu supporters were being subjected to offensive comparisons involving their political leader, arguing that the rhetoric reflected hostility toward the prime minister rather than legitimate criticism.
"People who vote for Netanyahu hear their leader being compared to someone whose name is followed by the expression 'may the name of the wicked rot,'" he said, referring to a traditional Hebrew condemnation. "A false messiah is someone who joins the 'Anyone but Bibi' camp."
Bismuth defends Netanyahu amid Egyptian intelligence warning controversy
The interview came amid renewed scrutiny of reports that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel had traveled to Israel shortly before Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack.
Netanyahu previously denied meeting or speaking with Kamel in the months leading up to the attack, but confirmed this week that an Egyptian aircraft had landed in Israel in September 2023. He maintained that he did not know whom Kamel had met, if the intelligence official had visited.
Asked why Netanyahu had acknowledged the aircraft's arrival only after previously rejecting reports surrounding the alleged visit, Bismuth defended the prime minister's handling of sensitive intelligence matters.
"Prime Minister Netanyahu is a very responsible person," Bismuth said. "Believe me, as chairman of the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, who is exposed to certain information, I know he does not disclose material that could benefit him and support his arguments."
He argued that the public debate had been dominated by a politically motivated effort to discredit Netanyahu, including through interviews with former senior security officials.
"What does this shallow campaign do from morning until night?" he asked. "It searches for arguments in interviews with former officials, through stories about Egypt and the Emirates that never happened."
The circumstances surrounding the Egyptian aircraft's arrival and the reported warnings remain disputed. While several international media reports have alleged that Egyptian officials sought to alert Israel to a possible escalation before October 7, Netanyahu has denied receiving such a warning directly from Kamel.
Bismuth condemns publication of Yonatan Urich's private WhatsApp messages
Bismuth also criticized the publication of private correspondence attributed to Yonatan Urich, a senior Netanyahu adviser whose communications have come under scrutiny amid the ongoing political controversies surrounding the prime minister's office.
"My conclusion is that when people want Netanyahu's head, they try to attack him through everyone close to him," Bismuth said.
"The public knows this, and people are already tired of it."
Bismuth alleged that the messages had been obtained through unauthorized access to Urich's WhatsApp account and claimed that some of the published correspondence had been altered. Those allegations have not been independently established.
"Whoever hacked Yonatan Urich's WhatsApp and published private correspondence, while adding and changing things, will pay the price," he said. "The same will happen to anyone who publishes it or cooperates."
He also accused journalists who reported on the messages of celebrating what he described as a criminal violation of an individual's privacy.
"Media figures who celebrate a criminal offense committed against someone should be ashamed of themselves," Bismuth said.
He recalled previous cases involving unauthorized access to mobile phones, including an alleged incident involving former prime minister Naftali Bennett, and suggested that similar privacy concerns had not received sufficient attention.
"Yonatan Urich did not harm Israel's security. I have absolutely no doubt about that," Bismuth said.
"Israel, under Netanyahu, attacked in Qatar, so perhaps it's time to stop with this nonsense?"
Urich has also publicly alleged that his phone was hacked and has threatened legal action against those responsible for distributing the correspondence. The allegations about the messages' authenticity and the circumstances of their release remain contested.
Likud MK rejects questions over loyalty to Netanyahu and party ranking
During the interview, Bismuth was also asked why he continued to defend Netanyahu so strongly despite being placed 21st on the Likud electoral list, after previously securing a higher position in the party's internal rankings.
Bismuth rejected suggestions that the placement had affected his relationship with the prime minister, saying he was satisfied with the party's reserved positions and the broader composition of its list.

Bismuth insisted that his support for Netanyahu was based on his political preference rather than considerations about his own parliamentary position.
"This has nothing to do with me. A seat in the Knesset is a seat you hold temporarily. Netanyahu is the prime minister I want."

‘Trying to dominate’: In Cyprus, some fear Israel’s growing influence
Israel now reaches into Cyprus’s water, gas, health and defence and a number of Cypriots fear their island is losing control.
Nicosia and Limassol, Cyprus – Heavily bearded and wearing a loose shirt, Christos Achniotis speaks about the history and demographics of Cyprus and runs off dates from memory.
He was 16 when Turkish troops landed in Cyprus in mid-1974. At one point, Limassol has long had a large Russian community, he said, but that revolved around property investments.
Now, he believes there is pressure from Israel, which he says is “trying to dominate as much as possible, land-wise, company-wise”, as well as politically and militarily.
Israel’s reach in Cyprus now runs through the state’s most vital systems.
Mekorot, Israel’s state water company, helps supply the island’s water. Israel Aerospace Industries, a state-owned arms maker, is supplying its new air defences. And Israeli firms run a growing hospital network and hold a stake in the country’s largest gasfield.
Israel’s economy is about 15 times Cyprus’s, according to the World Bank, and Israel’s military spending is about 73 times that of Cyprus.
Cyprus’s government presents the ties as a security alliance against Turkiye, but several Cypriots interviewed by Al Jazeera said they feared their country is handing another state control of systems it cannot live without.
Israel is “a small area with big money and a big military”. Cyprus is strategically placed in the Mediterranean and, just a 35-minute flight away, is an attractive piece of land, said Achniotis.
‘Our resources’
Cyprus gets about 80 percent of its drinking water from the sea.
With its dams just 21 percent full in March, desalination plants supply most of what comes out of its taps, according to the Water Development Department.
Agriculture Minister Maria Panayiotou said in June that desalination would cover almost all domestic demand by next year.
Mekorot has joint ventures with Cypriot firm Netcom that run two of the island’s five permanent plants, at Larnaca and Episkopi, according to the Water Development Department. In August, Mekorot expanded its cooperation with Cyprus, signing a memorandum with the Nicosia District Water Board to help manage water and sewerage in the capital.
For Danae Laou, who works in hospitality in Limassol, the water deals crossed a line.
“It’s terrifying to see, but at the same time, we have no power,” she said.
Today’s occupation of Palestine is in part facilitated by control of vital resources. “I can see the same thing happening here”, she said.
Palestinians know Mekorot well.
In the occupied West Bank, the company is on the United Nations list of businesses linked to illegal Israeli settlements.
Najla Abdellatif Vallander, a Swedish-Palestinian environmental advocate who founded Zero Waste Palestine, has tracked Mekorot’s work in Palestine and abroad and told Al Jazeera that its operations in the West Bank are akin to “water theft”, diverting Palestinian sources to illegal Israeli settlements.
“Israeli settlers are able to enjoy almost unlimited amounts of water while Palestinians are not allowed to use their own water sources,” she said.
Palestinians “have to buy back their own water sources from Mekorot”, and are mostly barred from digging their own wells. “This is water apartheid,” she said.
At the time of publishing, Mekorot had not responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
‘Leverage’
Israel’s economic footprint has grown fast.
Investors in Israel held 5.1 billion euros ($5.7bn) of investment in Cyprus at the end of 2024, more than six times what they held in 2017, according to the Central Bank of Cyprus.
The true figure may be higher as the data excludes Israelis living in Cyprus or elsewhere, and may miss money routed through companies whose owners are hard to trace.
The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange is also weighing a bid for the Cyprus Stock Exchange, which the government is privatising, Cyprus Mail and the Israeli business daily Globes reported this month.
The Cypriot exchange’s European Union licence would give Israel “greater access to the Eurozone market”, a source close to Cyprus’s Ministry of Finance told the Cyprus Mail.
Health is the newest.
Hadassah Medical Centre Limassol, the Israeli hospital group’s first centre in Europe, began seeing patients in July and was formally opened on Thursday.
Its opening was ratified in Israel by Hadassah’s governing bodies, including the Hadassah Women’s Zionist Organization of America.
Offshore, Israel’s NewMed Energy owns 30 percent of the Aphrodite gasfield, according to its filings to the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.
The two governments are also negotiating over the field, which Israel says extends into its waters.
‘Create a problem’
Israel has also been flexing its military muscle.
Israeli special forces have trained in Cyprus’s Troodos mountains, whose terrain resembles southern Lebanon, according to Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies.
In 2022, the two armies held their largest joint exercise yet, simulating a war with Hezbollah, The Jerusalem Post reported.
Cyprus is replacing its Russian-made air defences with the Barak MX, built by Israel Aerospace Industries, with deliveries beginning in late 2024.
Israel presents itself as a guardian against Turkiye.
Following a coup in Cyprus backed by Greece’s military government in July 1974, Turkiye invaded the island and has occupied its northern part ever since. Only Turkiye and its Turkish Cypriot leadership recognise Northern Cyprus.
In late December 2025, Israeli and Cypriot military officials signed a 2026 cooperation plan covering joint exercises, training, and “strategic military dialogue”, the Israeli military said.
On Tuesday, a pro-Israel advocacy group, the Israel Allies Foundation (IAF), launched a caucus of six Cypriot lawmakers from three parties in Nicosia. Its president, Josh Reinstein, told reporters after the group’s meeting with the Cypriot president at the presidential palace on Wednesday that Turkiye is a “common adversary”, according to the Cyprus Mail.
The opposition party AKEL called it “extremely provocative”, asking what credibility Cyprus has in demanding pressure on Turkiye while backing “another occupying and settler state”, the Cyprus Mail reported.
Last month, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told the United Nations General Assembly that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan “illegally occupies northern Cyprus, an EU member”.
Netanyahu “knows what he’s doing”, said Ioanna Lamprou, a writer in Limassol.
Cypriots who feel the world has forgotten the occupation, she said, will “become more sympathetic to Israel and to Netanyahu’s government because of this”, but they “don’t understand that what’s happening in the West Bank is illegal occupation as well”.
Laou understands the government’s reasoning; from its perspective, she said, “Cyprus can’t protect itself from anything.”
Ceylan Hassan, a Turkish Cypriot researcher and environmental social scientist, said the British had won over Cypriots the same way, by promising to keep them safe from a bigger threat.
Israel is doing “the whole colonial thing of let’s create a problem and then be the solution to it and never let it go”.
‘Athens or Crete’
In 1902, Theodore Herzl, the founder of political Zionism, presented a pamphlet to a British Parliamentary Committee with the idea of establishing a Jewish homeland in Cyprus. He offered a pamphlet with the title: The problem of Jewish immigration to England and the United States solved by furthering the Jewish Colonisation of Cyprus.
Britain’s colonial secretary refused, saying Greeks and Muslims lived there, according to Herzl’s diary.
Herzl mused, “The Greeks will gladly sell their lands at a good price and migrate to Athens or Crete.”
Achniotis has thought about that history more since the genocidal war on Gaza began.
Watching what is happening to Palestinians, he said, “I think it can happen to anyone.”
As the onslaught happened so easily, with the acceptance of the US and European governments, “you feel a kind of insecurity,” he said. “Why are they going to respect you?”

Norwegian teen sentenced to 20 years in prison for plotting murder in UK for Iran-linked gang
A Norwegian teenager convicted of traveling to Britain to carry out a contract killing on behalf of an international crime gang linked to Iran was sentenced Friday to 20 years in prison.
Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was found guilty in July of conspiracy to murder for agreeing to shoot an unknown target for 25,000 euros (21,500 pounds) last year. He was arrested at a hotel in Huddersfield in northern England with two guns and ammunition two days after arriving in the UK.
The target is not known.
Natland, who was working part time at a pizza restaurant at the time of his arrest, was recruited by a Swedish organised crime group known as the Foxtrot Network while he was playing a game online. The group has links to the Iranian government, according to counterterrorism officers from London’s Metropolitan Police.
Natland admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition but claimed he did not want to go through with the plan.
"You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself," Justice Bobbie Cheema-Grubb said at his sentencing hearing at Woolwich Crown Court in southeast London. "Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to."
Natland was hired by a 17-year-old known as "Generalen." A court in Norway last year convicted the teenager of attempting to “contribute to murder” and sentenced him to 14 years in custody. A 16-year-old is awaiting trial in Norway for his role in the conspiracy.
The UK government last year announced sanctions against Foxtrot Network and its leader "due to their involvement in violence against Jewish and Israeli targets in Europe on behalf of the Iranian regime."
The sanctions include an asset freeze that bars UK businesses from handling funds or other economic assets controlled by the organization.

IRCS, ICRC hold workshops to strengthen readiness for CBRN incidents
TEHRAN – The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) and the International Red Cross and Red Crescent (ICRC) have held the second and third training courses on Application of Personal Protective Equipment during Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) incidents.
The first round of the course was held in Tehran from June 7 to 21. The second and third courses were held from October 4-8 and 11-15, separately. The courses aimed to improve preparedness and the operational capacity of relief teams and has been attended by a total number of 150 members of rapid response teams from different provinces in the country, ICRC website announced in a press release on October 15.
During the closing ceremony, the attendees and instructors reviewed achievements, strengths, and ground for improvement. Stressing the need to repeat the exercises, organize the course in provincial levels, and to provide complementary equipment required, the attendees emphasized that the experience was different from previous maneuvers.
The instructors also expressed gratitude for the participants’ active involvement, reiterating their positive performance during practical simulation exercises in applying the learning points and following the decontamination process suited to each type of contamination.
Speaking on the sidelines of the ceremony, the head of ICRC’s Tehran Delegation, Marisela Silva Chau, highlighted the close collaboration between ICRC and the Iranian Red Crescent Society, citing the workshop a concrete example, putting together IRCS’ operational experience and ICRC’s academic expertise and technical, equipment support. She reiterated the ICRC’s readiness to throw support behind similar courses to be held at a provincial level, while stressing the importance of transferring learnings to operational teams and their application in daily activities.
The IRCS Deputy Director for Education, Research and Technology, Rouzbeh Rajaei, also stressed continued training, teacher training, and planning for similar course to be held for female participants, noting the participation of experts from different scientific institutions and centers.
 
The continued collaboration and transfer of knowledge and experience to operational teams is an important step in strengthening the incident preparedness and response capacity.
The first training course targeted basic health care unit (BHCU) team leaders from five high-risk provinces, namely Tehran, Qom, Markazi, Isfahan, and Bushehr, as well as passive defense trainers.
ICRC hails IRCS efforts, bravery during war
In April, the president of the ICRC, Mirjana Spoljaric Egger, commended the efforts, bravery, and accomplishments of the IRCS during the recent imposed war by the United States and the Zionist regime of Israel on Iran.
“I admire the courage and commitment of the Iranian Red Crescent Society aid workers to provide humanitarian relief to people affected by the recent war. Your efforts were both important and outstanding,” Mehr news agency quoted Spoljaric Egger as saying.

Highlighting the importance of respecting international humanitarian law (IHL), the official noted that the IHL is frequently violated in the region; the war impacts on civilians, particularly children, are unacceptable. There is no justified reason for depriving children of their rights.
The measures that lead to the breach of IHL, and the attacks that target civilians and humanitarian workers, have to be stopped and reversed, she added.
The official described the current situation as dangerous, saying that “We, and the Iranian Red Crescent Society’s staff, should use our capacity to reduce tensions, which is essential for the protection of civilians and children.
That is why we are here, staying here; we fulfil our responsibility inside and outside the country to change the situation, and offer assistance in any way that is possible.”
The IRCS is a leading, strong national society, equipped with good facilities. The ICRC representative in Iran will help meet the country’s medical needs to set up hospitals and facilitate the import of supplies that are not allowed under sanctions, she further noted.
The official went on to thank the head of the IRCS for his continuous follow-up on the issues and for providing the ICRC with information and reports.
Vincent Cassard, the representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), has highlighted the need to expand collaborations with the Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) in 2026.
In December 2025, Cassard met with Razieh Alishvandi, the director of the Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) for international affairs, lauding the IRCS for its efforts and enumerated joint activities, such as holding a conference on rehabilitation, establishing a rehabilitation secretariat by the IRCS, and co-hosting a webinar on ‘Early Rehabilitation in Conflicts and Disasters’, with the IRCS playing a key role in organizing the event.
Cassard went on to say that the ICRC office in Tehran has secured the budget to implement plans, such as rehabilitation services to vulnerable groups, particularly refugees. He added that the second conference on rehabilitation is planned to be held in the second quarter of 2026.
