A protest calling for the resignation of Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko is under way outside Kyiv City State Administration building in the centre of the capital.
According to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, several hundred participants had gathered outside the administration building at 36 Khreshchatyk Street as of 12:20. The rally began with speeches by activists and organisers.
The protesters are holding cardboard signs reading "Klitschko, resign," "Glass bus stops won't protect us from missiles and drones," "It's Time," "Mayor or Looter," "Kyiv Isn't Ready Even for Autumn," "Klitschko, It's Time for You to Go," "Who to Call When the Mayor Steals Money," "Schrödinger's Mayor – Klitschko exists separately from his powers," "Russia strikes, and you just add to it," and others.
The protesters are also chanting "Resign!"
Passing cars occasionally honk in support of the protesters.
At the same time, a small number of participants supporting the current mayor and opposing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are also present outside Kyiv City State Administration building. They are holding signs reading "Klitschko – Our Mayor" and "Hands Off Klitschko." Police asked them to move away from the main protest, but they refused.
Seven police minibuses and five patrol cars are parked near Kyiv City State Administration building. More than three dozen officers from the National Police, Patrol Police and Dialogue Police are present at the rally site, while others remain in patrol vehicles.
In addition, representatives of the OZON civil society organisation and the Red Cross Society are monitoring the protest.
"Klitschko has had the authority and resources for all 12 years. He must bear political responsibility and step down from office," a statement issued by the rally organisers the previous day said.
In particular, the statement points to what the protesters describe as systemic, long-standing problems in city governance, including the city's lack of preparedness for the challenges of war, such as insufficient mobile and stationary shelters, a lack of alternative water, heating and sewage systems, and failures to address the consequences of destruction and assist those affected. It also cites allegations of corruption involving the mayor's team, favouring developers' interests, the lack of decisions to protect valuable historic buildings, deterioration of the public transport system, disregard for petitions and public opinion among city residents, and other problems.
The organisers said populist strategies were being developed without any intention of implementing them, decisions were being postponed for years and responsibility was constantly being shifted. They said the division of powers between the city authorities and district administrations could not serve as an excuse for the lack of results.
According to the protest organisers, the mayor could resign voluntarily, lose office as a result of a court ruling or an election, transfer his powers to a military administration, or leave office as a result of voluntary mobilisation.
The organisers' demands were signed, among others, by the All-Ukrainian Association Automaidan, the Green Teremky Initiative, the Legal Platform Kyiv Ecological and Cultural Center NGO, the March for Kyiv Association, the Passengers of Kyiv NGO, the Right to the City NGO, the Repair Together NGO, the Seven-Tiered Mountain Youth Center, the Kyiv Heritage NGO and the Spalah! NGO.
Ahead of the event, the UDAR Vitali Klitschko faction in Kyiv City Council, citing the security situation, called on Kyiv residents to refrain from mass gatherings on Saturday, October 17.
The faction said those calling on people to gather for protests should consider who would bear responsibility if a Russian attack occurred during the gathering and people were harmed. It said destabilising the situation in the capital, which Russia was attacking and seeking to deprive of electricity, heat and water, would only benefit the enemy. It added that responsibility, unity and joint efforts were needed to ensure Kyiv's resilience.
In response, the rally organisers published instructions on what participants should do in the event of an air raid alert.
The organisers said people with access to a map showing enemy aerial targets would be present at the rally and would be able to provide additional warnings about potential threats to the city centre. In the event of a threat, the rally would be suspended and participants would be asked to take shelter. They identified the TSUM shopping centre car park, Khreshchatyk and Teatralna metro stations, as well as nearby underground passages if there was little time, as the nearest shelters.
As previously reported, Vitali Klitschko, who was serving as Kyiv mayor at the time, won the first round of the October 2020 local election with 50.9% of the vote. Klitschko was first elected mayor of the capital in a special election in May 2014.
Under the Law of Ukraine On Local Self-Government, a mayor's powers may be terminated early in the event of a personal resignation; loss of Ukrainian citizenship; a conviction becoming final; a final court ruling holding the mayor liable for a corruption-related offence or declaring assets to be of unjustified origin; recall through a popular initiative; a court ruling declaring the mayor legally incapacitated, missing or presumed dead; or the mayor's death.
The mayor's powers may also be terminated early if the mayor violates the Constitution or laws of Ukraine or the rights and freedoms of citizens, or fails to exercise the powers granted to the office, based on a local referendum or a decision by the relevant council adopted by secret ballot with at least two-thirds of council members voting in favour. Early termination is also possible in cases provided for by the laws of Ukraine On Military-Civilian Administrations and On the Legal Regime of Martial Law.

Iran women’s wheelchair basketball suffer loss against Thailand

Despite showing improved performance in the second quarter, Iran were unable to overcome Thailand, who maintained control throughout the contest to secure a convincing victory.

Thailand then closed out the game strongly, taking the final quarter 17–7 to seal a 64–33 victory.

Iran will look to bounce back when they face Cambodia on Monday in their next group-stage fixture, aiming to deliver a stronger performance and secure a better result.

Russian Ryazan oil refinery halts operations of one main unit after drone attack, Reuters reports
Russia's Ryazan oil refinery suspended operations at one of its main crude distillation units, CDU-6, following a drone attack on Oct. 15, Reuters reported a day later, citing unnamed industry sources.
The news comes amid a dispute between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil and energy infrastructure.
U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Ukraine to halt the attacks, reportedly threatening to cut intelligence sharing and weapons support, while blaming the strikes for rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by energy experts.
After Trump unilaterally announced an "energy ceasefire" between Moscow and Kyiv on Oct. 11, Ukraine initially paused refinery strikes. However, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 15 that Kyiv had lifted the pause due to Moscow's continued attacks against Ukraine's energy grid.
The same unit of the Ryazan oil refinery had already been shut down following a drone strike in September. The refinery's three other primary crude distillation units — CDU-1, CDU-3, and CDU-4 — reportedly continue to operate.
The oil refinery has been targeted repeatedly in recent months. It was struck on Sept. 6 and May 15, with repairs after the May attack lasting until around mid-July. A further attack on July 29 halted operations for several weeks.
Since Zelensky announced the resumption of strikes earlier this week, Kyiv has not reported any new attacks on Russian oil refineries or confirmed reports of such strikes.
Throughout the week, Moscow continued its near-constant drone attacks on Ukraine and launched a large-scale ballistic missile attack on Kyiv overnight on Oct. 13–14, damaging a residential neighborhood and targeting several energy facilities.
On Oct. 16, Russia launched one of its largest attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 key energy facilities across the country, Zelensky said. The attack came as Trump waived sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.

Egypt's Sisi says he will step down in 2030, rules out another term
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:17:00 UTC
19:17:00 KST

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Saturday that he would leave office when his current term ends in 2030, ruling out any further constitutional amendments to extend his rule as he also pledged to defend Saudi Arabia’s security and sovereignty if requested.
“The year 2030 will mark the end of my presidential term. This matter is completely settled,” Sisi said during a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital, according to state-run Al-Ahram newspaper.
“I said that the Egyptian constitution would not be touched,” he added. “This is an entirely settled matter and will not be discussed.”
The 71-year-old president, a former army general who has led Egypt since 2014, is serving a six-year term after winning re-election in December 2023. Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four years to six and allowed Sisi to seek an additional term, enabling him to remain in office until 2030.
The amendments reshaped Egypt’s presidential limits and drew criticism from opponents who warned they would consolidate power in the hands of the president.
Sisi came to power in 2013 after the military ousted Mohamed Morsi, Egypt’s first democratically elected president, following mass protests against his rule. Sisi subsequently won the presidency in 2014 and has maintained a tight grip on the country’s political system.
His latest remarks appeared aimed at ending speculation about whether he might seek another constitutional change to remain in power beyond his current mandate.
Sisi also spoke about the role of the military and the need to prepare a new generation of leaders, linking the armed forces to the protection of Egypt’s constitutional order and state institutions.
He said the constitution defines the military’s responsibility to safeguard democracy, the constitutional framework and the fundamental pillars of the state.
“I will not leave the Egyptian state until it is brimming with its own people capable of shouldering responsibility,” Sisi said, referring to efforts to prepare younger generations to take on leadership roles through the Egyptian Military Academy.
The comments did not provide further details about how the transition to new leadership would be managed or what role Sisi might play after leaving office.
Sisi also declared that Egypt was prepared to take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect the kingdom’s security and sovereignty, underscoring Cairo’s stated commitment to the defense of its Gulf partners.
“We will take any measure to protect Saudi Arabia,” he said, adding that he would call on parliament to convene an emergency session to authorize such action if Riyadh requested it.
“We stand firmly to protect and defend the territories of our brothers in the Gulf,” he added.
Sisi did not specify what measures Egypt might take or identify a particular threat that would prompt such a response.

The Vatican had also released on Friday pictures of the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small chapel in Gemelli Hospital.
The pope was scheduled to travel to South America next month, but his ability to make the trip has been in question since his diagnosis. However, on Friday the Vatican published the names of journalists accredited to fly on the papal plane to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, signalling that the trip appeared to be going ahead.

Solar power booms in Philippines as war on Iran spikes energy costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:12:01 UTC
19:12:01 KST

Solar power booms in Philippines as war on Iran spikes energy costs
With Southeast Asia’s largest electricity bills rising even higher, Filipinos invest in rooftop panels.
Manila, Philippines – Keith Cantera and his family have been thinking about having their own solar power grid at home for years. But spending up to $5,000 for solar panels was nothing to scoff at, so they put the idea on the back burner.
It all changed this year when the United States-Israel war on Iran rattled global energy markets and sent electricity prices soaring. From paying a monthly bill of about $150 before the war began in late February, Cantera said his family went to forking out as much as $220.
Eight months later, they are having solar panels installed on their rooftop.
“The cost is about the same as paying our electric bills for three or four years based on the current rate,” Cantera said. “But in the fifth year, we’ll have recovered our investment, and electricity will essentially be free.”
Cantera is one of a growing number of Filipino homeowners turning to solar power in a country that had Southeast Asia’s highest electricity costs even before the war. They were comparable only to Singapore, where the average income is more than 10 times higher.
A report by the energy think tank Ember estimated that rooftop panels had nearly doubled in the Philippines since early 2025.
And in the first months of the war from March to May, the rush for solar power led to $407m in panel imports, according to government trade data from China, where most panels are manufactured. The Philippines became the biggest single overseas market for that period. Only the Netherlands bought more, but it redistributes them to the rest of Europe.
Lexus Grepo, CEO of the solar power supplier Solarmaxx, can attest to the boom.
“There is a 30-day wait because solar panel shipments can’t keep up,” Grepo said. “In March, we had 40 projects, which was almost triple our monthly clientele. Since then, we have been setting up 25 to 30 systems a month.”
Grepo does not expect demand to slow down even if tensions in the Middle East ease and shipping routes for energy supplies reopen.
“I think people now realise that the world is an unpredictable place, so they have to be ready for any eventuality. Filipinos now see that they don’t necessarily have to be at the mercy of the global energy market.”
The Philippines, one of the few countries in the region where electricity is not subsidised, relies on imported coal and gas for more than 70 percent of its power mix. The value of its currency, the peso, which has slid to a record low of more than 63 to the US dollar, is making these imports even costlier.
In late March, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr declared a national energy emergency in response to the war and what he described as the “imminent danger” posed to the national energy supply. Still, electricity rates have continued to increase.
The shift to solar is also partly driven by anger at electric companies that have come under scrutiny for charging customers for so-called system losses, which include illegal connections.
Cantera said learning about having to pay for someone else’s electricity consumption was the last straw.
“Who would agree to paying for something that you did not use? It’s not like the money we spend for electricity just fell from heaven,” he added.
But while the soaring demand is real, the upfront cost of a solar power system is still too high for most Filipinos. The government in March launched a new initiative offering loans for residential rooftop installations, but these are available only to public sector workers.
What officials hope can bring power rates down for the majority of people are the dozens of renewable energy projects in the pipeline, including a 3,500-hectare (8,650-acre) solar farm north of the capital, Manila, that is projected to be the largest in the world. When fully operational, the project is expected to generate 850 megawatts of electricity for 2.4 million households.
But some consumers said such projects could take years to complete, leaving them with ballooning electricity bills unless they take action themselves.
“It’s just so unpredictable nowadays. You have the impending El Nino weather pattern. There’s still war, the continuing fuel price hikes and so much more,” Cantera said. “So why not utilise a natural resource?”

====================================================================================================

Zest is a Key Ingredient to Good Living
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Approaching life with positive expectations, a get-up-and-go attitude, and eagerness is related to many good things in life. This individual asset is often referred to as zest, and it can be purposefully developed to assist us in managing daily stressors as well as creating meaningful lives.
True zest is not due to hyperarousal or too much caffeine. It is a cultivated cheerfulness and joy. When we are stressed or not feeling well, it’s hard to avoid doing things halfway or halfheartedly. But there are ways we can increase zest even when it seems like the deck is stacked against us, the world is filled with conflict, and our social media feeds are thick with chaos and gloom.
Psychologists Christopher Peterson and Martin Seligman pioneered the field of positive psychology, the scientific study of human flourishing. One of the highlights of their initiatives was published in 2004, Character Strengths and Virtues, a groundbreaking text on the 24 universal character strengths. Zest is one of the 24 strengths.
When you cultivate zest, you’ll want to fully engage in life and not just view it from the sidelines, look forward to each day, and wake to anticipation over the day’s possibilities. Zest has also been referred to as vitality, exuberance, and joie de vivre, the French phrase for the joy of living.
In an analysis of data from 130 studies involving more than 275,000 people around the globe, most character strengths were associated with greater mental health. But zest was one of just two strengths (the other is hope) that had the strongest relationship to mental well-being across countries and age groups. Zest contributes to life satisfaction among children, adolescents, and adults. In addition, in a study of nearly 10,000 employed adults, those who scored high on zest had higher work satisfaction and were more likely to view work as a calling. People who score high on measures of zest are also more likely to view their lives as meaningful.
I reached out to Ryan Niemiec, a psychologist and author of several books, including The Power of Character Strengths and Character Strengths Interventions: A Field Guide for Practitioners. Niemiec is the chief science and education officer at the VIA Institute on Character, a non-profit focused on the science and practice of character strengths. I asked him about the most effective ways people can increase zest in their own lives.
“In terms of boosting zest, I turn straight to behavioral activation, one of the most proven strategies for depression,” Niemiec said. “In practical terms, this means to take action in some way to boost oneself—to take that one step forward in lifting one’s energy.” He encouraged people to engage every day in one healthy pleasure, one form of physical activity, and one action that makes you feel like you accomplished something.
Some of us seem to naturally have this irresistible aliveness, often invigorating those around us. Others work hard to cultivate zest. Research supports the idea that we are never too old to change. And we can learn how to cultivate zest.
We can learn to savor pleasures, set good intentions, and try to view life as an adventure. Other intentional ways to potentially lift our spirits include taking a brisk 10-minute walk every morning, doing cardiovascular or strength-building challenges, practicing Reiki or yoga, laughing with friends, and engaging in stimulating tasks and work. The VIA Institute on Character has activities, workbooks, videos, webinars, and courses—some of them free—on improving all the character strengths, including zest.
To be sure, practicing a zest for life can be harder for those who have physical illness and pain and those who engage in unhealthy lifestyle behaviors. And those striving for zest under these circumstances may benefit from assistance from a mental health professional like a psychologist, a physical health provider like a physician, or a personal trainer or fitness instructor.
For some of us, being hard on ourselves is second nature. We expect our mental health to stretch under strain. Rather than exclusively focusing on what’s wrong with our mental health, one approach is to develop skills, traits, and perspectives that can help us. Acquiring zest is a worthwhile investment and may help us not only through challenging times, but also help us to see beauty and soar in our lives and workplaces.

Pope Leo to leave hospital on Oct 17, four days after lung cancer surgery
ROME – Pope Leo is expected to leave hospital in the afternoon on Oct 17 following surgery for lung cancer, the Vatican said, after blood tests and chest imaging found him fit to return home four days after his operation.
The 71-year-old pontiff, who has not been seen in public since a procedure on Oct 13 to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, will also hold his first public engagement since surgery on Oct 18. He will lead weekly prayers with pilgrims in St Peter’s Square at noon.
Leo has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
The diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and raised questions about the future shape of his papacy as he deals with the illness.
The Pope’s doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications.
They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.
The Vatican signalled on Oct 16 that Leo, known for following a busy schedule, intended to keep up his commitments, as some cardinals began to publicly express concern about the Pope’s health.
It said work on his Nov 6 to Nov 17 visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, one of the most intense arranged for a pope in decades, was “going forward”.
It released a list of journalists accredited to travel with Leo and cover the trip.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican Secretary of State, said on Oct 16 that Leo may need to adjust the pace of his schedule going forward “according to the condition of his health”. It is unusual for a cardinal to say openly that a pope might need to modify his routine.
The Vatican on Oct 16 released the first images of the Pope since his surgery, showing him celebrating Mass and standing unaided. REUTERS

Gaza shelters deteriorate after repeated displacement as winter approaches: IOM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:54:15 UTC
18:54:15 KST

Repeated displacement during three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has left shelters across the enclave increasingly deteriorated, while restrictions and funding shortages are hampering preparations for winter, a senior UN migration official said late on Friday.
Karl Baker, regional crisis coordinator for the Gaza response at the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), said some Palestinians have been displaced as many as eight times, damaging or destroying tents and other temporary shelters each time families are forced to move.
“When they move, all those goods that they currently have or did have either get destroyed, or they have to seek new shelter,” Baker told UN News.
Even basic materials such as tarpaulins need to be replaced roughly every six months, but humanitarian agencies have been unable to bring replacements into Gaza at the required scale, he said.
Baker said agencies now need to move beyond temporary solutions toward more durable transitional shelters.
Materials needed for stronger roofing, concrete floors, and more substantial walls, however, are affected by Israel’s “dual-use” restrictions over security concerns.
“After three years of war, we do need to improve the level of shelter which is inside, and move further away from temporary and more toward transitional type of shelter,” he said.
Baker said IOM remains in constant contact with Israeli authorities, but some durable materials continue to be denied entry over security concerns.
He also cited funding shortages and disruptions to international shipping as obstacles, saying IOM relies on suppliers in countries including China, India, and Pakistan.
Although funding has begun to arrive, it remains insufficient to meet the needs of an estimated 1.8 million to 1.9 million people requiring shelter assistance, he added.
Baker said only around 30 percent of Gaza is currently accessible to most of the population, forcing displaced Palestinians into increasingly crowded and often flood-prone areas.
“The 30 percent in which they currently live is a very large displacement camp,” he said.
With winter rains already beginning, humanitarian organisations are working to address flood-prone areas and deploy water pumps, but Baker warned that getting displaced Palestinians through the winter would be the biggest challenge.
Earlier this month, IOM said available and incoming shelter supplies covered only 17 percent of Gaza’s winter needs, while more than half of tents and makeshift shelters were in poor condition.
A ceasefire has been in effect since October 10 2025, but Israeli attacks and restrictions on the entry of humanitarian and shelter supplies have continued.

A press release said the first 301 Tze-Chiang EMU3000 train departed at 6:30 a.m. for Kaohsiung. Ministry of Transportation and Communications Minister Chen Shih-kai (陳世凱), Mayor Huang Wei-che (黃偉哲), and Taiwan Railway Chair James Jeng (鄭光遠) boarded the southbound train.
The EMU 3000 train is an inter-city train designed by Hitachi Rail and purchased by Taiwan Railway to upgrade its fleet, per the Legislative Yuan. The trainset has 12 cars and 538 seats for 40% more passengers, per the Economic Daily News.
Chen said the Railway Bureau and Taiwan Railway sent more than 500 crew to switch rails and test the ticketing system. He added that the team worked throughout the night to ensure that the train left on time.
The city said it will continue removing old railway crossings and related structures while reconnecting roads and developing park lanes to improve transportation.
The 8.23-kilometer-long railway underground project covers North, East, and Rende districts and took nearly 16 years to complete. It will later expand to include Yongkang and Xinshi districts, per CNA.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Japan’s government has approved plans for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. to build the country’s first 3-nanometer chip plant, reports said Saturday.
The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry announced Friday it agreed to the proposal to establish a second fab for the TSMC-led joint venture with Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing in Kumamoto Prefecture, per CNA. The original plan had been to produce 12 nm and 6 nm chips at the new factory, but in February, TSMC announced it was planning for the more advanced 3 nm semiconductors.

Some of the changes were motivated by TSMC seeing an increased demand for chips for the development of AI products, Asahi Shimbun reported. The second plant is scheduled to start operations in December 2028.
Final production figures will be decided based on the scale of government subsidies, per CNA. The original plan was to provide NT$150 billion (US$4.63 billion) in subsidies.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Saturday that his presidential term will end in 2030, stressing that the country’s constitution will not be amended to extend his tenure, according to state-run Al-Ahram newspaper.
“The year 2030 will mark the end of my presidential term. This matter is completely settled,” Sisi said during a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital.
Sisi said the Egyptian constitution “will not be touched,” stressing the need to prevent any violation of constitutional and democratic principles.
He said the constitution defines the role of the armed forces in protecting the constitutional order, democracy and the fundamental pillars of the state.
“I will not leave the Egyptian state until it is brimming with its own people capable of shouldering responsibility,” he added, saying a new generation of leaders is currently being prepared through the Egyptian Military Academy.

Sisi also said Egypt is prepared to take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to defend the kingdom’s security and sovereignty.
“We will take any measure to protect Saudi Arabia,” he said, adding that he would call on parliament to convene an emergency session to authorize such action if requested.
“We stand firmly to protect and defend the territories of our brothers in the Gulf,” he added.

An international forum on the reconstruction of Ukraine will take place in Bucharest on October 22–23
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:32:34 EEST
18:32:34 KST

The international forum “Rebuilding Ukraine: Security, Opportunities, Investment” will take place on October 22–23, 2026, in Bucharest, Romania, at the ROMEXPO exhibition center, Pavilion C2. The event will bring together representatives of government agencies from Ukraine, Romania, and other European countries, as well as international financial organizations, investors, the business community, and experts.
The forum is organized by the Romanian think tank New Strategy Center in partnership with the Romanian Chamber of Commerce and Industry. The academic partner of the event is the University of Agronomic Sciences and Veterinary Medicine in Bucharest (USAMV).
According to the updated program, 31 thematic panel discussions are scheduled over the course of two days, focusing on attracting international capital for Ukraine’s reconstruction, the development of transportation and energy infrastructure, industrial cooperation, defense technologies, food security, and cross-border cooperation.
One of the forum’s key focuses will be a discussion of Romania’s role as a regional logistics and investment hub for Ukraine’s reconstruction. In particular, participants will examine the prospects for developing transport corridors between Ukraine, Romania, and Moldova; expanding the capacity of Danube ports; and creating new rail and road routes between the Baltic and Black Seas.
Special attention will be given to investment opportunities in Ukrainian regions. The program includes special presentations on projects in the Kyiv, Zakarpattia, Ivano-Frankivsk, Vinnytsia, Chernivtsi, Odesa, and Kherson regions. Representatives of local authorities, regional development agencies, and the business community will discuss attracting foreign investors, implementing infrastructure projects, and developing cooperation with Romanian partners.
On October 22, the main focus will be on economic recovery, financing, and investments. Participants will examine mechanisms for attracting private capital, opportunities offered by international development banks, support programs for Ukrainian businesses, and prospects for the restoration of residential and industrial infrastructure.
Among the announced participants for the first day are Gennadiy Chizhikov, President of the Ukrainian Chamber of Commerce and Industry; Marina Khlistun, Executive Director of UkraineInvest; Kateryna Glazkova, Executive Director of the Union of Ukrainian Entrepreneurs; and representatives of the European Investment Bank, the German development bank KfW, Japan’s JBIC, Poland’s BGK, and other international financial institutions.
As part of the discussion on financing the reconstruction, a remote presentation by a representative of the Ukrainian government is scheduled. Separate panels will be dedicated to the development of the agricultural sector, ensuring global food security, the modernization of the energy sector, and the development of renewable energy sources.
Also on October 22, there will be a presentation of the “Together for Ukraine” platform, initiated by the New Strategy Center to foster cooperation and support for Ukraine.
Human capital issues will be the subject of a separate discussion featuring Ella Libanova, director of the M.V. Ptukha Institute of Demography and Social Studies of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine. Participants will discuss challenges related to the return of Ukrainian citizens from abroad, workforce supply for the economy, and the training of specialists for reconstruction.
On October 23, the forum’s program will focus on security challenges, the development of the defense industry, energy resilience, and cross-border cooperation.
In particular, panel discussions are planned on international security guarantees for Ukraine, the prospects for ending Russian aggression, the use of unmanned systems, and the development of joint production of defense products by Ukrainian and European companies.
Participants in the discussion on security guarantees will include Igor Zhovkva, Advisor to the President of Ukraine on Foreign Policy; Kiril Petkov, former Prime Minister of Bulgaria; and representatives from the United States, Japan, and European think tanks.
A separate session will be dedicated to the reintegration of veterans and the utilization of their professional potential in economic recovery. Among the participants listed is Ruslan Prykhodko, Ukraine’s Deputy Minister for Veterans’ Affairs.
The energy segment on the second day will include discussions on preparing Ukraine’s power grid for the winter, protecting critical infrastructure, cooperation in the Black Sea region, and prospects for involving international companies in energy projects. Among the announced participants are representatives of Naftogaz of Ukraine, OMV Petrom, ROMGAZ, Japan’s JICA, and other energy companies and organizations.
Issues related to the participation of Romanian businesses in Ukraine’s reconstruction will play a significant role in the program. A special panel will be dedicated to financial instruments, institutional support, and opportunities for implementing joint investment projects.
The forum’s concluding discussions will address the prospects for post-war security in Europe, the development of defense-industrial cooperation, Russia’s international responsibility, and mechanisms for compensating Ukraine for damages caused by the war.
The organizers note that the forum’s goal is to create a practical platform for dialogue between Ukrainian and international companies, financial institutions, and representatives of government agencies and local authorities. Particular emphasis is placed on identifying specific investment opportunities and forming partnerships aimed at Ukraine’s long-term economic recovery.
The New Strategy Center is an independent Romanian think tank specializing in security, defense, foreign policy, energy, and regional cooperation. The organization hosts international conferences and expert events dedicated to strategic challenges in the Black Sea region and Central and Eastern Europe. This forum continues a series of events on Romania’s role in Ukraine’s recovery, organized by the New Strategy Center in 2023 and 2025.
The detailed forum program and information about participants are available on the event’s official website.
The Interfax-Ukraine news agency is a media partner of the event.

IMF urges support for poorer nations facing high inflation, war spillovers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:31:47 UTC
18:31:47 KST

IMF urges support for poorer nations facing high inflation, war spillovers
Low-income countries spend up to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, IMF chief says.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has a responsibility to help poorer nations struggling with rising debt, high inflation and price shocks caused by war spillovers, the head of the global lender says.
Speaking as the IMF’s annual meetings in Bangkok wrapped up on Saturday, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said discussions with global policymakers showed both “optimism and worry”.
“Optimism from the resilience of the global economy, the promise of AI, the dynamism of Asia,” Georgieva told reporters. “But AI is also recognised to be a source of worry and so are inflation, high levels of debt, wars, climate risks.”
Georgieva said vulnerable nations are missing out on the AI investment boom that is driving growth in richer countries while at the same time dealing with higher borrowing costs.
Higher global interest rates mean low-income countries now spend 8 to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, up from previous years, she said.
“I can tell you that people everywhere, but especially in poorer countries, don’t like inflation. Inflation is like a tax on the poor,” Georgieva said.
The warnings came as low-income, oil-importing countries take the strongest hit from rising global energy costs. Prices have soared since February when the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran, leading to retaliatory strikes in the Middle East and disrupted oil and gas flows.
“Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security,” said a statement issued by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, the chairman of the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC).
The IMFC is the main steering committee for the 191-member crisis lender.
Debt relief and regional support
Georgieva said her organisation has a responsibility to help countries restructure debt if needed to assist with domestic resource mobilisation, bring in international finance and create conditions for private investment.
Such countries need to set spending targets that prioritise growth and protect the most vulnerable people, she said, adding that the IMF has a “relentless pursuit of more resources for low-income countries”.
“When we do our best, it translates into better lives for people,” she said.
Georgieva also said the IMF plans to back Iraq “very firmly” with a requested loan programme while talks with Lebanese authorities are making progress.
“We will get to Iraq both money and policy support,” she said. “In the case of Lebanon, we are in very intense discussions with Lebanese authorities. We have made significant progress towards the programme. We have still a bit more work to do together, and I’m confident we will be successful.”

Russia suspected of an online influence campaign ahead of important elections in the United States
Kyiv • UNN
Researchers say that a Russian government-backed influence operation is stepping up its efforts to sow division in the United States ahead of the congressional elections. X blocked 13,000 related accounts.
The Russian online influence operation "Doppelgänger" has intensified the dissemination of social media posts addressing the issue of the United States’ support for Israel, in an effort to deepen divisions in American society ahead of the midterm elections to Congress. This was reported by The New York Times on October 16, citing the relevant study, UNN reports.
Details
"Less than three weeks before elections that could change the balance of power in Congress, there are growing signs that Russia and other foreign governments are again trying to influence American voters. An online influence operation backed by the Russian government is stepping up its efforts to sow division in the United States and inflame tensions surrounding Israel as a political wedge, according to a new study by an independent company that tracks digital threats and foreign propaganda campaigns," reads a NYT article titled "Russia Appears to Step Up Efforts to Influence U.S. Voters."
According to a study by Alethea, a company that tracks digital threats and foreign propaganda campaigns, the "Doppelgänger" operation is spreading posts on social media claiming that bipartisan support for Israel in the United States is weakening. Researchers believe that in this way the campaign is attempting to intensify political disputes surrounding the issue.
As the publication writes, the operation is linked to the Russian company "Agency for Social Design," which operates in the public relations sector. The U.S. government and the European Union have imposed sanctions on it.
"On Wednesday, the social network X announced that it had blocked 13,000 accounts linked to three separate influence operations associated with Iran, Russia, and China. The platform said that the fake accounts had distributed ‘content about U.S. politics targeting candidates and public figures across the political spectrum,’" the publication says.
According to people familiar with the matter, "on Thursday, U.S. intelligence officials attempted to hold a secret briefing for some government officials on threats related to the midterm elections." "However, the initiative encountered an obstacle when intelligence officials were unable to establish a secure virtual connection with election personnel, sources said. Although such briefings were commonplace in previous election cycles, Thursday’s would have been the first of its kind in more than two years," the publication writes.
According to available information, a U.S. official confirmed that the call had to be postponed due to a technical problem. He expressed hope that the briefing would take place next week. Current and former officials explained that such meetings usually involve providing background materials and information about possible threats. They are not intended to transmit intelligence requiring immediate action by local or state authorities.

Spain’s far left fails to unite ahead of November vote
Unknown

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez during a press conference following a government cabinet meeting at the Moncloa Palace, one day after announcing a snap general election, in Madrid on October 6, 2026. | Thomas COEX / AFP via Getty Images
MADRID – Parties on Spain’s far left have failed to reach an agreement to run on a joint ticket in the November 29 election, in a setback to Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who would need their support to form a new governing majority.
The Frente Amplio (or Broad Front), an alliance of several parties to the left of Sánchez’s Socialist Party, had hoped to recruit Podemos, which was a junior partner in government from 2020 to 2023. But with the deadline for electoral coalitions falling at midnight on Friday, the parties were unable to reach a nationwide accord.
Instead, the Broad Front and Podemos will run together only in the Canary Islands and the Valencia region.
Advertisement
The Broad Front is made up of Sumar, the current junior partner in the Socialist-led government, the Catalan Comuns, the Communist-led United Left and Más Madrid. Some smaller local parties have also joined the ticket. The lead candidate for prime minister will be Ada Colau, the former mayor of Barcelona.
Sumar, the dominant force in the alliance, has seen its vote share more than halve since 2023, to 5%, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.
Although Podemos has only been polling at 3%, its full involvement in the Broad Front would have meant a greater overall share of seats for the far left, according to analysts.
The PSOE has been trailing the conservative People’s Party and would need a strong performance by parties to its left in order to keep Sánchez in office. The more likely scenario, polls show, is that the PP will be able to form a majority with the far-right Vox, whose support has been rising.
“The Spanish left is caught up in a game of thrones that demobilizes [voters],” said Irene de Miguel, coordinator of Podemos in the western region of Extremadura, as the deadline loomed.

Anger over Kyiv's winter preparations fuels calls for Mayor Klitschko to resign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:10:00 UTC
18:10:00 KST

Anger over Kyiv's winter preparations fuels calls for Mayor Klitschko to resign
Local residents gathered on Oct. 17 in front of the city council to demand that Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko step down from the post he has occupied for over 12 years.
"Kyiv without Klitschko," hundreds of protesters chanted as they took to the streets in central Kyiv, according to Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground.
Kyiv's failure to prepare for the coming winter amid Russian attacks on critical infrastructure, coupled with broader mismanagement, were the main factors that brought people to protest.
The protest comes as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure and Kyiv struggles to ensure reliable access to basic utilities and adequate shelter.
The cardboard signs read "Where are the shelters?" "Resign" and "12 years of irresponsibility." Others mockingly called on Klitschko to "leave Kyiv," turning his recent advice that residents consider relocating ahead of a difficult winter back on the mayor himself.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticized Kyiv's preparations for winter, saying other cities are significantly better prepared. But despite growing public frustration, Klitschko's removal remains unlikely, as the city's complex governance structure limits the options for dismissing him during wartime.
The dispute also raises a broader question: who is ultimately responsible for ensuring Kyiv can withstand another winter?
Kyiv is less prepared than other cities
Zelensky said on Oct. 13 that "In almost all regions of Ukraine, including border and front-line areas, resilience plans have been implemented more effectively than in the capital."
Emergency power and water outages, triggering the hum of generators on almost every street, returned to Kyiv as Russia renewed its campaign against energy infrastructure as early as Sept. 30.
Power outages are not new to Kyiv, but near-daily water loss is unprecedented.
Serhii Gorkutsenko, deputy head of Kyivvodokanal, the capital's city-owned water supply company, explained the problem in an interview with Ukrainska Pravda.
"The entire electrical water utility system dates back to the 1970s. With such (voltage) fluctuations, it simply can't hold up — it burns out," he said.
This year's issue is not merely about restoring water supply but also about the sewage system, without which Gorkutsenko said there will be "an epidemiological disaster in three days, because no one will stop using the sewers."
Besides the lack of basic amenities, Kyiv also suffers from a deficiency in safety infrastructure, despite the full-scale war continuing for over 4.5 years.
The lack of shelters and the state of existing ones has been an echoing concern for months, if not years.
Klitschko told reporters on Sept. 11 that mobile shelters have been purchased and "within a month, the first batch — about 40 or 50 of them, as far as I recall — will be installed at public transit stops where there are no permanent shelters."
That promised number suddenly diminished. The Kyiv City State Administration (KMDA) told the media outlet Slidstvo.info on Oct. 6 that far fewer will arrive over a much longer timescale.
The first and so far the only new public mobile shelter appeared on Oct. 15, more than a month after Klitschko's claims.
The protest
The overarching message of the Oct. 17 protest was simple — Klitschko should resign.
However, the issues outlined by the organizers were plentiful. They addressed everything from safety to public transport issues, and the neglect of cultural heritage sites.
Corruption and the city's financial mismanagement was also on the list of protestors' grievances.
Klitschko has been in power since 2014 and was decisively reelected as Kyiv's Mayor twice, in 2015 and 2020.
During these terms, Klitschko has been widely criticized for failing to address the city's urgent needs, instead focusing on building developments that demolish "cultural heritage, green zones, and public spaces," wrote activist and veteran Dmytro Koziatynskyi on social media prior to the protest.
This is the second time in October that a protest has been held at the City State Administration's doorstep. In the evening of Oct. 7, people gathered in protest of the mass felling of trees during the construction of a heating pipeline in Teremky, a district fiercely targeted by Russian attacks.
"I just go around all week and tell people at work, and my foreign friends, and everyone about how Kyiv is an incredibly uncomfortable place to live," Kyiv resident Nadiia told the Kyiv Independent during the Oct. 7 protest.
read also
Likelihood of Klitschko's removal
Klitschko's ousting remains unlikely, however.
Kyiv is run in a convoluted manner, with numerous administrative bodies whose duties either overlap or omit certain areas entirely.
Klitschko is currently Kyiv's mayor and, due to the city's special status as the country's capital, is also the head of the Kyiv City State Administration, a post equivalent to a regional governor. According to the law, the elected mayor is usually appointed as the head of the city administration.
The city is also governed by the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA), a structure created by Zelensky following the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. Andrii Tkachov currently leads it and is responsible for "preparing the city for defense, maintaining public order and ensuring the safety of the civilian population, enforcing the legal framework of martial law, and ensuring the city's essential functions," as written on its website.
Only the heads of KMDA and KMVA can be appointed by the president, while the mayor is elected by popular vote.
Considering this, Klitschko cannot be fully dismissed by Zelensky, but can only resign on his own will. What Ukraine's president can do is strip Klitschko of his title as head of the administration, thus limiting his power over decisions in Kyiv.
Following Zelensky's latest criticism, the city's mayor had five minutes in Ukraine's parliament to address the growing issues.
"We, as the city government, are doing everything in our power to ensure the city's functioning, despite the setbacks the central government is constantly trying to inflict on us; unfortunately, this is what their so-called 'cooperation' looks like," he said on Oct. 14.
He also revealed that, so far this year, Kyiv's power grid has been struck nearly 50 times by missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), an increase since last year.
"Where is the capital's air defense? Where is the protection for Ukrenergo's (energy operator) facilities? Where are the billions you allocated for this?" Klitschko appealed, pointing the finger at the government.
In 2026, Kyiv was allocated over $2.3 billion for winter preparation, but only 51.1% had been used as of Sept. 1, according to the Finance Ministry.
The Kyiv Independent reached out to the Kyiv City State Administration and Klitschko with a request for comment, but has not received a response at the time of publication.

The woman, surnamed Chan, reported the case to police at around 8.30am on Saturday morning at their home in the Ocean One residential development in Yau Tong.
According to police, Chan suspected that her 40-year-old husband, surnamed Lam, had stolen goods worth HK$450,000 in total. The items involved were Chanel and Hermes bags worth HK$300,000 and a HK$150,000 Rolex watch.
Police later arrived at the scene and arrested Lam on suspicion of theft after a preliminary investigation. He is currently being detained for further investigation.

Morocco forms new government under 1st ever female prime minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
09:05:07 UTC
18:05:07 KST

Morocco announced a new cabinet on Friday, ushering in a historic era with the country’s first female prime minister leading a four-party coalition, Anadolu reports.
According to state-run Maghreb Arabe Presse (MAP), King Mohammed VI received members of the new cabinet, led by Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, and presided over their appointment ceremony at the Royal Palace in the capital Rabat.
El Mansouri is the first Moroccan woman to hold the country’s top government post.
She will lead a new government formed by a four-party coalition comprising her Authenticity and Modernity Party, the Istiqlal Party, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces and the Party of Progress and Socialism.
The new government includes seven women, including El Mansouri, compared with six in the previous government led by Aziz Akhannouch.
READ: Moroccan opposition leader: We are not Israelis; we support Palestine, King, government and people
The new government comprises 32 members, including ministers and ministers-delegate, according to official figures.
Abdelouafi Laftit kept his post as interior minister, alongside Nasser Bourita as foreign minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi as justice minister and Ahmed Toufiq as minister of Islamic affairs and endowments.
The new cabinet also established a Ministry of Artificial Intelligence, Digital Transformation and Administrative Reform, headed by Ahmed Rahhou.
On Monday, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, Istiqlal Party, Socialist Union of Popular Forces and Party of Progress and Socialism announced in a joint statement that they had formed the governing majority following the conclusion of the second round of consultations on forming a government, which began on Sept. 30.
On Sept. 29, King Mohammed VI tasked El Mansouri with forming a government after her party, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, came first in the Sept. 23 elections with 97 seats.

Sri Lanka to speed up gov't issuance of forensics reports by early 2027
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:57:03 CST
17:57:03 KST

COLOMBO, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka will reduce delays in issuing forensic reports to three months by Jan. 31, 2027, Justice and National Integration Minister Harshana Nanayakkara said on Friday.
The minister made the remarks during an inspection visit to the Department of Government Analyst, the country's central forensics laboratory under the Ministry of Justice and National Integration, where he reviewed progress in processing reports related to narcotic substances.
It took about approximately 18 months to issue a report when the current Sri Lankan administration came to power in late 2024.
Officials told the minister that they had cleared reports on narcotic samples weighing less than 5 grams, received up to August 2026. Work on the remaining cases had been accelerated.
Nanayakkara said faster issuance of analyst reports was important for speeding up court proceedings and reducing prison overcrowding.
He said staff shortages and limited facilities had previously contributed to delays. Measures introduced to address the problem include filling vacancies, upgrading facilities and providing allowances to employees working night shifts. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Para taekwondo athlete Li Yujie and para powerlifter Yan Panpan will bear the flag for China at the opening ceremony of the 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan on Sunday, the Chinese delegation announced Saturday.
Li, a student at Beijing Sport University, won bronze in the women's K44-58kg category at the Tokyo Paralympics in 2021, China's first-ever Paralympic medal in taekwondo, and gold in the K44-57kg category at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, the country's first Paralympic gold in the sport. She was also named 2025 World Para Taekwondo Female Athlete of the Year, becoming the first Team China athlete to receive the honor.
Yan, who graduated from Beijing Sport University earlier this year, took gold in the men's 97kg category at the Tokyo Paralympics in 2021, followed by gold in the 88kg category at the Paris Paralympics three years later. In 2025, he claimed the 88kg title at the World Para Powerlifting Championships in Cairo.
Competitions at the 5th Asian Para Games kicked off on Friday, two days before the opening ceremony. China beat hosts Japan 1-0 in the men's blind football, while wheelchair basketball, para table tennis and para badminton also got underway.
More than 300 Chinese athletes will compete in 335 events across 17 sports at the Games, which will run through October 24. ■

17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
The Trump administration warned California election officials Friday that they could face criminal prosecution for counting ballots cast by suspected noncitizens, escalating a dispute ahead of the Nov. 3 election, Newsmax reported.
Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter wrote in a letter to Los Angeles County officials: “If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.”
The warning followed a Justice Department lawsuit filed Thursday seeking to block the counting of mail ballots from individuals identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status is verified.
The administration cited a list of 20,000 names, while California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said it had provided no supporting evidence.
UCLA law professor Rick Hasen said the letter “ups the ante by threatening election officials with potential criminal prosecution.”
Justin Levitt, a Loyola Law School professor and former Justice Department official, said, “Courts haven’t been buying what DOJ has been selling, and nothing in this letter is calibrated to change course.”

Moscow welcomes Trump’s sanctions waiver as Ukraine voices alarm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:56:00 UTC
17:56:00 KST

Russia on Saturday welcomed U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to waive new sanctions targeting Moscow, calling it a historic move as Ukraine warned that easing economic pressure would encourage Russian President Vladimir Putin to continue the war.
Trump signed an executive order Friday suspending the application of sanctions provisions under the Lindsey Graham Act, a law designed to increase pressure on Russia’s energy and defense sectors, its officials and the network of tankers Moscow uses to circumvent Western restrictions.
The decision comes as Russian forces intensify attacks on Ukrainian cities and diplomatic efforts led by Washington remain deadlocked, raising concerns among Kyiv and its European allies that the Trump administration is easing pressure on Moscow without securing meaningful concessions.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy for investment and economic cooperation, praised the decision on social media, describing the suspension of the law as an “important and truly historic moment.”
Dmitriev argued that the sanctions would have caused serious damage to the U.S. economy and global markets. The Kremlin and Putin had not publicly commented on the decision as of Saturday.
The waiver followed an arrangement between Trump and Putin under which Moscow agreed to release substantial quantities of diesel onto global markets amid mounting pressure on fuel prices. Trump’s decision to suspend the new measures marks a diplomatic gain for Russia as Washington struggles to broker an end to the war.
The Graham Act, named after the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, was designed to tighten restrictions on Russia’s energy and defense industries, officials linked to Putin and its so-called shadow fleet of tankers. It also included provisions targeting countries that continue to buy Russian oil and gas.
Trump’s order suspends the application of the new measures under a national-interest waiver. It does not automatically remove sanctions imposed on Russia under earlier U.S. measures.
The decision has intensified concerns in Kyiv that Washington could weaken its leverage over Moscow while Russian forces continue their offensive.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the waiver Saturday, arguing that easing sanctions would reward Russia despite its continued attacks.
“A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin, all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” Zelenskyy said on social media, urging Ukraine’s allies to maintain pressure on Moscow.
The sanctions decision came as Russia stepped up its attacks on Ukraine, including repeated strikes on the capital, Kyiv, as the war enters its fifth year.
Russian forces struck the southern city of Kherson on Saturday, killing one person and wounding 22, local officials said. The attack underscored the continuing toll of the war even as Washington pursues negotiations.
The conflict, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. Russian forces occupy large areas of eastern and southern Ukraine, and Putin has repeatedly vowed to seize the remaining territory Moscow claims in eastern Ukraine.
Speaking to military leaders Friday while wearing military uniform, Putin said he saw a positive trend in the operations of Russian forces and reiterated that capturing the rest of the Donetsk region remained a major objective.
“Undoubtedly, one of the main objectives remains the liberation of the Donetsk People’s Republic,” Putin said, using the Kremlin’s term for the Ukrainian region.
Russian strikes have intensified in recent weeks, putting additional pressure on Ukrainian air defenses as the country prepares for another winter of war. Kyiv has struggled to intercept incoming missiles and drones while seeking additional defensive systems from its allies.
Putin’s remarks signaled that Moscow intends to continue its military campaign despite diplomatic efforts to secure a ceasefire.
European leaders responded to the growing uncertainty over Washington’s approach by reaffirming their support for Ukraine and calling for continued economic pressure on Russia.
Zelenskyy met European leaders in Brussels on Friday during a European Union summit, seeking sustained financial and military assistance as relations between Kyiv and Washington deteriorated.
European Council President António Costa warned against easing pressure on Moscow while Russian forces continued their attacks.
“This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” Costa said. “Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”
European leaders have argued that maintaining sanctions and strengthening Ukraine’s defenses are necessary to persuade Russia to accept a meaningful ceasefire and negotiate an end to the war.
The EU has also signaled that it intends to maintain its restrictions on Moscow while preparing further measures.
Zelenskyy has sought additional air defense systems, support for Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and continued funding to sustain the country’s defense effort. His appeal came as European governments weighed how to maintain assistance amid uncertainty over the future direction of U.S. policy.
The European response reflects growing concern that Washington’s willingness to ease sanctions could undermine the pressure intended to bring Putin to the negotiating table.
U.S.-led negotiations have yet to produce a breakthrough, with disputes over territory, security guarantees and the terms of a possible ceasefire continuing to obstruct progress.
Trump has expressed frustration with both Putin and Zelenskyy over the lack of progress toward ending the conflict. His increasingly strained relationship with the Ukrainian leader has added to concerns in Kyiv that Washington could press Ukraine to make concessions while offering Moscow economic relief.
The sanctions waiver has heightened those fears, particularly as Ukraine faces intensified Russian bombardments and questions over the reliability of some U.S.-provided military and intelligence support.
For Ukraine, the immediate concern is that easing economic pressure could give Russia greater room to sustain its military campaign. For European governments, the decision raises questions about how to maintain a unified strategy if Washington takes a more conciliatory approach toward Moscow.
Russia’s public celebration of the waiver reflects the potential diplomatic value of the move for Putin, even as the Kremlin continues to pursue its territorial objectives by force.

Switzerland advances bid to host 2038 Winter Olympics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:52:23 UTC
17:52:23 KST

Switzerland advances bid to host 2038 Winter Olympics
Switzerland is preparing a bid to host the 2038 Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games. Following approval by the Swiss House of Representatives, the relevant committee of the Senate has backed the proposal, which provides for federal financial support of up to CHF200 million ($242 million).
The Senate’s Committee on Science, Education and Culture has given the green light by 10 votes to 0, with 2 abstentions. It has made a number of clarifications to the House of Representative’s draft regarding funding and cantonal participation, according to a statement issued by parliament on Friday.
The privileged dialogue between the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and Switzerland allows the country to prepare a bid to host the Games without competition until the end of 2027. If the bid meets the IOC’s requirements, Switzerland will be awarded the right to host the Games. The IOC is expected to make its decision at its spring session in 2027.
The Games must meet the highest national and international standards of sustainability, transparency and governance. They will be held in a decentralised manner across the four linguistic regions. No new construction projects will be undertaken. The plan does not envisage putting the bid to a referendum of the Swiss people.
+ Switzerland names venues for 2038 Winter Olympics bid
It envisages a total budget of CHF2.2 billion over the next ten years, from the awarding of the Games until they take place. While the Games will be primarily funded by private sources, federal support will amount to CHF200 million. The cantons will be required to contribute at least the same amount.
Additional funds will be used to co-finance the Paralympic Games, reduce public transport costs and make competition venues available throughout Switzerland. The federal government will also be responsible for security measures, estimated to cost between CHF40 and 80 million.

The European Council has formally instructed the European Commission to formulate concrete proposals to bridge Ukraine’s projected €70 billion ($79 billion) budget deficit for 2027, European Council President António Costa announced in Brussels on Friday, Oct. 16.
Speaking at the conclusion of the European Council summit, Costa confirmed that EU heads of state reached a consensus on addressing Kyiv’s long-term fiscal requirements, acting on requests delivered by President Volodymyr Zelensky.

“We agreed that it is necessary to address Ukraine’s additional financing needs for 2027,” Costa told reporters. “And we asked the European Commission to present a concrete proposal for discussion and adoption.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reaffirmed the funding requirement, stressing that Ukraine’s international partners must coordinate to eliminate the looming fiscal shortfall.
“Now it is clear that we have a gap of €70 billion that has to be covered,” von der Leyen stated following the summit, urging allied nations to mobilize financial commitments.
A senior EU official familiar with the leaders’ discussions told European Pravda that the proposal remains in an exploratory stage, noting that formal adoption is not bound to a rigid year-end deadline.
The official explained that deliberations on sourcing fresh capital can progress while disbursements continue under the existing €90 billion ($102 billion) loan facility, which allocates €45 billion ($50 billion) for 2027.

The official added that it remains undetermined whether the forthcoming Commission proposal will incorporate recommendations to leverage Russian sovereign assets immobilized across the EU.
Allied coordination
French President Emmanuel Macron confirmed that international allies – including the Group of Seven (G7), European governments, and broader partner coalition – will review Kyiv’s €70 billion funding request.
“We will indeed be looking at the funding,” Macron told France 24.
“The funding that will be provided by the G7 countries, by our partners and, of course, by the Europeans.”
Macron also disclosed that European defense planners are accelerating programs to supply Ukraine with sovereign satellite imagery and early-warning architectures, noting that friction with Washington has highlighted Kyiv’s acute reliance on American technical capabilities.
“We are working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed,” Macron said.
Addressing recent diplomatic developments, Macron criticized the bilateral commercial diesel agreement reached between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, warning that granting Moscow market access harms allied cohesion.
“This decision is not good for anyone. It sends a negative signal. It is an element of division and doubt,” Macron stated.
Pre-winter air defense shortfalls
The drive to secure 2027 budgetary commitments unfolds as President Zelensky delivered an urgent appeal to European Union leaders in Brussels, requesting 300 Patriot surface-to-air interceptors alongside the multi-billion-euro financial package to shield municipal utilities ahead of winter.
Zelensky warned European leaders that Russian forces have expanded long-range standoff bombardments against civilian power grids, leaving municipal centers exposed as domestic interceptor stockpiles reach depletion.
“I ask you to really focus on helping us get PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors,” Zelensky said in his address to the European Council.
“Ukraine can’t get by on just two or four missiles from a country every few months. We need a winter package – we always spoke about it between us – of missiles: 300 Patriot interceptors specifically against ballistic missiles.”
The appeal coincides with reports that Ukrainian forces have nearly exhausted their inventories of US-manufactured Patriot interceptors, with supply strains compounded by production backlogs and high operational expenditures during US military operations in the Middle East.
While European defense coordinators have lobbied member states possessing Patriot systems – including Greece and Spain – to transfer aging interceptors approaching statutory shelf limits, southern European governments have expressed reluctance to release batteries, citing their own regional defense commitments.

Strait of Hormuz transits remain 70% below pre-conflict levels: UK maritime agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:49:20 UTC
17:49:20 KST

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained about 70% below pre-conflict levels as attacks on commercial vessels continued, a UK maritime agency said Friday.
In its weekly overview, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) reported 125 outbound and 129 inbound transits over the past seven days.
The figures marked a decline from 129 outbound and 146 inbound transits recorded the previous week, according to the agency.
UKMTO reported 12 attacks on vessels during the week, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz, one in the Gulf and one in the Gulf of Oman. Six vessels continued or reached port, one was lost, two were disabled or not under command, and three have unconfirmed outcomes.
Container ship sinks after projectile strike
UKMTO said a container ship was struck by an unidentified projectile near Ras Shaykh Masud on Oct. 13.
READ: Iran says container ship sank after striking naval mine in Strait of Hormuz
The vessel caught fire and sank the following day, according to the agency.
All crew members were evacuated, UKMTO said.
The agency warned that it was struggling to establish the actual number of attacks because most targeted vessels declined to report incidents.
UKMTO said it had recorded 84 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began in late February.
The reported attacks came amid continued tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.
The waterway is a major route for global energy and commodity shipments and remains a key issue in negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
The conflict began with US and Israeli attacks against Iran on Feb. 28, followed by a ceasefire in April.
Clashes between Washington and Tehran later resumed as negotiations stalled, although the two sides signed a framework agreement in June.

EU backs just peace in Ukraine, calls on Russia to cease fire, enter negotiations – summit conclusions
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
11:49:10 EEST
17:49:10 KST

European Union leaders have declared their support for a just peace for Ukraine, based on the principles of the UN Charter, and called on Russia to agree to a ceasefire and begin peace talks.
This position of EU leaders is set forth in the conclusions adopted following the European Council meeting held on October 15-16 in Brussels. "The European Union supports a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in Ukraine based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law and underpinned by robust and credible security guarantees for Ukraine. Only a solution that respects Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity can bring about a just and lasting peace," the document states.
EU leaders are convinced that "the path to peace in Ukraine cannot be decided without Ukraine," while the EU "will decide on matters of its competence or affecting its security."
"Borders must not be changed by force, the aggressor cannot be rewarded and Ukraine's long-term security and ability to defend itself must be guaranteed," the conclusions read.
The European Council reaffirmed its support for diplomatic efforts aimed at ending Russia's war of aggression and emphasized the EU's readiness to step up its involvement in this process.
EU leaders also stressed that Europe will play "a key role to play in a future settlement and will defend its interests." "The European Council urges Russia to show genuine willingness regarding peace, agree to a full, unconditional and immediate ceasefire and engage in meaningful negotiations towards a just and lasting peace," the document states.

Language matters in Hong Kong’s birth rate debate, not just money

Language matters in Hong Kong’s birth rate debate, not just money
Hong Kong’s fertility woes are not just about affordability. They might also involve language use and how it shapes our views of the future
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
Dr Zhisheng (Edward) Wen is an associate division head and senior lecturer in the College of Professional and Continuing Education at Hong Kong Polytechnic University, where he researches and teaches second language acquisition, translanguaging and cognitive science. 
When Hong Kong debates how to raise its birth rate, the conversation usually revolves around money: bigger baby bonuses, tax concessions, housing support, cheaper childcare and so on. These economic measures are necessary. Lowering the cost of raising a child removes some real and immediate barriers.
However, there is another, lesser-known factor that works more subtly and implicitly. It comes not from economics but from the structure of the language or languages we speak each day.
Consider a simple contrast. In English, one says, “Yesterday it rained. Now it is raining. Tomorrow it will rain.” In Chinese, the same three sentences need no such grammatical marking. The verb does not change. The future is not grammatically separated from the present.

How Switzerland became an organic farming pioneer
