How Switzerland became an organic farming pioneer
A visit to a supermarket in Switzerland leaves many visitors from abroad amazed. With a higher proportion of organic products on the shelves than elsewhere, organic food has become part of everyday shopping in the country.
Almost one in three eggs sold in Swiss shops is organically produced. For vegetables, lettuce and potatoes, the proportion stands at around 27%.
With organic products accounting for 12.3% of all food sold, Switzerland tops the international rankings. It is followed by Denmark (11.6%) and Austria (11.4%).
‘Organic’ is not clearly defined
However, international data is inconsistent. Countries use different survey methods, and terms such as ‘food retail’ and ‘total food market’ are not always defined in the same way.
Furthermore, even the definition of ‘organic’ is not standardised worldwide. A product bearing an organic label in one place often meets different standards to those in other countries. For instance, Swiss certification requirements are stricter than the European Union’s Organic Regulation or the US Organic Standard.
Bio Suisse, the umbrella organisation for Swiss organic farms certified under the Knospe label,External link also points out that Swiss figures have been based on a new dataset since 2024. Some earlier figures have been recalculated.
Despite these limitations, the overall picture remains clear: organic products account for a larger share of Swiss consumers’ shopping baskets than those of shoppers in other countries.
Furthermore, Switzerland has for years topped the rankings when it comes to per capita spending on organic products, at the equivalent of €494 (CHF461) per person per year.
“However, the general price level [in Switzerland] is high in any case,” states the 2026 industry report by the German Federation for Organic Food and AgricultureExternal link (BÖLW).
From niche market to political recognition
Switzerland’s success story did not begin with the sustainability boom. Local organic farming developed into an organised movement during the 20th century.
In 1981, five organisations founded the umbrella organisation for Swiss organic farming, which became Bio Suisse in 1997.
With its ‘Knospe’ (in the form of a bud), the association also created a common certification label. It is not simply the Swiss equivalent of the EU organic logo, but a private label with its own guidelines, which in several areas go beyond statutory minimum standards. The aim is to build trust in production methods and inspections.
Political recognition followed in 1992. At that time, organic farming was included in the Agriculture Act alongside integrated productionExternal link (IP label) as a form of production eligible for support.
Organic farming thus became an integral part of state agricultural policy. In Switzerland, organically produced products therefore moved out of the niche market and into the mainstream food system at a relatively early stage.
Supermarkets enter the fray
The market received perhaps its most significant boost in the early 1990s. Coop launched its own organic brand, ‘Naturaplan’, in close collaboration with Bio Suisse. From then on, the products carried the ‘Knospe’ logo. Organic produce was thus no longer available only in specialist shops, but also in supermarkets.
Later, Switzerland’s second retail giant, Migros, also entered the organic market. The two cooperatives have long dominated the Swiss food retail sector and have an extensive network of stores.
This made organic produce easily accessible and part of everyday shopping. Today, no retailer can afford to ignore organic products.
While organic products accounted for 7.1% of the total food market in 2007, this figure had risen to 10.8% by 2020. By 2024, it reached its record high of 12.3%.
Sales of organic food amounted to CHF4.266 billion.
Organic products accounted for 12.3% of the food market.
Consumers spend CHF468 per capita on organic food.
52% of all consumers buy organic products daily or several times a week.
7,467 organic farms, market gardens and beekeepers in Switzerland and Liechtenstein produce in accordance with Bio Suisse guidelines.
18.4% of Switzerland’s agricultural land is farmed organically.
Source: Bio Suisse
Trust and purchasing power as reasons for success
One reason for the success of organic products in shopping baskets is likely to be the high level of trust that Swiss consumers place in organic labels.
After all, when shopping, nobody can personally check how a field is farmed or how animals are reared. Customers therefore rely on inspections and credible labelling.
However, ‘organic’ does not automatically mean that products were produced in Switzerland. As not everything can be produced domestically, Switzerland also has to import organic raw materials and foodstuffs. Care is taken to ensure that foreign producers comply with the Knospe guidelines.
Another reason is likely to be the high purchasing power of Swiss consumers. Organic products are expensive, and price is one of the main barriers. Higher-income households are more likely to buy organic products; education and place of residence also influence consumer behaviour.
Taste is less important
According to a 2022 study by the Federal Office for Agriculture and the Research Institute of Organic AgricultureExternal link (FiBL), taste is not the primary factor influencing purchasing decisions.
Instead, for 85% of those surveyed, animal welfare and the avoidance of pesticide residues are key considerations. These are followed by environmentally friendly production and the avoidance of preventive antibiotic use in animal husbandry.
Liechtenstein has the highest proportion of organic production
According to figures from Bio SuisseExternal link, in 2025 almost 7,500 farms and market gardens in Switzerland and the Principality of Liechtenstein were producing in accordance with the organisation’s guidelines.
Although Switzerland is the world leader in organic consumption, it does not lead in production. In terms of the proportion of land farmed organically, Liechtenstein leads the worldExternal link at 43.5%. Spain, France and Italy have the largest areas of organic farmland in Europe in absolute terms.
Room for improvement in the catering sector
However, Switzerland’s leading position in terms of market share for organic products is by no means guaranteed. Market share is currently stagnating, prices are high, and some demand has to be met by imports.
The next challenge is to make organic produce more widely available outside supermarkets and affordable to broader sections of the population.
This also includes the catering sector: the aforementioned study by the federal government and FiBL identified strong demand among respondents for organic food in restaurants, canteens and takeaways.
For many people, organic food is less readily available when eating out than it is in supermarkets. Rising living costs can also lead even committed organic shoppers to opt for cheaper products.
Edited by Balz Rigendinger. Adapted from German by Alexandra MV Andrist/dos

Drone attacks on Moscow continue since last night
This was reported by the BBC’s Russian Service, according to Ukrinform.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin reported the drone attack on the city. On Saturday night, he initially stated that 69 drones had been shot down as they approached the Russian capital.
“Emergency service specialists are working at the crash sites of the UAVs,” Sobyanin wrote.
Toward morning, the mayor reported that another 75 drones attempting to attack Moscow had been destroyed. Thus, the total number of drones that Russian authorities claimed to have shot down reached 144.
According to ASTRA, shortly before midnight, Rosaviatsiya imposed restrictions on aircraft arrivals and departures at Moscow airports due to the drone attack. Restrictions were also in effect at other airports in Russia.
Around midnight, it was reported that five flights from Antalya to Moscow had been rerouted due to restrictions at Vnukovo Airport. In particular, passengers on one of the Pegasus Airlines flights from Antalya to Moscow reported that they had departed from Turkey at 7:35 p.m., and shortly before landing, they were informed that the airspace over the Russian capital was closed. Consequently, around 1:00 a.m., the plane landed at Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg. Since then, passengers have not been allowed to leave the plane. Flight attendants warned that they would have to remain on board “until the airspace over Moscow reopens.” It is unknown when that will happen.
An alert regarding drones was also issued in the Leningrad Region. At 2:10 a.m., the region’s governor, Alexander Drozdenco, announced an air raid alert and a reduction in mobile internet speeds.
In total, according to the Russian Ministry of Defense, air defense forces shot down 610 drones overnight. According to the ministry, the drones were intercepted over the territories of the Leningrad, Novgorod, Tver, Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Oryol, Kaluga, Voronezh, Rostov, Smolensk, and Tula regions; the Moscow region; the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug, the Krasnodar Krai, the temporarily occupied Crimea, and the Black Sea.
As reported by Ukrinform, yesterday Moscow’s airports suspended operations for the third time this week due to Ukrainian drones, and more than 200 flights were canceled.

Rubio’s Uzbekistan trip underlines Central Asia’s hunt for diverse partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:27:28 UTC
17:27:28 KST

Rubio’s Uzbekistan trip underlines Central Asia’s hunt for diverse partners
Can the United States reassert influence with pragmatic, transactional approach to Central Asia as C5+1 summit gets under way?
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is arriving in Samarkand, the fabled Silk Road city in what is now central Uzbekistan, for talks with key regional ministers on Saturday.
The C5+1 – Central Asia plus the US – summit to be held from Saturday to Tuesday heralds Washington’s new approach to the ex-Soviet region – pragmatic, purely transactional and devoid of speeches about democratisation and human rights.
At the dawn of Central Asia’s independence, Americans used to show up in the mostly Muslim region strategically stretched between Russia, China and Iran, bearing gifts – and giving lectures.
After the 1991 Soviet collapse, amid the region’s economic degradation, joblessness and poverty, US and European diplomats and businessmen were seen as ambassadors of the brave new world of capitalist prosperity.
They wanted reforms – and not just the economic ones.
Western diplomats made sure that former Communist apparatchiks-turned-new regional leaders understood that they’d get investments, technologies and international recognition only in exchange for abandoning the Soviet-era totalitarian ways of governing and building the economy.
The West held forums and workshops on human rights, democracy and decentralisation of governance, and sent thousands of students and officials to Western schools.
And the West accused regional leaders of losing their moral compass and threatened sanctions when they began to amend their nation’s constitutions to extend their presidential terms, appoint their family members and friends to key government jobs and help them create business empires that often competed with Western investors.
“When the West began moralising, teaching them about democracy, human rights, they immediately turned towards China or Russia,” Galiya Ibragimova, Uzbekistan-born, Moldova-based regional expert, told Al Jazeera.
Uzbekistan, the region’s most populous nation of 37 million, offers a perfect example.
Its iron-fisted President Islam Karimov was the first ex-Soviet leader to allow a US military base on its soil in 2001.
But four years later, he kicked it out after Washington lambasted his brutal suppression of a popular revolt in the eastern city of Andijan that killed hundreds of unarmed civilians.
In 2005, a leaked US diplomatic cable called Karimov’s daughter, Gulnara, a “robber baron” who forcibly took over lucrative businesses and was seen as her father’s successor.
Turning to Russia
As to moralising and lecturing, the tables have turned since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, observers say.
Moscow still has plenty of soft power in Central Asia – from movies and pop music to theatre festivals and propagandist TV shows that constantly lie about the war.
The Kremlin also uses its economic clout to promote the imperialist concept of the “Russian World”, where the region is seen as Moscow’s “near abroad”, and its pre-Russian heritage is snubbed as backwards and insignificant.
In 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed that Kazakhstan had “never had statehood”, and his ideological allies repeatedly threatened to annex its Russian-speaking northern part.
This year, Kazakhstan began extraditing Kremlin critics and supplying gas to Russia amid Ukrainian drone attacks on its oil refineries.
In January, Kremlin propagandist Vladimir Solovyov said Moscow should launch a “special military operation” – a term reserved for the war in Ukraine – in Central Asia and Armenia.
Critical remarks from minor political figures followed – but no rebukes from the halls of real power.
Meanwhile, Central Asian labour migrants have been duped or forced into enlisting to fight in Ukraine in droves, while Moscow uses Central Asian companies to import microchips, communications equipment and machine tools to build drones and missiles.
“These days, the US and Russia have switched roles. Today, it’s Russia that began building ties through moralising,” Ibragimova, the regional expert, said.
Return of the White House?
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump’s administration has abandoned the pro-democracy stance and now advocates a utilitarian, transactional approach to foreign policy.
“Under Trump, the American policy in Central Asia is all about ‘just business and nothing more’, without being nosy about human rights, reforms. They are content with everything,” Ibragimova said.
Earlier this month, Trump received Saida Mirziyoyeva, the daughter of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.
A year earlier, Mirziyoyev pledged to invest up to $100bn in the US economy, buy Boeing aircraft and even US-grown cotton, even though Uzbekistan is one of the world’s largest cotton growers.
Washington did not say a word about Mirziyoyev’s crackdown on critics or his daughter’s growing domestic clout.
After largely ignoring Central Asia during Trump’s first term, the White House wants to resume its presence.
“The interest is mostly geopolitical and military-strategic, considering the region’s location in the zone of Russia’s and China’s interests,” Alisher Ilkhamov, head of the London-based Central Asia Due Diligence think tank, told Al Jazeera.
“In the future, Washington apparently wants to have a military base here as a deterrent measure against China,” he said.
The economic interests seem to be focused on rare-earth minerals – crucial for manufacturing a wide array of technology – and other critical elements, especially since China uses them as a political cudgel in its ties with Washington.
The deposits are abundant, but need development, technologies and investment.
Meanwhile, the White House shows little interest in human rights violations in Central Asia, such as the jailing of political opponents and independent journalists.
“An interest in these issues, unfortunately, is absent from Rubio’s agenda, because these problems went missing from US foreign policy priorities since Trump returned to the White House,” Ilkhamov said.
A Norwegian human rights advocate echoes his concerns.
“There are uncomfortable similarities between Trump’s worldview and established authoritarian regimes like Tajikistan and Turkmenistan,” Ivar Dale, a senior policy adviser with the Norwegian Helsinki Committee, a rights watchdog, told Al Jazeera.
“However, Marco Rubio probably has a better understanding of Central Asia and the challenges there than does [Vice President] JD Vance and [Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth,” he said.
The US State Department “should bring back the focus [on human rights] if the C5+1 format is to be taken seriously going forward”, he said.

European Union leaders expressed their full and resolute support for the people of Ukraine in their struggle against Russian aggression and their intention to continue providing comprehensive assistance to the Ukrainian state.
This position is set forth in the conclusions adopted following the European Council meeting held on October 15-16 in Brussels. "The European Council held an exchange of views with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, President of Ukraine. It expressed its full and resolute support to the people of Ukraine as they face particularly brutal attacks by Russia," the document states.
The European Council also reaffirmed its "continued firm and unwavering support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders." "The European Union will continue to provide, in coordination with like-minded partners and allies, comprehensive political, financial, economic, humanitarian, military and diplomatic support to Ukraine and its people," the EU leaders affirmed.
The European Council strongly condemned Russia's "brutal attacks" on the civilian population and highlighted the resilience, determination, and fortitude of the Ukrainian people and their leadership in confronting Russian aggression and defending their homeland. "Exercising its inherent right of self-defence, Ukraine has managed to stand its ground and push back against Russia's enormous pressure, preventing Russia from achieving its military and strategic objectives," the EU leaders said.
In light of the approaching winter, the European Council called for further intensification and coordination of efforts to "urgently strengthen Ukraine's air and missile defence capabilities, the resilience of its critical infrastructure and energy system, including through the Ukraine Energy Support Fund, and to address other immediate needs."

Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said Friday that Doha is seeking to provide integrated solutions for Lebanon’s energy sector and activate projects previously agreed between the two countries, Anadolu reports.
Speaking after meeting Lebanese President Joseph Aoun in Beirut, Al Thani said their talks focused on relations and ways to implement joint projects that would contribute to the region’s security, stability and prosperity.
“The energy sector is a key priority for Lebanon,” he said, and added that a later meeting with Prime Minister Nawaf Salam would address activating projects previously agreed between Beirut and Doha.
Al Thani said he also discussed regional and international developments with Aoun, particularly the situation in southern Lebanon and “Israeli occupation practices” against the country.
He reaffirmed Qatar’s support for measures taken by Lebanon and stressed the need for the Israeli army to withdraw from Lebanese territory it occupies and hand it to the Lebanese army.
Al Thani also reiterated Qatar’s continued support for Lebanon.
Separately, Foreign Minister Youssef Rajji said that his country remains committed to maintaining an international force in southern Lebanon to replace the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) after its mission ends at the end of the year.
His remarks came during a meeting with UN Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations Jean-Pierre Lacroix, attended by UNIFIL commander Diodato Abagnara and an accompanying delegation, according to a Foreign Ministry statement.
READ: Lebanon presses US to push Israel for halt to attacks
The meeting addressed the situation in southern Lebanon and the future of the international presence there after UNIFIL’s current mandate ends.
Rajji praised UN peacekeepers’ sacrifices in maintaining security and stability in southern Lebanon.
Lacroix stressed the need to prepare for the next phase, saying the UN Security Council would soon begin negotiations on the future of the UN presence in Lebanon.
He reaffirmed the UN’s commitment to playing a constructive role in the coming period while fully respecting Lebanon’s position, according to the statement.
Both sides agreed to intensify efforts to overcome obstacles and ensure the continuation of an international presence in southern Lebanon under the UN flag.
Lacroix began a visit to Lebanon on Wednesday, with no duration announced, during which he has been meeting officials to discuss UNIFIL’s future and the possibility of extending its mission.
He met Aoun, Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, Salam and army commander Gen. Rodolphe Haykal.
On Monday, the Council of the European Union adopted a decision establishing a new support mission in Lebanon for an initial three-year period to strengthen the capabilities of the Lebanese army and Internal Security Forces and support the country’s sovereignty and stability.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, during a visit to Lebanon on Oct. 7-8, stressed the need to avoid a security vacuum in the south after UNIFIL’s mandate ends.
UNIFIL operates in southern Lebanon under UN Security Council resolutions, with duties including monitoring the cessation of hostilities and supporting the deployment of the Lebanese army in its area of operations.
Discussions about the force’s future come as its current mission nears its end, amid international consultations on the nature of the UN presence in southern Lebanon in the next phase.

Yagera woman Jayda Allen Bonner remembered at Melbourne vigil

'We're living with wars behind our doors': Jayda Allen Bonner remembered at Melbourne vigil
In short:
Hundreds of mourners have gathered in Melbourne to pay tribute to a young Indigenous woman one week after she was killed in an inner-suburban apartment.
Jayda Allen Bonner was remembered as "a beautiful soul" by her mother and aunt, who have called for Australians to do more to prevent violence against women.
What's next?
Police investigations are continuing.
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.
Hundreds have gathered in Melbourne to pay tribute to a young Indigenous woman killed at an inner-suburban apartment complex last weekend.
A smoking ceremony was held in honour of 21-year-old Jayda Allen Bonner, who was remembered as "a beautiful soul" by her mother and aunt.
This week, a 31-year-old man was charged with murder and appeared briefly in the Melbourne Magistrates Court.
Police say he was known to Ms Allen Bonner.
Supporters of the Bonner family then marched to Victoria's Parliament to demand changes to domestic violence procedures and reform to better prevent violence against women.
Ms Allen Bonner's mother, Jade Allen, took part in the vigil, wearing a t-shirt emblazoned with an image of her daughter and the phrase 'Justice for Jayda'.
"Jayda loved her family fiercely. She had a heart of gold — she would do anything for anybody," Ms Allen said.
"I want everyone to stand up and stop keeping all of this quiet.
"I want to make sure Jayda's name isn't forgotten. She was one-of-a-kind."
Ms Allen Bonner's aunt Kellie Carter Bell said all Australians need to do more to speak out against violence against women.
"We're living with wars behind our doors,"
she said.
"We need recognition, we need people to understand what this stuff looks like.
"The question should be: What can I do to help (victim-survivors) get out safely?"
Questions raised over police response
Antoinette Braybrook, chief executive of Melbourne-based Aboriginal family violence service Djirra, said the 21-year-old's death was "devastating".
She said it was "outrageous" and "shocking" that Ms Allen Bonner could "fall through the cracks".
Ms Allen Bonner's family has previously said the young woman had made a complaint to police about her safety which she later withdrew.
Her family has also said they tried to contact police themselves, but were told that because Ms Allen Bonner was an adult, there was nothing they could do.
Ms Braybrook said that wasn't true.
"They have the power to investigate violence in the home and initiate their own intervention orders and charge people; my question is, why didn't they do that?"
Ms Braybrook added that it was not uncommon for women experiencing violence to withdraw their complaints to police, even if they were still in danger.
Speaking generally, she said women experiencing violence might be pressured into doing so or be threatened with further violence by their abusers.
"The perpetrator has absolute control, power and control over her in that situation,"
Ms Braybrook said.
"It's a consistent issue in our work."
While Djirra was now in contact with the young Yagera woman's family, Ms Braybrook said given the history of concern for Ms Allen Bonner's safety, it was "extremely disappointing" police or other authorities had not connected her with the service before her death.
"That's one of the concerns that we have as a specialist Aboriginal community-controlled organisation working on the frontline of Aboriginal women and children's safety," she said.
"I am just at a loss — I sit at the table, many tables, with police, with corrections, with courts and others, talking about how we can improve the safety of women.
"When things like this happen to women, it just makes those talks that we participate in all of the time seem like a joke."
A Victoria Police spokesperson said the death of a young woman in Carlton on October 10 was suspicious.
"The investigation is being led by the Homicide Squad," the police spokesperson said.
"As part of investigations, Victoria Police will thoroughly examine any interactions between police and the victim in the lead-up to her death.
"We are unable to comment further while the investigation remains ongoing."

Italy launches probe against Israeli defense minister

Italy launches probe against Israeli defense minister
Italy has expended its probe into the alleged torture and sexual abuse of activists from the Gaza-bound aid flotilla by Israel’s security forces to include Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz and twelve other high-ranking military, police and prison officials, the Rome Public Prosecutor’s Office has said.
Israel intercepted dozens of yachts in international waters and arrested more than 800 volunteers from various countries in October 2025 and May 2026, who were attempting to break West Jerusalem’s naval blockade of the Palestinian enclave. They were held for days before being deported.
The investigation was launched by Rome earlier this year after some 50 Italian nationals, who were part of the Global Sumud Flotilla missions, complained about being mistreated in Israeli detention, among other things reporting at least 15 cases of sexual abuse and rape. The probe had initially beeen centered on the country’s far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. A similar inquiry was initiated by France.
The Rome prosecutor's office said in a statement on Friday that the case against the Israeli officials concerns suspected torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage.
The activists detained after the 2025 mission reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism, the statement read. The participants of the second mission claimed to have been subject to even harsher treatment by Israeli security forces, including beatings in the dark and the use of tasers and rubber bullets, it added.
Prosecutors said they had sent a request for judicial assistance in the investigation to Israel in June, but it remains unclear if they received a response from West Jerusalem.
Italian law allows crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens to be prosecuted by Rome. If the probe finds the charges warranted, the country could formally request a trial of the Israeli officials.
Katz and Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir, who is now also under investigation, haven’t yet commented on the development. Ben-Gvir brushed off the Italian probe in June, saying that he would “continue to stand proudly alongside our fighters.”
West Jerusalem has repeatedly rejected accusations of mistreating the activists and described the flotilla missions as political provocations designed to aid the Palestinian armed group Hamas. The Israeli prison service said that the detainees were held “in accordance with the law, with full regard for their basic rights.”
Israel claims the blockade of Gaza is necessary to prevent weapons from getting into the enclave. It also denies withholding supplies for Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, almost 2 million of whom have been displaced since the outbreak of the conflict in October 2023, according to UN figures.
West Jerusalem sent its forces into Gaza in retaliation for a Hamas-led incursion in which some 1,200 people lost their lives and 250 others were taken hostage.
Israel’s airstrikes and ground offensive have cost the lives of more than 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, in Gaza over the past three years, the local health ministry has said. Over 1,500 deaths happened despite a US-brokered ceasefire being in effect in the enclave since October 2025.

From a marriage proposal to a fight for survival: Israeli couple recounts flydubai terror
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:08:07 UTC
17:08:07 KST

"I told her, 'Baby, I love you.' I couldn't believe this was how I was going to die." That is how Adar Hayut, one of the passengers who subdued the terrorist pilot on a flydubai flight, described the terror he experienced about two weeks ago when the plane went into a steep dive and he began thinking about saying goodbye to his family and his fiancée, Michal, to whom he had proposed during their trip to Japan.
"We weren't supposed to be on that flight," Hayut told ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth. "We had flown to Japan for a monthlong trip, during which I proposed to Michal. We had originally been booked on a different flight, but were switched to this one. We were sitting on the plane, and I was reading an article on my iPad and taking notes while Michal was looking at the flight map on the screen, going through the cities displayed and checking what there was to do in each one. Suddenly, the plane started going crazy, making random turns in every direction."
At that point, he said, he was focused on calming the panicked passengers.
"Someone shouted to fasten our seat belts. I hadn’t fastened my seat belt yet, and very quickly I found myself floating between my seat and the ceiling for two full seconds. I saw people around me panicking and shouted, 'Breathe deeply into your stomachs. Everything is OK. Fasten your seat belts.'"
Hayut buckled up. At that stage, he had no idea it was an attempted terrorist attack. He said he was convinced there was a mechanical problem, possibly causing the plane to stall, and that the pilot was trying unsuccessfully to regain control.
"I was certain we were going to die. I thought that if I got up, Michal and I would die apart, and I couldn't bear not being with her in our final moments."
But as the dive grew steeper and the plane went into a spin, Hayut realized there was no way out.
"I understood that we were going to crash," he said. "So many thoughts were racing through my head. I thought about people in similar situations who chose to say goodbye to their loved ones. I looked at Michal and told her, 'Baby, I love you.' I repeated it several times. I couldn't believe this was how I was going to die, that my family would have to go on living without me and that I wouldn't get to see the AI bubble burst."
Michal said she, too, wondered whether this was really how their story would end.
"We had been talking about starting a family and were excited to begin planning the wedding," she said. "I was terrified and felt we were going to die. I thought maybe I should record something for my parents."
It was then that Hayut heard the screams of Tali Manes, the wife of Tzvika Manes, who also helped subdue the terrorist. According to witness accounts, she was the first to alert passengers to what was happening and call for help.
"Someone shouted, 'We need people up front. We need people to help,'" Hayut continued. "Meanwhile, one of the flight attendants was moving toward the front of the plane, shouting for everyone to fasten their seat belts. When he reached the front, he turned back. His face fell, as though he had just seen death itself. As he headed toward the back of the plane, apparently to get a first-aid kit, he shouted, 'I can't believe it.'
"When I saw his face, I realized something else was probably happening. But what went through my mind was that one of the passengers had stabbed both pilots and that death was certain. I thought that if I got up, Michal and I would die apart, and I couldn't bear not being with her in our final moments."
After the plane stabilized, Hayut heard people shouting that they needed a doctor and decided to get up and help.
"I turned to Michal and asked, 'Is it OK if I get up?' She said, 'Go.' I ran toward the front, and when people tried to stop me, I told them I was a medical student," he recalled.
"I squeezed past people and entered the passageway leading to the cockpit, where a chaotic scene was unfolding amid a lot of shouting. Slightly to my left, I saw the Indian pilot lying on the floor, bleeding. The terrorist was curled up over the Indian pilot's legs, with Assaf Rajuan and Yaniv [Hayun] on top of him.
"I asked them who was flying the plane, and they told me, 'The pilot.' I could see a pilot sitting in the left seat of the cockpit, with blood smeared across his right shoulder."
Hayut initially went to help the injured Indian pilot but realized the terrorist had not yet been fully subdued. He left the pilot and moved to restrain the attacker. Then people began shouting that the terrorist had a knife.
"The terrorist was struck several more times. A flight attendant lowered a set of plastic restraints onto his exposed hand, and I tightened one. Without hesitating, I grabbed the hand that posed the threat, secured it with the second restraint and tightened it. I tightened it so much that it could cause tissue necrosis because, as far as I was concerned, there could be absolutely no chance of him breaking free," he said.
'We're picking up the pieces'
But then, according to Hayut, the flight attendants asked the passengers to loosen the terrorist's restraints.
"The flight attendants started arguing with us. They wanted to loosen the restraints a little, which made us suspicious that they might be against us."
Hayut described a confrontation with the crew that continued until the flight attendants began listening to the passengers.
At that point, Hayut again went to reassure the other passengers.
"I told them, 'Everyone, there has been a terrorist attack. The situation is under control. There's a pilot flying the plane,'" he said.
"I felt I had succeeded, but when I returned to the cockpit, I realized the issue of loosening the restraints hadn't been resolved, and things were heating up again.
"During the argument, Yaniv [Hayun] said, 'Guys, if we don't take charge here, I don't know how this is going to end.' I started pulling one of the flight attendants away. We struggled while standing, and I decided to calm things down. When I calmed down, he calmed down too, and they began to come around."
Michal said that even after the plane stabilized and the situation was brought under control, she and the other passengers remained terrified.
"At that point, we thought the terrorist was one of the passengers, and we didn't know whether he had accomplices. I felt I needed to arm myself with something to defend myself, and I was afraid he had brought some kind of explosive on board.
"Everyone was suspicious of the flight attendants. We didn't know who was cooperating with whom. There was a lot of tension until the plane landed."
About two weeks later, the couple is still struggling with the trauma.
"I still haven't processed it, and I feel like my body is still in shock. I haven't cried yet or fully let it all out," Michal said.
"I'm having a very hard time concentrating, and I have nightmares at night. I'm taking sleeping pills. I've always had trouble falling asleep, so now it's even more overwhelming. Physically, I still feel the tension from what happened on the plane, and it's affecting me."
The couple returned home safely but have yet to celebrate their engagement.
"No one asks us about Japan or the engagement. They ask about what we went through on the plane," they said.
"Fortunately, it ended well. We're trying to pick up the pieces because we need to start planning the wedding, but we still haven't fully recovered."

Russia rebuilt its Blackjack bomber on a new tech base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
08:05:01 UTC
17:05:01 KST

- Tupolev’s chief said 80% of the Tu-160M bomber’s systems and equipment were modernized, including avionics, navigation and engines.
- He said the bomber’s modular avionics will allow newer systems to replace outdated ones without redesigning the whole suite.
Russia’s Tupolev says about 80% of the systems and equipment on its new Tu-160M strategic bomber have been modernized, and that the aircraft’s onboard electronics were designed as a modular architecture so newer systems can be swapped in later without rebuilding the whole suite.
Tupolev General Director Yuri Abrosimov made the claims in comments published by Russian state defense conglomerate Rostec and Tupolev’s parent, United Aircraft Corporation. The Tu-160M keeps the outward look of the Soviet-era Tu-160 supersonic bomber, known in NATO as the Blackjack, but most of its systems, including avionics, navigation and engines, have been upgraded, he said.
“Outside, the Tu-160M has kept that same recognizable silhouette, but inside it was created on an entirely new technological base with active use of digital technologies. 80% of the systems and equipment were modernized,” said Abrosimov, in remarks translated from Russian.
According to Abrosimov, the modular avionics will let Russia integrate newer equipment over time in place of outdated systems, which he said would allow the bomber to keep up with emerging requirements and take on a wider range of missions. He did not specify which systems are new or name any planned additions.
The Tu-160 is a four-engine, variable-sweep-wing bomber that can carry up to 12 long-range cruise missiles in internal rotary launchers and serves in the air leg of Russia’s nuclear triad. Under the Tu-160M program, Kazan Aviation Plant is both upgrading older Tu-160s and building new aircraft, and earlier upgrade phases have added a new radar, a digital glass cockpit, new navigation and communication equipment, and NK-32-02 engines.
Russia signed a contract in January 2018 for 10 new Tu-160M bombers worth a reported 160 billion rubles. The first newly built aircraft flew in January 2022, but deliveries slipped repeatedly, and Russia’s Aerospace Forces received two Tu-160M bombers in late 2025, The Defence Blog reported.
The bombers have been used to launch cruise missiles at Ukraine. Analysis by the Ukrainian aviation monitoring channel AviVector, published in May, found that only seven of Russia’s 18 Tu-160M bombers were flying combat missions, while seven to nine aircraft were at the Kazan plant at any given time for modernization, maintenance or construction, The Defence Blog reported.

====================================================================================================

Restoration reveals architectural secrets of Istanbul’s Süleymaniye Mosque
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:48:50 UTC
16:48:50 KST

Restoration work at Istanbul’s Süleymaniye Mosque, a landmark of Ottoman design, has uncovered hidden acoustic vessels inside its dome, 16th-century decorative paintings and calligraphy preserved on a metal surface, shedding new light on the engineering techniques of architect Mimar Sinan.
Commissioned by Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent and completed on Oct. 15, 1557, the mosque is regarded as Sinan’s “masterpiece of the journeyman period.” The wider Süleymaniye complex includes religious schools, a hospital, a public kitchen and a bathhouse, reflecting the Ottoman approach to urban planning and social welfare.
Kaya Üçer, an associate professor at Mimar Sinan Fine Arts University who participated in the restoration, said the work had helped distinguish architectural evidence from long-standing popular beliefs about the building. One discovery concerned the mosque’s renowned acoustics. During restoration, workers erected approximately 20,000 cubic meters of scaffolding, allowing specialists to examine parts of the dome inaccessible from the floor.
“By chance, during repairs to some cracks in the dome, we found pitchers at the bottom, used alongside bricks,” Üçer said. “When you look up at the dome from below, you cannot see them. But from above, you understand that the openings soften the sound coming from below and prevent echoes.” The vessels, installed vertically in a zigzag pattern with openings at their bases, were examined through acoustic tests.
The dome also contains elaborate Baroque and Rococo-style floral decorations, despite the building’s origins in the 16th century. Researchers examined its painted layers under ultraviolet light and through careful scraping to identify earlier designs. They found traces of another decorative scheme beneath the existing ornamentation, suggesting that different designs had been tested before one was selected. The restoration team preserved the surviving historic elements while repairing the visible decorations.
Another unusual feature was found in the structure supporting the dome’s calligraphic inscription. Although the writing is traditionally associated with calligrapher Ahmed Karahisari, historical records also name his student Hasan Çelebi, while later restoration work is said to have included corrections by Abdülfettah Efendi in the 18th century. Üçer said the inscription’s background included a zinc surface, fastened with large nails, beneath a gold-leaf-covered wooden frame. The writing on the metal surface appeared to have been designed for exceptional durability. The team also identified a missing letter in the inscription and, after consulting calligraphy specialists, restored it in accordance with the scientific committee’s assessment.
Elsewhere, scraping work in the mosque’s arcades and the imperial gallery revealed original decorative paintings from Sinan’s era, including rumi motifs widely used in 16th-century Ottoman art. Missing sections were reconstructed based on surviving examples. The team also located a broken piece of the fountain’s water-level measuring structure in a museum in Istanbul’s Fatih district and confirmed that it fitted the missing section.
Üçer said the restoration had taken a period comparable to the mosque’s roughly seven-year construction and had been designed to protect the historic structure from requiring another major intervention for approximately 50 years.

Edward Burtynsky’s ‘Shifting Topography’ to be shown at COP31 in Antalya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:47:40 UTC
16:47:40 KST

A special selection from Canadian photographer Edward Burtynsky’s “Shifting Topography” exhibition will be displayed in the southwestern Turkish city of Antalya from Nov. 9 to 20 as part of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), bringing large-scale photographic works examining humanity’s impact on the planet to the international climate summit.
The selection draws on Burtynsky’s 2025-2026 exhibition at Perili Köşk, an arts venue in Istanbul, and focuses on how human activity has reshaped the natural environment. Through expansive images of industrial production sites, mines and agricultural landscapes, the photographer documents the physical traces of economic development and the lasting consequences of human intervention.
The exhibition will be presented at Akra Antalya through a collaboration with Borusan Contemporary. A key section of the exhibition is the “Erosion” series, commissioned by the Borusan Contemporary Art Collection with contributions from the Turkish Foundation for Combating Soil Erosion (TEMA). Featuring aerial photographs taken across Anatolia, the series brings together the geological history of the land and the effects of human activity, portraying changes to landscapes shaped over thousands of years.
The Antalya exhibition will also feature “In the Wake of Progress,” a 22-minute immersive multimedia work combining Burtynsky’s photographic output spanning several decades with music composed by Phil Strong.
The project, which will be presented in Türkiye for the first time, combines visual storytelling with an examination of the environmental consequences of industrialization and development. It will be accessible throughout the COP31 period.
COP31 will bring government representatives, climate negotiators and other stakeholders to Antalya to discuss global efforts to address climate change. The exhibition will offer visitors an artistic perspective on the relationship between human progress, environmental transformation and the long-term sustainability of the planet.

YOUTH PROTESTS THREATEN RAMA'S RULE

"Our country is the Albanian people," she said, the air around her thick with acrid tear gas. "They create the future, they create the now, and they are the ones who can bring our country forward. Not a single person, not a single government." REUTERS

Year-old startup wins spot in U.S. Army interceptor fly-off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:45:23 UTC
16:45:23 KST

- Furientis was selected as one of four vendors for a U.S. Army fly-off at the end of fiscal 2027 for a second IFPC Inc 2 interceptor.
- The year-old startup recently won its first funded Pentagon contract, raised $25 million, and unveiled a CAML launcher with Rheinmetall at AUSA.
Furientis, a missile startup founded just last year, has been picked as one of four companies to fly interceptors in a U.S. Army shoot-off at the end of fiscal 2027, competing to supply a second missile for the service’s Indirect Fire Protection Capability Increment 2 air defense system.
Co-founder and CEO Brody Franzen announced the selection, describing it as a downselect for a fly-off at the end of a fiscal year that closes on Sept. 30, 2027, without naming the other three companies chosen.
The Indirect Fire Protection Capability Increment 2, or IFPC Inc 2, is the U.S. Army’s mid-range air defense system for protecting bases and troops from cruise missiles, drones, rockets and artillery. Its truck-mounted Enduring Shield launcher, built by Leidos subsidiary Dynetics, now fires RTX’s AIM-9X Sidewinder, and the U.S. Army has spent the past few years looking for a second, more capable missile that can handle fast, low-flying cruise missiles and be built in larger numbers.
Lockheed Martin and a team of Boeing and Anduril are already competing in the formal second-interceptor program, which moved into its demonstration phase in September after Rafael’s U.S. subsidiary was not selected to continue. At the Association of the U.S. Army conference this week, Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, the service’s portfolio acquisition executive for fires, said the U.S. Army would open a parallel path for companies that missed that first cut but kept investing in their own designs, inviting them to bring missiles to the range for a shoot-off in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, Breaking Defense reported, and Furientis’ selection appears to be part of that track.
Franzen and Aris Simsarian, both former engineers at Virgin Orbit and Castelion, founded Furientis in 2025 in the Los Angeles area to build interceptors designed for mass production from readily available parts. The company puts final assembly time at about 30 minutes and says it flight-tests prototypes roughly every two weeks instead of spending years on design before flying.
The startup came out of stealth in May with a $5 million pre-seed round, and on Oct. 6 it announced both a $25 million seed round led by Benchmark and its first funded government contract, a prototyping agreement with the U.S. Department of War for a 100-mile-range interceptor intended for homeland defense.
According to Franzen, the IFPC selection capped a busy two weeks in which Furientis flew its first horizontal flight test on a government range for the U.S. Army’s low-cost interceptor effort and, at AUSA, unveiled a containerized launcher developed with Rheinmetall for the U.S. Army’s Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher program.
He credited the U.S. Army’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Fires and its defensive fires team, led by Brig. Gen. Guy Yelverton, for opening the door to nontraditional vendors and giving them the resources to speed up development, and said Furientis is now hiring as it prepares its interceptor for the shoot-off due by the end of September 2027.

Senegal-sized Antarctic glacier melting faster than thought: Why it matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:43:19 UTC
16:43:19 KST

Senegal-sized Antarctic glacier melting faster than thought: Why it matters
Thwaites glacier has been losing ice for decades. Now there are concerns of rapidly accelerating loss.
The world’s largest glacier is melting much faster and could add twice as much to global sea levels as previously expected over the next century.
New research published this week by a team of glaciologists has found that the Thwaites glacier in West Antarctica is losing mass rapidly because warm seawater is pushing underneath it and melting its core. This could add 1.2 inches (30mm) to water levels even if global warming does not accelerate as predicted.
The findings, published in the journal Nature Communications, add to a growing body of evidence that shows that the glacier, which has been receding for decades, is now losing mass even faster than scientists thought.
Researchers at the University of California in the United States collaborated with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory for the study. Here’s what we know about the findings:
What is Thwaites and why is it important?
Nicknamed the “Doomsday Glacier”, Thwaites is the largest glacier on Earth, spanning an area of around 192,000sq km (74,130sq miles) or roughly the size of Senegal – and larger than the US state of Florida.
It is located on the Walgreen Coast of Marie Byrd Land in remote western Antarctica and forms part of the great West Antarctic ice sheet, which includes other glaciers and is 14 times the size of Thwaites.
The glacier was first mapped in 1947 and is named after the late American glaciologist Fredrik T Thwaites, although he never visited it.
In the 1980s, scientists discovered that Thwaites is melting rapidly and have closely monitored its melting process as concerns have grown ever since.
Because it is so big, the glacier’s collapse would sharply raise global sea levels by a catastrophic amount – although researchers don’t project that will happen for many decades, or even a few centuries.
Together, Thwaites and other glaciers such as the Pine Island glacier – an ice stream in West Antarctica which flows into Pine Island Bay in the Amundsen Sea – act as a barrier that holds back the vast and vulnerable West Antarctic ice sheet. If melted, the ice sheet could cause many coastal cities to be submerged around the world.
At present, ice loss from Thwaites contributes around four percent of all global sea-level rise. Studies have calculated that the glacier has lost more than 1,000 billion tonnes of ice since 2000, and continues to lose 50 billion tonnes of ice per year.
Why is the glacier melting?
The main drivers are warm ocean water which is actively melting the Thwaites glacier from underneath it, according to several studies.
Ocean warming is caused by human-induced climate change, in particular from the burning of polluting fossil fuels.
In a 2019 study, the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory discovered a giant underwater cavity beneath the Thwaites glacier that spread across an area two-thirds the size of Manhattan, which researchers said was likely speeding up the glacier’s thinning.
Rising temperatures have caused glaciers to lose about five percent of their ice since 2000, according to the European Space Agency.
What has the latest research found?
Thwaites could add as much as 1.2 inches (30mm) – double the current estimates – to sea levels by 2100, even without any additional global warming, the study found.
The researchers said they used new computer models that paint a clearer picture of melting activity under the threatened glacier at its grounding line – the boundary where it transitions from resting entirely on bedrock to spreading out over the sea in the form of ice shelves.
Where other ice sheet models conclude a grounding line is fixed, the scientists said they developed the concept of a broader “grounding zone” instead. In this scenario, seawater lifts and lowers the ice in a “tidal pumping” process that allows warm water to reach “deep underneath the ice sheets and causing vigorous melting,” lead author Mattia Poinelli, a project scientist at UCLA, told media.
That melting process is accelerating the Thwaites’ “unpinning” from the Mouginot Ridge – an important underwater bedrock currently stabilising the glacier from below. The study concluded that there is a 60 percent chance that Thwaites could unpin from the ridge by the end of the century.
However, experts say more studies are needed to accurately predict the volume of Thwaites’ ice loss.
In separate findings, scientists from the British Antarctic Survey concluded that Thwaites will continue losing ice for at least the next 150 years, even under the most extreme ocean cooling conditions imaginable.
The study, which used computer simulation models that examined the melting effects of the ocean over the next century and a half, was published in Geophysical Research Letters in July.

Pakistan's finance minister on Saturday said the country had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices due to the Iran war, but that attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were "worrying" for the country's longer-term economic outlook.
In an interview on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Muhammad Aurangzeb said the South Asian country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.
"The first-order impact has been negotiated well by Pakistan," he said.
"We've had no shortage, no queues at the gas stations, and no law and order situation, which at times we have seen in some of the countries."
He added that unless the government saw "an absolute dire need", it would not be procuring spot cargoes on the LNG front, which tend to be far more expensive than previously contracted shipments.
Since the United States and ally Israel launched the war on Iran in February, global energy prices have surged as Tehran's retaliatory action has targeted Washington's Gulf allies and curtailed oil and gas supplies.
With Yemen's civil war flaring back to life as well, the Houthis there have repeatedly attacked Saudi infrastructure, including energy facilities and airports, in recent days.
Aurangzeb expressed alarm at the escalation, saying damage to such sites would delay a return to economic normalcy.
"What is now (the) worrying part of it is when the energy infrastructure starts getting hit," he said.
"I, to be very honest, I don't know where that would go. But one thing is very clear: that if the infrastructure continues to get hit, the return to normalcy, even if things subside, will take longer."
'Pushback'
Pakistan has been a frequent customer at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the lender of last resort to countries on the brink of default.
It is currently in the midst of its 25th programme with the Fund, at least 11 of which have been outright bailouts, since gaining independence in 1947.
The current programme totals around $7 billion over three years, with the Fund reaching an agreement this month to release a $1.2 billion tranche.
With global debt stocks running high, the Fund has called at this year's annual meetings on all economies, even those most vulnerable to the Iran war shock, to engage in fiscal consolidation to avoid a potential crisis.
"Fortunately for us, we have been on this fiscal consolidation path for a while," Aurangzeb said with a rueful smile.
The country's tax revenues have grown significantly in recent years, and the finance minister said the government was targeting the theft of taxes by private sector businesses that collected sales tax from consumers but never deposited it in government accounts.
Such theft accounted for billions of dollars, Aurangzeb said, adding that there remained "room for improvement" on increasing income tax collection as well.
He said the government's reform agenda had faced resistance from industry, lobbying groups and vested interests.
"Every reform, everything that you try to do when you try to change the status quo, there is pushback," he said.
One of the major pillars of the IMF's programme criteria is privatising state-owned assets in Pakistan, where the military runs a vast empire of businesses in sectors from real estate to fertiliser.
Asked about those companies, Aurangzeb denied that they were receiving state funding.
"As far as we are concerned, whichever commercial enterprises (the military) are running, they are running on a standalone basis and profitable on their own basis," he said.
"So, I can confirm to you, we are not providing any funds from the exchequer."
Pakistan's military has directly ruled the country for roughly two-fifths of its history, and under current army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, it has tightened its grip over key pillars of power, even as a civilian government remains nominally in charge of the state.

Somer, an apprentice once again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:42:24 UTC
16:42:24 KST

Somer Sivrioğlu has closed his award-winning restaurant Efendy and opened an ocakbaşı, a traditional Turkish grill restaurant, in its place. What might initially seem like a move towards simplicity is, in fact, driven by a much bigger ambition: To rediscover the relationship between meat, fat and fire and the mastery born of years of repetition. Sivrioğlu no longer wants simply to make excellent kebabs. He wants to elevate the knowledge of the usta — the master craftsman we call a kebapçı — to its rightful place in the world of gastronomy
Having spent years introducing Turkish cuisine to Australia before establishing a contemporary culinary language for Anatolian food at Efendy in Istanbul, Somer Sivrioğlu is now entering a new chapter in his culinary journey. This time, however, moving forward means looking back, towards one of the oldest ways culinary knowledge has been passed down: The master-apprentice tradition. Somer has closed Efendy, where he spent five years interpreting Anatolian cuisine through the lens of a contemporary chef-driven restaurant, and opened an “ocakbaşı,” a traditional Turkish grill restaurant, called Baharat in the very same space.
Efendy had earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand, four pearls from the İncili Gastronomy Guide and two toques from Gault&Millau. From the outside, then, the decision seems genuinely radical: Why close a chef-driven restaurant recognized by prestigious gastronomic guides to become a kebab chef?
When I put this question to Somer, his answer provided the key to understanding Baharat: “I believe making a truly good kebab requires more mastery than many of the dishes we prepare in fine dining.” It sounds like a bold claim at first. But consider the anatomy of a kebab and his point becomes clearer. In fine dining, a chef has considerable room for intervention: Techniques, sauces, textures, garnishes, presentation… A kebab offers nowhere to hide behind such complexity. There is meat, fat, a skewer and glowing embers. Every decision, from preparing the meat and determining the proportion of fat to threading it onto the skewer, judging the embers, adjusting its distance from the fire and choosing the precise second to remove it, is reflected directly in the final mouthful. The fewer the ingredients, the fewer places a master has to hide.
At a time when gastronomy seems perpetually obsessed with the “new”, the idea of perfecting the same thing through thousands of repetitions feels almost radical. One remark Somer made during our conversation has stayed with me: “I love the word kebapçı. Pideci, baklavacı, kebapçı…” Each of these words describes someone who has devoted years of their life to mastering a single craft. In recent years, our conversations about gastronomy have revolved around chef-driven restaurants, creativity, signature dishes, techniques and stars. Yet there is another form of knowledge that has carried the cuisine of these lands into the present: Craftsmanship. While a chef often feels compelled to create, a master craftsman strives to perfect. One pursues the new; the other finds greater depth by repeating the same movements thousands of times. And it is precisely this depth that fascinates Somer today.
In Baharat’s kitchen, the meat comes from eight- to nine-month-old male lambs of the “Thracian Kıvırcık” breed, sourced from the northwestern province of Balıkesir. Whole carcasses are butchered in-house daily; the meat is never minced in advance but ground and threaded onto skewers only when an order is placed. Butchery and kebabs are entrusted to Tuncay Usta, while the oven and “lahmacun,” a thin flatbread topped with spiced minced meat, are the domain of Müslüm Usta, a master from the southeastern province of Şanlıurfa. Leading the kitchen is Başak Daldaban, a female chef from the southern province of Adana with a fine-dining background who has worked alongside Somer since Efendy’s very first day.
In the predominantly male world of kebab restaurants, having a woman lead the kitchen is certainly noteworthy. But to my mind, what makes Başak’s story particularly interesting is not so much her gender as the role she plays. She is not there to replace the traditional masters; she brings different forms of craftsmanship together under one roof. The master’s accumulated knowledge and the chef’s ability to build systems come together in the same kitchen. Perhaps this is where Baharat’s true modernity lies.
That is also why the menu extends well beyond the familiar Adana–Urfa repertoire. Lahmacun is made with onions in winter, fresh garlic in spring, aubergines in summer and walnuts in autumn. When “keme,” a prized desert truffle, is in season, there is keme kebab; when loquats arrive, there is loquat kebab. Because Anatolia’s kebab culture is far more deeply connected to the land and the seasons than we often realize. When we present kebab to the world as little more than minced meat threaded onto a skewer, we erase much of the story we have to tell.
One of Somer’s most thought-provoking remarks was this: “I hope that one day the gastronomic elite in this country will accord Küşlemeci Halil Usta the same respect they give Arguinzoniz.”
It is a point worth dwelling on. As the international gastronomic community has rediscovered cooking over fire, it has elevated figures such as Spain’s Victor Arguinzoniz to the ranks of the world’s most respected culinary masters. Yet in Türkiye, we have largely confined the craftsmen who have spent generations working in front of the fire to the category of “good kebab makers.” We do not extend the same intellectual curiosity to our own masters. Why should knowledge accumulated over decades — of ember temperature, the structure of meat and the behavior of fat — not become a subject of serious gastronomic study? Why do we not document a kebab master’s thirty years of experience with the same rigor we apply to the knowledge of a fire-cooking master elsewhere in the world? It is for this reason that Somer plans to invite a master from a different region to Baharat every month. The first gathering will feature Ciğerci Mehmet Usta, a renowned liver specialist from Adana.
Towards the end of our conversation, Somer told me, “I want to devote the remaining years of my career to this.” That sentence makes Baharat, to me, far more interesting than simply another new restaurant. Because the most radical change in Somer Sivrioğlu’s career is not his decision to close Efendy and open an ocakbaşı. It is his willingness, after years spent championing the role of the chef, to become an apprentice once again at this stage of his career — and to devote himself to the pursuit of true mastery.
