Hanged, electrocuted and poisoned: The killers who survived execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:39:11 UTC
16:39:11 KST

"Take it off! Take it off! Let me breathe!" cried Willie Francis, a 17-year-old boy from Louisiana, after an electric current intended to kill him passed through his body. The year was 1946. Francis was strapped into the electric chair and prison officials had already thrown the switch. But instead of dying, his body convulsed, the chair shook — and he remained alive. Prison officials were forced to release him from his restraints and return him to his cell. A year later, they tried again. This time, they succeeded.
Francis' case became one of the most famous episodes in the history of capital punishment in the United States, but it was far from the only one. Throughout history, there have been documented cases of death row inmates surviving hanging, electrocution or attempts to kill them by lethal injection. Some survived because of technical malfunctions, others because of mistakes by execution teams. In exceptionally rare cases, prisoners survived even after the execution method itself had been administered.
These stories have returned to the headlines following the extraordinary case of Christa Pike, the Tennessee killer who survived two doses of execution drugs last month. But behind these remarkable stories lies a far more troubling question: What happens when a state sentences someone to death, attempts to carry out the punishment — and fails?
Hanged, declared dead — and revived before her autopsy
One of the earliest and most astonishing cases occurred in England in 1650. Anne Greene, a 22-year-old servant from the Oxford area, was convicted of infanticide after becoming pregnant by the grandson of the man who employed her and suffering a miscarriage. At a time when unmarried women who concealed pregnancies could be regarded as murderers if they could not prove the circumstances of their babies' deaths, she was sentenced to death by hanging.
In December of that year, Greene was taken to the gallows in Oxford. A rope was placed around her neck and she was hanged before a crowd of onlookers. According to historical records, she remained suspended for about half an hour, and people at the scene even pulled on her legs in an attempt to hasten her death.
She was then cut down and delivered in a coffin to doctors at the University of Oxford, who intended to dissect her body. But it emerged that Greene was still alive. The doctors detected signs of breathing and a pulse and began trying to revive her. They warmed her body, treated her and monitored her condition. Against all expectations, she gradually regained consciousness and recovered.
Her extraordinary survival caused a sensation. Some saw it as divine intervention, and the doctors who treated her helped secure a pardon. Greene was not returned to the gallows. She was released, married and had three children. According to a study published in the Journal of Medical Biography, she lived until 1659 — nine years after her supposed execution.
Her case became a local legend, and pamphlets and poems describing the woman who survived hanging circulated in England for years. Centuries later, her story continues to be examined in medical studies, including efforts to understand how she managed to survive for so long after being hanged.
'The man they could not hang'
More than 200 years later, in February 1885, another extraordinary incident occurred in England. John "Babbacombe" Lee was convicted of murdering his employer, Emma Keyse, and sentenced to death by hanging.
He was brought to the gallows at Exeter Prison, where executioner James Berry prepared to carry out the sentence. Lee was positioned on a wooden trapdoor designed to open beneath his feet, dropping him through the gallows.
But when the mechanism was activated, the trapdoor failed to open. Prison officials attempted to repair the malfunction and operate the gallows again, but the second attempt also failed. The same thing happened a third time.
Eventually, officials decided to halt the execution. The case attracted widespread attention across Britain, and Lee became known as "the man they could not hang." The British home secretary commuted his death sentence to life imprisonment.
Although Lee escaped the gallows, he was not immediately freed. He spent another 22 years in prison before being released in 1907. His subsequent fate remains uncertain, but his story is one of the best-known cases of an execution thwarted by a mechanical failure.
The teenager who survived the electric chair
The case of Willie Francis, more than 60 years after the failed attempts to hang Lee, ended very differently.
Francis, a Black teenager from Louisiana, was convicted of murdering Andrew Thomas, a white pharmacy owner who had previously employed him. He was sentenced to death in 1945, when he was 16, and on May 3, 1946, he was taken to the electric chair.
According to official testimony later presented to the U.S. Supreme Court, Francis was strapped into the chair, a hood was placed over his face and the operator threw the switch. The teenager's body convulsed violently and he jerked in his seat. One witness described how officials demanded that the electrical current be increased after it became clear that the boy was not dead, but the operator replied that he was already delivering the maximum possible power.
Francis continued breathing. He cried out for officials to remove the hood and let him breathe. After the attempt failed, prison officials released him and returned him to custody.
It later emerged that a malfunction in the chair's electrical system had prevented a sufficiently powerful current from passing through his body to kill him.
His lawyers argued that Louisiana had no right to execute him a second time. They maintained that another attempt would constitute cruel and unusual punishment, prohibited under the U.S. Constitution, and would expose him to the risk of death a second time under the same sentence.
The case reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which rejected Francis' arguments in January 1947. The majority held that the unintentional malfunction during the first attempt did not make a second attempt a violation of his constitutional rights.
On May 9 of that year, Francis was returned to the electric chair. This time, the system worked and he died at age 18.
His case became a significant legal precedent that continues to shape legal battles involving death row inmates who have survived execution attempts.
Eighteen needle punctures, two hours of pain — and a return to death row
In recent decades, most botched executions in the United States have involved the very method intended to replace the electric chair: lethal injection.
One prominent case was that of Romell Broom, who was convicted of kidnapping, rape and murder in Ohio and sentenced to death in 1985.
On September 15, 2009, Broom was taken to the execution chamber, placed on a gurney and restrained. The execution team began searching for a vein into which they could insert an IV line to administer the lethal drugs.
But the task proved exceptionally difficult. Time after time, team members inserted needles into Broom's arms and legs but were unable to find a suitable vein.
A total of 18 needle punctures were documented over approximately two hours. In one instance, a needle even struck bone. Broom cried and complained of pain as the team continued its attempts.
Eventually, officials decided to halt the execution. Broom was returned to his cell, with his death sentence still in effect.
He subsequently launched a legal battle to prevent the state from attempting to execute him again, arguing that the suffering he had already endured should rule out another attempt.
In 2016, however, the Ohio Supreme Court rejected his arguments in a 4-3 decision, allowing the state to set a new execution date.
Broom was never subjected to another execution attempt. In December 2020, more than 11 years after surviving the first attempt, he died in prison from complications of COVID-19. He was 64.
Cancer patient warned of the risks — and his execution attempt failed
In February 2018, Alabama attempted to execute Doyle Lee Hamm, a 60-year-old prisoner convicted of murder. But Hamm had advanced cancer, and his lawyers had warned before the execution that his medical condition would make it extremely difficult to find suitable veins for a lethal injection.
Despite the warnings, the state decided to proceed.
For approximately two and a half hours, members of the execution team attempted to insert needles into his body, including his legs and groin.
According to a medical report subsequently submitted to the court, at least 11 puncture marks were found on his body, along with bruising and other injuries.
Eventually, prison officials were forced to abandon the attempt. According to reports, Hamm was in such severe pain that staff had to carry him back to his cell.
Unlike Francis and other condemned prisoners, Hamm did not have to face the execution team again. A subsequent legal settlement stipulated that Alabama would not make another attempt to execute him, and he remained in prison. He died of cancer in November 2021 at age 64.
A year before the failed attempt to execute Hamm, a similar incident occurred in Ohio.
Alva Campbell, a 69-year-old prisoner suffering from lung cancer and other serious illnesses, was taken to the execution chamber in November 2017. The team made four attempts to establish an IV line but failed.
Campbell was returned to his cell and a new execution date was set for 2019. However, he died of natural causes in March 2018, before the state could try again.
They survived lethal injection — but the state found another way to kill them
Not everyone who survived an execution attempt managed to escape the death penalty indefinitely.
Kenneth Eugene Smith, convicted of involvement in a contract killing in Alabama, was taken to the execution chamber on November 17, 2022.
For hours, the execution team attempted to establish an IV line but failed to complete the procedure before the execution warrant expired at midnight.
Smith was returned to his cell alive. His lawyers later argued that the failed attempt had caused him severe psychological trauma, but Alabama remained determined to carry out his sentence.
In January 2024, Smith became the first person in the United States to be executed by nitrogen hypoxia, a method in which the oxygen a person breathes is replaced with nitrogen gas.
Alabama presented the method as an alternative to lethal injection, but the execution drew fierce criticism. Witnesses said Smith shook and writhed for several minutes, contradicting authorities' claims that he would lose consciousness quickly.
A similar case involved Alan Eugene Miller, who was convicted of murdering three people.
In September 2022, Alabama authorities attempted to execute him by lethal injection but were also unable to establish an IV line. The procedure was halted after more than an hour.
Miller's obesity, with his weight reaching 159 kilograms (350 pounds), significantly complicated efforts to locate suitable veins.
Two years later, in September 2024, Miller was executed using nitrogen gas. He became the second person in the United States to be executed by that method, after Smith.
Both condemned prisoners who survived their initial lethal injection attempts ultimately died when the state used a different execution method.
Eight needle attempts — and a prisoner still awaiting his fate
In February 2024, Thomas Eugene Creech, one of the longest-serving death row inmates in the United States, was taken to the execution chamber in Idaho.
Creech, who was convicted of multiple murders, had spent decades in prison and was set to become the first person executed by the state in 12 years.
For about an hour, the execution team attempted to insert an IV line into his arms and legs. Eight attempts were made, but each time, the vein located proved unsuitable or the team was unable to insert the needle properly.
. (Tennessee Department of Correction)
Eventually, the prison warden decided to halt the procedure. Creech was returned to his cell, and Idaho began examining changes to its execution protocol.
His subsequent legal argument that another attempt would constitute prohibited punishment was also rejected.
He remains alive under a death sentence.
In May 2026, a similar incident occurred in Tennessee.
Tony Carruthers, convicted of murdering three people, was taken to the execution chamber. The team successfully established an initial IV line but was unable to insert the additional line required under the state's procedures.
After more than an hour of attempts, the procedure was halted.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee announced that he was granting Carruthers a reprieve of at least one year.
Four months later, the same state would find itself at the center of a far more extraordinary case.
Seven needles, two doses of lethal drugs — and Christa survived
On September 30, 2026, Christa Pike, 50, was taken to the execution chamber in Tennessee.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
Despite difficulties inserting the needles, the execution team administered two doses of pentobarbital, a drug intended to cause her death.
But Pike continued breathing.
She was rushed to a hospital unconscious and in critical condition, and doctors and her lawyers feared she would not survive.
Emergency call recordings released afterward revealed that efforts to save her life were also marred by failures.
After the execution attempt failed, more than half an hour passed before emergency responders were allowed into the prison, partly because dispatchers initially suspected the call was a hoax.
Witnesses continued to hear Pike breathing heavily even after the curtain in the execution chamber was closed. It remains unclear what medical treatment she received during those minutes.
On October 10, Pike was discharged from the hospital and returned to prison, where she continues to receive medical care.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, she is the first known person to survive an execution attempt after lethal drugs were administered.
Experts believe the drugs may not have properly entered her bloodstream, but the official cause of the failed execution has yet to be determined.
Following the incident, Tennessee's governor ordered a suspension of further executions pending an investigation into the failures, and the state's corrections commissioner resigned.
The question of whether the state will attempt to execute Pike again remains unresolved.
Can a person be executed twice?
Pike's case brings the American legal system back to a question considered nearly 80 years ago following Willie Francis' survival: Does a failed execution attempt effectively constitute the carrying out of a person's sentence, and would another attempt violate the constitutional prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment?
The ruling in Francis' case established that the mere failure of an execution attempt does not necessarily prevent a second attempt.
However, legal experts point to the distinction between a case in which equipment fails before the punishment is administered and one in which a lethal substance has already been injected into a person's body, causing suffering and other consequences.
The issue becomes even more pressing in light of data on botched executions.
A study by Amherst College professor Austin Sarat, which examined 8,776 executions in the United States between 1890 and 2010, found that 276 had gone wrong in some way — approximately 3.15%.
The highest failure rate was recorded in lethal injections, long considered a more advanced and humane method of execution: approximately 7.2%.
The stories of Francis, Greene, Broom, Smith and Pike differ greatly.
Some took place centuries ago, others in recent years. Some of the condemned prisoners were convicted of particularly brutal crimes, and victims' families waited years for their sentences to be carried out.
Yet all these cases point to a single reality: Even a procedure designed to end a human life is not immune to mistakes, malfunctions and unexpected failures. For some condemned prisoners, survival meant genuine salvation. For others, it was merely a temporary postponement of death.
Willie Francis survived the electric chair but died in it a year later. Kenneth Smith and Alan Miller survived lethal injection attempts but were ultimately executed using nitrogen gas. Others died in prison without the state ever succeeding in carrying out their death sentences.
Now, nearly 80 years after Francis cried out to be allowed to breathe, the United States once again faces the same question: What happens when a person the state has decided to kill refuses, against all expectations, to die?

- UK Defence Innovation launched a £2.45 million Tactical Power Challenge for the British Army to find better battlefield power generation, storage and charging technologies.
- The competition, run with Australia’s ASCA, closes for first-stage bids on Nov. 10, 2026, with funded demonstrations due by March 2028.
The British Army is looking for new ways to power its troops in the field, offering £2.45 million ($3.26 million) to companies that can develop better batteries, faster chargers and quieter alternatives to the diesel generators units rely on today.
UK Defence Innovation, the Ministry of Defence’s innovation arm, launched the Tactical Power Challenge on Oct. 15 on behalf of the British Army, with support from the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory, known as Dstl. The competition is being run alongside Australia’s Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator, which has its own parallel effort on distributed tactical power, and first-stage bids are due by noon GMT on Nov. 10, 2026, according to the UK government announcement.
The push stems from how much more electricity armies now use. Radios, drones, sensors, electronic warfare kit, counter-drone systems and battlefield computers all need power, and research and experimentation by the British and Australian armies found a sharp rise in power demand driven by digital and autonomous systems. Most of that power still comes from fuel-burning generators, which are noisy, hard to move and depend on regular fuel deliveries.
“Reliable and deployable power is fundamental to maintaining operational advantage,” said John Cunningham, director of innovation responsible for UK Defence Innovation.
The challenge has two parts. The funded strand, called Innovative Tactical Power, is a two-stage competition for technologies at an early-to-middle stage of development, roughly from lab prototypes to systems tested in a relevant environment, which winners would mature and demonstrate by March 2028. A separate, unfunded strand called Immediate Power is aimed at more mature products that could meet current needs quickly, and companies with promising systems may be invited to join British Army trials and experiments in the UK.
The Army’s wish list includes safer battery chemistries that hold at least as much energy as lithium-ion cells, high-speed charging, new types of power generation, and equipment to store, manage and distribute electricity across dispersed units. It also wants technology that lets troops operate silently, cuts the fuel they need to haul, supports uncrewed and robotic systems, and includes power sources soldiers can carry themselves. Both complete systems and individual components are eligible.
“British industry is central to delivering the capabilities our Armed Forces need for the future. This challenge will help identify and develop sovereign technologies that can improve operational energy resilience, support deployed personnel and strengthen the UK defence innovation ecosystem,” said Cunningham.
The British Army has a requirement for more than 4,000 Lightweight Field Generators and is studying how to modernize its tactical power as current systems near replacement, giving companies that perform well a possible route into future procurement.
Bids may be shared with Australia’s Department of Defence for assessment, and results from funded projects may be passed to Australian and U.S. defense partners under information-sharing arrangements. Second-stage submissions will be by invitation only, with demonstration work due to finish by March 2028.

Sweden extradited 52-year-old Russian citizen Alexandr Suvorov to the U.S., where he is accused of illegally supplying American microelectronics to Russia in circumvention of sanctions.
This was reported by the U.S. Department of Justice.
According to the U.S. investigation, from March 2022 to April 2023, he ran a procurement network that supplied dual-use electronic components to Russia through GS Group Limited, a company registered in Hong Kong. According to the investigation, some of these components can be used in military communications and radar systems, as well as in high-precision positioning systems.
“According to the charges, Alexandr Suvorov organized an international procurement network that illegally supplied U.S.-manufactured electronic components with military applications to buyers in Russia,” said Roman Rozhavsky!, assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division.
Suvorov was extradited to the Northern District of New York on October 15. The next day, he was scheduled to make his first court appearance in Albany.
He faces three charges: conspiracy to launder money in international transactions, illegally exporting goods from the United States, and violating the Export Control Reform Act.
Under the first and third counts, Suvorov faces up to 20 years in prison; under the second, up to five years. He may also face a fine.
More than three-quarters of the onboard computer in Russian Geran-4 drones consists of electronic components manufactured by American companies.
Products from Texas Instruments account for the largest share, along with components from National Semiconductor, which it acquired—more than half.
In early October, the U.S. Department of the Treasury imposed sanctions against the A7 shadow banking network, which is linked to Russia and Iran.
A7 developed a large-scale network of front companies that allows Russia to circumvent Western sanctions and purchase goods for its military-industrial complex.

Türkiye seeks inclusion as France, Germany agree on car rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:22:16 UTC
16:22:16 KST

Türkiye has been left outside a Franco-German automotive proposal announced on Oct. 16 that would give Britain conditional access to the EU’s planned “Made in EU” support scheme.
The agreement brings France and Germany closer on rules governing which vehicles qualify for public procurement and financial support. For Türkiye, a major production base supplying European markets, the concern extends to future model allocations and factory investment.
The proposal still needs support from other EU member states and the European Parliament before becoming law.
Under the Franco-German plan, the automotive provisions would cover the EU’s 27 members and allow European partners that were part of the single market on Jan. 1, 2020, to opt in.
That definition provides a route for Britain, which left the single market at the end of 2020, but does not include Türkiye.
Participation would require reciprocal treatment and continuing alignment with EU rules on investment from third countries and trade protection.
For Britain, this could mean adopting the bloc’s measures restricting imports of Chinese-made electric and hybrid vehicles.
The agreement narrows a longstanding difference between Paris and Berlin.
France had sought to reserve support for production within the EU, while Germany favored including trading partners closely integrated into European automotive supply chains.
The wider rules are being negotiated under the Industrial Accelerator Act, which would introduce European-content requirements for vehicles benefiting from public purchasing and support schemes.
A joint statement released by French President Emmanuel Macron’s office said the aim was to reduce emissions while strengthening Europe’s capacity to develop and manufacture the next generation of electric vehicles.
It linked that transition to investment, research and production in France, Germany and across Europe.
Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa had advocated a similar approach at the Paris Motor Show, calling for incentives for companies investing in European design, research and development, factories and suppliers.
He also urged a swift agreement on emissions rules and measures supporting European production.
The Franco-German compromise combines that industrial preference with concessions on emissions.
It would retain the European Commission’s proposed 90 percent reduction in CO2 emissions from new cars by 2035, compared with 2021 levels, while removing the requirement to offset the remaining emissions through measures such as low-carbon steel and alternative fuels.
That change would give manufacturers greater flexibility to continue selling combustion-engine and hybrid vehicles beyond 2035, in line with German industry demands.
For Türkiye, the debate concerns its largest automotive export market. The sector exported $41.5 billion in 2025, with EU countries accounting for $30.1 billion, or 72.5 percent, according to the Uludağ Automotive Industry Exporters’ Association.
Trade Minister Ömer Bolat pressed Türkiye’s case during talks in Brussels earlier in the week.
“Türkiye must be accepted from the very beginning as an equal partner within the framework of the ‘Made with Europe’ concept,” he said on Oct. 14.
Bolat said European companies accounted for nearly 75 percent of Türkiye’s automotive production.
He warned that excluding the country could disrupt the production and supply relationships established through its three-decade customs union with the EU, harming investment, employment and exports on both sides.
The Commission’s March draft already provides for content from customs-union and free-trade partners to receive equivalent treatment in certain procurement and support schemes, subject to conditions.
Bolat said that restrictive automotive provisions nevertheless remained and that Ankara was seeking changes through talks with EU institutions and manufacturers.
Toyota also called for a broader agreement on Oct. 16.
Its European division welcomed discussion of Britain’s inclusion but said the arrangement should extend to other trusted partners, including Türkiye and Japan, whose cooperation could support European competitiveness.
The company said wider inclusion would also benefit future investment decisions, including a battery production study.

France rolls out fifth new nuclear attack submarine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:22:01 UTC
16:22:01 KST

- Naval Group rolled out Rubis, the fifth of six Barracuda nuclear attack submarines for the French Navy, at Cherbourg on Oct. 16, 2026.
- Four boats have already been delivered since November 2020, and France plans to receive all six by 2030.
Naval Group has rolled out Rubis, the fifth of six Barracuda nuclear-powered attack submarines it is building for the French Navy, moving the boat out of its construction hall at the company’s shipyard in Cherbourg on Oct. 16, 2026.
The submarine was transferred onto the yard’s floating shiplift platform in the presence of Catherine Vautrin, France’s minister for the armed forces and veterans. Naval Group will now finish outfitting the boat and run a series of trials alongside the quay and then at sea before handing it over to the French Navy.
“It is with great pride and a deep sense of responsibility that we today transferred the Rubis, the fifth Suffren-class nuclear attack submarine, to its launch platform. This crucial milestone comes just 17 months after that of the nuclear attack submarine De Grasse, a symbol of our commitment to our customers,” said Pierre Éric Pommellet, chairman and CEO of Naval Group.
The program is known as Barracuda, and the boats themselves are called the Suffren class after the first submarine in the series. It is replacing the six Rubis-class attack submarines France put into service from the 1980s, and the new Rubis takes the name of the boat that led that older class. France’s defense procurement agency, the DGA, runs the program with the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission, which handles the nuclear reactors, and the plan calls for all six submarines to be delivered by 2030.
Four are already in service or delivered. Suffren was handed over in November 2020, followed by Duguay-Trouin and Tourville, and De Grasse was delivered in June 2026, about 13 months after its own rollout in May 2025 and four months after it first went to sea. If Rubis follows a similar path, it will spend the coming months on quayside testing, reactor startup and sea trials. The sixth and final boat, Casabianca, is also under construction.
The Suffren-class boats are about 99 meters (325 feet) long and displace roughly 5,300 tonnes submerged. They carry F21 heavyweight torpedoes, Exocet SM39 anti-ship missiles and MBDA’s naval cruise missiles, which give the French Navy the ability to strike targets on land from a submerged submarine, and they can carry and deploy special forces.
Naval Group designs and builds the submarines and produces the main components of their nuclear propulsion plants with TechnicAtome. It also provides logistical support and maintenance for the boats in Toulon, the home port of France’s attack submarine force on the Mediterranean.
About 3,000 people are working on the design and construction of the submarines, including around 800 from Naval Group subcontractors, up from the 2,500 the company cited when De Grasse rolled out last year.

Australia's first Vietnamese heritage museum opens in Melbourne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:21:12 UTC
16:21:12 KST

Australia's first Vietnamese heritage museum opens in Melbourne after decade-long push
In short:
The first Australian museum dedicated to the Vietnamese refugee experience has opened Melbourne.
Vietnamese-Australians are one of the country's largest migrant groups and many fled after the country's civil war ended.
A community campaign helped galvanise interest in the museum concept, with bipartisan support for the new centre.
Before the days of bánh mì takeaways and discount flight holidays, to most Australians Vietnam was known only for the horrors of conflict and conscription.
That was to change with the end of the Vietnam War.
Thousands of Vietnamese refugees made the perilous journey to Australia in the mid-1970s, saying an abrupt goodbye to Saigon and an apprehensive hello to Melbourne's Sunshine and St Albans or Sydney's Cabramatta and Canley Vale.
Five decades on, refugee beginnings and generational achievement were recognised with the opening of the nation's first museum dedicated to Vietnamese-Australian history.
Constructed on a council car park in Sunshine, the unveiling of Vietnamese Museum Australia marked the culmination of a decade-long campaign to establish a permanent monument to the community's pioneering generation.
The parents of the museum's chief executive, Tammy Nguyen, escaped Vietnam on a perilous six-day, seven-night boat journey.
"There are more than 350,000 people of Vietnamese-origin living in Australia and everyone has their own unique story to tell," Ms Nguyen said.
"This museum is a living monument to all those who courageously left their homeland behind — often as refugees on overcrowded and unseaworthy boats — seeking freedom and a better future."
The project has received bipartisan support, with Victorian Premier Ben Carroll officially opening the centre on Saturday alongside MPs from across the political divide.
Both the federal and Victorian governments contributed millions to the project, alongside grassroots community contributions.
Liberal MP Trung Luu, who represents the Western Metropolitan Region in the state's upper house, said the museum's opening was a significant day for the Vietnamese community.
"As someone who came to Australia as a refugee from Vietnam, today is deeply personal for me," he said.
"This museum honours the courage of every family who made that journey."
University of Melbourne development studies professor Lan Anh Hoang said public attitudes towards Vietnamese refugees in the 1970s and 1980s were mixed as the nation adjusted to life post-White Australia policy.
"In the immediate aftermath of the fall of Saigon, there was a great deal of sympathy and compassion, particularly because of Australia's own involvement in the war,"
she said.
"But as boat arrivals continued towards the end of the 1970s, concerns grew about uncontrolled migration, and the legacy of the White Australia policy meant that racial anxieties still lingered."
Professor Hoang said Vietnamese migrants to Australia who relocate in 2026 find themselves in a more welcoming environment.
But she added that they also tended to be more educated or skilled, with better English proficiency than the refugees who came in the 1970s.
"Many describe the kindness and generous support of churches and community organisations (in the 1970s)," she said.
"At the same time, Vietnamese families and their children faced more than their fair share of racism in the community and at school.
"It was not easy to be a Vietnamese kid growing up in Australia at that time."
University of Technology Sydney sociology professor Andrew Jakubowicz said the mid-1970s intake of Vietnamese-Australians under the Fraser Government was the first real test of the post-White Australia policy consensus.
Malcolm Fraser became a champion of the Vietnamese-Australian diaspora and members of the community paid tribute to the ex-PM at his 2015 funeral.
"(Vietnamese-Australians) were admitted as the first big group of refugees from a group that had almost no prior presence," Professor Jakubowicz said.
"Initially, most were Catholic southerners and pro-Saigon. Their actual travel to Australia was traumatic — they were the first modern boat people.
"They arrived in the shadow of the end of White Australia into a country that was trepidatiously ready to accept Asians.
"Before then, most Asians admitted after 1967 were English-speaking professionals."

Greece will do everything possible to support Ukraine but will not take steps that compromise its own national defense capabilities, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in Brussels on Friday, Oct. 16.
Speaking to Radio Liberty on the sidelines of the European Council summit, Mitsotakis addressed questions regarding whether Athens would transfer Patriot surface-to-air interceptor missiles from its military stockpiles to Kyiv.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Mitsotakis declined to comment publicly on whether the Ukrainian government had submitted a formal request for the systems, while emphasizing Greece’s security priorities in the Eastern Mediterranean.
“You know that we have supported Ukraine by providing significant air defense assets from our stockpiles,” Mitsotakis told reporters.
“At the same time, I want to be completely candid: we will do everything possible to support Ukraine without undermining Greece’s defense capabilities. We are also in a security-sensitive region, we have other obligations, but we stand by Ukraine and always try to do everything possible.”
While Greece has previously transferred shorter-range air defense systems to Ukrainian forces, Athens has not officially announced or authorized deliveries of long-range Patriot interceptors.
According to Greek newspaper Kathimerini, Kyiv approached Athens with a request to acquire up to 200 Patriot PAC-2 missiles.
General Staff Reports 222 Clashes on Wednesday as Russia Continues Pressing Pokrovsk Axis
Ukrainian defense planners noted that after 23 years of operational service in the Hellenic Air Force, portions of the Greek PAC-2 stockpile are nearing the end of their certified operational shelf life.
Allied pressure on aging Southern European stockpiles
The statements by the Greek head of government follow coordinated diplomatic efforts by NATO and EU defense officials to persuade Greece and Spain to transfer aging surface-to-air missiles to Ukraine.
Athens and Madrid maintain some of Europe’s largest national inventories of Patriot PAC-2 interceptors, systems that Ukrainian defense planners require to defend urban population centers and electrical grid infrastructure from Russian ballistic and cruise missile strikes.
Military data cited by The Telegraph indicates that Greece holds at least 200 Patriot PAC-2 missiles whose certified 23-year lifespan is approaching expiration.
Allied defense coordinators have argued that transferring aging munitions before they exceed statutory operational limits represents a practical arrangement, noting that expired missiles require expensive, logistically complex factory recertifications.
“We know that some countries have interceptor missiles that will expire soon,” EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas stated during multilateral consultations in Ireland last month. “So it would be very good if they were transferred to Ukraine.”
While Spanish military stockpile figures remain classified, Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares confirmed last month that Madrid agreed to deliver five Patriot interceptors to Kyiv.
Zelensky appeals for 300 Patriot interceptors ahead of winter
The Greek position comes as President Volodymyr Zelensky delivered an urgent appeal to EU heads of state in Brussels on Friday, Oct. 16, calling for 300 Patriot interceptors alongside €70 billion ($79 billion) in financial assistance for the upcoming year.
Addressing the European Council summit, Zelensky warned that Ukrainian forces have depleted critical stockpiles of surface-to-air interceptors capable of neutralizing Russian ballistic missiles, leaving civilian energy networks vulnerable as winter temperatures approach.
“I ask you to really focus on helping us get PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors,” Zelensky said in his address to EU leaders. “Ukraine can’t get by on just two or four missiles from a country every few months. We need a winter package – we always spoke about it between us – of missiles: 300 Patriot interceptors specifically against ballistic missiles.”
Ukrainian officials have emphasized that defending regional electrical generation and distribution nodes against combined ballistic missile and turbojet drone strikes requires steady munition supplies, warning that piecemeal transfers remain insufficient to ensure persistent airspace defense.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

A senior Hamas official told the London-based Saudi newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat that Ali al-Amoudi, who is considered the terrorist organization's leader in the Gaza Strip, was wounded in an Israeli strike targeting him two weeks ago.
According to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, Amoudi, dubbed "Sinwar's successor," was inside the apartment targeted in the strike but survived because he was in a separate part of the residence.
According to the report published Saturday morning, the official said Amoudi was in good condition and receiving treatment at a secure location. This marks the first time a senior Hamas official has acknowledged that Israeli intelligence correctly identified the target of the strike.
Amoudi, Hamas' former head of public relations, was released in the 2011 Gilad Shalit prisoner exchange and has emerged over the past year as one of the central figures overseeing Hamas' affairs in Gaza. He is competing against Nizar Awadallah for the leadership of the terrorist group's political bureau in the Strip.
The strike, carried out on a Saturday morning two weeks ago in western Gaza City, exactly three years after the October 7 massacre, reportedly killed five people, including four women. At the time, Asharq Al-Awsat quoted three Hamas sources who expressed doubts that Amoudi had been killed. One believed he had been at the scene but may have survived.
The assassination attempt was part of an Israeli military campaign targeting senior Hamas figures in recent weeks, including the commander of Hamas' northern Gaza brigade, Izz al-Din Bik, the head of Hamas' finance department, Mohammed Abu Alwan, and the commander of Hamas' Rafah Brigade, Nael Abu Obeid.
Two days after the strike, senior Hamas official Ghazi Hamad said Amoudi had survived. Speaking to the Saudi news channel Al Arabiya, Hamad accused Israel of violating the Gaza ceasefire agreement by continuing its policy of targeted killings. "The Israeli assassinations are putting the Gaza agreement at risk of collapse," he said. He also placed responsibility on Washington, saying, "The United States is responsible for saving the Gaza agreement and must pressure Israel to stop the assassinations."
Amoudi was born in the Gaza Strip and lives in Khan Younis. He was linked to the murder of Shin Bet security coordinator Noam Cohen and was arrested in 1994 by troops from the IDF's undercover Duvdevan unit in the village of Abu Dis, east of Jerusalem. While his accomplices exchanged fire with the soldiers surrounding the house, Amoudi emerged with his hands raised and sustained only minor injuries in the incident.
He was sentenced to life in prison but was released in the 2011 Shalit prisoner exchange, along with Yahya Sinwar and approximately 1,000 other terrorists.
His ties to Sinwar are considered a defining feature of his career within Hamas. The two met while serving prison sentences in Israel and maintained their relationship after their release. During Sinwar's first term as head of Hamas' political bureau in Gaza, from 2017 to 2021, Amoudi served as his bureau chief.
In 2021, Amoudi was elected to Hamas' political bureau and was appointed head of the group's public relations department that same year. In that role, he helped formulate Hamas' communications strategy and messaging and coordinated between the group's political leadership and operational units.
Following Sinwar's killing in October 2024 and the deaths of numerous other senior Hamas leaders in Gaza during the war, Amoudi's standing within the organization grew. According to reports, he assumed responsibility for managing the affairs of Hamas' political bureau in Gaza and became a central figure in overseeing the group's operations on the ground.
During this period, his name was linked to a series of organizational changes and appointments within Hamas' structures in Gaza. Reports also indicated that some of these moves sparked disagreements among senior officials, with questions raised within Hamas over how he had acquired his authority.
Amoudi is now competing with Nizar Awadallah for Hamas' top leadership position in Gaza. The first round of voting ended without a clear winner, and the decisive round was suspended after Awadallah appealed aspects of the election process.
According to sources cited by Al Arabiya and Al Hadath, Khaled Mashal and Zaher Jabarin support Awadallah, while Amoudi has the backing of Khalil al-Hayya, head of Hamas' political bureau. However, Asharq Al-Awsat reported that it remains unclear whether al-Hayya supports either candidate.
Despite his longstanding ties to Sinwar and his involvement in managing Hamas' affairs in Gaza, Amoudi is not regarded as a commander of the group's military wing. Rather, he is a senior political and organizational figure whose influence has grown significantly following the killing of much of Hamas' top leadership during the war.

‘I cannot carry all of this alone’: the couples kept apart by the war in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:00:24 UTC
16:00:24 KST

Wijdan Abu Matar, 43, was forced to leave Gaza in November 2023 with her eight children for medical treatment, while her injured husband, Hatem, remained behind.
Wijdan and her family were living in the Nuseirat refugee camp when the Gaza war began with the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. Ten days later, on 17 October that year, an Israeli strike hit the al-Muhandseen tower, near their home, injuring Wijdan and every member of her family.
“We were sitting together, just about to start lunch when the bombing happened,” Wijdan recalled. “The ceiling collapsed over our heads. Everything went dark. I couldn’t see anything. I just started screaming the names of my sons and daughters.”
Her daughter Nour, 15, suffered the most serious injuries, including a fractured skull and bleeding in the brain. Five-year-old Amna suffered severe burns to her chest. The family was initially separated after the strike.
Nour spent about 33 days in intensive care, with Wijdan by her side. Amna and Aysel, three and a half, were at a different hospital for 15 days.
On 30 November 2023, Wijdan travelled with Nour to a hospital in Egypt for treatment. For months, the family remained scattered across Egypt, receiving medical treatment and staying with other relatives.
“I felt completely helpless,” Wijdan said. “There was a fire in my heart because I was away from my husband and my family was scattered.”
Eventually, Wijdan managed to bring her children together in an apartment in Egypt. Three years on, however, she is still separated from her husband, who remains in Gaza. “I have become both the mother and the father to my children,” she said. “The responsibility is exhausting me, and I am constantly worried about my husband.”
Hatem suffered a serious leg injury that limits his mobility and is now displaced in a tent in Nuseirat. Even speaking to him is difficult because of Gaza’s unreliable internet connection. “When he manages to get online, he calls me and the children. He tells me, ‘I am counting the days until I can see you again.’ I can see the tears in his eyes,” Wijdan says.
Wijdan has no regular source of income and relies on donations. Hatem stopped receiving a salary 10 months ago and his injury prevents him from working.
In Egypt, life is difficult for Wijdan and her family. She says she cannot afford transportation to send five of her children to school. “I see my children’s future slipping away in front of me, and there is nothing I can do.”
Nour still requires medical treatment, but Wijdan often cannot afford her medication. She sometimes considers returning to Gaza to be with Hatem, but fears exposing her children to further suffering.
“I dream of getting my children the treatment they need, and I hope we can reunite with my husband as soon as possible so he can also receive treatment,” Wijdan said. “I cannot carry all of this alone. Psychologically, I am exhausted. I have lost 35 members of my family in this war.”
Since the war began with Hamas’s attack on Israel that killed 1,200 people, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry. Earlier this year an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continues to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.
Sami Abu Tabaq, a 29-year-old Palestinian photojournalist, was forced to leave the Gaza Strip in April 2024, leaving behind his family and his fiancee, Ola.
“Loneliness kills me every day,” he said. “Life away from the woman I love and my family is incredibly hard. I’m desperately waiting for the day God brings us together again.”
Sami became engaged to Ola five months before the war began. They had met by chance when he chose her family’s home as a location for a photoshoot. Before the war, they saw each other constantly. They went to the sea, had dinner at restaurants in Gaza, and spent months preparing the house where they planned to live after their wedding, which was scheduled for November 2023.
Sami and his family fled their home in Tal al-Zaatar, Jabaliya, early on in the war. Their home was badly damaged and later destroyed, along with the house Sami and Ola had been planning to move into once they got married.
When his sister decided to flee south with her children, Sami accompanied her but he could not reach Ola to say goodbye.
The separation became unbearable. Days, sometimes weeks, passed without Sami knowing whether Ola was alive. Once, he saw reports that an entire residential block near her home in Gaza City had been bombed. “I almost lost my mind. I had never felt so helpless,” he said. Unable to return north, he asked his brother to check on her. Eventually, his brother confirmed that she and her family were alive.
Sami continued working as a photojournalist from southern Gaza. Four journalists who had shared his tent were later killed, including Hamza al-Dahdouh, a son of the Al Jazeera journalist Wael al-Dahdouh.
As Israel threatened a ground invasion of Rafah in 2024, Ola began urging Sami to leave Gaza, fearing he would be killed. Sami paid a company coordinating exits at the time for both of them to cross into Egypt. But Ola could not reach southern Gaza to travel through Rafah. “She told me, ‘You go, and I’ll follow you,’” Sami said. “And here we are, still waiting, nearly two and a half years later.” They still have not managed to get married.
By his second day in Egypt, Sami was overwhelmed by guilt. “The overthinking kills me,” he said. “I felt ashamed to turn on the lights or eat proper food while my fiancee and my family were struggling to find the most basic things.”
In Egypt, his life has become dominated by loneliness and sleeplessness. “There is safety in Egypt and there are beautiful places, but I stay home. Happiness has no meaning without her. I cannot enjoy anything while she is not here,” he said.
Despite the war, Ola completed her bachelor’s degree in nursing at the Islamic University of Gaza. She has also endured enormous loss: her cousin, the journalist Ayat Khadoura, was killed, along with about 50 other members of her extended family.
From Egypt, Sami tries to create moments of happiness for her. For her latest birthday, he contacted her brother in Gaza and secretly arranged a cake, gift and flowers. “When she woke up and saw everything, she was so happy. I love her reaction when she’s happy.” The only problem was the flowers. “They were artificial,” he said. “I wasn’t happy with them, but natural flowers can’t get into Gaza because Israel does not allow them in.”
Sami says he has tried every possible way to get Ola out, without success. She is now applying for scholarships abroad, hoping education might provide a route to evacuation and, eventually, to him.
Sami recently travelled to Mecca for Umrah, where one prayer remained constantly on his mind. “I prayed, ‘God, please bring us together soon,’” he said. “But one thing I know for sure: I will wait for her for the rest of my life, until God brings us together.”

Plan to make firms pay more to train older workers than youth apprentices in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:00:24 UTC
16:00:24 KST

Employers in England are to be forced to pay more to train an older worker than a youth apprentice under plans being drawn up by the government to tackle the youth jobs crisis.
The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training by 25% for a worker over the age of 25 in order to encourage businesses to train young people instead.
Aiming to reverse a 40% drop in youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade, the proposal is being developed as part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are out of work.
With his final report delayed until after the budget, the former Labour cabinet minister this week signalled that boosting access to apprenticeships would be critical for fixing the first rungs of the career ladder for young people.
The chancellor, John Healey, is preparing to include measures to tackle soaring youth unemployment in his highly anticipated tax and spending statement to the Commons in less than a fortnight’s time.
After a rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training to almost 1 million, Andy Burnham has made supporting youth job opportunities central to his agenda for power, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and apprenticeships.
Ministers have been clear they want to rebalance the apprenticeship system back towards younger people. More than half of new starts are now for over-25s and the number of under-19s enrolling has almost halved in a decade.
Under the changes being planned to the growth and skills levy – the £4bn a year tax used to fund the national apprenticeship system – employers in England will face a new “co-investment” rule restricting the funding they can access.
Aiming to tip the balance to incentivise youth apprenticeships, the change is controversial because employers have for years been told by successive governments they were free to spend their levy funds on training as they saw fit.
“Employers are not going to like it,” said one senior policy expert close to the government. “They were told ‘it’s your money, you get to decide’. But the system is not working at the moment.”
Earlier this year Labour revamped the apprenticeship levy introduced by the Conservatives in 2017, with changes handing more flexibility to employers over the types of training the system can be used for – including new foundation apprenticeships and shorter courses.
Under the levy, large employers (those with yearly wage costs totalling more than £3m) must pay 0.5% of their total annual pay bill into a dedicated digital pot that they can draw from to fund training and assessment costs.
Following the proposed change, money from the pot would still be available to cover eligible training costs for apprentices aged 16 to 24. However, for older apprentices, the funds would cover only 75% of the cost and employers would need to pay for the remainder. It is believed the measure is under consideration for a phased launch from the start of the next academic year, in September 2027.
Labour has been warned that its skills strategy to tackle youth unemployment risks failure without a change in course. Official figures show its flagship foundation apprenticeship scheme has enrolled just 160 young people in the first eight months, against an ambition for 30,000 starts over the course of the parliament.
This month the Fabian Society thinktank called on ministers to increase the rate of the growth and skills levy to 0.7% to raise an additional £2.5bn, which could be used to target more funding towards youth apprenticeships.
However, it is understood that ministers are wary of heaping additional costs on businesses after the backlash suffered over employer national insurance contributions and as firms press for budget support to help them hire more young people.
Alongside tight constraints on the public finances, this has shifted the focus to restricting levy funds as a way to support young people without further adding to the costs for the public purse.
A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “We remain determined to address the 40% decline in apprenticeship starts among young people and give them the skills they need to succeed.
“We are already pivoting the system towards the next generation, including by creating 50,000 additional apprenticeships for young people, and introducing a new hiring payment of £2,000 for SMEs who take on a 16-24-year-old apprentice.
“The Milburn review is due in the autumn. We will not pre-empt its findings.”

No money for Ukraine and EU budget cuts: What could a Le Pen victory mean for the EU?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:00:24 UTC
16:00:24 KST

Le Pen is campaigning on a platform that would reshape France’s relationship with the EU ahead of the 2027 presidential election, potentially setting Paris on a collision course with Brussels with far-reaching implications.
Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is seeking to become France’s next president on a hardline anti-EU platform, pledging to cut the country’s contributions to the EU budget and end funding for Ukraine.
On Ukraine, Le Pen has repeatedly pledged to end financial assistance. Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Wednesday, she said that if elected, France could only sustain funding for six months because of the “perilous” state of its public finances.
“This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell [Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy] the truth,” she told Euronews.
Zelenskyy hit back in an interview with the Financial Times on Thursday. “The price to pay is not as high as the value of people’s lives,” he said. “That is why I think Ms Le Pen is not fully familiar with certain details.”
He added that, if Le Pen were elected president, she should have access to “the most powerful European system that works”, stressing that Ukraine’s battlefield experience could benefit European countries.
Le Pen has also called for an end to EU sanctions against Russia, while saying France could continue training Ukrainian troops and supplying military equipment to Kyiv.
Her comments signal that Le Pen is prepared to take a hardline stance, pledging to end French funding for Ukraine in a position similar to that of US President Donald Trump.
Her stance also contrasts sharply with that of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who is often compared to Le Pen but has advocated continued support for Kyiv.
Speaking in the Italian Senate on Wednesday ahead of an EU summit in Brussels, Meloni delivered a forceful defence of Ukraine’s right to self-defence.
“Supporting Ukraine is not an alternative to peace, it’s what makes it possible,” Meloni said. “The peace we want is one that is sustainable, just and also safeguards Europe and our interests.
“Therefore, the position of this government will not change: support for Ukraine, pressure on Russia and Euro-Atlantic unity.”
‘France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid’
“France’s support for Ukraine goes far beyond aid alone. It is primarily diplomatic,” Elie Tenenbaum, director of the French Institute of International Relations’ Centre for Security Studies, told Euronews.
He highlighted France’s leading role in initiatives such as the Coalition of the Willing, launched alongside the United Kingdom, as well as other mechanisms that “help keep Ukraine afloat”.
These include the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan (USL), whose implementation and disbursement depend on the political backing of major countries, including France.
Tenenbaum stressed that cuts to EU-level funding would have a greater impact on Ukraine than a reduction in France’s bilateral aid.
“If France were not only to stop providing bilateral aid and contributing to the EU budget, but also to actively oppose these kinds of mechanisms, then the entire framework of European assistance to Ukraine would be put at risk.”
According to figures from the German think tank Kiel Institute, France has committed an estimated €27 billion to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. This includes €7.9 billion in bilateral aid and €19 billion through European mechanisms.
Germany remains Europe’s largest provider of aid to Ukraine in absolute terms, having pledged more than €50 billion since February 2022, well ahead of France, Italy and the Netherlands. Relative to GDP, however, Denmark and Estonia provide the highest levels of bilateral aid.
Cutting France’s contributions to the EU budget
With six months to go before France’s presidential election, Le Pen is campaigning on a platform centred on tighter immigration controls, greater national sovereignty and measures to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, as rising fuel prices fuel public discontent.
Her party has backed capping France’s net contribution to the EU budget at €5 billion a year, down from €8 billion, according to figures published by the French Senate. Such a move would mark a departure from recent years, during which France’s contributions have generally increased, despite annual fluctuations.
Under President Emmanuel Macron, France has backed a larger EU budget, unlike countries such as Germany, which favour tighter spending limits. Paris has also called for new EU own resources, meaning additional sources of revenue beyond member state contributions.
Although France is a net contributor to the EU budget, it also receives substantial funding for its farmers through the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).
“France stands out among the major contributors as it is the only one that has so far supported an ambitious EU budget,” Eulalia Rubio, a senior research fellow at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.
She said Le Pen’s proposals reflected a “lack of understanding” of EU institutions.
“Spending varies slightly every year, so you can’t say, ‘We’re only going to pay €5 billion every year from now on’,” she commented.
Rubio warned that if France overcame the legal obstacles to cutting its contributions, other member states would have to make up the shortfall. Such a prospect could prove particularly contentious given that France is the largest recipient of farming subsidies.
On Wednesday, France’s National Assembly rejected the National Rally’s proposal to unilaterally reduce the country’s contributions to the EU budget for 2027, instead backing the government’s planned level of funding.
Thierry Chopin, an adjunct professor of European studies at Sorbonne University, said a National Rally victory could mark a break with France’s traditional role as a driving force within the EU and with the “intellectual contributions championed by Paris” in recent years, which had gained traction in response to global events.
Chopin pointed to France’s role in promoting European sovereignty, strategic autonomy in defence and trade protection measures. However, he said France’s influence had waned during Macron’s second term as its economic credibility declined.
“This credibility was not particularly strong to begin with, but it has worsened given the country’s budgetary situation, public debt and the difficulties facing its public finances. And then, once again, there are political considerations, because the executive branch has been weakened,” he said.
EU budget for 2028-2034
Speaking to the Financial Times on Wednesday, Le Pen described efforts to reach an agreement on the EU’s 2028-2034 budget by the end of 2026 as "anti-democratic."
She accused the European Commission of undermining “democratic processes” by advancing the budget ahead of elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland.
Ahead of the vote, Macron has moved to secure key positions, including at the central bank, by appointing allies. On Thursday, the French president told EU leaders during a closed-door meeting that Paris favours reaching a deal this year.
Beyond the timeline, Le Pen is also focused on the substance of the EU budget. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, she said she hoped to “build new coalitions” with like-minded parties to challenge what she described as an anti-growth mindset in Brussels.
She also suggested that the European Central Bank (ECB), led by Christine Lagarde, should revise its mandate to give greater weight to economic growth. The ECB is independent and its primary mandate is to maintain price stability.
Experts told Euronews they are sceptical that member states would support another major overhaul of EU fiscal rules following the sweeping reform of the Stability and Growth Pact in 2024.
“In my view, member states show little appetite for another major reform,” Andreas Eisl, a senior research fellow in European economic policy at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.
He added that “future changes are likely to involve reinterpretations of the existing rules rather than a fundamental overhaul of their legal foundations”.
Le Pen has repeatedly criticised EU regulations and standards, describing them as “regulatory hell” or a “regulatory shantytown”, and has pledged to strip them back to the bare minimum. Such an approach could undermine the bloc’s legal framework if adopted across member states.
“Obviously, if every member state does this, the EU can no longer function as a union based on the rule of law,” Chopin said.
The National Rally leader has also vowed to “stop” the European Green Deal, the EU’s flagship programme to cut emissions and achieve climate neutrality by 2050.
Le Pen argues that the Green Deal undermines economic growth. She has also proposed abolishing institutions such as the European Committee of the Regions (CoR), an advisory body representing local and regional authorities involved in implementing EU policies, including climate measures.
“The dismantling of the European Green Deal is already underway. If Marine Le Pen were to be elected, this would only be further accentuated, according to certain analyses,” Phuc-Vinh Nguyen, head of the Energy Centre at the Jacques Delors Institute, told Euronews.
Maria Tadeo contributed to this report

Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev has called the decision to put the sanctions on hold a "significant and truly historic moment."
US President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order to waive a new package of sanctions and tariffs on Russia shortly before it was due to take effect, telling Congress it was in the US' national interest.
Trump had signed the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026" into law in September in a push to increase pressure on the Kremlin and the Russian economy.
The legislation - named in honour of the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the measures - had sought to impose sanctions on Russian government and military officials, major banks, and vessels in Russia's shadow fleet. It also provided for duties on Russian goods and goods from certain countries continuing to buy Russian oil and gas.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev has called the decision to put the sanctions on hold a "significant and truly historic moment," adding that the package could have "brought economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a complete standstill."
Trump's move comes amid his increasing criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
It also follows a controversial announcement from Trump, who is gearing up for the US' midterm elections, earlier this month on a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to release large flows of diesel into global markets in an effort to bring down fuel prices.
"It was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account. "Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel."
Zelenskyy in Brussels
The Ukrainian leader has been in Brussels this week, where he has been meeting with European leaders to discuss the ongoing war.
Taking questions from the media on Friday, Zelenskyy was asked whether he felt he had been made a "scapegoat" for Trump's "own problems" ahead of November's midterms.
He gave a wry smile and said: "This is my answer."
Addressing the US-Russia diesel deal, Zelenskyy added that Ukraine "can’t accept diesel deals, because gas deals will come next."
"I’m absolutely sure of that," he said. "After gas, sanctions will be lifted on other things. It will eventually extend to the banking system, specific individuals, and the chemical industry. And there are risks around the frozen assets. If I don’t defend that through diplomacy – who will do it for us?"

Ukraine and Europe have little choice but to work with Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:36:03 UTC
15:36:03 KST

Ukraine and Europe have little choice but to work with Trump
Despite growing tensions over Russia, Kyiv and European leaders remain dependent on US military support and diplomatic leverage.
“It’s painful when President [Donald] Trump chooses one side, not our side,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday. The United States president’s much-discussed diesel deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, has become another source of tension between Washington and Ukraine and its European backers.
The reported disruption of Starlink/Starshield services on October 13-14, which wrongfooted Ukraine’s military, has added to those tensions. Service was later restored, and reports that the restrictions were imposed at the White House’s behest to pressure Kyiv remained unconfirmed.
Nevertheless, the two episodes have reinforced the impression of a widening rift between Ukraine and the US. On Friday, Zelensky accused Washington of continuing to throttle Starlink and promising the Russians new concessions.
Obviously, one needs to wait until the dust settles. Trump has tilted towards Moscow before, notably at his August 2025 summit with Putin in Anchorage, Alaska, only to return to conditional support for Ukraine amid Russian intransigence and diplomatic efforts by Kyiv and European leaders. The arrangement under which Europe pays for US weapons delivered to Ukraine is working, and the US continues to share intelligence with Kyiv despite reports that some critical information has been withheld.
The White House has also walked back proposals to recognise Crimea as de jure Russian, floated in its April 2025 peace framework, or to require Kyiv to withdraw from the entirety of its Donbas region. For their part, Ukraine and Europe have continued to go along with Trump’s diplomatic overtures to Moscow, led by his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
The diesel deal itself may yet unravel, given bipartisan opposition in Congress, including from Republican senators. Washington’s latest shift towards Moscow may, therefore, prove less significant than it currently appears.
The above is no reason for complacency on the part of Ukraine and its principal backers in Europe. They have plenty of reasons to worry beyond Trump’s unpredictability.
Chief among them is Putin’s resolve to ramp up the war. Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure are coming under daily attacks from ballistic missiles and upgraded jet-propelled drones while its air defences are struggling. The country is bracing for yet another tough winter. A propaganda war is unfolding in parallel, fuelled by the diesel deal.
Unlike Ukraine, Russia never embraced Trump’s proposal for a partial ceasefire on strikes against energy facilities. Yet Moscow is now portraying Kyiv as the spoiler after Ukrainian attacks resumed, including an attack on a refinery in the city of Ryazan on Thursday which Trump slammed as “a disgrace”.
Fighting has spilled over onto NATO’s eastern flank with ships transporting Ukrainian grain through the Black Sea attacked in Romanian waters. Russia is expanding its hybrid attacks in Europe to disrupt supplies of weapons and ammunition to Ukraine and sway public opinion in key countries such as Germany by sowing fear. In some corners of the European Union, there is a push to re-engage with Moscow. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico confirmed that the Slovak-Russian intergovernmental economic commission would resume work. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, praised Trump’s diesel diplomacy, even as Russian drones carried out strikes near Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast.
Paying for Ukraine is another headache for the Europeans. The 90-billion-euro ($101bn) loan the EU authorised in April might be exhausted well before the end of 2027. Some estimates suggest Kyiv would require an additional 70 billion euros ($79bn) for defence and civilian purposes in 2027.
That threatens to open a can of worms for EU member states, which are already negotiating the bloc’s 2028-2034 budget.
With some calling for deep cuts in spending, the controversial question of whether aid for Ukraine should come from Russian financial assets frozen in Europe is coming back with a vengeance. Trump is meanwhile calling for some of the money to be released.
The squabble comes before several major elections, notably the French presidential election in April and May as well as polls in Spain, Italy and Poland.
Given the fragility in Europe, it is remarkable that diplomatic and financial support for Ukraine has remained rather steady. “This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” European Council President Antonio Costa said on Friday while appearing alongside Zelenskyy and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels. “If we fall, 20 million Ukrainians will come to Europe,” Zelensky reminded everyone, “Stay strong, defend our country.”
In the run-up to the summit, the EU opened two clusters in accession talks with Ukraine and imposed a new round of sanctions on Russia. Zelenskyy came to Brussels after talks with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III in London on Wednesday.
But there is a limit to how much more the EU and the United Kingdom can do beyond what they are already delivering. They have already replaced the US as the principal international champions of Ukraine and de facto guarantors of its survival as a state. Becoming a member of the EU – or, at the very least, a closely integrated partner like Norway – is the best-case scenario for Kyiv in the long run.
At the same time, Europe lacks the political heft and the military capabilities to substitute for the US in the short term. That is abundantly clear on the battlefield. Although top European intelligence agencies can probably supply Ukrainians with some data, there is no EU alternative to Starlink. Europe cannot deliver enough air-defence systems and interceptors to fend off Russian attacks without US support. Faced with US unreliability, Europe is investing in these capabilities in pursuit of strategic autonomy, but even in the best-case scenario, these efforts will take a decade to bear fruit.
Most crucially, Europeans have little leverage they can use to bring Putin to the negotiating table. Sure, there might be positive incentives in the form of sanctions relief and the restoration of oil and gas flows. But any Russian response is likely to require pressure of some kind. The US has thus far failed to twist Putin’s arm – and under Trump has moved from sticks to carrots, dangling all kinds of “deals” mixing diplomacy and business. Part of the failure is due to the fear of escalation with another nuclear power; part of it is the current US administration’s opportunism. But the bottom line is that there is little reason to expect Europe can do a better job.
In light of all this, both Zelenskyy and the Europeans will probably fall back on the familiar approach: trying to keep Trump onside and smoothing over their differences as much as possible. They are probably hoping and praying that the current White House overture to Russia will fizzle out after the midterm elections. They will also tell Trump that the best way to secure his legacy is to stand firm against Moscow, a position that enjoys support among his fellow Republicans. The strategy is to wait it out: first the winter, then the Trump presidency.

U.S. Osprey fleet gets new flight computers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:35:39 UTC
15:35:39 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Bell Boeing $90.8 million to continue redesigning the V-22 Osprey flight control system, including new flight control computers.
- The upgrade addresses aging electronics, cybersecurity and parts obsolescence for U.S. and Foreign Military Sales Ospreys, with work running through October 2030.
The U.S. Navy has awarded the Bell Boeing joint venture $90.8 million to continue redesigning the V-22 Osprey’s flight control system, including new flight control computers and cockpit interface units for the tiltrotor aircraft flown by the U.S. Marine Corps, U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and a foreign customer.
The order, signed on Oct. 15 by Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, also covers new test equipment, software, technical documentation and logistics products needed to buy and support the redesigned system later. The U.S. Department of War said the upgrade is meant to deal with aging electronic components, cybersecurity requirements and parts that are no longer being made, so the Osprey fleet can keep flying for the rest of its service life.
The flight control system is the core of the V-22’s fly-by-wire design. Its computers turn pilot inputs into commands for the aircraft’s rotors, wings and engine nacelles, which tilt between helicopter and airplane modes in flight, so the computers have to keep working reliably for the Osprey to fly at all.
Bell Boeing will perform 52% of the work in Ridley Park, Pennsylvania, where Boeing builds the Osprey’s fuselage, and 42% in Mesa, Arizona, with smaller shares in Fort Worth, Texas, where Bell assembles the aircraft, and at other U.S. locations. Work is scheduled to finish in October 2030.
The government obligated about $4.9 million at signing, including roughly $3.1 million in U.S. Air Force research and development funds, $369,250 in U.S. Navy research funds and $1.4 million from the Foreign Military Sales customer. Japan is the only foreign country flying the Osprey, with V-22s in service with its Ground Self-Defense Force, though the contract notice did not name the buyer.
The award, issued as a sole-source order under an existing basic ordering agreement, extends work that began five years ago. In September 2021, the U.S. Navy gave Bell Boeing a $214.4 million order for the redesign and development of the V-22 flight control system, flight control computer and cockpit interface unit, citing functional obsolescence, cybersecurity and parts shortages. That work was due to be completed in June 2026.
The U.S. Marine Corps flies the MV-22B for troop and cargo transport, Air Force Special Operations Command uses the CV-22B for special operations missions, and the U.S. Navy operates the CMV-22B to carry people and supplies to aircraft carriers. The services plan to keep the aircraft in service for decades after production wraps up, which makes replacing electronics that suppliers no longer support a recurring task for the program.
Bell Boeing is expected to complete development of the redesigned flight control system, along with the software and support products needed to field it across the fleet, by October 2030.
