Israel faces a nationwide mental health crisis post-October 7, Clalit experts warn - study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:19:37 UTC
15:19:37 KST

The outrageous massacre committed by Hamas terrorists on October 7, 2023, inflicted many hidden wounds – traumas almost as painful as being stabbed with a knife or shot with a gun.
Haim Ben-Arye was one of these undetected victims. A longtime school-bus driver who was deeply devoted to his young passengers, Haim was happily married to Irit for 30 years and a loving father of six adult children.
Not long before the attack, Haim’s daughter had shared joyous news: she was pregnant with his first grandchild. He had so much to look forward to.
Yet on October 25, just 18 days after the massacre, Haim drove to a remote location and ended his life.
“He loved his job and his passengers,” his wife, Irit, recalled. “On the morning of October 7, our son, a first responder, told us, ‘Something terrible has happened.’
“Haim went to shul to be with the children whose fathers had gone to fight. He played with them and sang songs. But after Shabbat, we sat in front of the TV, and he just wept.”
Later that evening, Haim’s boss asked if he could drive his bus to evacuate children from Kibbutz Be’eri to safety. He agreed immediately. He returned home at 5 a.m., devastated and in shock.
“I couldn’t help them,” he told Irit. “My passengers were in total silence for over two hours.”
While Irit returned to her job at Clalit Health Services on October 8, Haim stayed home and watched horrific scenes on television. He hardly turned it on before.
On October 25, schools reopened for half-days, and Haim was scheduled to return to his bus route. When Irit called him later that day, he didn’t answer. Shortly after, a friend messaged that someone had died by suicide.
“I knew it was Haim,” Irit said. “I rushed home and saw people gathered in front of our house. My instincts were right. Haim was all heart.”
During the shiva mourning period, a man came to pay his respects and shared how Haim had once saved his child’s life.
The man’s son had seemed withdrawn on the bus, and Haim was the only person – including family and teachers – who noticed the boy felt profoundly alone, ensuring he got the help he needed.
“I told my children that their father shouldn’t have taken his life, but his heart simply broke,” Irit shared. “To me, he is still a hero.”
Irit shared her family’s tragic story with about 100 English-speaking journalists worldwide during a recent online seminar (webinar) hosted by the Clalit Research Institute, titled Israel’s Mental Health Front: Three Years Since October 7.
The event highlighted how personal grief reflects a widespread psychological emergency across the country.
The scale of the challenge
Prof. Amir Krivoy of the Geha Mental Health Center emphasized the scale of the challenge. Clalit, Israel’s largest public health insurer, serves five million members, half the nation’s population, and maintains comprehensive electronic data on their mental health.
“The population has endured cumulative stress since 2020, from coronavirus lockdowns and social tension over judicial reforms to the Hamas incursion, the war in Gaza, and Iranian missile attacks,” Prof. Krivoy explained.
“This sequence generated immense acute and chronic stress. While the peak occurred on October 7, Israelis were already in a fragile state.”
According to Clalit’s findings, the last baseline “normal” years were 2018 and 2019. Since then, chronic stress and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) have surged, particularly along the southern and northern borders.
Evacuated residents experienced a tenfold increase in psychological distress compared to those who remained in their homes. Furthermore, health professionals have observed an unprecedented rise in PTSD among children and adolescents, who usually suffer rarely from it.
All four public health funds have estimated that there are 60,000 Israelis who developed clinical PTSD between October 2023 and December 2025; half were Clalit members.
Krivoy recalled that he ran a clinic in the southern city of Sderot, where during the Hamas attacks and the subsequent battles, 53 people – including 37 residents of and visitors to Sderot, 11 police officers, three IDF soldiers, and two firefighters – were murdered or killed.
“I learned that 90% of the population didn’t sleep at night. They were afraid there would be another attack. Even two years afterward, many didn’t go for diagnosis because they were afraid to leave their homes.
“There will be more like them in the coming years unless they get relief. There must be follow-up. We know from experience that Israelis are resilient, but we have to be able to detect crises early and treat them in time.
“Israeli society will recover, but we have to help them.”
Living in a traumatic reality
Nufar Bar-Lipshatz, a developmental psychologist in a Clalit clinic in Beit She’an, told the Webinar audience that “we still live in a traumatic reality. My own husband has done a lot of reserve duty during summers and the High Holy Days, and the war isn’t over.”
She continued, saying that “delegations of Clalit therapists were sent to evacuated families who spent months in Eilat after the massacre.
“For some, it was the first time that they met a therapist. They were living in hotels, and they didn’t know when they could return. We encouraged them to talk; we encouraged their children to build toy houses so we could better understand their problems.
“In 20 years, these children will help run our society. Some of their family members were murdered, injured, and taken hostage. When the siren sounded, the difficulty continued. The child still struggles to feel safe. Some parents didn’t talk about it, but the kids can ‘read’ the stress in their parents’ faces and voices.”
Saying everything is fine doesn’t work, continued Bar-Lipshatz.
“They may develop fears that someone will kidnap them when they’re asleep or that their father could die in the army, but they won’t tell their parents, so they keep these fears to themselves.
“It can cause aggression and a hard time in preschool and school. Parents must give honest explanations, even though it’s hard.
“We can give the child a sense of meaning, recall their moments of bravery, that they went to the safe room fast; that they called the police or a relative even if they cried on the phone.”
Toddlers who are not yet verbal have difficulty expressing their experiences.
“We observe how they play and function every day,” the psychologist continued. “They may have nightmares, show aggression and withdrawal, play soldiers, hide, run to the shelter. Not every difficulty began in war. Some had problems before, but war can intensify it.”
A growing number of children who were emotionally affected by it all began to stutter.
“We didn’t have the personnel to treat each one individually, so we decided to organize a group of three- and four-year-olds with their parents,” recalled Bar-Lipshatz. “A siren sounded during the session, so we took them all to a shelter and did yoga, encouraging movement, play, and laughing.”
Challenges faced by health funds over the past decade
Prof. Ran Balicer, the founder and director of the research institute, Clalit’s chief innovation officer, and deputy director-general who also teaches at Ben-Gurion University in Beersheba, noted that mental health reform was added to the “basket” that insurers must pay for only in 2015.
Then COVID came and created a big burden. With the massacre, the health funds found that the mental-health care they were supposed to provide was underbudgeted, understaffed, and had long waiting times.
The 9/11 attacks on New York and Washington caused emotional harm in only 4% of Americans. In comparison, 15% of Israelis were directly affected. Not a single family wasn’t shocked by the barbarity.
When Iranian and other terrorist groups’ missiles fell, some Israelis took knives to the “safe” room. They felt nowhere was safe.
Clalit conducted a nationwide study with the Myers-JDC-Brookdale Institute that included 2,500 respondents. In January 2024, depression had affected 34%, and even today, it is clinically high.
Anxiety was 27%, and today it affects 20%. PTSD was 32% and has declined to 20%. One in five adults continue to report severe impairment in their daily functions, Balicer reported.
“We retrained primary care doctors so they could help treat patients. We added mental-health coaches, digital innovation, and used an AI tool to screen patients. Digital data helps us know who has a problem and predict future illness.
“Instead of waiting for patients to come in sick, doctors call and tell them they may have a medical problem. Not all doctors were willing to use them, but now they like the preventive-medicine technique because it can save lives.
“So many patients had been silent after October 7 that we created proactive preventive mental-health outreach and followed up treatment for 1,500 per week out of 8,000. We will continue to do this.”

Exclusive: Watchdog lists ships carrying Russian gas, blasts Trump sanctions waiver
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:13:18 UTC
15:13:18 KST

Exclusive: Watchdog lists ships carrying Russian gas, blasts Trump sanctions waiver
The NGO Urgewald has identified what it says are all the 134 vessels involved in Russian gas trade since 2022, which have carried over 150 million metric tons of cargo since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to data shared with the Kyiv Independent.
As of Oct. 15, around 1.5 million metric tons more were in transit.
The news comes as U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 16 issued a broad waiver of Russia sanctions that were set to take effect two days later under a law championed by the late U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham.
The law authorized the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five countries buying Russian gas and oil, and also provided for extensive sanctions against Russian officials, banks, and the energy sector, including ships involved in the Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) trade.
"Republicans and Democrats passed this law in Lindsey Graham's name to squeeze Russia's war revenues. Trump has now hollowed it out before its main sanctions could bite," said Alexander Kirk, a sanctions campaigner at Urgewald, on Oct. 17.
"That is a betrayal of the bipartisan effort behind this law and a lifeline to (Russian President Vladimir) Putin."
Between the law's signing on Sept. 18 and Oct. 15, 42 tankers had transported Russian gas, according to the analysis.
These include Boris Davydov, an Arc7 tanker that departed Russia's Yamal terminal on Oct. 6; Konstantin Posiet, which departed Arctic LNG 2 on Sept. 21; and Clean Horizon, which left Yamal the same day with a cargo later delivered to the French port of Dunkerque.
U.S. lawmakers from both parties have urged the White House to impose sanctions under Graham's law in order to pressure Moscow toward ending the war in Ukraine. For LNG tankers, this would enable Washington to target those ships and restrict their access to international shipping services.
Instead, Trump has taken increasingly accommodating steps toward Russia, announcing a deal earlier in October to purchase Russian diesel.
"Congress must challenge this retreat and demand that the administration explain whose interests are served by shielding Russia's energy trade from the pressure this law was designed to impose. Ukraine should not have to pay the price for Washington's unwillingness to act," Kirk said.
The list of 134 ships carrying Russian gas between Feb. 24, 2022, and Oct. 15, 2026, includes 17 Arc7-class LNG carriers, an advanced tanker type designed to export product from the Russian Yamal LNG terminal in the Arctic.
The EU paid 7.88 billion euros (about $8.9 billion) worth of gas from the Arctic project in the first nine months of 2026, Urgewald reported earlier.
While the U.S. has never been a major buyer of Russian fossil fuels and banned all imports in 2022, the EU remains the leading buyer of Russian LNG, followed by China, Japan, and South Korea, according to the CREA think tank.
But the EU has been phasing out Russian LNG imports, with a full import ban to take effect in January 2027.
Urgewald's latest findings underscore how much Russian LNG trade continues to rely on Western services.
Of more than 2700 voyages undertaken since February 2022, about a third were taken by ships owned by either the Greek shipping company Dynagas or the U.K.-based, U.S.-owned company Seapeak, according to data.
Both account for roughly 17% of the voyages each, with the Dutch Anthony Veder gas shipping company coming in third.
Greece has secured a sanctions exemption for Dynagas, allowing the company to continue shipping Russian LNG to non-EU countries even after the EU ban takes effect.
Other operators include Russian companies such as Gazprom and Novatek, as well as China's Cosco.
LNG trade has faced weaker sanctions pressure than Russia's oil exports, which have been constrained by an EU- and G7-imposed price cap, forcing the country to rely increasingly on its shadow fleet to ship its oil.
"Europe must now act with urgency. Sanction the tankers, cut off the services that keep them operating, and close the loopholes sustaining Russia's LNG exports," Kirk said.

Russia has lost 1,562,970 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 17.
The number includes 1,950 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,415 tanks, 25,554 armored combat vehicles, 163,883 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,266 artillery systems, 2,221 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,710 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,962 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

The chatbot murder guide: AI’s struggle between privacy, reporting violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:50:37 UTC
14:50:37 KST

The chatbot murder guide: AI’s struggle between privacy, reporting violence
The deadly Tumbler Ridge shooting in Canada raises questions about when AI companies should report threats of violence to police, and the potential risks to an individual’s privacy.
For months before carrying out Canada’s deadliest school shooting in almost four decades, Jesse Van Rootselaar was consulting an unlikely adviser on how to perpetrate mass murder.
“In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 [Remington shotgun] is brutal … Close quarters is its playground,” OpenAI’s ChatGPT guided the 18-year-old, according to reports.
On February 10, 2026, Van Rootselaar shot his mother and half-brother at home before going to a school in the small British Columbia town of Tumbler Ridge, where he killed another six people – including five students – before taking his own life.
Earlier this week, on October 14, US authorities charged a Washington State man with allegedly conspiring with Van Rootselaar to plan the attack. But the mass shooting incident has raised questions that go beyond the traditional legal understanding of culpability.
The British Columbia government in September filed a civil lawsuit against OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman, accusing them of failing to prevent the incident and claiming they were aware of the conversations that turned deadly. Families of the victims also filed separate lawsuits. OpenAI’s leadership issued a public apology for their failure to notify authorities.
The company has not responded to requests from Al Jazeera for its comments on the lawsuits.
But as the case against OpenAI progresses, it has spurred a familiar debate: Where should a line be drawn between reporting potentially dangerous behaviour and protecting an individual’s privacy?
“The question of whether companies should be required to turn such information over to law enforcement is extraordinarily difficult, particularly if they don’t already screen chats for indications of such types of threats,” United States-based civil liberties lawyer Jenin Younes told Al Jazeera.
“Forcing companies to implement a surveillance system implicates very serious civil liberties concerns, and that’s probably a bridge too far for me,” Younes added.
“On the other hand, AI gives individuals access to types and quantities of information they didn’t have previously that may facilitate the commission of mass casualty events, a concern it’s not easy to dismiss.”
AI’s ability to distinguish thoughts from threats
One of the biggest challenges facing AI companies is determining whether a user expressing violent thoughts actually intends to act on them.
In August, Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, flagged a user to San Francisco police after discovering conversations allegedly threatening its CEO, Dario Amodei.
According to the San Francisco Standard, citing a police report, the user had claimed to possess an AR-15 gun and suggested he had Amodei “in his sights”.
However, when contacted by the newspaper, the man said he was joking and had no intention of carrying out any form of violence. The person was neither charged nor detained, the Standard said.
Fazl Barez, a senior researcher at the University of Oxford specialising in AI safety and governance, said current AI models cannot “reliably” determine whether an interaction with an AI chatbot “is purely hypothetical or is likely to lead to harmful behaviour”.
“Suppose you are a creative writer working on a fictional story and want to explore how a murder plot might unfold. From the context, it may be clear that this is simply a fictional narrative. If the threshold for flagging potentially harmful content is too low, such a writer could be wrongly flagged,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Similarly, consider a graduate student in biology or chemistry studying pathogens that, if misused, could have serious consequences. They might be trying to understand the risks associated with these pathogens and how to mitigate them. Such discussions may be necessary for legitimate research and education. Even when the subject matter is sensitive, they should not automatically be flagged without considering the broader context.”
The researcher said identifying a credible threat may require examining a user’s interactions across multiple conversations, rather than relying on isolated statements.
Barez said someone experiencing intrusive violent thoughts might turn to a chatbot for support, while another person planning an attack may reveal their intentions gradually across several conversations.
“Distinguishing between the two requires careful consideration of context, intent and patterns of behaviour, rather than relying on individual statements alone,” he added.
Chinmayi Sharma, a law professor at Fordham University, said the debate has parallels with the duty imposed on mental health professionals to warn identifiable third parties about credible threats.
However, she said there was a key difference – therapists have professional training, knowledge of their patients and enforceable standards governing their conduct. AI companies do not necessarily have comparable safeguards.
“My concern with AI companies is that right now there’s not a concerted effort to hire mental health professionals, sociologists, individuals that would have the unique expertise on what the indicators of threat are here,” Sharma told Al Jazeera.
“Secondly, licensed professionals are accountable to concrete, legally enforceable standards in their discipline. We don’t have something like that for AI companies.”
The privacy dilemma
The privacy implications extend beyond whether AI companies can accurately identify threats. Millions of people use chatbots to discuss relationships, emotional distress, mental health concerns and deeply personal experiences.
Civil liberties lawyer Younes said many users may not realise how vulnerable those conversations could be to disclosure.
“They often reflect a person’s innermost thoughts, questions, and desires. The majority of people assume that these dialogues will never be viewed by another person,” Younes, president and legal director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, said.
Younes warned that the consequences of greater monitoring could extend well beyond those planning violence.
“If people fear their chats can be turned over to law enforcement simply because they express disturbing thoughts/violent fantasies etc, many will be dissuaded from using them,” she told Al Jazeera.
Younes argued that forcing companies to establish systems for monitoring users and reporting conversations could raise serious constitutional concerns in the US, including protections against unreasonable searches.
Meanwhile, Fordham’s Sharma also raised an issue about who could be disproportionately affected by heavy monitoring by AI chatbots.
“The concern is always there about either intentional or unintentional targeting, because if you have models trained on what we consider dangerous speech, they’re almost always going to reflect biases,” she said. “Certain minorities’ speech is over‑flagged as a threat, while other comparable speech is not.
“Even in a world in which everyone is benevolent, we should still be concerned about disparate outcomes,” she said, warning that machines could reproduce such disparities at scale.
‘Not a licensed therapist’ – When do AI companies become liable to report?
While AI companies may face moral pressure to prevent violence, their legal obligations are less clear, legal experts say.
Bryan Choi, a professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder, said US law recognises a duty to warn in certain circumstances, including when mental health professionals become aware of imminent threats or when a special relationship exists between parties.
But those principles do not necessarily apply to AI companies.
“Under present case law, it seems unlikely that a company such as OpenAI would be held to have such duties to warn,” Choi told Al Jazeera. “The chatbot is not a licensed therapist. There is no special relationship between the company and the victims.”
Choi said existing negligence and product liability laws could potentially be applied to AI companies, but proving responsibility would present significant challenges.
Finding a balance
Fordham’s Sharma suggested that independent institutions could help establish reporting standards rather than leaving decisions entirely to private companies or requiring immediate disclosure to police.
Such bodies she said could develop procedures for assessing threats and explore ways of sharing only relevant information while protecting users’ identities and other personal details.
Meanwhile, Younes argued that users should, at a minimum, be clearly informed about whether their conversations are monitored and what circumstances could lead to information being shared with law enforcement.
“This is almost certainly an issue that will be wrestled with over the coming years, and I’m not sure anyone knows the solution at this particular point in time,” she said.
“Events that have not yet occurred will likely influence how these policies are shaped.”

Bulgaria offers a true culinary journey in mid-October
Unknown

PHOTO BNT
Font size
Bulgaria offers a true culinary journey in mid-October, bringing together traditional recipes, local producers, folklore and cooking demonstrations. Bulgarians celebrate autumn with Elena dry-cured ham, Smilyan beans, roasted chestnuts and a variety of pumpkin delicacies.
PHOTO facebook.com/elenski.byt
The popular Elena Ham Festival takes place in the town of Elena in northern Bulgaria from October 16 to 18. Visitors can sample a traditional Bulgarian dry-cured pork delicacy made from a hind leg of pork and characteristic of the Elena region.
Locals say the recipe is simple: meat, salt, spices and a little patience. Yet the ham’s distinctive flavour is closely tied to the local climate, traditional curing methods and generations of experience among local producers.
PHOTO BTA
Vegetarian food lovers may be tempted to visit the Rhodope village of Smilyan, home to the traditional Smilyan Bean Festival, held from October 16 to 18.
PHOTO Facebook/ People and traditions - Brezhani
Meanwhile, the village square in Brezhani in southwestern Bulgaria hosts the Brezhani Chestnut Festival. The famous local chestnuts are smaller and have lighter-coloured shells than other varieties, but boast a much sweeter taste. Roasted on the spot, they are served with young wine made from the latest grape harvest.
PHOTO kazanlak.com
The 11th National Walnut Festival will take place this weekend in the centre of Golyamo Dryanovo, a village in the Kazanlak region. The event was first held in 2014 in honour of what was once the oldest walnut tree on the Balkan Peninsula, estimated to be 500 years old and which survived until 1993. A special postage stamp was issued in Bulgaria in 1965 in three print runs in honour of the tree. Today, Golyamo Dryanovo is still home to one of Bulgaria’s largest walnut plantations featuring local varieties, covering an area of more than 2,500 decares (250 hectares).
PHOTO nesebar.bg
The flavours of the sea will take centre stage at the 13th Autumn Fish Festival, “Autumn Shoals”, in Nessebar from October 16 to 18.
PHOTO facebook.com/festivalnazhitenatapitka
To mark World Bread Day and World Food Day on October 16, the town of Strazhitsa is hosting the Wheat Loaf Festival. The event is inspired by The Wheaten Loaf, a popular fairy tale by Angel Karaliychev, a writer born in Strazhitsa.
PHOTO BTA
The Pumpkin Festival is being held for the seventh time in the village of Dalboki, near Stara Zagora in southern Bulgaria. The programme includes a cooking competition, a variety of pumpkin dishes and a tasting of traditional rachel, a sweet pumpkin preserve.
PHOTO BTA
No visit to the town of Radomir, known as the boza capital of Bulgaria, would be complete without sampling this distinctive sweet, fermented drink popular across the Balkans. Located near Sofia, the town will host its 11th Boza Day on October 17, featuring a farmers’ market and a craft fair.
PHOTO visit.varna.bg
Varna is the destination of choice this weekend for lovers of Bulgarian wine. The coastal city is hosting the Urban Wine Fest 2026 on October 16–17, one of a series of events dedicated to Bulgarian wines in the run-up to International Mavrud Day on October 26.

The ‘Maid of Ghent’ has been the city’s symbol for 700 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:48:00 UTC
14:48:00 KST

The ‘Maid of Ghent’ can be seen in various places around the city, but fewer and fewer people are familiar with the figure that has adorned the city’s coat of arms since 1991. “She first appeared as early as the 14th century. She is not a single person, but a symbol. She embodied both the rebellious city and nationalism,” says Nina Uelpenich of Ghent University, who has now delved into her history.
In the city centre, there are several references to the Maid of Ghent. There is the café ‘De Maecht van Ghent’ on the Korenmarkt, the Corn Market. Her image adorns the tower door of the post office building and the base of the statue of Jacob of Artevelde on the Vrijdagmarkt, the Friday Market.
Historian Nina Uelpenich researched the origins of the figure and the meanings it has taken on over the past centuries. “The very first mention dates back as far as the 14th century, in a poem by Boudewijn van der Lore. At that time, the Maid was a symbol of Ghent during a conflict with the Count of Flanders.”
From a figure of the Virgin Mary to a nationalist symbol
The female figure is based on the Virgin Mary. She does not refer to any real person. “Several cities were depicted as a virginal figure. They appear everywhere: in books, during ceremonies – in Ghent and elsewhere.” She is also a popular figure in works of art from that period.
‘Even during the Calvinist period – when idols were destroyed – she endured. She is no longer merely a Catholic symbol.’ When Napoleon came to power, most city maidens lost their significance. ‘In Ghent, however, there was a revival during the 19th century.’
“At the time of Belgium’s formation, the Maid was a symbol of the region’s medieval history. Images began to appear in which she is depicted waving the tricolour. She was the face of the illustrious past that was to shape Belgian identity. She became a nationalist figure.”
The female figure was used on posters advertising the 1913 World Exhibition in Ghent. In this way she also became an international symbol of Belgium during the period between the wars.
“Chosen to tell a particular story”
The Maid lost that significance in the decades that followed. “All sorts of maidens emerged, co-existing side by side: there is a liberal Maid of Ghent, a socialist Maid of Ghent… It really became a popular symbol that could serve any form of identity formation.”
“The Maid of Ghent shows how symbols are used to shape identity. This is not a fixed reality, but a construct. They are chosen and magnified to tell a story.” A story that still resonates today, for since 1991 the Maid has adorned Ghent’s official coat of arms.

Indian woman jailed over son’s fatal stabbing faces possible deportation from UK

Vickrum Digwa's mother Kiran Kaur was jailed for three years in July for assisting an offender
An Indian woman jailed for helping her son after he fatally stabbed an 18-year-old student in Southampton could face deportation to India following her early release from prison, British authorities have indicated.According to new agency PTI, the UK Home Office said it would seek to deport foreign criminals at the earliest opportunity, although it did not refer specifically to Kiran Kaur, 53. Foreign nationals sentenced to at least 12 months in prison are generally considered for deportation, subject to exceptions and legal challenges.Kaur was sentenced to three years in prison in July for assisting an offender by removing the weapon used by her son, Vickrum Digwa, to kill Henry Nowak on December 3, 2025. She is expected to be released early under a government scheme aimed at reducing overcrowding in British prisons.Digwa, 23, was sentenced to life imprisonment in June, with a minimum term of 21 years before he becomes eligible for parole.Both Kaur and her son have been granted permission to challenge their sentences, with their appeals scheduled to be heard by the UK Court of Appeal on November 5.Kirpan argument sparks controversyThe case drew widespread attention after Digwa sought to invoke a religious self-defence argument involving the kirpan, a ceremonial knife that Sikhs are legally permitted to carry in the UK.
During Kaur’s sentencing, Justice William Mousley stressed that the kirpan was a symbol of religious faith and was not intended to be carried for offensive purposes. He said any use of the weapon in self-defence would have to be justified by circumstances involving great seriousness and urgency.The judge also criticised Kaur for removing the weapon rather than challenging her son’s actions and encouraging him to do the right thing.He acknowledged that she had experienced a difficult life in India before marrying and moving to the UK nearly 30 years ago. He said she had acted to protect her son rather than for personal gain and was unlikely to reoffend, while making clear that her actions warranted punishment.British Sikh organisations and parliamentarians subsequently condemned what they described as the misrepresentation of the kirpan, stressing that religious protection did not justify the violence in this case.Police conduct under investigationThe killing also triggered scrutiny of police conduct after body-worn camera footage showed officers handcuffing Nowak following Digwa’s allegations that he had been subjected to racism. Those allegations were subsequently rejected in court.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct is investigating the officers’ handling of the incident amid allegations of “two-tier” policing, referring to claims that different communities were treated unequally.The case has heightened tensions in Southampton and the wider Hampshire and Isle of Wight area.Kaur’s potential deportation remains subject to the applicable immigration process, while the outcome of the appeals against her sentence and Digwa’s life term is awaited.

Iranian, Algerian central banks governors discuss enhancing economic cooperation
TEHRAN- The Governor of the Central Bank of Iran met and held talks with Mohand Bouri, Governor of the Central Bank of Algeria, on the sidelines of the Annual Meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
At the meeting, the two sides discussed and exchanged views on the latest status of monetary, banking, and trade relations between the two countries. Enhancing the level of joint economic cooperation and utilizing mutual capacities to strengthen bilateral trade interactions were among the most important themes of the meeting.
The Governor of the Central Bank of Iran, referring to the historical and political commonalities between Iran and Algeria, emphasized the serious determination of the Islamic Republic of Iran to develop and consolidate economic relations with friendly and brotherly countries.
The Governor of the Central Bank of Algeria, while expressing satisfaction with the meeting, emphasized his country’s readiness to expand economic and banking cooperation with Iran and the need to follow up on mutual agreements in line with the interests of the two nations.
In late December, Saeed Zare’ Haghighi, the head of Iran Trade Center in Algeria, said that Algeria’s infrastructure needs offer significant opportunities for exporting technical and engineering services, making the North African country a largely untapped economic market.
He said Africa — and Algeria in particular — should be seen as a strategic destination for the private sector, noting that limited numbers of commercial counsellors made targeted entry into new markets essential.
He described Algeria as a geopolitically secure country with a strategic location close to Europe, adding that after the decline in Russian energy exports, about 20 percent of Europe’s oil and gas is now supplied by Algeria.
Zare’ Haghighi said Algeria’s foreign currency revenues had risen from around $50 billion to more than $300 billion in recent years, generating a trade surplus of $20 billion to $30 billion and creating broad scope for economic cooperation.
He pointed to strong demand in Algeria for technical and engineering services, infrastructure projects, and the construction of silos and storage facilities linked to food security, saying Iranian companies had the technical know-how and experience to meet these needs.
He also highlighted Algeria’s industrial and mining potential, including steel and phosphate, and said the trade center was ready to identify opportunities, guide exporters and promote participation in specialized exhibitions, drawing on models used by countries such as Turkey that combine trade with on-the-ground investment.

Students, trade unions and Yellow Vests set to protest across France

French protesters take to streets over rising prices and social strain
- Protests spread across France on Oct 17 over high prices, weak public spending and falling standards, with tens of thousands expected to join and police heavily deployed in Paris.
- Anger began in Paris high schools over poor facilities and teacher shortages, then grew into a wider revolt over inequality, fuel costs and the cost of living.
- The government fears unrest and blames far-left France Unbowed, while police face criticism over violence and injuries, including one teenager who lost a hand.
AI generated
PARIS – Demonstrations began across France on Oct 17 in what was expected to become a major nationwide protest against high prices and the fraying of a model intended to provide a basic level of opportunity and social security.
The protests began in September at high schools in Paris’ poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.
A large police presence was visible in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as the Avenue des Champs-Elysees and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of the two official demonstrations.
Hundreds of other protests were planned across France, with tens of thousands set to participate.
Protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, an echo of the unrest that dogged President Emmanuel Macron’s previous term, while in Marseille, rubbish cans were set alight.
“We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions,” said a 19-year-old protester in Paris who gave her name as Lola.
Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, leaving behind a polarised electorate and a badly fragmented political landscape.
A long struggle to reduce rising public debt has not impressed investors, who are ditching French bonds, driving borrowing costs to their highest levels in more than two decades.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Oct 15 that the authorities fear unrest during the protests. The government blames the far-left France Unbowed for inflaming the protests, an accusation the party denies.
High level of violence in French student protests
The police have drawn criticism for their response due to a grisly list of injuries among demonstrators, including one adolescent who had his hand blown off after picking up a stun grenade. Lecornu said more than 900 police personnel had also been injured.
The internal police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen cases of alleged police violence. France suspended the use of stun grenades for the student demonstrations, but Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said they could be used in the protest on Oct 17.
“If there were to be clashes, all types of intermediate weapons can be used,” he told Telematin on Oct 16.
Calls on social media for members of past protest movements to join the fray appear to have worked, raising questions about just how large the protests could grow.
The Yellow Vest movement started in 2018 as a protest against taxes on diesel before morphing into an outpouring of anger at high living costs and income inequality.
However, things have been largely quiet since Macron agreed to billions of euros in tax cuts.
Yannick Maillou, a teacher from La Creche in western France, joined the Yellow Vests in 2018 and remains involved in the movement.
He said there were several nearby meeting points for protesters to gather on Oct 17, with unions also calling on their members to join.
“Groups of people providing medical assistance are forming in anticipation of police violence,” he said.
Myrtil Devillers, another Yellow Vest protester, said he was sympathetic to the protesters’ “explosive catch-all of grievances”, although he will not be protesting on Oct 17 as he is abroad.
“I was a Yellow Vest protester when petrol cost €1.40 a litre, so imagine how I feel now that it’s €2.20,” he said.
“The justice system is complaining; the education system is complaining; the healthcare sector is complaining; my friends who run businesses are complaining.” REUTERS

German minister seeks debt-brake exemption to sustain Ukraine aid
BANGKOK, Oct 17 - Germany's development minister is seeking an exemption from the country's debt brake, a constitutional limit on government borrowing, for Ukraine funding, arguing that much of Germany's civilian support for Ukraine comes from her ministry's budget.
"The Russian attacks are more severe than ever, leading to more deaths, more destruction, more suffering. But as budget cuts for development assistance continue, we simply will not be able to maintain our support for Ukraine at this level," Reem Alabali Radovan told Reuters on Friday, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank meetings.
Funding for Ukraine in her ministry's budget amounts to about €330 million ($371 million) this year, down from €670 million in 2022 and €750 million in 2023.
"At this point, it is not a political decision; we just face massive cuts and it will no longer be possible," Alabali Radovan said. "This is especially hard as the money is wisely invested in Ukraine's and Europe's stability."
Alabali Radovan is a member of the Social Democrats, the junior partner of the governing coalition led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU.
Her proposal has the backing of Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, a member of the conservative CDU, but faces opposition from other members of the party who oppose further exceptions to borrowing rules beyond those already approved, such as for defence spending.
"I am already prioritising support for Ukraine, but there are many other crises and conflicts, too. And we work in the long term, which means large parts of our budget are already committed," Alabali Radovan said.
"That means the cuts hit crisis instruments above all, because – naturally – they work with flexible funds that are not yet pre-committed."
Alabali Radovan added that she supports Merz's call for other countries to contribute more.
"We are the strongest supporters, and I believe others can and should contribute more," she said. REUTERS

746 aftershocks recorded in Panama after 7.5 earthquake

746 aftershocks recorded in Panama after 7.5 earthquake
More than 740 aftershocks have been recorded across Panama since a powerful magnitude 7.5 earthquake struck on Oct. 9, with scientists monitoring ongoing seismic activity and investigating reports of significant changes along the country's Pacific coastline, Qazinform News Agency cites Anadolu Agency.
Nestor Luque, director of the Institute of Geosciences at the University of Panama, said aftershocks from an earthquake of this magnitude could continue for up to two months. The shallow quake, which occurred at a depth of less than 10 kilometers, released enough energy to trigger ongoing adjustments within the Earth's crust, though aftershocks are gradually weakening.
Authorities stressed that recent tremors detected in the provinces of Chiriquí and Bocas del Toro appear to be linked to separate fault systems and are not necessarily connected to the Oct. 9 earthquake.
Meanwhile, geologists are assessing reports from coastal communities where residents have observed exposed rock formations and what appears to be a retreat of the sea. Experts say tectonic movements can cause land to rise or sink, potentially altering coastal landscapes.
Scientists are also examining unusual changes in seawater color, including grayish shades reported by some residents. One possible explanation is that underground water mixed with minerals released during the earthquake, although laboratory analysis will be needed to determine the exact cause.
On Isla Cañas in Los Santos Province, residents have reported that the island may have developed new fractures following the quake. Researchers plan to conduct field studies to determine whether any cracks extend across the island and into surrounding waters, which could indicate fault displacement.
The Institute of Geosciences has called for stronger seismic monitoring infrastructure, estimating that around 150 additional instruments would be needed to improve earthquake observation nationwide. A comprehensive early-warning network, meanwhile, could require as many as 700 sensors across the country.
Earlier, an earthquake with an intensity of up to four magnitude points was registered in Kamchatka.

The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by Trump in September.
But the US president issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US "national interest", prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel. Ukraine then accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.
Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy, giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.
It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.

Many of these provisions have now been waived by Trump.
Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called the waiver "an important and truly historic moment".
Posting on X, he said the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" primarily on the US and global market, and that economic cooperation benefits both nations.
Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer have criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X.
The move is likely to draw further anger from Ukraine, where Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding Russia can use in its war effort.
Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end".
He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter."
Zelensky said was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground.
He later told reporters that he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.
He also said negotiators Ukrainian spoke to their US counterparts on Friday and that both teams could meet next week.
Trump was initially criticised by Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies for temporarily suspending some US sanctions to import Russian diesel in a bid to bring down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.
Trump has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Middle East conflict, which has sent fuel costs soaring ahead of the US midterm elections. Rising inflation has soured Trump's standing with the American public.
Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.
A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel.
Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Kyiv says this is to limit revenue for Russia's war machine, while Moscow claims it only targets facilities used by the Ukrainian military.
Zelensky initially expressed surprise at Trump's announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days which saw several fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
This prompted scathing condemnation from Trump, who called the strikes a "disgrace". Zelensky replied that he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests".
Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine.
Last week Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield missions, Ukraine said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.
During the slowdown, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying these came with no prior warning.
Zelensky said on Friday that Starlink speeds had still not been fully restored.
Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing and deliberately slowing down Ukraine's Starlink network.
Ukrainian authorities have confirmed that at least nine people have been killed and around 60 injured in Russian strikes across the country over the past 24 hours.
They said an ambulance driver was killed and 20 others were injured in Russian strikes on the city of Kherson on Saturday morning.
Russia's defence ministry said it had targeted industries linked to Ukraine's defence industry - including steel works, an electrical sub-station and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.

Europe’s sponge cities are turning rain from waste into a valuable resource
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:01:57 UTC
14:01:57 KST

The EU is creating a ‘Sponge Facility’ to help implement nature-based projects that aim to make cities less prone to droughts and floods.
Wild weather swings have turned water into a dual threat for Europe’s cities. When storms hit, there’s too much of it. When droughts come, there’s too little.
But some experts believe that the ‘sponge city’ model – a nature-based approach to urban planning pioneered in China two decades ago – could help cities put a new spin on the old saying ‘save for a rainy day’.
The model involves retrofitting urban areas with green spaces, permeable surfaces and water storage systems to absorb, retain and reuse rain rather than letting it drain away. This eases pressure on drainage systems and conserves water to use during dry spells.
“One of the most impactful ways cities can adapt is by reversing a century of urban design that treated rainfall as waste rather than as a valuable resource,” says Justin Abbott, fellow and Europe water leader at engineering consultancy Arup.
What is a ‘sponge city’?
The sponge city model was developed in the early 2000s by Chinese landscape architect Kongjian Yu.
He proposed using features such as ponds, wetlands and planted drainage channels to catch rainfall before it rushed into sewers and rivers. Slowing the runoff would reduce flood risk during storms, he argued, while rainwater could be used to replenish groundwater supplies or irrigate parks during dry spells.
The greenery would also help cool city streets during heatwaves, and in some cases, healthy soil and wetlands could help protect against wildfires.
After catastrophic flooding killed 79 people in Beijing in 2012, his ideas gained greater attention.
In 2014, China adopted national guidelines for sponge city development, and the next year the country launched a 16-city pilot programme, including Wuhan, Xiamen and Chongqing. Another 14 cities, including Shanghai and Shenzhen, were added in 2016.
By 2030, China now aims to have 80 per cent of its built-up urban areas function as sponge cities.
Could sponge cities make Europe more resilient?
Europe has been experimenting with similar water management projects for decades.
Between 1998 and 2002, the southern Swedish city Malmö transformed its flood-prone Augustenborg neighbourhood by installing green roofs, wetlands, retention ponds and six kilometres of water channels. During major storms in 2007 and 2014, it suffered much less flood damage than other neighbourhoods.
In the Netherland’s Rotterdam, the Benthemplein water square – opened in 2013 – doubles as a basketball court and recreational space in good weather, but during heavy rains, its three basins temporarily hold up to 1.7 million litres of water.
Opened one year later in Denmark, Copenhagen’s Tåsinge Plads collects water from nearby rooftops using underground storage and rain gardens – shallow, planted areas that allow rain to soak into the soil.
The European Commission hopes to expand projects like these across the continent. Its 2025 Water Resilience Strategy called for more sponge cities, as well as to restore more wetlands, and now the bloc is developing a ‘Sponge Facility’ to help develop them.
The changes won’t necessarily be easy. Protected buildings, crowded streets and buried utilities make it difficult to retrofit historic city centres. But Abbott says that’s no excuse for failing to think outside the box.
“These challenges should encourage better targeting, not inaction,” he says, suggesting smaller interventions such as removing courtyard paving, planting more trees and installing green roofs partially or completely covered with vegetation.
Sponge cities are a ‘powerful’ tool but not a fix-all
Even the greenest city can only absorb so much rain, though. During extreme storms, soil becomes saturated and storage systems fill up, leaving excess water nowhere to go.
The catastrophic floods around Valencia in 2024 revealed the tragic consequences that can occur when extreme rainfall overwhelms a city’s defences like this.
“Sponge measures are powerful, but they cannot address every challenge independently,” Abbott explains.
Cities also need conventional drainage systems, larger reservoirs and designated routes that can carry floodwater away when rain gardens and wetlands reach capacity, he says.
That’s a matter of more than engineering. Abbott argues that city authorities, water utilities, developers and landowners all have a responsibility to manage rainfall. Decisions made by one entity, he explains, can affect entire neighbourhoods.
“In planning and designing cities, we need to put water first,” he says. “We need to ‘design with water’.”

Three Mexicans jailed for 158 years each for killing Australian, US surfers
A Mexican judge sentenced the three men for the 2024 murders a week after they were found guilty.
Three Mexican men have been sentenced to more than 158 years in prison each for the murder of two Australian brothers and their American friend during a surf trip on Mexico’s Baja California coast in 2024.
A Mexican judge in the coastal city of Ensenada, in Baja California state, ruled on Friday that Jesus Gerardo Garcia, alias “El Kekas”, Irineo Francisco “N” and Angel Jesus “N” would each serve 158 years and nine months in prison for homicide, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
The defendants were found guilty a week ago of the murders of Australian brothers Callum and Jake Robinson, aged 33 and 30, respectively, and their American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, 30.
The case impacted Mexico’s tourism industry by exposing the risks foreigners face when visiting the country.
Previously, the Baja California State Attorney General’s Office requested the “exemplary sentence” of 210 years in prison for each defendant.
Antonio Otanez, president of the Baja California surfers’ association, welcomed the outcome, saying “justice has been served.”
Otanez acknowledged that the killings had caused a “major drop” in tourist visits, particularly by surfers, to the region known for its beautiful beaches.
The Robinson brothers and Rhoad travelled to Mexico in late April 2024 to surf at a beach in Punta San Jose, near the popular tourist city of Ensenada.
The three friends camped on the beach on the night of April 27, 2024. Authorities launched a multi-day search with help from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) after the men were missing for several days.
The bodies were found on May 3 in a well more than 15 metres (50 feet) deep, all with gunshot wounds to their heads.
Last week, the brothers’ father, Martin Robinson, said the “guilty verdict is a significant moment in our long and painful journey to seek justice for our beautiful sons, Callum and Jake, and their friend Carter Rhoad, whose lives were so cruelly taken from them in 2024.”

The Israeli politicians seeking to replace Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:00:58 UTC
14:00:58 KST

The Israeli politicians seeking to replace Netanyahu
A look at Israel’s main opposition leaders, their parties and their largely shared positions on Gaza and other wars before October 27 election.
Do any of these Israeli candidates support a Palestinian state?
On September 26, five leading members of Israel’s self-styled Zionist opposition signed a non-aggression pact, seeking to oust incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in the October 27 election.
Gathered at the Tel Aviv home of opposition leader Yair Lapid were his co-runner, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, leader of Beyachad; former Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the new Yashar party; Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party; and Avigdor Liberman, head of the Yisrael Beiteinu party.
In the statement of principles published after the hours-long meeting, the leaders said, “Despite ideological differences among us, the formation of a Zionist, statesmanlike government dedicated to repair and reconstruction is our shared overarching goal.”
However, how long that pact might last — Liberman has already accused frontrunner Eisenkot of seeking a deal with Netanyahu — how meaningful a change in substance as well as style they offer, and which of them might lead a future coalition, remain open to question.
With the exception of Golan, all take a fundamentally right-wing approach to Israel’s challenges.
None is committed to establishing a Palestinian state, with only the Democrats acknowledging it as a distant, unspecified goal. None, Golan included, accepts that Israel’s war on Gaza amounts to genocide or that it has committed war crimes in killing more than 74,000 people there. Nor has any questioned Israeli military actions against Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Qatar and Iran, instead reserving criticism mostly for how those actions have allowed Israel to be perceived internationally.
“The dominant forces in the opposition such as Bennett, Liberman or Eisenkot represent right-wing politics,” said Ahron Bregman, an Israeli analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London. “They are not willing to touch the real, fundamental issue which is at the heart of everything: the Palestinian issue, and the Palestinian aspirations for independence.” He likened them to Netanyahu, but without the corruption allegations and support of far-right figures, such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. “Israel as a whole is a right-wing nation,” he added.
So, who are the main opposition figures and what do their parties stand for?
Gadi Eisenkot – Yashar
Credited with originating the Dahiyeh Doctrine in 2008, involving “disproportionate force” and large-scale destruction of civilian infrastructure against groups such as Hezbollah and Hamas, Eisenkot served as Israeli military chief from 2015 to 2019.
The 66-year-old entered politics in 2022 with former Defence Minister Benny Gantz’s National Unity alliance and later joined the war cabinet assembled by Netanyahu after the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on October 7, 2023. In December that year, his son Gal, 25, and two nephews were killed while participating in the genocide in Gaza, losses commentators say have helped forge a connection with an electorate that has come to see itself as scarred by war.
In June 2024, he quit the war cabinet alongside Gantz, accusing Netanyahu of lacking a strategy to end the war. A year later, Eisenkot founded the centrist Yashar (Straight/Honest), advocating for professional government, military service for all – including ultra-Orthodox Jews – and a state commission of inquiry into the failings before October 7.
While notoriously ambiguous on many of Israel’s foreign policy positions, he has been critical of the government’s reliance upon the United States in achieving its war aims, while not questioning those aims themselves. In June, he characterised Washington’s mediated negotiations with Tehran to end the war against Iran that Washington had embarked upon with Israel as “a deal taking shape far from here and far from Israeli interests” and, the same month, railed against US restrictions on Israel’s freedom of action in Lebanon.
Eisenkot has ruled out including the United Arab List, or Ra’am party, in a post-election coalition. In a September 26 Channel 12 interview, he said no Arab party would accept his conditions, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish state.
Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid – Beyachad
Beyachad (Together) is the joint list announced in April 2026 by former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, who served for a combined 18 months in 2021-2022 between Netanyahu governments.
Bennett, a 54-year-old longtime supporter of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, leads the list, with Lapid, the 62-year-old founder of the centrist Yesh Atid party, in second place.
Lapid has called his partner “a right-wing politician, but an honest one”. Neither has prioritised resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict or supported a Palestinian state. Though their 2021 coalition included Ra’am, Bennett has acknowledged that this broke an electoral promise.
Lapid has been one of Israel’s most outspoken critics of how its genocide and multiple strikes upon its neighbours are perceived internationally, while rarely questioning the rationale behind those actions. Bennett, in contrast, is more outspoken in his hawkish views. A full-throated supporter of the country’s war on Iran, he also congratulated Israel’s military and security services for a September 2025 attack on Qatar’s capital, Doha, that targeted senior Hamas leaders as they met to consider a Gaza ceasefire proposal put forth by the US. A Qatari security official was killed in the attack, which drew condemnation from across the region and beyond.
They now seek a government composed solely of Zionist parties, also ruling out reliance on Arab parties.
Avigdor Lieberman – Yisrael Beiteinu
The most hawkish voice at Lapid’s table, Lieberman, 68, founded Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) in 1999 to represent right-leaning Russian-speaking immigrants.
Once Netanyahu’s protege, Lieberman has ruled out serving under him or joining a coalition that includes the ultra-Orthodox or relies on Arab parties, which he calls anti-Zionist. He has also rejected a minority government, reportedly making him a principal obstacle to Eisenkot becoming the bloc’s prime ministerial candidate.
In November 2023, Lieberman repeated his 2018 assertion, made then as defence minister, that there were “no innocents in Gaza”. In February, he visited the Karem Abu Salem crossing, known as Kerem Shalom to Israelis, and accused Netanyahu’s government of funding Hamas by allowing the minimal humanitarian aid that has been permitted into Gaza.
The Yisrael Beiteinu leader has been a consistent supporter of Israel’s genocide and subsequent military actions. In September 2025, he joined other Israeli politicians in criticising Netanyahu for the apology to Doha that he had been forced to make by the Trump administration for that month’s strike, saying the apology was instead owed to the Israeli public. Equally, he has argued against any restraint in its invasion of Lebanon, telling the Jerusalem Post in March: “If once again we go for a limited operation, some manoeuvre near the border, maybe talk about a security zone, it’s complete madness.”
“Lieberman does not belong in this bloc,” said Shaiel Ben-Ephraim, an Israeli analyst with Atlas Global Strategies, arguing that his main motivation was hatred of Netanyahu.
However, Ben-Ephraim said, Lieberman “maintains a loyal base and is a crucial force in Israeli politics”. His core constituency is the former Soviet electorate, but he has gained wider trust through his perceived independence.
Observers say he could potentially return to Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc.
Yair Golan – Democrats
The only leader at Lapid’s table from the Zionist left and the only one open to working with Palestinian parties, Golan heads the Democrats, a liberal party that was formed in 2024 through the merger of Labor and the social democratic, secular Meretz.
A retired major-general and former deputy chief of staff, Golan, 64, earned domestic plaudits for driving south during the 2023 Hamas-led attack and helping repel it.
Golan is alone among many in the anti-Netanyahu bloc in his criticism of the government’s war aims, arguing that military achievements are being squandered without a coherent diplomatic and political strategy
In May 2025, two years into the genocide in Gaza, Golan sparked controversy when he told a news conference that a “sane country does not kill babies as a hobby”, accusing ministers of celebrating the starvation of Palestinian children in the territory. He later walked back the comments after widespread criticism in Israel. In October, while praising the achievements of the previous year’s 12-day war against Iran, he told party members that the assassination of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei at the beginning of the conflict was a “mistake”. “Not because he didn’t deserve to die,” he caveated, “only because it doesn’t serve the interests of the State of Israel.”
Despite his openness to working with Palestinian parties, in September, Golan backed the disqualification of Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Arab Balad party, over an article about October 7, drawing criticism from the Joint List – an alliance of the Arab-led Hadash, Ta’al and Balad parties – and commentators.
Roi Zur, a University of Essex specialist in Israeli politics, said that despite Golan and Lieberman’s ideological differences on security and conflict, there will be “no winning coalition without these two”. He added that concerns about a clash between them miss the point, noting that both oppose Netanyahu, favour secularisation and strongly oppose exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews.

Jackson Boxer’s vegan recipe for poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
05:00:25 UTC
14:00:25 KST

I have a great respect for the leek, which is possibly the most demanding vegetable in its need to be freshly cooked before consumption. A warm leek, fresh from the pot, is an ethereal, collapsing sigh of diaphanous veils, whereas cold it can all too easily become a slippery and almost slimy mess of hopelessness.
Poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnuts
All the various elements can be made ahead of time except the leeks, which should be just warm from their poaching, and the dressing, which should be made at the last minute. Vegetable bouillon may seem a bit of a faff to make just to poach some leeks (if you prefer, simply cook them in two litres of seasoned water with a dash of white wine instead), but a good, light vegetable broth is a useful thing to have around, and a batch will keep happily in the fridge for three or four days. To toast nuts successfully, cook them on a tray in an even layer in a 170C (150C fan)/335F/gas 3½ oven for 15-20 minutes, which will toast them evenly to the core without scorching.
Prep 25 min
  
Soak and chill Overnight
  
Cook 1 hr, plus cooling
  
Serves 4
For the hazelnut miso
 
250g hazelnuts
  
40g white miso paste
 
25ml olive oil
 
5g flaky sea salt (about 1 tsp)
For the vegetable bouillon (optional; see recipe introduction)
 
1 medium carrot, peeled and quartered
 
1 medium onion, peeled and quartered
 
1 medium shallot, peeled and left whole
 
2 garlic cloves, peeled
 
4 leek tops (from trimming the leeks below)
 
1 bay leaf
  
5 thyme sprigs
  
2 parsley sprigs
  
1 star anise 
  
150
 ml white wine
  
2 litres filtered water
  
40g flaky sea salt
For the pickled pears
 
2 conference pears
  
150ml white-wine vinegar
  
50g sugar
For the leeks
  
4 leeks
 , trimmed, roots removed and thoroughly cleaned, then cut in half across the middle
 
2 litres vegetable bouillon (see above and method)
 
Minced chives and chopped chervil, to finish (optional)
For the dressing
 
200g pear pickling liquor (see above and method)
 
100ml extra-virgin olive oil
  
5g flaky sea salt (about 1 tsp)
  
2g ground black pepper
  (about ½ tsp) 
  
50g minced shallot
  
10g minced garlic
  
100g toasted hazelnuts
 , chopped
The day before, put the nuts in a container or bowl, add a litre of water and leave overnight to soften. Next day, strain the nuts, reserving the soaking liquid.
Put all the bouillon ingredients in a large pot (again, you can do this a day before), bring to a low simmer and cook gently on a medium heat for 25 minutes. Take off the heat, leave to rest and cool for four hours, then strain.
Peel, quarter and core the pears, then cut each quarter in half lengthways and put in a container, for which you have a lid. Put the vinegar, sugar and 75ml water in a saucepan, bring to a simmer, then pour the pickling liquor over the pears, cover and chill for 12 hours.
Put the drained nuts, miso, olive oil and salt in a food processor, dribble in just enough of the soaking liquid to lubricate, then blitz to a smooth, rich puree the consistency of mayonnaise; add a drop more liquid to loosen, if need be.
Submerge the leeks in the bouillon, bring it to a low simmer and cook for 15 minutes, until the leeks show only gentle resistance to the tip of a sharp knife. Take off the heat and leave to cool to room temperature for about half an hour.
Meanwhile, make the dressing. In a stainless-steel bowl, whisk the pickling liquor and oil to a smooth and coherent emulsion, then stir in all the other dressing ingredients.
Lift the just-warm leeks out of the poaching liquid and cut lengthways into quarters. Spoon some hazelnut miso on each plate, then arrange the leeks on top. Dot pieces of pickled pear between them, spoon over the dressing and garnish with minced chives and, if you’re lucky enough to have some, chopped chervil.
- Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House, Vesper and Dove, all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London

Trump puts on hold new Russia sanctions he signed into law
US president’s executive order comes two days before sanctions deadline and a week after diesel deal with Putin.
United States President Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia that he signed into law last month, telling Congress the pause is in the national interest.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday, two days before a deadline in the law that would put the sanctions into effect.
The law – named after Lindsey Graham, the Republican senator who died unexpectedly in July after returning from Ukraine – passed in the House of Representatives and the Senate by large margins. The bipartisan legislation was drafted by Graham and Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal.
It seeks to starve Moscow of money for its war on Ukraine by sanctioning Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers carrying its energy exports.
It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the five biggest importers of Russian oil or gas with an exception for countries that import less than 15 percent of Russia’s natural gas exports and are taking steps to cut them.
Kirill Dmitriev, special envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin, said on social media that Trump’s move was “an important and truly historic moment”.
“The US-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue,” he added.
Diesel deal and criticism
The decision to suspend the sanctions came a week after Trump said the US signed a deal to buy diesel from Russia to try to lower global fuel prices.
Both Republicans and Democrats criticised the deal, saying it would help Russia’s war effort without affecting fuel prices.
Democratic Representative Don Beyer said he and other politicians had “warned” that Trump might do this, referring to Trump’s deal with Moscow.
Beyer called on Congress to “fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine”.
Trump recently has also increasingly criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to reach a deal with Russia.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Oleksandr Merezhko, the chairman of the Ukrainian parliament’s Committee on Foreign Policy and Interparliamentary Cooperation, linked Trump’s latest moves, which put Ukraine at a disadvantage, to next month’s midterm elections in the US and predicted an improvement in relations after the voting.
“President Trump is a difficult partner, but we are dependent on the United States, and we need to have constructive, respectful relations even with Trump, no matter how difficult it might be,” he said.
“I believe that after the midterm elections, the situation will be better, the emotions will subside and we will be able to return to constructive dialogue with President Trump,” Merezhko added.
Polls have suggested that Trump’s Republican Party will have a hard time keeping its majorities in Congress in the November 3 elections due to voters disapproving of Trump’s handling of the US-Israel war on Iran and blaming him for higher prices.

Why one of NYC’s longstanding symbols is set to disappear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17

Why one of NYC’s longstanding symbols is set to disappear
New York City’s horse-drawn carriages could disappear under legislation proposing a ban from June 2028, as concerns over passenger safety and animal welfare fuel efforts to end the familiar tourist attraction, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent.
The proposal, known as Romanch’s Law, is named after 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who died after being thrown from a runaway carriage in Central Park in June. He was visiting New York to celebrate his high school graduation. His death brought renewed urgency to the debate over whether carriage rides should continue operating in the park.
“His death was heartbreaking, and it was preventable,” City Council Speaker Julie Menin said in an official statement announcing her support for the legislation in July.
Menin became the first sitting City Council speaker to publicly endorse ending horse-drawn carriage rides in Central Park. She said the transition should protect New Yorkers, international visitors and the horses, while providing employment opportunities for people whose livelihoods depend on the industry.
The teenager’s death followed the death of a carriage horse in Central Park a week earlier. The incidents intensified scrutiny of an industry already facing longstanding concerns over animal welfare and public safety.
Under the proposed legislation, sponsored by Council Member Christopher Marte, horse-drawn cab operations would be prohibited from June 1, 2028. The measure would wind down the industry by stopping the issuance of new operating licenses, with existing driver licenses eligible for limited renewals until the deadline.
The proposal also addresses what would happen to the animals. Carriage horses could not be sold or transferred for slaughter, or sent to another horse-drawn cab business.
For drivers and other affected employees, the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection would administer a workforce development program to help them move into other fields of employment.
Menin has identified hospitality and tourism among the sectors where displaced workers should have access to quality jobs. The planned phaseout therefore seeks to combine an end to carriage rides with protections for both workers and horses.
The ban has not yet become law and remains subject to legislative approval.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that site preparation is underway for a 102-meter-tall detention facility in New York City’s Chinatown, expected to become the world’s tallest correctional facility.
