New menopause guidelines designed to cut through misinformation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
03:21:20 UTC
12:21:20 KST

Australia has new guidelines for managing menopausal symptoms
Hot Flushes. Night sweats. Vaginal dryness. Painful sex. A frequent need to wee.
Menopause marks the end of a woman's reproductive years and is associated with a range of symptoms that can affect their quality of life.
There's a lot of information and misinformation about the best treatments to help ease the severity of symptoms.
In a bid to make things easier, the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG) has developed a new set of clinical guidelines.
Loading...
The guidelines clarify when to use menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) over other medicines and what options are available for those with a history of breast cancer.
RANZCOG guideline development group chair Catriona Melville said they wanted to "cut through the noise" and provide clear, evidence-based recommendations for clinicians to discuss with their patients.
"If your clinician is not clear about where the evidence lies and what's safe and what isn't safe, and what's recommended and what isn't recommended, then they're not in a position to have that patient-centred discussion about what the available [treatment] options are," she said.
What do the guidelines cover?
The new guidelines provide evidence-based advice for managing the symptoms of menopause, which begins 12 months after a woman's last period.
The guidelines cover vasomotor symptoms (such as hot flushes and night sweats) and genito-urinary symptoms (such as vaginal dryness and the frequent need to urinate) of menopause in women 40 years and above.
They do not cover the management of bone density, joint pain, libido, depression or anxiety.
Magdalena Simonis, a practising GP and women's health expert from the University of Melbourne, said not all women experienced the same type or severity of symptoms.
While she was not involved in developing the guidelines, she said they reinforced the need for clinicians to treat the whole person in front of them, not just the symptom.
"We should also be looking at lifestyle and other risk factors around the time of the menopause," Dr Simonis said.
"This is a really important time to talk about [cholesterol] lipid control, bone density management and lifestyle activities.
"Looking at family history of other cancers, breast screening, cervical screening and having that conversation around chronic conditions."
How do the guidelines work?
The guidelines list a range of possible treatment options for different menopausal symptoms, including menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), acupuncture and hypnosis, ranking available evidence on a scale of very low to high.
The guidelines recommend that women taking MHT have an annual review with their doctor.
But there's not enough evidence that weight loss or physical activity alone will improve hot flushes or night sweats, or that hypnosis will improve sleep.
Dr Melville, a specialist gynaecologist and sub-specialist in sexual and reproductive health, said the new guidelines would hopefully make it easier for clinicians and patients to understand their options.
For example, women with a history of breast cancer can be offered vaginal oestrogen to ease menopausal symptoms.
Although RANZCOG had previously released statements about managing menopausal symptoms, Dr Melville said these were their first evidence-based guidelines.
How will it improve patient care?
Women should receive the same standardised recommendations no matter who they see or where they live if clinicians across Australia use the same guidelines.
Jean Hailes for Women's Health chief executive Sarah White, who was not involved with the guidelines, said this was important because clinicians wanted to give their patients the very best support, but there was a lot of online misinformation to wade through.
"It really will help the health professional to have these new guidelines sitting in front of them so that they can talk them through and reassure women that they are getting the very best advice," she said.
The guidelines also encourage clinicians to ask women approaching menopause if they experience any "troublesome" symptoms, especially if patients are First Nations, Māori and Pacific Islander women and others who may experience barriers to treatment.
This will make it easier for women to get help, even if they find it hard to ask.
Won't there be new national guidelines soon?
The Australian government has funded separate perimenopause and menopause guidelines expected to be released next year.
These guidelines, which RANZCOG is contributing to, will be continually updated as new evidence emerges.
Dr Simonis welcomed the spotlight on the health of menopausal women.
She encouraged anyone experiencing troublesome symptoms to book an appointment with their GP and advised women approaching mid-life to schedule a check-up.
"Menopause is not a stage to be afraid of or to dread; it's a natural phase of life,"
she said.

Cameroonians await government reshuffle after Biya’s return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
03:14:28 UTC
12:14:28 KST

Cameroonians await government reshuffle after Biya’s return
After 10 weeks abroad, Biya returned to Cameroon but has yet to appoint a new government or vice president.
Yaounde, Cameroon – Every weekday at 5pm, Elvis Mbi tunes in to the state broadcaster’s flagship radio bulletin, hoping to hear an announcement from President Paul Biya that could signal a change in Cameroon’s political leadership.
Biya, 93, returned to Cameroon on August 20 after spending about 10 weeks abroad. His prolonged absence fuelled speculation about his health and whereabouts, including unverified claims that he had died.
His return raised expectations of a government reshuffle, but no new government had been appointed by October 6. The vice presidency, restored through a constitutional amendment in April, also remained vacant.
“Every Cameroonian was expecting that upon his return home, he was going to change government, but nothing up to this moment,” 39-year-old Mbi told Al Jazeera.
In his December 31, 2025, address to the nation, Biya promised that a new government would be formed “in the coming days”. More than nine months later, the promised change had yet to materialise.
Succession fears grow
The vacant vice presidency has drawn particular attention since politicians approved a constitutional amendment in April restoring the position abolished in 1972.
Under Law No. 2026/002, promulgated on April 14, the president may appoint and dismiss a vice president.
The amendment provides for the vice president to assume the presidency on an interim basis if the office becomes vacant because of the president’s death, resignation or permanent incapacity.
The vice president serves the remainder of the seven-year presidential term under the conditions set out in the Constitution.
The reform establishes a formal succession mechanism while leaving the appointment of the vice president to Biya. The amendment does not set a deadline for filling the post.
“We all know the president needs assistance in order to execute state duties and that’s why we are anxiously waiting for the appointment, but nothing has happened yet to our greatest dismay,” Mbi said.
A disputed presidential decree purporting to appoint a vice president has added to the speculation.
In June, an individual delivered a sealed envelope to Cameroon Radio Television (CRTV) in Yaounde containing a purported presidential decree appointing a vice president.
The document appeared to bear the official seals of the presidency and a signature attributed to Biya, according to a government statement published by state newspaper Cameroon Tribune on July 1.
CRTV did not broadcast what the document said. The government said the decree had not been issued through the proper official process and confirmed that the individual had been detained and an investigation was under way.
For Jude Mutah, a Washington-based governance and democracy expert and director of member relations at the Corporate Council on Africa, the attention paid to the state broadcaster’s evening bulletin reflects public expectations of political change.
In the absence of clear information, rumours can gain traction, he said.
Cabral Libii, leader of the Cameroon Party for National Reconciliation and an opposition figure in the 2025 presidential election, has argued that appointing a vice president would matter beyond filling a vacant post.
“The vice presidency is not just another administrative post to be filled. Appointing your vice president means securing your leadership,” Libii said in a public appeal.
“A vice president of this calibre could help to mitigate the succession struggles that are currently paralysing collective action,” he added.
Economic uncertainty
The leadership questions are unfolding as Cameroon faces other challenges, including a separatist conflict in its English-speaking regions and an armed rebellion linked to Boko Haram around the Lake Chad Basin.
Jason Healy, a sub-Saharan Africa country risk analyst at BMI, part of Fitch Solutions, said uncertainty over political leadership could weigh on investor confidence.
Healy warned that prolonged uncertainty could discourage some investors from committing to large, long-term projects. He also suggested that delaying appointments could be a political calculation by Biya, allowing him to retain control over the timing and composition of any changes.
Mbi Aziseh Azimboh, executive director of the Policy Lab for Civic Innovation and Community Solutions (POLITICOS), said prolonged uncertainty could slow government decision-making and delay reforms and public policies.
Government defends president’s prerogative
The government has defended Biya’s authority to decide when to make appointments.
In an interview with RFI in August, Communication Minister and government spokesperson Rene Emmanuel Sadi said the president had the authority to form a new government and determine when to do so.
“It is surely quite normal for him to take his time when entrusting such a high office to one of his fellow citizens,” Sadi said.
Elvis Ngolle Ngolle, a former minister and coordinator of the ruling Cameroon People’s Democratic Movement’s academy, said citizens’ concerns were legitimate but maintained that the president had the constitutional prerogative to act when he chose.
The presidency did not respond to an Al Jazeera request for comment.
For Mbi, his radio-listening ritual continues.
“No one knows anything any more. It is so disheartening when I tune in each time but don’t get the big news,” he told Al Jazeera.

Sukkot in Florida offers an Israeli family joy, community, and a reminder of war - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
00:56:03 UTC
09:56:03 KST

On the eve of Sukkot, I find myself not in Jerusalem but in Kissimmee, Florida, in a gated vacation home community called Encore at Reunion.
Our youngest grandchild, Ye’ela, now seven, has convinced her family that it’s her turn to visit Disney World. Her older siblings have already been. My son, daughter-in-law, and their four children can all take off the days of Sukkot. My physician son even has a lecture to give for Hadassah in Miami. We decide to go for it.
I admit to having a weakness for Disney World. Walking down Disney’s Main Street, U.S.A., riding through the African savanna on Kilimanjaro Safaris in Animal Kingdom, and watching For the First Time in Forever: A Frozen Sing-Along Celebration in Hollywood Studios when the snow comes down (twice!) offer an invigorating vacation break from the Middle East. I like refilling my Disney popcorn bucket at every stop, eating Mickey Mouse-shaped ice cream, and being silly enough to decorate my hat with a Minnie Mouse headband.
Seven-year-old Ye’ela has spent most of her life either in a pandemic or wartime, and I want to see her pose with those Disney princesses and ride the Slinky Dog Dash roller coaster with her siblings.
So I take on the job of logistics, which has to include Sukkot observance, of course.
Where to stay? We want a house, not a hotel, partly because it’s less expensive, but also because we can prepare kosher food for kids used to Israeli cuisine and celebrate the holiday our own way. There are literally tens of thousands of vacation home rentals in the Orlando area, but only a handful of rental communities allow or tolerate the building of those strange shacks called sukkot on their property. Hence, we decide on Encore at Reunion.
For most of the year, Encore is a regular vacation resort village for American and foreign guests. But on Jewish holidays, particularly Sukkot and Passover, hundreds of observant Jews abandon their already chilly backyards in colder states to erect their sukkot in Florida.
Encore is 18 km. from the Magic Kingdom and closer to the other three Disney parks. It is not only sukkah-friendly but has an eruv, making carrying possible on Shabbat. Over the last decade or so, this has become a popular holiday venue for religious Jews. The resort also includes shuttles to the parks and a large, free water park with impressive waterslides for all ages.
I arrange for an unassembled sukkah to be delivered by one of several local suppliers (Klein’s, if you’re interested). Ironically, we live on a Jerusalem street with a bustling Four Species marketplace, but fear violating import laws by bringing an etrog into the Citrus State. So I order the Four Species from a pop-up Chabad distributor, also at Encore.
We bring some pots and pans and buy others. With 337 km. separating Miami International Airport from Encore, I search for and find a reliable, reasonably priced van service (DNR Limousine Services, in case you’re interested; ask for Vladi) that also stops at a kosher supermarket so we can pick up our large online order of food supplies and sushi lunch.
By the day before the holiday, the nondescript vacation village has been transformed into a Sukkot hub. Thatched-roof booths are ubiquitous, mostly in driveways, but also in backyards beside the private swimming pools.
Nearly all those rental homes also have golf carts in their driveways, not for golfaholics, but for families to use as transportation and entertainment on the resort’s streets. Many of the drivers look dangerously underage.
Despite jet lag, we spend our first two happy days in Disney parks. Then it’s Sukkot eve. Our sukkah is up and, thanks to my daughter-in-law, our holiday food is sizzling on a hotplate delivered by Amazon Prime.
One neighbor insists that we come inside and eat a plate of cholent. Another invites my husband to walk with him to one of the pop-up synagogues for the Mincha prayer. My granddaughter Eliana, 18, and I try to follow them soon after candlelighting, but never find the synagogue.
The air is balmy, with no Florida hurricanes threatening tonight. There are few cars on the street. Passersby wish us “gut Shabbos” and “gut yom tov.”
'Strange and unexpected'
“How strange and unexpected it is to be in Florida and to be surrounded by religious Jews,” Eliana says.
Most of those strolling like us are girls and women, their cooking done, their menfolk off to synagogues. The teenage girls look a lot like Eliana, in holiday dresses, long hair, and welcoming smiles. We stop to chat with a few of them along the way.
Then, when we are alone, Eliana says something that changes the mood.
“I see these girls. In most ways, they’re just like me, but none of them has been through what we teenagers in Israel have gone through. We’ve dodged rockets, cared for families where the father was gone for months, and, worst of all, we’ve gone to so many funerals and shiva calls. We’re all going to national service and the army. How different our lives have been.”
We walk quietly after that, her words bringing us back to Israel, to her hometown of Modi’in.
Modi’in has suffered devastating military losses during the war. So many young residents have fallen that the military cemetery has required expansion. When you’re 18, you know many of the soldiers from school or youth movements. The names on the gravestones are not strangers.
Eliana herself is spending the year at Tzahali, a pre-military preparatory academy for religious young women, founded in 2006. The academy is named in memory of combat navigator Tamar Ariel, whose youth group was led by Eliana’s aunt and uncle. Its program combines Torah study with preparation for meaningful leadership and service in the IDF.
Eliana already has her future army placement.
Our somberness fades as we sit around the holiday table, enjoying the home-cooked food and the novelty of having our own sukkah so far from home. Sukkot is, after all, the holiday of joy, reaffirming our reliance on the Almighty. Through the thatched roof of our Florida sukkah, the same stars we see at home are abundant and reassuring.
Little Ye’ela does get to see the princesses. She turns out to be a roller coaster enthusiast, riding with siblings Matan, 10; Ariel, 16; and Eliana on the famous roller coasters.
By the time we reach the finale, the magnificent fireworks over the Magic Kingdom, no one thinks of comparing them to the Iron Dome squiggles of light that have so often illuminated the heavens over Modi’in. Watching the bursts of light align in the air to create hearts and Disney characters, the children are able to look up at the sky and focus on the beauty.
We, too.
The writer is the Israel director of public relations at Hadassah, the Women’s Zionist Organization of America. Her latest book is A Daughter of Many Mothers, cowritten with Holocaust survivor and premier English-language witness Rena Quint.

Missiles struck Aden International Airport in southern Yemen on Friday, while a Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile headed for the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz.
The coalition said it had also destroyed two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and three drones in Saudi Arabia's Southern and Riyadh regions. It did not identify those behind the attacks.
In Aden, two missiles landed on the airport grounds, the Aden Security Department said, blaming the Iran-backed Houthi group. It said the incident was the second attack on the facility in less than a week. The Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility.
No casualties were reported. A Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for takeoff when the missiles landed, the security department said.
Yanbu key to Saudi oil exports
Yanbu is a key outlet for Saudi oil exports, allowing the kingdom to ship crude to international markets via the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz, where heightened regional tensions and security threats have raised concerns over the safety of shipping.
Brent crude briefly touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May, as worries over escalating Middle East tensions raised concerns about tighter global supplies.
Saudi Civil Defense authorities earlier issued alerts in the Jazan region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, where such warnings have become frequent since fighting resumed last month.
Houthi attacks raise concerns over deteriorating humanitarian crisis
Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has raised fears of a further deterioration in the country's humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions are worsening rapidly.
The Yemen conflict has become another front in the wider regional war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Yemen's war began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and forced the internationally recognized government south. A Saudi-led intervention began the following year, leading to years of stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.
The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since the conflict reignited, targeting airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure. In recent days, the group has also targeted sites in government-held parts of Yemen, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital.
A spokesperson for the Houthi-run health ministry said on Friday that 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what he described as "Saudi aggression" since the escalation began on September 3. Reuters could not independently verify the figures.

Two rivals in the pivotal race for New York’s 17th Congressional District are aggressively courting Jewish voters, each seeking to present themselves as a champion of Israel and a defender against antisemitism.
Rep. Mike Lawler, a two-term Republican incumbent, and Democratic challenger Cait Conley are neck and neck in polls, with both within the margin of error, in a race that could help determine which party controls the House in the last two years of President Donald Trump’s second term.
Continued Republican control of Congress would give Trump a more favorable setting for advancing his legislative agenda. A Democratic House majority would give the opposition control of House committees and their investigative powers.
NY-17 comprises Putnam and Rockland counties and parts of Westchester and Dutchess counties. An estimated 19% of the district’s residents are Jewish, according to a 2024 study commissioned by the Jewish Electorate Institute.
Each candidate is trying to tie the other to polarizing figures in their respective parties. Lawler is asserting that Conley refuses to separate herself from New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the increasingly progressive wing of the Democratic Party. Conley is accusing Lawler of being a rubber stamp for Trump’s legislative priorities.
Jewish voters emerge as key constituency in New York House race
For Conley to win, she’ll have to convince Jewish voters that not only is she a staunch Israel ally and determined to protect the Jewish community from antisemitism, but that she can distance herself from the left wing of the Democratic Party and the members of the Democratic Socialists of America, such as Mamdani and others who have been widely critical of Israel.
One reason is that most Orthodox Jews, a major constituency in Rockland County, identified as Republican or leaned Republican, according to a 2020 Pew Research national survey. Another is that a September poll by the Jewish Electorate Institute found that 57% of Jewish voters believe antisemitism is increasing within the Democratic Party, despite about 70% of Jewish voters favoring Democrats. The same national poll found 60% believed antisemitism was increasing in the Republican Party.
When the two candidates squared off in a televised debate hosted by PIX11 on Wednesday night, Lawler brought up the New York City mayor’s statement on Oct. 7, which mourned those killed and abducted on the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks before accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza and saying US tax dollars funded war crimes.
Lawler, noting that Conley repeatedly declined to condemn Mamdani in their previous debate, said the mayor issued “the most vile antisemitic statement on Oct. 7th, blaming Jews for their butchering on Oct. 7th.” Turning to Conley, Lawler asked, “Do you denounce Zohran Mamdani’s recent statement on Oct. 7th, which blamed Jews?”
“Yes, I do denounce Mamdani’s statement on October 7th, a day that we should be honoring and mourning the loss of life, the greatest loss of life to our Jewish community since the Holocaust,” she responded. “I condemn antisemitism from any party or anyone.”
Lawler, Conley clash over Mamdani, support for Israel
Both candidates spoke strongly in support of Israel. Debate moderator Dan Mannarino asked if US taxpayer money should still be used “to send offensive and defensive weapon funding to aid Israel.”
“Israel is our greatest ally in the world,” Lawler replied. “The fact is, they’re the only democracy in the Middle East.”
He then accused the Democratic Party of ambivalence toward Israel. “I am opposed to any effort by the Democrats and the DSA to defund the strategic partnership between the United States and Israel, and I will fight it tooth and nail,” he said.
Conley agreed with Lawler that the US should continue funding offensive and defensive weapons for Israel.
“I believe in Israel’s right to exist,” she said. “It is the only democracy in the Middle East. It is a strategic partner for American national security, and I believe America has a responsibility to help ensure the safety and security of the Israeli people.”
New York House candidates diverge over Netanyahu, Iran war
Even so, she sought to distinguish herself from Lawler by affirming her willingness to chastise the Israeli government when warranted. “I also will criticize the Netanyahu administration when I believe it is doing the wrong thing for Israel and America,” she said.
Conley said that although she supported the Trump administration’s military strikes on targeted locations associated with Iran’s nuclear weapons development program, she believes that the “feckless execution” of the war has drawn the country “into this reckless conflict without clear military objectives or an exit strategy.”
Lawler defended voting against congressional efforts to end the war, while trying to tie Conley to Iran’s ability to fund terrorism. He argued that while Conley served as director for counterterrorism on President Joe Biden’s National Security Council, the US “eased sanctions on the illicit oil trade between China and Iran, allowing them to accumulate hundreds of billions of dollars. That’s what funded Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis. That’s what financed the October 7th terrorist attack.”
Conley defended her record by noting that the head of ISIS was killed during her tenure. She also said that similar attacks on Iran have been on the table for both Democratic and Republican administrations for decades, but they were never carried out because those administrations determined such attacks would threaten national security.

Norwegian teen jailed for 20 years in UK for Iran-linked murder plot after being recruited online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
00:55:43 UTC
09:55:43 KST

A Norwegian teenager who flew to Britain to commit murder after being recruited online by a Swedish organized crime group linked to Iran was jailed on Friday for 20 years.
British prosecutors said Johannes Natland, now 19, was recruited by the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish criminal group that pays young people to carry out "violence as a service" on behalf of clients, including the Iranian state.
He was convicted in July of conspiracy to murder. Natland had not been told the identity of the person he had agreed to kill in return for a payment of 270,000 Norwegian kroner, around $28,600, prosecutors said.
The case was one of a number in recent years involving young adults who have stood trial in Britain over serious criminal acts carried out after being recruited online. Britain says some of them have ended up acting as unwitting proxies for foreign states such as Iran or Russia.
Foxtrot has been linked to several murders across Europe, and Britain and the US allege the group was behind attacks against Israeli and Jewish targets on behalf of Iran, which denies the allegation.
Teen said 'it will be cool to kill'
Natland had only just turned 18 when he flew from Norway to Britain, having responded to an advert which offered money to kill and said "nothing can go wrong."
He admitted possessing a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver and ammunition, but denied conspiracy to murder, saying he did not intend to carry out the plan and had considered shooting himself in the foot to get out of it.
But prosecutors said Natland was an enthusiastic recruit, who boasted to a friend that "it will be cool to kill someone."
Judge says she was sure Natland would have carried out attack if not caught
Natland was sentenced at London's Woolwich Crown Court to detention for 20 years by Judge Bobbie Cheema-Grubb, who said she was sure he would have carried out the murder if he had not been arrested by police.
"This was not an impulsive act lasting a few moments ... your conduct demonstrated purpose and persistence," she said, adding that Natland would serve at least 13 years in custody.
Natland's Norwegian lawyer Farid Bouras said in a statement: "Our priority now is to bring him home. We will be working to secure his transfer to Norway as quickly as we possibly can."
Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said there was no evidence of any direct link to Iran in Natland's case, which served as a warning to those who may be recruited to become criminal proxies.
"As Natland found, the people orchestrating these crimes will not protect you from the consequences," she said.

Defense firm Elbit Systems expands operations in Europe with new Swedish facility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
00:55:22 UTC
09:55:22 KST

Elbit Systems Sweden AB announced on Wednesday that it plans to establish the Israeli defense company's first European production and maintenance center for laser warning systems (LWS) in Sweden, as part of efforts to strengthen European defense manufacturing and support the security needs of NATO member states.
The facility, expected to become operational in 2027, will provide local integration, assembly, maintenance, and long-term technical support for laser warning systems supplied to European customers.
The initiative is part of Elbit Systems' long-term strategy to expand its industrial presence across Europe and strengthen local manufacturing and technological capabilities. The company said the facility would help improve system availability, shorten delivery times, and enhance support for European customers.
The establishment of local production capabilities also comes as European countries increase defense spending following Russia's invasion of Ukraine and pressure from US President Donald Trump for NATO allies to raise their military expenditure. Local manufacturing could strengthen Elbit's position in European defense procurement programs that prioritize domestic or regional industrial participation.
Elbit Systems to produce next-generation laser warning technology in Sweden
The planned facility will focus on Elbit Systems' next-generation passive laser warning systems, designed to immediately detect and locate laser threats directed at military platforms. The technology provides crews with additional time and operational flexibility to deploy protective measures.
According to the company, the new systems are designed to integrate seamlessly with existing command-and-control infrastructure. Their decentralized architecture reduces the number of components, minimizes modifications required to military platforms, and is intended to improve reliability and operational durability.
Armed forces worldwide already deploy Elbit's laser warning systems as key components of advanced self-protection suites for military aircraft, vehicles, and other platforms.
Sweden becomes a key hub for Elbit's European defense operations
Established in 2020, Elbit Systems Sweden has become an increasingly important part of the company's European operations, employing more than 100 people across the country. The subsidiary serves as a regional hub for Elbit's activities in Northern Europe and works closely with Sweden's defense industry.
In recent years, Elbit Systems Sweden has supported the Swedish Armed Forces through advanced defense and digitalization programs, strengthening its position as a long-term industrial and technology partner.
The expansion follows other Elbit initiatives in Europe. In June 2026, the company conducted major demonstrations of its digital battlefield networking capabilities in Sweden for representatives of NATO militaries and European defense companies.
Elbit has also expanded its European business through defense contracts involving Greece and Sweden, reflecting growing demand for Israeli-developed military technology and locally supported defense systems.
Elbit Sweden CEO highlights local manufacturing and NATO supply chains
Tobias Wennberg, CEO of Elbit Systems Sweden, said the initiative represents an important step in expanding the subsidiary's industrial capabilities and strengthening its ability to develop, deliver, and manufacture systems locally.
"This initiative represents an important step for us and reflects our commitment to strengthening our capabilities to develop, deliver, and produce locally," Wennberg said. "It also aligns well with our core technologies and enables us to expand our scope going forward."
"Through the establishment of this center and the transfer of advanced technologies, we aim to support Swedish, European, and NATO customers with reliable, long-term, and locally supported self-protection solutions with secure and sovereign supply chains," he added.

Bill tabled in US Congress to block deal on Russian diesel fuel
Gregory Meeks, a Democrat and Ranking Member of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, has introduced a bipartisan bill aimed at blocking the US-Russia deal on diesel fuel.
Source: the US House Foreign Affairs Committee's website
Details: The bill would prohibit the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) from investing in Russia's energy sector; revoke general licences issued by the US Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) and prohibit future licences; and require US President Donald Trump's administration to impose sanctions on Russia's energy sector.
The bill has 17 co-sponsors in the House of Representatives.
Quote from Meeks: "This deal won't lower costs for the American people, who are already paying for Trump's failed war of choice in Iran. It will hand Putin millions of dollars to continue slaughtering Ukrainian civilians with impunity."
"At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cosying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine. This goes against everything the United States stands for. Congress must act. Every Member of Congress who claims to be outraged by this should join in passing this legislation."
Previously: Twenty-two Democrat and Republican members of the US House of Representatives wrote to Trump demanding the full and immediate implementation of the sanctions against Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
Background:
- In September and October, Trump repeatedly urged Zelenskyy to scale back attacks on Russian oil refineries, linking the strikes to fuel shortages and rising prices in the US.
- On 8 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that talks would take place in the US involving a Ukrainian delegation. This delegation included Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People party; Rustem Umierov, Head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service; Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine; and Serhii Kyslytsia, First Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine.
- Ahead of the meeting, Axios reported, citing US and Ukrainian officials, that US President's Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were planning to present "new ideas and proposals" in Miami to break the diplomatic deadlock.
- On 9 October, Trump said he had had a "highly successful discussion" with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement on lifting sanctions on Russian diesel fuel.
- US Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick announced that a new bipartisan bill was being prepared to block any purchases of Russian oil. Fitzpatrick's fellow Republican Don Bacon said Trump's decision to purchase Russian diesel fuel looks like weakness.
- On 15 October, the Kremlin announced that Russian diesel fuel had begun reaching global markets following an agreement with Trump.

Albanian PM blames ‘foreign hands’ for unrest as student protests intensify
Riot police clash with protesters for fourth day, as young Albanians protest corruption and poor university conditions
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has blamed “foreign hands” for the increasingly violent student-led protests that are calling on him to resign.
Riot police clashed with protesters outside the education ministry for the fourth day in a row, as thousands of young Albanians marched through the capital, Tirana, on Friday to protest government corruption and poor university conditions.
“This is not a student phenomenon,” Rama said in a video address on Friday. He said there were “foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace”.
Rama insisted that the protest had “absolutely nothing to do with the hardships, problems or legitimate aspirations of anyone who desires a better life”.
Police officers used water cannon and tear gas as demonstrators hurled rocks.
The protests have spread beyond the capital to Elbasan, Shkodra and Korca, where demonstrators broke windows and set fire to rubbish bins, local media reported.
The ongoing escalation follows months of mostly peaceful demonstrations, originally sparked by the sale of part of Albania’s coastline to a luxury resort development linked to Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.
Days of unrest have increasingly targeted banks and government buildings. Protesters hurled bricks and concrete blocks at the education ministry on Tuesday. They also set fire to several buildings across the city, including the prime minister’s office, the finance and justice ministry buildings and branches of several banks.
According to a police statement, 160 people were detained over alleged acts of violence on Thursday evening.
The EU question
Demonstrators are demanding Rama’s resignation, as well as electoral and education reforms.
The prime minister, whose government denies corruption, said he would be ready to discuss rising education costs but rejected the calls to resign.
He said on Thursday, “My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward.”
His dismissal “would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership”, he added.
Corruption scandals have complicated Albania’s efforts to join the EU. Analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking.
Rama won a fourth term last year on promises to take Albania into the EU, aiming for membership as early as 2028.

WASHINGTON, October 17. /TASS/. A group of the US House of Representatives members has introduced a bill aimed at halting agreements on the supply of Russian diesel fuel to the United States, according to a document published by Gregory Meeks, a senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee (New York).
The document provides for the revocation of a general license issued by the Treasury on October 9, under which supplies of Russian diesel fuel to world markets are exempted from US sanctions until April 7. Other licenses related to the easing of restrictions on Russian energy are annulled, and the US financial authority is prohibited from issuing new ones for three years.

Grynspan holds lead for next UN chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
23:16:30 UTC
08:16:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Grynspan holds lead for next UN chief as race enters decisive stage
An informal poll by the United Nations Security Council on Friday placed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race to become the 10th UN secretary-general, two people close to the process said.
But there was no clear winner as all candidates received two or more opposing votes from the ultimately decisive five permanent members of the council — Russia, China, the US, France and Britain — opening the door for new candidates to join the race, diplomats and observers said.
Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including several wars, cutbacks in American contributions to the UN, and the 193-member body's declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of dozens of its agencies.
This was the sixth secret ballot organized by council officials, who have less than three months to pick the successor to UN chief Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on December 31.
Securing the council's recommendation requires at least nine positive votes of the 15 countries and no "discourage" votes from the five permanent members.
The race has entered a decisive stage, as Friday's poll for the first time used color-coded ballots revealing whether a veto power opposes a candidate.
Four of five polls in recent months showed Grynspan, 70, narrowly ahead, with one poll in August placing Guyana's UN ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett in the top spot.
This dynamic did not fundamentally change on Friday, with Grynspan receiving nine "encourage," five "discourage" and one "no opinion" vote, with two of the five opposing votes coming from the Security Council's permanent members, people close to the process said.
Rodrigues-Birkett received eight votes in favor, six against, and one "no opinion," with two opposing votes from the permanent members.
Rafael Grossi, director general of the UN nuclear watchdog, received a near-identical result to Rodrigues-Birkett, but with one fewer permanent member supporting his bid.
Four more former UN officials and senior diplomats are vying for support, but they have received more opposing than supporting votes, indicating waning enthusiasm for their candidacies.
Diplomats say several senior figures, including former and current foreign ministers and country leaders, are considering entering the race. Any new entrant will face a steep challenge of convincing the divided council in short order.
On the question of new contenders joining the race, Washington's envoy to the UN, Mike Waltz, said after the vote: "Countries, if they want to put more candidates in, that's certainly within their sovereign rights."
When Guterres was chosen in October 2016, it took six straw polls for the council to reach agreement.
In the more than 80-year history of the UN, there has never been a female secretary-general.
In an interview with Reuters on Thursday, Grynspan said she "wouldn't be surprised" to receive a veto and said that it would be just the start of negotiations as such blocking votes have been overcome by winning contenders in past races.
"The game is not over -- we will have to continue working," she said.
The Costa Rican economist added that the UN has become too risk-averse and its next leader must be prepared to bear the cost of diplomatic failure and try again.
She also said the UN must cut top jobs, curb bureaucracy and stop agencies duplicating work, arguing that cost-cutting alone would not revive an institution struggling with shrinking resources and declining political clout.

Drone strike kills 30 at cattle market in Sudan's Darfur

Breadcrumb
Drone strike kills 30 at cattle market in Sudan's Darfur
A drone strike on a cattle market in Sudan's Nyala killed 30 people on Friday, AFP reported, in one of the deadliest attacks on the paramilitary stronghold in the western Darfur region.
The Rapid Support Forces blamed the attack on the army, while a military source acknowledged an uptick in strikes on the area, without claiming responsibility.
Both the RSF and the army, at war since April 2023, have increasingly used drones to launch far-reaching attacks without sacrificing their fighters.
Nyala, Sudan's second-largest city and the capital of South Darfur state, serves as the seat of the self-declared administration established by the RSF last year.
"The drone strike on the city's cattle market today killed 30 people and wounded 47 others, who are receiving treatment at the hospital," a medical source at Nyala Hospital told AFP on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to brief the media.
The source did not say who was responsible for the attack.
The strike hit the livestock market on a Friday morning, when traders and shoppers typically crowd the area and roadside stalls serve grilled meat, a popular breakfast in Darfur.
The RSF accused the Sudanese army of carrying out Friday's attack using a Turkish-made drone.
In a statement, the paramilitary group said the strike targeted a densely populated civilian area, adding that preliminary reports indicated 17 women and five children were among the dead.
A military source, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that the army had intensified strikes against RSF positions inside Nyala on Friday.
The source said the military had also targeted Nyala airport 48 hours earlier, adding that all attacks were aimed at military objectives.
Drone warfare
Sudan's war, now in its fourth year, has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced more than 11 million and triggered what the United Nations has described as one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
More than 1,100 people were killed in drone attacks across Sudan during the first half of this year alone, according to the UN.
Nyala has come under repeated drone attacks in recent months as the army seeks to challenge RSF control over Darfur.
The paramilitary group seized most of the region last year after capturing El-Fasher, the last major Darfur city previously held by the army, in an offensive that UN experts said bore "the hallmarks of genocide".
The latest strike comes as fighting intensifies in several parts of the country, including the strategic Kordofan region linking Darfur to central and eastern Sudan.
On Thursday, an army Antonov aircraft struck a house in the paramilitary-controlled village of Abu Zaeima in North Kordofan, killing five children from the same family and wounding their mother, according to the rights group Emergency Lawyers.
Recent attacks in Kordofan have also hit a shelter for displaced people and a university dormitory, killing at least 15 people, the group said.

Russia Seeks New Gas Buyers in Africa After Losing More Than Half of Gazprom’s Exports

- Category

Russia Seeks New Gas Buyers in Africa After Losing More Than Half of Gazprom’s Exports
Russia is turning to African countries in search of new markets for Gazprom after the state gas giant lost more than half of its exports outside the former Soviet Union following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, The Moscow Times reported on October 16.
Russian Energy Minister Sergei Tsivilev announced that Moscow was prepared to supply gas to African countries while offering exploration, extraction, and broader energy infrastructure services.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Our country can offer a comprehensive solution: modernize existing hydroelectric plants, build solar and thermal power stations, lay networks, supply substations and transformers, and create power-system management and dispatch centers,” Tsivilev stated.
Tsivilev added that Moscow views Africa as a “long-term market,” The Moscow Times reported.
The push comes as Gazprom struggles to replace European customers lost since 2022. According to estimates from Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development cited by The Moscow Times, Russian gas exports are expected to total about 77 billion cubic meters in 2026, down from 185 billion in 2021 and roughly 200 billion at the end of the 2010s.
The ministry projects exports falling further to 72 billion cubic meters by 2028, after the EU gas embargo takes effect. The Moscow Times noted that this would return Russian gas exports to levels last seen in the second half of the 1980s.
Russia has also struggled to secure a major new gas agreement with China. The Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, has sought to increase annual supplies to China to as much as 100 billion cubic meters, but negotiations have stalled over pricing.
According to sources cited by the South China Morning Post, Beijing wants Russian gas priced at around $50 per thousand cubic meters, close to what Russian households pay, or roughly $120-$130 for industrial consumers.
Moscow, however, wants pricing closer to the approximately $250-$260 per thousand cubic meters China currently pays for gas delivered through Power of Siberia 1. That price already represents a discount of roughly 40% compared with Gazprom’s contracts with other foreign customers, which average about $420 per thousand cubic meters.
The Moscow Times reported that negotiations over the proposed Power of Siberia 2 pipeline, which Putin has renamed “Power of Baikal,” are currently suspended because of the disagreement over price.
On October 13, Zelenskyy warned that Russia’s blockade of maritime routes could trigger food shortages across parts of Africa, Asia, and the Middle East within one to two months by restricting Ukrainian grain exports.

Zelensky’s diesel burnout, Nord Stream on trial, Russiagate revived: RT stories that shaped the week

Zelensky’s diesel burnout, Nord Stream on trial, Russiagate revived: RT stories that shaped the week
Zelensky’s diesel-fueled burnout
This week did not start well for Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, who was apparently blindsided by US President Donald Trump’s decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel supplies after talks with the Kremlin. The deal won’t alleviate the global diesel shortage, but it’s already cooling speculative markets and easing pressure on Trump ahead of next month’s midterm elections.
For Zelensky, it’s a “diplomatic nightmare,” as Russian analyst Sergey Poletaev wrote for RT. Trump rubbed salt in the wound on Saturday when he openly suggested that Ukrainians “get a new leader who can make a deal” and halt attacks on Russian oil refineries. Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump went on to claim, “wants to make a deal more than Zelensky.”
Backed into a corner, Zelensky began throwing haymakers. Accusing the American president of empathizing with dictators, Zelensky demanded air defense missiles from the US before vowing to continue his drone campaign against Russia’s refineries – with or without American support.
The US apparently sent a warning signal to Zelensky by throttling the Ukrainian military’s access to SpaceX’s high-speed Starlink and Starshield satellite communications services, which are vital tools in guiding attack drones used against Russia, and in detecting incoming retaliatory strikes. Neither Trump nor SpaceX CEO Elon Musk would take responsibility for the communications drop-off, but even if they had, their message would likely have fallen of deaf ears.
Zelensky escalates the energy war
The Ukrainian leader followed through on his promise to keep hitting Russian refineries, despite Trump’s announcement of an “energy ceasefire” between Moscow and Kiev (which neither side confirmed). Ukrainian forces attacked facilities in Russia’s Saratov and Ryazan regions on Wednesday, before firing a barrage of four long-range Flamingo cruise missiles and 69 fixed-wing kamikaze drones at the Ryazan refinery again on Thursday.
Debris from an intercepted UAV triggered an intense fire at the facility, according to the Russian Defense Ministry.
Retaliation was swift, from both Moscow and Washington. Russian forces used missiles and drones to strike six power plants in Kiev, Kharkov, and the surrounding regions, as well as military logistics hubs and data centers. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that it shot down four missiles out of 39, confirming reports that Zelensky launched the refinery strikes knowing Ukraine lacked adequate air defense supplies to repel the retaliation.
Trump went on to savage Zelensky in a Newsmax interview on Thursday. “I’m not a big fan of Zelensky. They’ve destroyed that country,” he said, before accusing the Ukrainian leader of selling missiles given to him by the US “on the open market.”
“Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with,” Trump concluded.
Nord Stream trial begins
As Ukraine doubles down on its infrastructure war, the costliest infrastructure attack in history is finally being litigated in a German courtroom. Sergey Kuznetsov, a Ukrainian military officer, went on trial in Hamburg this week, accused of leading the team that sabotaged the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines in September 2022, an act that German prosecutors consider a “war crime.”
Kuznetsov is staying silent, refusing to admit or deny a role in the bombing. The evidence against him is circumstantial, and his lawyers are confident that without a confession, he “cannot be convicted.”
As RT has explored in depth, the prosecution’s version of events is riddled with plot holes and inconsistencies. However, to pick apart the alternative story – that the pipelines were destroyed in a CIA operation – would call the relationship between Washington and Berlin, the foundation of the postwar liberal order, into question.
While a guilty verdict against Kuznetsov would directly implicate the Ukrainian military in a war crime against its largest foreign donor, the trial, at least at this stage, appears set up to avoid this outcome.
Russiagate resurrected
Speaking of reopening old wounds, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham dug up the bloated corpse of ‘Russiagate’ this week to bolster his efforts to undo the 2016 Brexit referendum and rejoin the EU. Burnham claimed that he had “clear” evidence that Russia interfered in the vote, in which Britons voted by 51.89% to 48.11% to leave the union.
Just as the original ‘Russiagate’ claims against Trump fell apart under questioning, Burnham’s allegation crumbled once subjected to some basic scrutiny. The British PM was unable to back up his accusation when grilled in Parliament, and his foreign secretary, Stephen Doughty, humiliated himself on national television when he attempted to evade questioning on the claim.
The final nail in the coffin came when Burnham’s own domestic intelligence chief cautioned against exaggerating “Russian influence” on Brexit, arguing that debating the influence of “Russian trolls” on the vote “play[s] into our adversaries’ hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall.”
However, Burnham couldn’t be faulted for his timing and opportunism. As he spoke of Russian bots and influence campaigns in Parliament on Monday, Zelensky, his Polish and Baltic backers, and his army of internet supporters claimed that a Ukrainian strike on a Yandex data center in Russia the previous day had wiped thousands of “Russian bots” from social media.
As it turned out, none of this was true. The strike interrupted the activity of Yandex’ web crawler bots, which archive websites for search users, but with the help of an AI-created graph and some creative interpretation of the word “bot,” the hoax made it all the way to the Warsaw Security Forum.
French riots spread
French students took part in a fifth wave of demonstrations this week, which they say are aimed at securing more school funding and better learning conditions. Every wave of protests thus far has descended into rioting and vandalism, and this week’s marches were no different, with participants torching cars and battering police officers with cobblestones and fireworks in Paris.
RT’s Nadege Abderazzak watched heavily armored police baton-charge crowds of rioters in the French capital on Wednesday, noting that officers now outnumber protesters two-to-one at some rallies.
With French President Emmanuel Macron determined to increase military spending and continue arming Ukraine, France’s financial situation is in dire straits, and right-wing National Rally leader Marine Le Pen is on track to win the country’s next presidential election.
Meanwhile, Albanian students have taken a page out of their French counterparts’ book. After large protests demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama and opposition leader Sali Berisha over corruption allegations, a crowd of students breached the fence of the Education Ministry in Tirana on Wednesday and torched the building.
Rama’s response has also drawn from the Western playbook, with the Albanian PM accusing protesters of waging “hybrid war” against the country.
What we’re watching
Zelensky may be in Trump’s bad books, but he can still count on the support of Macron, Burnham, and the rest of his European backers, whom he met in Brussels on Thursday and Friday. In his address to the European Council on Friday, the Ukrainian leader asked for another “70 billion euros” for ammunition, missiles, and air defense. Should Ukraine “fall,” Zelensky warned, another 20 million Ukrainian migrants will flood into the EU.
We’ll be keeping an eye on what kind of promises the cash-strapped Europeans make after this blatant shakedown.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will fly to Tehran on Monday for talks with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi. The two diplomats are expected to focus on de-escalating the simmering US/Iran conflict in the Middle East, and any progress on this front will likely be reflected in global energy markets.
Lavrov will also meet Serbian Interior Minister Ivica Dacic on Friday, ahead of critical parliamentary elections on October 25. Amid student protests, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic called the election early and stepped down to run as prime minister, a high-stakes move that turned the vote into a referendum on his nine years in power. With pro-Western students and right-wing ‘patriotic’ forces squeezing Vucic from either side, we’ll be keeping an eye out for polls, protests, and interference from the usual suspects.

Streets quiet in Bend city
A woman identified as his mother told the local Fox affiliate she was "very proud" and that her son was "an absolute hero" before she read a prepared statement.
"He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," she said.
On Friday, the small city in the US northwest was struggling to come to terms with a tragedy that took the lives of children aged five, eight and 11, as well as a teacher, the latest victims of America's epidemic of gun violence that all-too-frequently afflicts the nation's schools.
Streets were quiet in an area known for its natural beauty, with hiking trails and ski pistes nearby that attract tens of thousands of visitors every year.
Kristen Vanetsky, 52, told AFP news agency she was in shock over the shooting at her grandson's school.
"My grandson should be in his classroom, with all of his friends," she said.
"Everybody should be in there learning, having fun, looking forward to their weekend, and it's just vacant," she said. "There's nothing. Even the birds are not here."
Gun violence debate
Even as the city tried to process the tragic events, the familiar contours of an argument that plays out after every school shooting in the US began to harden.
The NRA has invested millions of dollars campaigning for gun rights and supporting politicians who block the limits on ownership that the vast majority of Americans support.
Gun control advocates again lamented the ready availability of weaponry in a country where the number of gun-related deaths far outpaces most of the developed world.
The United States holds the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership globally, making it the world's most heavily armed society.
Persistent mass shootings in the US have repeatedly heightened public calls for stricter federal gun control measures.
Despite repeated calls over the years, the US Congress has yet to enact such restrictions.
"America's gun violence crisis is killing our babies. Enough is enough," gun-control group GIFFORDS said on X.
More than 360 mass shootings have been recorded across the United States this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines them as incidents in which at least four people are shot, excluding the gunman.
Griffin's neighbours told AFP they had seen his mother taken away from the house she shared with the suspect on Thursday afternoon in a police patrol car.
That woman, Shauntai May Nickerson, was seen on her apartment and crying.
"If I could have prevented this, I would have," a tearful Nickerson said, according to The New York Times.

Nirit is travelling 14,000km to vote in Israel's election. She's not alone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:38:26 UTC
04:38:26 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Nirit Eylon immigrated to Australia 21 years ago. This month, for the first time, she’s flying back to Israel specifically to vote.
The country does not allow citizens living abroad to vote from outside its borders.
But with an election many view as the most consequential in its history fast approaching, estimates from the US-based Fly&Vote initiative, which helps facilitate their travel, suggest as many as 53,000 Israeli expats are expected to return.
Eylon is among them.
"There is a perception that this election is about right and left. I don't believe it's so. I believe it's between right and wrong," the 52-year-old, who lives in Melbourne, tells SBS News.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Eylon believes Israel is at a crossroads. She views the election as a contest between competing visions of the country’s future: one grounded in liberal democratic values, and another shaped by religious nationalism.
She believes Israel's leaders must be held accountable for failures surrounding the October 7 attacks, and that political change is necessary for Israel to begin to heal.
Eylon is far from alone in viewing this election as pivotal.
Israeli political science expert Shahar Burla, a contributing editor at The Jewish Independent, is one of more than 11,000 Israeli-born people living in Australia.
He tells SBS News he knows around 20 people in his immediate circle who are planning to return to Israel for the election — a circumstance he describes as "very unusual".
"I think that the main motivation is fear," he says.
There is a fear that if the Netanyahu bloc will win again, that will be the end of Israel as we know it as a democratic, liberal, free state.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government has pursued sweeping changes to Israel's institutions, including moves to curb the judiciary’s oversight of government decisions, while pushing increasingly hardline policies towards Palestinians and expanding Israeli military operations across the region, including in Lebanon and Iran.
Ongoing geopolitical tensions and fractured alliances mean the election will be watched closely by many outside Israel too.
SBS News has spoken with nine people from Jewish, Israeli, Palestinian, Lebanese and Iranian communities in Australia about what is at stake for them in this election, as conflict continues to reverberate across the Middle East.
While their views on peace, security and coexistence vary, they share one common belief: that Israel cannot continue on its current path.
For Palestinian Australian academic Shamikh Badra — who lost his father, his brother and his brother’s family to the war in Gaza — a change of government would be welcome, but he cautions it's not a simple fix.
"I am not saying that [the] next government will automatically be better, but removing this government is the first step," he says.
The electoral landscape
Netanyahu, as leader of the Likud party, has served as Israel's prime minister for nearly 20 non-consecutive years since he was first elected in 1996.
In the lead-up to the 27 October election, a relatively new, centrist party called Yashar has been polling neck and neck with Likud.
Former Israel Defense Forces (IDF) chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot leads the party, which takes its name from the Hebrew word for 'straightforward' or 'honest'.
Eisenkot is Netanyahu’s primary challenger to lead the country, and has a personal stake in Israel's ongoing conflicts, having lost both his son and nephew in the Hamas-Israel war.
He's running on a platform of accountability for the October 7 attack, promising to restore trust in Israel's institutions and strengthen national security.
But neither party is close to winning enough seats for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.
That means coalition-building will be crucial to forming government.
Currently, Israel’s parties are divided over their willingness to govern alongside Netanyahu rather than splitting along traditional left-right lines. Two distinct camps remain: those willing to join a Netanyahu-led coalition, and those who may be willing to join one led by Eisenkot.
But neither bloc appears to have a clear path to a parliamentary majority, raising the prospect of political deadlock.
Burla notes that while Eisenkot has positioned himself at the political centre, his prospective coalition spans the political spectrum and includes right-wing parties.
That limits how far a new government could go on issues such as recognising Palestinian statehood and negotiating territorial compromise.
Among Israel's major Jewish-led parties, support for Palestinian statehood remains limited. Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats, is the only major party leader to have endorsed a future two-state solution.
Burla believes changing Israel's leadership could remove a "first obstacle" to peace with Palestinians, but does not expect significant progress in the coming years.
"None of them will speak about a Palestinian state at this stage, or any territorial compromise with the Palestinians.
"But I think that Eisenkot has at least the potential, the political potential, to move forward some kind of a peace process."
High stakes for those with a vote — and those without one
Yasmeen Abu Fraiha is a medical doctor who works with humanitarian missions in the Middle East.
She's one of roughly two million Palestinian citizens of Israel, a group that makes up around 20 per cent of the country’s population.
Fraiha tells SBS News many "feel the urgency in these elections". She believes Palestinian voters will turn out in higher numbers than they have for previous polls.
Palestinian citizens of Israel have historically voted at lower rates than the wider population. In the 2022 election, just over half of Arab and Druze voters cast a ballot, compared with more than 70 per cent nationally, according to the Israel Democracy Institute.
Fraiha, too, feels democracy is at stake. But for Palestinians, she says, the consequences are more fundamental.
"I don't know if it will be necessarily better if [Netanyahu] loses, but it will definitely be worse if they win again," she says.
It’s really a matter of life and death for us as Palestinians, for sure in the West Bank and Gaza, but also inside Israel.
Yet many Palestinians who will be directly affected by the election’s outcome will have no say in it.
Badra, the Sydney-based researcher and community organiser from Gaza, says his family paid the ultimate price under Israel’s current government. His priority is to see it removed from power.
Beyond that, a path to peace will not be easy. But Badra says any lasting solution must address Palestinian rights and security, including an end to occupation and settlement expansion.
"Security for Palestinians means being able to live in your home without fear of bombing. It means children have food, medicine, education. It means people being able to move freely and live with dignity," he says.
"It also means real political and human rights for Palestinians."
On 7 October 2023, Hamas killed 1,200 people and took another 251 captive during its attack on southern Israel.
Israel's retaliatory bombardment of Gaza has decimated much of the strip and killed more than 74,000 people, including more than 1,400 since a ceasefire began last October, according to the local health ministry.
The humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain dire, with critically limited access to food, water and essential services. UNICEF estimates nearly 84 per cent of Gaza’s population continues to live in overcrowded displacement sites or damaged shelters.
Far from Israel, but close to home
The election’s outcome will be felt far beyond Israel. For many Australians like Sam Hoballah, the results will be deeply personal.
Born in southern Lebanon, in a town close to the Israeli border, the Sydney-based interpreter moved to Australia 40 years ago.
However, much of his family still lives in Lebanon, a country scarred by civil war and decades of regional conflict.
As a child, Hoballah says he grew accustomed to periods of recurring war and insecurity. Last August, before Israel launched its ground invasion of southern Lebanon, he returned to his hometown to visit family.
"This time it was different," he tells SBS News of the conflict in recent years.
"While [they] have been living in a difficult, insecure situation in that part of Lebanon, this time it is catastrophic."
Following the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, a new chapter began in the decades-long conflict between Israel and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah.
Despite a ceasefire in November 2024, the conflict flared again in March this year, after Israel and the US initiated war with Iran.
The Iran-backed Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel in support of its ally, triggering a major Israeli air and ground offensive in Lebanon.
More than 4,300 people have since been killed in Lebanon, according to the country’s health ministry, while dozens of Israelis have been killed in the conflict.
Israel’s occupation and bombardment of southern Lebanon has flattened villages and displaced hundreds of thousands of people.
Hoballah says his own siblings are among them; parts of his hometown, Shaqra, have been reduced to rubble.
"It's a total misery there now," he says.
"So you can imagine the psychological impact this has on our community here [in Australia]."
The 66-year-old says he can’t recall a time in his life when people in southern Lebanon felt safe under any Israeli government.
"To be honest, there was some differences, but no major difference."
He has little faith the election will bring meaningful change, but hopes to see Israel led by a more moderate coalition.
I'm a person who believes that people of different nationalities, race, faith, they can live together, and we can live with the people in Israel.
For Australians with ties to Iran, the war has also brought Israel's political future into sharp focus.
Suren Edgar, vice president of the Australian Iranian Community Alliance, says the conflict has affected many in his community very personally.
"You are consistently checking the news, trying to contact people and worrying about what may happen next," he tells SBS News.
He says decisions made by Israel’s next government "could have direct consequences" for his friends, family and the wider region.
"For me, what is at stake is whether the region moves toward another cycle of war, or towards greater stability."
Edgar hopes Israel's next government will balance its security concerns with the need to protect civilians and infrastructure, recognising that long-term security cannot come from permanent regional conflict.
"I hope it understands that weakening the Islamic Republic and weakening Iranian society are not the same thing."
Across different diaspora groups, the election is also being viewed as a vote on the direction the country will take in managing its foreign relationships and conflicts into the future.
Ric Benjamin is chair of the New Israel Fund Australia and a longtime organiser within Australia’s Jewish community.
He says many Jewish Australians feel "strongly connected to Israel" and are passionate about its elections, even if they can’t cast a ballot.
Benjamin points to the work of Jewish and Palestinian Israelis who continue to cooperate despite the conflict, such as those in the health and humanitarian sectors, as a rubric for Australians navigating their own divisions.
"If it's possible for people who are on the ground in the conflict, who have on both sides lost people through war or terror, if they are able to come together, why is it that our communities, 15,000 kilometres away, can't find that when they cry out for help?
Let's focus on the common causes and the common issues we have, and through that build trust and and build an acceptance.
That desire to break the cycle of conflict at the ballot box is one of the reasons Israeli Australian Limor Fayena has extended her trip to Israel. It will be her first time voting in Israel in 20 years.
The Sydney-based 50-year-old software engineer, who is also Burla's partner, says she hopes her vote will help bring about a "more responsible government" — one that will consider the future being created for the nation's children and grandchildren.
"How can we minimise the option of another war and sit down and think about the future — not the current and not the past?"

EU vows satellite support for Ukraine but cannot yet replace Starlink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:34:21 UTC
04:34:21 KST

The European Union has pledged to help Ukraine reduce its dependence on US-owned satellite communications, while acknowledging that it cannot replace Starlink in the short term.
Speaking at an EU summit in Brussels on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said services were still being restored after disruptions he described as “a very unpleasant and dangerous surprise”.
Ukraine reported restrictions this week on some Starlink internet terminals, saying they had hampered its ability to defend against Russian forces.
The disruption came amid renewed tensions between Kiev and Washington even as US President Donald Trump denied ordering temporary disruption of Starlink service for Ukraine’s military.
EU leaders rallied around Zelenskyy but acknowledged limits to the support Europe could immediately provide.
“We are working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed,” French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters after the talks.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Europe had no readily available replacement.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine, and unfortunately in the short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” she said.
Europe’s satellite plans
EU countries currently pool and share satellite communications capacity through GOVSATCOM, a programme in which the bloc wants to fully include Ukraine, EU spokesperson Thomas Regnier said.
The EU also plans to incorporate commercial services into GOVSATCOM early next year to help meet military needs while it develops its own satellite network.
That network, known as IRIS², is intended to rival Starlink. Launches are planned for 2029, with full operations targeted for 2030.
Ukraine uses SpaceX’s military satellite service, Starshield, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-controlled territory and interceptor drones.
It also uses the company’s civilian Starlink system, though not for offensive operations.
SpaceX owner Elon Musk, whose stance on Ukraine has shifted repeatedly since 2022, said this week that any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his company.
Limited alternatives
European support extends beyond EU programmes. France’s Eutelsat already provides satellite communications services to Ukraine through its OneWeb network, although it has disclosed little about government and military uses.
Its constellation of 648 satellites, however, is far smaller than Starlink’s network of more than 10,000.
According to specialist publication Via Satellite, OneWeb cannot support drone and ground robot operations because of limited capacity and a lack of compact satellite terminals.
Kallas said the European Defence Agency had identified critical capabilities that Europe lacked, stressing that those gaps needed to be filled “as soon as possible”.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also underscored Ukraine’s dependence on the service.
“Starlink is the key for Ukraine, actually, to fight or fight back,” he told reporters. “It takes time for us to have the same capabilities. We do have it, but not enough.”
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said he had discussed Starlink with Macron on Thursday, including how European countries could provide more such services in the near future.
