Major Bathla lender La Trobe sells $31.2m loan as private credit firms seek to recover funds
In short:
La Trobe Financial has sold its senior loan facility, tied to a Bathla Group development, to investors through a fund managed by 360 Capital.
The $31.2 million purchase would give 360 Capital greater influence over the Marsden Park project.
What's next?
Morningstar expects private credit fund growth to slow substantially.
The fallout from the collapse of property developer Bathla Group continues to reverberate through Australia's private credit market, with lenders taking matters into their own hands to recover money tied up in the failed construction giant.
In one of the latest deals, property investment and funds management group 360 Capital has revealed it acquired a senior loan facility for about $31.2 million through its private credit fund, funded by private investors and entities within the 360 Capital group.
A senior loan facility is the first mortgage debt in a commercial investment and ranks highest in repayment priority.
The ABC understands the debt was acquired from major private lender La Trobe Financial, relating to a Bathla development at 137 South Street, Marsden Park, in Sydney's north-west.
The Marsden Park project comprises 72 apartments and is nearing completion, according to two sources close to the construction.
Half of the apartments have already been pre-sold under contracts worth $25.8 million (excluding GST), 360 Capital said in a statement.
In August, La Trobe disclosed it had $38.1 million in loans to Bathla, comprising four residential loans and one development loan.
The ABC understands through this deal, La Trobe has sold its development loan, recovering all outstanding principal, interest and late-payment charges and significantly reducing its exposure to the collapsed developer.
Deal gives 360 Capital greater control
360 Capital's ASX-listed mortgage investment trust, the 360 Capital Mortgage REIT, already held an $8.9 million loan secured against the development, which ranked behind La Trobe Financial for repayment.
The trust has invested a further $5.2 million in the deal.
"The step was not taken lightly, but is very important to protect the value of the trust's subordinated position," the company said.
The deal means entities associated with 360 Capital now control both the first and second mortgages over the development, giving them greater influence over how the project is completed and the debts recovered.
Morningstar equity analyst Winky Tan said lenders holding first mortgages were in a much stronger position to recover their money, while mezzanine lenders further down the repayment queue risked losing most, if not all, of their investment.
"When you're able to finish the project, you can sell it as a finished product, which will have a much higher valuation than a half-finished project," she said.
Following the purchase, advisory firm Wexted was appointed as receiver, with a focus on speeding up the process of obtaining occupancy certificates and settling the 36 pre-sold apartments.
360 Capital executive chairman Tony Pitt said the group expected to recover the full amount owed to it under the loan.
Ms Tan cautioned that the ultimate financial outcome for any lender would depend on whether the remaining apartments could be sold and at what price, particularly given the downturn in the property market.
'Perfect storm' unfolding in private credit sector
Lenders including Centuria Bass and CVS Lane suspended withdrawals from some funds in August amid concerns about their exposure to Bathla.
MA Financial, which says it has no exposure to Bathla, also introduced withdrawal limits on some of its funds amid concerns more investors could seek to pull out their money.
Major private credit manager Metrics Credit Partners, which also says it has no exposure to Bathla, suspended withdrawals from some unlisted funds amid scrutiny of asset valuations.
Corporate regulator ASIC has previously warned of poor practices across the private credit sector, including questionable asset valuations, opaque fees and inadequate disclosure.
ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said the Bathla collapse highlighted the need for stronger oversight, warning the industry was now "beyond warnings" and should prepare for enforcement action.
Ms Tan described the sector as facing "a perfect storm" of higher interest rates and falling property prices, with developers potentially struggling to refinance their debts just as nervous investors sought to withdraw their money.
Morningstar expects growth in private credit funds to slow substantially in the near to medium term, potentially make it harder for developers to secure financing and further worsening Australia's housing shortage.

EU plans new tool to restrict market access in potential trade war
Unknown

2026-10-16
19:23:18 UTC
04:23:18 KST

The European Union will develop a new tool to swiftly block access to the bloc’s market in the event of a trade war, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has said.
Her announcement came after France and Germany said on Friday that they wanted to strengthen the EU’s legal armoury in case of a potential trade conflict with China.
"We will develop a new instrument for decisive action by limiting access to the single market where this is in the union’s interests fast and immediately," she told reporters after EU leaders met in Brussels.
Von der Leyen also reiterated calls for Europe to change the way it consumes energy, warning that the bloc’s dependence on imported fossil fuels has increased costs by $119 billion without delivering any additional energy.
Speaking at a press conference after the summit, she said Europe’s reliance on imported oil and gas continues to expose its economy to geopolitical developments beyond its control.
She said gas prices had surged by around 140 percent since late February, while diesel prices had doubled, highlighting the economic consequences of the ongoing energy crisis.
"We must also change the way we consume energy," von der Leyen said, calling for the replacement of foreign fossil fuels with electricity produced in Europe.
Energy transition
She stressed that Europe must remain committed to its energy transition, focusing on affordable, clean and domestically produced energy sources, including nuclear power and renewables.
European Council President Antonio Costa also highlighted the impact of high and volatile energy prices on households and businesses, describing energy costs as a crucial component of Europe’s competitiveness.
He said the bloc was paying the price of its dependence on fossil fuels and the absence of a fully integrated single energy market.
Costa also announced that he would convene another informal meeting of EU leaders in Alden Biesen, Belgium, in February 2027 to assess progress on defence and competitiveness following previous discussions.
Short-term measures
Von der Leyen outlined several short-term measures agreed upon to mitigate the impact of rising energy prices.
These include the release of 100 million barrels of oil and diesel over the next four months, managed by the International Energy Agency, extending the scope and duration of a temporary state aid framework introduced in February, and postponing implementation of the methane regulation by one year.
The EU will also launch a strategic dialogue on European refineries, with the aim of strengthening refining capacity within the bloc and helping bring prices down.
Von der Leyen also addressed concerns over the EU’s trade relationship with China, calling for a substantial and rapid rebalancing of economic ties.
She said the bloc’s trade deficit with China reached €1 billion per day in 2025 and warned that the imbalance was expected to worsen in 2026.
Costa said the bloc’s commitment to Ukraine remained strong and that the EU had identified the means to cover the country’s financial needs for this year. He called on the European Commission to propose measures addressing additional financing needs for 2027.

How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm elections
Through statements in English, Iranian officials are emphasising gas prices and issues with the US economy.

“It’s not necessarily that they’re trying to get Democrats in power or manipulate US politics in a certain direction, other than just overall increasing the costs on this issue of the Iran war, and just playing that game of information warfare and getting out their own narrative and propaganda as well,” Toossi told Al Jazeera.
Trump’s Republican Party is looking to retain control of the Senate and House of Representatives in next month’s midterm vote. But the Democratic Party, which largely opposes the war with Iran, is mounting a strong challenge across the congressional electoral map, including in areas that have been conservative strongholds for decades, such as Texas.
On Wednesday, Ghalibaf shared a news story on inflation rising to 3.7 percent last month along with a collage of negative headlines on the US economy.
The social media post also featured a comic strip from the Road Runner cartoon showing Wile E Coyote building a catapult that misfires and launches a boulder at him.

Ghalibaf’s remark referred to the increase in inflation, underscoring that the cost of living keeps rising due to the war despite Bessent’s assertions.
Days earlier, he shared an image of a ghost shaped like a bell curve, with diesel prices rising and housing affordability and consumer confidence falling.
Since the start of the war on February 28, Iran has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, sending energy prices soaring. In the US, the price of diesel is at an all-time record of $6.33 per gallon (3.8 litres), according to the American Automobile Association, and gas is $4.33, up from less than $3 before the war.
Iran has intensified its attacks on vessels around the strait in recent days after Trump and his aides repeatedly stressed that the waterway is under US control.
The uptick in energy prices has fuelled overall inflation in the economy, leading the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates last month at a time when Trump has been calling for them to be cut to stimulate economic activity.
In a letter to the American public on September 29, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) accused Trump of lying about the cost of the war and the state of the US economy, dismissing the president’s claims that oil prices would soon nosedive.
“Countries around the world have lost their faith in the US economy. Demand for American bonds has plummeted. In fact, countries are starting to offload their US bonds. “I don’t think they’re hedging their bets either way, and I don’t think it necessarily affects their overall strategy of increasing the costs [of war] regardless of whatever happens in November,” Toossi told Al Jazeera.

President Donald Trump has fired his newly appointed White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, after just five days on the job, U.S. media reported Friday, following a troubled debut and growing controversy over her claims about her legal career. The reports came shortly after Trump publicly suggested she should reconsider remaining in the position, saying she had been treated unfairly by the media. Trump later said he was in no rush to appoint a new White House press secretary to replace Zacharia, Fox News reported.
Speaking to reporters on the White House lawn before departing for a campaign rally in Georgia, Trump said he had spoken with Zacharia about the intense criticism she faced since taking the job.
"I told Katie, in my opinion, she was treated very unfairly," Trump said, adding that she had been "brutalized by the media."
Recounting their conversation, Trump said: "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy.'" He added: "I want her to have a good life. I don't want her to have a life like she's led the last three days."
The president also addressed Zacharia directly through reporters, saying: "Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this."
At the time, Trump stopped short of announcing her dismissal, saying he would make a final decision after returning from his campaign trip. "When I get back, we're gonna talk," he said.
CNN reported, citing a source familiar with Trump's private conversations, that the president had been more decisive behind closed doors, telling advisers that Zacharia "wasn't ready for prime time," According to the report, Trump initially believed her first briefing had gone better than his advisers thought, but changed his assessment following her interview with Sean Hannity.
White House communications director Steven Cheung confirmed Zacharia's departure, telling The New York Times that she was "transitioning into a new role that will be announced at a later date."

No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to." She concluded: "It was an honor to work for him."

Just before 1 p.m., as she discussed her plans for the position, senior Trump adviser Jason Miller knocked on her door. "JD wanted to chat with us real quick," he said, referring to Vice President JD Vance. According to the newspaper, Zacharia never returned to the interview or to her position.
Before her dismissal became public, Zacharia appeared calm and spoke enthusiastically about her close relationship with Trump. "That's what matters," she said. Discussing her plans for the press team, she added: "There are no staffing changes that are happening. I'm trying to keep everyone cohesive." Less than an hour later, she was out of the job.

Zacharia said she found it difficult to turn down the assignment because she wanted to be a team player, describing how she scrambled to gather the necessary information and prepare for the briefing on short notice.
Nevertheless, Zacharia told The Wall Street Journal that she did not believe Trump had made a mistake by sending her into the briefing room on such short notice and stressed that she did not blame the White House.
Zacharia, who replaced Karoline Leavitt, began her new position Monday and held her first White House press briefing Tuesday. The briefing lasted just 14 minutes, during which she read extensively from prepared talking points and took questions from only three news organizations, all considered friendly to Trump. Critics said she appeared nervous and stumbled over some of her answers, although Trump initially defended her performance.
During the briefing, Zacharia mistakenly referred to her husband as the president before correcting herself. She also said her role was to highlight Trump's accomplishments, emphasizing that the president was best equipped to speak for himself.
When she abruptly ended the briefing, Zacharia told reporters they could direct further questions to Trump on the White House's South Lawn before his departure for a campaign event in Alaska.
Zacharia's five-day tenure was the shortest in White House press secretary history, surpassing Stephen Early, who served as acting press secretary for 14 days in 1950.
Her brief stint also drew comparisons to Anthony Scaramucci, whom Trump fired as White House communications director after just 11 days in 2017. Scaramucci, who later became a Trump critic, expressed solidarity with Zacharia in a post on X.
"Dear Katie — speaking as the world's leading expert on short White House tenures: turn off the news and go enjoy your family. In time you’ll realize that the Universe did you a major favor," he wrote.
The controversy intensified over questions about Zacharia's legal qualifications. She had previously described herself as having practiced law, and Trump himself had referred to her as an attorney. However, during an interview Thursday with Fox News host Sean Hannity, she acknowledged that she had failed the bar examination and had never retaken it.
Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University's law school in 2011. While a law degree is generally required to become an attorney in the United States, graduates must also be admitted to a state bar before they can practice law.
The watchdog group Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California, calling for an investigation into whether Zacharia had violated the law by repeatedly presenting herself as an attorney despite lacking a license to practice law.
The organization's executive director, Michelle Kuppersmith, said Zacharia had described herself as an attorney during appearances on Fox News, CNN and Newsmax and had identified herself as chief legal counsel for a California-based conservative nonprofit.
"Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility," Kuppersmith said. "The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has."
The California bar confirmed to U.S. media outlets that it had no record of Zacharia holding a license under either her married or maiden name.
Before joining the White House, Zacharia had worked as a conservative media commentator and communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group, the parent company of Truth Social. Trump announced her appointment on October 9, praising her loyalty and predicting she would do an excellent job representing his administration.
Zacharia, 41, previously worked at a law firm in Beijing after moving to China with her husband. Foreign nationals are not permitted to take China's bar examination, although they may perform certain legal work at local law firms.
Asked Tuesday where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia replied: "When I moved to China." In a subsequent statement, she said she had "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," but did not clarify whether she held a U.S. law license or where, if anywhere, she had been admitted to practice.
Zacharia told The New York Times that when she began appearing on cable news, she consulted Pepperdine University's president about how to describe her legal qualifications. She said she was advised that she could call herself a "lawyer" but should not use the terms "attorney" or "esquire." However, legal experts have questioned whether someone who has not passed the bar exam can properly describe themselves as a lawyer.

====================================================================================================

Control of Congress: How past midterms shine a light on Republican challenge in November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:04:39 UTC
03:04:39 KST

The US midterm elections, scheduled for November 3, will determine control of Congress and shape the last two years of President Donald Trump’s final term.
All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives, the lower chamber of Congress, will be up for grabs in the midterms – the informal term for the nationwide polls held in the middle of every four-year presidential term.
Elections will also be held for 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate, the upper chamber of Congress, on the same day.
Currently, the Republican Party has a slim majority in both chambers.
Without a majority in Congress, the incumbent president finds it difficult to pass legislation or make key appointments.
But historical patterns show that the party of the sitting president usually loses House seats in midterms. That has been the case in roughly 20 of the last 22 midterm cycles.
Experts say the trend is likely to continue, even though rising polarisation in US society, along with other factors, complicates any major shift in voting patterns.
“During the past 10 years with Trump dominating the political scene, many of the old rules and historical traditions have been defied,” John Zogby, a public opinion pollster and co-founder of the Arab American Institute, tells TRT World.
Since 1982, every first-term president – with the sole exception of George W Bush in 2002 – has lost seats in the first congressional election after his ascendancy, he notes.
Presidents Ronald Reagan, Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Trump himself in 2018 “lost a huge number of seats” in the midterms.
“As things stand right now, all of the ingredients appear to be in place for the opposition Democratic Party to continue this legacy,” Zogby says.
Trump’s approval ratings are at a low point. They are particularly low on affordability, the economy, and the war in Iran, which are issues that “matter most to American voters”.
Barely a fortnight before the election, “the president’s party appears to be in trouble,” he says.
According to David Schultz, a professor of political science at Hamline University and editor of Presidential Swing States: Why Only Ten Matter, the historical pattern of the president's party losing House seats in midterms should be treated only as a “strong tendency”, and not a law.
The exceptions of 1998 when backlash to Clinton’s impeachment helped Democrats – and 2002 when the September 11 attacks created support for George W Bush – show that “unusual external events” can override the ordinary midterm referendum dynamic.
“As of (now), the major polling averages put Trump’s approval between about 36 and 38 percent,” Schultz tells TRT World.
He points out that the share of swing voters in the electorate has shrunk from 10-15 percent in earlier decades to closer to 0-5 percent.
Meanwhile, the number of truly competitive House seats has fallen from around 120 to about 30.
With fewer voters available to switch sides, outcomes depend more heavily on who turns out on the day of election.
“Detachment from Trump is not the same as attachment to Democrats,” Schultz says.
He expects Republicans to lose House seats, but the size of their seat losses is “far less certain” at this point.
Trump’s name on the ballot?
Presidential approval among voters in midterms ranks among the strongest single predictors of the outcome, experts say.
Zogby points to past cycles in which weak presidential approval, paired with economic stress or unpopular policies, produced large losses: Reagan amid a recession in 1982, Clinton in 1994, and Obama after the Affordable Care Act in 2010.
Trump has reinforced the personal nature of the contest, telling supporters to “vote like his name is on the ballot”, Zogby notes.
Schultz cautions that the relationship between the presidential approval and midterm outcomes is not automatic.
Presidential approval works better when paired with economic perceptions, he says.
Both signals are negative for Republicans this year: voters are sour on the economy and the country’s direction, he adds.
A survey by Quinnipiac University, a non-partisan polling service, has shown only about 32 percent approving of Trump’s handling of the economy against 65 percent disapproving.
But Schultz notes many reasons why poll numbers may overstate Democratic gains.
Roughly 79 percent of Republicans still approve of Trump, according to Quinnipiac polling.
Disapproval does not automatically translate into a vote for the other party, he insists, adding that independent voters now make up a smaller, more disengaged share of the electorate than in earlier eras.
Issues that matter
Zogby describes the top concerns among the electorate as having “melded into one super issue”, as affordability, the war in the Middle East, and inflation.
This goes against Republicans because they currently hold power at House, Senate, and presidential levels.
Even on issues long favourable to Republicans – such as immigration and crime – the Republican Party’s ratings have slipped, he says.
For Schultz, core concerns among the US electorate are grocery and gas prices, housing, and the cost of health care.
Other than immigration and tariffs – which have contributed to the overall affordability problem – another important issue for the electorate is the war against Iran.
The so-called war of choice – now in its eighth month – remains unpopular among voters. Polls show only 29 percent approving of Trump’s handling and 65 percent disapproving.
What distinguishes 2026 from past midterms is that a “small set of issues is nearly inseparable from President Trump himself”, Schultz notes.
“The election, therefore, functions as a referendum on a person more than a contest between issue platforms,” he says.
“Because Democrats have not offered a clear alternative economic message, affordability may produce disengagement as often as it produces Democratic votes,” he adds.
The wild cards
Several conditions can possibly allow Republicans to limit losses or retain at least one chamber of Congress, experts say.
Zogby identifies Democratic vulnerabilities as a major wild card.
“Voter trust for the Democrats is at the lowest point ever,” he says.
Overall, the Democratic Party has a 26 percent positive rating, which includes about 65 percent of Democratic voters – down from 85 percent who trusted their own party in November 2024, Zogby says.
“Democrats also lack an agenda going forward. Those that do have an agenda for action are the progressive wing, and even moderate Democrats are attacking them for being too radical,” he says.
This leaves open the possibility of “last-minute revulsion” by late-deciding voters, he says.
Trump himself remains a wild card who has “rewritten the rule book many times”, he adds.
Schultz outlines a number of factors that can possibly affect the midterm outcomes.
One, partisan loyalty can outlast disappointment with the president, he says.
Many unhappy Republicans will still support their candidate for Congress when they think the alternative offers no clear programme.
Two, the “Democratic brand” imposes a ceiling: only about 21 percent of voters approve of Democrats in Congress, but more than three-fourths of Democratic voters describe their vote primarily as “opposition to Trump”, he says.
Three, a change in the news, such as a durable settlement of the Iran war, falling gas prices, or easing inflation, can improve Trump’s standing by a few points in key places, Schultz says.
Schultz also points to the structure of the Senate. It favours Republicans, while Democrats must defend all their seats and gain a net four, several of them in states Trump carried comfortably.
Finally, polling and turnout error can be consequential if low-propensity voters who dislike Trump decide to stay home on the day of the election.
“Taken together, my judgement is that Republicans are far better positioned to hold the Senate than the House,” he says, adding that maintaining the majority in the House would require a combination of strong Democratic abstention and durable Republican loyalty – something the current polling does not show.

Saudi Arabia’s biggest problem may be its enemy’s smallest weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:03:43 UTC
03:03:43 KST

Saudi Arabia’s biggest problem may be its enemy’s smallest weapons
The Houthis continue to strike Saudi Arabia despite Riyadh’s threats of a forceful response and promises to enlist outside partners to defend the kingdom.
By targeting airports and oil infrastructure, Ansar Allah is seeking to raise the cost of Saudi involvement in Yemen’s conflict and force the kingdom’s leadership to reconsider the terms of a settlement.
The latest wave of Houthi attacks has targeted facilities of particular importance to Saudi Arabia. On the evening of October 13, a strike hit Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, home to the company’s key management operations. The Saudi Energy Ministry reported a fire, though miraculously no one was killed.
Ansar Allah also claimed strikes on an oil refinery in Riyadh and King Khalid International Airport. The choice of targets suggests the Houthis want to put virtually all of the kingdom’s oil revenue at risk and disrupt its international air connections.
These targets also suggest that the movement is trying to influence Saudi leaders’ decisions directly. Oil infrastructure generates government revenue, airports connect the country to the outside world, and confidence in the kingdom depends on the security of both. Even limited damage can therefore produce an impact far greater than the cost of the weapons used.
What is driving the conflict?
The Houthis have their own history of confrontation with Saudi Arabia. The movement emerged in northern Yemen, fought a series of wars against the central government between 2004 and 2010, and seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Its rise was rooted in Yemen’s political system, local conflicts, and the collapse of state institutions. Iranian support strengthened an already established force with its own social base and political objectives.
The Saudi intervention in 2015 cemented Riyadh’s position as the movement’s principal foreign adversary. For the kingdom, the aim was to prevent a hostile force from consolidating power along its southern border and to support Yemen’s internationally recognized government. For the Houthi leadership, the war became both a threat to its survival and a rallying cause. Invoking foreign aggression allowed the movement to portray its struggle for domestic supremacy as a defense of national sovereignty.
That logic remains relevant to the current escalation. Saudi support for an offensive by Yemeni government forces threatens the Houthis’ territorial gains and bargaining position. Striking deep inside the kingdom allows them to raise the price of that support. Their apparent calculation is to make continued Saudi involvement in the war carry a recurring cost on Saudi soil.
The movement’s demands are concrete: an end to strikes, limits on assistance to its Yemeni adversaries, the lifting of transportation and trade restrictions, and agreements on revenues and payments. These issues were under discussion long before the latest escalation. The framework for a roadmap presented by the UN in December 2023 included a nationwide ceasefire, payment of public-sector salaries, the resumption of oil exports, and an easing of restrictions on Sanaa airport and the port of Hodeidah.
By increasing Riyadh’s costs, Ansar Allah hopes to extract concessions and retain control of the territory it has seized. A ceasefire on those terms, however, would consolidate the movement’s position without resolving how power should be shared in Yemen.
Attacks on Saudi Arabia also serve Ansar Allah’s domestic political interests. The movement uses its ability to strike deep inside the kingdom to bolster its standing among supporters. Confrontation with Riyadh also allows the Houthis to cast themselves as Yemen’s defenders against foreign intervention and use that claim to justify their bid for power.
Iranian military and technological assistance has undoubtedly expanded Houthi capabilities considerably. But the relationship with Tehran does not erase Ansar Allah’s own interests in Yemen’s power struggle or its confrontation with Saudi Arabia. Reducing the movement’s actions to the execution of Iranian orders fails to explain either the conflict’s local roots or the Houthi leadership’s objectives.
A more accurate description would be a partnership with unequal resources in which the Yemeni side retains substantial autonomy. Weakening Saudi Arabia may serve both partners’ interests, but their preferred terms for ending the war may differ. Ansar Allah must consider conditions on Yemen’s battlefields and the survival of its own rule. Agreements between Iran and outside powers therefore do not guarantee an automatic halt to Houthi operations.
The economics of war
The development of domestic missile production and an expanding network for procuring components make it harder for Riyadh to bring Houthi attacks to an end. If the movement can replenish its arsenal from several sources, restricting Iranian supplies will have only a partial effect. An agreement with Tehran alone would therefore be insufficient to secure Saudi facilities. Much will depend on whether the Houthis themselves believe continued strikes serve their interests.
Nor do the Houthis need to match Saudi Arabia in the quantity or quality of their weapons. They can choose their targets and pause between attacks, while the kingdom must continuously defend airports, oil facilities, and cities across a vast territory. Even a single hit can disrupt a facility’s operations, trigger flight cancellations, or bring business activity to a halt. Purchases of American air defense systems reduce that threat but do not eliminate it. Riyadh’s problem is that military superiority has yet to deprive its adversary of the ability to inflict economically painful blows. That is precisely the capability the Houthis are trying to turn into negotiating leverage.
Saudi military spending exceeds $82 billion per year, yet the kingdom still struggles to protect its infrastructure from Houthi attacks. This exposes the gap between the cost of the weapons it has purchased and their effectiveness in this particular war. Advanced fighter jets and missile defense systems give Riyadh a considerable advantage, but detecting small drones and low-flying cruise missiles requires extensive radar coverage and rapid information sharing between units. Without those capabilities, expensive equipment cannot reliably detect and engage targets in time.
In a prolonged confrontation, the disparity in weapons costs also becomes significant. According to cited estimates, a Patriot interceptor costs more than $3 million, while some Houthi drones cost just $15,000–25,000. Defenders have to use such interceptors against cheap aircraft to protect far more valuable assets. But sustained defensive operations deplete stocks that cannot be replenished quickly, particularly amid strong global demand for air defense systems. This gives the Houthis an opportunity to wear down the kingdom’s defenses even when most of the aircraft they launch fail to reach their targets.
Technical difficulties are compounded by the structure of the Saudi armed forces. The separation of the regular military and the National Guard has historically served, in part, to protect the monarchy against a coup. But separate chains of command and highly centralized decision-making can hinder coordination and limit commanders’ initiative. Another weapons purchase, then, will not solve the problem on its own. Even additional detection and interception systems will deliver limited results if information arrives late and coordinating a response takes too long.
The Houthis can reasonably expect these shortcomings to take time to address, leaving them able to continue inflicting painful blows in the meantime. Domestic production and broader supply networks help sustain that campaign. The movement does not need to destroy major industrial facilities or shut down air travel altogether; a recurring threat is enough to make airlines reconsider routes, investors postpone decisions, and Saudi leaders spend more on protecting infrastructure.
Will help come from abroad?
Statements by Türkiye and Pakistan expressing their readiness to defend Saudi Arabia do not yet provide grounds to expect either country to enter the war fully, much less fight the Houthis inside Yemen. At an October 5 meeting, the parties to the Mecca Agreement announced that they would provide forces and equipment for the kingdom’s defense. The political weight of those promises, however, will depend on whether the allies can actually reduce the number of attacks and the damage they cause. As long as the strikes continue, Houthi leaders may view such declarations as rhetoric unlikely to be followed by a dangerous expansion of the war.
Ankara’s position reinforces that calculation. Turkish Foreign Affairs Minister Hakan Fidan outlined possible assistance with air defense, electronic warfare, and technical support, while explicitly ruling out Turkish troops taking part in offensive operations on foreign soil. Türkiye has thus set clear limits on its role from the outset.
Pakistan also has reasons to avoid direct intervention. Joining the war in Yemen would mean additional military spending and the risk of worsening relations with neighboring Iran. It would therefore be premature to expect Islamabad to take on the task of defeating the Houthis on Riyadh’s behalf. Its commitments to the kingdom leave room for a role limited to defending specific facilities and providing military assistance.
A similar distinction applies to the American position. Intelligence sharing and targeting assistance support Saudi operations, but they do not mean Washington is willing to stop the attacks at any cost. The Houthis appear to be counting on precisely these limits to outside involvement. Their bet is that the kingdom’s allies will help it defend itself but will be reluctant to become embroiled in a prolonged war to achieve Saudi objectives in Yemen.
Until that support produces a substantial reduction in attacks, threats to bring in allies may carry little weight with Ansar Allah.
***
The Houthis are seeking to demonstrate that continued Saudi intervention will bring losses that neither a vast defense budget nor foreign partners can prevent. If that pressure prompts Riyadh to scale back assistance to their adversaries or accept settlement terms favorable to them, the movement will have an opportunity to translate its battlefield gains into lasting political advantages.
Such an outcome would also benefit Iran by weakening Saudi Arabia’s position. Its most immediate consequence, however, would be to strengthen Ansar Allah itself in the struggle for power in Yemen.

Saved from Nazi-occupied Prague, thousands of Torah scrolls find new life through a Satmar scribe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:26:33 UTC
02:26:33 KST

On an overcast London morning in February 1964, Satmar hassid David Eliahu Brand passed by the Westminster Reform synagogue. Looking for work as a sofer (scribe), Brand took a chance and knocked on the front door. Ruth Shaffer, a native of Warsaw, Poland, and the coordinator for the Westminster synagogue Torah restoration project, answered the door.
Speaking in his native Yiddish, Mr. Brand asked her: “Es gibt Torahs?” Do you have any Torah scrolls that have to be repaired? Ruth replied in the affirmative, but added that the synagogue possessed not just one scroll, but 1,564 Torah scrolls that had been rescued from Czechoslovakia after the war.
After that astounding revelation, Ruth introduced Brand to the synagogue’s spiritual leader, Rabbi Dr. Harold Reinhart. Thus began the most unlikely arrangement between a Satmar hassid and a Reform synagogue that would last for 27 years!
The story begins: Demise of Jewish communities of Czechoslovakia, Moravia and Bohemia: March 15, 1939
On March 15, 1939, Nazi German troops violated the Munich Agreement and marched into the capital city of Prague. This began the official annexation of Czechoslovakia. Wherever German troops entered, the Jewish communities were in danger as well.
Until 1939, the Jewish communities of Czechoslovakia, Moravia and Bohemia numbered over 120,000 Jews and boasted over 350 synagogues, including the famous Maharal synagogue in Prague.
Prague was also the home of the Old-New Synagogue, which was built in the year 1270, and the Pinkas synagogue, built in 1479.
Almost overnight, Jews were stripped of their civic rights, banned from most jobs (including the medical field), and children were expelled from all public schools.
Then, in July 1939, the Nazis established the Central Office of Jewish Emigration in Prague (directed by Adolf Eichmann), thus forcing many to abandon their communities, leaving behind their beautiful synagogues (containing hundreds of Torah scrolls) and houses of study.
The first miracle: Gathering all Torah scrolls and artifacts to the Prague Jewish Museum
The Prague Jewish Museum was built in 1906 and in 1939 was under the directorship of Dr. Karel Stein and curator Alfred Engel. Fearing that the holy and beautiful Torah scrolls in the hundreds of Czech Jewish communities would be totally lost, Stein and Engel asked permission from Nazi authorities to centralize all Jewish ritual objects in Prague in order to protect them from widespread plundering.
Over 1,800 Torah scrolls and 212,000 artifacts were transferred to the museum.
Whether the Nazi intent was merely to amass valuable silver and gold for its treasury or to build a museum to recall an extinct race (once all Jews would be murdered) is a matter of question, but nonetheless all of the Czech Torah scrolls and artifacts were brought to Prague.
There, many Jews were employed to sort, catalogue, and store all the items that arrived from over 100 synagogues in Czechoslovakia, Moravia and Bohemia. Tragically, almost all of the employees were later deported to Terezin and other death camps and perished during the Shoah.
The second miracle: Procurement of the Torah scrolls
Following the end of World War II, the Torah scrolls lay abandoned and unattended for almost 20 years in a damp, moldy warehouse in Prague.
That all changed with a tap on the shoulder in 1963. A British art dealer, Eric Estorick, was approached by a representative of the Czech State Agency to purchase some ritual objects that had been kept in storage. The Czech government, then under Communist rule, was badly in need of money and felt that this was a golden opportunity.
Estorick contacted Ralph Yablon, a British philanthropist and member of the Westminster synagogue in London. Yablon consented to provide the £30,000 necessary for the purchase and shipping of all the Torah scrolls and other religious objects that had been stored away for so long.
Yablon, aware that many of the scrolls were badly in need of repair, contacted his rabbi, Harold F. Reinhart, in order to determine which scrolls were totally unusable and which could be designated for restoration.
Finally, on February 7, 1964, two enormous trucks carrying the 1,800 stained and tightly packed scrolls arrived in London. The original idea was that these Torah scrolls would be repaired and then returned to the communities from which they came.
But soon after their arrival, it was determined that almost all of the former Czech shuls were either destroyed or the communities no longer existed.
The third miracle: Restoration of the 1,800 scrolls
By the early part of 1964, all of the Torah scrolls and hundreds of other religious objects (including 400 wimples or binders) arrived in the Westminster synagogue. That is when the divine hand of God directed David Brand to knock on the door of the synagogue.
As in the book of Shir Hashirim, which says: “the voice of my beloved knocks,” it was a most unlikely but divinely ordained moment. That is when the major work began in order to determine how many of the scrolls could actually be repaired.
Of the total of 1,800 scrolls, Brand, along with other professional scribes, slowly and meticulously determined that hundreds could simply not be repaired-the decades of storage in horrible conditions had made many unusable.
It should be noted that even if one letter of a Torah scroll is written incorrectly or if the ink dries up, the scroll cannot be used at all until repaired. Imagine what happened to the Czech scrolls when they were not used or opened for so long.
The fourth miracle: Founding of the Memorial Scrolls Trust
Of the entire collection of the 1,800 Torah scrolls, 1,564 were deemed to be usable, but then the decision had to be made as to how they would be used and to whom they would be given. In 1964, after several months of meticulous work by the scribal team, Ruth (1910-2006) took over the directorship of the Memorial Scrolls Trust (MST).
Ruth would spend almost 40 years managing, documenting, and distributing the scrolls to communities worldwide. Amazingly, the initial filing and tracking were done on index cards only, and only many years later was the entire system transferred to a digital database.
One of her early decisions was that each scroll would be given to a community or synagogue on permanent loan in order to memorialize the communities from which they came originally. In addition, since the Torah is described as a “tree of life,” the scrolls would be read and would become a living memory for all the communities that were destroyed during the Holocaust.
About six months ago, I contacted the MST to find out more information about the scrolls and where they are today. I was fortunate that Jeffrey Ohrenstein, MST trustee and chairman, wrote back, and so began a series of discussions and amazing stories.
Jeff said the oldest known scroll in the collection is one from the 13th century, and that today about 150 scrolls still remain in the museum in London. Over 1,400 Torah scrolls have been loaned out to communities around the globe, including 1,000 to the US, as well as Israel, Italy, Argentina, Chile, and the UAE (Dubai).
Over the last 62 years, these communities have become part of the ongoing memorial to the former Jewish centers, but they have also transformed the Torah scrolls into living and eternal messengers of all who perished at the hands of the Nazis.
The scrolls are not stored in the holy ark, but are read and celebrated everywhere where they have been adopted.
Like the famous and tragic death of Haninah ben Tradyon (tractate Avodah Zarah 18A), when he is asked by his students what he saw as he was being tortured by the Romans, he replied: “The parchment is burnt, but the letters are flying heavenward.” Those letters, he was saying, are eternal; they can never be destroyed by our enemies.
In the case of the Czech collection, both the scrolls and its holy letters have survived, been lovingly cared for, and preserved for eternity.

Civil war has returned to Yemen.
The ceasefire of 2022 is over and open warfare has returned to the country. The Iran-backed Houthis have ceased large areas of the western coast and are encircling the city of Taiz. The Saudi-backed government has now launched its counteroffensive, but can they defeat the Houthis?

AI has enhanced Iran’s intelligence and targeting capabilities: Taeb
TEHRAN— Hossein Taeb, head of Iran’s Basij Organization, says the use of artificial intelligence in defense and intelligence operations has improved the accuracy of target identification and precision strikes, highlighting the technology’s growing role in Iran’s military capabilities.
Speaking on Thursday at the first Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity Conference in the southeastern city of Kerman, Taeb said AI had strengthened intelligence gathering and target assessment, adding that its applications had extended to the naval and aerospace divisions of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) and other branches of the armed forces.
Taeb also discussed 'the objectives of the US-Israeli war against Iran,' arguing that attacks on military commanders, scientists and air-defense systems were intended to weaken the country’s defenses and undermine the scientific foundations of its development.
Protecting Iran’s scientific capabilities
Referring to the 12-day war, Taeb said the simultaneous targeting of military commanders and scientists was part of a strategy to weaken Iran’s security infrastructure and damage the scientific capabilities underpinning its technological progress.
He said the campaign against Iranian scientists had failed to eliminate the country’s nuclear expertise. According to Taeb, the scope of attacks expanded during the 40-day war, extending to other scientific fields and claiming the lives of researchers.
Taeb argued that the objective of such attacks went beyond military damage, encompassing efforts to undermine public security and weaken the country’s capacity for scientific and technological advancement.
"Targeting one scientist would not halt the country’s progress, as more specialists would emerge to continue the work," he said.
AI and the changing landscape of military operations
Taeb described investment in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity as a strategic decision for Iran’s future, calling for these priorities to be translated into practical action by government institutions, policymakers and leading experts.
He said AI had already produced tangible results in the defense sector by improving intelligence assessment and the accuracy of target identification.
He further said AI-assisted systems had improved the detection of military vessels operating near the Strait of Hormuz and helped increase missile accuracy. Taeb argued that these capabilities had affected US military calculations and contributed to the relocation of American naval vessels farther from the area.
His remarks underscore the growing importance of AI-enabled intelligence, surveillance and targeting systems in contemporary military operations. Such technologies can help process large volumes of information, identify patterns and support faster operational decisions, although their effectiveness depends on data quality, system reliability and human oversight.
Taeb highlights disparity in military spending
Taeb also contrasted Iran’s defense resources with the much larger military budgets of the United States and Israel. He cited figures for US military spending and additional wartime funding requests, and said Israel had received $22 billion in additional US assistance for the conflict.
Despite Iran’s limited defense resources in foreign-currency terms, Taeb said the country had been able to withstand the military campaign. He argued that a comparable emphasis on scientific capability, technological innovation and strategic planning was necessary to sustain progress in the fields of AI and cybersecurity.
He called for artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to move beyond isolated technological initiatives and become part of a coordinated national strategy involving public institutions and the country’s scientific community.
The conference’s focus on young technology specialists, Taeb said, reflected Iran’s intention to expand its pool of skilled researchers and developers. In his view, strengthening domestic expertise in emerging technologies is essential not only to defense preparedness but also to the country’s broader scientific and technological development.

‘Mother of all bombs’ will not rescue Trump from Iran war quagmire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:49:46 UTC
01:49:46 KST

‘Mother of all bombs’ will not rescue Trump from Iran war quagmire
TEHRAN — The possible use of America’s largest non-nuclear bomb against Iran may offer President Donald Trump a dramatic display of military power, but it is unlikely to resolve the strategic predicament facing Washington, analysts have warned, arguing that a spectacular explosion cannot substitute for a viable path out of a protracted war.
CNN reported on October 14 that the US military had developed strike plans that could include the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, commonly known as the “mother of all bombs,” against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if Trump orders a resumption of combat operations. The report cited multiple US officials familiar with the planning.
The prospect of deploying the weapon has raised questions about whether Washington is seeking a decisive military outcome or a dramatic action that could allow the president to declare victory without achieving his stated strategic objectives.
 
Even within US military planning circles, doubts have emerged over the weapon’s effectiveness in changing the course of the war, CNN reported. Reuters subsequently reported the story, noting that it had not independently verified CNN’s account.
A dramatic explosion, but what strategic result?
Dani Citrinowicz, a former Israeli military intelligence official, told the BBC that even using the “mother of all bombs” would not force Iran to surrender.
“Even the use of the [mother of all bombs] will not force Iran to surrender; although such an attack could have psychological effects and give Trump an opportunity to claim an imaginary victory,” he said, according to the quotation provided in the BBC-attributed report.
The assessment points to a fundamental distinction between the destructive power of a weapon and its ability to achieve political objectives. A strike can cause extensive damage without compelling an adversary to accept the attacker’s demands or bringing a conflict to a favourable conclusion.
Sina Azodi, director of the Middle East Studies Program at George Washington University, similarly questioned the strategic logic behind the reported option.
“Trump has a strange fascination with the symbolic use of American military power and wants to advertise it on his personal social media account through a grand spectacle and a massive explosion,” Azodi said, according to the quotation provided.
He also highlighted the weapon’s limitations against deeply buried targets, noting that it detonates in the air and has limited capacity to penetrate far underground.
The distinction matters because the MOAB was designed primarily to produce devastating blast effects over a broad surface area. It is not the same as a specialised penetrator designed to attack deeply buried, hardened facilities.
In an October 15 Al Jazeera explainer, military analyst Elijah Magnier said that using the MOAB would not guarantee the destruction of Iran’s deeply buried nuclear installations and could amount to little more than “political theatre.”
A weapon cannot resolve a strategic deadlock
The reported plans have emerged as the Trump administration faces pressure to demonstrate progress in a war that has failed to produce a clear political resolution.
In a CNN broadcast on October 15, senior national security reporter Zachary Cohen said Trump and his advisers had spent months discussing options that could be presented to the American public as a “definitive end” to the war.
Cohen said the military had been tasked with developing fresh strike options amid the absence of a diplomatic resolution and growing unpopularity of the conflict.
He also reported that the administration’s stated strategic goals remained unfulfilled.
That assessment raises a central question: what would a MOAB strike actually accomplish that previous attacks and existing military pressure have not?
The bomb’s destructive capacity is not in dispute. The uncertainty concerns whether its use would change Iran’s calculations, compel Tehran to capitulate or create conditions for a durable settlement.
A dramatic strike might generate powerful images and headlines. But if it does not achieve its declared objectives, it could instead expose the gap between the administration’s military capabilities and its ability to translate them into a political outcome.
The limits of spectacle
The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. Its deployment would represent a major escalation, but its size alone does not make it an appropriate weapon for every target.
CNN military analyst and retired Air Force Colonel Cedric Leighton explained in a broadcast on October 15 that the MOAB is designed to inflict damage over a large surface area, whereas Iran’s hardened and deeply buried nuclear facilities present a different targeting challenge.
He contrasted the MOAB with the Massive Ordnance Penetrator, a different weapon specifically designed to attack hardened underground targets.
Leighton also questioned the suitability of the aircraft required to deliver the MOAB for the Iranian operational environment.
The technical limitations reinforce the broader strategic problem. A weapon capable of producing an enormous explosion is not necessarily capable of destroying every intended target, still less of compelling a country to surrender.
A face-saving exit is not the same as victory
The most consequential possibility raised by the reporting is that the proposed strike could be intended partly to shape the political narrative of the war.
CNN’s reporting suggested that the administration was examining military options that could enable Trump to present the conflict as decisively concluded. Such a scenario would make the distinction between a battlefield achievement and a politically useful declaration of victory particularly important.
Citrinowicz’s assessment, as quoted by the BBC, captures that concern: the attack might provide an opportunity to claim victory without necessarily producing the underlying result.
This is the danger of treating military spectacle as a substitute for strategy. An attack can be visually overwhelming and still leave the fundamental dispute unresolved.
For Washington, the question is not simply whether the United States can deploy a powerful bomb. It is whether doing so would bring the war closer to an outcome that can be sustained politically and strategically.
 
The quagmire remains
The possibility of using the MOAB does not, by itself, demonstrate that Trump has authorised such an attack. The reports describe contingency planning, not a confirmed decision to deploy the weapon.
Reuters said it could not independently verify CNN’s initial report. CBS News separately reported on October 15 that the White House and Pentagon had prepared plans for possible use of the weapon if ordered by the president.
If the bomb fails to achieve its intended military objectives, the administration could find itself confronting the same fundamental problem after an even more dramatic attack. If it is used primarily to create the appearance of a decisive outcome, the gap between the declaration of victory and the realities on the ground could become harder to conceal.
The “mother of all bombs” may offer Trump a spectacle of overwhelming force. But an explosion, however large, cannot by itself deliver a political settlement, compel an adversary’s surrender or guarantee a way out of war.
The real test is not the size of the blast. It is whether the strategy behind it can produce an outcome that military power alone has so far failed to secure.

Egypt discovers parts of giant pharaoh statues (PHOTOS)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:45:52 UTC
01:45:52 KST

Egypt discovers parts of giant pharaoh statues (PHOTOS)
Egyptian archaeologists have uncovered the remains of two royal statues, at least one depicting Pharaoh Ramses II, during excavations in the Nile Delta, the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced on Wednesday.
The discovery was made in the village of Behbeit el-Hagar in Gharbia Governorate after a local resident, Khaled el-Shahat Khalil, found an inscribed stone block on his property and alerted the authorities. Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy later visited the site and rewarded the man and his wife with a pilgrimage to Mecca for reporting the find.
According to Hisham el-Leithy, secretary-general of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, the first find is a 1.6-meter-high head of Ramses II wearing the double crown symbolizing the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. Part of the statue’s back pillar was also recovered, bearing an inscription of one of the pharaoh’s royal titles. Archaeologists estimate that the complete monument, including its base, may have stood around 8.5 meters tall.
The second discovery includes a 2.4-meter section of another royal statue, also believed to depict Ramses II. The figure is missing its legs and base, but its head remains well preserved, with facial features resembling those of the first statue. Excavators also uncovered a 1.3-meter block of pink granite bearing hieroglyphic inscriptions with two of the pharaoh’s titles, including “King of Upper and Lower Egypt” and “Son of Ra.”
The ministry said archaeologists are continuing to study the artifacts, and their exact age has yet to be determined. However, the discovery sets clear links to Ramses II, who ruled Egypt from 1279 to 1213 BC. It’s not the first finding of the kind. In February 2024, archaeologists uncovered the upper section of a statue of the pharaoh in Minya Governorate, nearly a century after its lower half was discovered in 1930. The restored statue, standing about 6.7 meters tall, was re-erected in 2026.
Other recent finds in Egypt include three New Kingdom tombs uncovered at Saqqara in July and a Roman-era tomb discovered in the Dakhla Oasis in September, containing pottery, funerary inscriptions and a coin depicting Emperor Constantine.

Breadcrumb
FIFA fines Spain over anti-Muslim chants at Egypt game
FIFA has fined world champions Spain $20,000 over Islamophobic chants by supporters during a friendly against Egypt earlier this year.
The chants were heard during Spain's 0-0 draw with Egypt at Espanyol's RCDE Stadium in Barcelona on 31 March.
Sections of the crowd chanted "Whoever doesn't jump is Muslim", while Egypt's national anthem was also jeered before kick-off.
Spain winger Lamine Yamal, who is Muslim, condemned the chants after the match as disrespectful and intolerable.
"Using a religion as a taunt on the field makes you look ignorant and racist," he said.
FIFA said its appeals committee had upheld the sanction following an earlier ruling by its disciplinary committee.
The Spanish Football Federation has been ordered to pay a $20,000 fine and must also close at least 15% of the seating at Spain's next home friendly.
FIFA said the affected seats could instead be allocated to groups including families, students and anti-discrimination organisations.
The governing body's disciplinary judges said "harsh sanctions were necessary", while acknowledging that it was the Spanish federation's first offence and that officials had acted quickly after the chants began.
Stadium announcements were made during the match calling on supporters to stop discriminatory behaviour.
The Spanish federation also condemned the chants and co-operated with authorities seeking to identify those responsible.
Spanish police opened an investigation the following day into what they described as "Islamophobic and xenophobic" chanting.
The incident came amid wider debate over racism and discrimination in football. FIFA's current anti-racism framework includes a crossed-arm gesture allowing players and officials to report racist abuse during matches.
FIFA rejected the Spanish federation's argument that the word "Muslim" was not inherently insulting, ruling that otherwise neutral language can become discriminatory when used as a taunt or marker of inferiority.
The federation said on Friday that it considered the punishment disproportionately severe and would appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
FIFA has also imposed sanctions elsewhere this year for breaches of anti-discrimination rules, including a fine against the Israeli Football Association over its handling of racist behaviour by Beitar Jerusalem supporters.
The March incident came before Spain went on to win the 2026 World Cup, defeating Argentina in the final in July.
The Egypt match had already drawn wider attention to anti-Muslim sentiment in European football, an issue TNA has examined in the context of the growing far-right backlash against Muslim players and supporters.

Did Egypt's Sisi hint at stepping down in 2030?

Breadcrumb
Did Egypt's Sisi hint at stepping down in 2030?
A series of statements by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has raised questions over whether the former military general will step down when his current term ends in 2030.
Speaking at the 44th Armed Forces Educational Symposium on Wednesday, Sisi reaffirmed that Egypt's constitution would remain protected and unchanged, remarks that were welcomed by supporters but also drew scepticism.
The president said the constitution would remain untouched, and warned against attempts to incite unrest in Egypt.
“There is a constitution for this state, there is a constitution that we approved for this state, no one will touch it … no one will touch it," Sisi reiterated.
The remarks have sparked debate in Egypt, with some interpreting them as a sign that he does not plan to pursue constitutional changes that would allow him to remain in power for longer.
Here, The New Arab takes a closer look at what the constitution states and what his comments could be hinting at.
What does the constitution say?
Egypt's 2014 constitution, prior to being amended in 2019, stipulated in Article 140 that the country's president is elected to serve a four-year term, with the possibility of re-election only once.
In 2019, an amendment that maintained the two-term limit but extended each term to six years forwarded by a pro-government bloc, was approved by parliament.
The amendment was later approved in a public referendum which saw 88.8 percent of voters vote in favour and 11.1 percent against, with a turnout of 44 percent.
Rights groups and monitors warned at the time that the moves would entrench repression in Egypt, with reports of intimidation of referendum voters and journalists, arrests of opponents of the amendments, and vote buying by state-aligned entities.
Why is Sisi making these statements now?
Sisi's latest statements come amid calls from supporters for him to extend his rule over the country, including the launch of an online petition calling for the president to stay in his post until 2050.
This, however, has prompted widespread backlash, as many have decried it as undemocratic and have cited Sisi's crackdown on dissent.
Saeed Sadek, a professor of political sociology, told The New Arab that the president's statements appear to be aimed at closing the door to speculation about his political future.
The comments also come at a time when Egypt is facing several challenges, particularly from upheaval in the region and a sustained domestic economic crisis.
Sadek added, however, that the statement raises the political cost of any attempt to amend the constitution in the near future, though it does not completely shut the door to changes.
The constitution, he highlighted, contains mechanisms for amendments which can be activated with the necessary political will and backing of parliament.
Sadek notes that Sisi had made similar statements prior to the 2019 amendments.
What has been the response?
While Sisi did not explicitly say he would step down or rule out standing for re-election in 2030, his words have sparked some optimism for many.
Hamdeen Sabahi, Karama Party founder and former presidential candidate who stood against Sisi in 2014, described the president's comments as the "best of words", and expressed his hope that they would be followed up by the "best of actions".
In statements to the press, Sabahi expressed hope that Sisi would hand over power in 2030, paving the way for a new era in Egypt.
Amr Hashem Rabie, an expert at the Al-Ahram Center for Political and Strategic Studies, also told The New Arab that Sisi's statements indicate that Egypt is heading towards the election of a new president in 2030, unless unforeseen circumstances alter this course.
He added that some political parties, such as Nation's Future Party, Homeland Protectors, and the National Front Party, might push for street rallies to demand the president's continued rule, in addition to the role of some media figures who might promote the idea that there is no viable alternative to the president.
Sisi's remarks were also welcomed by Justice Party leader Abdel Moneim Imam, who similarly expressed hope for a peaceful transfer of power.
Egypt's Civil Democratic Movement was among those who welcomed the remarks, though cautioned that the constitution should not be subject to amendment according to circumstances or individuals.
Many Arabic-language reports from outside of Egypt have further expressed skepticism about the president's remarks, given that he holds such a tight grip on the state's institutions.
Sisi took power after removing Egypt's first democratically elected president, Mohamad Morsi, in 2013, and has led a crackdown on dissent within Egypt. By 2030, the former military general would have served as Egypt's president for 16 years.

Starlink Speeds Rise Again in Ukraine—but Key Frontline Missions Are Still Disrupted, Zelenskyy Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:17:34 UTC
01:17:34 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Starlink Speeds Rise Again in Ukraine—but Key Frontline Missions Are Still Disrupted, Zelenskyy Says
Starlink connectivity has improved in Ukraine following reported signals from the White House to restore higher operating speeds, but the system remains restricted, and Ukrainian forces still cannot carry out some frontline missions as before, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said during a briefing in Brussels on October 16.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s partners said there had been signals from the White House regarding the restoration of Starlink’s higher-speed capabilities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Have they returned to the previous speed? No. But has the speed increased? Yes,” Zelenskyy said.
The restrictions have become a significant battlefield issue because Ukraine uses high-speed Starlink connectivity on rapidly moving unmanned systems. Zelenskyy stressed that Ukrainian forces do not currently use Starlink for deep strikes inside Russia.
“No, we do not use Starlink for attacks or retaliatory strikes on the territory of the Russian Federation. That is precisely why we appealed to SpaceX and the White House to open up such a capability for us. If we had it, we obviously would not be asking,” he said.
Zelenskyy described the sudden restrictions as an unpleasant and dangerous “surprise,” particularly because Starlink is used in operations intended to intercept Russia’s new jet-powered Shahed-type drones.
“We use Starlink to intercept jet-powered ‘Shaheds’ that fly in and strike our civilians, killing our families. We use special interceptors—drones that move at high speed and use Starlink,” Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that the service was not completely switched off. Instead, its effective speed limit was sharply reduced, which prevented some Ukrainian interceptor drones from keeping their satellite connection while pursuing fast-moving Russian targets.
“And when the speed was reduced, we were unable to shoot down a certain number of these ‘Shaheds.’ That is very painful and unpleasant. In other words, we were unable to provide protection for the population. The ‘Shaheds’ were flying at more than 400 kilometers per hour, while our speed was reduced to 78 km/h,” he said.
That means Russian jet-powered drones were traveling at more than 249 mph, while Ukrainian Starlink-equipped systems reportedly faced connectivity restrictions at around 48 mph.
The restrictions have also affected Ukrainian middle-strike operations against Russian military targets in occupied Ukrainian territory. Zelenskyy said Starlink connectivity had previously supported those missions, but the new limits made some of them impossible.
“And we can no longer do this,” he said.
Beyond combat missions, Zelenskyy emphasized that the restrictions have also complicated battlefield logistics. Ukrainian units use drones connected through Starlink to deliver food and water to troops holding isolated or difficult positions.
“Many people are within reach of enemy drones; we use UAVs to deliver water and food to people who have been holding positions for a long time. We use drones and Starlink. So this affected our ability to protect the population,” Zelenskyy said.
Previously, Germany called for speed restrictions affecting Starlink service in Ukraine to be lifted, stressing that Berlin itself finances part of the satellite communications equipment used by the country.

Starvation killed 466 Palestinians since 2024, says Gaza Health Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:47:37 UTC
00:47:37 KST

At least 466 Palestinians, including 157 children, have died from malnutrition and starvation since 2024, Gaza’s Health Ministry said Friday, Anadolu reports.
The figures were released on World Food Day, observed annually on Oct. 16.
At least 189 elderly people died of starvation, representing 40.5% of the deaths, it said.
In August 2025, the UN declared famine in Gaza.
More than 1.4 million people are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026, the ministry added.
Starvation as a weapon
Israeli authorities have used starvation as a weapon during the genocide in Gaza since October 2023, according to Palestinian government bodies and rights organizations.
Israel tightened restrictions on crossings in March 2025, preventing thousands of aid trucks waiting at border crossings from entering the enclave.
The restrictions followed widespread hunger in northern Gaza caused by the blockade and limits on food and relief supplies, forcing some residents to eat animal feed and wild plants.
In late May 2025, Israel allowed 87 aid trucks to enter Gaza for the first time after 81 days, according to Gaza’s government media office.
Aid later continued to enter on a limited and intermittent basis under strict restrictions until February 2026, when Israel allowed a limited increase in the number of trucks entering the enclave under a ceasefire agreement.
Palestinian officials said the shipments still lacked sufficient quantities of essential food items.
According to Gaza’s government media office, Israel has allowed in only about 34% of the humanitarian aid trucks agreed upon.
OPINION: The ceasefire that keeps killing children: Gaza one year on
Malnutrition reaches ‘catastrophic levels’
“Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached catastrophic levels that are killing children, the elderly and vulnerable groups,” the Health Ministry said.
More than 1.4 million Palestinians, around 67% of Gaza’s population, are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026.
More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition were recorded among children under 5 from 2024 through August 2026, the ministry added.
Of them, 18% of children were suffering from severe acute malnutrition that threatened their lives, while 12.2% of children were affected by stunting, indicating the impact of food shortages on their development.
The mortality rate among children under 5 rose from 13.6 to 33.4 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2022 and 2025, the ministry said.
It estimated that 74,200 children will need treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027.
Pregnant women
Among pregnant women, the ministry said the prevalence of anemia rose to 61% in 2026, compared with 41% before the war.
“Around 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded during the first half of 2026, more than three times the number recorded during the previous six months,” it added.
“One in three pregnancies in Gaza is now classified as high-risk,” the ministry continued.
“The figures show that the health consequences of the food crisis are increasingly affecting mothers and unborn children, in addition to children,” it said.
Calls for urgent international action
“The right to food is a fundamental human right that does not cease to exist during war,” the ministry said.
It called on the international community and the UN to take immediate action to ensure the safe, sustained and unrestricted entry of food, therapeutic nutritional supplements and medicines into Gaza.
The ministry urged that children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and the elderly be given priority as the groups most vulnerable to malnutrition.
It also called for support to revive local food production to help curb the worsening humanitarian crisis.
The figures come amid the humanitarian consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, which has caused widespread destruction to infrastructure, health facilities and food production sources.
The war has also damaged farmland, food production facilities and water networks, undermining residents’ ability to meet their basic needs locally.
Repeated displacement, loss of income and soaring prices have further increased families’ dependence on humanitarian aid, while access remains irregular.

UK clears way for German media group Axel Springer’s planned purchase of Telegraph Media Group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Aysu Biçer
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The UK government has cleared the way for Axel Springer’s planned purchase of Telegraph Media Group after deciding not to refer the deal for a more detailed competition investigation.
Culture Minister Lisa Nandy said Friday that she would not refer the proposed acquisition to a Phase 2 investigation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), the UK’s competition regulator.
“I will not be referring this matter to a more in-depth ‘Phase 2’ investigation by the Competition and Markets Authority,” Nandy said in a written statement.
She also said the Public Interest Intervention Notice (PIIN), issued in January 2024, and the related public interest merger reference order had ceased to be in force following her decision.
The decision reduces regulatory uncertainty surrounding one of the UK media industry’s high-profile ownership transactions and allows Axel Springer to proceed with its planned purchase without a more detailed competition investigation at this stage.
Axel Springer is one of Europe’s largest media groups. It owns major German newspapers, including Bild and Die Welt, as well as international digital outlets Politico and Business Insider.
The acquisition would bring one of Britain’s most prominent newspaper groups under the ownership of the Berlin-based company, marking a significant change in the UK media landscape.
The Telegraph Group was placed under receivership in 2023 after its former owners, the Barclay family, accumulated substantial debts to banks. Since then, the newspaper’s future has remained highly uncertain.
Before Axel Springer entered the picture, the UAE-backed RedBird IMI consortium had sought to acquire the newspaper.
However, the prospect of a long-established conservative British newspaper coming under the control of Gulf capital — and, indirectly, a foreign state — triggered a major political controversy in the UK.
The British government subsequently introduced legislation banning foreign state ownership of newspapers, prompting RedBird IMI to step back and transfer its acquisition rights to Axel Springer.

He argued that the EU must strengthen its internal market while developing measures to protect European industries against unfair external competition.
According to De Wever, integrating the European market and protecting it must go hand in hand, while avoiding excessive protectionism.
"Only when we have a unified market will we be able to protect it by avoiding the pitfalls of senseless protectionism. We must not copy the follies of others," he said.
The premier acknowledged that European decision-making was slower than that of major powers, but said this reflected the bloc's democratic structure. "But Europe is not a dictatorship. It is not a country where one president can decide one thing on Monday, the opposite on Wednesday, and something else again on Friday," he said.
