Defense Minister Israel Katz and senior military, police and prison officials have been placed under investigation in Italy over the treatment of Gaza flotilla activists, Italian prosecutors said on Friday.
The move expands an investigation that was previously focused on far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
The case concerns suspected torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage when Israeli forces intercepted small fleets of boats headed towards Gaza in 2025 and 2026, the Rome prosecutors' office said in a statement.
Investigators opened the probe after complaints from 50 Italian citizens who were detained by Israeli authorities following two Global Sumud Flotilla missions in September to October 2025 and April to May 2026.
Katz did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Ben-Gvir in June dismissed news that he was under investigation, saying he would "continue to stand proudly alongside our fighters."
Death threats and beatings
Prosecutors said activists detained after the first mission had reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism.
Activists involved in the second mission reported even harsher treatment, including beatings in the dark, the use of tasers and rubber bullets, the statement said.
Investigators had identified various individuals forming the military and police chains of command involved in the operations, prosecutors said.
Besides Katz and Ben-Gvir, prosecutors named 12 senior Israeli military, police and prison officials as suspects, including military chief Eyal Zamir.
Zamir also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Prosecutors said they had sent Israel a request for judicial assistance in June, seeking information needed to reconstruct events and establish individual responsibility. They did not say whether Israeli authorities had responded.
The prosecutors said they also held talks with the European Union's judicial cooperation agency, Eurojust, because similar investigations into the two flotilla missions were underway in other unnamed European countries.
Under Italian law, crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens can be prosecuted in Rome.
Being placed under investigation in Italy does not imply guilt and does not automatically lead to a trial. However, if the probe determines that charges are warranted, prosecutors could lodge a formal request for trial.
Flotilla organizers say they aimed to break Israel's blockade of Gaza by delivering humanitarian assistance. Israel says its naval blockade on Gaza is lawful.

Gaza malnutrition and starvation at ‘catastrophic’ levels: Health Ministry

Gaza malnutrition and starvation at ‘catastrophic’ levels: Health Ministry
About 67 percent of Gaza’s population is projected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026.
Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached “catastrophic” levels, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, despite a United States-brokered “ceasefire” that aims in part to allow more food and medical supplies to enter the Strip as Palestinians face famine.
At least 466 Palestinians have died of malnutrition and starvation since 2024, with children accounting for one-third of the deaths, the Gaza Health Ministry said on Friday, in a statement released for World Food Day.
Elderly Palestinians accounted for the largest share of malnutrition-related deaths in the Strip, with 189 deaths, representing 40.5 percent of the total. The ministry said 11 percent of older people went without a meal for an entire day and 48 percent reduced portions so their families could eat.
The ministry estimated that 74,200 children would require treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027.
Malnutrition was also driving up rates of anaemia among pregnant women to 61 percent in 2026, up from 41 percent before the war began in October 2023. Nearly 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded in the first half of 2026, more than three times the number recorded in the preceding six months.
More than 1.4 million Palestinians – 67 percent of Gaza’s population – are projected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026 as winter months approach, the ministry warned.
Gains in tackling hunger crisis at risk
The United Nations children’s agency, UNICEF, said that gains in tackling Gaza’s hunger crisis were fragile. It warned that the situation could worsen due to disruption of supplies entering Strip, and urged that crossings remain open.
A UNICEF report published on Friday found that while the so-called “ceasefire” between Israel and Hamas last October had allowed more humanitarian aid and commercial supplies to enter, acute malnutrition remains a risk.
The report said scaled-up food and nutrition response and the easing of restrictions on the entry of food and nutrition supplies helped to avert a prolonged famine after it was declared in August 2025.
Speaking to reporters in Geneva, UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires said the flow of both commercial and humanitarian supplies must remain predictable and continuous.
“The impact on children obviously will be felt if this situation is not resolved,” he said. “We can’t go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods, and services that they require.”
Israel said on Wednesday that no commercial goods had entered the Strip in days, blaming the supply shortages on a tax dispute between local merchants and Hamas. The Palestinian group dismissed Israel’s claims as “baseless” while Gaza’s Government Media Office condemned Israel’s “blatant disinformation campaign and false statement”.
Israel’s move to halt supplies has cut off a vital source of food and other goods in a territory where most depend on humanitarian assistance after three years of war, repeated displacement and stringent Israeli restrictions on aid deliveries.
Even before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in 2023, an Israeli land, sea and air blockade restricted the flow of food, clean water, fuel and medical supplies from entering the Strip.
Gaza’s Health Ministry has called for international action to ensure unrestricted entry of food and medicine into the Strip. It also called for support to revive local food production.

The Bedouin shepherd who claimed he was a kidnapped Jewish child
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:17:01 UTC
00:17:01 KST

Had this been a TV drama, someone would probably have asked the writers to tone it down. In 1956, a little boy disappeared from Tirosh, a farming community between Beit Shemesh and Kiryat Malachi. His mother had left him playing in the yard with a neighbor while she went to the clinic. When she returned, he was gone.
The boy was Yitzhak Gabay, 2. His brother David was 7 and his sister Aliza was 4. “We were going for tetanus shots,” David, now 78, recalled this week. “Mom told the neighbor, ‘I’m taking David and Aliza to get vaccinated. Keep an eye on Yitzhak.’ We were gone seven minutes. When we came back, Yitzhak wasn’t there. We asked the neighbor where he was. She said, ‘I gave him a tomato, and he headed back toward the house.’”
Relatives, neighbors and police searched for the child, but found no trace of him. “There were dozens of police officers and even a tracking dog, which died after a snake bit it,” David said. His parents spent years looking. “There wasn’t a rabbi, a sorcerer or a medium we didn’t go to.”
Of all those visits, David remembers one in particular, to the rabbi known as the Baba Sali. “We went to him right after the kidnapping,” he said. “He told us exactly when we would find Yitzhak. How many years, how many months, how many days. Even how many hours.” David remains convinced that the prediction came true.
Their mother, Zohara, had been pregnant 16 times; only David, Aliza and Yitzhak had survived. Nine years after her youngest son vanished, she died at 32. The family says she died of a broken heart. Her husband, Yisrael, stayed in Tirosh while David and Aliza married and moved to Tel Aviv. As the years passed, the family kept hoping someone would come forward with information, or recognize the boy and bring him home.
About two decades after the disappearance, an argument broke out in a Bedouin family. A young shepherd named Abdullah was quarreling with a relative when the relative snapped: “Who asked you? You’re not even Bedouin. Your mother is Jewish.” Abdullah could not forget it. He began to wonder whether the people who had raised him were his parents, and whether they had kept something from him.
He later said he began dreaming of an elderly Jewish man who told him he was Jewish. Eventually, Abdullah left his family and went to the home of Rabbi Yitzhak David Grossman in Migdal HaEmek, in northern Israel. He told Grossman he believed he was Jewish and had grown up with a family that was not his own. He wanted the rabbi’s help finding out who he was.
Word spread, and the story appeared in Yedioth Ahronoth. Families with missing children began arriving at Grossman’s door. Among those who heard about the shepherd was Yisrael Gabay. Twenty-one years had passed since his son’s disappearance.
David was then serving as an army personnel officer in Sharm el-Sheikh. “One day I got a call from the police: ‘Where are you? Get on the first flight. We need you back in Israel,’” he recalled. “As soon as I landed, Dad said, ‘We need to go to Migdal HaEmek.’” His father told him about the newspaper report and the shepherd who claimed his mother was Jewish.
“Thousands came to the rabbi, all saying he was their son,” David said. “The line stretched from Tel Aviv to Petah Tikva. Everyone had identifying marks. We arrived on Thursday, almost at the end, and we had the clearest signs. My brother had had treatments on his back as a child, and they’d left scars.” Abdullah had scars on his back, too.
Grossman had invited Yisrael to come with two friends from Tirosh. The family stayed through the Sabbath, and on Saturday night the rabbi arranged an informal identification lineup. David remembers a larger group taking part. “They brought in six or 10 men who looked more or less like Dad, but this young man went straight to him. He didn’t even look at the others. And I said, ‘That’s my brother.’ He was huge, like Dad.”
For Yisrael and Abdullah, that settled it. Abdullah began calling himself Yitzhak and moved into Yisrael’s home in Tirosh. He was also known as Abdullah-Yitzhak or Ovadia Ben Yisrael. “I remember we had a party, and Bedouin families came carrying weapons,” David said. “Then he stayed with us in Tirosh, where my father lived.”
Newspaper reports from 1977, however, said a police investigation had found no family connection. They cited a new blood test that had ruled out a biological relationship between Abdullah and the Gabays. Nearly half a century later, relatives interviewed this week dispute those reports. The story is still vividly remembered by the family and by Grossman’s assistant, who first brought it to public attention.
Abdullah tried to adjust to Jewish life with the Gabays, and they tried to help him settle in. But living together was difficult. “Abdullah was bored at Yisrael’s,” said Bracha, David’s wife. “He spoke only Arabic, and the father spoke only Hebrew. There was nothing for them to do at home in Tirosh. Back in his village, there were horses and sheep.”
David said Abdullah’s Bedouin family never explained how he had come to live with them, and the Gabays never asked. “My father died knowing he had found his son, and that this was the right child,” he said. Abdullah began spending time with the people he now regarded as his brother and sister. After a serious argument with David, he moved in with Aliza, who was raising five children.
Aliza has since died, but her son, Shimon Ben Khalifa, remembers Abdullah-Yitzhak well. To him, he was simply his uncle. “I was a baby when they found him, so I grew up with the whole story,” he said. “My mother was sure he was her brother. Nobody ever thought otherwise.”
Asked about the blood-test reports, Ben Khalifa said: “I never heard of a test like that. On the contrary, I think they did another test that showed he was my mother’s brother. There was also an older aunt, his mother’s sister, who always said that was the child. That was Yitzhak.”
Life in Tel Aviv did not suit Abdullah. By then, he had married a woman from the village where he had grown up. Relatives say she was a teacher and had even considered converting to Judaism for him. The couple tried living in Tirosh, but they were far from the families who had raised them. They eventually returned to Zarzir, where Abdullah did well raising calves and tending olive groves.
He stayed in touch with Aliza’s family. “We visited his home several times,” Ben Khalifa said. “His son was at my house two months ago. My younger brother got married two years ago, and he was at the wedding.”
“To this day, I’m sure he’s my brother,” David said. “He named his eldest daughter after our mother. Once he told me he lived between two worlds, Jewish and Bedouin.” Yisrael died 12 years ago, still carrying a childhood photograph of Yitzhak in his wallet. “Until the day he died,” David said, “he believed he had found his child.”

Ousted US general warned before Iran war of missile defense shortages lasting until 2030: Report

Ousted US Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned months before the US-Israeli war against Iran that American missile defense stockpiles were critically low and could take until 2030 to recover, CBS News reported Thursday.
George raised the warning in late December, two months before the conflict began, according to US officials familiar with his assessment. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed him from his post in April as the war was underway.
The general’s assessment, included in the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 force allocation planning, identified shortages of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors and Patriot missiles, with supplies expected to remain at strategically low levels until 2030.
The officials reportedly attributed the shortfall to weapons transfers to Ukraine, US military support for Israel, and limited defense industry production capacity.
The war with Iran has further strained supplies, according to the report. A Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimate found that US forces entered 2026 with approximately 2,300 Patriot interceptors and used between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict.
READ: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran: Report
The country’s prewar THAAD inventory stood at around 355 interceptors, of which an estimated 190 to 290 were expended.
Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, told CBS News that these systems would be crucial in a potential conflict with China.
“Air defense — missile defense — that will be huge,” he said, explaining that a major confrontation with Beijing would demand substantial interceptor supplies.
Replenishing the stockpiles remains a lengthy process, the report said. The CSIS estimates that new THAAD interceptor contracts take over four years to fulfill, while Patriot PAC-3 orders take an average of 3 1/2 years.
The Pentagon rejected claims of a shortage. Chief spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: “Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false.”
He added that Washington retains “everything required to strike at the time and place of the President’s choosing.”

====================================================================================================

Is Israel fighting the wrong war? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:02:18 UTC
00:02:18 KST

What if Israel is winning the military battles but losing the war that ultimately determines its survival?
Since October 7, 2023, Israel has demonstrated extraordinary military capabilities. Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran have suffered significant blows.
Yet the fundamental question remains: Has military superiority brought Israel closer to enduring security? This may be one of the most important questions for Israelis in the upcoming elections.
Or, perhaps the question should be: Are we fighting the wrong war? It is fascinating that this question is not a significant part of the political debates leading up to the decision regarding who will lead the country.
The early Zionist movement understood something that modern Israel may have forgotten.
Nation-building was a generational undertaking. Theodor Herzl, Chaim Weizmann, and David Ben-Gurion invested decades in diplomacy, institution-building, immigration, and international legitimacy.
They understood that establishing a Jewish state required more than winning individual confrontations.
Today, Israel often approaches existential threats through military operations measured in days, weeks, or months.
Our ideological adversaries are operating on an entirely different clock.
Consider the historical memory of the Crusades. European armies conquered Jerusalem, but ultimately lost their foothold in the region.
The lesson for movements committed to a generational struggle is straightforward: survive today, regroup tomorrow, and eventually your enemy will lose his will to fight and leave.
Iran’s revolutionary leadership has demonstrated comparable strategic patience, investing decades in regional proxies, ideological networks, and the pursuit of influence.
Israel cannot assume that its adversaries define victory, defeat, or acceptable sacrifice as we do.
That brings us to the first strategic trap: deterrence.
Traditional deterrence assumes that sufficiently painful consequences will discourage aggression.
But what happens when an adversary embraces martyrdom, accepts devastating casualties, or considers organizational survival itself a victory?
Yahya Sinwar understood that October 7 would provoke an overwhelming Israeli response. Yet the resulting devastation did not necessarily negate the broader political and ideological objectives of his attack.
Israel must then employ increasingly substantial military force to defeat an adversary willing to absorb extraordinary losses.
Now introduce the second trap.
When terrorist organizations embed military operations within civilian environments, Israel faces difficult operational choices. Protecting civilians, as international law requires, by definition extends military campaigns.
Civilian casualties and destruction, whatever the military circumstances, produce images that travel around the world within seconds.
A Hamas command center may be the military objective. A destroyed building becomes the television image.
CNN, Al Jazeera, TikTok, Telegram, and countless smartphones transmit those images into millions of homes.
Military time and political time are no longer synchronized.
The longer Israel fights, the more international pressure can accumulate. The more force required, the greater the potential reputational consequences. And the more international legitimacy erodes, the less strategic freedom Israel retains.
Israel can win the battlefield while losing the conditions necessary to achieve and sustain victory.
But there is another battlefield, one extending thousands of miles beyond Israel’s borders.
The Jewish Diaspora
Jewish communities in New York, London, Paris, and elsewhere are increasingly drawn into conflicts they neither initiated nor controlled.
As the war continues, images of Palestinian suffering circulate globally, accompanied by accusations against Israel that can spill over into hostility toward Jews generally.
And what is their response?
Too often, they follow Israel’s traditional hasbara (public diplomacy) playbook.
More facts. More explanations. More historical context. More attempts to correct the latest accusation.
Necessary? Absolutely.
Sufficient? Clearly not.
Because while we are explaining yesterday’s military operation, our opponents are organizing tomorrow’s political campaign.
An October 10 Fox News investigation by Asra Nomani exposed the organizational machinery behind a coordinated international anti-Israel mobilization starting this past October 8 to the 15.
The investigation identified 179 participating organizations and 322 scheduled events across three days. Organizers had prepared graphics in seven languages, common slogans, media guidance, and political demands.
The campaign extended beyond street demonstrations into universities, workplaces, corporations, and government institutions, calling for sanctions and arms embargoes.
This was not simply spontaneous outrage. It was evidence of a prepared, interoperable international network capable of transforming individual demonstrations into coordinated political pressure, just as it did on October 8, before Israel even responded to the attacks of October 7.
Our enemies have spent years building what we now know is an extremely effective ecosystem.
Not every participant shares the same ideology. But organizations with different political identities can cooperate around common objectives without surrendering their independence.
That is the power of an ecosystem. And it exposes another weakness in our approach.
We are fighting not merely an information war, but a competition for meaning.
Psychiatrist and Holocaust survivor Dr. Viktor Frankl described the existential vacuum: the emptiness people feel when they struggle to find meaning and purpose.
He suggested that our modern society, with all its technological advances, was driving this feeling of emptiness among millions.
Ideological movements can fill that vacuum by offering something more compelling than information: identity, belonging, community, moral purpose, and agency.
Their message effectively becomes: Here is who you are. Here is what is wrong. Here is who is responsible. Here are your people. And here is what you can do.
This is why a “Free Palestine” chant at a huge Ed Sheeran concert so quickly engaged tens of thousands both at the concert and via their social media platforms.
Traditional hasbara too often responds: Here are the facts you should know.
You cannot defeat a meaning system merely by correcting its facts. This is where Israel’s strategic doctrine requires fundamental reconsideration.
Military superiority remains indispensable. But Israel and global Jewry also need a permanent, decentralized, interoperable global ecosystem supporting Jewish safety, Israel’s legitimacy, and long-term societal resilience.
Further strengthened by those who realize that the anti-Israel ecosystem is focusing on Israel first, with the West next in line.
Not another government-controlled public relations campaign.
Not another emergency fundraising appeal following an antisemitic incident.
And certainly not an organization demanding that everyone agree with their view of the world.
Instead, an international network of independent Jewish and non-Jewish institutions, educators, influencers, researchers, philanthropists, cultural leaders, public-private initiatives, and civil society organizations connected by a shared agreement on fundamental principles.
The Jewish people’s historical continuity matters. Jewish safety matters. Israel’s legitimate existence matters. Human dignity and coexistence matter.
Participants can disagree on politics while sharing those foundations.
Such an ecosystem must operate continuously, building relationships, credibility, community, and meaningful participation before the next crisis erupts.
It must strengthen the Diaspora rather than leave Jewish communities perpetually defending military decisions made thousands of miles away.
And it must become an additional dimension of deterrence.
An adversary contemplating aggression should encounter not merely a formidable Israeli military, but a society and international network capable of enduring political pressure, resisting isolation, and sustaining legitimate security interests.
The Zionist movement understood the importance of building the future before the decisive moment arrived.
We must rediscover that strategic patience.
Israel cannot fight a generational ideological conflict exclusively through military campaigns measured in months.
Our military protects our ability to survive in the short term. Our ecosystem must help protect our ability to endure for the long term.
The writer is a global strategist and a strategic adviser at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs. Follow him on X: @jeffkahn2020

Poll: right-wing People’s Party, and polarisation, growing ahead of 2027 elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Poll: right-wing People’s Party, and polarisation, growing ahead of 2027 elections
A year ahead of Swiss federal elections, pole parties from the right and left are gaining ground while centre-right parties lose out, a new poll finds.
The Sotomo institute’s election barometer, carried out on behalf of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (Swissinfo’s parent company), took the pulse of voters’ opinions and priorities just over a year ahead of parliamentary elections set for October 24, 2027.
The big takeaway: polarisation is growing as centre-right parties lose ground. If elections were held today, the right-wing Swiss People’s Party would be the big winner with 29.9% of the vote – a score that would surpass its own record of 29.4% set in 2015.
And in terms of progression since the last elections in October 2023, the People’s Party has also recorded the biggest jump, strengthening its electoral share by two percentage points.
The left-wing Social Democrats and Greens also currently look to be making slight gains which would boost the left’s combined strength by 1.5 percentage points in total. The increase is mainly down to the Social Democrats, currently backed by 19.3% of voters (up one percentage point since 2023); this would be the party’s best result since 2007, Sotomo notes.
Struggles for centre-right
The Centre Party, which stands at 12.6% of voting intentions, and the Radical-Liberal Party, at 13.3%, continue to shed electoral support. The two parties currently look set to lose 1.5 and one percentage point respectively compared to 2023.
Compared to a similar poll in 2025, the Radical-Liberal Party has in fact managed to gain a place and move slightly ahead of the Centre. However, its 13.3% score would still be its worst result in its entire history of House of Representatives elections, Sotomo notes.
And taken together, the Radical-Liberals and the Centre – the two traditionally dominant conservative parties – currently come to a total of 26%, an electoral share which is four percentage points lower than that of the Swiss People’s Party alone.
Climate change back on the agenda
The survey also indicates that the shake-up of support for political parties only partially reflects the population’s major concerns.
Migration, a traditional policy priority of the Swiss People’s Party, is notably moving down the list of the population’s concerns. The two political challenges currently considered most urgent by voters surveyed are the cost of health insurance premiums (39%) and climate change (36%).
The latter, “which seemed to have gone out of fashion in recent years”, has risen sharply following the heatwave-hit summer of 2026, according to Sotomo director Michael Hermann. The proportion who see it as a major challenge has jumped nine percentage points in a year.
At the same time, climate concerns have not yet translated into electoral support; while the Green Party has progressed only marginally, the centrist Liberal Greens have even dropped.
While not predicting another “green wave” like in 2019, Sotomo nevertheless notes that the current trend for the two ecological parties is “more positive than it seems at first glance” – mainly because both have “at least managed, thanks to environmental ‘branding’, to pull themselves out of the dip they were in”, the research institute writes.
Almost two-thirds (65%) of respondents in the poll think measures taken by politicians to mitigate the consequences of climate change are not sufficient. However, support for additional measures, as well as the perception of the urgency of the situation, varies greatly depending on affiliation – nearly 90% of Green voters consider climate action a priority, compared to just 5% of People’s Party voters. Concern about rising health insurance premiums, on the other hand, cuts across party lines.
Immigration and crime still big issues for the right
Behind the two prominent themes of climate and health insurance, four other issues are all cited by around a quarter of respondents: asylum policy, relations with the European Union (EU), immigration, and housing.
Concern about housing has notably progressed in recent years – from 13% in 2023 to 23% today – as has concern about crime, which has jumped from 10% to 19%. This latter is particularly mentioned by right-wing voters.
On the other hand, immigration has largely declined as a priority, after having been cited as a major challenge by 35% of respondents in 2023. But it is still the top issue for People’s Party voters.
‘Too friendly’ towards the US and Israel?
Given the importance of foreign policy issues during the current legislative term, the poll also asked about citizens’ perceptions of how the Swiss government is faring on the international stage.
Here, the population is most critical of Bern’s attitude to the US, with over 80% believing the Federal Council is too friendly with Washington – a perception which is quite uniform across party affiliations.
Similarly, nearly three-quarters of survey respondents consider the official Swiss attitude towards Israel to be too cordial. This opinion is also seen across most party bases, although less clearly for People’s Party and Radical-Liberal Party supporters.
Russia and the EU are the source of much bigger differences and ideological splits. Overall, just over half of all respondents consider Bern’s attitude towards Moscow to be too friendly: but for People’s Party voters it is less than 30%, for left-leaning voters over 70%. Meanwhile nearly 90% of People’s Party supporters consider the government to be too friendly towards the EU, compared to just 10% of Social Democrat and Green voters.
Survey respondents were also asked about their perception of the degree of influence and popularity of each member of the seven-headed federal government. Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter (Radical-Liberal Party) is still clearly on top for influence (63%), ahead of Environment Minister Albert Rösti (People’s Party), at 53%, and his party colleague, Economics Minister Guy Parmelin, at 42% – up from just 17% a year ago.
Parmelin, who currently holds the rotating Swiss presidency, and who is stepping down from the government at the end of this year, also now tops the popularity rankings (more than 60% of respondents like him) ahead of Defence Minister Martin Pfister (50%) and Keller-Sutter (46%).
The barometer – methodology
Data collection for the SBC election barometer was carried out online from September 10-23, 2026. Poll respondents were recruited partly via SBC web portals and partly via Sotomo’s online panel. Responses from 25,092 voters were used, and statistical weighting was used to make the sample conform to sociodemographic characteristics like place of residence, age, gender, education and political characteristics.
The poll’s margin of error is +/- 1.2 percentage points for an observed percentage of 50% with a 95% confidence interval.

CineCrossroads: What to watch this weekend - “Heart of the Beast,” “City of God” and “Fantastic Mr. Fox”

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:32:15 UTC
23:32:15 KST

CineCrossroads: What to watch this weekend - “Heart of the Beast,” “City of God” and “Fantastic Mr. Fox”
The weekend is approaching, bringing three stories about survival in worlds where danger can emerge from nature, violence or one’s own choices. In this edition of CineCrossroads, a soldier and his dog fight their way through the Alaskan wilderness, a young photographer searches for an escape from the violence surrounding him, and a clever fox risks everything by returning to his criminal ways. Qazinform News Agency correspondent wishes you an enjoyable viewing.
Movie of the Week: Heart of the Beast (2026)
In the wilderness, survival depends on trust between a man and his most loyal companion.
Directed by David Ayer, Heart of the Beast stars Brad Pitt as James Belmont, a Special Forces officer who survives a devastating plane crash alongside his combat dog, Odin. Stranded deep in the Alaskan wilderness, the pair must confront extreme weather, dangerous terrain and the physical limits of their endurance.
Belmont’s military experience gives him the skills needed to stay alive, but the isolation forces him to rely equally on Odin. Their relationship forms the emotional center of the film, transforming a traditional survival thriller into a story about loyalty, trauma and the bond between humans and animals.
Released in cinemas on September 25, Heart of the Beast reunites Pitt with Ayer after their collaboration on the 2014 war drama Fury. It is a fitting choice for viewers seeking action, striking natural landscapes and an emotional story about companionship under the most difficult circumstances.
Classic Pick: City of God (2002)
In a neighborhood ruled by violence, a camera offers one young man a different path.
Directed by Fernando Meirelles and Kátia Lund, City of God follows several interconnected lives in a housing project outside Rio de Janeiro. At the center of the story is Rocket, a quiet boy who dreams of becoming a photographer rather than joining the criminal world surrounding him.
As rival gangs compete for control, Rocket documents a community shaped by poverty, ambition and fear. His photographs gradually become both a record of the violence and a possible route out of it.
Driven by energetic editing, vivid performances and an unforgettable visual style, City of God presents violence without turning it into simple entertainment. More than two decades after its release, it remains a powerful examination of how opportunity, environment and personal choices can determine the course of a life.
Family Pick: Fantastic Mr. Fox (2009)
Some animals are simply not made for an ordinary life.
Directed by Wes Anderson and based on Roald Dahl’s beloved book, Fantastic Mr. Fox follows a former thief who has promised his wife that he will leave his dangerous habits behind. Years later, frustrated by domestic routine, Mr. Fox secretly begins stealing from three wealthy and ruthless farmers.
His actions place his family and the entire local animal community in danger. To protect them, he must use the same intelligence and daring that created the crisis in the first place.
Featuring stop-motion animation and the voices of George Clooney, Meryl Streep and Jason Schwartzman, Fantastic Mr. Fox combines dry humor, family adventure and carefully crafted visuals. Beneath its playful surface is a thoughtful story about identity, responsibility and learning to protect the people who depend on us.

The parties have clashed over the National Health Insurance Act, the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act, land expropriation and proposed value-added tax increases. They have also traded accusations over consultation and the handling of major government decisions.
The DA has repeatedly criticised what it sees as unilateral action by the ANC, while the governing party has continued to advance policies that the DA opposes.
These disputes have tested a coalition formed after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority in the 2024 national elections. Mbalula’s demand puts the DA’s role in the coalition under renewed political scrutiny.

In space, no one hears Zelensky scream: No euros can buy Kiev options in orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:28:53 UTC
23:28:53 KST

In space, no one hears Zelensky scream: No euros can buy Kiev options in orbit
No matter how European leaders pledge to support Ukraine come hell or high water and let the taxpayers foot the bill, the cold hard fact is that there are things no euros can buy, such as US intelligence and satellite communications.
Kiev’s critical reliance on American space capabilities came to the fore this week when the long-standing feud between US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Zelensky flared up again. Trump, who had struck a diesel supply deal with Russia, called Zelensky a hindrance to peace who should be replaced. Zelensky called Trump a weakling who had betrayed Ukraine, if not in those exact terms.
According to lamentations from Kiev corroborated by media reporting, the White House put a chokehold on the Zelensky government by suspending early warning about incoming Russian ballistic missiles and temporarily suspending access to Starlink satellite internet for fast-moving objects – such as drones used in Kiev’s “middle strike” operations inside what Washington recognizes as part of Ukraine.
It’s not like Kiev was not warned. During a meeting in Miami last week, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly told the Ukrainians the diesel deal announcement was coming and that Kiev should not have ignored Trump’s multiple requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Accounts shared with Axios and Reuters suggest the Americans were polite enough not to say “what a nice deal to get intelligence and internet you have; it would be a shame if something happened to it.” But they mentioned “all that the US has done for Ukraine.” The Ukrainians did take it as a threat.
Here are the alternatives Kiev would have, should Trump push the issue further.
No match for US intelligence
Intelligence that European NATO members can provide is a far cry from what the US has been delivering for years. Already, early warning about Russian ballistic missile launches has stopped coming, just as Zelensky is complaining.
The US operates the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS), whose backbone is six geosynchronous orbit satellites equipped with thermal sensors that detect launch signatures, complemented by two active and two reserve payloads in a highly elliptical orbit.
SBIRS helps identify and estimate the trajectory of a weapon, but has limited ability to track missiles after the intensive boost phase. But knowing one is incoming helps ground and airborne radar systems that guide interceptor missiles.
Other NATO members rely on SBIRS intelligence and never thought they would need their own alternative.
Satellites operated by the US National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) and the Air Force’s electronic reconnaissance aircraft, such as the RC-135U Combat Sent, also collect intelligence about Russian air defense systems. It’s unclear how much data it shares with Kiev, but the media has said the US helps plan Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia to minimize Moscow’s ability to intercept.
European NATO members do have some similar capabilities, including France’s three CERES electronic-intelligence satellites, the UK’s three RC-135W Rivet Joint aircraft, and Germany’s SARah radar-reconnaissance space program, but there is only so much they can do to measure up to the world’s largest military spender.
OneWeb not to rule them all
On the connectivity side, Starlink and its military twin Starshield remain the most capable today. It has over 11,000 satellites in low Earth (LEO) orbit that can use lasers to route traffic between each other, boosting their bandwidth.
The Starlink Mini terminal weighs just 1.1 kg and has an integrated antenna, making it usable even on even smaller military drones. Even larger variants are compact, which makes them harder to spot, and they typically consume under 100 watts of power – both valuable features in frontline applications.
The most direct non-US alternative is Eutelsat OneWeb, which already complements Starlink access in Ukraine. It only has 600+ satellites in its constellation, but nevertheless offers a high-speed connection.
However, OneWeb’s orbital component “remains rooted in an outdated architecture and technology conceived a decade ago, without any evolution of its underlying design,” Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant, told Reuters.
OneWeb ground hardware is likewise no match for Starlink in price, size, or appetite for energy. The relatively small Hughes HL1100W terminal weighs over 10 kg and consumes around 130 watts, though there are efforts to produce smaller and less power-hungry equipment.
Kymeta Corporation announced a OneWeb terminal in March whose 100-watt consumption it said was optimized for mobile platforms. Its “compact and lightweight design” means it weighs less than 11 kg, and the producer itself is Redmond, Washington.
Dark horses in orbit
In September, EU co-founder Luxembourg announced the successful launch of the final three of a planned 13 satellites of its O3b mPOWER communication system. The low number is misleading, since the constellation is being positioned in medium Earth orbit and requires fewer satellites for coverage.
The trade off is latency, which is higher by an order of magnitude compared to LEO-based systems, but Luxembourg’s system is still good enough for some military applications and is used by NATO.
O3b mPOWER’s potential for Ukraine’s war effort is limited due to its coverage, which is between 50° north latitude and 50° south latitude. Luxembourg is right on the northern border of the band, but a large part of Ukraine, including Kiev, is outside of it. As they say, geography is destiny.
GOVSATCOM, the EU’s program to band together communication satellites owned by several member states, is somewhat of a dark horse, but public data suggests its capabilities are too limited to replace Starlink.
Amazon Leo is currently in limited preview, but it’s hard to expect an American company and a major Pentagon contractor to publicly defy Trump at Brussels’ call. Russia’s in-development Rassvet system is obviously not an option.
The EU’s proposed IRIS² system is years away from being operational, as is Canada’s Telesat Lightspeed.
In short, should Ukraine lose Starlink, in the short term Europe cannot replace it, as EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas acknowledged on Friday.

Can Russia help ease tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:56:43 UTC
22:56:43 KST

Can Russia help ease tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan?
Russia has close ties with the Taliban and is courting Islamabad, but analysts say its leverage remains uncertain.
Islamabad, Pakistan – Sitting with his elbows on his knees, Russia’s Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev leaned towards Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, for talks in Rawalpindi on October 14.
While Kolokoltsev was in Pakistan, Sergey Naryshkin, director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), flew into Kabul to meet the Taliban’s intelligence chief, Abdul Haq Wasiq.
Officially, Russia, Pakistan and Afghanistan have issued little beyond standard statements about the meetings. But the signs are clear: Pakistan and Afghanistan have spent the past year exchanging fire and public threats. Qatar and Turkiye brokered a ceasefire in Doha last October and China hosted talks in Urumqi in April, but attacks inside Pakistan continued. Islamabad again struck Afghan territory in June, September and this month.
Russia now appears to be stepping in as a mediator.
Moscow’s special representative for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, told Russia’s TASS news agency earlier this month that his country was ready to play peace broker between Kabul and Islamabad if both sides requested it.
Pakistan’s ambassador to Russia, Faisal Niaz Tirmizi, said in March that Islamabad had approached Moscow. The Taliban, though, have not publicly requested Russian mediation, raising questions about how much and in what capacity Moscow can push Pakistan and Afghanistan to talks when other mediators have struggled.
A complicated history adds to the challenge Russia faces.
A diplomatic opening
Pakistan’s military media wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), said the Rawalpindi meeting discussed issues of “mutual interest and the regional security environment, with particular emphasis on strengthening bilateral security cooperation.”
The statement did not mention Afghanistan and neither Russian officials nor the Taliban have disclosed what the intelligence chiefs discussed. Moscow has, however, voiced concern about the fighting.
“We are seriously concerned about the ongoing military confrontation between Pakistan and Afghanistan, which affects civilians, including children,” the Russian embassy in Kabul posted on X earlier this month.
The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said Pakistani strikes between September 30 and October 1 killed at least 10 civilians, mostly children.
In decades past, the idea of Russia mediating between Pakistan and the Taliban might have been unthinkable. Throughout the Cold War and even after the collapse of the Soviet Union, Russia was – and remains in many ways – one of the closest strategic and military partners of India, the neighbour Pakistan has fought multiple wars against. While in Afghanistan, Russia backed the Northern Alliance against the Taliban throughout the 1990s.
But in recent years, Russia has significantly strengthened relations with both Pakistan and the Taliban. Then Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan was in Moscow when Russian forces invaded Ukraine in 2022. Last year, Russia became the first country in the world to officially recognise the Taliban government in Afghanistan.
Those shifts have been driven by Russia’s desire to broaden its options in South Asia, at a time when India has embraced the United States and to counter the rise of the Afghan branch of ISIL, also known as the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or ISKP. While the Taliban are concerned with ruling Afghanistan, ISKP has broader territorial ambitions and carried out an attack in Moscow in 2024 that killed nearly 150 people. The Taliban and the ISKP are sworn enemies.
Fighting between Pakistan and the Taliban created regional instability and Moscow was worried that could make it easier for armed groups to spill into Central Asia, said Taimur Khan, a research associate at the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad (ISSI).
“Mediation also helps Moscow preserve its regional influence and avoid a vacuum that could invite renewed extra-regional involvement,” he told Al Jazeera.
Why mediation stalled
Qatar and Turkiye brokered a ceasefire between Pakistan and the Taliban in Doha last October, but talks in Istanbul collapsed the following month and skirmishes resumed. Islamabad also launched air raids inside Afghanistan. China hosted talks in Urumqi in April.
In mid-September, Turkiye’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin, met Taliban officials in Kabul and Kandahar before travelling to Islamabad.
An attack in Kohat followed on September 18, with Pakistan striking Afghanistan on September 24 and October 1.
“Other actors have so far achieved more tangible mediation results in this conflict,” Eldaniz Gusseinov, a Central Asia analyst and head of research at the geopolitical foresight agency, Nightingale Int, told Al Jazeera.
Russia’s own effort stalled at a Moscow meeting on October 5.
Kabulov told TASS that the Afghan delegation objected to Afghanistan being mentioned too often in connection with “terrorism”.
“For Pakistan, this is a substantive security issue, not merely a matter of wording,” Pakistan’s Foreign Office spokesperson, Sajjad Haider Khan, said on October 9 at a weekly media briefing.
Kabul-based security analyst Tameem Bahiss said the objection reflected Kabul’s longstanding position.
“Accepting language that repeatedly associates Afghanistan with terrorism could be seen as an acknowledgement of the very allegations Kabul has consistently denied,” he told Al Jazeera.
The TTP problem
At the Moscow meeting, Pakistan’s special representative for Afghanistan, Mohammad Sadiq, said “terrorism” remained at the core of Afghanistan’s problems.
Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi said the two countries’ problems could be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, according to Afghan media.
Pakistan says the Pakistani Taliban and other armed groups shelter in Afghanistan.
Kabul rejects the allegation, saying it does not allow its territory to be used against other countries and that Pakistan’s security problems are largely internal, Bahiss said.
Moscow’s public warnings have focused on the ISKP.
“There is no visible public pressure from Russia on the Taliban over Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), and Moscow is unlikely to exert such pressure,” Gusseinov said. TTP is the official name of the Pakistani Taliban, which is behind dozens of the deadliest attacks Pakistan has suffered in recent years.
He argued that pressing the Taliban hard on Pakistan’s behalf would undermine Moscow’s standing as a neutral mediator and its partnership with the Taliban against ISKP.
“Russia’s primary concern is ISKP and it appears satisfied with the Taliban’s efforts to counter the group,” Abdul Sayed, a Sweden-based analyst specialising in armed groups and security dynamics in Afghanistan and Pakistan, told Al Jazeera.
What Moscow brings
Still, Russia has something earlier mediators did not. In July 2025, it became the only country to recognise the Taliban government.
Taimur Khan said that could give Moscow another source of influence.
“The Taliban authorities’ interest in preserving that recognition and expanding cooperation with Moscow could give Russia additional influence in seeking action against the TTP and other terrorist groups operating from Afghanistan,” he said.
In May, the two sides signed an unpublished military-technical agreement covering, according to Kabulov, the repair and maintenance of equipment the Taliban already hold, mostly Soviet and Russian-made.
Three days after the signing, the Taliban’s Defence Minister, Mohammad Yaqoob, said Pakistan would soon no longer dare to launch strikes.
On June 9 and 10, Pakistani aircraft struck Kunar, Khost and Paktika provinces, killing 13 civilians, according to the Afghan government.
“Russia has greater access to the Taliban than any other major power, but its actual leverage is considerably more limited than is often assumed,” analyst Gusseinov said.
Sayed said senior Taliban leaders continued visiting Russia and India as fighting escalated, seemingly signalling they could offset Pakistan’s military superiority through new alignments.
“While the military and political significance of these ties remains unclear, the Taliban present such diplomatic developments to the Afghan public, particularly their supporters, as political achievements that reinforce their image of strength,” he said.
Why the SCO matters
Pakistan chairs the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) for 2026-27 and will host the 10-member bloc’s summit in Islamabad next year.
The Taliban were not invited to this year’s summit in Bishkek, where members called for an inclusive government in Kabul.
On July 16, then-Foreign Office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said Afghanistan first needed diplomatic relations with member states, when asked whether Pakistan was blocking its inclusion in the SCO.
In September, Tirmizi, the Pakistani envoy in Moscow, said he did not see full SCO membership for Afghanistan as an option under the current Taliban government.
“The chairmanship strengthens Moscow’s reasons to invest in its relationship with Pakistan and manage differences over Afghanistan constructively,” Taimur Khan said.
The Foreign Office did not answer Al Jazeera’s questions about whether the Taliban would be invited next year.
“I cannot recall an instance where Kabul has explicitly requested Moscow to mediate between the two countries,” Bahiss said. “Nevertheless, Kabul’s repeated calls for diplomacy and its relatively close relations with Russia suggest that it would likely welcome Russian mediation if Moscow offered to play such a role.”

Britain Is Taking Too Long to Blame Russia for Sabotage, Labour MP Warns
Britain is taking too long to publicly attribute sabotage and arson to Russia, leaving businesses supporting Ukraine without timely warnings that they may themselves become targets, Labour MP Graeme Downie told UK Defence Journal on October 16.
Downie, author of The Putin Tax report, contrasted Britain with countries such as Estonia, which recently blamed Russia within days of an arson attack on a drone manufacturer.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We’ve seen other NATO countries like Estonia blaming Russia and attributing blame within days without the need to publish all of the raw intelligence,” he said.
Downie argued that Britain effectively applies a criminal standard—“beyond reasonable doubt”—when deciding whether to attribute hostile-state activity, when a lower civil standard could allow the government to act faster.
“Rather than apply the criminal bar of beyond reasonable doubt, you probably apply a civil legal bar of overwhelming evidence, and on the balance of probabilities,” he said, adding that the current approach “delays it.”
That delay can have practical consequences for British companies supplying Ukraine. Downie said firms should not necessarily be afraid, but they need to understand that they could be targeted and receive better guidance on protecting themselves.
“I think it’s not they should be worried, but they should be aware,” he said. Publicly identifying attacks more quickly, he argued, would signal to companies supporting Ukraine “that they need to get protection.”
He also warned that Britain’s subsea energy and communications infrastructure faces a serious threat from hostile activity.
“The threat to subsea infrastructure is entirely real,” Downie said, warning that even short disruptions to internet cables or energy networks could inflict major economic damage.
His comments follow the March 2024 arson attack on a warehouse in Leyton linked to aid for Ukraine. Men were later convicted over the fire, which prosecutors said had been organized on behalf of Russia’s Wagner Group.

Ukraine Tests First Aerial Drone Designed to Evacuate Wounded Soldiers From the Front
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:55:41 UTC
22:55:41 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Tests First Aerial Drone Designed to Evacuate Wounded Soldiers From the Front
Ukraine has begun front-line testing of StarGate, its first aerial drone designed to evacuate wounded soldiers from areas too dangerous for conventional vehicles or evacuation teams, the Associated Press (AP) reported on Octobe 16.
Ukraine is increasingly using unmanned ground vehicles to evacuate wounded troops from areas where Russian FPV drones make conventional rescue missions too dangerous. In April, the First Separate Medical Battalion completed six casualty evacuations with ground robots in a single day under constant drone threat.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
AP received exclusive access to a field demonstration of the system before StarGate was handed to a Ukrainian combat brigade for testing under front-line conditions.
“The idea came directly from the front line, from the trenches,” a SkyFall spokesperson told AP.
The drone was developed over the past year by Ukrainian defense technology company SkyFall after a request from the commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, known as Code 9.2.
In some sectors, the battlefield “kill zone” under constant drone and artillery threat extends 10 to 15 kilometers or farther, AP reported. StarGate has a one-way range of 15 kilometers and is designed to reach wounded troops inside those areas without exposing an evacuation crew.
“Covering 10 kilometers in minutes would be a drastic change on the front line,” KVN, a commander with Code 9.2, told AP.
StarGate can carry up to 150 kilograms, enough for a wounded soldier wearing body armor and combat equipment. Its evacuation compartment is built around a medical-grade stretcher.
According to AP, the drone cruises at 65 kilometers per hour and can reach 105 kilometers per hour. SkyFall states that it can be prepared for flight in about 10 minutes.
The system uses Starlink and SkyFall’s proprietary L-Link communications system, alongside AI-assisted navigation designed for environments where GPS is unavailable, spoofed, or jammed.
During the demonstration observed by AP, FPV drones simulated attacks on StarGate while electronic jamming was active. The evacuation drone deployed a net against one approaching FPV, knocking it off course.
SkyFall also states that StarGate can return toward a safe area if communications are completely lost. The drone is equipped with thermal cameras for night operations and is designed to fly in rain and snow.
The company has demonstrated that the aircraft can continue flying after losing one of its arms, although AP noted that SkyFall has not released data showing how reliably it can survive damage under combat conditions.
Each system is expected to cost at least $50,000, depending on its configuration. SkyFall aims to produce up to 1,000 StarGate drones per month by the end of 2026.
“It’s a completely new method of evacuation,” KVN told AP. “It’s difficult to talk in depth about the pros and cons right now. We need to work with it more.”
Unmanned systems already play an expanding role in Ukrainian casualty evacuation, particularly where ground vehicles face mines, craters, destroyed roads, rivers, and drone attacks. AP reported that ground robots can take two to three hours to reach some positions, while StarGate is designed to cover comparable distances in minutes.
The StarGate tests build on Ukraine’s growing use of unmanned systems for casualty evacuation. In June, the Third Army Corps reported that its ground robots had evacuated more than 600 wounded soldiers during their first year of operations, while completing more than 18,000 missions overall.

Ethiopia announces instalment of interim government in Tigray
Unknown

2026-10-16

Ethiopia announces instalment of interim government in Tigray
After military pushed back TPLF uprising, PM Abiy Ahmed promises free elections within six months.
Ethiopia has announced that an interim government will take control of the state of Tigray, after its armed forces retook control of the northern region.
The installation of the six-month administration was announced in a statement by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Friday. He pledged that free elections would then be held in the state.
The move comes after the Ethiopian military pushed back an uprising launched last month by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Tigray’s main political party had launched the insurrection after announcing in April that it was retaking control of the region, effectively ending a peace deal with Ethiopia’s federal government.
The government promised that the interim government would create “a stable political situation” in Tigray so that free elections could be held. It has appointed five officials to run the state, including the mayor of the capital, Mekelle.
The officials will carry out “directives and instructions” delivered directly from the federal government.
The TPLF has yet to respond to the announcement. The rebel group launched an ambitious offensive in September in alliance with several other armed groups aimed at toppling the Abiy government. The Ethiopian government has accused the breakaway state of Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, accusations that Eritrea has denied.
After some early gains in the Afar region, its fighters were defeated and lost Tigray’s major cities. They surrendered in Mekelle in early October. Eritrean troops who had entered Tigray withdrew after heavy drone strikes from the Ethiopian armed forces.
The TPLF governed Ethiopia for nearly 30 years until 2018, when Abiy’s party came to power. Tigray, in response, boycotted national elections and rejected the central government, creating a severe rift.
The region remains scarred by the 2020-2022 war between federal forces, backed at that time by Eritrea, and the TPLF, which resulted in the killing of almost 600,000 people.
A peace deal ended the fighting, but key promises were not kept, including the return of displaced people and the disarmament of the TPLF.
Since the recent escalation, Ethiopia and Eritrea have accused each other of inciting war, raising fears of a wider conflict.
On Wednesday, the United States urged both sides to “de-escalate” during a phone call between Abiy and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

EU decision could drive more Sika deer to Zurich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:31:31 UTC
22:31:31 KST

EU decision could drive more Sika deer to Zurich
The spotted Sika deer from Japan could soon be migrating to the Swiss canton of Zurich in greater numbers. This is due to a European Union directive for member states to cull the animals.
In Germany and Austria, the EU decision announced in the summer of 2025 caused quite a stir. The media were already referring to an “extermination and culling plan”. The EU had classified the spotted sika deer as an “invasive alien species”.
Private ownership of these deer will therefore only be permitted until August 2027. Furthermore, wild populations are to be “intensively hunted”. In this way, the EU aims to prevent damage to native forests and to stop the Asian deer from interbreeding with native red deer.
More
How Switzerland is battling invasive species
Around 40 Swiss Sika deer
The decision from Brussels could have implications for the canton of Zurich. “We will notice the increasing hunting pressure in Baden-Württemberg,” says Reto Muggler, co-head of the cantonal Fisheries and Hunting Administration. This means that more sika deer could migrate into the area.
This Asian deer species already lives in the canton of Zurich, albeit only in a small area of just over 2,300 hectares. The animals can be observed north of the Rhine in the Rafzerfeld in the canton of Zurich and in the canton of Schaffhausen. This population numbers just over 40 animals.
Unlike in the EU, where culling plans are a recent development, sika deer have, however, been hunted in the canton of Zurich for years. Last year, 19 animals were shot to prevent the population from spreading. “If more sika deer were to enter the canton of Zurich, they would continue to be hunted as part of normal management,” said Muggler.
The canton does not currently fear any significant geographical spread. According to Muggler, the sika deer remains within its territory. As such, it has not yet swum across the Rhine.
Nor does Zurich regard the possibility of Sika deer interbreeding with red deer as a threat. This is because the species live far apart and are unlikely to cross paths.
Gift from Japanese Emperor
The Zurich sika deer population descends from a population in the Black Forest that has lived there since 1939. The spotted deer actually originate from South-East Asia and the Far East. They arrived in Europe – more specifically, in France – in 1890 as a gift from the Japanese Emperor. There, they managed to escape from the grounds of Rambouillet Castle near Paris.
Around 1900, sika deer were brought to Germany because it was fashionable to ‘enrich’ the native wildlife with non-native species. Many sika deer lived in parks, where – as had happened in France – they once again managed to escape. There are now five populations in Germany.
Sika deer are related to red deer but are significantly smaller. From May to September, they have a summer coat with white patches.

‘They kept kicking me’: Washington Post photojournalist beaten in West Bank settler attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:28:29 UTC
22:28:29 KST

American photojournalist Heidi Levine, who works for The Washington Post, was injured Friday in an attack by masked Israeli settlers on Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank, according to witnesses and Palestinian reports. The assault near the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, was one of several violent incidents reported during the annual olive harvest, with Israeli authorities opening an investigation into the clashes.
Witnesses said approximately 80 settlers, many wearing masks and some carrying gas canisters, descended from a hill overlooking terraced olive groves where Palestinian villagers had gathered to harvest olives. Some settlers allegedly set olive trees on fire and used slings to hurl stones at the harvesters, who retreated downhill before throwing stones back. "The settlers want to attack us and force us from our homes," Palestinian farmer Moutaz Abdelhadi told Reuters.
Levine, a Jerusalem-based photographer who has covered conflicts across the Middle East for decades, was among those injured. Footage from the scene showed masked individuals beating her with sticks as she lay on the ground. Other journalists and Palestinians subsequently approached her, and she could be heard saying, "I'm not okay. They took all my stuff." Her camera equipment was reportedly stolen and her vehicle damaged.
Speaking from a hospital in Ramallah, where she was reported to be in stable condition, Levine described the attack. "I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me," she said. Levine said her Palestinian colleagues eventually intervened, ending the assault. She was initially taken to a clinic in Abu Falah before being transferred to the hospital. Palestinian reports said a second person was also injured in the attack.
Witnesses said Israeli military vehicles arrived during the confrontation but that the violence continued, with soldiers firing tear gas toward Palestinians. The IDF said troops and Border Police officers had been dispatched following reports of a violent confrontation and used riot control measures to disperse those involved. At another nearby location, soldiers fired warning shots into the air before shooting at a Palestinian suspect who allegedly ran toward them carrying a sharp object and posed a threat. The military said all circumstances surrounding the incident would be examined.
The Binyamin Regional Council disputed the Palestinian account, describing the incident as a "planned provocation" organized by the Palestinian Authority. It claimed that hundreds of "terrorists and anarchists" had confronted Israelis, throwing stones and firing fireworks directly at them while journalists filmed the violence. The council also alleged that Palestinian Authority vehicles were present in the area and that left-wing activists had planned confrontations during the olive harvest to promote allegations of settler violence. These claims were not independently verified.
Israeli police said they had opened an investigation into violence in Abu Falah and nearby Turmus Ayya, including suspected stone-throwing and vehicle arson. Investigators and forensic teams were sent to collect evidence and witness statements under military escort. "The Israel Police and the IDF view any manifestation of violence gravely, particularly when it involves journalists carrying out their work," police said, pledging to bring those responsible to justice.
In Turmus Ayya, Palestinian reports said settlers set fire to olive trees and several vehicles, including one belonging to the Palestinian Civil Defense. The organization said one of its members was attacked while trying to extinguish a burning vehicle. Additional violence was reported near Burqa and Birzeit, where Palestinians said olive harvesters had been assaulted. The Palestinian Red Crescent reported treating four injured people near Burqa, while Palestinian media said a 70-year-old man was injured in the Birzeit area. The incidents come amid heightened tensions across the West Bank during the olive harvest, which has repeatedly been disrupted by attacks on Palestinian farmers and their property.
The U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack on American photojournalist Heidi Levine and was monitoring the situation. "The Trump administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans," an embassy spokesperson said, adding that the State Department provides appropriate consular assistance to Americans facing difficulties abroad. "We are in regular dialogue with partners about improving stability and security in the West Bank. We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests and convictions of those responsible." The embassy declined further comment, citing privacy and other considerations.
The Washington Post also condemned the attack and called for a full investigation. "This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank," said Matt Murray, the newspaper's executive editor. "She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist." Murray said the newspaper was relieved that Levine had received medical care and was safe, but was "outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job," urging authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and take appropriate follow-up action.

Israel picks between 'secular democracy or theocracy' in election, chess master Garry Kasparov says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:27:27 UTC
22:27:27 KST

When Israelis head to vote on October 27, they won't just be picking the next government; they will be deciding whether Israel becomes "a secular Hebrew democracy, or a rigid, rabbinical theocracy," Garry Kasparov, a Russian chess grandmaster, political activist, and writer, wrote in an op-ed for the New York Times published on Thursday.
"Just as Abraham Lincoln observed that the government could not persist 'half slave and half free,' Israel cannot go on half theocratic and half secular," Kasparov, whose father was Jewish, argued.
"Americans resolved that contradiction over four years of brutal civil war. Israel’s election on Oct. 27 offers a bloodless way out of this morass," he wrote.
"Democracies are built on compromise," Kasparov said. "But sometimes a compromise can turn dangerous."
Growing up in the Soviet Union shaped Kasparov's view of Israeli democracy
He explained that his upbringing in the Soviet Union shaped his perception of both the US and Israeli democracies. "I see this dynamic at play in two democracies with which I closely identify: the United States and Israel."
"As a young Soviet with a Jewish father, I grew up to become a staunch supporter of Israel, an outpost of liberalism surrounded by illiberal, Moscow-backed Arab states," Kasparov wrote.
"While I rejected the anti-Americanism and anti-Zionism of the Communist regime under which I was raised, I also sought a textured understanding of the United States and Israel."
Israel faces a breaking point, risk of permanent rupture
"I learned early on that the United States had reached a breaking point just 84 years after independence. America’s founders included men who owned slaves and men who did not. They could not both midwife the union and challenge the 'peculiar institution.' This guaranteed the birth of the United States but cursed the young nation with an affliction that nearly caused a permanent rupture."
Kasparov believes that Israel is also facing this affliction and risk of permanent rupture. Rather than the divisive issue being slavery, the divisive issue that Kasparov says has placed Israel at this crossroad is the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) draft to the IDF. He clarified in the NYT that "There is, of course, no moral equivalence between the haredim, as the ultra-Orthodox are called in Israel, and slave owners."
He cites then-prime minister David Ben-Gurion's original agreement with the haredim as the thing that set in motion the aforementioned split. In 1948 Ben-Gurion approved a temporary agreement with haredi yeshiva students, granting 400 people an exemption from army service to study Torah. Today, upwards of 50,000 people evade IDF draft to study Torah.
"The pact haunted their descendants and today is sustained by a nationalist far right and an unscrupulous prime minister willing to bend the law to stay in power," Kasparov said.
Haredi draft is 'corroding' Israel's social compact
"In Israel today, ultra-Orthodox political power is corroding the social compact that holds the country together."
"Israelis of Ben-Gurion’s generation may not have understood the kind of foundation they were laying," Kasparov argued. "They may have presumed they were simply handing out draft exemptions to a few hundred young men. Many of the American founders similarly expected slavery to peter out over time."
"Instead, slavery expanded significantly after 1776, just as religious influence in Israel exploded in the decades following 1948. The draft exemption became especially infuriating to secular Israeli Jews after Oct. 7 and the war in Gaza."
The haredi draft is not the only way Kasparov thinks that religious influence is corruptive to Israel. He argues that their power over Israeli law, from marriages, divorces, and funerals to transportation and public services on Shabbat, is "toxic" and unfair to the millions of Israelis who do not observe Shabbat.
"The ultra-Orthodox parties in the Knesset are so single-minded that it seems they will support anyone, no matter how clouded by accusations of misdeeds, who preserves their special privileges," Kasparov wrote in the NYT. "This is how the haredim have become indispensable accomplices and supporters to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition."
Netanyahu's relationship with the haredim in Knesset
"Without the ultra-Orthodox, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would not have backing for many of his authoritarian endeavors," he argued, and similarly, "Without Mr. Netanyahu, the ultra-Orthodox would lose their protected status."
Despite his comments that Israel is choosing between secular democracy or rigid theocracy, Kasparov added that he does not want religion and culture to be suppressed. "When I was growing up in the Soviet Union, Communist thugs enforced atheism and suppressed Jewish culture. This is not what I want for Israel."
"I simply believe in equality before the law and an Israel that embodies its founders’ aspirations of being a 'light unto the nations,' rather than an international pariah held back by far-right and religious special interests," Kasparov wrote.
"Israel’s election on Oct. 27 offers a bloodless way out of this morass."

Palestinians, US journalist attacked in West Bank pogrom: What we know
Unknown
